Elazar Yair Wilensky, 14, identified as student killed by Hezbollah ordnance explosion in North
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:39:17 UTC
13:39:17 KST

Elazar Yair Wilensky, 14, was identified as the student killed on Monday when an unexploded munition detonated during a school trip in the Ramim Ridge area of northern Israel, near the Lebanese border.
Wilensky, the youngest of five siblings, was described by his family as "a boy who loved life. Smart and intelligent, full of joy, a good and beloved friend, whose entire future was still ahead of him."
He is survived by his parents, three sisters, and a brother.
In a statement, the Ma'alot-Tarshiha Municipality said that Mayor Moti Ben-David and the rest of the city "share in the profound grief of the Wilensky family and extend their condolences at this difficult and painful time.
"The Ma'alot-Tarshiha Municipality continues to closely support the families of those affected. At the same time, welfare teams and educational psychological services continue to provide emotional support and assistance to students, families, and educational staff."
The incident occurred when a group of students and teachers from ORT Ma'alot High School's yeshiva program was struck by an explosion involving unexploded ordnance during a hiking trip.
Some 24 teachers, children injured in explosion meters from Lebanese border
According to the initial reports, 24 teachers and students were injured in the incident. One person was critically injured and pronounced dead shortly afterward. Two others were seriously injured, 10 sustained moderate injuries, and another 12 were lightly injured.
The victims suffered injuries of varying severity, including serious injuries. A medical evacuation helicopter was dispatched to the scene. The IDF declared the incident a mass-casualty event and sent helicopters to the area.
The incident occurred near the Paar Lookout, approximately 50 to 100 meters from the Lebanese border.
A nearby military outpost had been manned by Combat Engineering Corps soldiers throughout the war, leading Hezbollah to direct heavy fire at the area during the fighting.
The assessment is that the explosion was caused by a Hezbollah missile or artillery shell that had landed in the area but failed to detonate at the time.
The area is densely vegetated, which is believed to explain why the unexploded munition had not been discovered previously.
A preliminary investigation showed evidence that one of the students put the Hezbollah cluster munition into his bag, which later detonated.

Panama earthquake affects over 6,000 people — president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:26:58 UTC
13:26:58 KST

MEXICO CITY, October 13. /TASS/. The earthquake in Panama affected more than 6,000 people but caused no fatalities, President Jose Raul Mulino said in an address to the nation.
"So far, 1,744 homes have been inspected, and 6,174 people have been affected. This figure will be updated as inspections continue," he said.
Mulino stressed that the quake’s destructive force was considerable and that specialists are still assessing the damage. Meanwhile, the government is delivering food and drinking water, restoring roads and bridges, and providing electricity.
"I will spare no resources needed to ensure that assistance and solutions reach those who need them most," the president said. He added that authorities would provide materials for housing repairs and hire local contractors to build new two-and three-room homes designed by National Police specialists.
Mulino also urged residents to rely solely on official reports and avoid spreading false rumors. "Nothing of the kind happened, and these reports caused only unnecessary alarm and concern," he said, referring to false social media claims about a tsunami and the closure of the Bridge of the Americas over the Panama Canal.

DSB warns of longer travel times between Odense and Fredericia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:23:48 UTC
13:23:48 KST

The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.
The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.

Taiwan says Chinese drills will not affect regional shipping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:17:06 UTC
13:17:06 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Maritime and Port Bureau said on Monday that China’s military drills will not affect ships operating around Taiwan.
Beijing announced live-fire exercises in the Bohai Sea, the northern Yellow Sea, the East China Sea, the South China Sea, and the southern Yellow Sea between Monday and Saturday.
The bureau said the Bohai and Yellow Seas lie outside Taiwan’s search-and-rescue zone, CNA reported. It added that the designated firing zones in the East and South China Seas are close to China's coast and also outside of Taiwan’s search-and-rescue zone.
The bureau said the nation's commercial ports are operating normally. To ensure navigational safety, it is closely monitoring vessel movements in waters around the country and will issue timely advisories reminding ships to consider rerouting around the affected areas, per CNA.
Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) condemned the drills. He said an initial assessment suggests they involve artillery exercises along China’s coast and pose a relatively low threat to waters around Taiwan. The Ministry of National Defense will continue to monitor China’s military activities.

Taiwan secures Saudi crude for November as CPC assures year-end supply
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:16:56 UTC
13:16:56 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan has secured Saudi Arabian crude oil for November delivery, while state-owned CPC Corp. says domestic oil and natural gas supplies are assured through year-end despite rising risks to Middle Eastern energy shipments.
Two sources told Reuters that Saudi Arabia had sold November-loading crude to refiners in Taiwan and India. Some cargoes sold on a delivered basis carried premiums of about NT$640 (US$20) per barrel above November official selling prices.
Saudi Arabia typically announces official selling prices at the beginning of each month and asks buyers with long-term contracts to nominate their purchase volumes. However, security concerns linked to the Iran war have made buyers reluctant to charter vessels to load crude inside the Strait of Hormuz, prompting Saudi Arabia to shift some volumes to the spot market.
CPC Corp. said Tuesday that it has diversified crude purchases, adjusted tanker schedules, and increased procurement from outside the Middle East to maintain stable domestic energy supplies. The company said oil and natural gas supplies are secure through the end of the year and that it has begun planning procurement for Q1 2027.
It began purchasing alternative crude from multiple non-Middle Eastern sources after the US-Iran war began in February. In mid-September, after a bombing of Saudi Aramco’s East-West Pipeline disrupted supplies under September and October term contracts, CPC purchased additional spot crude to cover the shortfall.
Crude prices have remained elevated and volatile, while freight and insurance costs have risen sharply, CPC said. As the Northern Hemisphere approaches peak winter demand, European countries are replenishing liquefied natural gas inventories, intensifying competition for energy cargoes and tankers.
CPC has also increased sourcing from the Americas, West Africa, and the Asia-Pacific region as part of its long-term diversification strategy.

Taiwan probes alleged repackaging of Chinese software for government contracts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:16:39 UTC
13:16:39 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Four people suspected of passing off Chinese-developed software as locally developed to win government contracts were released on bail Tuesday after being questioned by prosecutors.
The prosecutors set bail at a combined NT$850,000 (US$26,463) for the suspects and imposed travel restrictions on their departure from Taiwan, per UDN.
On Monday, the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office searched 10 locations and questioned four people from three companies over suspected violations of the Government Procurement Act, Liberty Times reported.
Taiwan prohibits government agencies from procuring or using information and communications technology products, including software, from China.
The suspects allegedly repackaged Chinese-developed software as Taiwanese-made and secured Ministry of Foreign Affairs contracts worth more than NT$20 million over three years, prosecutors said.
The ministry said the software, called IP-Guard, had been installed on computers at Taiwan’s representative offices abroad, but no confidential information had been shared.
A man surnamed Lu (呂) allegedly worked with Chinese companies to develop the software and arranged for it to be repackaged, according to the prosecutors. Another man was suspected of modifying its user interface, while two others allegedly submitted bids for MOFA contracts involving the software.
MOFA said it would hold the companies accountable under the terms of their contracts, according to UDN.
The case came to light last December, when MOFA discovered irregularities during a security audit and reported them to the Investigation Bureau. The ministry said several files within the software bore stamps from the company Guangzhou TEC Solutions Co.

Taipower urges quicker investment planning for Taiwan AI demand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:16:33 UTC
13:16:33 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipower Chair Tseng Wen-sheng (曾文生) said Monday that the country's power industry must speed up investment decisions to keep pace with the technology sector, shortening planning horizons from about 10 years to five or even three years.
Speaking at a press conference ahead of the Net-Zero Taiwan and Energy Taiwan exhibition, Tseng said electricity security would depend not only on having sufficient generation capacity but also on whether the grid could deliver power to where it is needed while coordinating with renewable energy sources and energy storage facilities, per CNA.
As AI drives demand for computing power, electricity is becoming an increasingly important part of the semiconductor and technology supply chains, Tseng said. Thus, Taipower can no longer act solely as an electricity supplier, he said.
Parts of its operations must become more closely aligned with the technology industry, including understanding companies' investment schedules, financial arrangements, and supply chain needs. Businesses seeking more renewable energy also need to coordinate with suppliers on green electricity purchases, renewable energy certificates, and storage systems, Tseng said.
Tseng said Taiwan's existing power resources and investment plans were sufficient to support current domestic industrial development, citing Taiwan's investment in natural gas-fired power generation, which ranked third globally in 2024 and sixth in 2025. However, he warned that electricity demand from AI applications could grow rapidly and prove difficult to predict.
He said computing demand will not only be concentrated among large cloud service providers, as some companies may build their own data centers to conduct computing locally to protect confidential information. This could spread electricity demand across multiple locations, complicating grid planning, per UDN.
Taipower is closely monitoring growth in distribution networks and general high-voltage electricity consumption, Tseng said. If demand for computing power rises rapidly, the challenge will be ensuring that the grid can deliver electricity to customers in time, rather than simply increasing generation capacity.
Tseng said Taipower hopes to establish more communication platforms with technology companies, renewable energy developers, and other industries through exhibitions and forums to discuss future market arrangements and commercial cooperation.
Asked about speculation that Taipower might ask major electricity users such as TSMC to finance power plant projects, Taipower Spokesperson Huang Mei-lien (黃美蓮) said the company would continue discussing potential electricity investment plans with high-tech businesses, per TechNews.
Such discussions do not mean Taipower is transferring responsibility for future electricity supply to manufacturers, she said.

Yair Wilensky identified as teen killed by unexploded munition during school hike near Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:13:33 UTC
13:13:33 KST

The teenager killed Monday when an unexploded cluster munition detonated during a school hike on Ramim Ridge in northern Israel has been identified as Yair Wilensky, the youngest of five children.
His family described him as "a boy who loved life. Bright and wise, full of joy, a good and much-loved friend, with his whole future ahead of him." He is survived by his parents, three sisters and a brother.
Wilensky, whose full name was Elazar Yair, had previously competed in fencing and was ranked among Israel's leading athletes in his age group about two years ago. His older brother, Dov Wilensky, is one of Israel's top épée fencers and is considered an Olympic prospect.
Yair was a ninth-grade student at ORT Ma'alot Yeshiva High School. The Ma'alot-Tarshiha municipality issued a statement expressing condolences to the family on behalf of the mayor, his deputies, city council members and municipal employees.
Teacher remains seriously wounded after surgery
Rambam Medical Center in Haifa said Tuesday morning that a 61-year-old teacher injured in the explosion underwent surgery overnight and remained in serious condition.
One teenager was hospitalized in moderate condition with a shrapnel fragment lodged in his neck. He was fully conscious. Two other teenagers remained hospitalized with minor injuries.
Six people injured in the explosion were taken to Galilee Medical Center in Nahariya.
Dr. Nadav Sleifer, head of the hospital's pediatric surgery department, told ynet Monday that medical teams had encountered complicated injuries caused by the blast.
"The teenagers suffered blast and shrapnel injuries," he said. "They are all stable now and out of danger. Each will need a period of recovery, depending on the nature of their injuries. I expect the first patients to be discharged as early as tomorrow, while others will need several more days before they can return home."
Sleifer explained that although the cluster munition was small, roughly the size of a beverage can, it was capable of causing devastating injuries.
"It causes blast injuries and shrapnel wounds. We're talking about very small fragments that can penetrate all the layers of tissue, travel deep into the body and damage vital organs," he said.
"Even a tiny fragment can cause a very serious injury if it enters the wrong place. That's what we saw in some of these cases. There weren't necessarily many fragments, but some caused severe injuries."
Students used tourniquets and CPR to save their friends
Students who survived the explosion described extraordinary efforts by the wounded to help one another in the chaotic moments after the blast.
Several teenagers applied tourniquets to their injured friends, while one student performed CPR on another.
One injured boy, bleeding heavily from shrapnel wounds to his leg, made a video call to his father and asked him to explain how to apply a tourniquet to himself.
The group had set out on a three-day hike along the Israel National Trail, a long-distance walking route stretching across the country. They left their school in Ma'alot at dawn Monday.
The explosion occurred while the group was taking a meal break near Pe'er Lookout in the Upper Galilee, close to the Lebanese border.
According to the students, they had not noticed a sign beside the area where they stopped warning of unexploded ordnance and prohibiting entry.
In addition to Wilensky, who was killed, three people were reported seriously wounded, 10 moderately wounded and another 10 lightly injured.

====================================================================================================

Explainer: Why the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics honors scholars tackling economic shocks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:07:37 CST
13:07:37 KST

STOCKHOLM, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel was awarded to American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford for their decades of work developing models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks.
In its announcement on Monday, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences credited the two economists with laying "microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization."
"The laureates have helped us smooth out the economy's peaks and troughs," the academy said in a statement, adding that their work had "significantly improved" policymakers' ability to implement well-timed fiscal and monetary measures.
WHAT THEY FOUND
Hall, a professor at Stanford University, and Woodford, a professor at Columbia University, helped reshape macroeconomic modelling by grounding it in microeconomics.
Rather than relying solely on statistical relationships between broad economic indicators such as inflation, output and consumption, their approach examines how the decisions and expectations of households and businesses shape the wider economy.
In a 1978 paper, Hall examined how household consumption decisions are shaped by expectations about future economic conditions. His work helped establish the microeconomic foundations for understanding consumption, while Woodford's research on firms' price-setting behaviour helped bring the demand and supply sides together in a framework for macroeconomic stabilization.
Together, their work contributed to the development of New Keynesian models, which provide a framework for analysing how households and businesses respond to economic conditions and how monetary policy affects economic activity.
"Robert Hall worked on the demand side, studying consumption, whereas Michael Woodford studied the supply side, the price-setting behaviour of firms, and put all the pieces together in a whole," Timo Boppart, a professor at Stockholm University and a member of the prize committee, was quoted by the Financial Times as saying.
The academy said it was recognizing the pair for bringing about "a paradigm shift in stabilization policy." The prize is worth a combined 12 million Swedish kronor (about 1.2 million U.S. dollars).
"The laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world," said John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.
Because of their research, "we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," he added.
WHY IT MATTERS
The award comes at a time of heightened geopolitical uncertainty and a fragile global economy, with frequent shocks posing persistent challenges for policymakers.
"Your research on economic stabilization has greatly improved our understanding of people's economic decisions and strengthened the foundations for effective policy," Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, wrote in a note of congratulations to the economists on social media.
For decades, governments have sought to cushion economic shocks by following the prescriptions of British economist John Maynard Keynes, whose ideas gained prominence during the Great Depression. Cutting taxes and increasing government spending can stimulate demand by encouraging households and businesses to spend and invest, helping revive economic growth.
The oil shocks of the 1970s, however, posed a major challenge to existing economic thinking. Many Western economies experienced high inflation alongside high unemployment, while growth remained weak. The combination raised doubts about the effectiveness of established approaches to economic stabilization.
This year's award winners brought renewed relevance to economic stabilization theory, showing how a better understanding of real-world economic behaviour can help explain the effects of policy decisions.
Their research also helped shape the theoretical basis for forward guidance, a policy tool through which central banks signal their expectations for future interest rates. The approach gained prominence in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis.
"That was an important part of the policy response in the years from 2009 onward, and I think it did contribute to better stabilization," Woodford told the committee by phone from New York.
He added that one of the main themes of his work was helping policymakers appreciate the importance of understanding individuals' behavior in the market: How they make decisions about spending and what they understand about future economic policy. ■

In 2019, Beijing, home to over 20 million residents, launched a "swift response to public complaints" initiative aimed at addressing public concerns promptly and resolving everyday challenges efficiently. It has integrated more than 60 hotline services into the single hotline number 12345, which serves as the primary channel for residents to voice their concerns.
Official data shows the Chinese capital has handled about 200 million public appeals in just over seven years, with resolution and satisfaction rates both exceeding 97 percent.
Beijing's "swift response to public complaints" reform began with a single hotline and platform and has since evolved into an urban governance system integrating big data and AI, one that has tackled a range of pressing public concerns, Gao Xiang, president of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, said in his opening address.
"Digital empowerment of people-centered urban governance is the prevailing trend in urban governance worldwide," he said.
This year's forum unveiled a batch of research outcomes on urban governance, including theoretical studies of the reform itself, an evaluation of global city hotline services, and case studies of governance innovation worldwide.
It also rolled out two English-language publications on the reform -- the monograph "How Urban Governance Works: the Case of Swift Response to Public Complaints in Beijing," and a special issue with the "Journal of Comparative Policy Analysis: Research and Practice." Both signal a move from lessons learned to theoretical exposition, and from Chinese practice to international comparison.
"The experience of Beijing's citizen service system offered valuable lessons for Athens in advancing people-centered urban governance and building a city that listens to its citizens and responds to their concerns," said Georgios K. Giannaros, first deputy mayor of Athens, Greece.
Held every two years, this year's Beijing Forum on Swift Response to Public Complaints featured six parallel sub-forums, where participants noted that the reform has driven changes in mega-city governance, offering the world a window into China's approach to governance. ■

NEW YORK, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- At the conclusion of a concert in New York, young singers from China and the United States were embracing, exchanging farewells and posing for photos.

The concert presented a series of renowned vocal and instrumental works from both countries, including the Circle of Life, Bridge Over Troubled Water and As Wished.

For 17-year-old Sylvie, a member of the New York chorus, the evening's most meaningful moments came from reconnecting with friends she had made in China.
Sylvie began learning Chinese six years ago. In 2024, she traveled to Guangzhou, Shenzhen and Zhuhai with her chorus, where she made Chinese friends.
"I'm so happy that we've met again. We've kept in touch on WeChat and talked in both Chinese and English," she told Xinhua.
Now Sylvie has added Beijing, Shanghai and Chengdu to her wish list for the next trip. "I really like China and wanna go back soon. It's definitely a different experience," she said.
The reunion reflected a relationship that has grown for more than two decades between the two choirs. Their story began with an international choral competition in Japan and has since expanded through online collaborations, student exchanges and reciprocal visits.
In autumn 2024, Francisco J. Nunez, founder and artistic director of Young People's Chorus of New York City, led the U.S. choral ensemble to China at the invitation of Guangdong Experimental High School Choir. This year, he welcomed the Chinese singers to New York.
"This is like ping-pong," Nunez said with a smile. "It's not a tour. It's a relationship."
"Each time in these steps, our relationship has grown stronger, with more singing, more families and more friendship," he said.
Quan Hanyan, chairman and principal of Guangdong Experimental High School Group, said continued cultural exchanges offered young people in both countries valuable opportunities to foster mutual understanding and a deeper bond.
"In a world with so much noise, these young people have chosen to listen to each other. That is how a bridge is built across the Pacific," Nunez said.
Chinese Consul General in New York Chen Li praised the sister choirs' longstanding partnership as an example of friendship between Chinese and U.S. youth.
He encouraged young people from both countries to learn from one another and grow together, and use their youthful voices to write a new chapter in China-U.S. friendship.
As the Chinese singers prepared to head home, Nunez offered once again his best wishes.
"Tomorrow, you'll get on an airplane," he told them. "But it's not goodbye. It's until we sing again." ■

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet has urged relevant authorities to treat disaster management as a core priority, calling for a significant strengthening of human and material resources to combat rising climate change risks.
In an official message marking National Disaster Management Day on Tuesday, which coincides with both the ASEAN Day for Disaster Management and the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction, Hun Manet warned that the world faces increasingly complex and fast-evolving disaster risks driven by environmental, social, and economic factors.
"Climate change, rapid urbanization, and environmental degradation pose serious threats to sustainable social and economic development," he said.
Hun Manet said that Cambodia continues to face extreme weather conditions, including rising temperatures during the rainy season, erratic rainfall patterns, strong winds, lightning strikes, riverbank collapses, infectious diseases, and fires -- all of which threaten human lives and community property.
To mitigate these impacts, Hun Manet directed authorities at all levels to prioritize flood and drought management, emphasizing the need to upgrade local water infrastructure and closely monitor vulnerable households to build stronger climate resilience across the country.
Furthermore, the prime minister called on citizens to actively strengthen their own household resilience. He urged families to develop "safety and preparedness plans," which include assembling home emergency kits stocked with clean water, dry food, medicine, a radio, and vital documents.
He advised citizens to inspect and reinforce their homes against wind and lightning, while paying close attention to the safety of children, the elderly, people with disabilities, and pregnant women in times of emergency.
Hun Manet also advocated for increased public investment in housing resilience for vulnerable families, saying that establishing robust social safety nets, providing adequate and safe shelter, and ensuring timely community access to risk information are critical steps to sustaining the nation's economic growth.
According to data from the National Committee for Disaster Management (NCDM), Cambodia has recently been dealing with severe weather impacts. Last month, heavy rainfall triggered widespread flooding across portions of 10 provinces, directly affecting nearly 60,000 families and forcing approximately 5,000 families to evacuate to designated safe areas.
The rising waters also inundated roughly 52,000 homes and damaged more than 72,000 hectares of rice paddies. ■

====================================================================================================

Europe’s big election season is about to kick off. It could change everything | Nathalie Tocci
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:00:15 UTC
13:00:15 KST

When it comes to Europe’s economy or its peace and security, it is obvious that decision-making has to be done largely at the European level to be meaningful. Yet electoral politics is still conducted mostly at the national level. The silver lining of this mismatch is that from country to country in Europe we have governments with different political priorities and leanings. Unlike in the US, where one presidential election can radically change the entire country’s course, as we have seen so vividly under Donald Trump’s leadership, the same drama has not so far unfolded in Europe. This may be about to change.
Pedro Sánchez rolled the dice in Spain last week, calling a snap election for next month after an unholy alliance of the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox and Catalan pro-independence party Junts blocked his big housing reform package in parliament. If the socialist prime minister, hailed by progressives globally but demonised by Europe’s right and Trump’s US, loses his election gamble, Spain could fall into the hands of a conservative/far-right coalition, which is currently ahead in the polls.
In addition to Spain, France, Italy, Poland, Finland, Greece, Estonia and Slovakia will all head to the polls in the coming year. The four largest of these, France, Italy, Poland and Spain, could see far-right or nationalist populist parties either confirmed in power (Italy), returned to it (Poland) or elected for the first time (France and Spain). This could dramatically change the face of Europe.
Europe has been tilting to the right for some time, with far-right parties entering coalition in different countries at different times. Centre-right and far-right groups are now able to form a majority in the European parliament, coalescing in particular around an anti-climate and anti-migration agenda. But while this tilt has slowed European integration, its policy effects have not been as rapid and radical as those we have seen in the US under Trump.
This is because the rightward shift has so far not been homogeneous. In the Netherlands last year, Geert Wilders’s far-right Freedom party was punished at the polls and the liberals made a comeback. This year, Hungary’s slide into authoritarianism was halted, and is now being reversed, after Viktor Orbán was ousted in a landslide election. Most recently, in Sweden, support for the far right, which had backed the outgoing centre-right government, slipped. The opposition bloc, led by the Social Democrats, scraped a victory. So, while the rise of the far right is a continent-wide trend – Alternative für Deutschland’s recent victory in eastern Germany sent shock waves across Europe – it does not hold everywhere, at all times.
But if the coming round of elections were to bring Marine Le Pen to the French presidency, confirm Giorgia Meloni as Italian prime minister, possibly backed by a coalition even further to the right than the current one, return the Law and Justice party to power in Poland, and produce a conservative/far-right government in Spain including Vox, the face of Europe could change dramatically.
If all these countries, plus several smaller ones, elected far-right or nationalist populist governments, they would not reach a qualified majority able to steer the EU’s policy course. But they would form a blocking minority, putting an end to any ambition of deeper EU integration in such areas as finance, energy, defence and technology.
And it is not just a question of numbers. These far-right leaders would have a galvanising and radicalising effect on each other, propped up by Maga America and Silicon Valley’s algorithms. The common perception outside Italy is that Meloni has mellowed in power. To the extent that this is true, it is in no small measure because she has been surrounded by the likes of Emmanuel Macron, Donald Tusk and Sánchez, among others. If these leaders were replaced by the likes of Le Pen, Jarosław Kaczyński and Alberto Núñez Feijóo, backed by Vox’s Santiago Abascal, Meloni herself would act differently, more in line with her true political instincts. All this could trigger not simply a slow erosion of the European integration project – a muddling through with the unambitious agenda we have seen in recent years – but a hollowing out, if not an outright implosion. The EU as we know it would struggle to retain its purpose, especially if no agreement is reached on its next seven-year budget in the coming months.
The irony is that European political heterogeneity persists, but outside the EU it is not only Canada that wants more proximity. More importantly, the UK may have begun the slow journey of retracing its steps. It took 10 years for a British prime minister to call a spade a spade, publicly recognise that Brexit has done more harm than good and open the door to rejoining the EU, as Andy Burnham has now done.
It has taken a decade to remember the purpose of European unity and the emptiness of petty nationalism – just as Europe risks losing the memory of its dark past and teeters on the brink of falling apart. Now is perhaps the moment for the UK to remind its European neighbours what it means to be out there, all alone.
- Nathalie Tocci is a Guardian Europe columnist

A new messaging and payment “super app” marketed at British students uses servers owned by a Chinese company that has been put on a US military blacklist for its alleged affiliation to the People’s Liberation Army.
ZyMix, which is being pushed on university campuses as the UK’s first super app designed “for gen Z”, combining chat, payments and community features, has a contract with a German-based subsidiary of Tencent Holdings, a Chinese conglomerate in Shenzhen.
Tencent Holdings was added in January 2026 to the US Department of Defense’s (DoD) list of Chinese military companies, which is formally known as the section 1260H list.
The citation on the DoD list says that the company, which is a gaming and social media conglomerate, is indirectly affiliated to the Chinese People’s Liberation Army.
The blacklist is part of a US attempt to counteract what it regards as Beijing’s efforts to increase its military power by using technology from Chinese firms, universities and research programmes.
The DoD is prohibited from entering into, renewing or extending contracts for goods, services or technology with any entity on the list although wider sanctions are not automatic.
A Tencent spokesperson said: “Tencent’s inclusion on this list is clearly a mistake. We are not a military company or supplier. Unlike sanctions or export controls, this listing has no impact on our business. We will nonetheless work with the Department of Defense to address any misunderstanding.”
China’s footprint in higher education in the UK has become a controversial issue. MI5 recently warned British universities to cut ties with the China General Technology Research Institute.
The domestic intelligence service claimed it was secretly channelling funding from Beijing’s intelligence apparatus to UK-linked academics to improve the technical espionage capabilities of China’s ministry of state security.
The link between the Chinese-owned infrastructure and ZyMix was initially disclosed in the company’s privacy policy at the time of its launch last week.
The document, which is legally required, said that Tencent (Frankfurt) stored user-generated content and messages. After the Guardian approached the company, the privacy policy was rewritten and mention of Tencent was removed.
The policy now states that users’ personal data is stored and processed primarily in the United Kingdom and the EU, adding that “some of our service providers are located in other countries, including the United States”.
It goes on to say that “auxiliary infrastructure providers, hosted in the EU, receive only encrypted user messages and limited technical data, such as technical statistics, licence validation when the app starts”.
A spokesperson said: “As a newly launched startup, we are updating our privacy notice as we develop our services, including clarifying that Tencent, Twilio and the other providers concerned are used solely for performance testing.”
The spokesperson added: “Our agreement is with Tencent Cloud Europe BV, which we use for auxiliary services, rather than as the provider that stores ZyMix user data. We take our obligations under UK data protection law seriously.”
The new privacy policy invites those who wish to know the identity of their suppliers to request the information from the company.
In response to a request from the Guardian, Tarique Ghaffur, a former assistant commissioner at the Metropolitan police, who described himself as a security consultant for ZyMix, responded.
He said: “We have reviewed your request as against our private privacy [sic] you mentioned. Unfortunately, at the present time for reasons of commercial confidentiality, contractual obligations and legal privileges, we are not able to provide you with the requested information.”
Fraser Sampson, a professor of security and national governance and formerly the UK’s biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner, said he was “sceptical when ‘commercial confidentiality’ arguments are used to duck basic policy questions and amending policy on the fly is never reassuring”.
He added: “When companies ask us for our personal data, they should expect us to ask them where it’s being kept, for what purpose(s) and who they’re going to share it with – and be prepared to answer fully.”
Sam Dunning, the director of the UK-China Transparency NGO, said: “There are serious questions about whether ZyMix have taken due care before launching this product.”
A spokesperson for ZyMix said: “Whilst still in its beta stage, the ZyMix app has been developed to fully comply with all UK data, privacy and financial regulations.”
ZyMix is heavily targeting the university market and is offering £200 to £400 a month to people who agree to be brand ambassadors on campuses. Staff roles have also been advertised in the UK by ZyMix for Mandarin-speaking applicants.
One advert on LinkedIn for the job of operations manager (Mandarin speaking) required “excellent written and verbal communication skills in both English and Mandarin (required for daily communication with the China team)”.
Separately, a distinct company appeared to be recruiting on behalf of ZyMix on WeChat, the Chinese instant messaging service, saying: “The product, R&D, design and testing team is in Greater China, with branch-company bases covering: Taipei / Shenzhen / Guangzhou / Hangzhou / Chengdu / Zhengzhou.”
Ghaffur said that Flicknmix, the UK company that publishes the ZyMix app, “does not have any subsidiaries or branch offices in China. Our aim is to create opportunities within the UK”. A spokesperson for ZyMix described it as “British born”.

====================================================================================================

Women ‘more likely to be told autoimmune conditions are psychological’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:00:14 UTC
13:00:14 KST

Women with autoimmune conditions are up to 74% more likely than men to be told their symptoms are psychological or psychosomatic, and face much longer waits for a diagnosis and treatment, a study suggests.
Hundreds of millions of people – about one in 10 globally – are affected by autoimmune conditions, which can cause a range of health issues including fatigue, muscle pain and rashes.
But research by the University of Cambridge and University of East Anglia suggests a stark gender divide when it comes to how signs of the conditions are handled by doctors.
Women are more likely to have their conditions wrongly attributed to psychiatric causes, more likely to have symptoms misdiagnosed as psychosomatic, and more likely to experience delays in getting a diagnosis, according to the study.
The lead author, Melanie Sloan, said: “The damage caused to women by these types of misdiagnosis can be very long lasting in terms of trusting doctors and their own self-esteem.”
Sloan, a researcher in the department of public health and primary care at Cambridge and UEA, said some women were forced to wait years before finally getting a diagnosis, causing long delays to treatment for their condition.
The study, published in the Lancet eClinicalMedicine journal, included more than 6,600 people with autoimmune conditions. Most were female and from the UK.
Patients listed their main condition, with almost a quarter of the women having autoimmune thyroid disease, which can cause the gland to become underactive – known as Hashimoto’s disease – or overactive, known as Graves’ disease. Hashimoto’s disease can cause weight gain, hair loss, fatigue and joint pain, while the symptoms of Graves’ disease include bulging eyes, palpitations and weight loss.
One in seven women in the study had systemic lupus, which can cause tiredness, rashes and muscle pain.
Among male patients, rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), also known as “sticky blood” syndrome, were the most common conditions.
Researchers found 43% of women reported being told their condition was down to a psychiatric cause compared with a third of men (33%).
A third (34%) of women also reported having symptoms misdiagnosed as psychosomatic – meaning they were triggered or worsened by stress or anxiety – compared with 22% of men.
Overall, after accounting for factors including age, disease group, continent and household finances, researchers said women were 46% more likely to report having received a psychiatric misdiagnosis, and 74% more likely to report a psychosomatic misdiagnosis than men.
Researchers also found women reported much longer periods between the onset of symptoms and receiving a diagnosis, as well as more healthcare consultations. Among men, the most frequently reported time to diagnosis was less than three months. Among women, it was one to two years.
Autoimmune conditions, which happen when the immune system attacks the body by mistake, can be complex to diagnose as they often present with symptoms common in the wider population.
The study team said “broader diagnostic challenges affect both sexes” but “females may face additional disadvantages”.
They added: “Historical biases in medicine may persist, including positioning females as less credible and emotional reporters of symptoms than males.”
Sloan said the findings “highlight that psychological or mental health explanations can be given too soon”.
She added: “This is true for both sexes, but our study suggests that females may be particularly vulnerable to these types of misdiagnoses.
“It is really important that symptoms are not automatically assumed to be psychological and for doctors to just say, ‘I believe you,’ to patients with symptoms that the doctors cannot see.”
Shaista Tayabali, a patient affected by an autoimmune condition who was part of the research team and a co-author of the study, said: “The differences between the sexes in misdiagnoses for people with autoimmune diseases is stark.
“The fact that females reported higher rates of psychiatric and psychosomatic misdiagnoses than males … suggests that historical gender biases remain a challenging aspect of the diagnostic journey.
“Although labels such as hysteria are outdated, and fortunately rarely used nowadays, as women we still often have a harder time having our symptoms believed and therefore addressed accurately.”

I was kidnapped and held hostage for 977 days. Could I forgive my captors?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:00:14 UTC
13:00:14 KST

I knew Mohamed Tahlil as a gentle pirate who oversaw a team of guards during the first months of my life as a hostage in 2012. I had travelled to Somalia to report on the outbreak of modern piracy off the coast. On the 10th day, along a dusty road near Galkayo, in the centre of the country, I was kidnapped by pirates. For the next two and a half years, I was a hostage.
I spent most of my time on a thin, sweat-soaked foam mattress on the floor of a dusty room. The dim concrete prison houses changed, but the filth and the circumstances didn’t. Sometimes my captors moved me into the Somali savannah – where we camped in the open and slept on the ground – and for a six-month stretch, I was held on a hijacked tuna vessel, where I joined 28 fishers from east Asia who had been captured about three weeks before I was placed on board. (They had captured me on land, but they were a pirate gang, organised to capture ships at sea.) In each location, pirate guards would sit around with AK-47s and listen to the radio, or else chew khat, a narcotic plant.
Tahlil was a skinny, almost cheerful man who spoke little English and swept the junk-littered yard of his unfinished prison house with a grandmotherly calm. When he came into my room, he would give me his snaggletoothed smile and teach me a few Somali words (for “sun”, “cloud” and so on). He carried rifles but never threatened to shoot me. Tahlil did not seem particularly tough – he would cook and wash dishes alongside lower-ranking guards – but he commanded respect. I thought of him as a low-ranking guard leader in the vast school of clan pirates in central Somalia, who ranged from foot soldiers to a handful of top bosses, warlords who travelled with armed escorts. Tahlil said the men who had captured me were the “bad group”, while he and his guards were the good group. He promised to keep me safe in “his” house until the real pirates negotiated the ransom. I heard this kind of thing all the time in Somalia.
The “bad group” of rougher and fiercer guards was led by a squat man with rotten teeth named Ahmed Diriye. I had understood Tahlil and Diriye as team leaders of the “good” and the “bad” – so it surprised me when, one day, I saw both men squeeze into the front seat of a crowded SUV to visit some random part of the Somali bush, laughing and joking in the seat like old friends. It would be years before I understood how wrong my impression of Tahlil had been.
During my years in captivity, I was usually kept alone. I was beaten on multiple occasions. I saw a friend of mine being tortured. I was frightened most of the time. I was also livid – at my captors, and at myself, for getting kidnapped.
For two separate periods I had access to a short-wave radio, and I could listen to whatever programming came into range. One day, on the BBC World Service, I heard a story about Abraham Lincoln. He supposedly gave a speech during the US civil war in which he referred to southerners as fellow human beings who were simply in error. A Yankee woman criticised his meekness and wondered if southerners were not mortal enemies of the union, who ought to be destroyed. “Why, madam,” Lincoln replied, “do I not destroy my enemies when I make them my friends?”
I resisted this story at first. I wasn’t interested in edifying tales of secular saints. I lived through most of my days in a state of quiet fury.
In September 2014, after 977 days as a hostage, I finally walked free. Two months later, back home in Berlin, I received a Facebook message. It began: “hello michael i am ur friend mohamed”. The author was Tahlil.
Had it come from any other pirate, I would have dumped this message in the digital garbage can. But I was curious what Tahlil could want. He wrote: “I am happy u r out of bondage” and wished me a “happy and joyous life”. The message raised my temper. He was trying to ingratiate himself with me, to dissociate himself from the “real” pirate gang, and pretend we were all OK. After 32 months of horror he still thought I would believe his fairytale about “good” and “bad” pirates in Somalia.
I did not lash out. I wanted information. During the sporadic, long-running conversation that followed, I asked Tahlil to shore up my memories and correct my sometimes blurred impressions of the most squalid phase of my life. He gave names. He sent pictures. He answered questions, not always honestly. He helped me research a book about the ordeal, The Desert and the Sea, which took two years to write.
Of course, Tahlil did want something. He must have known that asking for cash wouldn’t work, since my family, friends, benefactors and various magazines I’d worked for had together sent $1.8m in ransom money to Somalia to have me released. But in the spring of 2015, he asked to come to the US. “I live in constant fear,” he wrote, “and I have no one to help me … I am left with only two options: to flee the country illegally or to continue living this way.”
At the time, the FBI had an open investigation into my kidnapping, and I had informed them about my ongoing online conversation with Tahlil. I was not about to help him immigrate. But it did sound as if he might cooperate with the government. So if I were to help Tahlil come to the US, it would be to help the FBI arrest him upon arrival. For a journalist it’s no small thing to participate in an operation with the feds, but when the pirates took me hostage, they converted me from a journalist to a kidnapping victim, and I felt that the ethical line had already blurred.
I was conscious that Tahlil was not the most important man to throw in jail. On the other hand, piracy is organised crime, and I hoped that a smaller boss, under pressure of evidence, might cough up dirt on his higher-ups. I wanted the right people to be punished. But I knew it was a gamble, in both practical and moral terms.
The FBI set up an operation to lure Tahlil to New York, where he would be arrested. “If you have second thoughts about all this,” one agent told me in the fluorescent-lit Manhattan field office one afternoon, “just let us know.” He meant that once Tahlil was arrested, any question of punishment or forgiveness would be out of my hands. The FBI would have a case to prosecute, and my one-time jailer would be subject not to my sense of right or wrong, but to US law.
In the summer of 2018, the FBI made covert arrangements for Tahlil and flew him to New York City, where he expected to stay in a hotel for two weeks. There was no promise of payment, but I helped lure him with a fake story about the hotel and “final factchecking” on the book. He, in turn, acted vague about his purposes in America. He seemed to vacillate between hope and despair. He would regularly check in to see if his visa and plane ticket were ready. Sometimes he would say he wondered whether he might get arrested. But he never seemed too interested in seeing me. I think we lied to each other for weeks.
On 10 August 2018, when he landed at JFK airport, the FBI arrested Tahlil. The agents said he seemed genuinely surprised. I hoped he would accept a plea and help the Bureau arrest one of the top pirate bosses, such as Mohamed Garfanji. Garfanji was an infamous figure in the state of Galmudug who had tortured my friend Rolly Tambara, an elderly hostage from Seychelles, by dangling him from a tree by his ankles and beating him with a bamboo cane. Garfanji also threatened to sell me to the terrorist group al-Shabaab. I have not forgiven him.
By November, three months after his arrest, Tahlil had still not cooperated, and I was having profound second thoughts. If the full weight of the US government came down on the shoulders of a seemingly gentle and low-ranking boss like him – and no one else’s – the whole operation would seem pointless and cruel. In late 2018, the New York Times published a short article about the case. “I’m not as happy as you might imagine that he’s in jail”, I told the journalist.
In the comments beneath the article, readers wondered whether I had “Stockholm syndrome”. Some people could not understand how a former hostage could wish anything short of savage vengeance on his captors. He must be hypnotised; he must be traumatised; he must be out of his mind.
But forgiving your captors is not the same thing as “Stockholm syndrome”. Not even close.
In my first few months as a hostage, my companion in captivity was Rolly Tambara, a 69-year-old fisher with tattoos on his forearms and a dry but unwavering sarcasm. He spoke English in a French-inflected island pidgin. He knew how to be a hostage, having been at it three months longer than me. At this point in my captivity I was still charged with a hair-trigger rage, and he would try to calm me down. Whenever our guards acted in an arbitrary or cruel manner, he mumbled, ironically: “We are the devil, Michael. And they are like God.”
He was right. The first thing a criminal needs to clarify once he has you under his violent control is that he is right, and you, by definition, are wrong. As hostages, we lived in a world turned on its head, and the consequences of rejecting its hierarchy could be lethal. “Within a matter of hours, the hostage is treated like an infant and has a kind of regression to infantile emotions,” the influential psychiatrist Frank Ochberg has said. “They can’t eat, they can’t talk, they can’t use a toilet, they can’t move without permission. To do it risks death and they accept the feeling that ‘this is the giver of life just like my mother was’.”
Ochberg was talking about Stockholm syndrome. The term has its origins in a six-day hostage standoff that followed a failed bank robbery in Sweden in 1973. The robber, Jan-Erik Olsson, took several employees hostage at a bank in Stockholm, using a knife and a submachine gun. He demanded freedom for an incarcerated friend, a great deal of money and a Ford Mustang for a getaway car. One captive was a 23-year-old stenographer named Kristin Enmark, who seemed to empathise with him from the start. The Swedish authorities met most of Olsson’s demands within a day. By this point, Olsson had been joined by a friend; when he asked if they could drive away with two hostages – to reduce the chances of the cops shooting him dead – the answer was no. Enmark, during a phone call from inside the bank to Swedish prime minister, Olof Palme, said that she and another woman genuinely wanted to leave with Olsson and his friend in the Mustang. “We are more afraid of the policemen than these two boys,” she told a journalist in another phone call from the bank.
Enmark seemed angrier with her own government than with her kidnappers. This posture mystified both Swedish authorities and the general public. But a psychiatrist named Nils Bejerot – who had worked as a negotiator for the Swedish government – told journalists that all the hostages suffered from a syndrome that led victims to stick up for their abusers. He called it “the Norrmalmstorg syndrome” after the bank’s location on Norrmalmstorg Square. To the rest of the world it became “Stockholm syndrome”.
It wasn’t until the following year that the term took hold in the US and beyond. Patty Hearst, the 19-year-old granddaughter of the newspaper tycoon William Randolph Hearst, was taken from her Berkeley apartment by a far-left gang called the Symbionese Liberation Army (SLA). Two months later, Hearst appeared on a bank surveillance video as “Tania”, threatening customers during an afternoon heist in San Francisco. “Up, up, up against the wall, motherfuckers!” she hollered. People wondered if the privileged daughter of a rich American publishing family had lost her mind. Was she brainwashed? Acting under duress? Had she started to work for the SLA? (She had.) Did she have Stockholm syndrome?
After Hearst’s arrest in September 1975, a famous defence lawyer named F Lee Bailey took up her case. He wielded the term “Stockholm syndrome” to keep her out of jail. It didn’t work in the courtroom, but she went free after 22 months because of a commutation by President Carter. Bailey’s headline-making arguments in the Hearst case are the main reason that people all over the world know the phrase “Stockholm syndrome”. But it’s never been listed in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, because evidence for it has never been clear enough for a formal definition.
Whether or not the term is valid, there is no dispute that the pressures on a hostage’s mind are real. Humans can have any number of reactions to absolute rule – rebellion, peacemaking, sympathy, obedience, rage – and no single response is “wrong” in a short-term crisis. Hostages who fall in love with their persecutors, convert to another religion, or identify with a gunman’s delusional notion of the world all give up their sense of self out of self-preservation. The mental strain has to resolve itself somehow.
What helped deliver me from my overwhelming sense of murderous anger, after more than two years in Somalia, was something I heard on the shortwave radio. It was a homily by Pope Francis about forgiveness. I was suffering not just from feelings of outrage, but also from a self-lacerating guilt about my own mistakes, which had led me to this miserable existence. I lived with a recurring urge to grab one of the Kalashnikovs and shoot either the pirates or myself. “How many of us perhaps deserve condemnation!” said the pope, adding that a person’s sins were like the stars at night. “We look at the sky, so many stars, but when the sun comes in the morning with so much light, the stars are no longer seen.”
This homily woke up a dormant Catholicism within me – not the whole system of belief, but a living river of feeling. I did not have road-to-Damascus conversion, and I wasn’t about to sit down with the pirates for an earnest chat about guilt and reconciliation. But after thinking about the pope’s homily for a few days I noticed how bitterness and anger were acts of will, like suffering itself, and how a slight step backwards, an unhooking of the mind, could let in a flood of mercy and light. I did it in silence. But I found that this mental shift made it easier to smile at the guards in the morning when they delivered a Thermos of oversweet tea and unlatched the steel shutters on my window. Whatever else I was condemned to suffer, I came to see that rage and self-pity were not mandatory aspects of the sentence.
When people ask if that isn’t just a “version of Stockholm syndrome”, I argue it was the opposite: to forgive a persecutor helps maintain your sense of self. It isn’t the same as adopting a false view of the world, or identifying with enemy interests. It’s a cool-headed resolution that dissolves the need for vengeance.
In retrospect, Enmark understood how strange her state of mind must have seemed to others. When the bank robber came up with the bright idea of shooting another hostage through the leg – promising not to hit any bone – Enmark tried to convince the hostage that it might turn out fine. (“But Sven, it’s only in the leg,” she said.) In an interview many years later, she pointed out that she was in a situation where “all your values, the morals you have, change in some way”. But in a matter of days she had found a working survival mechanism. It’s worth noting that in spite of the criminal’s lunatic threats, no one died in this standoff. Enmark found the right tone to handle an erratic, narcissistic gunman for almost a week.
When it was over, the gunman couldn’t believe he was the captive, sentenced to a decade in jail. “It was the hostages’ fault,” he later complained. “They did everything I told them to do. If they hadn’t, I might not be here now. Why didn’t any of them attack me? They made it hard to kill.”
In February 2019, six months after they had picked up Tahlil at JFK, the FBI arrested a Somali-American citizen named Abdi Yusuf Hassan in the frozen parking lot of a Starbucks in Minneapolis. In Somalia, he held a formal title, minister of interior of the state of Galmudug, where I was kidnapped and held. Hassan had lived between the US and Somalia for years.
The FBI believed Hassan had made off with about $250,000 of the ransom money that had been paid to release me. After that, he had retreated to Minnesota, which left the pirate bosses in Somalia to argue about the remaining cash. (Five ranking bosses died in a shootout over the ransom after I was gone.) I pieced this story together in vague outline when I wrote The Desert and the Sea, but after Hassan’s arrest in Minneapolis, and particularly after the trial of Tahlil and Hassan, I started to see there were whole dimensions of my case that I knew nothing about.
Both men were charged with conspiracy to kidnap an American, “terrorism” (in the sense that I was threatened with death in Somalia) and related firearms offences. Neither accepted a plea deal. They each faced 30 years or more, against a mountain of damning evidence.
I had rebuilt my life in Berlin and California, and I was anxious to get the trial over with. It should have run for two weeks in the spring of 2020, but Covid and other unexpected troubles delayed things until February 2023. By the time it finally came around, I was sick of hearing cliches about pirates as “protectors of the Somali coast”, and I wanted to see some semblance of official justice.
In court, Tahlil looked well-fed and wore a Covid mask. Hassan had grey in his hair. My job on the witness stand was to tell the story of my captivity as I remembered it, from start to finish. The defence objected a handful of times, first at my constant use of the word “seems” or “I had the impression …” and then, sharply, at a comment I mumbled into the microphone: “A lot of this is impressionistic.” All I meant was that it was difficult to know absolute facts in Somalia while I navigated that world as a hostage, without my glasses. But the judge agreed that I should stick to facts, rather than trying to interpret them for the jury.
It was cathartic to tangle with defence teams on the witness stand. A lawyer for Tahlil, Steve Lynch, spent part of his cross-examination asking me about guards at Tahlil’s house. “The dozen or so men who were in the house,” he said, “some of these men did not appear to have military training; is that right?”
“It was always hard to tell about military training with the guards,” I said, trying not to use Lynch’s own word “appear”.
“But some of them seemed to be, you know, people who were fishers – right?” he suggested. I felt a bolt of outrage, because the pirates I met were overwhelmingly not fishers trying to protect their livelihoods. That was propaganda, repeated by well-meaning journalists in the west from the moment pirates had made headlines in 2005. In the 1990s and early 2000s it had an element of truth, but by the time they were hijacking oil tankers and cargo ships, pirate gangs no longer consisted primarily of poor fishers defending the Somali coast from illegal fishing vessels. They were clan soldiers with Kalashnikov training – poor men who needed jobs, certainly, but still members of brutal organised criminal networks.
I leaned into the microphone and said, low and clear, so no one in the courtroom would miss it: “Absolutely not.”
“Let me ask you this,” he said. “Did some of the people who were there … did they seem to be relatively simple people?”
“They were clan soldiers,” I said.
Not what the defence wanted to hear. Other witnesses echoed this point during the two-week trial: most pirates were clan soldiers, not simple fishers. The witnesses were Somali spies, informants from the ranks of local Galmudug police or the pirate network itself. One key witness told the court that Tahlil was more sophisticated than the cheerful guard leader he had played around me. In fact he was a captain in the Somali army, the witness said, and he ranked as a mid-level boss in the pirate network.
After the trial, as I read the 2,000-page court transcript, Tahlil came into focus. He’d spent a surprising amount of time on the hijacked tuna vessel, out of my sight. The ship, called the Naham 3, was a long-line tuna vessel run by owners in Taiwan and Oman. It had been hijacked in open water near Seychelles, more than 700 miles from Somalia. (Territorial waters for any nation reach 12 miles out.) The ship was 50 meters long and had a vast maze of fish freezers in the hull, which, according to witness testimony, Tahlil had converted to an armoury. “Tahlil was responsible for collecting all those weapons at the end of the guards’ shifts and locking them overnight in the ship’s freezer,” said one US prosecutor, Gillian Grossman, in her summation, “which the pirates used as a sort of makeshift gun locker. Tahlil controlled access to those weapons. He was the only one with the key.”
Remarkable. This mass of information shifted my impression of him. I no longer thought of my skinny, mild-mannered Facebook informant as a minor boss. If he stashed weapons in the freezer hold, he was involved in the Naham 3 case, too. I doubt he had hijacked the ship, just as he hadn’t physically kidnapped me – but as an armourer he was responsible for all the pirates’ weapons, and in that sense he was also partly responsible for the long captivity of the 28 fishers held hostage on the ship. Twenty-six of them were finally released in 2016, having spent nearly five years as hostages. Two died in captivity.
It also turned out that Tahlil and Hassan were friends, although I had never seen them together. The feds had a binder full of Facebook correspondence and phone calls between them. The defendants called each other “brother” and “my friend”. But Tahlil seemed to acknowledge his own lower rank by using “minister” and “my respected leader”.
My urge to forgive Tahlil eroded like a salt statue in the rain. Not that anger or vengeance rushed back; but I was less interested in showing grace. The released fishing crew members that I spoke to had little interest in forgiveness. One Filipino, Arnel Balbero, wrote to me that he hoped “all of the pirates are put in jail … Because of them there’s a lot of dreams in life broken.”
As for Hassan, it came out in court that he owned a home in Galkayo just down the road from one of my prison houses. According to a pair of Somali witnesses, it was a hideout and a meeting point for some of the highest-ranking pirates I encountered. Alongside his work as the long-distance interior minister for the state of Galmudug, in his capacity as a local landlord Hassan found a way to profit from my presence in the neighbourhood by renting a house to my kidnappers.
I expected to hear some kind of plausible counter-narrative in court about Tahlil and Hassan. It never came. Both men argued that they had infiltrated the pirate gang with some hope of giving me comfort or helping me escape. If that were true, why had they not aided the FBI, never mind the prosecution team? Why did Hassan own a house in Galkayo that was full of ranking pirates? And how did Tahlil come to work as an armourer, responsible for every Kalashnikov I saw, every grenade launcher, every machine gun?
The Somali witnesses said Tahlil had reached out to me on Facebook because the top pirate bosses had paid a final, insulting compensation of $8,000 for his armoury services. He had felt stiffed. So he messaged me in 2014 and began to help me with my book, dreaming about a new life in the US. That made sense. I still felt a measure of pity for him that I didn’t feel for Hassan. I had learned some illuminating facts from Tahlil and convinced him to board a plane. After I absorbed the evidence against him, the Tahlil in my mind had become a less hapless, more calculating man, but I didn’t think he deserved a minimum sentence of 30 years.
Getting these punishments “right”, whatever that meant, felt important for the same reason that forgiveness on the floor of a filthy prison house had felt liberating. It was a form of agency. I had lost my desire for revenge, but not for justice. But, by this point, justice was out of my hands.
People talk blithely about closure, as if a criminal case in a bland federal courtroom can bring peace to the victim of a violent crime. I don’t think it can. You have to find peace on your own. The US Department of Justice did a tremendous job in prosecuting my captors, but psychological comfort wasn’t part of the deal.
On the day of his sentencing, in late 2024, I read out a terse letter for Tahlil in court. I asked Judge Allyne Ross to hand him less than 30 years if she could. “I know what it is to be held against my will,” I said. “I also learned mercy in Somalia as a means of survival … This is not the same as forgetting what happened.”
Tahlil gave a speech insisting on his innocence, insisting (still) that he had wanted “to help Michael”. Ross listened to everything. At last she handed out two 30-year sentences. Tahlil’s would have been lower if a minimum of 30 on one firearms charge were not strict law in New York state. For Hassan, given the weight of evidence, the 30-year sentence was “appropriately severe”, she said, “in contrast to Tahlil’s”.
Another of my captors, Bashko, had been arrested in 2021, this time by FBI agents and local police in Djibouti, a nation north-west of Somalia. He was sent to the US, where he faced similar charges in New York – involving conspiracy to kidnap, terrorism and firearms – but pleaded guilty for a lighter sentence.
I first became aware of Bashko as a lean and clever young gunman on the Naham 3 who wrapped his head in flamboyant turbans to keep the sun off. He was good-humoured and smart, a ground-level guard from start to finish. For two years, he guarded me almost every day with his Kalashnikov, sitting cross-legged on the floor of a given prison house. We used to hold long, sometimes entertaining conversations in fractured English and Somali during our sweltering prison-house afternoons. Our worldviews rarely lined up – he justified my captivity with the most violent, infidel-phobic verses of the Qur’an – but we had lively arguments.
If the poverty trap applied to any pirate I met, I believe, it applied to him. He did not fit the desperate-fisher profile, but he’d signed on as a foot-soldier because he was poor and had few other options. Bashko faced a sentence ranging from zero, or time served, to 25 years, and I saw no reason for him to spend a third of his life in jail. So I wrote a letter to the judge, emphasising his low rank.
“His willingness to talk and joke also made my captivity easier,” I wrote. “He ordered samosas for me as a snack. He mediated between me and more aggressive guards, and he sometimes arranged for me to sleep without chains. Once, in a fit of temper, I flushed the keys to those chains down the toilet, which I think caused him a little trouble.”
Bashko was sentenced in the fall of 2023. The judge gave a long assessment of the case. “There is a word for the inhumanity of Mr Moore’s kidnappers, all of them, leaders and followers,” said Judge Paul Engelmayer. “The word is ‘evil’. We don’t use that word often in courthouses, and we don’t use it often in criminal sentencing. It is reserved for the worst of the worst crimes. It fits here.”
He went on to say that my letter was not the final word. “A court can never subcontract its determination of the just sentence to a victim, whether the victim seeks vengeance or mercy.” But the letter perhaps had some effect. Engelmayer slashed Bashko’s maximum sentence from 25 years to 12 and a half.
I couldn’t be at the hearing in New York, but I was told that Bashko was agitated in the courtroom – and that he wanted to give me a “postcard”. His lawyers would be sending it to me, I learned. I was away at the time, and for a couple of weeks I imagined Bashko’s message would be a screed about how I had ruined his life.
When I returned home, I found a thick envelope, not a postcard. I opened it with some trepidation. It was a handcrafted greetings card with no language at all, no English or Somali, just a sliding pop-up contraption made of pink and white paper, which, when you opened it, unfolded into an eloquent flower.
After his trial, Bashko was moved to Leavenworth federal correctional institution in Kansas, and I tried to visit him while writing this essay. The bureaucratic system was sluggish and unresponsive, but we did manage to speak on the phone.
Bashko’s voice was deeper than before, and his English was now strong. He thanked me for writing to Engelmayer. “I know you were helping me, for real, Michael. I want to say I’m sorry … Bashir from 10 years ago? He’s different, for real. Before, I knew nothing. You remember?”
“I remember.”
“God bless you. Everything is good now,” he said.
It was strange, but he sounded excited, even happy.
“I can’t hate the jail. I know what I did before,” he said. “I did bullshit.”
I raised my eyebrows. In Somalia he had been full of doctrinaire, self-righteous religious beliefs. It sounded as if, in prison, he had arrived at some deeper revelation. “I told the judge: ‘I’m guilty.’ I say: ‘If you give me 30 years, I don’t care. If you give me 15,’ that’s what I told him. I said: ‘Judge, I did wrong. I’m sorry.’”
He had no chance of remaining in the US after his prison term. He wasn’t angling for anything in return. He was serious.
“Thank you, Bashko. You sound like a new man.”
“Your family, everything is good, right?” he said.
“My family is good right now, thank you.”
“I hope you can forgive me, please.”
I hesitated. I’d grown so used to not hearing confessions for this period in my life that I had no idea what to say. A forgiveness that had been completely personal, inward – a form of self-liberation – turned shy in the face of a spoken request. But the piece of mail he had sent was still on my sideboard; in fact I could see it from where I sat with my phone.
“Well, yeah,” I said at last. I cleared my throat. “Yes, Bashko.”
“Thank you, Michael Scott Moore.”
It cost me nothing to grant. I thought about Lincoln and his vaporised enemies. For the first time, I felt something had shifted out in the world – something beyond my own life had transformed because of this halting, doubting, uncertain trajectory of forgiveness I had been writing about for years – and it was more powerful, in its effects, than any project of vengeance.

Das Bas-Beben: Neuer Groll zwischen Union und SPD

Der überraschende Rücktritt erschüttert die Koalition: SPD-Arbeitsministerin Bärbel Bas gibt ihren Rückzug von allen Ämtern bekannt. Ausgerechnet kurz vor dem wichtigen Arbeitgebertag heute. POLITICO-Chefkorrespondent Rasmus Buchsteiner ordnet zusammen mit Maximilian Stascheit ein, wie diese Personalie das zerrüttete Regierungsbündnis belastet und warum mit der eiligen Ernennung von Alexander Schweitzer die Proporzregeln der SPD über Bord geworfen werden.
Währenddessen läuft in der Berliner Landespolitik weiter der Richtungsstreit. Die Linksfraktion im Abgeordnetenhaus streitet nach wie vor über den Umgang mit Antisemitismus und israelfeindlichen Protesten. Im 200-Sekunden-Interview stellt sich der Co-Vorsitzende im Bund, Luigi Pantisano, den Fragen zu offenen Briefen, fragwürdigen Demo-Aufrufen von Mitgliedern und erklärt, wieso er keine drohende Spaltung der Partei sieht.
Nach eigentlich viel zu langer Vakanz besetzt die Bundesregierung den Posten der Antisemitismusbeauftragten neu. Rixa Fürsen beleuchtet die Hintergründe der Personalie Katharina von Schnurbein und erklärt die Erleichterung bei vielen Beteiligten, weil die erfahrene Expertin aus Brüssel nach gescheiterten Anläufen mit anderen Kandidaten nun diese drängende Aufgabe übernimmt.
