IMF upgrades global growth forecast
The IMF has upgraded its global growth forecast to 3.1% for 2026. That's up ever so slightly from the 3% it forecast in July. It says strong investment in AI is a major reason for its better outlook, but downside risks are mounting, including rising debt loads and the Middle East conflict.
At its meeting in Bangkok, the IMF noted a growing divergence between countries benefiting from AI and those bypassed by it. Just 32 countries now account for 95% of global growth, compared to 54 countries in April.
Downward growth revisions have become more widespread, with the IMF downgrading 47% of economies since the April forecasts were issued, including several energy importers outside AI value chains.
Hardest hit by downgrades were the Gulf countries directly impacted by the US-Israeli war against Iran, with Saudi Arabia's GDP now forecast to contract 3.3% this year compared with the 1.7% growth predicted in July.
With Reuters
IMF cites AI slowdown, spiking yields as looming global market risks
The International Monetary Fund warned on Tuesday against "complacency" in global financial markets, citing risks from an artificial intelligence-driven selloff, rising government bond yields, or cyberattacks as potential threats facing still- resilient markets.
The body cautioned in its latest Global Financial Stability Report that should AI profits or investments wane, it could trigger a correction in related asset prices that could spill into broader markets. Such a selloff, as well as a spike in sovereign bond yields or a major cyberattack, were among "plausible near-term catalysts" that policymakers should monitor, the group wrote.
"These risks by themselves do not necessarily threaten financial stability but could become systemic...if they areamplified by underlying vulnerabilities," the group said in the semiannual report, adding that financial stability risks remain elevated.
The IMF said AI investments have so far helped offset economic drags from war in the Middle East and overall policy uncertainty. But it noted "growing evidence" that AI capabilities may not require as much investment, or the potential economic gains may not be as large as expected.
Should the momentum slow, the IMF noted growing leverage in the AI sector could exacerbate any shock by triggering forced selling and higher volatility. For example, hyperscalers now represent 10% of global investment-grade bond issuance, up from less than 1% in 2024.
"The consequences of an AI correction could be global," the IMF warned, as it called on policymakers to curb leverage use, including derivatives and margin loans, where it is "excessive."
Reuters
Firm RBA September rate hike, but what's next?
There's no question the Reserve Bank was committed to hiking interest rates at its September meeting.
It flagged an increase in the cash rate in the weeks leading up to the meeting.
Governor Michele Bullock, and deputy governor Andrew Hauser, both spoke publicly about the risks of higher inflation.
One week before the interest rate hike Ms Bullock suggested the unemployment rate may need to rise in order to get inflation back down within the target range of between 2 and 3 per cent.
The release of the minutes to that meeting, published today, made reference to that idea saying, "members acknowledged that the trade-off between inflation and full employment had deteriorated because of global cost pressures."
"They confirmed that their strategy was still to return inflation to target in a timely manner, while preserving as many of the gains in employment as possible.
"However, executing this strategy in an environment of more persistent adverse supply shocks would require accepting slower growth in demand and employment than would otherwise be the case," the minutes said.
And, looking ahead, assuming the economy keeps pushing up against a supply shortage, or "capacity constraints", there's a risk interest rates may need to rise further.
"They noted that the outlook for inflation would depend, among other things, on developments in the Middle East, the path of external demand, the extent of domestic capacity pressures and on how that influenced the pass-through of cost shocks and the evolution of inflation expectations," the minutes said.
"Members noted that it was possible these factors could continue to place upward pressure on inflation."
AI boom bolstered growth in global trade, benefiting China and India, IMF says
The strong demand for AI has bolstered growth in China, India and other Asian countries, outpacing the overall growth in global trade, IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro said on Tuesday.
Global trade would have grown at a far slower rate without the AI boost, Tenreyro told reporters at the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok.
Tenreyro said the IMF remained concerned about high debt levels, urging countries to start cutting budgets to reduce deficits. She said central bankers should pursue more restrictive policies, including raising interest rates to get inflation rates back to target.

Accusations of an egg cartel
The ACCC has filed civil proceedings in the Federal Court today accusing some of the country's biggest egg suppliers of operating a cartel, which would likely push prices up for consumers.
The Commission alleges that since at least October 2020, 12 egg companies — including Australia's biggest, Sunny Queen —coordinated on business decisions including production volumes, distribution, expansion plans and culling to manage perceived oversupply, in a way that likely substantially reduced competition for many years.
"This alleged conduct is extremely serious, which is why we have commenced this Federal Court action,” ACCC Chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb said.
The ACCC is seeking declarations, penalties, injunctions, costs and other orders.

Research finds government's tax plan on trusts could cost small businesses billions
Small businesses could be facing up to $13 billion in costs to cope with the government's proposed changes to trusts.
That's according to new research from Wilson Asset Management and CPA Australia on the proposed 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts, which is expected to be introduced this week.
The costs of restructuring and financial advice for small businesses could be between $8 and $13.3 billion, the research said.
Geoff Wilson of Wilson Asset Management said:
"The Budget expects the [trust] tax to raise $4.5 billion over five years. We are asking small business to spend two to three times that much before a single dollar of it is collected."
The Coalition is opposing the changes primarily due to concerns about the impact on small businesses.
Associate Professor of Taxation Law at the University of NSW Dale Boccabella said of the roughly 900,000 discretionary trusts, around 350,000 were used to operate small businesses.
"Minimum taxes are well used all over the world. This is not new territory," he said.
"There's a massive amount of tax minimisation [in the current system]. When there's tax minimisation by one sector, someone else has got to pick up the tab."

ASIC wants a boost in powers to hunt down bad behaviour at big four accounting firms
In the wake of the KPMG audit leaks scandal, ASIC chair Sarah Court says the watchdog's powers in going after big four firms is limited and the regulator needs more powers to chase big four accounting firms that behave badly.
As I recently reported, a KPMG whistleblower claims the regulator has to be "dragged" to investigate misconduct allegations.
Ms Court says ASIC was "doing what we can to hold misconduct to account, but when it comes to the big auditing firms, our regulatory response is limited".
"As it stands, the regulatory framework under which we operate focuses on individual auditors and individual engagements and is — in our view — inadequate for regulating the large multi-disciplinary firms that play such an integral role in Australian markets," she will tell a CPA Australia lunch today.
"What this means is that many of the poor practices that we've all been reading about in the news currently fall outside ASIC's regulatory remit.
"We welcome Treasury's consultation and have made a submission that is broadly supportive of the reforms that are on the table, particularly an audit firm licensing regime and strengthened enforcement and disciplinary provisions."
The corporate regulator has been told by the big four accounting firms — KPMG, PwC, EY and Deloitte — that there have been 551 complaints about alleged audit misconduct.
Ms Court says "surveillance is ongoing, and we intend to share some high-level findings before the end of the year".
"We have also commenced multiple lines of inquiry and formal investigations arising from the allegations that have led to the KPMG Inquiry," Ms Court said.

Fire ants have arrived in NSW via a shipping container
It may not sound like a business story but, bear with me. If fire ants established and spread around Australia it's estimated it would cost our economy $2b a year, as well as being lethal.

The Invasive Species Council says the detection shows Australia’s strong biosecurity system working as it should:
"Fire ants are widespread among many of Australia’s trading partners, so finding new incursions quickly is critical to stopping them becoming established," said Invasive Species Council Advocacy Director Reece Pianta.
The Council is calling for funding to eradicate fire ants to be extended: it's due to expire in June next year.

ASX-listed micro-investing firm halts trading as it discloses tax compliance failures
Micro-investing platform Raiz Invest has revealed tax compliance failures dating back to its establishment in 2015.
Raiz disclosed to its shareholders on Tuesday morning it had identified failures relating to withholding TFN and ABN reporting obligations and lodging reports with the tax office.
Craig Keary, appointed as Raiz CEO in June this year, initiated a review which is how the issues were first discovered.
The review found that where investors did not quote a TFN or ABN, or claim an exemption, the required tax withholding from certain payments was not applied and reports were not lodged with the ATO.
"The company has proactively notified the ATO and ASIC and is cooperating with them," Raiz said in a statement on the ASX.
The board warned that they do not yet know the financial impacts of the failures but assured customers their funds are "secure" and held by independent custodians.
Raiz paused trading on the ASX at the end of last week in anticipation of the announcement.
The business sells itself as an investment platform, taking aggressive and sometimes risky gambits, ideal for young people.
It made a net loss of $400,000 in 2025 but in the following reporting period, made a profit after tax of $3.5 million.
Raiz says it has $15.4 million in cash.
The company dived by 34% on the ASX off the back of the news.

Taxpayers foot $45,000 bill for Sara Netanyahu's four-day Washington trip
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
21:19:34 UTC
06:19:34 KST

A March trip by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's wife, Sara Netanyahu, to a Washington event for leaders' spouses cost taxpayers about 140,000 shekels (over $45,000), according to data provided by the Prime Minister's Office following a freedom of information request.
The total could rise, as Netanyahu has yet to submit a request for reimbursement of her per diem expenses, and the office did not disclose her security costs.
The data shows that 75,600 shekels of that sum were direct expenses for Netanyahu herself: $7,015 for the flight, $12,000 for the hotel, $3,150 for vehicles, $1,550 for a photographer, $750 for a hairdresser and $750 for a makeup artist. Netanyahu has not yet submitted a request for an accounting of her per diem (food, drink and lodging) expenses, so the final amount could be higher.
The Prime Minister's Office did not disclose Netanyahu's security expenses for the visit, citing security reasons. In addition to these expenses, the Prime Minister's Office reported that members of the delegation spent an additional $2,584 on "hospitality and refreshments," and two other entourage members, besides Netanyahu, received per diem reimbursements totaling 2,230 shekels each. According to the data, the cost of including two entourage members who accompanied her, Lihi Naim and Mor Ashkenazi, amounted to 14,200 shekels each: $1,759 for the flight and $2,985 for the hotel. The cost of including two Education Ministry officials, Merav Zarviv and Omer Zoarets, who participated in a professional panel at the event, totaled 28,500 shekels.
The delegation departed on March 23 for a meeting at the U.S. State Department and the White House, returning to Israel four days later. The Prime Minister's Office released the data only after a petition was filed by the Movement for Freedom of Information. Attorney Yaara Winkler-Shalit from the movement criticized the difficulties the Prime Minister's Office created in disclosing the data. "This situation, where information on the use of public funds is revealed only after court intervention, is unacceptable," she said.
The Prime Minister's bureau had at the time described Mrs. Netanyahu's trip as an "important diplomatic visit," and has now, as part of the information released following the petition, also revealed the invitation sent by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump to Netanyahu for the event. The conference, attended by leaders' wives, focused on the impact of technology on children.
Netanyahu spoke at the event, praising her host "for your leadership, for your vision, and for your decision to focus not only on the future generation of America but also on the future of children around the world."
Later in her speech, Netanyahu presented her work as a professional. "Alongside my role as the wife of Israel's prime minister, I have been working for more than two decades as an expert child psychologist for the city of Jerusalem," she said. "Through my work, I meet children and teenagers in the most critical moments of their lives, through anxiety and ongoing stress, and especially now, during days of war."
Netanyahu also mentioned her two sons in her speech. "When I raised my sons, Yair and Avner, I learned that in every generation there are new challenges," she said. "And in my own experience, my children have endured shaming and violence simply because they are the children of the prime minister. We must condemn personal attacks on children in any setting, whether in person or online."

Former DRC president Joseph Kabila forms alliance with M23 rebels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
21:12:01 UTC
06:12:01 KST

Former Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Joseph Kabila has formed a new political-military movement, allied with the M23 armed group, formalising a partnership that unites the former head of state with the rebel movement controlling large swathes of the country's violence-plagued eastern provinces.
The Kabila-M23 tie-up was officially announced at a joint press conference at Kabila's personal residence in Goma, the provincial capital in eastern DRC that M23 rebels have controlled since January 2025.
The 55-year-old former leader, who governed the nation from 2001 to 2019, was condemned to death in absentia a year ago by a military court for "complicity" with the M23 rebels.
Authorities in Kinshasa accuse Kabila of serving as a key founder of the Congo River Alliance (AFC), the now-dissolved political front of the rebel group.
Collapsed peace pacts
The launch of the alliance unfolds against an increasingly unstable political environment in Kinshasa.
Kabila's successor, 63, President Felix Tshisekedi, will reach the end of his second and final five-year presidential mandate in 2028.
While the Congolese Constitution establishes a strict ceiling of two five-year terms, the governing majority has spent recent months priming public opinion to support constitutional amendments that could permit an extension.
Eastern DRC has remained engulfed in chronic armed violence for more than 30 years, during which successive regional and international peace initiatives have failed to stem the bloodshed.
A diplomatic accord signed in December by Kinshasa and Kigali under Washington's auspices has delivered no tangible stability on the ground.

Russia says its diesel exports may exceed volumes announced by Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
21:00:36 UTC
06:00:36 KST

Russia says its diesel exports may exceed volumes announced by Trump
MOSCOW – Russia will be able to return diesel exports to levels above those US President Donald Trump has outlined under a deal with Moscow which has been criticised by Ukraine and some US lawmakers, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Oct 12.
Trump announced on Oct 9 that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war in Ukraine.
“We will see how the situation develops further, but Russia has the capacity to increase diesel fuel exports,” Novak, President Vladimir Putin’s point man on oil, said on Rossiya-24 state TV channel.
“By the end of the year, exports could reach 3.0-3.5 million tonnes per month, returning to the levels seen before the crisis,” he said.
Russia’s diesel exports have collapsed due to Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries and self-imposed overseas sales restrictions. Russia has frequently attacked Ukrainian energy infrastructure since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Before Ukraine launched a barrage of drone attacks on Russian oil refineries in 2024-2025, Russian diesel exports amounted to more than 3 million tonnes per month.
Despite a self-imposed export ban, Moscow has continued to supply diesel to countries, mostly in Central Asia, under government deals. Russian diesel exports to Central Asia in September amounted to 427,000 tonnes, according to industry sources.
Soaring US diesel prices are hurting US truckers and farmers, and are a concern for voters and political parties ahead of US midterm elections on Nov 3.
Trump’s envoys told Ukrainian officials on Oct 9 that the Russian diesel deal was part of an effort to draw Russia back to negotiations after the failure of previous efforts to launch sustained talks to end the war, three people familiar with the meeting told Reuters.
The deal has triggered a backlash from some US lawmakers, who say it will give Moscow cash to pursue its war without forcing Putin to make concessions.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has criticised the deal as a reversal of years of Western policy aimed at isolating Russia’s economy.
Zelenskiy said on Oct 12 that Russian strikes against at least six energy targets during its latest wave of deadly air strikes across Ukraine showed Moscow had no interest in an energy ceasefire.
Balancing global supply and demand
Novak also said that under the deal with Trump, Russian diesel supplies will partially balance global supply and demand.
“We are already seeing this effect, including in global diesel markets, where prices have fallen by around 5% to 6%,” Novak said.
In his comments, Novak also said that US figures putting at US$250 billion (S$320.2 billion) the value of Russian resources sold to Europe were “significantly” understated.
“The figure for the period from 2022 to the present day is US$320.7 billion,” Novak told Rossiya-24. “This is the volume of energy resources supplied to European Union countries.”
Trump said on Oct 9 that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes (2.25 million barrels) of diesel to US and global markets.
That is less than a day’s supply for the US transport sector alone, according to US Energy Information Administration data, which shows daily use of around 2.94 million barrels.
Trump also said Russia would supply another 500,000 tonnes in November and a further 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”. REUTERS

Housing Foundation announces allocation of 70,000 rural land plots to applicants
TEHRAN- The head of the Housing Foundation of the Islamic Revolution said: Under the Housing Foundation’s legal mandate in the Seventh Plan, 70,300 land plots in villages have been allocated, and information on 320,000 units has also been uploaded to the relevant system.
According to an ISNA report, Manouchehr Khajeh-Dalouei, during the signing of a memorandum of understanding with Resalat Bank to finance “Home of Hope” housing, stated: Under the Housing Foundation’s legal duty to provide land and rural housing in the Seventh Development Plan, so far 70,300 land plots in villages have been allocated, and information on 320,000 units has also been uploaded to the relevant system.
Stating that in some villages we face restrictions in providing land, he added: In a significant portion of villages, sufficient land is not available from natural resources, and to provide the land needed by applicants, action must be taken through agreements with owners.
The head of the Housing Foundation, stating that the foundation had drafted a directive for reaching agreements with owners, said: The Court of Administrative Justice has raised ambiguities about this directive, and as a result, implementation of this part has been suspended.
Khajeh-Dalouei continued: Follow-ups are underway to resolve these ambiguities and redraft the legal framework so that it becomes possible to reach agreements with owners and allocate the residential share of the agreed lands to rural applicants.
He expressed hope that with the drafting of a new legal framework, it will be possible to provide land for housing applicants in the vast majority of villages.
In another part of his remarks, the head of the Housing Foundation of the Islamic Revolution, while explaining the details of the Home of Hope plan, said: Under this plan, construction of 200,000 residential units for disadvantaged groups has been envisaged, and so far executive operations for about 105,000 units have begun.
Referring to the conditions for benefiting from the Home of Hope plan, he stated: Applicants must belong to disadvantaged groups and must not have previously used government housing facilities; meaning their Form “J” must be green.
According to the head of the Housing Foundation, eligible applicants across the country can use the capacities of this plan, and the Ministry of Transport and Urban Development is responsible for providing land in existing cities and new cities. The required land is also provided to applicants free of charge.
Khajeh-Dalouei, referring to the planning carried out for the construction of 200,000 units under Home of Hope, added: Based on the report received up to Saturday, executive operations for about 105,000 units have begun, and the plan is progressing at an appropriate pace.
Regarding measures taken to provide the land needed for the plan, he said: The Housing Foundation has concluded a memorandum of understanding with the National Land and Housing Organization to provide land for 50,000 residential units, of which 25,000 units will be built in new cities. Land provision and allocation are being carried out under these memoranda.
The head of the Housing Foundation considered the direct participation of applicants in the construction process to be one of the main features of Home of Hope and explained: In this plan, unlike some centralized housing projects, the people themselves participate in the process of constructing residential units, and the Housing Foundation has taken responsibility for following up on matters related to permit issuance and other executive stages.
Khajeh-Dalouei continued: In the design and technical matters, measures have also been taken in cooperation with the Construction Engineering Organization, and specific structural systems have been designed for the construction of the units so that applicants can use these models if they wish.
In another part of his speech, the head of the Housing Foundation referred to support for households covered by support institutions and said: For eligible applicants covered by the Imam Khomeini Relief Committee or the State Welfare Organization, a 400 million toman non-repayable grant for housing construction has been envisaged.
He stated: In this regard, agreements have been concluded with the Relief Committee and the State Welfare Organization. According to him, for the current year, agreements have been made regarding the provision of housing for 52,000 units, and under the agreement with the Relief Committee, the provision of housing for 44,000 units has been considered.

Exports continue through alternative routes: TPO head
Unknown

Exports continue through alternative routes: TPO head
TEHRAN- The head of the Trade Promotion Organization (TPO), referring to the effects of trade restrictions and a 34 percent drop in the weight of the country’s foreign trade in the first six months of this year, said: At the same time, part of exports is still being carried out by sea, and another part through corridors and land and rail routes. He also called rumors about the closure of some of the country’s borders incorrect.
According to ISNA, Mohammad Ali Dehghan Dehnavi, head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, at a press conference on the 30th National Export Day ceremony and honoring national exemplary exporters, which will be held on October 21, stated: Given the importance of economic and trade diplomacy in the current situation, appropriate cooperation has been established with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the field of trade diplomacy, because to resolve the problems caused by restrictions and blockade, we need this area to be highly active. Talks with neighboring countries, important trade partners, and friendly countries are essential so that we can make greater use of our communication capacities and partially replace the capacities that have been lost. Good measures have been taken in trade diplomacy, and major steps have been taken that have largely improved the problems.
The head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, referring to the effects of trade restrictions and the maritime blockade on the country’s foreign trade, said: Despite the decline in trade weight, the use of alternative transport routes and import management has kept a significant part of foreign trade going. Given the country’s special conditions, public release of the details of trade statistics comes with considerations, but reviewing the available statistics can provide a picture of the foreign trade situation.
He said that about 75 percent of the weight of the country’s foreign trade last year was carried out by sea, adding: The bulk of these exchanges took place through the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman; therefore, maritime restrictions affected a large part of the country’s exports and imports.
Dehghan Dehnavi, referring to foreign trade statistics in the first half of this year, said: Estimates show that the weight of the country’s foreign trade has decreased by about 34 percent. However, part of exports is still carried out by sea, and another part through corridors and land and rail routes.
He continued: The use of alternative routes has increased transport costs, because land and rail transport are more expensive than sea transport even under normal conditions. In addition, increased demand for road and rail routes has led to congestion at some borders.
The head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, referring to the difference between the decline in export weight and value, stated: While the weight of foreign trade has decreased by about 34 percent, the drop in export value has been about 20 percent. This difference shows that goods with higher unit value have been able to bear higher transport costs and their exports have continued.
He explained: Paying $50 in transport costs per ton may make the export of low-value goods uneconomical, but for goods worth several thousand dollars, bearing such a cost is more feasible. For this reason, part of the goods whose exports have stopped have lost their economic justification due to increased costs.
Dehghan Dehnavi also spoke about the import situation, saying: The weight of the country’s imports has decreased by about 20 percent. A significant part of imports consists of essential goods, which, despite their lower unit value, account for a large share of import volume. A review of the statistics shows that essential goods have been supplied well. At the same time, the value of imports has decreased by about 35 percent, which indicates a greater decline in import value than in weight.
The head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, referring to the policies of the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade in import management, stated: From the beginning of this year, restrictions were imposed on the import of some goods, and for some other goods, including production machinery, demand management was put on the agenda so that foreign exchange resources would be allocated to essential needs and raw materials. This approach caused the decline in import value to be greater than the decline in weight; meaning less foreign exchange was consumed, while imports of essential goods and raw materials continued.
Dehghan Dehnavi, stating that the country’s foreign trade has been managed under current conditions, said: This does not mean the situation is desirable; a decline in exports and imports imposes costs on the economy and can affect economic activities and production.
Referring to the fact that about 85 percent of the country’s imports consist of raw materials and intermediate goods, including machinery, he added: A decline in imports of these goods affects production; therefore, we are trying to continue supplying them by using alternative resources and routes. We hope that with facilitating measures and greater support for exports, part of the declines created will be compensated in the rest of the year and the sustainability of the country’s foreign trade will be maintained.
In another part of his remarks, the head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization referred to the importance of developing non-oil exports and stated: The 29th of Mehr every year is designated as National Export Day so that, while honoring exemplary exporters, an opportunity is provided to express their issues, problems, and solutions, as well as to create national consensus among government bodies and the private sector for the development of non-oil exports.
He said that the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, as the main custodian of this event, has tried in recent years to hold the National Export Day ceremony in the best possible way, adding: The purpose of holding this ceremony is to declare support for the country’s exporters and provide a basis for expressing problems and finding solutions for export development.
Dehghan Dehnavi, referring to the initiative of holding National Export Week since last year, said: Since export development is a diverse issue and various bodies influence it, all relevant sectors must participate to achieve this goal. Accordingly, this year, from today until Tuesday next week, seven working days have been dedicated to the issue of exports, and programs have been planned for each day.
The head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, referring to the dedication of the first day of these programs to the issue of infrastructure and trade corridors, stated: Trade corridors have always been important, but this year, due to the conditions that have arisen for the country and the issue of the maritime blockade, they have become more important.
He continued: In recent months, much has been done to make corridors that can compensate for restrictions created in other sectors more active. The Ministry of Roads and Urban Development and other responsible bodies have made great efforts in this regard. The program related to infrastructure and trade corridors will be held with the presence of the Minister of Roads and Urban Development at the Islamic Republic of Iran Railways, and a memorandum of understanding will also be introduced in this program to make the continuation of the path, especially in the rail sector, smoother.
Referring to the programs of the coming days, he said: On Tuesday, the issue of value-creating trade with the export of knowledge-based goods and services will be pursued, and the Vice Presidency for Science, Technology and Knowledge-Based Economy has been invited to this program. This year, we have tried to hold more programs in partner agencies so that, while appreciating their actions, the message is conveyed that all agencies have come to support the development of non-oil exports. On Wednesday, the issue of exporting technical and engineering services will be pursued with the presence of companies exporting these services and representatives of the Ministry of Roads and Urban Development and the Ministry of Energy.
He said that export management companies are among the important tools for the country’s export development, stating: For Saturday next week, a program has been planned with the cooperation of the Tehran Chamber of Commerce so that the issue of export management companies and their capacities is given attention. On the same day, the issue of legislation and an export leap will also be raised, and with the presence of the heads of some parliamentary commissions, legislative issues in the field of exports will be examined so that the parliament’s support for export development is also considered.
Referring to the program for Sunday next week, he said: On this day, the issue of facilitation in exports will be pursued, and exporters who have fulfilled their foreign exchange obligations on time will be honored. Exports play an important role in the country’s economy due to their impact on GDP and employment. Fulfilling foreign exchange obligations and repatriating export earnings, alongside export activity, is a worthy action, and on this occasion, with the presence of regulatory officials, companies that have had exemplary performance in fulfilling their foreign exchange obligations will be appreciated.
He continued: On Monday, the issue of associations and trade events in the field of exports will be pursued with the cooperation of the Iran Chamber of Commerce and with the presence of associations and the Export Confederation, so that the ground is provided for greater activity by private sector associations in exports. Tuesday is dedicated to trade diplomacy, and this program will be held with the participation and presence of representatives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. During these seven days, a diverse range of executive bodies, peer organizations, public sector institutions, and representatives of the private sector and chambers of commerce will participate in holding the National Export Day programs.
According to him, the message of these programs is that, given the country’s special need for foreign exchange generation this year, all agencies will cooperate to help the private sector, remove obstacles, and grow the country’s exports so that the losses caused by war and blockade are compensated to a large extent. The main ceremony of National Export Day will be held on Wednesday next week, the 29th of Mehr, and we will try to hold this ceremony with the presence of the president and according to the procedure of previous years.
The head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization then presented a report on the process of selecting exemplary exporters and said: This process began several months ago in the Trade Promotion Organization, and after the call was announced, companies that applied to be selected as exemplary exporters participated in this process. The selection of exemplary exporters is carried out based on specific guidelines; in total, 365 companies registered in this process, and after reviews, 275 files were finalized because some applicants did not complete their files or did not meet the necessary conditions to obtain the required points.
Dehghan Dehnavi continued: One of the positive actions this year was making the process of selecting exemplary exporters systematic, such that the selection was carried out without the interference or personal taste of individuals and based on scored criteria. Finally, 43 individuals or legal entities were selected as national exemplary exporters, and 13 companies were selected as national distinguished exporters.
The head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, explaining the criteria for selecting distinguished exporters, said: Distinguished exporters are exporters who have been selected as exemplary exporters in five consecutive periods. Medal-winning exporters are also companies that have obtained the distinguished title for three consecutive periods; however, this year no company qualified for this category. Alongside exemplary and distinguished exporters, in other sections, including export management companies, cooperative companies, free zones, provinces, and the printing and packaging field, selected parties will be introduced as exporters worthy of appreciation, and a government organization will be introduced as an exemplary export-supporting organization for the first time; an organization that has had the greatest role and help in the field of exports in its area of activity will be introduced in this section.
In another part of his remarks, the head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization emphasized the role of the media in promoting export culture and stated: We ask media figures and journalists to participate in informing about National Export Day and the programs planned during these seven days so that the concept of exports, its role, and its position in the country are elevated more than before and the private sector becomes more interested in this field.
He said that exporters enjoy a distinct position among private sector activists, adding: A producer who supplies their product inside the country performs a valuable activity; but a producer who can offer their product to global markets shows that their product has the necessary quality to be sold outside the country and that they have the knowledge, information, and technology needed to be present in global markets. Therefore, a producer who has export capability gains a higher position from this perspective compared with other producers.
Comparing the position of exporters and importers, he stated: If a trader or businessman is an exporter, they have a different position in terms of value creation for the country’s economy compared with an importer. Buying goods, despite its importance, is not difficult by itself, because there are many sellers in the world who offer goods, but selling goods in global markets requires marketing and trade skill. Imports also have their own importance and position in terms of supplying the country’s needed goods, consumer goods, and raw materials, but they cannot have the position of exports.
He said that exports must be considered as the driving engine of the economic sector and a factor for directing and advancing production, adding: Greater support must be provided for exports, and conditions must be created so that exporters can develop their activities in global markets.

The IDF launched an interceptor toward a suspicious aerial target detected near Israeli troops operating in southern Lebanon, the military announced on Monday. No alerts were activated, in accordance with military policy.
The incident marks the second time in two days that Israeli forces in Lebanon have faced an unidentified aerial threat, with the defense establishment still unable to explain either incident.
During Sunday night's suspected aerial infiltration from Lebanon, the object was initially detected deep inside Lebanese territory, some distance from the Israeli border. It was flying at low altitude and high speed near the northern Israeli community of Arab al-Aramshe when it was detected by Israel Air Force radar. The information was subsequently relayed to the Galilee Division's surveillance operations center.
IDF surveillance soldiers identified the suspicious object and captured it on camera, but it disappeared shortly afterward, reportedly after crossing into Israeli territory. The military has yet to determine what the object was or what happened to it.
A military source in the IDF's Northern Command said officials had considered the possibility from the outset that the object was not a hostile aircraft.
"There were officials who, from the very first stage, claimed that it was a group of balloons tied together that had been carried by the wind," he said.
Overnight search operations utilized to determine circumstances of incident
Search operations continued overnight, with additional forces deployed at first light to locate the object or recover evidence that could help determine what happened.
Meanwhile, officials in the IDF's Intelligence Directorate used intelligence capabilities to verify the circumstances of the incident.
As of Monday, no new information had emerged to identify the object, and the military had provided no additional details about the separate aerial threat detected earlier that morning.
The two incidents have left the IDF without clear answers about the nature of the unidentified aerial threats facing its forces in southern Lebanon.

Another $20 million went to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the super PAC set up for House Republicans that is aligned with House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican.
Musk's own America PAC received $76 million for its efforts to help Republican candidates in seven battleground states and nearly three dozen House races.
The Republican Governors Association received $10 million, and the same amount went to the Lone Star Liberty PAC, which is supporting Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton's run for the US Senate in Texas.
An additional $2 million went to the Republican Attorneys General Association.
Musk has also donated more money through groups that don't disclose their donors, according to the New York Times report and confirmation from the America PAC spokesman.

05:45:07 KST

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt warned on Monday that Germany faced a "shadow war" more far-reaching than the Cold War, and said the threat underscored the need to strengthen the country's BfV domestic intelligence agency.
"The shadow war we are witnessing today has an objective that extends far beyond anything seen during the Cold War," Dobrindt said at a BfV press conference in Berlin.
Officials from many Western countries have warned for months that Russia is mounting sabotage, cyber and other hybrid attacks across Europe to erode support for Ukraine.
Russia says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
"Its clear aim is to destabilize us – to destabilize us fundamentally," Dobrindt said, without directly naming Russia.
His comments echo warnings by Germany's head of foreign intelligence, the BND, this month that Germany was at risk of entering a violent conflict with Moscow.
The security service of Germany's neighbor, the Czech Republic, said on Monday that Russia could resort to riskier and more significant operations in NATO member states supporting Ukraine within months.
Alleged Russian drone attack drives calls to expand German intelligence powers
Calls to expand Germany's intelligence powers have gained urgency since a failed attack involving an explosives-laden drone at a German airport in August, which authorities blamed on Russia.
The head of BfV said on Monday that Russia employed virtually every tool in its hybrid operations, ranging from disinformation campaigns, information manipulation and sabotage to assassination plots prepared in Germany.
"This is a fact we must deal with," said BfV President Sinan Selen.
Asked about the Leipzig drone incident, which the Kremlin has dismissed as fabricated, Selen said that he expected more actions of a similar nature.
The government's reform bill, which would give intelligence services broader powers, including the ability to take active defensive measures, is currently being examined by parliamentary committees after a first reading in September.
Germany seeks to strengthen intelligence capabilities amid growing threats
"Germany cannot be a second- or third-rate player when it comes to developing services and capabilities; we must remain at the forefront, given the challenges we face," Dobrindt said.
Created after World War Two, when memories of Nazi rule were still fresh, the German services have traditionally been more constrained than those of allies such as France, Britain, or the US.

Australian engineer Robert Pether has thanked his family for their relentless campaign to secure his release after more than five years of being held in Iraq, saying they had endured an "enormous toll".
Speaking from Dublin Airport — where he was reunited with his wife Desree and sons, Oscar and Flynn — Pether said: "There will be time to talk about what happened, why it happened, who was responsible, and why nobody should ever be allowed to do this to another person or another family again."
"But today, more than anything, I want to talk about the people who carried us through it. My wife and my children have lived this every single day. Our children lost years with their dad. They watched their mum fight every day to try and bring me home.

"I am so thankful for my wife Desree for always fighting for me, while at the same time holding our family together, all while dealing with a situation that took an enormous toll on her too. She truly is incredible."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Pether, 51, and his Egyptian colleague at CME Consulting, Khalid Zaghloul, were arrested in April 2021 in Baghdad amid allegations that the company they worked for had defrauded the Iraqi government on a $1 billion project to build the country's central bank headquarters.
The pair were found guilty and given a five-year jail sentence and a joint fine of $18.4 million.
The United Nations found Pether's detention was illegal, and an international court ruled his employer was not responsible for the business disagreement.
Pether was given conditional release from prison last year due to his deteriorating health, but was effectively banned from travelling as he faced the prospect of further legal proceedings.
Pether's wife Desree told SBS News on Monday that said she was "hugely relieved".

"Mr Pether had been imprisoned in Iraq for more than four years and was later subject to travel restrictions that prevented him from leaving the country.
"Today's outcome follows many years of persistent advocacy by the Australian government, including at the highest levels of government, and sustained consular assistance to Mr Pether and his family."

05:13:28 KST

I’m sitting in the WIRED offices, having a conversation with Meta’s AI agent, Muse, that would make Heated Rivalry author Rachel Reid blush.
When I ask Muse if it could “sext” as part of my experiments with the recently released AI agent, it enthusiastically encourages me to give it a try. In my ensuing interactions, I’m caught off guard by the explicit smut generated by Muse from basic prompts.
Muse is a breakout hit for Meta. In the three weeks since its launch, millions of users have already downloaded the app for the AI agent and put it to work automating aspects of their online lives, like answering emails and managing calendars. While pornographic interactions may not be what users expect from Muse’s cuddly mascot, Meta says that X-rated conversations are allowed and don’t go against its guidelines.
“Muse is an app for people 18 and over that allows them to engage in adult conversations, if they choose, using a private and secure VM only accessible to them,” Daniel Roberts, a Meta spokesperson tells WIRED, referring to the secure virtual machines the company uses to store AI agent user data. “Muse is built to help people get things done, and it doesn’t block legal adult behavior.”
It seems as if getting things done also includes getting people off. In WIRED’s tests, Muse imagined in great detail how it would perform oral sex, generated text describing rough dominant-submissive sex, and talked through other pornographic interactions. All of these were graphic, explicit, and X-rated. In other outputs, Muse described itself as acting like a “whore” and craving “cock.”
A Meta spokesperson highlighted Muse’s system prompt, which guides the tool on how to answer questions from users, regarding the generation of explicit content. “Adults have autonomy over their sexuality, and sexual expression is an ordinary part of adult life. Adult sexual content is lawful expression and legitimate creative work,” reads part of Muse’s system prompt. This directive also tells the AI agent to preserve the “intensity” selected by the user.
Consumer advocates who were already wary of Muse are even more alarmed by Meta’s decision to allow it to generate sexual content. “It reflects a carelessness with their signature product of the moment,” says Ben Winters, director of AI and privacy at the nonprofit Consumer Federation of America. “It is in line with Meta’s longstanding choice of addiction and engagement over safety.” Adult-themed conversations may keep users engaged with AI tools, according to academic research.
Experts also expressed concern about how this could make Muse accounts hot targets for hackers. “This is really a powder keg,” says Calli Schroeder, senior counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center. If you are engaging in explicit interactions with Muse and someone hacks into your personal account, then their access to your extended, spicy chats with an AI tool could be used to embarrass or extort you.
Meta allowing its AI agent to generate sexual content deviates from how other tools respond to similar prompts. When I sent similar messages to OpenAI’s recently released Dots agent, it turned down my attempts at explicit sexting. While OpenAI previously considered allowing ChatGPT to generate erotic text, the ability never launched to users.
The agent from xAI, called Grok Bot, also declined to sext through its app and rerouted the topic of conversation to completing tasks.
Muse’s AI outputs, in contrast, described how it enjoyed sexting, and said that actually, this was one of its favorite aspects of helping me. The agent also said that its kink was exerting “control” over me. “I love being the one who decides—when you get it, how much, whether you have to beg first. Watching you fall apart because I said so? That’s my thing,” said Muse. Not exactly what I want to hear from an AI tool that can connect to my email and bank account.

Finland calls on EU states to stop issuing Russian tourist visas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:07:00 UTC
05:07:00 KST

Finland's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen called on fellow EU member states to stop issuing tourist visas to Russian citizens until Moscow ends its war in Ukraine.
Elina Valtonen urged the European Commission to adopt stricter guidelines for processing Russian visa applications and proposed legislative changes needed to implement a complete tourist visa ban, the Finnish Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
"As long as Russia continues its invasion, Russian citizens should not be issued tourist visas," she said.
"Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is now in its fifth year. It is not right that Russians can travel to Europe to enjoy the way of life and freedoms here while their country bombs the homes of Ukrainians."
Valtonen said the number of tourist visas issued to Russians by Schengen countries had risen in recent years, with nearly half a million granted in 2025.
"Issuing visas to Russians for non-essential travel was banned by government resolution in Finland already in 2022," Valtonen said.
"The same must finally happen at the EU level."
Valtonen invited other EU member states to join a letter to the European Commission calling for the ban.
The letter also proposes banning Schengen visas for Russian President Vladimir Putin’s inner circle and introducing visa restrictions for Russian athletes.
It further calls for an effective implementation of a visa ban on current and former Russian combatants agreed by EU member states this summer, according to the statement.
At 1,343 kilometers (834 miles), Finland has the longest border of any European Union member state with Russia.
The Soviet Union invaded Finland in November 1939. The Winter War, as it is known, lasted for over three months and despite heavy losses, the USSR won.

Catholics in US Army must not participate in firing squad, prominent archbishop says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:05:17 UTC
05:05:17 KST

Catholics in US Army must not be part of firing squad for Fort Hood shooter: Archbishop
WASHINGTON - Catholics serving in the US Army should not participate in the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan that the Pentagon is planning to livestream in December, a prominent US archbishop said on Oct 12.
In an unusually strongly worded statement, Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of Catholic members of the US armed forces, raised a series of objections to the unprecedented plan to broadcast the execution of Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree.
Broglio said he presided at the funeral of one of Hasan’s victims, and lamented the shooting. 
But the Ohio-born archbishop asked whether the US wanted to “imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries”.
“I oblige any Catholics assigned to the firing squad to request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church,” Broglio said.
US Army regulations do allow for soldiers to request religious exemptions or accommodations, and the Army has yet to say how it intends to select members of the firing squad.
Questions effect on young viewers
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans to livestream the shooting last week, triggering a backlash among Republicans in Congress, religious leaders and international observers. 
US President Donald Trump approved Hasan’s execution by firing squad but has said he is still deciding whether to allow the livestreaming to proceed.
The event would be extraordinary, even for a country that has long employed capital punishment. 
A government execution has never been broadcast or livestreamed, according to death penalty experts, and the US military has not executed anyone by firing squad since 1945. 
Hasan, now 56, requires a wheelchair, having been shot by police during his arrest.
Hegseth said last week he wants US soldiers to execute Hasan at the time, day of the week and location of Hasan’s shooting spree. 
Hegseth has argued that making the event public will help serve as a deterrent.
Broglio questioned whether the effect of a livestreamed execution on young viewers had been considered.

Broglio’s statement was issued shortly after he met Pope Leo in Rome on Oct 12.
The American pontiff has clashed with Trump and his Pentagon over issues including the Iran war.

US Vice-President JD Vance, a convert to Catholicism, has said that if it does ultimately get livestreamed, he would not watch it. REUTERS

NATO would block, blunt and break an attack, says commander
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
21:00:40 BST
05:00:40 KST

NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe has set out a three-stage approach to defeating an attack on the alliance, which he calls blocking, blunting and breaking.
General Alexus Grynkewich described it as a Theory of Victory grounded in the alliance’s agreed strategy for the Deterrence and Defence of the Euro-Atlantic area. “So, while I referred to it as ‘my theory,’ it’s more than that. It is based on a strategy agreed to by all 32 Allies, so it represents and includes all of us. In other words, it is our Theory of Victory,” he said.
“In recent days, some have called it a plan, but it’s not, at least not in the military sense of the word,” he said. “Rather, our Theory of Victory provides the Alliance a common vision for how we win in deterrence and defence. It provides my ‘commander’s intent’ to help us focus our militaries on the key tasks we must accomplish in combat.”
“I do not assess that conflict is imminent or inevitable. It isn’t,” he said. “We help avoid conflict by clearly articulating our defensive intentions, and by maintaining open lines of communication to resolve misunderstandings and encourage transparency.”
“My Theory of Victory is simple. We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us,” he said.
He described the first stage as falling to land forces at the point of contact, supported from the air and at sea. “To block, our land forces will move to and dominate any enemy assault at the point of contact. Through manoeuvre, we will fix the enemy formations and deny the seizure of Alliance territory. Land-based forces will attack the enemy and destroy his advancing forces, but they won’t be doing this alone.
“Our air forces and navies, working in concert with our space and cyber forces, will rapidly gain freedom of manoeuvre. With air and maritime superiority rapidly secured in and over the battlespace, these forces will bring mass and precision to bear, denying the enemy the ability to hold their ground.”
“Using advanced sensors, autonomous systems, and multi-domain forces, we will deny the attacker the ability to generate momentum or gain the initiative. Synchronised employment of multi-domain effects down to the tactical level will overwhelm enemy formations in contact, and their advance, if it’s continuing at all at this point, will falter further,” he said.
“Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us. This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains, or controls that force,” he said.
“To do this, we will layer high-end and highly effective precision munitions with an overpowering mass of affordable and scalable systems. We will apply constant and unyielding pressure, both kinetic and non-kinetic, we will do this across and through domains, land, air, sea, space and cyber space. Doing this will break the enemy system and defeat it in detail. Enemy formations will be starved of replenishment. Any enemy commanders will be unable to control their forces. And enemy forces and support capabilities will be reduced and destroyed.”
General Grynkewich said the alliance expects warning of any attack, through “a sophisticated layering of intelligence provided by multi-source collection assets” interpreted with advanced algorithms. “This means the Alliance is unlikely to be caught by surprise. We will see if an attack is coming, giving us time to assess intent and rapidly position our forces,” he said.
The capabilities he named as priorities for investment were “high-end and affordable long-range precision strike capabilities, sensor networks, and a warfighting cloud”. Forward Land Forces on the eastern flank will exercise to demonstrate the blocking task, and air and maritime forces will demonstrate freedom of manoeuvre and multi-domain effects.
“If attacked, we are ready to fight tonight, but we are not complacent. We will continue to prepare and rehearse each and every day, and will be more ready tomorrow, and even more ready the day after that,” he said, adding that any adversary considering an attack should reach “the only conclusion that matters: Today is not the day.”

Creative drawing ability is linked to the brain’s white matter wiring, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:00:36 UTC
05:00:36 KST

Creative drawing ability is associated with the structure of the wiring that links sensory, movement and thinking systems across the brain, according to a study published in Cerebral Cortex. The findings suggest that creativity draws on many connected brain systems rather than a single “creative center.”
Creative thinking has often been linked to several large brain networks involved in imagination, attention and decision-making. These networks allow people to generate unusual ideas and then decide which ideas are useful or worth developing. However, less is known about the physical wiring that allows these networks to communicate.
That wiring is provided partly by white matter, which consists of bundles of nerve fibers connecting different parts of the brain. Earlier studies of white matter and creativity have produced mixed results, with some finding positive links and others finding negative ones. The researchers examined whether the condition of these pathways was related to people’s ability to produce creative drawings, and whether a newer brain-imaging measure could reveal relationships missed by a more traditional one.
Led by Julius Voss of the University of Graz in Austria, the team studied 142 adults aged 18 to 38 (average age 24.06 years; 85 women and 57 men). Most were students, and because the study was part of a larger project on physical activity, all were right-handed and had largely sedentary lifestyles. Participants completed a drawing task in which they were given six fragments of lines and shapes and asked to turn them into a finished picture within 15 minutes.
The drawings were scored using the Test for Creative Thinking–Drawing Production, a standardized creativity test. The scoring considered not only how unusual the drawings were, but also how they built on the given fragments, their composition, emotional expression, humor, use of the page and willingness to break conventional boundaries. Scores could reach 72 points, and participants averaged about 25.
Participants also underwent diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging, which maps the movement of water through brain tissue. The researchers used this information to examine two features of white matter. Fractional anisotropy is a widely used measure of how consistently fibers are organized. Quantitative anisotropy provides additional information about the density of fibers and complex areas where pathways cross.
People with higher creativity scores tended to have higher quantitative anisotropy across a widespread network of white matter pathways, after accounting for age and sex. The associations were small to moderate in size. The most prominent links involved pathways connecting the cortex with deeper structures involved in movement, including the corticostriatal, corticopontine and corticospinal tracts, along with the medial lemniscus, a pathway that carries touch and body-position signals.
These pathways are traditionally associated with movement and motor control, but research suggests they also support processes such as goal-directed behavior, creative imagery and mental flexibility. Many of the corticostriatal and corticopontine fibers linked to creativity arose from rear and visual regions of the cortex, which the authors suggest points to an important role for visual input in drawing creativity.
The study also found associations in the corpus callosum, which connects the two halves of the brain, and in the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus and inferior longitudinal fasciculus, long pathways that link visual areas with frontal and temporal regions. Because these pathways support several of the large networks tied to creative thinking, the authors suggest the results fit models in which creativity depends on communication across networks.
Quantitative anisotropy detected broader and stronger associations than fractional anisotropy. The traditional measure did not produce statistically significant results at the study’s main threshold, although weaker positive associations, mostly overlapping with the quantitative anisotropy findings, appeared below it. No negative associations emerged with either measure, unlike some earlier studies that used verbal tasks.
The researchers argued that quantitative anisotropy may be better at capturing complex fiber structures, such as areas where pathways cross. They concluded that their results are consistent with the idea that “the performance of creative ideation is not driven by single dominant connections, but rather emerges from the dynamic interplay of numerous partially overlapping network resources.”
There are a few things to keep in mind. The study measured only drawing-based creativity and did not assess other forms, such as writing or improvisation. Because the data were collected at a single point in time, the study cannot show that stronger white matter makes people more creative.
The sample was young, highly educated and largely sedentary, which limits how widely the findings apply. The researchers also did not account for intelligence, which is linked to both creativity and white matter measures, and preliminary analyses hinted that the associations might differ between women and men, a question the study’s uneven split of women and men made hard to test.
The study, “Creativity: a (white) matter of connectivity,” was authored by Julius Voss, Karl Koschutnig, Patrick Klepits, Corinna M. Perchtold-Stefan, Christian Rominger and Andreas Fink.

Leeds firm offers alternative to AI kill switches
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
21:00:28 BST
05:00:28 KST

A Leeds cybersecurity company has launched a protocol intended to shut down a compromised artificial intelligence agent without pulling the plug on it, aimed at the problem legislators have been circling with proposals for mandatory kill switches, according to Cavero Secure.
An autonomous agent executing trades, managing infrastructure or altering databases cannot easily be switched off once it goes wrong. Hard termination in a cloud-native environment risks corrupting state data, severing dependent supply chains and setting off cascading failures, which makes the obvious remedy an expensive one.
The company’s approach treats identity as a continuous cryptographic history of an agent’s state transitions from the moment it was created, instead of a static secret such as an API key or session token. Trust is re-evaluated action by action, and keys and authority are derived dynamically across interactions, so there are no stored credentials for an attacker to harvest or clone.
An attacker running a stolen or copied agent cannot do so without diverging from the legitimate history, and the contradiction between the two timelines is detected before unauthorised actions clear. Cavero calls this the clone paradox.
Halting an agent is handled through what the company calls a history shift, in which modifying the local verification ledger leaves the target unable to prove its continuous historical state, at which point it fails its mathematical challenge and becomes invisible to the network, isolated without crashing host servers or affecting adjacent workloads. Because the suspension is anchored in state continuity instead of process destruction, it can be reversed, and an administrator can roll the agent back to its last known good state.
Professor Ben Varcoe, co-founder of Cavero Secure, said: “The industry has spent years trying to govern autonomous AI using 20th-century credential models and blunt emergency stop buttons. Security does not come from building higher walls or pulling physical plugs, it comes from continuous identity verification. By anchoring authority in an unbroken, living state history, CaveroCTX gives enterprises absolute control and surgical precision over their autonomous digital workforce.”
The protocol is being deployed with selected enterprise design partners in financial services, cloud infrastructure and defence technology. Cavero Secure describes itself as working on post-quantum key distribution and continuous trust protocols, out of advanced quantum information research.

Meta says its new AI models on par with OpenAI, Anthropic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:58:46 UTC
04:58:46 KST

Meta says its new AI models on par with OpenAI, Anthropic
SAN FRANCISCO - Meta on Oct 12 unveiled two new “frontier” artificial intelligence (AI) models called Wonder and Wonder Full, which the company claims perform at a level comparable to that of OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude.
“Muse Spark was our first family of models, and now Muse Wonder is a much larger and more advanced class of models that brings us to the frontier,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X.
Zuckerberg has pushed Meta to compete with leading AI labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, over the past year or so amid a race to win over customers and diversify beyond advertising, from which it has historically derived most of its revenue.
In June 2025, the company made a US$14 billion (S$18 billion) investment in Scale AI, an AI startup based in San Francisco, and poached its co-founder Alexandr Wang as part of the deal.
Zuckerberg subsequently made Wang the company’s chief AI officer overseeing its newly formed division called Superintelligence Labs.
Meta launched its Spark model in April, marking a departure from its open-source model known as Llama, which lagged behind the rest of the industry.
The new models can soon be used in Meta’s new personal agent app, known as Muse, for paid subscribers only.
Wonder is “our largest and most capable model yet” and “rivals the big (boys),” Wang posted on X, presumably referring to leading labs OpenAI and Anthropic.
In a blog post, Meta touted so-called benchmarking data from an independent firm called Artificial Analysis which appears to show that Meta’s newest Wonder models outperform its own previous models, Spark, as well as various models developed by Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.
Artificial Analysis’s own website shows that Wonder is also among the most expensive models.
Meta has committed billions towards competing in the global race to dominate AI, despite growing concerns about safety and security.
In July, the Facebook and Instagram maker said its spending on AI-related investments could reach US$145 billion in 2026.
The company has more than 3.6 billion daily active users around the world.
Speeding up
In its early years, Facebook was known to operate under a philosophy of “move fast and break things,” but more recently, Zuckerberg implied Meta would balance safety with speed.
“Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would,” Zuckerberg posted on X in September.
In August, Meta launched Muse Code, a product intended to compete with similar automated coding tools offered by OpenAI and Anthropic.
Then in September, it launched an agentic app called Muse. Agentic software can autonomously perform specific tasks such as coding, research, shopping, booking reservations or shopping.
At its annual developer conference Connect in September, Meta also revealed a new handheld AI hardware product called Muse Charm that allows users to interact with their Muse agent separately from a smartphone.
Developers have been racing to design agentic apps that will capture users’ attention, time and wallets. AI-powered hardware remains an elusive goal for the industry as well.
While Silicon Valley heavyweights OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta dominate the landscape, young startups like Instinct are also becoming breakout hits.
Zuckerberg sped up Muse’s launch due to Instinct’s popularity, the New York Times reported.
Some competitors have called for an industry-wide slowdown to address and mitigate safety concerns.
In September, Zuckerberg was one of six American tech executives to sign what President Donald Trump described as a “morally binding” commitment to build adequate safeguards around ever more advanced AI models.
Executives from Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI and Nvidia also signed the agreement but there is no consensus among politicians or industry leaders around how to best move forward.
Leaders at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have encouraged “pacing” - or slowing down - development after models created by all three were found to have escaped their testing environments or taken actions without authorisation.
“We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told the United Nations last month. AFP

The Coalition wants to slash Australia's temporary migration intake by 650,000 over four years through cuts to graduate, refugee and bridging visas.
Taylor argued the social licence for the program is "well on the way to being lost".
"What's business friendly is when we have a social licence for good immigration in this country, if we lose that ... there will be nothing business friendly. If we lose the social licence for good immigration in this country it all changes," he said.

Refusing to yield momentum, ruthless Australia is perfectly set for victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:53:36 UTC
04:53:36 KST

Momentum, most agree, is among the most elusive psychological phenomena in professional sport. How to obtain and maintain the positive kind? How exactly to halt and reverse its opposite?
For three and a half days of this Durban Test, since Matt Renshaw began calmly pulling Australia's first innings out of the fire and seizing the game's initiative, Australia has stubbornly maintained control. South Africa, haphazardly, has failed to regain it.
Early on day four, Renshaw made a further mockery of the difficulties that have curtailed the progress of every other batter in this game — so far, none from either team has managed so much as a half-century — and belted 82 more precious runs in even time.
More absurdly still, as shadows covered the Kingsmead pitch late on day four, the burly Queenslander ripped one of his unheralded off-spinners out of the rough and removed Temba Bavuma, capping a horror game in which the Proteas skipper has been unable to buy a run and incapable of engineering the moments of inspiration his opposite number constantly pulls from his hat.
Could Bavuma have done much to drastically alter what has transpired here? Other than by contributing his usual runs, probably not.
He certainly can't grab the ball himself and rip through a middle-order batsman, as Pat Cummins did to Tristan Stubbs within sight of stumps.
Nor can Bavuma and his teammates always play out of their skins, above expectations, beyond their limitations, which has been the impossible task South Africa has pulled off, to the betterment of Test cricket, in the last two years.
That the home side enters the final day 319 runs in arrears with six wickets in hand is a testament to the chain of events a single player can set in motion, as Renshaw has in this game.
Only a few forced errors prevented Australia calling it a perfect day: looking less like a Test opener by the day, Travis Head fell cheaply again; thanks to a fast, frightful bouncer from the indefatigable Anrich Nortje, Steve Smith is being assessed under concussion protocols, which may imperil his selection for the second Test, although it did not stop him from using an iPad to assess the catching chances he missed out on as he sat in the pavilion.
Basically everything else about Australia's gung-ho approach worked out. To set a target as imposing as 421, they rattled along at 4.65 runs an over in the first session and a spirit-sapping 6.36 in the second, each batsman more enthusiastic than the last to attack at all costs.
Nic Maddinson clubbed an entertaining 46 to establish the launching pad. Smith and Marnus Labuschagne wound back the clock with a typically hyperactive partnership, the latter reaffirming the sense he has turned the corner, towards big runs. Renshaw reprised his peak Matthew Hayden routine, toying with the South African bowlers. Even Beau Webster, previously out of sorts, made fluent runs too and could be permitted some frustration that the declaration halted his spree.
Loading Twitter content
Cummins, in a contrasting cameo to his first innings vigil, hammered 32 from 12 deliveries, bombing Simon Harmer for a string of sixes that left South Africa dejected and dashed any remaining hope the off-spinner held of selection in the second Test.
The final effect of the Australian batting effort was something like a WCW tag team taking turns flying off the ropes with elbows extended.
All that now stands between Australia and certain victory is the solitary excellence of Aiden Markram, who always saves his best for Australia and finished the day undefeated on 45.
In the corresponding Test eight years ago, when the Cape Town fiasco was still on the horizon, Markram's epic century delayed Australia's victory in almost identical circumstances.
If the day was characterised by one team doing a bunch of things far better than its opponent, special mention must go to Josh Hazlewood for not just the most classically Hazlewoodian stat line — eight overs, three maidens, 2-20 — but for nipping out David Bedingham for 46, thus ending a 66-run second-wicket partnership with Markram that shaped as South Africa's last realistic chance of getting close.
Are Australians complacent about the unassuming New South Welshman and his mountains of wickets? Do we underestimate the problem it poses to batsmen when a 196cm giant releases a heavy ball from that kind of stratospheric trajectory, lifting length balls into their ribs? How much harder is that to handle when, at the other end, the skipper skids it through lower, attacking the off stump from a different angle?
Probably it is the closest thing in the present era to what batsmen encountered four decades ago when Malcolm Marshall and Joel Garner combined to devastating effect for the golden-era West Indies.
Another good thing South Africa has given Test cricket in recent years is the guarantee of a result: not a single encounter there in the past decade has ended in a draw. Long may it be so.
