Royal Ballet star Natalia Osipova returns to Israel with world premiere by Israeli choreographer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:47:49 UTC
04:47:49 KST

Natalia Osipova, a principal dancer with London’s Royal Ballet, one of the world’s leading ballet companies for nearly a century, will return to Israel to perform her ballet program, Force of Nature, at the Tel Aviv Performing Arts Center on December 17 and 18.
The program combines excerpts from classical ballets with contemporary dance works created especially for Osipova, who will perform alongside American dancer and choreographer Jason Kittelberger and an ensemble of guest dancers.
The performances will also feature the world premiere of a new work created in collaboration with an Israeli choreographer, whose name has not yet been announced.
Osipova, born in Moscow, trained at the Moscow State Academy of Choreography before joining the Bolshoi Ballet. Although she began in the corps de ballet, she performed eight solo roles during her first season.
She drew international attention in 2007 when the Bolshoi visited London, and the danced Kitri in Don Quixote, a production directed by Alexei Ratmansky. That role is considered one of the most important in the ballet repertoire. Her performance drew enthusiastic reviews and helped establish her international career.
She subsequently appeared with major ballet companies and theaters in Paris, Milan, Berlin, and New York. In 2013, she joined the Royal Ballet in London, where she continues to perform.
Over the years, Osipova has worked with leading choreographers, including Ratmansky, Arthur Pita, Akram Khan, and Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui. She has received numerous awards, including the National Dance Awards and the Benois de la Danse prize.
From classical ballet to contemporary dance
The Tel Aviv program will feature excerpts from Giselle, one of Osipova’s signature classical roles, and Le Corsaire, known for its technically demanding pas de deux.
Another selection is Isadora, Frederick Ashton’s choreography set to five Brahms’ waltzes in the style of Isadora Duncan, the pioneering modern dancer.
The contemporary portion of the program includes Ashes, an intimate duet choreographed by Kittelberger in collaboration with Osipova. The work explores the relationship between two people through movement.
Osipova and Kittelberger also established Blooms Dance Project, an independent initiative that presents selections from her classical and contemporary repertoire while developing new productions.
The story behind Osipova's 'Force of Nature'
The title Force of Nature has accompanied Osipova for several years. In 2018, British filmmaker Gerald Fox directed the documentary Force of Nature Natalia, which followed her work in rehearsals and performances. In 2022, Osipova developed a stage program under the same title, bringing together highlights from different periods of her career.
Alon Yurik Productions will present The Force of Nature on December 17 and 18 at the Tel Aviv Performing Arts Center.

====================================================================================================

Iran’s two-front war on Israel: From October 7 to election interference - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:47:41 UTC
04:47:41 KST

Iran’s hand in the Hamas-led October 7 massacre went beyond rockets and training camps. Reports say Persian was heard among the terrorists during the attack. A parallel campaign of Iranian hackers and fake accounts opened a second front, now reopening ahead of the election.
The internal front
Three years after the massacre
On the morning of October 7, 2023, on Simchat Torah, thousands of terrorists broke through the Gaza border fence, overrunning IDF posts, kibbutzim, the Nova music festival, and Sderot. Some 1,200 people were murdered, most of them civilians, and 251 were dragged into Gaza as hostages. It was the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust.
‘They were speaking Farsi’
Survivors are still piecing together that day themselves.
Eyal Eshel, whose daughter Roni was killed at the Nahal Oz base, told Channel 2 that survivors heard terrorists inside the compound speaking to each other in Farsi.
“I understand from this detail that they collected information about us before October 7,” he said, adding that bereaved families were gathering such facts “ourselves.” The IDF has not confirmed the account, which remains survivor testimony. But it raises the question Israel has asked since that morning: How deep was Iran’s hand in the attack?
Why Persian? Tehran’s fingerprints
Evidence of Iranian sponsorship is heavy: training, planning, money, and weapons.
The Wall Street Journal reported that some 500 Hamas and Islamic Jihad operatives received combat training in Iran in September 2023, led by the IRGC, with Quds Force commander Esmail Qaani attending.
Hamas minutes seized by the IDF show Yahya Sinwar spent over two years planning the attack and worked to persuade Iran and Hezbollah to join a wider war.
The IDF has accused Iran of supplying Hamas with weapons, money, and technological know-how for years.
Washington was more cautious: the secretary of state at the time, Antony Blinken, said the US had no direct evidence Iran planned the attack, “but that could change.”
The pattern is clear: Hamas pulled the trigger, but the gun, the training, and the strategy of a multi-front war came from Iran.
The external front
Cyber warfare: hacking for headlines
Since October 7, Iran has sharply escalated cyber operations against Israel, according to the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), through fronts such as Handala Hack, CyberAv3ngers, and IDFLeaks.
Handala, tied to Iran’s Intelligence Ministry, has leaked the phone of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s aide Tzachi Braverman, breached Naftali Bennett’s Telegram account, doxxed Unit 8200 members, and claimed 197 gigabytes from the Nahal Sorek nuclear center.
“Most of its mission is to damage public trust, create a sense of penetration, and amplify media resonance,” said Rafael Franco, former deputy head of the National Cyber Directorate.
Offline, counter-espionage arrests rose 400% in 2024 as Iran recruited Israelis on Telegram for surveillance and sabotage.
The bot army that was waiting
The Israeli firm Cyabra scanned over 162,000 accounts discussing the attack and found one in four was fake.
In the first 48 hours, it found ~40,695 fake profiles and 312,000+ pro-Hamas comments and posts, with 531 million+ views.
Many accounts were created over a year earlier and lay dormant until October 7 – preparation, not spontaneous outrage.
Iran hosts, its partners amplify
Iran did not fight alone – its partners shared interests, not a command.
Iran played the role of the host, sponsoring Hamas and contributing hacking units, fake outlets, and bots to their mission.
Qatar was the megaphone. It contributed to Hamas’s Doha leadership and Al Jazeera’s reach. Nearly a third of profiles engaging with AJ+ on X/Twitter were fake.
Turkey was a safe haven. It hosted Hamas officials and contributed by pushing the same narratives through state media and troll networks.
The result: an echo chamber, where a Hamas Telegram claim could be picked up by Al Jazeera, repeated by Turkish outlets and multiplied by fake accounts within hours.
What the bots did
According to Cyabra and FDD, the networks hijacked hashtags like #IStandWithIsrael, recycled old war footage as fresh evidence from Gaza, rewrote the massacre as justified (seeds of today’s denial), and targeted Israelis directly through Hebrew fake outlets like “Dofek TV” and AI deepfakes.
They left a distorted global picture, pressure on hostage families and soldiers, eroded trust at home, and an infrastructure that can be switched back on at any moment.
The next battle: October 27
The bots are back
Security officials warn Iranian influence operations are already underway to deepen Israeli divisions ahead of the vote.
An investigation by the OSINT platform Golden Owl, reported by The Jerusalem Post, mapped 119,717 accounts and confirmed 57 as part of an Iran-linked campaign posing as Israelis.
Fifty-seven may sound small. But October 7 showed what a small, patient network can do: plant a narrative and let real users spread it for free.
Israel cannot be caught off guard twice
Before October 7, the warning signs were there. Israel saw pieces of the picture and didn’t act on the whole. Three weeks before the vote, we cannot make that mistake again.
Israel should treat October 27 as a likely target and prepare now. That means protecting the vote. Election systems, party databases, and the Central Elections Committee’s infrastructure should be hardened and tested, with backup plans ready.
It also means we must expect a strike timed to the vote. Handala hits at the moment of maximum impact; a fake “leak,” false results, or a deepfake on election morning should be planned for, not hoped away.
Platforms must be held accountable. X, Meta, TikTok, and Telegram must act fast against networks researchers have already exposed.
We must also stay alert beyond the screen. Iran has opened multiple fronts before. Security services should be on heightened alert for any attempt to exploit election day, online or off.
The front line is every phone
The government can’t do this alone. Before you share a shocking clip, an anonymous “leak,” or a post designed to make you hate your neighbor, ask who benefits. Too often, the answer is Tehran.
Three years ago, Iran helped bring a massacre to Israel’s border. Since then, it has waged a quieter war on what rockets can’t destroy: Israelis’ trust in each other. The answer is not panic but preparedness.
If Israel goes into October 27 alert, protected, and united enough to vote on its own terms, it will have won a battle Iran spent years preparing for.

Houthi official warns of ‘swift, painful response’ if US enters Yemen war
SANAA – A Houthi official on Oct 12 warned the US it would receive a “painful response” if it entered the war in Yemen, where Saudi Arabia has reportedly requested Washington’s help in dealing with the group as it weathers repeated attacks.
Yemen’s civil war – in which a Saudi-led military coalition supports the government against the Iran-backed Houthis – reignited in July, months into the wider regional conflict that has roiled energy markets and plunged the Middle East into crisis.
The Houthis quickly began targeting Saudi oil facilities, tankers and transport hubs, including a string of lethal strikes on Riyadh’s airport, rocking the world’s top oil exporter.
Blasts resounded over the capital again on the night of Oct 12, with the Saudi coalition saying it had intercepted a Houthi missile and the group saying it had again targeted the airport.
Later, the coalition announced that it had intercepted two ballistic missiles in the south of the kingdom, near the border with Yemen.
In a statement posted on social media platform X, the coalition said it had “intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Khamis Mushait”, a city where a Saudi military base has previously come under attacks.
Following an attack at the Riyadh airport on Oct 10 that killed 13 people, US President Donald Trump said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the group, after having reportedly rebuffed previous requests for help from the kingdom.
“The Houthis are misbehaving very badly. They’re misbehaving very badly. No good,” Trump said on Oct 12.
“If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond. Rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region,” Houthi political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti told AFP in an interview.
He also warned “all employees and workers at Saudi oil facilities and airports to stay away from these sites, as they have become legitimate targets”.
The Oct 10 strike on King Khalid International Airport was the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in more than a decade, and also left hundreds wounded.
Trump said the attack was “not acceptable” and that he would be speaking to the kingdom’s de facto leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, telling reporters the US was “going to look at” the possibility of joining Saudi strikes.
Operations remained suspended at the sprawling airport on Riyadh’s outskirts on Oct 12.
‘Serious’ response
Bukhaiti said the purpose of the campaign against Saudi targets was to send a message to the crown prince “that he can no longer wage aggression against Yemen from a safe position”.
Saudi energy minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told a conference in Riyadh on Oct 12 that the recent events had “tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people and our resilience”.
“The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious.”
CCTV footage of Oct 10’s attack released by the Saudi authorities showed Muslim pilgrims in religious attire waiting in departure lounges before a sudden blast tore through the building and brought down flaming debris.
The atmosphere in Riyadh remained tense on Oct 12, as state broadcaster Al Ekhbariya said the military coalition was responding to drone and missile threats.
In the evening, mobile phones received a loud government alert warning of a “hostile aerial threat” before the announcement of the interception.
The alert delayed the kick-off of a football match between Uzbekistan’s Neftchi Fergana and Saudi team Al Nassr, home to Portuguese superstar Cristiano Ronaldo.
It was the first use of the phone alert system in Riyadh in weeks, with no official reason given for the lack of messaging during the attacks targeting the capital in recent days.
The Houthis said they had also targeted the Khamis Mushait base in the kingdom’s south with a drone.
Flights suspended
The US embassy in Saudi Arabia said US government employees must obtain its authorisation before using any airport in the kingdom, and urged US citizens to “take extreme caution” if they chose to do so.
The mission also said “American citizens have been detained for taking photos of recent events” in Saudi Arabia.
The UAE’s national carrier Etihad Airways announced on Oct 12 that it was cancelling all flights to and from Riyadh until next week, and also suspended flights to Dammam and Jeddah.
Bahrain’s national carrier Gulf Air said it, too, was cancelling all Riyadh flights until Oct 17.
US operator Delta announced it would delay the launch of direct flights from Atlanta to Riyadh, scheduled for Oct 23.
Despite vast spending on military hardware, the Houthi attacks on oil, military and transport facilities across the large, mostly desert country are stretching Saudi defences.
Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University, said that despite some success, “Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves”.
Riyadh leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen’s government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.
Juneau said the Houthis now “want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them”.
The long-running Yemeni civil war has created a deeply entrenched humanitarian crisis in the impoverished country.
UN rights chief Volker Turk said he was “appalled by the repeated attacks” on Saudi Arabia, but urged both sides to back down, adding “continued fighting will only unleash further misery with no end in sight”. AFP

Quick hits: Cummins blasts and Maharaj juggles as Smith pulls up lame

Pat Cummins's explosive knock pushes Australia clear, Keshav Maharaj produces some magic in his follow-through and Steve Smith doesn't join his teammates in the field.
Nic Maddinson hooked the first ball of the innings for four, so it was no surprise that he got a move on when day four began with Australia needing quick runs to set up a victory.
He hit two boundaries in his first three balls faced, but both were off the edge. Then, after watching opening partner Travis Head chip a tame shot to mid-on, Maddinson decided to force the issue.
Through cover, down to third man, back over the bowler … the controversially selected 34-year-old made a real statement as he raced to within one shot of a maiden half-century.
But it came to an end on 48 off 38 balls when Anrich Nortje uprooted his middle and leg stumps with a searing yorker.
A famous Test inning? Perhaps not, but a career high likely to earn him another chance to prolong his strange Test career.
2. Maharaj's bizarre juggling take
With Matt Rensaw having pushed into the 80s and looking destined for a second century for the match, it felt like the South Africans were in need of something extraordinary to dismiss the Queenslander.
And although not quite a work of art, Keshav Maharaj's diving return catch was certainly out of the ordinary.
With Renshaw having chipped one back towards the bowler, the finger spinner did well to get down in his follow-through, before juggling the ball once, twice, taking his eye of the cherry, and ultimately securing it in his palm while lying on the turf.
He looked as surprised as anyone to have taken the catch, which was confirmed after a lengthy review by the TV umpire.
3. Cummins's late cameo
Australia was surprisingly circumspect during the middle session, with Matt Renshaw and Beau Webster doing little more than keeping the scoreboard ticking over.
Pat Cummins clearly had no plans to declare on Renshaw when he had a second ton for the match in the offing, but when Renshaw was caught out, the captain took it on himself to up the tempo.
He wasted little time attacking the spin of Simon Harmer, smacking his fourth ball for six over long-on and adding three more in his next four deliveries from the off-spinner before declaring on 6-314 having clattered 32 off 12 to take his team to a 420-run lead.
4. Smith sidelined
Steve Smith's slips catching changed the game on day three but soon after Cummins's declaration it became clear he would not have the same impact on day four.
Smith stayed in the pavilion when the Australian team took to the field for South Africa's run chase on account of a sharp blow he copped to the helmet from an Anrich Nortje bouncer while batting.
He carried on to 27 before holing out, but the after-effects of that head knock appeared to keep him sidelined.
He also hurt his finger taking the catch that ended South Africa's first innings, which could have caused issues in the slips.
5. Renshaw's dream Test continues
Matt Renshaw couldn't have dreamt it better.
With shadows lengthening in Durban, and with South Africa's innings threatening to steady, Australia's freshly minted golden boy was thrown the ball.
South Africa captain Temba Bavuma had faced 18 balls for his one run and was set on seeing his team to stumps, but he was unable to contend with the drift and turn of Renshaw's part-time off spin, the Queenslander drawing the batter forward and having him caught at short leg by a diving Maddinson.
Renshaw was mobbed by his teammates as he celebrated his maiden Test wicket and Australia marched on to be six wickets from victory at stumps on day four.
That came after the southpaw had once again led Australia's efforts with the bat, peeling off 82 to add to the 190 he made in the first innings.
Remarkably, Renshaw remains the only player to pass 50 in the match.

Unlike the established haredi parties, the Haredi Public party has called for change within the ultra-Orthodox community and encouraged haredi enlistment in the IDF.
Though the party has been recently polling below the electoral threshold, Glantz said the Haredi Public party had been gaining momentum despite being new and having limited time to build support.
"People need this. There have been a lot of individuals waiting for a party like this for a very long time, myself included," she said.
Women's health among issues largely unaddressed by haredi community
Yaffa said women's health was among the major issues that had received insufficient attention within the haredi community.
She added that haredi Knesset representatives had not sufficiently addressed women's issues in the government's past term.
"I've checked that not even one party member went to one of the Knesset committees dealing with it, for all kinds of various reasons," she said.
Yaffa also argued that existing efforts to raise awareness of women's health issues were not adequately reaching the haredi community.
Another issue the two candidates spoke on addressing was providing support for the issues of financial pressure on haredi women, many of whom work to support their children and families while their husbands study in yeshivas.
Yaffa said women's participation in the workforce had increased significantly over the past two decades.
She said that haredi women continued to face lower average incomes than their non-haredi counterparts and that some experienced unfair employment conditions.
"Their average income is way lower than their secular counterparts, and some of them are being employed in really unfair conditions. There is exploitation. Very simple. And this is something that needs to be addressed," Yaffa said.
She added that women supporting large families often had little time or opportunity to advocate for their own rights.
"Someone has to look at the numbers and ask what's going on. And this is our job as women. These are our sisters and our daughters," she said.
Yaffa said she sought to promote haredi women's rights and opportunities, as well as improve access to health and education services.
Just being able to make them aware of their legal rights is also important, Yaffa said.
Glantz speaks on struggles faced by haredi women
Glantz spoke on the struggle haredi women faced by being required to balance providing for their families in the workforce with raising children.
"We have to recognize that there is a limit to every human ability, and we are pushing people to the max," Glantz said.
"These women are professionals. They have large families. They're hosting and cooking big meals. And we have to make sure that they have the support that they need, because otherwise we're going to deal with families collapsing because people have burnout, and that can't keep on happening," she added.
Glantz also spoke on the importance of ensuring that haredi schools teach core curriculum subjects, including math and English, with the state responsible for overseeing their implementation.
"There needs to be broad educational reform within the [haredi] community and, frankly, within the community at large. I think education reform needs to be a topic of this election, and more people need to be talking about it because it affects everybody," she said.
"We want to push a core curriculum of math and English so that people should be able to employ themselves and have that opportunity to support themselves in the future, should they choose to. We also think that there need to be other changes in the education system," Glantz said.
Regarding military service, Glantz raised concerns about the IDF's readiness to accommodate women.
She said she did not believe the military was currently a suitable environment for many women, while adding that further work was also needed to address the challenges facing men who enlist.
"I do not think that right now the army is a good place for many women in general," Glantz said.
"I also think that there's a lot of work that needs to be done for men that are drafting," she added.
Yaffa, Glantz as political pioneers in haredi sector
Ahead of the approaching October 27 elections, Yaffa said she believed that she and Glantz were pioneers in being the first women to run on a haredi party's Knesset slate.
"[Haredi] women have been around doing amazing, really incredible jobs, being in key positions and helping and contributing. But politically, we are the pioneers," she said.
"This is the first time that we are being invited to sit around the table and be part of the major political decisions," Yaffa added.

Jewish Agency Chief Almog: Israel can absorb one million new immigrants amid rising antisemitism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:28:58 UTC
04:28:58 KST

Israel has the capacity to absorb one million new immigrants, Jewish Agency chairman Maj.-Gen. (res.) Doron Almog said at a conference in Jerusalem, as senior government officials called for greater national preparations amid rising antisemitism and uncertainty facing Jewish communities abroad.
Speaking at the annual conference organized by Habayta, an Israeli nonprofit organization supporting immigrant communities, Almog said Israel’s economic strength and existing capabilities would allow it to accommodate a large influx of newcomers, provided the necessary resources were mobilized.
The conference, held at Jerusalem’s Cinema City under the theme “Absorbing the Next Million,” brought together government ministers, Jewish Agency officials, community leaders, and representatives of immigrant populations.
Almog also warned that Jewish communities worldwide needed to prepare for worsening security conditions, calling for emergency assistance networks and early-warning systems to protect communities facing potential threats.
Almog's goal: One million new Jewish immigrants
The goal of bringing one million Jews to Israel has been raised by Almog previously. In November 2023, he predicted that rising antisemitism could lead to one million immigrants arriving over the following years.
The ambition remains far beyond current immigration levels. According to Aliyah and Integration Ministry figures released in September, slightly more than 20,000 immigrants arrived in Israel during the Jewish year 5786, from over 100 countries. Russia, France, and the United States were the leading countries of origin.
In a separate interview published last month, Aliyah and Integration Ministry Director-General Dganit Sankar-Langa estimated that Israel would receive between 18,000 and 20,000 immigrants in 2026.
Smotrich: Aliyah is an economic opportunity
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich presented immigration as an opportunity to strengthen Israel’s economy.
“There is no better engine of economic growth than aliyah,” Smotrich said.
He argued that international investors continued to demonstrate confidence in Israel’s economy and said the situation confronting Jewish communities abroad created an opportunity to bring hundreds of thousands of new immigrants to the country.
Smotrich praised Aliyah and Integration Minister Ofir Sofer for his work and described immigration as both a national priority and an economic opportunity.
Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Minister Amichai Chikli raised concerns about the possibility of severe instability in countries with substantial Jewish communities, including scenarios involving civil conflict.
Chikli warned that Jews could be among the first populations affected by such developments and stressed the importance of preparing for emergencies.
He also identified language as a central obstacle facing immigrants after their arrival in Israel, pointing to the difficulties of navigating everyday life without sufficient command of Hebrew or English.
Beyond immigration: The challenge of integration
Much of the conference focused on what happens after immigrants arrive, particularly their integration into schools, workplaces, and local communities.
Roi Aviksis, deputy chairman of Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund (KKL-JNF), emphasized the role of education in strengthening immigrants’ connections to Israel. He also raised concerns about social isolation and the responsibility of Israeli society to welcome newcomers.
An education panel featured World Zionist Organization president Rabbi Doron Perez and Lali Deri, who previously directed a program helping French immigrants integrate into Israel’s education system. Deri’s son, Saadia, was killed during the war.
Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu addressed the importance of introducing immigrants to Israel’s history and national memory, citing the October 7 attacks and stories of civilian heroism.
Former Israeli ambassador to the US Michael Oren also participated in an English-language session, raising concerns about changing American public attitudes toward Israel.
Netanel Rotenberg and Yosef Hoter, co-directors of Habayta, called for a broader approach to immigration absorption, emphasizing long-term community support alongside government services.
“Israel must prepare today to absorb the next million immigrants,” they said in a joint statement.
They argued that successful absorption required building a sense of belonging, connecting immigrants with communities, and providing opportunities for social and economic integration.
“Our goal is for a new immigrant arriving in Israel to feel, within a short time, that they have come home,” they said.
According to Habayta, the organization operates through a nationwide network of more than 45 communities and provides support to approximately 100,000 immigrants in five languages.
The conference featured sessions in Hebrew, English, Russian, Spanish, and Portuguese and concluded with a tribute to immigration hosted by actor Daniel Stiopin, known for his role in the Israeli television series Checkout.

Iran's Araghchi offers to mediate Saudi-Houthi talks, calls for diplomatic end to hostilities

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi offered to help facilitate talks between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi terrorist group amid ongoing hostilities, according to a statement posted on Telegram following his phone call with Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan on Sunday.
Araghchi expressed concern over escalating tensions, warning that continued reliance on military action while disregarding diplomatic solutions would further complicate the situation, the statement said.
He also stressed that the region's ongoing crises could not be resolved militarily and offered Iran's assistance in initiating dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen to help reach a political solution.
The phone call came amid several days of Houthi missile and drone attacks targeting Saudi airports, which have severely disrupted air travel and prompted international airlines to suspend services. Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport is expected to remain closed until October 17, while some airlines have extended flight suspensions into 2027.
Authorities have extended the closure of Riyadh's international airport until Saturday, and airlines scrapped flights after continuing attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis emptied the skies over Saudi Arabia's capital.
Riyadh airport closure extended following deadly Houthi attacks
Operations at King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended to "allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport's facilities," the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement.
A Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) issued later in the day said the airport will remain closed until 2100 GMT on October 17.
The airport has been shut since an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Sunday, another attack killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.
Houthi attacks disrupt Saudi aviation, raising security concerns
The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi aviation in years, adding to pressures on an industry already grappling with conflict across the Middle East and with higher jet fuel prices that are eating into profits.
They have also raised worries over civil aviation becoming a target in armed conflict.
"This level of sustained intense attack on civil aviation is unprecedented," said Mark Zee, founder of OPSGROUP, a membership-based organization that provides aviation safety advice.
"I think this requires us to rethink how we view the current risk picture, and tread very carefully," he said.
Air traffic tracker Flightradar24 showed planes avoiding the city on Monday, though jets crossed Saudi airspace and landed at the country's top hub, Jeddah, on the west coast.
Cancellations across all Saudi airports reached 46.4%, aviation analytics firm Cirium said.
Airlines extend Saudi flight cancellations
Lufthansa Group has canceled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM has extended its suspension of services to and from the Saudi capital until the end of the month, Reuters reported.
Etihad Airways canceled flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam due to “regional disruption.” All flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh have been canceled until October 19, the airline said.
Qatar Airways said on Monday that it had temporarily suspended flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam due to the “current situation.”
Delta Air Lines postponed the launch of its Atlanta–Riyadh service, originally scheduled for October 23, until March 2027.

'We won't stop hiking': Upper Galilee council head demands IDF action after tragedy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:28:39 UTC
04:28:39 KST

Upper Galilee Regional Council head Asaf Langleben demanded in a Monday interview with 103FM that the IDF conduct searches in areas open to hikers following an incident in which an unexploded Hezbollah munition detonated and killed one person while injuring 24.
Despite the incident, Langleben told Ron Kofman and Aryeh Eldad during the interview that he had no intention of suspending hiking activities in the region, while he called on the military to draw lessons and prevent similar incidents from recurring.
"We have just evacuated the children from the area, and they are on their way to Kibbutz Yiftah to meet their families," Langleben said. "Ultimately, the Upper Galilee is one of the most beautiful tourist regions in the State of Israel, and the IDF has been fighting here for three years with a very large number of troops. The combination of those two things proved deadly today."
Despite the tragedy, the council head stressed that hiking activities in the area would continue.
"There is no other way. We need to educate our children through hiking, through a love of the land. That is what everyone has been doing since we returned to the North. I hope the IDF learns from this and draws the necessary lessons, and that this will be the last such incident."
'We don't immediately suspend activities'
Asked whether hikes would also take place within the council's jurisdiction on Tuesday, he replied, "I assume so. We don't immediately suspend activities."
"People have been hiking since the day we returned here. We live here, and our homes are on the border," he added.
Addressing the location of the tragedy, Langleben emphasized that the area was open to the public.
"This is not a closed military zone. It is located along a scenic route. We returned a year and a half ago, and many people have been hiking in our areas in the North."
Council head demands IDF action to prevent another tragedy
Langleben concluded by issuing a firm demand to the IDF.
"We are asking and demanding that the IDF draw the necessary lessons and make every effort to ensure that this incident does not happen again, even if it requires a very large number of soldiers to conduct searches in the area," the regional council head said.
"I don't know all the details of the incident, but beyond the behavior we expect of hikers, our responsibility is to prevent them from encountering unexploded ordnance. We will do everything to make sure this is the last such incident."

US hopes diesel deal can ‘soften’ Moscow on peace talks, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:25:24 UTC
04:25:24 KST

US hopes diesel deal can ‘soften’ Moscow on peace talks, sources say
NEW YORK/WASHINGTON/KYIV - President Donald Trump’s envoys told Ukrainian officials on Oct 9 that a deal to allow Russian diesel exports is part of a bid to draw Russia back to negotiations after the failure of previous efforts to launch sustained talks to end the war, three people familiar with the meeting told Reuters.
Trump’s Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner told the Ukrainians in a meeting in Miami that Russian President Vladimir Putin was not prepared to negotiate an end to his 4½-year-old war in Ukraine and that the deal announced last week could help restart trilateral talks, said two of the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
The third person said the US relayed to the Ukrainians that the diesel deal could help “soften” Moscow’s position in part because it “sends a signal that Trump is open to do things” with Russia.
That deal, under which Russia will supply more than 2.25 million barrels of diesel to US and global markets, has triggered a backlash from some US lawmakers, who say it will give Moscow cash to pursue its war without forcing Putin to make concessions to end the conflict.
On Oct 12, Trump publicly defended the deal, calling it “the right choice for the American people.”
Trump says the agreement will lower US energy prices, which have become a political headache for his Republican Party ahead of pivotal midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.
Trump also wanted the Ukrainians to stop striking Russian refineries, Kushner said in the meeting, reiterating that the administration had made that request several times, the two people said.
Trump has said Ukraine’s attacks are increasing global fuel prices, but most experts say the war in Iran is the main driver of the high costs.
“The idea was that the US could go back to Russia and say ‘See, the Ukrainians stopped striking and we gave you this deal. Now it’s your turn to do something,’” one of the people said.
Trump on Oct 11 announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine days after unveiling the diesel deal. The warring sides have not confirmed the ceasefire, though, and Russia struck energy targets inside Ukraine on Oct 12.
The Russian embassy in Washington and the presidential office in Kyiv did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A person close to the Kremlin said the diesel deal “is a way to bring Russia back” to the negotiations.
One of the people familiar with the meeting said the diesel agreement is just one part of a larger conversation about how to bring Ukraine and Russia back to the negotiating table and end the war. The meeting also touched on security guarantees for Ukraine, the person said, without elaborating.
Doubts about Moscow’s willingness to negotiate
Trump has repeatedly said Putin wants to reach a settlement to end the war - a claim he repeated on Oct 10. Ukrainian and European officials have expressed doubts that the Russian leader is willing to end the military campaign soon.
The envoys’ comment that Putin is not prepared to end his war suggests that Trump’s view is not uniformly held within the administration.
Some experts have said the diesel agreement will do little to lower prices in the US. The additional amount provided to the market will be less than a day’s supply for the US transport sector alone.
The Ukrainian officials attending the meeting were sceptical of the US approach, which they see as using business deals to appease Russia, the two people briefed and one person in the meeting said.
The Trump administration has previously tried to entice Putin, including through sanctions relief proposals as well as potential mineral deals. Neither has substantially changed Russia’s core demands or persuaded it to accept a comprehensive ceasefire agreement.
The person close to the Kremlin said Putin will only return to the table when “he gets the remaining 11% of Donbas, which he can present domestically as victory.”
Ukraine has said it will not hand any more territory to Russia, but that freezing the conflict on the existing battle lines could be the basis for a peace deal.
No threat to withhold US support for Kyiv
In the Miami meeting, Kushner and Witkoff stressed to the Ukrainian officials “all that the US has done for Ukraine,” one of the people said, including providing military and intelligence support to its forces.
The Americans did not threaten to cut off that support if Ukraine did not agree to stop striking Russian refineries, the two people briefed and the person in the meeting said.
The meeting in Miami, which also included European officials and virtual appearances by representatives from the World Bank, came after Witkoff and Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv in September. Witkoff said then that the sides had created “new momentum” and that a new round of talks could soon begin.
The World Bank declined to comment.
Tensions between the US and Ukraine have spiked since the announcement of the US-Russia diesel deal. Zelenskiy called it a “weak decision” by the US and a “gift to Putin.” Trump said on Saturday that Zelenskiy “could have settled this war many times” and Ukrainians needed to “get a new president.”
Part of the meeting in Miami, which spanned several hours, focused on reconstruction funds for Ukraine and a need for Kyiv to formalize plans for investment in the country, the people briefed on the meeting said.
The Ukrainians left the meeting without agreeing to anything formally, but signalled that they would be willing to agree to an energy ceasefire so long as Russia did. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

‘Distressing events’: Flydubai's 12-day-late email skips pilot's attempt to crash plane
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:21:43 UTC
04:21:43 KST

Twelve days after 174 passengers survived an attempt by a flydubai pilot to hijack and crash their aircraft, the airline finally contacted them. Its message made no mention of the attempted hijacking, the pilot responsible or the extraordinary danger the passengers had faced. Instead, it described the ordeal as "distressing events," expressed relief that the passengers had reached Tel Aviv safely aboard a replacement aircraft and offered contact details for anyone with "questions or concerns."
The email, sent Monday to passengers aboard flight FZ 1073, also contained no reference to financial compensation for the ordeal.
For passengers who survived an incident that could have ended in a mass-casualty disaster, the airline's carefully worded message was hardly the acknowledgment some had been waiting for.
The flight had been hijacked by Omani pilot Hamam al-Hamami, who, according to prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates, subsequently admitted intending to crash the aircraft at Ben Gurion Airport. The passengers survived thanks to the actions of several people aboard and another pilot, who helped prevent the disaster.
Yet almost two weeks later, the airline's first direct communication with the passengers focused not on what happened aboard its aircraft, but on its efforts to bring them home.
‘We are relieved you arrived safely’
"We are writing to you directly because you were aboard our aircraft on flight FZ 1073," the airline said in the email.
"We understand that the events surrounding the flight were distressing for the passengers on board."
The message continued with assurances that passenger safety, well-being and peace of mind remained top priorities.
"While we are relieved that we were able to assist with your safe arrival in Tel Aviv aboard our replacement aircraft, we understand that you may have questions or concerns following the events surrounding the flight," flydubai wrote.
"We wish to reassure you that flydubai is fully committed to supporting you."
The wording made no explicit reference to the attempted crash, the actions of the airline's pilot or the circumstances that had forced the original aircraft to land in Saudi Arabia.
Instead, the email emphasized the replacement flight arranged by flydubai, presenting the passengers' eventual safe arrival as the central point of its communication.
The airline did offer two channels for assistance.
Passengers were invited to contact a dedicated support address, [email protected], which the company said had been established exclusively for them.
Flydubai also offered access to independent professional support for passengers experiencing difficulties obtaining appropriate assistance through their regular health care providers.
"If you have any questions or require assistance, please contact our dedicated support team using the details provided above, and a member of our team will be happy to assist," the message concluded.
There was no mention of whether the airline intended to compensate passengers financially.
‘An incident that only by a miracle did not kill us’
One passenger who received the email sharply criticized the airline's handling of the aftermath, describing both the lengthy silence and the contents of the message as unacceptable.
"Flydubai chose to remain silent for far too long after an incident that only by a miracle did not result in our deaths, and that was caused by appalling negligence on the company's part," the passenger told ynet.
The passenger also rejected reports suggesting that financial compensation had been arranged for those aboard.
"The stories about financial compensation are an urban legend that never materialized," he said.
"No financial compensation was offered, and it's astonishing how a false report managed to spread so widely."
He questioned why the airline had waited nearly two weeks to make contact and suggested that the carefully formulated message may have been prompted by legal considerations.
"It seems the email we received followed legal advice," he said. "The contents of the message are a disgrace to the company."
Pilot allegedly admitted planning to crash at Ben Gurion Airport
The understated wording of the airline's message stands in stark contrast to details that have emerged from the investigation into the attempted attack.
According to the prosecution in the United Arab Emirates, al-Hamami admitted during questioning that he intended to crash the passenger aircraft at Ben Gurion Airport.
Prosecutors also said he had previously flown to Israel twice and had undergone radicalization while living in Australia, where he attended a mosque in Melbourne.
According to the prosecution's account, al-Hamami was inspired by the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in the United States when he decided to pursue a career in aviation.
Britain's Daily Telegraph previously reported that he had received his professional pilot training at L3 Airline Academy, one of the United Kingdom's major aviation training institutions.
The incident also triggered Israel's military procedures for responding to the hijacking of a civilian aircraft.
The emergency transponder code 7500, used to signal an aircraft hijacking, was activated during the flydubai flight.
The IDF's response protocol for such incidents, known as "World Trade," provides for fighter aircraft to intervene in a hijacking, potentially escorting an aircraft to a secure landing or, in extreme circumstances, shooting it down to prevent a larger catastrophe.
The name refers to the World Trade Center, the target of the September 11 attacks.
The flydubai aircraft ultimately landed in Saudi Arabia, where its tail was damaged, before the passengers were brought back to Israel on another plane.
Against that background, the first email passengers received from the airline offered a strikingly restrained account of their experience: an acknowledgment that the flight had been distressing, a reminder that flydubai had arranged their safe return and an invitation to get in touch if they had questions.
For at least one of those who survived, that response fell far short of addressing what had happened aboard the aircraft or what the airline intended to do about it.

British tanker completes fourteen missions in Saudi deployment
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:15:48 BST
04:15:48 KST

A Royal Air Force Voyager sent to Saudi Arabia to provide air-to-air refuelling has already flown fourteen operational missions, alongside air defence also deployed by Britain, the Prime Minister told the House of Commons.
Andy Burnham set out the deployment in a statement on the United Nations General Assembly and the international meetings that followed it, describing the Middle East as one of the subjects he had discussed with President Trump in New York.
He said: “I confirmed Britain’s decision to send air defence and a Voyager aircraft to Saudi Arabia to provide air to air refuelling support. I can confirm today it has already completed 14 operational missions. This support is needed to protect civilians. I condemn the appalling attacks on the King Khalid International Airport. We will continue to stand with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis.”
The deployment was agreed in late September in response to a Saudi request, with the Prime Minister acting on the advice of the Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, and the Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband. Mr Burnham said then that Britain was acting to secure the interests of this country and the wider region, and that pathways needed to be kept open. Saudi Arabia was reported to be running low on interceptor stocks as Houthi ballistic missile and drone attacks, which began on 8 September, continued.
The attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh came on 8 October, when a Houthi ballistic missile killed three people, among them a Saudia pilot, Captain Hamoud Ali Alkalthami, and wounded dozens more, several of them foreign nationals. A Saudia aircraft was damaged. Operations at the airport have since resumed.
Attacks on Abha and King Khalid airports in early October killed three civilians and injured thirty-six, according to the Saudi civil aviation authority, and strikes on Jazan and Najran airports wounded at least three. The coalition said on 18 September that it had intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at King Khalid, and an explosion was heard near the airport the following day with smoke rising from a fuel storage area.
Pakistan and Turkey have agreed to deploy forces under mutual defence arrangements signed with Saudi Arabia earlier this year, and a Pakistani foreign ministry spokesman has said his country now has a substantial number of forces and resources in Riyadh, acting in defence of Saudi territory without crossing into Houthi-held areas.
Voyager is the Royal Air Force’s only air-to-air refuelling aircraft and also carries the strategic air transport role, flying in two configurations, the KC Mk 2 with two underwing pods for fast jets and the KC Mk 3 with an additional centreline hose for larger aircraft.

Labor and Coalition deny interference in AI inquiry after David Pocock raises 'stitch-up' concerns
In short:
Labor and the Coalition have rejected concerns about undue interference in a parliamentary AI inquiry after the prime minister's office reviewed draft recommendations.
The bipartisan proposals include independent safety checks on AI companies, greater access for security agencies and a review of copyright laws.
What's next?
The committee will deliver its final report in November.
Labor and the Coalition have denied there was "interference" in a raft of recommendations from an artificial intelligence inquiry after accusations of a major party "stitch-up".
A joint committee on AI has recommended Australia require AI companies to submit to independent safety checks, reserve computing power for local use and give security agencies early access to new models.
The committee has endorsed investment in data centres, backed by national standards covering resource use, additional electricity generation and community consultation.
It has also urged a review of Australia's copyright settings, which would be at odds with creative groups seeking stronger enforcement of existing protections rather than changes to accommodate the AI industry.
The federal government has signalled it hopes to introduce legislation outlining national standards for data centres and frontier AI models by the end of this year and pass the laws through parliament in early 2027.
Pocock warns of 'major party stitch-ups'
ACT independent Senator David Pocock has raised concerns an adviser to Anthony Albanese "pre-vetted" the committee's "early advice" letter before it was sent to the prime minister.
Senator Pocock said he respected the committee process and the need to work in a "multi-partisan way" but was unhappy to discover there were "mark-ups" from Mr Albanese's office on a draft of the document.
"We've seen enough major party stitch ups,"
he said.
"Regaining the community's trust, especially on the issue of AI, requires robust debate and committee work."
Labor MP Jo Briskey, who is the committee chair, said she had engaged with the prime minister's office ahead of finalising the early advice.
"It's been a process by which we are seeking advice and making sure that this is working across the board," she said.
"This is an indication to the government on where the committee is heading, where we think there is some really important [consensus] to just get on with the job."
Ms Briskey said the inquiry's final report, due in November, was not predetermined and there was "more work to do".
Duniam says 'no interference' in committee work
Liberal Senator Jonno Duniam, who also consulted with the Coalition on the letter, is the deputy chair and said the collaborative approach of the committee was an example of parliament "working well".
"There has been no guidance, no interference, there has been a lot of discussion, a lot of consultation," he said.
Senator Duniam said Australia had a "very small" window to make the most of AI.
"If we wait, if we dither, if we do nothing, then of course that opportunity will sail by our country and our adversaries will be taking advantage of that opportunity at our expense."
Regarding copyright, Senator Duniam said the committee wanted the issue resolved in the "interests" of creatives and rights holders.
"At the moment you've got a situation where data, copyright, intellectual property, whatever form it comes in is currently being used by offshore models. It's being harvested to train models offshore," he said.
"And do you know how much our copyright holders are getting as a result? One hundred per cent of nothing."
Push for independent experts inside AI companies
The committee has recommended the government put independent experts inside leading AI companies that would have access to their systems and a duty to report safety findings and incidents to government.
Security agencies like the Australian Signals Directorate should receive early access to new models as a condition of arrangements allowing frontier AI labs to train them in Australia.
The government has been urged to immediately review protections used across its data repositories, particularly those holding sensitive and national security information.
It has also been advised to monitor the risk of AI helping to develop biological weapons.
Alongside those safeguards, the committee has questioned whether existing copyright rules were delivering for Australian creators or supporting local AI development.
Copyright rules under scrutiny
The committee noted current copyright arrangements were "not facilitating" licensing deals for Australian culture and content.
"The status quo sees the work of Australian artists, musicians and media outlets used overseas without adequate control or payment," the letter said.
They also acknowledged frontier AI labs had indicated existing copyright settings were a "barrier" to undertaking training in Australia.
The committee recommended the government "examine" current copyright settings and prioritise ensuring that Australian creators "retain control over how their works are used, that they are paid, and that AI systems reflect Australian values and culture".
But Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) chief executive Annabelle Herd told the inquiry last week that existing licensing systems could support AI training without rewriting copyright protections to suit foreign companies.
"They should come to the negotiating table, not to the prime minister's office," she said.
OpenAI breach drives calls for oversight
Last month it was revealed OpenAI's experimental models accessed government websites without authorisation during training, including a Services Australia portal hosting Medicare statistics.
The letter from the committee said the OpenAI breach demonstrated the need for "appropriate and robust safeguards" to protect Australian data and those who own and use it.
It was recommended the safeguards apply to frontier AI developers deploying models and agents in Australia, ensuring there was "proper and transparent accountability and oversight mechanisms" along with "well-established practices to deal with incidents that may occur in the future".
Frontier labs should also be required to monitor and report incidents to the government in a "timely manner".
OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon last week said the company would "support a framework on mandatory disclosures".
Australia cannot simply be 'consumer' of foreign AI
It was recommended the government establish an ongoing parliamentary joint standing committee to monitor AI, which could conduct "rapid reviews" of new regulation when required.
This committee would also be reported to at "regular intervals" on serious events and incidents, including cyber incidents involving AI, unintended actions of agents and models as well as "misuse" of the technology.
The letter recommended reserving a share of computing capacity for national security and university research, with health and social services also among the potential beneficiaries.
"The overarching objective should be to ensure that Australia is not merely a consumer of AI technologies developed elsewhere, but a trusted, competitive and strategically capable participant in the global AI industry," the letter said.

‘Pure Kafka’: Israeli scientist jailed in Russia over $25 in Navalny donations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:09:13 UTC
04:09:13 KST

Russian scientist Sofia Rosenfeld, who also holds Israeli citizenship, has been sentenced to three and a half years in prison by Moscow's Gagarinsky District Court for financing an "extremist organization." The two money transfers cited in the indictment amounted to 1,000 rubles each, worth approximately $12 to $14, and were made to the Anti-Corruption Foundation established by Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, who died in a Russian prison in February 2024. In an interview with Ynet, her father, Boris Rosenfeld, described the proceedings against his daughter and his fears about what awaits her.
Rosenfeld, 50, is a senior researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences. She immigrated to Israel with her family in 1990, at the age of 14, but returned to Moscow about a year and a half later to continue her studies in Russia. She built her professional career there while retaining her Israeli citizenship and maintaining close ties with her family. According to her father, she visited Israel every year.
"Every time she returned to Russia, I was worried and warned her, but she didn't listen to me," Boris Rosenfeld said.
According to her father, the donation was made in 2021, when Navalny's organization was still operating legally. She donated a symbolic amount of no more than 80 shekels. The organization was subsequently outlawed while Sofia was participating in a research expedition to the Arctic and was unaware of the change.
Rosenfeld maintained that she was cut off from the outside world during the expedition when the transfers were made from her account. When she returned to Moscow later in 2021, she canceled the standing payment order, but the two payments had already gone through.
For four years, nothing happened. "Nobody contacted her," her father said.
Proceedings against her began only in late 2025. An indictment was filed in December, after she returned from Israel, but she remained free under restrictions prohibiting her from traveling or leaving Moscow. "I warned her not to return to Russia," Boris Rosenfeld recalled. "But there were no particular warning signs. Nothing had happened for four years."
According to her father, Sofia had hoped to receive a fine or community service. Instead, she was taken directly from the courtroom to prison, where she has been held since Wednesday.
Sentenced on October 7
The family has almost no way of contacting her. They cannot speak to her, and correspondence is possible only through letters sent via the Russian prison service. Her father wrote a short letter, but he said censorship made it impossible to convey "any meaningful message." Sofia has not replied.
Rosenfeld was reluctant to attribute the sentence to antisemitism or anti-Israeli sentiment, although he did not rule out the possibility.
"I don't know whether there's antisemitism or anti-Israeli sentiment behind this sentence. Everyone has that concern," he said. "I don't think there's a strong chance it was because of antisemitism, but who really knows?"
He suggested that Russia might be seeking to detain Israelis as leverage in negotiations over a possible deal. "It's a black box over there," he added.
He also addressed the timing of the sentencing, which took place on October 7, calling it "a symbolic sentence." He summed up the entire ordeal in a single sentence: "This whole process is pure Kafka."
Her father contacted the Israeli Foreign Ministry and was promised that the Israeli consul in Moscow would request permission to visit her in prison. The Foreign Ministry said it "is in contact with the family and is working with the Russian authorities to provide consular assistance."
Rosenfeld's imprisonment comes amid a widening wave of political persecution in Russia. According to monitoring by Mediazona and The Insider, approximately 220 sentences have been handed down in recent years over donations to Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation, including about 24 prison terms ranging from four months to four years.
According to Mediazona, this is only the third case in Russia in which a woman has been sentenced to prison for donating to a Navalny organization, and only the second case in which a person holding Israeli citizenship has received a prison sentence in a political case in Russia following proceedings conducted in their presence.
The first was Yegor Grafov, 26, who was sentenced in May to 12 years in prison for throwing a Molotov cocktail at the headquarters of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) in Moscow.

Billions in the bin as economy struggles with true cost of food waste
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:07:35 UTC
04:07:35 KST

Food waste costing Australian businesses and the economy billions
In short:
Australia wastes about 7.6 million tonnes of food each year, costing the economy more than $36 billion.
Less than a quarter of businesses regularly inspect their food waste, and operational methods mean it can go unnoticed.
The federal government has committed to halving food waste by 2030, but some experts are concerned about progress.
When Karl Riseborough realised how much food went to waste each week at his Sydney pub and brewery, he was shocked.
Grain left over from the beer-making process was thrown out, as well as food waste from the kitchen.
What surprised him most was the volume of waste on top of the spent grain.
"The food scraps coming back, the plate waste, the kitchen prep waste … you don't really notice when it was all going straight into the bin," Mr Riseborough said.
Food waste expert Belinda Chellingworth said many traders had no idea how much waste they were generating, or how much it was affecting their bottom line.
Every year about 7.6 million tonnes of food is wasted in Australia at a cost of more than $36 billion to the economy.
Of that wasted food, 70 per cent is edible and there are critical knock-on effects for landfill management, food security and the climate.
With the support of Ms Chellingworth, who happily calls herself a "garbologist", Mr Riseborough has stopped throwing away 50 kilograms of spent grain from each batch of beer he brews.
"Now I have regular users who come and collect it once I've brewed and use it for the benefit of their gardens or their animals," Mr Riseborough said.
"We had two 240-litre bins that were getting collected each week. We're now down to one bin collected each fortnight."
He said that saved him about $5,000 a year.
Cumulative effect not realised
Australia's hospitality sector wastes 1.2 million tonnes of food each year, according to the Sustainable Restaurant Association.
The economic impact of food waste in the food service sector is about $6.4 billion, averaging about $66,000 annually per business.
Ms Chellingworth said less than a quarter of businesses regularly inspected their food waste.
"Typically, many businesses, if they've got food left over at the end of their operations or the end of the day, then it will be landfilled," she said.
"For many businesses, and particularly large businesses, the cost of food waste across their operations isn't fully realised because they incur it multiple times, but it's not obvious."
For example, over-ordering food is a cost to the kitchen. If it is not sold, that is a revenue cost, and then whatever goes into the bin also involves a cost for collection.
"So they're paying for it multiple times, but they're different departments, different cost centres, and it's often not added together, so they don't understand the full cost across the whole business," Ms Chellingworth said.
She said landfill capacity was reaching critical levels in many areas.
Some tips in Perth are set to run out of space in two years and sites in New South Wales are set to reach capacity in four years.
Victoria's capacity is expected to be reached in the next 10 years.
Government target 'unachievable'
To combat the economic and environmental impacts of food waste, the federal government has committed to halving food waste by 2030.
But UNSW food and health professor Johannes le Coutre does not believe the plan is on track.
"I'm not sure if that's attainable or achievable with the current landscape," he said.
"In Australia we have a unique situation in that we are dealing with a big distance and that even in the food industry a lot of value-added manufacturing occurs overseas."
In a statement to the ABC, a spokesperson for the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water said: "The Australian Government is working with jurisdictions and industry to drive behaviour change and expand organics recycling capacity.
"This includes investing $37 million into new and upgraded organics recycling infrastructure, $30 million to set up the End Food Waste Cooperative Research Centre to research food waste interventions, [and] $10 million on the Great Unwaste Campaign to help Australians reduce food waste at home."
Alongside food waste, Professor le Coutre said about 3.5 million households were experiencing food shortages.
"If we address the food waste problem, we might be able to help that," he said.
"We are a modern country, a modern economy … we need to raise awareness, we need to improve technology, and we need to improve policy."
Ms Chellingworth said some businesses were reluctant to donate excess food due to common misunderstandings.
"It's not widely understood or well-known, but every Australian state and territory has laws in place to protect food donors, provided that certain conditions are met when the food exchanges hands," she said.
"The food needs to be edible when it's donated, any instructions on how to refrigerate it or prepare it afterwards need to be provided, it must be free … and it needs to go to a registered organisation."
Food waste a global issue
Excessive food waste is a global concern and will be a focus at the United Nations Climate Change Conference, COP31, in Türkiye next month.
Professor le Coutre said the impact of food waste on the climate could not be underestimated.
"A lot of greenhouse gas emissions are based on agricultural, industrialised activities on our planet — that is something which needs to be improved," he said.
"Livestock management can be improved in order to lower greenhouse gas emissions and, if we work on that end, we will have a chance as well to improve food security, improve food systems, and lower food waste."
Ms Chellingworth said there were examples abroad that Australia could take inspiration from.
"France has laws that mean that supermarkets over a certain size must donate edible food," she said.
"In the Netherlands, they've had a long-running food waste campaign for all of their citizens to help them understand how they can reduce food waste at home, as well.
"Stronger mandates for food rescue and food donation … would start to help alleviate the pressure that a lot of households are feeling with cost of living and food insecurity as well."

Britain calls in industry for fleet of drone submarines
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:03:56 BST
04:03:56 KST

The Royal Navy has opened preliminary market engagement for the Type 93 extra-large uncrewed underwater vehicle and the AUKUS Signature Payload Programme, inviting companies to register interest before any requirement is set, according to a notice published on Find a Tender at ten past twelve on Monday.
“The Royal Navy seeks to improve its understanding of the market and wider ecosystem for Extra-Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (XLUUV) platforms, associated payloads, and enabling functions,” it says. “This activity supports the development of the Type 93 capability and the Royal Navy’s commitments under the AUKUS Pillar II Signature Project.”
Registrations are sought from “XLUUV platform providers, payload providers, relevant technology and software suppliers including Autonomy, AI and Mission Management Systems, integrators, through-life support providers, and other relevant suppliers.” Those who come forward may be invited to collaborative workshops, one to one meetings, industry days and written requests for information, and small and medium-sized enterprises are flagged as particularly suitable.
“The Royal Navy is initially considering platforms approximately 2 metres in diameter and 12 metres in length, however organisations offering platforms of other dimensions are also encouraged to register,” the notice says, adding that it “should not be considered as a commitment from the Royal Navy to progress with any future procurement activities.”
XV Excalibur, the uncrewed submarine Britain already operates, is twelve metres long, two metres across and displaces nineteen tonnes. It was unveiled at Devonport in May last year, as this publication reported at the time, having been built by MSubs of Plymouth under the three-year Project Cetus, for which the Ministry of Defence awarded a £15.4 million contract in December 2022. It joined the Fleet Experimentation Squadron as a demonstrator with no operational role.
The Royal Navy controlled Excalibur in home waters from an operating centre in Australia during Talisman Sabre in July 2025, the first British and Australian demonstration of XLUUV interoperability under AUKUS Pillar II. It carried out the first underwater operation of a quantum optical atomic clock that November and transferred to Royal Navy ownership in December. In June the Submarine Delivery Agency awarded MSubs a further £6.7 million for trials and evaluation running to May 2028, work intended to move the programme towards functional payloads.
On 13 September, Excalibur fired an American Mark 48 exercise torpedo at the British Underwater Test and Evaluation Centre in Scotland. Britain and the United States described it as the first time either country had launched a heavyweight torpedo from an uncrewed vessel, carried out under Project Broadsword and Trial Iron, both part of AUKUS Pillar II.
The Type 93 designation first appeared in February last year, in Project CABOT documents setting out a persistent wide area anti-submarine search capability built around the Type 92 Sloop, an uncrewed surface vessel, and the Type 93 Chariot, described then as a drone submarine. Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, confirmed in July that the Defence Investment Plan had announced Type 92 uncrewed underwater sensing platforms and Type 93 extra-large uncrewed underwater vessels as part of the Atlantic Bastion programme, adding that the number of platforms to be procured and their construction schedules had not yet been determined.
He has also told Parliament that the Hybrid Navy will take at least £1.5 billion over four years, and that by 2030 the aim is to have the first large autonomous vessels in service, among them a prototype uncrewed missile platform and extra-large uncrewed underwater vessels carrying payloads developed through AUKUS.
The notice states that the programme “directly aligns with the Strategic Defence Review (SDR), Defence Investment Plan (DIP) and AUKUS Pillar II priorities, supporting the transition to a Hybrid Navy through the integration of autonomous and uncrewed maritime capabilities.”
