‘Kids went flying, fell into the bushes’: Wounded teen recounts blast as classmates rushed to help
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:01:29 UTC
04:01:29 KST

The Education Ministry announced Monday that school trips near the Lebanese border and in the northern Golan Heights would be suspended for 48 hours following an explosion that killed a 14-year-old student and injured 23 others during an excursion in the Upper Galilee. Education Minister Yoav Kisch said the trip and its route had been approved in advance but that safety procedures would now be reassessed.
The announcement came as 14-year-old Eitan Masaouri, who was wounded by shrapnel in his neck, described the terrifying moments of the explosion to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a visit to Rambam Medical Center in Haifa.
"We stopped to eat, and one of the students noticed something that could be unscrewed. He unscrewed it, and then it exploded," Masaouri recalled.
"Kids went flying and fell into the bushes. There were about two seconds of shock, and then someone told me I was bleeding too."
Netanyahu noted that Masaouri had remained conscious throughout the incident.
"I realized blood was coming from my neck, so I took off my shirt," the teenager continued. "I saw a friend lying on the ground. He was bleeding from his leg and head, and I wanted to help him. Then we sent our location."
The explosion occurred during an annual school trip by students from the ORT Ma'alot-Tarshiha religious high school near Mitzpe Pe'er, close to Israel's northern border.
One student was killed, three were seriously wounded, 10 sustained moderate injuries and another 10 were lightly hurt.
Security officials increasingly believe the explosion was caused by an old unexploded Hezbollah cluster munition. According to earlier witness accounts, a group of students found the device, handled it and posed for photographs before it detonated.
Education minister orders 48-hour suspension of school trips
Speaking at Rambam Medical Center hours after the explosion, Kisch said the circumstances of the disaster would be thoroughly investigated.
"We will examine in depth all the implications of what happened on the ground," he said.
The minister praised the students' response to the emergency, saying they had taken an active role in helping their injured classmates.
"The students managed the incident," Kisch said. "There were children there from seventh through ninth grade. Together with Magen David Adom, they helped speed up the evacuation to hospitals."
He emphasized that the excursion had received official authorization.
"According to the preliminary examination, the trip was approved by the Education Ministry's situation room. The route and everything else had been approved in advance, and hiking there was permitted."
Nevertheless, Kisch announced an immediate suspension of school excursions in the northern border region for 48 hours to allow officials to reassess the safety of the routes.
"Trips that were planned will be moved to other locations," he said.
The minister stressed that the existing approval policy had been based on IDF safety guidelines.
"These guidelines were in place. I'm not blaming anyone," he said. "There is unexploded ordnance that can detonate. Extra caution is needed, just as people know they must be careful around scorpions."
Kisch said the areas had undergone examinations involving the IDF, the Jewish National Fund and the Home Front Command, but acknowledged the possibility that the students had strayed from the designated trail.
"The students may have crossed beyond the trail," he said, emphasizing that this had not yet been established.
"The disaster requires us to stop and examine everything again. We will speak with the IDF and ask about these specific areas. The military will conduct its examination, we will conduct ours, and then we will reach conclusions."
Trips on October 13 and 14 rerouted
Following Kisch's announcement, the Education Ministry issued detailed instructions to schools and educational institutions.
The ministry said all excursions scheduled for October 13 and 14 in northern confrontation-line communities and the northern Golan Heights would be redirected to alternative routes.
Groups already hiking in those areas were instructed to leave their trails and move to alternative destinations in coordination with the ministry's trip coordination center.
School trips elsewhere in Israel will proceed as scheduled.
The ministry also reiterated nationwide safety instructions concerning unexploded ordnance, stressing the importance of avoiding suspicious objects and military remnants.
Any requests to change a route or obtain an exemption from the temporary restrictions must be reviewed by the ministry's trip coordination center.
In the coming days, the ministry will work with the military and other relevant authorities to reassess the procedures used to approve educational activities in areas affected by the war.
The ministry expressed condolences to the family of the student who was killed and wished the injured a speedy recovery.
It also said emergency procedures had been activated immediately after the explosion, including the convening of a special situation room led by Kisch and the ministry's director-general.
Students helped stop their friends' bleeding
Emergency responders described an exceptionally difficult scene in which injured students helped their classmates even while struggling with their own wounds.
Magen David Adom emergency medical technician David Radko, who was among the first responders to reach the site, said the injured were scattered along the trail.
"I arrived first on an MDA motorcycle and immediately saw the scale of the incident," he recalled.
"The wounded were scattered along the route. Some were holding their injured friends and trying to help them. Farther along the route, I saw the more seriously wounded students."
Radko began triaging the injured and attempting to stop severe bleeding.
Despite the chaos, he said the students demonstrated remarkable composure and cooperation.
"Some had even applied tourniquets to their friends to stop the bleeding. I gave them instructions on how to help, and they listened and followed them," he said.
"It was an extremely difficult and complex scene. Seeing injured children in that condition is never easy."
MDA paramedic Orly Ben Simon described the desperate efforts to save the 14-year-old boy who died.
"There was tremendous commotion and shouting," she said.
"Among the cries for help, we identified several casualties with injuries of varying severity, including a 14-year-old boy who was unconscious and in critical condition."
Paramedics immediately began prolonged resuscitation efforts, but his injuries proved fatal.
"Unfortunately, his injuries were critical, and we had to pronounce him dead at the scene," Ben Simon said.
The wounded were evacuated to Rambam Medical Center in Haifa, Ziv Medical Center in Safed and Galilee Medical Center in Nahariya.
The investigation now faces two central questions: how an unexploded munition remained accessible along a school hiking route near the Lebanese border, and whether the group stayed within the route that had been authorized.
For now, the Education Ministry's temporary restrictions remain in place while the military and civilian authorities reassess the safety of school excursions in the north.

Australian engineer speaks after being freed from Baghdad jail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:54:37 UTC

Australian engineer Robert Pether speaks after being freed from Baghdad jail
In short:
Robert Pether has spoken for the first time since being allowed to leave Iraq, ending a five-year ordeal including time in a Baghdad prison.
The Australian engineer paid tribute to his family's efforts to free him.
Mr Pether was arrested in 2021 and later found guilty of what his family says were trumped-up fraud charges.
Australian engineer Robert Pether has paid an emotional tribute to his family for maintaining their fight for his freedom, moments after touching down in the Irish capital Dublin.
Mr Pether was finally allowed to leave Iraq on Monday, after an ordeal lasting more than five years, most of which was behind bars in a Baghdad jail.
He was arrested in 2021 along with an Egyptian colleague, and later found guilty by an Iraqi court of what his family long argued were trumped-up fraud charges relating to his involvement as a contractor working on the massive Central Bank of Iraq headquarters construction project.
His jail sentence came with a massive fine, worth $16 million.
Mr Pether, 51, was released from jail in June last year, but was banned from leaving Iraq until this week.
Speaking to the media at Dublin Airport, and fighting back tears shortly after his reunion with his family, who are based in Ireland, Mr Pether said his wife and children had "lived this every single day with me".
"Our children lost years with their dad. They watched their mum fight every day to try and bring me home," he said.
"They grew up with uncertainty, fear and circumstances that no child should ever have to carry.
"I am so thankful for my wife Desree, for always fighting for me, while at the same time holding our family together, all while dealing with a situation that took an enormous toll on her too."
Mr Pether said his focus was on his family, even though he appreciated there would be many questions about his circumstances.
"There will be time to talk about what happened, why it happened, who was responsible and why nobody should ever be allowed to do this to another person or another family again," Mr Pether said.
"But today, more than anything, I want to talk about the people who carried us through it."
'We were innocent'
Mr Pether's wife Desree had been his most vocal advocate, campaigning for years for his release.
She had repeatedly raised concerns about his physical and mental health behind bars, and flagged serious flaws in his prosecution — particularly arguing he was forced to sign a confession, written in Arabic, without knowing what the document said.
In 2021, the United Nations investigated the situation facing Mr Pether and his Egyptian colleague, Khalid Zaghloul, and said the pair had been subjected to "acts of torture and ill treatment".
"Today I don't want to spend too much time talking about courts or governments or everything that was done to us," Mr Pether said in Dublin.
"I do need to say something about the injustice of what happened, because coming home today should never be mistaken for that injustice somehow having been corrected.
"It wasn't. Not even close."
He said the convictions against him and Mr Zaghloul had not be overturned, and neither man "has been exonerated".
"We were innocent when we were taken on 7th April 2021, and we remain innocent today," Mr Pether said.
"I was released from prison hours away from death, my body shutting down, after months of critical illness and excruciating pain, but I remained trapped in Iraq.
"I didn't have my passport, visa or identity documents, and I had no ability to move around freely or safely, leave the country or even go to a hospital."
'Thank you seems completely inadequate'
Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong had welcomed Mr Pether's release earlier in the day, and said she spoke to him before he left Baghdad.
"I know this has taken a real toll on him and his family," she said in Canberra.
Ireland's Taoiseach, or prime minister, Micheál Martin posted on social media Mr Pether's release would "come as a great relief" and said he appreciated "the Iraqi Government responding to the calls for his release from both Ireland and Australia".
Ms Pether had accused the Australian government, under prime ministers Scott Morrison and Anthony Albanese, of dragging their feet in pushing for his release, saying at times the family felt abandoned by their home country.
She turned to the Irish government for help, despite the fact Mr Pether does not share the Irish citizenship his wife and children have.
"One of the things this experience has taught me is that governments are ultimately made up of people," Mr Pether said.
"And sometimes an individual deciding to care, to pick up a telephone, to keep asking a question or simply refusing to give up can change the course of somebody else's life.
"There are some people who went so far beyond anything we could ever have asked of them that saying thank you seems completely inadequate."

Tyyne Karjalainen, a researcher at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs, said that Ukraine could face more severe consequences if the ceasefire broke down, including the risk of Washington withdrawing security support.

Nevertheless, the commentary noted that expanding the ceasefire from oil refineries to all energy infrastructure could help ease Ukrainian civilians' suffering during the approaching winter.
Such a move could pave the way for a broader ceasefire, it suggested, although a negotiated settlement to the conflict remained a distant prospect. ■

ESafety says it can't prevent Australians from seeing execution live stream
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:48:57 UTC
03:48:57 KST

eSafety office says it cannot prevent Australians seeing execution live stream
In short:
The office of eSafety says it does not have the power to proactively block the live streaming of a US execution from being available in Australia.
It says online services have the responsibility to protect users from harmful material.
What's next?
There are calls for the Australian government to make representations to the Trump administration opposing the death penalty.
Australia's online safety regulator eSafety says it does not have the power to "proactively prevent" the live stream of a firing squad execution in the United States from being shown in Australia, but argues platforms have a responsibility to protect users from harmful content.
Last week, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at a military base in Texas in 2009, would be available for the public to watch.
Across the political divide in Canberra there has been widespread concern about Australians seeing the December 3 live stream.
Loading...
The eSafety office said there were limits to its powers.
"While eSafety does not have powers to proactively prevent a live stream from occurring online, online services have responsibilities under Australia's online safety regulatory framework to protect users from harmful material," a spokesperson said.
"As the regulator responsible for enforcing these obligations, eSafety is in regular contact with online platforms and will continue to monitor the situation, considering any action as appropriate."
Experts agreed eSafety's power was more geared towards being able to take down content rather than pre-emptively blocking it.
Government says Australians 'rightly expect' to not see live stream
The ABC has contacted Google, Meta and TikTok to see if they have plans to restrict the content, but has not received responses.
The federal government said Australians "rightly expect" the content would not appear on their screens, and platforms have a responsibility to meet those expectations.
"Vision of an execution being live streamed here would be deeply distressing to many Australians," a government spokesperson said.
"No-one should be confronted with it, particularly younger Australians."
The government's response followed Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young writing to the communications minister and eSafety commissioner, demanding they "take whatever action is necessary" to block the "barbaric" event from being shown in Australia.
One Nation's Barnaby Joyce said it was "Roman amphitheatre stuff" that he did not want anyone to witness, while Liberal Tim Wilson said it was "enormously problematic" and Australia "shouldn't be promoting that sort of violence".
Expert says it highlights need for Digital Duty of Care
Swinburne University media lecturer Belinda Barnet believed the most the eSafety commissioner could do was issue take down notices, as was done in the case of a Sydney church stabbing in 2024.
"I don't see how they can take pre-emptive action," she said.
However, Dr Barnet acknowledged that take down powers were limited because content could run away as soon as it existed online.
"It's just a Band-Aid solution but we don't have a lot else in our armoury,"
she said.
Dr Barnet said it highlighted the need for the government's Digital Duty of Care Bill, which is being introduced into parliament this week, as it will require platforms to take steps to reduce the risk of harm to users on their sites.
"At the moment there is no onus on the platforms to protect all of us in Australia from what you could call harmful content," Dr Barnet said.
Government facing calls to make representations to US over death penalty
It is Australian policy to oppose the death penalty in all circumstances for all people, which includes supporting the universal abolition of the death penalty.
Monash University lecturer and vice president of the Capital Punishment Justice Project, Sara Kowal, said Australian officials should be telling the United States, whether it is publicly or privately, that they oppose the death penalty.
"This would be a perfect example of a case where the Australian government should be making strong representations to the Trump administration," she said.
Iran and Afghanistan are among the few countries that still carry out public executions.
"It's really abhorrent to see the United States trying to join this club,"
Ms Kowal said.
At the weekend, US President Donald Trump said he had not yet made a final decision about live streaming the execution.

Loophole allowing new coal and gas to avoid stricter climate laws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:46:30 UTC
03:46:30 KST

Coal and gas avoiding stricter laws by expanding existing mines, Climate Council warns
In short:
Coal and gas mines have to follow less strict emissions laws when they are expanded compared to outright new mines.
The Climate Council says that amounts to a "loophole" being used by the industry to add new emissions without having to follow "best-practice" limits.
What's next?
The Safeguard Mechanism, which sets emissions laws for heavy industry, is under review.
Coal and gas mines are using what the Climate Council warns is a "loophole" to expand operations and add new emissions while avoiding stricter laws imposed on new coal and gas projects.
The Climate Council says unless emissions from mine expansions are treated the same as emissions from new mines, it will cause an additional 4.5 million tonnes of CO2 a year by 2035.
Coal and gas mines are among the roughly 200 facilities covered by the Safeguard Mechanism — climate laws that require Australia's biggest polluters to cut or offset emissions by about 5 per cent a year or else face heavy penalties.
Under the laws, which are currently being reviewed, new coal and gas facilities are required to follow more strict, "best-practice" limits that take into account the most efficient technologies available for mines.
But existing facilities are not required to meet that higher standard when expanding or extending the life of an existing mine.
Modelling by Reputex has estimated that across 22 planned coal and gas expansions and extensions over the next decade, which will be treated as existing facilities, they will be able to emit 11 times more than if they were treated as new facilities.
The Climate Council says expansions are being used widely across the industry, taking advantage of that favourable treatment and leading to more emissions.
"Companies have an incentive to characterise everything as an expansion rather than a new facility," chief executive Amanda McKenzie said.
"We're arguing that is one of the loopholes that needs to be shut."
The Safeguard Mechanism is under review and due to be revisited next year, when the government will decide whether to set a steeper trajectory towards net zero emissions by 2050.
The Climate Council says when that time comes, "best-practice" CO2 limits should be applied to all new coal and gas emissions, regardless of whether they come from a new mine or an expanded one.
It says fossil fuel facilities are not doing enough to transition to net zero, and those covered by the Safeguard Mechanism actually increased emissions in the most recent year.
Most new coal and gas emissions from expansions
The council says since the Safeguard Mechanism laws were amended in 2022, more than three quarters of all new coal development have been expansions or extensions to projects.
It pointed to last month's approval for an open-cut coalmine in the Hunter Valley, which owners Yancoal and Glencore applied to extend by more than a decade.
Its life extension into the 2040s, which includes the mining of deeper coal seams, represents an additional $2.7 billion capital investment and will add an extra 809 megatonnes of CO2 emissions — or a bit less than two years' worth of Australia's annual emissions.
Because the Yancoal-Glencore owned coalmine was already covered by the Safeguard Mechanism, the extension will be treated under rules for existing projects, which the Climate Council estimates will result in emissions 60 per cent higher than if it was treated as a new project.
The NSW Independent Planning Commission, which approved the life extension, said while it would contribute to climate change and add to Australia's emissions, that was outweighed by its benefits, including supporting up to 1,400 local jobs and ongoing tax revenue from the mine.
"Despite these new investments being significant enough to require a new environmental approval, the vast majority of their pollution will not be considered 'new' by the Safeguard Mechanism," the council said.
Mining sector rebuffs Coalition promise to scrap Safeguard Mechanism
The Coalition has vowed to "take a chainsaw" to the Safeguard Mechanism, saying they would scrap the laws claiming they are driving up costs for heavy industry and manufacturing.
But after more than a decade of policy instability, the mining sector has urged not to up-end climate laws again.
On Friday the Minerals Council of Australia said the Safeguard Mechanism should be retained, saying it was working as intended to reduce emissions.
"The industry seeks change that is manageable, orderly, and establishes an appropriate regulatory framework for industry and the nation to achieve medium- and long-term emissions targets," MCA chief executive Tania Constable wrote on Friday.
The Minerals Council also urged the government not to push big polluters to cut emissions even harder after 2030, when requirements to cut emissions by about 5 per cent a year will soften to 3.3 per cent a year.
The industry argues existing projects should not be asked to meet "best-practice" emissions requirements since expansions and extensions are still using existing infrastructure, whereas new facilities are able to invest in more efficient technologies.
The Climate Council says if mining operations cannot be expanded under "best-practice" rules, then they should not seek to do so.
"We have to have laws that are genuinely getting us out of coal and oil and gas, so finding ways to enable the companies to continue to expand is nonsensical," Ms McKenzie said.
A spokesperson for Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen said the government's reforms to the Safeguard Mechanism were "working well".
"The focus of the review set out in the consultation paper is ensuring they continue to deliver," the spokesperson said in a statement.
"No decisions have been made to change current settings and our department is engaging with stakeholders to hear their views."

President Isaac Herzog has reportedly raised the possibility of forming a unity government bringing together Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot after Israel's October 27 election, according to sources in Eisenkot's party who spoke to ynet. The President's Office categorically denied the report, insisting that Herzog has not discussed any future coalition arrangement with politicians.
According to candidates from Eisenkot's Yashar party who encountered Herzog at various events, the president spoke about the need for national unity if the election produces no clear winner, suggesting that cooperation between Netanyahu's Likud and Eisenkot's party could prevent another election.
The reported proposal would bring together two political rivals whose parties are positioned on opposite sides of Israel's electoral divide, despite repeated declarations by Eisenkot and other opposition leaders that they will not join a government led by Netanyahu.
Sources familiar with the discussions told ynet that Herzog intends to use his influence after the election to encourage cooperation between the two parties, potentially applying pressure on lawmakers from Eisenkot's party if neither political bloc can assemble a governing majority.
The President's Office rejected the claims.
"We categorically deny the report," it said. "The president has not discussed a unity government with any candidate or Knesset member. At this stage, the president is not dealing with any potential government composition. All of this will be discussed during consultations at the President's Residence after the election results are received."
The office maintained that Herzog had spoken only about the importance of establishing a stable government, without expressing a preference for any particular coalition.
Eisenkot also rejected the prospect of serving alongside Netanyahu, declaring that the prime minister "cannot serve as prime minister, minister or deputy minister."
Herzog: ‘I will do everything I can to prevent another election’
The report follows remarks Herzog made earlier Monday during a special interview at the People of the Nation conference organized by ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth.
Asked about the possibility of another election if the October 27 vote ends without a clear majority, Herzog emphasized his determination to prevent Israel from returning to the polls.
"I am doing everything I can to ensure Israel has a stable government," he said.
"But I will say more than that: I really, really will do everything I can to prevent repeat elections. We need to understand that the national challenges facing us are enormous."
Herzog stressed that political leaders must first wait for the election results.
"We need to wait for the outcome and not pass judgment in advance, but we must do everything possible to avoid going back to elections again and again and again," he said.
The remarks immediately raised concerns among parties in the anti-Netanyahu bloc, whose leaders fear that the president could use his role in the government formation process to encourage cooperation with Likud.
Following an election, the president consults representatives of the parliamentary factions before assigning a lawmaker the task of forming a government.
According to the sources cited by ynet, Herzog could seek to use that political leverage to persuade lawmakers from Eisenkot's Yashar party, described as the largest faction in the opposition bloc, that a unity government is necessary if the election produces a deadlock.
Opposition leaders reject ‘fake unity’ with Netanyahu
The prospect of a coalition involving Netanyahu provoked an immediate backlash from opposition leaders.
Democrats chairman Yair Golan issued a sharply worded statement on X, rejecting any possibility of joining forces with the prime minister.
"There will be no unity government with Netanyahu," Golan wrote, warning that anyone even considering such an arrangement would be "stabbing the democratic public in the back."
Yair Lapid, the Yesh Atid chairman who is running alongside former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett as part of the Together party, also responded forcefully to Herzog's remarks.
"I very much hope President Herzog will not try to push another 'fake unity' government in which Netanyahu once again deceives his partners and brings more disasters upon Israeli citizens with the votes of people who voted to remove him from power," Lapid said.
"We will not cooperate with this," he added, calling on the other parties in the opposition bloc to announce in advance that they would refuse to join such a government.
Other parties in the anti-Netanyahu bloc, as well as Netanyahu's political allies, had not publicly responded to the reported proposal.
Opposition politicians have repeatedly ruled out participating in a government that includes Netanyahu, particularly citing his responsibility as prime minister during the failures preceding the October 7, 2023 Hamas massacre.
For most of those parties, another election would be preferable to entering a unity coalition with him.
The concern among opposition leaders is that Herzog's determination to prevent repeat elections could translate into pressure on individual lawmakers, particularly those less firmly opposed to a unity arrangement.
Eisenkot prepares for a minority government rather than another election
Despite the reported unity discussions, Eisenkot and his political allies are preparing for other scenarios after the election, including the possibility of establishing a minority government.
Eisenkot has said on several occasions that if forced to choose between leaving Netanyahu in office as caretaker prime minister and forming an alternative government supported by a Zionist parliamentary majority, he would pursue the latter option.
Members of the opposition bloc are also preparing to move quickly to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a senior Likud lawmaker, as one of their first steps following the election.
According to previously reported plans, they intend to secure the support of at least 61 lawmakers to demand the speaker's replacement.
The strategy draws on a previous confrontation involving former Likud Knesset Speaker Yuli Edelstein, who refused to convene the legislature for a vote on replacing him during a political transition.
After the matter reached the High Court of Justice, judges ordered the Knesset to convene. Edelstein subsequently resigned rather than carry out the court's directive.
Speaking at the People of the Nation conference, Eisenkot said that one of his immediate priorities after the election would be to take control of the Knesset and its main decision-making mechanisms.
Ohana, who also attended the conference, acknowledged that his replacement would be legitimate if a parliamentary majority supported it.
"If there are 61 votes to replace me, it will be legitimate to do so," he said.
Asked whether another dispute over the speakership might reach the High Court, Ohana dismissed the possibility.
"I don't think it will get there. We are law-abiding," he said.
The approaching election therefore presents two competing strategies for the day after the vote: Herzog's stated determination to avoid another round of elections, and opposition parties' efforts to establish a government without Netanyahu, even if doing so requires a minority coalition.
Whether a unity proposal is ever formally raised will depend on the election results and the subsequent coalition consultations. For now, the President's Office insists that no such discussions have taken place.

They moved to Australia. Years later, they developed an unexpected condition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:43:22 UTC
03:43:22 KST

In brief
- Nearly one in four Australians experience hay fever, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.
- For some migrants, hay fever doesn't appear until years after they move to Australia.
Zoe had never experienced hay fever before moving to Australia.
But a few years after arriving, she began experiencing red and itchy eyes. At first, she assumed they were a reaction to her contact lenses.
When the symptoms worsened and returned year after year, she started looking for another explanation.
Along with itchy eyes, she said she developed severe nasal congestion and an urge to sneeze. After seeking medical advice, she was told she had hay fever.
"It took me years to realise," Zoe, who asked for her last name to be withheld for privacy reasons, told SBS Thai.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Allergic rhinitis, commonly known as hay fever, occurs when the immune system reacts to airborne allergens. Common triggers include pollen, dust mites, mould and animal dander (flakes of skin in fur, hair or feathers).
Nearly one in four Australians experience hay fever, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.
For some migrants, the condition only emerges after several years of living in the country, with research suggesting exposure to new environmental allergens may play a role.
Why allergies can emerge years after migration
Dr Jason Yu, a Sydney-based general practitioner and clinical allergist, became interested in allergy medicine after moving between countries. He had not experienced allergies as a child but developed them years later.
He said allergies can develop at any stage of life, although they often first appear in childhood.
"We don't know the exact reasons why people develop allergies," Yu told SBS Thai.
One possible explanation for developing new allergies after migration is exposure to a novel environment, which can introduce people to allergens they hadn't previously encountered.
Yu said dust mite allergies are common in Sydney and other coastal areas, while grass pollen, including ryegrass pollen, was another prominent trigger in Australia.
"Pollen can be blown kilometres away," he said.
Yu said there isn't yet a definitive explanation for why some people develop allergies and others don't.
Genetics and the development of the immune system may also play a role. Infections can also influence immune responses, although their relationship with allergy development is complex.
Research has previously documented the development of allergic conditions among people who migrate to Australia.
A 1996 study found up to 60 per cent of people who moved from South-East Asian countries to Australia developed hay fever, while 15 per cent developed asthma within their first 10 years in Australia.
A 2015 study from Curtin University also reported similar findings, suggesting people who migrated from China were more prone to allergies after moving to Australia.
For Hansa, whose last name has been withheld for privacy reasons, the first signs of hay fever were easy to mistake for a cold.
"One day, all of a sudden, my nose wouldn't stop running, my eyes were watering, and I kept sneezing," she told SBS Thai.
While living in Thailand, Hansa occasionally reacted to construction dust, but she hadn't experienced the same symptoms after moving to Australia.
About three years after her arrival, the symptoms began.
She had assumed that if she was allergic to something, the reaction would appear straight away, rather than emerge several years after the move.
Antihistamines are commonly used to manage hay fever, but Yu said the ideal form of treatment depends on a person's symptoms.
For those whose main symptom is nasal congestion, corticosteroid nasal sprays may be more effective than antihistamines alone, he said.
For persistent or more severe allergies, allergen immunotherapy may also be an option.
When hay fever becomes more serious
Hay fever and asthma are different but closely related conditions.
Hay fever primarily affects the eyes and upper airways, while asthma affects the lower airways and causes symptoms such as wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath.
"If you feel short of breath, you feel like heaviness on your chest, you definitely should see someone about it," Yu said.
He said this was particularly important because, in rare circumstances, exposure to grass pollen can trigger a potentially life-threatening event known as thunderstorm asthma.
Under certain weather conditions, storm outflows can concentrate grass pollen into smaller particles. When inhaled, those particles can penetrate deeper into the lungs, triggering inflammation and narrowing airways.
"It doesn't happen often, but if it does happen, it has really deadly consequences," Yu said.
Melbourne experienced what's considered the world's largest recorded epidemic of thunderstorm asthma in November 2016. Thousands of people developed breathing difficulties, placing significant pressure on the city's emergency services and hospitals.
The event also highlighted the disproportionate impact thunderstorm asthma can have on some migrant communities.
A study published by The Lancet in 2018 found people of Asian or Indian ethnicity were disproportionately impacted, representing 39 per cent of people who attended hospital. Six of the 10 who died were of South or Southeast Asian ethnicity.
Hay fever and asthma can also occur together, and Yu said some people may not realise they have both conditions.
"I've had a few patients come in; they didn't realise they had asthma as well; they thought they just had hay fever.
"But because I checked, I could actually identify they actually have asthma."

The country coming for a $20-billion Australian export market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:43:14 UTC
03:43:14 KST

IN BRIEF:
- Brazil is the world's leading beef exporter and producer.
- Commentators warn that shifts in global markets could see the country absorb Australia's markets.
Australian beef could face its toughest competition yet, as the world's leading producer encroaches on its traditional export markets.
Since the early 2000s, Brazil has consistently ranked as the world's leading beef producer, with an enormous 230 million-strong herd in 2024, more than the country's estimated population. The South American country is also the world's leading exporter, sending its beef to 130 different countries.
Australia has long prided itself on its beef exports: in 2025, 1.5 million tonnes of beef were sent to 83 countries. In 2025, the value of Australian beef exports was $19.6 billion, according to Australia's red meat research and marketing body, Meat and Livestock Australia (MLA).
But commentators are suggesting South American exporters are expanding in Australia's most important export markets — South Korea and Japan — which could have significant impacts on price competition over the coming months.
Speaking on a recent agribusiness podcast, Angus Gidley-Baird, senior animal proteins analyst at food and agribusiness bank Rabobank, said Australia’s beef sector should closely monitor developments in Brazil.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Over the past few years, we’ve seen Brazil increase its presence in several of Australia’s export markets," Gidley-Baird said.
"Combined with changing trade dynamics involving China, the United States and Europe, it is becoming increasingly important for Australian producers and exporters to understand what is happening in the Brazilian beef sector."
Brazil already has a big presence in the Australian meat industry, through worldwide giant JBS. It's the biggest meat processing company in Australia, owning a series of foodlots and abattoirs, as well as the smallgoods company Primo Foods.
More than half of Brazil's beef exports are to China, and it hit its annual quota of 1.1 million tonnes for shipments to the country last month.
China's commerce ministry said it would start collecting an additional 55 per cent tariff on Brazil's beef shipments on 1 October after the South American country reached its annual quota of 1.1 million tonnes.
Rabobank Brazil animal protein analyst Wagner Yanaguizawa said that new quota restrictions significantly reduced Brazilian shipments during the second half of 2025, creating surplus volumes that would need to be redirected elsewhere, and could translate into greater competition for Australia in alternative destination markets.
Yanaguizawa said the United States was likely to absorb some of the displaced volume, while the Middle East, Indonesia, Vietnam, Chile and the United Kingdom also presented opportunities. Those markets would not be sufficient to offset reduced Chinese demand, though, he said.
Yanaguizawa said the potential opening of Japan and South Korea to Brazilian beef also warrants close attention from Australian industry participants.
"Japanese and South Korean inspections of Brazilian processing plants had been completed, and final reports were pending before market access decisions could be finalised. Industry expectations are that access could be granted later this year," Yanaguizawa said.
"These two markets are very important for Australia, and soon Australia may have a new competitor," he said.
The MLA is aware of the shift. On an August 2026 podcast, the corporation's regional manager for Southeast Asia, Valeska, said that as global trade patterns shifted, Australian beef volumes had been redirected from China into Southeast Asia.
At the same time, competition across Southeast Asia was intensifying, as exporters from South America actively pursued new opportunities across the region.
"The South Americans are really active and quite aggressive. At the [World Food Expo in the Philippines] yesterday, we spoke with Brazilian packers who indicated they're looking at alternative markets."
Valeska said she believed Australia's long-term investment in Southeast Asia positioned the industry well.
"We're not resting on our laurels. Australian beef is definitely ramping up activities across Southeast Asia, and I think it's an opportunity to really secure the premium segment while continuing to grow demand through other channels."

Carrie gets a bloody 2026 remake just in time for Halloween
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

What to watch in October, from classic horror reboots to shocking docs
Welcome to what to watch, where we take you through what's on the box in October.
This month brings a heartbreaking story of charity betrayal from the UK and an Australian horror-comedy about killer gnomes. Plus, Mike Flanagan has a go at rebooting Carrie and Catherine Zeta Jones gets to pull out her Welsh accent for Kill Jackie.
Here's what we're watching this month.
Believe In Magic: The Mother of All Cons
What's it about? A mother and daughter in the midst of a nightmare, or a cruel scam? Believe in Magic tells the story of Megan Bhari and her mother Jean O'Brien, founders of a UK charity supporting seriously ill children and their families.
The organisation, built in 2012 around the story of Megan's own battle with a brain tumour, raised hundreds of thousands of pounds and was praised for its work. Megan was dogged in her efforts to promote the organisation.There were tea parties at Buckingham Palace and a princess ball hosted by One Direction’s Louis Tomlinson and his mother.
In 2015, Jean reported that Megan’s condition had worsened. Pleading for funds as part of a Save Meg appeal, she gave little detail on Megan’s care and treating doctors. It prompted suspicion from members of the charity’s community who said they “smelled a rat”.
One mother’s doubts led her to dig deeper into the charity, as well as Megan and Jean’s claims. What she and other parents found was explosive. The charity was investigated and ultimately shut down.
But there’s a bigger twist in this new three-part investigative series by the BBC. No spoilers here, other than to say, at times it's hard to keep your jaw off the floor at what is an unbelievable and ultimately tragic story.
Perfect for: Lovers of true-crime stories like Inventing Anna, Catfish or Apple Cider Vinegar.
Where to watch: The first episode premieres on ABC TV and iview on Tuesday, October 13.
Carrie
What's it about? There are few stories in the modern horror canon that are more revered than Carrie. First as Stephen King's groundbreaking debut 1974 novel and then Brian De Palma's landmark 1976 film adaptation.
Modern adaptations of the girl with telekinesis haven't fared ,as well, with the 1999 sequel, The Rage, the 2002 TV movie and 2013's modern reboot all being resoundingly poo-pooed, but if there is one thing Hollywood will do it's capitalise on established IP. Which is how we arrive at Carrie (2026) an extended miniseries helmed by Mike Flanagan, who has proved himself very handy at adaptations with The Haunting of Hill House and The Haunting of Bly Manor.
All the familiar beats are here, just transported to high school in 2026. Carrie (Summer H Howell) is now not just an outcast, but a complete recluse kept prisoner in her home with her overly religious mother (Samantha Sloyan, a Flanagan fave who is born for this role). They're both exposed to the world after the untimely death of Carrie's construction worker father, who is a new addition to the story. So the timid teen is even more raw when she's pushed into the cruel world of bullies with smartphones.
King's original story is pretty tight, so Flanagan pads the eight-episode run time by expanding on some overlooked details about a coven of similarly gifted girls, which gives off the hint that the director is sniffing out a season two. Carrie purists might revolt, but Mike Flanagan fans remain fed.
Perfect for: those who like a very expanded horror universe.
Where to watch: Carrie is streaming on Prime Video now.
Dustfall
What's it about? This gritty mystery drama follows detective Antigone "Tig" Pollard (Anna Torv, The Newsreader) as she tries to solve a brutal sexual assault on a schoolgirl, revealing small-town secrets and dredging up her own past in her pursuit of the truth.
Given the subject matter, Dustfall makes for uncomfortable viewing at times, but it dares you to not look away. It's also punctuated by charming lighter moments which will likely feel distinctly familiar for anyone who grew up in regional Australia.
Dustfall spotlights layered female characters through Tig's often-complicated relationships, with her lifelong friend Shayna (Alice Ansara), her force of nature mother Olivia (Juliet Stevenson); and victim-survivors Edie (Zoe Phillips) and Maya (Gemma Chua-Tran).
Tig's also navigating a blossoming romance with local Mitch (Ben Knight), learning the ways of her detective partner Remi (Bert La Bonte), and can't escape Andy (Peter Fenton), the much older local rock star who has held an unsettling power over her since her teenage years.
Each episode leaves you wanting more, with a genuinely gripping storyline that builds in intensity until the very end, delivering a shocking but satisfying twist.
Based on Vikki Petraitis's novel The Unbelieved, Dustfall features stellar performances from a cast of established and up-and-coming actors and is bound to open doors.
Perfect for: Those who want their next bingeworthy series with a side of sharp social commentary that will stay with you long after the credits roll.
Where to watch: All episodes of Dustfall are streaming now on ABC iview.
Gnomes
What's it about? If you like your Australian comedy zany and silly, then you might have just been handed your favourite show of the year in Gnomes.
Senior Sergeant Arnold Kipps (Asa Butterfield) is perfectly happy acting as the big dog top cop in the tiny regional town of Nompton. His peaceful, if not a bit under-respected, life is interrupted when his ex-partner and old flame Ellie McKay (Megan Smart) comes down from the city to announce that Arnold's station is to be shut down due to lack of activity and they're only keeping one local police officer on.
And this is before an evil gnome queen is unleashed during prep for the annual gnome festival and animates all the garden gnomes in town into vicious killers.
Written by wife and husband duo Tegan Higginbotham and Paul F Verhoeven, the laughs are so smooth and fast it's easy to forget that Gnomes is a horror — that is until one of the titular terrors slices a man's face off with DVDs.
While UK import Butterfield is very much at home with the frustrated nerd slapstick he perfected on Sex Education, ditzy police duo consisting of Higginbotham and Matt O'Kine nearly steal the show (do we see a spin off on the horizon?).
Perfect for: Some smooth brain, halloweeny laughs.
Where to watch: Gnomes is streaming on Stan now.
Kill Jackie
What's it about? For the first time in her 40-year career, Welsh actor Catherine Zeta-Jones is using her real accent on screen. It's to play the titular Jackie in revenge thriller Kill Jackie, about a one-time "rich, sexy dealer of cocaine" turned art dealer who is trying to evade the seven assassins on her tail.
Except she's not really that interested in evading them, even though the so-called Seven Demons are psychopaths, hell-bent on killing not only her but the people she loves and even those with whom she has only a mildly inappropriate professional relationship, like her tax accountant (Daniel Ings; Lovesick).
Instead, Jackie is going to destroy them herself. And considering the assassins have torched her apartment and art collection, and stolen a lot of her money, she doesn't have much to lose.
It's fun to watch Zeta-Jones return to a Chicago-style role as a woman scorned, although Jackie is much happier to fly under the radar than the fame-hungry Velma Kelly, who she played when she was just 32.
Described by one assassin as "more resourceful than expected", Jackie has more friends and well-wishers than you would expect from someone who boasts "the most important thing about me [is] I don't give a f***".
Now 56, Zeta-Jones seemingly doesn't give a f*** either.
Perfect for: Fans of the spate of recent woman-assassin-slash-badass TV, from Furious to The Assassin and Killing Eve.
Where to watch: Kill Jackie is streaming on Stan now.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met on Monday with victims of the detonation of an unexploded Hezbollah cluster munition in northern Israel earlier that same day, according to the Prime Minister's Office (PMO).
The explosion, which killed a 14-year-old boy and injured 24 others, occured during a field trip for ORT Ma’alot Yeshiva High School students.
One of the victims being treated at Haifa's Rambam Health Care Campus, 14-year-old student Eitan Masouri, described his experience to the prime minister, who was joined at the hospital by Education Minister Yoav Kisch.
"I realized I was hurt; I saw that a friend was injured, and I tried to help him," said Masouri, who was injured by shrapnel in his neck.
Masouri told Netanyahu that one of his fellow students was handling the unexploded Hezbollah ordnance before it detonated.
"He unscrewed it, and then it exploded; the guys were thrown back," explained Masouri. "There was a moment of shock, about two seconds, and then I was told I was bleeding. I realized I was bleeding from my neck."
Masouri's account follows a preliminary investigation by the Israel Fire and Rescue Authority, which showed evidence that one of the students put the Hezbollah cluster munition into his bag, which later detonated.
Education Ministry: All group trips to area to be diverted over next two days
Also on Monday, the Education Ministry announced that group trips to the area along the Israel-Lebanon border on Tuesday and Wednesday would be diverted elsewhere.
"Groups currently traveling in these areas are instructed to leave their routes and move to alternative routes in coordination with the Education Ministry's travel center," the ministry stated. "In the rest of the country, trips will take place as usual."
The ministry added that it had "sharpened" safety guidelines "with an emphasis on caution against munitions throughout the country."
Israeli politicians respond to explosion incident in North
Several Israeli politicians reacted to the explosion, with Israeli President Isaac Herzog calling the incident a "horrific disaster" in an X/Twitter post on Monday.
"A student who left his home for a trip with his classmates, for a day of experiences amid the landscapes of our country, and will not return to his family's embrace," he wrote. "This is part of the heavy and painful price of the complex security reality in which Israel finds itself, one that leaves its marks even in places where our children should be protected and safe, free to wander, discover, and rejoice."
Also on Monday, Defense Minister Israel Katz wrote in an X post that he wished "a swift and full recovery to all the injured."
"I thank all the teams in the field who are working to save lives and treat the casualties," wrote Katz. "In this difficult hour, my heart is with the family, the injured, and their families."
Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot also responded to the explosion earlier on Monday, saying in an X post that his "heart is with the family of the deceased, the injured, and their families."
He added that he is praying "together with all Israeli citizens for the swift recovery of the injured."
Education minister: Trip was approved despite concerns of unexploded ordnance
Kisch issued a statement later on Monday, noting that the students' field trip, including the route, was approved despite concerns over unexploded ordnance, according to Maariv.
"In the briefing and in the notes, there was a note that we should be careful of unexploded ordnance, and this will probably be with us for a long time," he said.

Yisrael Beytenu chairman MK Avigdor Lieberman declared universal conscription a prerequisite for forming a government after the next elections and unveiled a plan to establish an Israeli constitution through a team of experts and a national referendum, bypassing Knesset approval, during a pre-election conference for students at liberal pre-military preparatory programs in Haifa on Sunday.
The remarks came at the first conference of its kind for students from liberal pre-military preparatory programs, held throughout the day in Haifa.
"The choice in the elections is between conscription and draft evasion. That is the choice. We must win, because otherwise we will not have a liberal state but a state governed entirely by Jewish religious law, with all that entails," Lieberman said.
"I have been talking about conscription for everyone for many years, not just haredim. Conscription through two tracks: military service or civilian service. But the Defense Ministry will also administer the civilian track, without nonprofit organizations or middlemen. Without this, there will be no government. It is a prerequisite for forming a government. There will be no compromises on this issue," he said.
Lieberman emphasized that the obligation would apply to everyone, including the haredim (ultra-Orthodox), Arabs, Christians, and Circassians.
He attacked coalition members over demonstrations against the conscription of haredim into the IDF.
"A week ago, a group of haredi rioters, draft dodgers, and deserters marched through Jerusalem. They organized a procession in honor of the deserters, handed them NIS 1,000 in cash per day, and held up signs saying 'The IDF is the enemy army' in Jerusalem, the capital of Israel. Nobody in the coalition condemns this. Why? Because for them, remaining in power is more important than security."
Lieberman proposes constitution approved by referendum
"The only reform that must take place is a constitution. We cannot continue without a constitution. I oppose all these piecemeal initiatives," Lieberman declared.
"When the State of Israel was established, they announced that there would be a constitution by October 1, 1948. How much water has flowed down the Jordan River since then? A constitution would address all the problems that have emerged in recent years, rather than dealing with every issue separately. Relations between religion and state, relations between the three branches of government, all the fundamental values of Zionism - all of these would be included in the constitution."
Lieberman also outlined the practical framework he proposed.
"The Knesset is incapable of legislating a constitution. Therefore, the way forward is for the government to appoint a team of experts that will produce a draft constitution within six months, while at the same time passing a referendum law to approve the constitution. It must be approved through a referendum outside the Knesset."
Lieberman also criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other members of the governing coalition, rejecting their identification with the political Right.
"Netanyahu has nothing to do with the Right. All these stories about Ben-Gvir and Smotrich supposedly belonging to the Right, there is no connection," Lieberman said.
"The problem with this government is not Right or Left. For them, remaining in power comes before everything else. This is the most sectoral government, one that destroys and divides the country. Goldknopf cares about nothing but his own sector, and the same goes for Deri and Smotrich, while Netanyahu wants to maintain his political bloc. Security is not even a consideration here, only power."
Asked whether he would agree to sit in a government with Ra'am or its chairman, Mansour Abbas, Lieberman said: "Anyone who defines Hamas as a charitable organization rather than a terrorist organization is conveying exactly the same message as senior Hamas officials inside the Gaza Strip."
At the same time, he said: "We need to do a great deal to bring the Arab public back into being an integral part of society. We are heading toward becoming like Lebanon, a federation of minorities. That is the dismantling of the state."
Iran, Lebanon, and the question of military victory
Addressing the question of achieving a decisive victory and ending the war, Lieberman said: "In Iran, a decisive victory means only overthrowing and replacing the regime. For most countries, nuclear weapons are solely a political question for the country itself. The problem is a regime that wants nuclear weapons for the purpose of war."
Turning to Lebanon, he said: "In Lebanon, Israel should have developed a coordinated operation with the moderate tribes and moderate countries. It should have built a comprehensive plan, known how to deliver a painful opening blow to Hezbollah, and the partners would have completed everything else."
"I am not speaking theoretically, but based on good relations with many people in the region," Lieberman added.
Lieberman declined to commit in advance to the identity of the candidate he would recommend for prime minister after the elections, arguing that focusing on the question served Netanyahu's interests.
"Netanyahu does not want us discussing the question of responsibility, the collapse of governance, personal security that is in complete collapse, October 7, or the fact that we are a pariah state, isolated in the world almost like North Korea and Iran. He wants us to discuss who will be prime minister."
"In 2021, we went to elections and won without coordinating who would be prime minister. In 2022, Yair Lapid won 24 seats, and we lost. Right now, the bloc's strategy is that every party must do everything it can to maximize its electoral potential."
"After the elections, we will know how to work things out within a few hours. We will know how to put the pieces of the puzzle together, who will be prime minister, who will be defense minister, and so on. The most important thing is that we secure 63 to 64 seats. We need to ensure a solid majority."
Lieberman also addressed the students attending the liberal pre-military preparatory programs, urging them to vote and avoid wasting ballots on parties that would fail to cross the electoral threshold.

Engaging Raz: Themes in Normative Philosophy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:14:00 UTC
03:14:00 KST

Engaging Raz: Themes in Normative Philosophy is a posthumous Festschrift for Joseph Raz (1939–2022), collects papers from “two highly selective, international conferences held in Raz’s honor after his passing.” It is a splendid volume: an entirely fitting tribute to, as its editors aptly write, a “towering figure in late twentieth century and early twenty-first century analytical philosophy”, whose work “profoundly influenced the discipline”.
The range of topics covered alone is a testament to the reach and significance of Raz’s contributions. There are essays, to give an incomplete list, on the relation between reasons and values, the nature of practical reason and action, exclusionary reasons, autonomy, the rule of law, the interest theory of rights, multiculturalism, and authority. It is also a striking, indirect testament to the reach and significance of Raz’s work how much, through no fault of the editors or contributors, the book leaves out. Two highly selective, international conferences and over 500 pages were not enough to allow for coverage of such topics as normative powers as such (although there are two excellent papers on promises and contracts), skepticism about the moral, criticism of the ideal of equality, the myth of instrumental reason, and incommensurability, among much else.
Many of the papers offer close readings of Raz’s work, most assess and develop Razian theses, and all engage with Razian themes. The result is a surprisingly cohesive volume; nothing feels shoehorned in. Each of the essays is of exceptionally high quality, from some of most distinguished thinkers in moral, political, and legal philosophy, as well as the philosophy of action, along with a few newer voices who, to judge from the strength of their contributions, will have much to teach us in coming years. None of the papers reads as dashed off or opportunistically unloaded. All are digestibly clear and concise. The joint effort and self-discipline of editors and contributors are remarkable; anyone who has edited or contributed to a collection of essays must marvel at how quickly the talks materialized on the shelf.
Many of the essays develop and advance, in conversation with Raz, their authors’ own ongoing work. Anyone interested in, for instance, T.M. Scanlon’s “buck-passing” account of goodness and value, Ralph Wedgwood’s attempts to reconcile ethics and decision theory, Elinor Mason’s notion of taking responsibility, Andrei Marmor’s elevation of accountability to philosophical attention, David Owens’s rethinking of the significance of commands, Massimo Renzo’s theory of alienated action, David Enoch’s distinction between “sovereignty” and “nonalienation”, or Daniel Viehoff’s fiduciary reading of the relation of state and citizen—and the list could go on—will want to read their essays.
Many of the essays, including some of those just listed, provide, directly or indirectly, opinionated surveys of the state of the art on Razian themes, along the lines of the most helpful handbook or encyclopedia entries. If someone with passing familiarity with Raz’s discussions of, say, exclusionary reasons, the rule of law, the interest theory of rights, multiculturalism, or the “adequacy” of an option set were to wonder, “Where has the debate gone since?” they could not do better than to read the papers on those subjects by Ulrike Heuer, Michael S. Moore, Emad H. Atiq, Kimberley Brownlee, Daniel Weinstock, and Steven Wall, respectively.
The wide-ranging nature of the collection would frustrate any attempt to engage with its content as a whole. So, I will confine myself to a question provoked by Enoch’s and Wall’s revisiting of Raz’s account of autonomy, presented in his seminal The Morality of Freedom. It is whether autonomy, as Raz articulates it, is really something of value, in the way that he suggests it is.
In Raz’s own words, the
ruling ideal behind the ideal of personal autonomy is that people should make their own lives. The autonomous person is a (part) author of his own life. The ideal of personal autonomy is the vision of people controlling, to some degree, their own destiny, fashioning it through successive decisions throughout their lives. (The Morality of Freedom, 369)
An autonomous life thus contrasts with “a life of no choices, or of drifting through life without ever exercising one’s capacity to choose” (The Morality of Freedom, 371). Enoch derives a natural methodology from this ideal, so described. In matters of autonomy, he suggests,
Whenever questions come up, whenever it is necessary to adjudicate between competing ways of filling in details, we should return to the underlying ideal, even if somewhat metaphorically put, and ask which way of filling in the details is more loyal to that underlying ideal. (247)
Let that be our methodology too.
There can be little debate that there is such an ideal, of an autonomous life. My question is whether one’s life necessarily goes worse for one insofar as one’s life does not realize that ideal. Of course, we need an “other things equal” qualification. And we might need to restrict our attention to life in cultural settings such as those of “western industrial societies” (The Morality of Freedom, 369). So, let us ask: other things equal and within such cultural settings, does one’s life go worse for one if and because one does not lead it autonomously, independently (as Wall clarifies, 273) of one’s attitudes toward living an autonomous life?
This is what I wonder. Imagine that someone leads the life that is otherwise best for them. It makes them happier, in a hedonic sense, than any other life would, and it is perfectly matched to their talents, so that they succeed in what they set out to do, more than they would in any other life. They willingly endorse it. But still this person has drifted into the life, or left it to chance, or was reared into it. To illustrate the last possibility, suppose that, from childhood, the siblings worked at the family business. As they reached adulthood, the others left the business for other things, something the parents wholeheartedly welcomed. But one sibling, content with the life they had, just continued in the business, doing each day what they had done the day before. While perfectly aware of alternatives—after all, the other siblings were pursuing them—this sibling, happy with what they had, never deliberated about whether to pursue such an alternative, never so much as to reject it.
Let us imagine further that this contented sibling enjoys the conditions for an autonomous life, even if, by hypothesis, they do not do anything further to make use of those conditions to lead an autonomous life. Those conditions, as Enoch lists them, are “appropriate mental abilities, an adequate range of options, and independence from coercion and manipulation” (248). Enoch and Wall do a real service in elaborating and amending these conditions. Enoch and Wall part ways with Raz in suggesting that the availability of even bad options can contribute to the autonomy of a life (253; 290), and Enoch goes so far as to suggest that the pursuit of a bad option can do so (258).
The last condition, of independence, that one is not coerced or manipulated into the life that one leads, reflects the fact that, as both Enoch and Wall note, leading an autonomous life is, at least in part, an interpersonal or, as Enoch puts it, a “relational”, matter. To lead an autonomous life is to lead it not subject to the will of another. Enoch and Wall observe (260; 293) that the adequacy of a range of options is itself in part a relational matter. Suppose that one is not coerced or manipulated into leading the life that one leads. To that extent, one is independent. Nevertheless, suppose, options have been removed from one’s menu (or, one might add, their costs increased) “intentionally” (Enoch) or by “unjustified interference” (Wall) (although perhaps without coercion). This seems more compromising to the autonomy of the life that we choose from the menu than if the same options were removed (or made more costly) by, say, natural forces or the uncoordinated, market choices of others. (Parenthetically, though, I’m a bit puzzled by Wall’s suggestion that this effect on our autonomy occurs only through interference that is unjustified on other grounds. One might have thought that the reason why such interference is unjustified is precisely that it had this effect on our autonomy.)
To these three conditions—capacities, options, and independence—Enoch adds a possible fourth, concerning “the conditions under which the preferences guiding the choice were shaped” (248). This references his paper “False Consciousness for Liberals, Part I: Consent, Autonomy, and Adaptive Preferences”, in which he argues, roughly, that when the preferences guiding the choice were shaped by injustice, the resulting life suffers from an autonomy deficit. This is another way in which one might live a life subject to the will of another.
So, in sum, there is a great deal of complexity and nuance in the conditions for autonomy. But imagine that these conditions are met. One is “living one’s best life”, as they say, one is not, in doing so, subject to the will of another, and one has an adequate range of options. Still, one has drifted into the life, or left it to chance, or was brought up into it. So, one is not living an autonomous life. While one “willingly endorses” one’s pursuits, this is not enough for autonomy, the ideal of which “transcends the conceptual point that personal well‐being is partly determined by success in willingly endorsed pursuits and holds the free choice of goals and relations as an essential ingredient of individual well‐being” (The Morality of Freedom, 369, reading this passage perhaps differently from Enoch at 249–250).
Recall that, following Enoch, our methodological lodestar in articulating the relevant value is the metaphor of authoring one’s life. And as we are imagining things, the metaphor does not fit. One is not the author of one’s life. One has simply let stand the text that one has found oneself with, as a biographical subject might let stand the offerings of a ghostwriter, rather than composing it oneself. As Wall writes, “they will not realize autonomy, even if they are very successful in realizing these other goods, if they do not pursue these other goods in certain ways and under the right conditions” (273), and while one has pursued these other goods “under the right conditions”, one has not pursued them in the “certain ways” that distinguish an autonomous life.
To be sure, there might be a kind of ideal that one does not realize, an achievement one has not achieved. But such is life. No one can realize all ideals or achieve all things. The question is whether one leads a worse life than they would if they stopped, deliberated, and chosen it. Is there reason to pity one for not doing so? Does someone else have reason to see to it that one chooses the life: to say, “Yes, I realize that this is the best life you could lead, but you really need to stop, deliberate about other options, and choose it, for its own sake—your well-being depends on it”? To insist on this, I worry, may be to betray a kind of fetish for planning or predilection for a studied way through life, which may not suit everyone. It is important that people live their lives under conditions of autonomy: with options and without being subject to the wills of others. But this is not because their lives are necessarily better if they are autonomously lived. Or so I speculate. In any event, if this collection leads us to return to Raz’s ideas with fresh eyes and new questions, then it is surely a success.
