Moscow sentences Russian-Israeli scientist to prison over funding Navalny-connected foundation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:45:10 UTC
01:45:10 KST

Dr. Sofia Rosenfeld, a Russian scientist who also holds Israeli citizenship, was sentenced to three and a half years in a penal colony by Moscow's Gagarinsky District Court last Wednesday after being convicted of financing an "extremist organization," it emerged on Monday.
According to the indictment, the charges concerned two donations of 1,000 rubles each, approximately NIS 30-35 per donation, to the Anti-Corruption Foundation associated with Alexei Navalny.
Navalny, a Russian opposition leader and outspoken critic of Russian President Vladimir Putin, founded the organization, which published investigations into government corruption in Russia over the years. Russian authorities designated the foundation an "extremist organization" in 2021. Navalny died in a Russian prison in February 2024.
According to a courtroom report by Mediazona, an independent Russian-language online news outlet, Rosenfeld said she did not intend to support extremism but wanted to help fight corruption.
"Even in my work, which involves scientific research and nature conservation, I have seen what monstrous forms this evil can take," she said.
When the judge asked her, "What, don't we have law enforcement agencies for that?" she replied that public assistance also had a place.
Rosenfeld argues time in Arctic made her unaware of transfers
Rosenfeld argued that she had been out of contact with the outside world while participating in a scientific expedition in the northern Arctic when the transfers were made from her account. She said she canceled the standing payment order as soon as she learned that the foundation had been outlawed.
According to Mediazona, she is the third woman known to receive a prison sentence for making small donations to the foundation.
She was taken into custody immediately after the hearing. She is currently being held in Moscow pending a decision on whether to transfer her to a penal colony.
Her lawyers intend to appeal the sentence, although an appeal hearing is not expected for several weeks at the earliest.
Rosenfeld, 50, holds an advanced doctorate in biology and is a senior researcher at the Institute of Ecology and Evolution of the Russian Academy of Sciences.
She immigrated to Israel with her family in 1990, when she was 14, but found it difficult to leave her life and studies in Moscow behind.
While in Israel, she studied from books mailed to her so she would not fall behind the Russian curriculum. After about a year and a half, she persuaded her parents to let her return.
She has lived in Moscow ever since, initially staying with her grandmother and aunt.
"She really loved studying in Russia and wanted to go back," said her father, Boris Rosenfeld, 78, who lives in Israel.
"I feel very bad. It's a serious shock for me and for her," he said. "She didn't expect the punishment to be so severe."
Although Dr. Sofia Rosenfeld built her professional life in Russia, she retained her Israeli citizenship throughout the years, maintained close ties with her family, and visited Israel frequently.
Doctor traveled to Israel every year, father says
According to her father, she traveled to Israel every year. In her younger years, she even represented Israel in international equestrian competitions.
She previously worked with wildlife researchers in Israel, volunteered at the Hula birdwatching center, and is also known to staff at the bird-ringing center in Eilat.
About three or four years ago, she and her partner, Arthur, 53, also her research colleague, produced a nature documentary about Israel titled The Country Without Hunting, available in Russian and English on YouTube.
The couple has no children.
Rosenfeld graduated from Moscow University in 1998 with a degree in biology, specializing in vertebrate zoology, and has worked as a researcher at the Institute of Ecology and Evolution ever since.
Her research focuses on Arctic waterfowl, including geese, ducks, and swans, and involves expeditions to remote areas within the Arctic Circle.
Early in her career, she also worked on Wrangel Island.
A light aircraft was specially built for her research, which she uses to count birds and track migration routes.
"Over ten research seasons, she and her team covered more than 100,000 kilometers in the light aircraft across the Arctic and on their way there," her father said.
Her father, a mathematician and retiree of Israel Aerospace Industries and its subsidiary Elta, worked in Israel's defense industry for 25 years.
He worked on the Arrow and Iron Dome projects, along with other defense programs.
Sofia's mother, an electronics engineer, died nine years ago. Her brother, Lev, 49, lives in Israel.
The last conversation between Rosenfeld and her father took place the day before the hearing.
"She told me she hoped it would end with a fine or community service," he recalled.
"I told her, 'Good luck.' Neither she nor her lawyers expected an actual prison sentence."
Since the sentencing, communication between them has been limited to email, with exchanges taking place sparingly and under highly restrictive conditions.
Her father said he was pessimistic about the appeal prospects.
"I find it hard to believe she'll be acquitted. Maybe they'll reduce the sentence by a few months; I don't know. The hope is that the public attention will have a positive effect."
After the indictment was filed, Sofia contacted the Israeli Embassy in Moscow to request assistance.
Following her imprisonment, her father contacted the Foreign Ministry.
He said he was informed that an Israeli consular official could visit her if she submitted a formal request.
"I want her to be here in Israel," he said.
"That's what I'm asking for: that they help her leave Russia and come to Israel."

German artist Barbara Hines unveils first solo exhibit in Israel after discovering Jewish roots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:44:57 UTC
01:44:57 KST

German-born artist Barbara Hines will debut her first solo exhibition in Israel, Jerusalem In My Soul, at the Moshe Castel Museum of Jewish Israeli Art.
The exhibition, which runs October 15 to December 31, is the culmination of a profound spiritual and personal journey that began when Hines discovered her family’s hidden Holocaust history.
Raised as a Christian in Australia, Hines spent years exploring various faiths, including Hinduism and Buddhism. Her life took a dramatic turn following a phone call between her son and her mother. When her son called his grandmother to share his decision to convert to Judaism, she casually revealed that her own mother and grandmother were Jewish.
Unbeknownst to Hines, both of her parents were Jewish survivors who hid in plain sight as German Christians to evade the Nazis. Her father had been dismissed from the Luftwaffe after his Jewish lineage was discovered, and her mother hid him throughout World War II.
Traumatized by the war and fearing another Holocaust, they immigrated to Australia and kept their true identity a secret.
Artist Barbara Hines debuts first solo Israel exhibition
This revelation deeply transformed Hines’s life and art. Her work shifted from depicting nature to exploring biblical, Zionist, and Israeli themes.
As her religious observance grew, she even began mixing physical earth from Israel into her paint to imbue her artwork with deeper meaning. Her art has since been featured in prominent global institutions, including the Holocaust Museum Houston and the Jerusalem Biennale.
Following the passing of her husband, Gerald Hines, in 2020, Barbara fulfilled a lifelong dream of moving to Israel. She later met and married Rabbi Dr. Natan Ophir on May 29, 2026. Fittingly, they had their first date at the Castel Museum, the exact location where she was offered this milestone exhibition.

French defence contractor Thales will establish a maintenance and operational support base in Japan in what is seen as the first such move by a foreign firm in the country, a report said yesterday.
Thales chairman and CEO Patrice Caine told the Nikkei business daily that the base “will mark a milestone toward Thales’ long-term engagement in Japan.”
It is believed to be the first time a foreign defense company has established a dedicated base in Japan for the maintenance and operation of Japanese defense equipment, the Nikkei said.
Photo: Reuters
It added that Thales might also expand its Japan-based business to civilian use. The report comes as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi boosts defense spending in the face of China’s rapid military expansion and an unpredictable North Korea, moving away from the traditional pacifist stance that limited the use of force to self-defense.
Thales already supplies equipment to the Japanese Self-Defense Forces, the Nikkei said.
Caine cited technologies such as radar and sonar as possible areas to share with Japan, saying that he hoped to “provide support in areas where Thales has an advantage in terms of performance.”
Thales is to transfer its technology to partner Japan Steel Works and production of the 2R2M heavy mortar system is to begin in Japan from next year, the Nikkei said.

Taipower head wants power sector at the table in tech decisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:41 UTC
01:42:41 KST

The electricity industry should be included in technology-sector decisionmaking as soon as possible, Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) chairman Tseng Wen-sheng (曾文生) said yesterday.
Energy would become increasingly important to the technology industry because computing power depends on electricity, Tseng told a news conference ahead of the Net-Zero Taiwan and Energy Taiwan exhibitions, which open tomorrow.
Electricity would also become a critical part of the semiconductor and technology industries’ supply chains, he said.
Photo: Lin Jing-hua, Taipei Times
As industrial power supply and demand patterns evolve, Taipower should play a greater role in industrial decisionmaking rather than simply providing electricity, Tseng said.
Parts of Taipower’s operations should take a more industry-oriented approach, enabling the company to better understand the technology sector’s operating models, business challenges, financial arrangements and supply chain partnerships, he said.
As businesses’ demand for renewable energy grows, electricity suppliers and consumers should jointly discuss energy procurement, the acquisition of renewable energy certificates and energy storage, Tseng said.
Because the industry sector changes rapidly, the time frame for electricity investment decisions has shortened from about 10 years to five years, or even three, he said.
Tseng said he hopes to hold more talks with the technology and renewable energy industries, as well as others, to discuss electricity market rules and ways to cooperate.
Taiwan’s electricity supply is sufficient and Tapower can meet the country’s industrial development needs, Tseng said.
He cited Taiwan’s global ranking in investment in natural gas-fired power generation, third in 2024 and sixth last year, as evidence of the rapid pace of investment in power generation.
However, he said that electricity demand from artificial intelligence applications could grow exponentially.
If companies build their own data centers or keep computing operations on-site to protect trade secrets, demand for computing power in Taiwan could also become more difficult to predict, he said.
Taipower is closely monitoring electricity distribution and the growth in demand for high-voltage power, Tseng said.
Meeting the rapidly growing demand for computing power would require not only enough electricity generation, but also a grid that can deliver power where and when it is needed, while coordinating with renewable energy sources and energy storage systems, he said.

NZ bank in free speech row over sheep memes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:38 UTC
01:42:38 KST

A bank in New Zealand has found itself at the center of an unlikely free speech row after an attempt to remove “explicit” memes about its sheep mascot from social media.
Kiwibank unveiled the mascot “Buck” this year in an ad campaign urging consumers to “bank Kiwi.”
However, the cute sheep with green wool quickly drew some unwanted attention online, with viral posts on social media alluding to Buck’s good looks — and uncharitable references to stereotypes about New Zealanders.
Photo: AFP
The state-owned bank responded by sending takedown requests, removing the image of Buck in the offending posts and leaving only the phrase: “this media has been disabled in response to a report by the copyright owner.”
Users responded by barraging the platform with dozens more in its place, and the original post has now garnered more than 4 million views.
A social media user said: “what if we ALL say the kiwibank sheep is sexy. They can’t get us all.”
Commentators described it as a classic example of the so-called “Streisand effect” — in which an attempt to hide something draws even greater attention to it.
Kiwibank spokesman Ben Mabon said the company had been responding to “explicit and harmful content being shared using Buck’s image.”
“Our concern was a serious one, and we believed it was important to address it,” he said in a statement. “We recognise that the response became part of a conversation. We felt doing nothing wasn’t the right thing to do because of the harmful content.”
In an open letter to Kiwibank, New Zealand’s Free Speech Union accused the company of censorship.
“Copyright protects creative work from being copied. It does not protect a brand from being laughed at, even by people who like it a bit too much,” the letter read. “Using copyright to remove speech a company dislikes is censorship, even when the subject is a sheep.”
New Zealand has long been known for having more sheep than people, with a ratio of 4.5 sheep to every person as of last year.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:42:38 UTC

The Philadelphia Eagles kicked a go-ahead field goal with 8 seconds left in London.
And they lost.
That is how things have been going for the Eagles these days.
Photo: AP
The Jaguars pulled off an improbable 19-17 victory on Cam Little’s 57-yard field goal as time expired at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Sunday.
The Eagles have lost three in a row and are 2-3 for the first time since 2021.
Jalen Hurts had led a late-game drive to set up Jake Elliott’s 48-yard field goal, giving the Eagles a 17-16 lead.
All they had to do was finish off the final 8 seconds, but the ensuing kickoff was kept inbounds and Ameer Abdullah returned it 53 yards, leaving 1 second on the clock.
Enough time for Little to send it through the uprights.
Eagles coach Nick Sirianni did not sugarcoat it.
“I didn’t make the right decision, and it cost us the game,” he said. “There’s no other way around it. There’s nothing really else to say about that. It’s just I didn’t do my job good enough in that situation.”
Sirianni fielded several questions about the fateful kickoff, owning the loss.
“There’s really nothing else to say. I didn’t make the decision — the right decision in that situation,” he said. “They returned it to where they returned it, and then they made a kick. You know, credit to them on that. Again, bad job by me.”
In some ways, Sunday’s game had seemed a tough task for the Eagles. They only arrived in London on Saturday and were undermanned.
They played without injured leading rusher Saquon Barkley and his backup, Tank Bigsby, who was placed on injured reserve this past week. They were missing wide receiver DeVonta Smith and had a patchwork offensive line after the retirement of Lane Johnson and the trade of Cam Jurgens.
The Eagles rushed for only 22 yards but Hurts kept them in contention by spreading the ball around to multiple receivers and converting on 6 of 15 third down attempts — a week after going 0 for 12 on third down.
Hurts completed 21 of 40 passes for 220 yards and one touchdown. His 62-yard touchdown pass to Darius Cooper gave Philly a 14-7 lead in the second quarter.
However, he missed open receivers.
“We didn’t perform well enough. I didn’t perform well enough, and that obviously starts with me,” Hurts said. “I’ll be thinking about all the different things that ultimately I could have done. I always use them as learning lessons, so I think that’s what’s great. We’ve got to learn from it.”

Man City defeat Liverpool amid future uncertainty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:37 UTC
01:42:37 KST

Manchester City survived a hostile reception at Anfield in their first match since a guilty verdict on widespread financial impropriety, but a 3-0 win over Liverpool highlighted the uncertainty that surrounds the Premier League season.
Enzo Maresca’s men are sitting pretty at the top of the table with six consecutive wins, including away victories at their two biggest rivals after also beating Manchester United last month.
Yet those points could count for nothing unless City successfully appeal the findings of an independent commission that found them guilty of more than 100 Premier League charges.
Photo: AP
No sanction has yet been decided. However, if City’s appeal fails, a severe points deduction that could lead to relegation or even expulsion from the English top-flight is on the table.
There is even the prospect of three Premier League titles City won between 2009 and 2018, the period to which the charges relate, being stripped.
For a league that frequently boasts of its huge global audience, the prospect of an appeal process dragging on for months, leaving a question mark over every City result and what it means for other Premier League clubs, is a damaging one.
“This is not good for the Premier League right now. That’s what I’ve just recognized today,” former Manchester United captain turned pundit Gary Neville told Sky Sports. “This is really bad for the Premier League and it’s going to continue for a few months.”
Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola said that “the uncertainty is not good for anyone”.
Defeat leaves the Reds nine points behind City, down in ninth in the table.
Even if Liverpool turn out to be not strong enough to challenge for the title, the three points lost on Sunday could be vital in the battle for a place in the Champions League.
Sanctions against City could have an impact on the battle for relegation.
“That today, what does it mean going forward?” Former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher told Sky Sports. “This has to be done before the end of the season. There’s no way this can carry on to the end of the season because we’re all getting kidded.”
Liverpool feel scorned by the revelations of City’s wrongdoing more than most, having finished second to them three times in the past 12 years.
City’s rivals say that the illegal spending during that 2009-2018 period built the foundations for a golden era that continues to bear fruit.
Liverpool were toothless without the injured Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo on Sunday, forcing Andoni Iraola to give 21-year-old Lewis Koumas his Premier League debut up front.
By contrast, Maresca had the luxury of bringing Jeremy Doku off the bench early in the second half in a substitution that transformed the game.
Moments later the Belgian winger provoked a second yellow card for Ryan Gravenberch and Liverpool never recovered.
Doku had a hand in the first and third City goals, scored by Erling Haaland and Rayan Cherki, either side of his own sumptuous strike into the top corner.
That strength in depth has been fundamental in City’s rise to becoming the dominant force in English soccer since an Abu Dhabi-backed takeover in 2008.
As chants, banners, flags and scarves at Anfield showed, City stand accused of cheating their way to the top.
But the investigation has left the rest of the Premier League stuck in stasis, waiting for a case that began eight years ago to finally be over.

Qīngqīng: Zhè jǐ nián lùyíng yuèláiyuè liúxíng le. Yóuqí shì “háohuá lùyíng”, búyòng zìjǐ dā zhàngpéng, hěn shìhé xīnshǒu.

Huáhua: Nà gēn zhù fàndiàn hǎoxiàng méi shénme bù yíyàng.
清清：露營最大的好處就是可以親近大自然，晚上還能看滿天星星。
Qīngqīng: Lùyíng zuì dà de hǎochù jiù shì kěyǐ qīnjìn dàzìrán, wǎnshàng hái néng kàn mǎntiān xīngxing.
華華：聽起來很吸引人，我也想去體驗看看。

清清：秋天的天氣最適合露營，不管是山上還是平地的露營地都很搶手，你要去的話，得提早預約才行。
Qīngqīng: Qiūtiān de tiānqì zuì shìhé lùyíng, bùguǎn shì shānshàng háishì píngdì de lùyíngdì dōu hěn qiǎngshǒu, nǐ yào qù dehuà děi tízǎo yùyuē cái xíng.
翻譯 Translation
Huahua: Lately, I’ve seen lots of friends sharing camping photos on Instagram. The beautiful starry sky and warm campfire make the whole scene look amazing.
Qingqing: Camping has become more and more popular in recent years, especially “glamping.” You don’t have to set up your own tent, so it’s great for beginners.
Huahua: Really? I’ve always thought camping was a lot of trouble. There’s nothing I hate more than a hassle.
Qingqing: These days, many campsites have beds and air conditioning, and some even have cafes.
Huahua: That doesn’t sound much different from staying at a hotel.
Qingqing: The best thing about camping is that you can get close to nature, and at night you can enjoy a sky full of stars.
Huahua: That sounds really appealing. I’d like to give it a try too.
Qingqing: Autumn weather is perfect for camping. Whether you want to camp in the mountains or on flat ground, campsites are in high demand. If you want to go there, you have to book early.

1. 露營 (lùyíng) go camping; camp
2. 分享 (fēnxiǎng) share
3. 星空 (xīngkōng) starry sky
4. 豪華露營 (háohuá lùyíng) glamping; luxury camping
5. 搭帳篷 (dā zhàngpéng) pitch a tent; set up a tent
6. 吸引 (xīyǐn) attract; appeal to
7. 體驗 (tǐyàn) experience; try out
8. 搶手 (qiǎngshǒu) in high demand; highly sought-after

====================================================================================================

AI will make ‘bad things’ happen, Sam Altman says. Exhibit A: needless death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:35 UTC
01:42:35 KST

OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman has some words about his company and the future of artificial intelligence (AI).
“One of the differences between us and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency” to use it, Altman told Politico’s new technology podcast and newsletter Decoded.
The statement — and the approach it represents — is problematic, to say the least. It is also emblematic of precisely the kind of world-building and world-destroying that is happening with today’s technology in front of all our eyes, with precious little input from the rest of us.
Illustration: Yusha
Altman’s mention of the “bad things” that AI might bring makes it sound like AI’s failures mistakenly create innocent, minor problems or even silly little episodes, such as the time when Google’s “AI Overviews” told users to put nontoxic glue on pizza so the cheese would be less likely to slide off. Good advice is helpful. Bad advice? Chalk it up to being a bad thing.
However, culinary adventurism is hardly the only realm that AI operates in and the damage AI is inflicting has already and repeatedly proven itself to be dangerous and even potentially deadly to humans.
OpenAI is embroiled in a lawsuit after the tragic suicide of Adam Raine, a 16-year-old student who initially began using OpenAI’s ChatGPT to help him with his homework. The family’s lawsuit says that the teenager took his own life with the chatbot’s encouragement. (OpenAI has claimed Raine misused the platform.)
Raine’s action is not the only one. OpenAI is facing multiple lawsuits filed by different families of victims of suicide and self-harm.
Nor is suicide the only “bad thing” to emerge in the AI universe. On Feb. 28, on the first day of the war in Iran, two Tomahawk missiles struck the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Iran, killing at least 120 children. (A UN fact-finding mission concluded that the US was probably responsible for the strike.)
In an investigation into the attack, Bloomberg News reported that an AI-linked system — Palantir’s Maven — was used to target the school.
Unnamed defense officials told Bloomberg that “inside Centcom [US Central Command], which conducted the US attack, some personnel relied too much on the artificial intelligence embedded in Maven Smart System.” The report added that “in the past year, the Defense Department has rapidly made Maven a cornerstone of the US military apparatus.”
AI is helping to produce these tragic and needless deaths, but bad things happen.
There is also the little detail that the US might have come within a hair’s breadth of starting a major war against a superpower, all due to an AI error.
CNN last month reported that an unidentified AI chatbot used by the US military determined that a Chinese ship in Middle Eastern waters was carrying components of a nuclear weapons program. CNN US planes took off on an interception mission and US military personnel were preparing to board the ship, CNN said.
Only then did the military look more closely at the report they were basing the mission on and realize the chatbot’s mistakes.
Also found in CNN’s story is that the analyst who used the chatbot to come up with the shoddy analysis then used AI again to write the report, which set the whole thing in motion. A twofer of bad things.
Why does it seem that these technologies — which an executive order by US President Donald Trump said are “empowering Americans to achieve what was previously impossible across science, medicine, and nearly every other domain of human endeavor” — get such serious stuff so wrong and so often?
Is it not true that the more people rely on AI, the more dangerous these little mistakes become? Why were Americans never consulted about any of this in the first place?
Could it be that what is behind the AI revolution might be less about the utopian or dystopian future that is just around the corner and more about the enormous amount of money that is being poured into these companies in the present?
AI might be the only thing keeping Trump’s economy afloat right — and it is paying dividends. According to the New Yorker, OpenAI “is reportedly preparing for an initial public offering at a potential valuation of a trillion dollars” and Sam Altman “may become one of the wealthiest and most powerful people on the planet.”
Those bad things? They only happen to other people.
Meanwhile, we are being warned almost every day that AI systems are getting so smart that they would end humanity.
Maybe the real worry is not that the machines are taking over, but that the humans are giving up, ceding control and responsibility in the name of hyping up a product that has shown itself as being really good at taking jobs away from people, stealing the intellectual property of others, writing some piss-poor undergraduate essays, spying on you and your license plates, and bringing us to the brink of World War III because God forbid humans should actually question the output from machines — or the makers of those machines.
What we need is real, tangible and enforceable government oversight over these technologies, which are quickly becoming a dominating force in all our lives. We must collectively have the right to decide how AI should be used.
Despite what you might hear, China already regulates its AI companies quite aggressively.
Instead, Trump, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang believe that the AI companies should regulate themselves, so they have come up with something called the AI Accords.
Signed by leaders of Meta, Nvidia, Google, Anthropic, xAI and OpenAI, the accords ask tech companies to “implement robust internal controls and monitor the capabilities and alignment of its models,” among other things. “Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations,” it states.
I am not holding my breath.
Trump, who has ordered the term artificial intelligence be discarded for “super intelligence,” posted the accord on social media on Sept. 29. The document, titled The White House Accord on Super Intelligence, can still be seen on his account and the White House’s official account. It is signed by all six tech leaders and Trump, who in the document is labeled “President of the Unites States.”
Super intelligence, indeed.
Moustafa Bayoumi is the author of How Does It Feel To Be a Problem? Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. He is an English professor at Brooklyn College, City University of New York.

Four questioned over software used in government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:33 UTC
01:42:33 KST

Prosecutors yesterday searched 10 locations and questioned four people over allegations that Chinese-developed software was repackaged and marketed as Taiwanese for use by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Three companies allegedly disguised Chinese-developed endpoint security management software as a Taiwanese product to secure more than NT$20 million (US$627,058) in ministry procurement contracts over three years, prosecutors said.
The Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office directed the searches and questioning as part of an investigation into suspected violations of the Government Procurement Act (政府採購法).
Photo: Wu Sheng-ju, Taipei Times
The software, called IP-guard, was developed by Chinese company Guangzhou Yixin Technology (廣州溢信科技), investigators said.
A person associated with Information Security Technology Corp (安和科技), surnamed Lu (呂), allegedly arranged for the software to be repackaged through other companies, investigators said.
Ewill Technology (鎰威科技) allegedly modified the user interface, allowing a product with Chinese technological origins to be marketed as Taiwanese-developed, they said.
Kunyou Technology (坤侑科技) allegedly tendered the software for ministry information technology (IT) asset management software contracts from 2023 to last year, winning more than NT$20 million in contracts over the three years, prosecutors said.
Potential uses of the software include inventorying computer equipment, monitoring software usage and controlling access to data.
The issue came to light in December last year, when the ministry discovered irregularities during a routine inspection of its information systems.
The software was installed on computers at the ministry’s overseas missions for internal IT asset management.
Some of the software’s code was reported to be linked to a Chinese company, raising suspicions that the product supplied differed from the Taiwanese-developed software described in the bid. The ministry subsequently notified the Ministry of Justice Investigation Bureau.
The bureau’s New Taipei City Field Division traced the software’s development, modification and bidding processes to clarify the relationships between the three Taiwanese companies and Guangzhou Yixin.
As of press time last night, Lu; two people associated with Kunyou, surnamed Chiang (江) and Chan (詹); and a person associated with Ewill, surnamed Wu (吳), were being questioned.

China’s unequal treatment
Twenty-seven Japanese lawmakers, led by Keiji Furuya, chairman of the Japan-Taiwan Friendship Parliamentary League, visited Taiwan this month for the Double Ten National Day celebrations, where they met with President William Lai (賴清德) and other senior Taiwanese officials. Such visits have become routine for Japanese lawmakers, drawing little public reaction from Beijing. However, for South Korean lawmakers, it has been a different story.
Recent visits to Taiwan by South Korean members of the National Assembly have prompted not only strong protests from China, but also tangible diplomatic repercussions.
In August, Beijing refused to issue visas for South Korean lawmakers Kim Gi-hyeon of the People Power Party (PPP) and Kwak Sang-eon of the Democratic Party after they visited Taiwan earlier this year. The controversy drew attention in South Korea because both lawmakers are prominent figures domestically. Kim previously led the PPP when it was South Korea’s ruling party under former South Korean president Yoon Suk-yeol. Kwak is the son-in-law of former South Korean president Roh Moo-hyun.
Accordingly, no South Korean lawmakers were listed among the foreign parliamentary delegations attending this year’s National Day celebrations.
Last year, South Korea was Taiwan’s third-largest trading partner, while Taiwan was South Korea’s fourth-largest. In both countries’ rankings, their trade with each other surpassed their trade with Japan.
Instead of forever making concessions to Beijing, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung’s administration should recognize that Chinese diplomatic pressure has crossed party lines, with Kwak, a member of Lee’s Democratic Party, among the lawmakers targeted over visits to Taiwan.
Moreover, China treats Seoul and Tokyo differently. In 2016, Seoul agreed to deploy the US Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system, in response to North Korea’s growing nuclear missile threat. China fiercely opposed the decision. South Korea subsequently faced severe economic pressure affecting tourism, retail and entertainment. Japan has long maintained its own ballistic missile defense architecture, the US Aegis Ballistic Missile Defense system, which is similar in function to THAAD. Yet South Korea faced particularly intense Chinese economic sanctions over its missile defense decision.
That Beijing bullies South Korea in particular while applying different standards to Japan should raise questions among Seoul’s decisionmakers.
Alan Jeong
Northwestern University, Illinois

Machinery exports rising: industry group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:32 UTC
01:42:32 KST

Taiwan’s machinery exports rose again last month, driven mainly by shipments of electronic equipment amid strong demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications and semiconductors, the Taiwan Association of Machinery Industry said yesterday.
Outbound shipments of machinery products increased 29.9 percent from a year earlier to US$3.437 billion, the 20th consecutive monthly increase, the association said in a report.
Last month’s strong performance led third-quarter machinery exports to grow 22.14 percent year-on-year to US$10.184 billion, data from the association showed. In the first three quarters, overall exports reached US$27.98 billion, up 20.3 percent from a year earlier, the data showed.
Photo: EPA
Driven by strong orders the industry has received, shipments in the fourth quarter are expected to continue showing positive growth, the association said. In addition, full-year exports and output value are forecast to hit record levels, it said.
Taiwan’s machinery products comprise mainly electronic equipment, inspection and testing equipment, power transmission components and machine tools.
Shipments of electronic equipment saw the largest growth, rising 61 percent to US$700.57 million last month and increasing 46.1 percent to US$5.55 billion in the first three quarters, association data showed.
Machine tool exports were relatively low compared with other product categories, down 1.8 percent to US$167 million last month and down 1.9 percent to US$1.492 billion in the first three quarters, the data showed.
The association attributed the decline to an unfavorable New Taiwan dollar exchange rate compared with the Japanese yen and South Korean won, undercutting Taiwanese competitiveness.
The US remained the largest buyer of Taiwanese machinery products in the first three quarters, with purchases worth US$7.287 billion, accounting for 26 percent of exports, association data showed.
China ranked second, with purchases of US$5.895 billion for a 21.1 percent share of exports. Singapore followed with purchases of US$2.122 billion and accounting for 7.6 percent of the total, the data showed.
The association said the local machinery industry should be able to maintain steady growth ahead, thanks to strong demand for semiconductors and AI servers boosting shipments of electronic equipment and inspection and testing equipment.
However, geopolitical conflicts and export control policies of some countries, such as those concerning high-tech and rare earths, could impact global supply chains. If the availability of key components becomes an issue, it might affect Taiwanese manufacturers’ order visibility and export outlook going forward, it said.

Digital expense refund service portal launched
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:30 UTC
01:42:30 KST

The Ministry of Digital Affairs yesterday launched a digital expense reimbursement service portal to reduce the time needed to process reimbursements of social welfare subsidies.
Ministry data showed that the government processes about 4,000 requests from 1,300 social welfare groups for reimbursement of social welfare subsidies a year, with the amount of funds involved topping approximately NT$1.5 billion (US$47 million).
Under the traditional system, applicants must submit paper documents, invoices and receipts, all of which have to be manually sorted, attached and checked item by item.
Photo: CNA
“Taiwan is known for being a digital nation, but social welfare groups still have to manually attach supporting documents to application forms for reimbursement of subsidies. As such, the government has decided to digitize the administrative process to meet the needs of social welfare workers,” Minister of Digital Affairs Lin Yi-ching (林宜敬) said in a news conference in Taipei.
The portal allows applicants to upload images of invoices, uses artificial intelligence to identify information on the receipts and automatically enters the information to their respective fields, reducing data entry time and errors, the ministry said.
The digital expense reimbursement service portal is only the beginning of the digitization of administrative procedures, Lin said, adding that the ministry could use similar models in other government systems that also need fund reimbursements.
With the newly developed portal, the processing time for a reimbursement request for welfare subsidies could be reduced from 10 days to one day, the digital affairs ministry said.
The portal also allows applicants to upload documents missing in the applications and application status, it added.
The digital affairs ministry and the Ministry of Health and Welfare discussed the development of the service portal for two to three years, said Chen Shu-mei (陳淑美), chief secretary of health ministry’s Social and Family Affairs Administration.
“We are planning to migrate to the new system in phases. National welfare organizations that handle reimbursement of subsidies from the Public Welfare Lottery surplus and other welfare programs would first use the portal as a trial operation. We will also test the portal at the local level by working with government officials in Tainan, Chiayi and Yunlin counties,” she said.
“When the portal officially operates next year, both paper-based and digital application processes would remain in place. The goal is to achieve full digitalization by 2028,” Chen said.

Six of new F-16s complete factory test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:30 UTC
01:42:30 KST

Six of Taiwan’s 66 newly purchased F-16V Block 70 jets from the US have completed factory acceptance and rolled off the production line, Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo (顧立雄) said yesterday as he expressed hopes for more deliveries later this month.
Two arrived at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung County on Oct. 2, he said at a meeting of the legislature’s Foreign Affairs and National Defense Committee meeting.
Under the air force’s Phoenix Rising program, US defense contractor Lockheed Martin and Taiwan’s Aerospace Industrial Development Corp (漢翔) upgraded 140 F-16A/B jets to the F-16V configuration, completing the program in December 2023. Separately, the air force’s Phoenix Soaring program allocated NT$247.23 billion (US$7.751 billion) to procure 66 new F-16V Block 70 jets.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) lawmakers Lai Shyh-bao (賴士葆) and Ma Wen-chun (馬文君) asked about the delivery schedule for the F-16V jets and whether the aircraft were equipped with the Viper Shield electronic warfare pods.
Koo said six aircraft had passed flight tests and completed acceptance procedures. Of those, two had returned to Taiwan, two were at a US base for training, and two were undergoing testing.
More aircraft were expected to pass acceptance procedures this month, he said.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
The Ministry of National Defense hopes additional jets would arrive in Taiwan this month, he said, adding that the ministry would work with the air force’s project office to expedite the arrival of aircraft that have passed flight tests.
Lai asked whether all 66 aircraft could be delivered by the end of next year, to which, Koo said the ministry would make every effort and continue coordinating with the US, but he could not make any commitments.
Air Force Chief of Staff Lieutenant General Lee Ching-jan (李慶然) said some Viper Shield AN/ALQ-254(V)1 electronic warfare pods had been installed, while software development was ongoing. Both were proceeding according to the schedule, he said.
The electronic warfare system needs to be integrated with the new aircraft’s other systems, and integration testing was proceeding as scheduled, Koo said.
Meanwhile, the ministry in a report to the legislature has proposed scrapping the maximum length of service for air force pilots amid a shortage of experienced pilots, many of whom leave the military to fly for civilian airlines.
It cited defense needs in proposing to remove the cap, which would apply to some experienced pilots.
If the Cabinet approves the proposal and it takes effect, the ministry aims to retain 74 pilots ranked lieutenant colonel or colonel in service longer, according to the report.
Under the Act of Military Service for Officers and Non-commissioned Officers of the Armed Forces (陸海空軍軍官士官服役條例), pilots holding the rank of lieutenant colonel can serve a maximum of 26 years and colonels a maximum of 30 years.
That means pilots at these ranks must generally leave military service at about 48 and 52 years of age, respectively, the report said.
As a result, many military pilots leave the air force before reaching their service limits so they can join civilian airlines sooner. Airline pilots can work until 65 and earn significantly higher salaries, the report said.
It said the ministry proposed adding positions under a special staffing program and extending service for experienced lieutenant colonel and colonels who have served for at least 14 years and meet high qualification standards. Under the proposal, they could retain their current rank and voluntarily extend their service until age 58, without being subject to the usual service-length limits.
Based on publicly available data, colonel and lieutenant colonel-level pilots earn up to about NT$300,000 a month with additional allowances and retention bonuses. The average monthly salary for airline captains is NT$400,000 to NT$500,000.

IMF boss gases up economic, job changes from AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:27 UTC
01:42:27 KST

Strong investment in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure is keeping global growth at about 3 percent, yielding major benefits for many Asian economies that supply the hardware, such as Thailand, IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva said yesterday.
The AI investment boom was already delivering a “demand shock, an investment shock” that could boost growth in advanced Asian economies by a half to one full percentage point, and emerging Asian economies by 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point, she said.
“AI, love it, hate it. It’s already here,” Georgieva said.
Photo: EPA
“That shift into higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at around 3 percent, despite the fact we are being dragged down by the energy supply shock,” she told hundreds of participants on the first day of a weeklong set of meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok.
The IMF in July forecast global growth at 3 percent for this year. It should release an update today.
Georgieva said AI amounted to a “slow-moving tsunami” that would have profound consequences for jobs, growth, education and even how governments generate revenue through taxation, given the expected shift from labor to capital.
The IMF estimates that AI could lead to 40 percent of jobs being augmented, downgraded or eliminated over time, she said. A study said that 10 percent of jobs in the US already required AI skills. While routine, repetitive jobs were shrinking, low-paying jobs were increasing in two lower-paying sectors, construction and data centers.
“It is a transformative technology. It so completely changes how we work, how we live,” she said, saying that an AI assistant gave her a 30 second message about her schedule each day.
Many of the firms building the needed infrastructure are in Asia, Georgieva said, speaking of Thailand, host of this year’s annual meetings.
World Bank president Ajay Banga, who has made jobs a central focus of his presidency, said the development bank was focused on leveraging “small AI,” which is not dependent on large language models, to generate enormous productivity gains for farmers, healthcare systems, educators and others in emerging markets.
Singaporean President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking at the same event, said governments should address how AI was reducing jobs for graduates.
“There is a particular problem that we have to address very soon... and that is that, the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand,” he said.
He said the world should guard against AI resulting in a “new divergence” in growth and job creation between developing and advanced economies.
“AI is going to widen the divergence if we are too passive about it,” he said. “So we’ve got to do everything we can to first use AI to create good jobs and to create jobs that can be done well by human beings, can allow them to ride up a career ladder despite AI.”

Taiwan building bridges of peace, knowledge: Lai
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:27 UTC
01:42:27 KST

The Taiwan Bridges Program has built bridges of knowledge, generations and peace, President William Lai (賴清德) said at the program’s closing ceremony at National Taiwan University in Taipei yesterday.
The program was launched by Academia Sinica and the university in November last year in collaboration with 12 academic or research institutions and the International Peace Foundation.
A total of 31 Nobel Prize laureates were invited to Taiwan for exchanges within seven months of the program’s launch.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
Lai, serving as the program’s honorary chairman, said in his address he expects Taiwan to become an anchor around which international scientific exchanges and conversations revolve.
“The program has built three bridges,” he said.
Firstly, “the bridge of knowledge” invited the world’s cutting-edge knowledge into Taiwan while bringing Taiwan’s academic researchers to the world, Lai said.
Faced with climate change, artificial intelligence, pandemic threats and shifting geopolitics, no country can find all of the answers on its own, he said, adding Taiwan must work with the world to ask the right questions and seek solutions together.
Secondly, “the bridge between generations” brought 31 world-changing academics to school campuses in Taiwan to deliver lectures, Lai said.
The students attending the lectures could become influential scientists in two decades and contribute to the world, he said.
Third, “the bridge of peace” encourages researchers of different fields to think how they can leverage their expertise to add to global peace and prosperity, he said.
Referring to the vision he outlined in November last year of Taiwan producing three more Nobel laureates within 30 years, Lai said the government would enhance basic research and higher education, support researchers in exploring the unknown, and expand international research collaborations and talent exchanges.
It would seek to turn initial encounters into long-term partnerships and bring together the government, foundations and broader society to build a stable, long-term support system, he said.

Brewers lead Dodgers 1-0 in league championship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:26 UTC
01:42:26 KST

Brice Turang homered and Milwaukee’s bullpen kept the Los Angeles Dodgers in check on Sunday as the Brewers triumphed 2-1 in game one of baseball’s National League Championship Series.
One year after they were unceremoniously swept by the Dodgers in the NLCS, the Brewers thrilled fans in Milwaukee, landing the first blow in the best-of-seven series that sends the victor to the World Series.
The Dodgers are chasing a rare World Series three-peat. The Brewers, who led the MLB with 103 regular-season wins, showed they do not plan on going quietly this year as they seek to return to the championship showcase for just the second time, 44 years after their 1982 loss to the St. Louis Cardinals.
Photo: AFP
The game was billed as a duel between the Dodgers’ two-time Cy Young Award-winner Tarik Skubal and the Brewers’ flamethrowing ace Jacob Misiorowski, but neither pitcher made it to the sixth inning.
The Dodgers wore down a sometimes shaky Misiorowski but were rewarded with just one run against him in the second inning.
Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani walked on four pitches to open the frame, advanced to second on a Teoscar Hernandez single and scored on a one-out single from Andy Pages.
Kyle Tucker worked a walk in a 10-pitch at-bat to load the bases. However, Enrique Hernandez hit into a double play, and Misiorowski escaped the inning without any more damage.
“I didn’t think I had my best stuff,” Misiorowski said. “Obviously good enough to make it work. Props to my defense behind me and all the support they gave me.”
Turang tied it with a solo homer off Skubal to open the bottom of the fourth inning, and the Brewers seized a 2-1 lead in the fifth on Luis Lara’s run-scoring single off Skubal.
Turang, who had fouled a ball off his knee in his prior at-bat, said he was trying to avoid a repeat when he delivered his second career postseason homer.
“I was like, I’m going to stay inside of this one,” he said. “Not try to do too much, just drive back up the middle and get inside of it. I just got it... sometimes less is more.”
One inning later, Lara put the Brewers ahead. Garrett Mitchell had walked to open the bottom of the fifth and reached second on a sacrifice bunt from Cooper Pratt before Lara cracked a ball up the middle that allowed Mitchell to score.
The Brewers bullpen made the lead stand up with four relievers combining for four and two-thirds scoreless innings.
“That bullpen really showed up today and did amazing,” Misiorowski said. “And then just the guys laying down a sac bunt to get a guy over and a clutch base hit by Lara — just, you know, our way.”

Russia hits Ukraine despite Trump deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:24 UTC
01:42:24 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy yesterday said that Russia has continued to strike Ukraine’s energy facilities even after US President Donald Trump said a day earlier that the warring countries had agreed on an energy ceasefire.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, Zelenskiy said Ukraine had learned through media reports that Trump had secured an energy ceasefire deal with Russia, which would involve a mutual pause in strikes on energy sites.
Zelenskiy said he would be willing to honor such an agreement, if Moscow did the same.
Photo: AFP
“We support it, but I have not heard approval of this proposal from the Russian side,” Zelenskiy said.
Trump’s brief social media post on Sunday claiming the purported agreement offered few details, but said that the energy ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: “Do not break it!”
However, Zelenskiy said Ukraine had been “horribly surprised” that following Trump’s “sudden but very important post,” Russia had struck numerous energy facilities including a power plant in the northeastern city of Kharkiv, as well as a gas production facility and a civilian gas station.
“It was clear that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin does not read Truth Social,” Zelenskiy said, referring to Trump’s social media platform.
Trump previously announced a similar agreement on ceasing energy strikes that did not come to fruition. In a social media post on Sept. 14, he said both countries had agreed “not to hit” each other’s energy infrastructure, but offered no details on that proposal either.
Russia has used attacks on energy facilities to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as “weaponizing winter,” and fear Russia could ramp up such attacks as cold weather approaches.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has leveled strikes against Russian energy sites like oil refineries, sometimes deep within Russian territory, prompting Trump to blame Zelenskiy for high diesel prices on world markets.
On Friday, Trump struck a deal with Putin to import Russian diesel to address high fuel prices just weeks ahead of US midterm elections.
Yesterday, Zelenskiy said Kyiv was ready to comply with Trump’s requests to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine’s energy system, and asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree. He added that if Moscow does not agree to an energy ceasefire this winter, “we will respond.”
“We are waiting for the details of the conversation between the Americans and the Russians, and we are waiting to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take,” he said. “This energy ceasefire can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war.”
The EU’s top diplomat yesterday welcomed the prospect of a pause in energy strikes in Ukraine, particularly as winter approaches, but said she sees no sign that Russia would be willing to respect it.
“We haven’t yet seen that also Russia will stick to it,” EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said at a meeting of the bloc’s foreign ministers in Luxembourg. “Personally, I would also welcome that the ceasefire would include people not being killed, not only energy.”
Ukrainian and European officials reacted with dismay to Trump’s diesel deal with Putin, saying it would help fund Russia’s war effort.
Estonian Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna yesterday told reporters in Luxembourg that he does not believe the deal “is actually going to change anything” in terms of fuel prices, and that it is ”much more connected to the domestic situation in the US.”

16:42:24 UTC
01:42:24 KST

A fresh Houthi strike on Sunday hit Riyadh’s international airport, killing one person and wounding 11 others, a day after a deadly attack claimed by the Yemeni group forced authorities to suspend operations there.
Saturday’s attack, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, was a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Riyadh has long militarily supported the internationally recognized government against the Houthis.
The Iran-backed group on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the previous 24 hours, including on the airport, and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom’s transit hubs, calling them “a theater of operations for our forces.”
Photo: the Saudi Ministry of Media via AFP
Hours later, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group reported that a projectile struck King Khalid International Airport, sparking a fire.
Air defenses also intercepted a missile nearby, it added.
The fresh attack on the airport killed one person — a Pakistani resident — and wounded 11 others, Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said on social media.
“The attack also caused property damage, the extent of which is currently being assessed,” it said.
Authorities have extended the closure of the airport by 24 hours, the tracking site Flightradar24 said on social media.
Multiple blasts were heard in the Saudi capital on Sunday.
“The birds went into a frenzy after the sound. The whole house shook,” a resident said.
The civil aviation authority also reported another attack on Dammam airport in the east — which the Houthis also said they had targeted — a day after the Saudi coalition reported a projectile landing nearby.
Shortly afterward, the coalition reported shooting down a drone, also in the east.
It said early yesterday that it had also “intercepted and destroyed” a Houthi ballistic missile heading for the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, home to a major military base.

Business travel pumping up guest numbers: hotelier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:24 UTC
01:42:24 KST

A surge in travel fueled by Taiwan’s artificial intelligence (AI) boom is driving record guest numbers at Formosa International Hotels Corp (晶華國際酒店), showing the technology sector’s growing impact beyond just the chip industry.
The company, led by chairman Steven Pan (潘思亮), is on track for record revenue and profit this year, he said in an interview at the Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore on Thursday last week. Room revenue has increased 10 percent year-to-date, while sales at its luxury retail business have jumped 20 percent due to the AI boom, he said, declining to provide specific figures.
“What it means for the hotel industry is a tremendous increase in business travel because people have to come and buy stuff from Taiwan, make deals in Taiwan,” Pan said.
Photo: CNA
Beyond corporate travel, demand for luxury retail business is being driven by newly affluent domestic customers, whose spending power has been boosted by strong economic growth and a surging stock market, he added.
Taiwan raised its economic growth forecast for the year to more than 11 percent, putting the island on track for its first double-digit expansion since 2010 as demand tied to AI continues to fuel the chip hub’s economy. The upgraded outlook follows growth of 8.76 percent last year.
The AI-driven boom has made Taiwan a standout destination for equity investors. Taiwan’s benchmark stock index has surged more than 70 percent this year, making it the top performer among more than 90 equity gauges tracked by Bloomberg.
International luxury hotel operators are expanding their presence in Taiwan, including InterContinental Hotels Group PLC, which opened a new hotel in Taipei this month.
Pan plans to open two hotels next year in New Taipei City’s Linkou District (林口), where he describes as a future technology hub, as companies including ASML Holding NV and Micron Technology Inc expand their presence in the area. He is also looking to buy a luxury hotel in San Francisco, another tech hub.
“We are looking at undervalued luxury hotels in major gateway cities in America,” Pan said, declining to comment on the deal size. The group plans to open two hotels in Japan next year.

Market rebalancing AI boom investment risks: DBS chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:19 UTC
01:42:19 KST

The market is repricing the risks around investments related to the buildup of artificial intelligence (AI) that could lead to more discipline in financing, according to DBS Group Holdings Ltd chief executive officer Tan Su Shan (陳淑珊).
“The market has spoken,” Tan said in an interview yesterday. “It’s not a bad thing because now, people are asking for higher returns, and people are also looking at structures. They’re making sure that whatever money is now being hoovered into the whole AI capex ecosystem will lead to some kind of long-term ROI [return on investment] that can then be repaid back to debt or bond or equity holders.”
Tan, who leads Southeast Asia’s biggest lender, said weaker firms might see their credit ratings revised downwards, although this risk repricing is “healthy” as the market wants to make sure that big financial commitments are sustainable.
Photo: Bloomberg
Her comments come as tech giants spend billions on AI, and as market gains concentrate in a handful of stocks. Interest rates are rising and bond yields around the world have surged to the highest in decades, increasing the cost of funding the enormous investment needed to build AI infrastructure. PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP estimates Asia’s spending on data centers could reach US$8.2 trillion by 2050.
DBS has originated about S$25 billion (US$19.5 billion) of AI deals this year, often as lead manager on syndicated loans and has held only a fraction of that, Tan said. The financing is mostly for hardware, from semiconductors and memory chips to data centers, she added.
Tan was speaking on the sidelines of DBS’ conference in Singapore focused on key topics such as AI and geopolitics. In her opening comments, Tan said she has not seen this kind of volatility in interest rates for a long time, with equity investors whipsawed by swings in AI stocks.
Tan has made AI key to her strategy since taking the helm in March last year. The Singapore-based bank is starting to see results from large AI projects that are underway to overhaul its work flows and processes, including fee growth and new accounts being opened at a faster pace, she said.
Tan said the wealth management business has long term structural tailwinds as Asia creates more wealth, capital markets deepen and intergenerational wealth transfer happens. While market swings would affect flows in the short term, net new money growth has been “consistently strong,” she added.

Taiwan closely monitoring China drills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:18 UTC
01:42:18 KST

The military is monitoring a series of Chinese live-fire drills along the country’s coast this week, Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo (顧立雄) said yesterday while accusing China of stoking tensions.
Starting from Thursday, the China Maritime Safety Administration announced no-sail notices for five areas, from the South China Sea up to the northeastern province of Liaoning, but none around Taiwan itself.
The closest area to Taiwan is off China’s eastern province of Zhejiang. The drills are scheduled to last all week, according to the notices.
Photo: CNA
Speaking to reporters at the Legislative Yuan, Koo said the preliminary assessment is that these activities were firing drills by coastal artillery and related units.
“However, we adhere to the principle of ‘anticipating the enemy as broadly as possible,’ so we will continue to closely monitor their activities, whether firing or military training,” he said.
China’s repeated military drills aimed at stirring tensions in the Indo-Pacific region warrant close scrutiny and condemnation, he added.
President William Lai (賴清德) in his National Day speech on Saturday said Taiwan cherishes peace but will not give up its freedom, and there must be respect for the right of Taiwanese to exist.
China condemned his remarks, as it always does.
While China has not linked the drills this week to Lai’s speech, on Sunday the Chinese Ministry of National Defense said he was exaggerating the threat from China and trying to “seek independence through force.”
“The People’s Liberation Army’s regular training and exercises around Taiwan are meant to deter reckless ‘Taiwanese independence’ moves and outside interference, and to safeguard the security and well-being of the Taiwanese people. This is entirely justified,” it said.
China’s military operates around Taiwan on an almost daily basis, although it has not held full war games since late December last year, which were in response to an US$11 billion arms sale announced by Washington, the largest ever.
Last week, the US Department of State said China’s maritime actions off Taiwan’s east coast are “deeply destabilizing” and only worsen tension, after Reuters reported the first known sighting of a Chinese militia boat in those waters in August.
Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokeswoman Mao Ning (毛寧) yesterday said those waters belonged to China and its activities there were “beyond reproach.”
“It has never been China that stirs up trouble and undermines stability in this sea,” she told reporters, without elaborating.
Meanwhile, during a meeting of the legislature’s Foreign Affairs and National Defense Committee yesterday, Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Huang Chien-pin (黃建賓) raised concerns over the report of the Chinese maritime militia vessel in August.
Huang asked whether the navy or the coast guard would be responsible for firing the first shot if a militia vessel entered Taiwan’s territorial waters.
Koo said the Coast Guard Administration would take the lead in handling and expelling Chinese maritime militia fishing boats and coast guard vessels that enter Taiwan’s waters, while the navy would provide support under an established assistance agreement.

Brussels finally reads the documents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:14 UTC
01:42:14 KST

On Wednesday last week the European Parliament did something Beijing has spent decades trying to prevent: It read the documents. By 454 votes to 86, with 110 abstentions, members of the European Parliament adopted a recommendation to the European Council, the European Commission and the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas that sets out what EU policy on China says and, more usefully, what it has never said.
Start with the phrase the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) most enjoys misquoting. The EU has a “one China policy,” which acknowledges Beijing’s claim to Taiwan without endorsing it, a distinction any 12-year-old grasps and the Chinese foreign ministry has failed to absorb in 50 years. The “one China principle,” under which Taiwan is already Chinese and merely awaits invasion, belongs to Beijing alone. The parliament notes that the EU has never signed on to that and that this still needs saying is the quiet triumph of Chinese diplomacy: repeat a falsehood in enough joint communiques and people begin apologizing for not believing it.
Then there is UN Resolution 2758. The 1971 General Assembly text decided who would hold China’s seat at the UN, and it says nothing about Taiwan or its sovereignty. Beijing wields it anyway, as a skeleton key to lock Taiwanese out of bodies whose business is health and aviation, forgetting that a virus does not check passports and a plane does not care which flag the controller salutes. The parliament rejects the distortion and the pressure on international organizations that enforces it. It also condemns transnational repression and the extraterritorial reach of Chinese law, which assumes that statutes travel with their citizens, and occasionally with other people’s, to whatever country they land in.
Add the language on forced labor in Xinjiang, repression in Tibet, China’s stance on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and resilience against espionage and hybrid threats, and the text reads less like diplomacy than a well-kept ledger of grievances, itemized and accurate, which in this field counts as a surprise.
A little sobriety is in order. A recommendation binds no one, and the council might nod gravely before returning to lunch. Several member states treat Beijing’s displeasure as weather to be managed with trade delegations and soft adjectives, and the 86 votes against and 110 abstentions suggest that some parliamentarians still mistake silence for prudence, usually until the next cyberattack or tariff retaliation corrects them.
Even so, the direction is correct. Taiwan has been asked for decades to be patient, flexible and creative about its own existence, so it is a relief to see Europe asked, for once, to be clear. The parliament opposes any change to the “status quo” by force or coercion, or against the will of the Taiwanese people, and it urges deeper cooperation on semiconductors and cybersecurity. None of this is radical. It is merely the absence of a lie.
Beijing will answer as it always does, with interference in internal affairs, the wounded feelings of 1.4 billion people and a stern spokesperson using the word “resolutely” at least twice. The facts will not move. The People’s Republic of China was founded in 1949 and has never governed Taiwan for a single day, and a claim to own what you have never ruled is not a principle, but an ambition with a press office.
The time has come for democracies to stop negotiating the meaning of words and decline to repeat the CCP’s rhetoric. Strasbourg has made a start, and a modest one, but starts are where these things begin. Taipei should not thank it too effusively, since Europe has merely done its homework, and the point of homework is that someone eventually hands it in.
Clive Hazell is a Kaohsiung-based writer and educator.

Taiwan condemns Beijing’s political coercion on diplomatic partners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:14 UTC
01:42:14 KST

Taiwan yesterday condemned China for interfering in other nations’ sovereignty and foreign policy through political coercion after Beijing sanctioned ministers from Paraguay and Belize over their diplomatic relations with Taiwan.
Paraguay and Belize are two of just 12 countries to maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan.
At a routine news briefing in Beijing yesterday, Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokeswoman Mao Ning (毛寧) said the sanctions against Paraguayan Minister of Information and Communication Technologies Gustavo Villate and Belizean Minister of Foreign Affairs Francis Fonseca were designed to “penalize them and serve as a warning to others.”
Photo: Lu Yi-hsuen, Taipei Times
“Certain politicians in Paraguay and Belize have willingly served as pawns of the Taiwan authorities in their attempts to seek independence through external support,” she said.
The measures against the Latin American ministers include the freezing of their assets in China, visa denials and the banning of Chinese organizations from doing business with them, the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said earlier.
The ministers had “taken a series of egregious actions and statements ... damaging China’s core interests,” it said, adding that the sanctions were to “safeguard national security” and “oppose separatist activities.”
Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA
The move comes two days after Taiwan celebrated the Double Ten National Day, with President William Lai (賴清德) delivering a speech that promoted the nation’s increasing investment in defense.
Villate marked the Double Ten National Day on social media saying: “Paraguay reaffirms its relationship of friendship and cooperation, based on shared values and principles: the self-determination of peoples, human rights and democracy.”
Fonseca last month met Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) in Belize.
In June, Villate met Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Chen Ming-chi (陳明祺) in Paraguay.
Neither the Paraguayan minister of communications nor the Belizean foreign ministry immediately responded to requests for comment outside of regular office hours.
In Taipei, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned China’s sanctions against the two ministers, describing the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ statement as utterly absurd.
The move openly interfered in other countries’ sovereignty and foreign policy, violated the principles of international law, and showed Beijing’s attempt to force other nations to submit to its political agenda through intimidation and transnational repression, it said.
The foreign ministry reiterated that Taiwan is a sovereign, independent country, and that it and the People’s Republic of China are not subordinate to each other. This is an internationally recognized fact and an objective reality across the Taiwan Strait, it said, adding that China has no right to interfere in Taiwan’s diplomatic relations.
It said Taiwan’s engagement with countries such as Belize and Paraguay has always been based on equality, mutual benefit and respect for each other’s sovereignty, principles it described as a consensus in the international community and a fundamental norm of international relations.
China’s coercive tactics only expose its high-handed and unreasonable behavior, make the world more aware of Beijing’s efforts to undermine the international order through hegemonic practices, and strengthen Taipei’s diplomatic allies in their resolve to support Taiwan, it said.
Hung Pu-chao (洪浦釗), director of the Center for Global Strategy and Democratic Resilience at the University of Taipei, said that Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) last month said at the BRICS summit that international rules should be written collectively by all countries, and that the logic of “might makes right” no longer works and should have been abandoned long ago.
By Xi’s own standards, China’s latest actions amount to the very power politics that Xi himself has said should be abandoned, Hung said.
The sanctions also show how China uses its domestic laws as a tool to exert pressure on other countries, he added.
Additional reporting by Chen Yu-fu

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:13 UTC

A 33-year-old man suspected of stabbing his aunt to death in New Taipei City’s Sinjhuang District (新莊) on Sunday was yesterday arrested in Taoyuan, police said.
The New Taipei City Police Department’s Sinjhuang Precinct said it received a call at about 7pm on Sunday about a stabbing at a home on Yongan Street.
Officers found the victim, a 59-year-old woman surnamed Lin (林), dead in the kitchen, with more than 10 stab wounds to her neck and abdomen, police said.
Photo: Wu Jen-chieh, Taipei Times
The victim’s husband, who found her when he returned home from work, said that their nephew, surnamed Lee (李), had recently moved in with them and had quarreled with Lin earlier that day, police said,
Police used surveillance footage to track Lee’s movements after he left the home at about 2pm on Sunday. He ate at a hot pot restaurant and took the MRT railway to Taipei Main Station, local Chinese-language media reported.
From there, Lee took a train to Taoyuan Station, and then allegedly switched between several forms of transport, traveling to Fengming Station in New Taipei City and Neili (內壢) in Taoyuan before returning to Taoyuan Station, in an apparent attempt to evade surveillance, the reports said.
Lee was arrested in Taoyuan at about noon yesterday, police said.
A preliminary investigation found that Lee was unemployed, and his aunt and uncle had occasionally quarreled with him over his daily habits, police said.
Lee also frequently asked for money to buy alcohol and tobacco, which had led Lin to consider asking him to move out, police said.
Police said they believe that on the day of the killing, Lin allegedly bumped Lee with her shoulder, which he interpreted as deliberate and insulting.
After that, Lee allegedly went out to buy a knife, returned home and stabbed Lin to death, police said.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:13 UTC
01:42:13 KST

Pope Leo XIV on Sunday announced that he would have an operation “in the coming days” for a lump on his lung, saying it had been located “at a very early stage.”
“During recent medical checks, a nodule on my lung was found. It has been detected at a very early stage and is very localized,” the 71-year-old said in a weekly address in St Peter’s Square.
“The doctors believe it would be right to intervene and so, following their advice, I have decided to have the operation to remove it. The operation is already planned in the coming days,” he said.
Photo: Vatican Media via Reuters
Following the pope’s statement during his Angelus prayers, the Vatican press office said the pontiff was expected to have surgery in the next few days, and the expected recovery time from the operation would be about one week.
The operation was to take place in the Gemelli hospital in Rome, which has treated popes since John Paul II.
No information has been given as to whether the surgery would affect the pope’s agenda for international trips. He is next due to go to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov. 6 to 17.
In Chiclayo, a city in Peru that Leo is due to visit, Catholics expressed hope for his quick recovery.
“A lung nodule is no small matter. Let’s hope God grants him the ability to travel by air and that he gets better soon,” Olga Pol, 62, said.
“The people of Peru are eagerly awaiting him,” she added.
“I’m certain that all of Peru is praying for the pope and that he’ll pull through,” retired journalist Diana Celi said. “God willing, we will have him here, because these preparations have been going on for several months — not just on a practical level, but also on a spiritual one.”
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said in a statement that the “calmness with which he spoke during today’s Angelus reassures us.”
She expressed to the pope her “personal closeness, and that of the Italian government, as he confronts this ordeal of the coming days.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy wished Leo a “successful surgery and a swift, full recovery” in a social media post.
“Our thoughts and prayers are with him, and we hope he will soon be back in good health and strength,” he added.
Archbishop Daniel Sturla of Montevideo called on Catholics to pray for the pope’s “speedy recovery” and to continue preparations for his upcoming visit to Uruguay “with even greater enthusiasm.”
Argentina’s bishops’ conference also urged Catholics to join in a special prayer for Leo ahead of the surgery, asking that it “go well” with a “swift and full recovery.”
Chicago-born Leo became the first US pope last year, following the death of his Argentine predecessor, Francis, on April 21.
Leo was elected leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics on May 8 last year.
The former Robert Francis Prevost, while less ebullient than his predecessor, has gradually imprinted his style on the leadership of the Catholic Church, finding his voice as he takes on some of the world’s most pressing issues, from bloody conflicts to artificial intelligence.
After the US and Israel launched a war against Iran in February, the pope became a high-profile critic of the conflict.
