EDITORIAL: Cyberdefense a whole society effort
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:11 UTC
01:42:11 KST

Media reports about personal data breaches affecting at least 68,000 people at several South Korean financial institutions have linked the attacks to the Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) cybersecurity tool ARTEX. The stolen information included customers’ names, phone numbers, annual income and loan application details, data that could be sold to scammers or traded online in other forms, the South Korean Financial Services Commission said.
The incident has drawn significant attention in South Korea and raised concerns globally about what happens when powerful AI tools fall into the wrong hands. Reports of some AI agents — originally designed to find previously unknown software vulnerabilities and weaknesses in their own systems — hacking companies, government agencies and public infrastructure in the past few months have been in the global spotlight, as leading AI labs continued to release ever more advanced models.
However, the South Korean incident is raising eyebrows because it is one of the first confirmed uses of AI tools in large-scale financial sector breaches. It should serve as a wake-up call for Taiwan’s financial institutions, as the nation is a frequent target of similar cross-border, AI-assisted cyberattacks.
ARTEX is an open-source penetration testing program designed to connect with external large language models, such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic PBC’s Claude and DeepSeek’s models, to help organizations automate vulnerability discovery, analyze potential targets, find infiltration routes and deploy security tools in their networks.
US security firm CrowdStrike on Wednesday last week said that the suspect behind the attacks from late last month to early this month was likely a China-based 26-year-old who used ARTEX and Claude Code and was financially motivated. Beyond conducting cyberattacks, the suspect used Claude Code to ask where stolen data in South Korea is traded and to search for Korean Telegram data sales groups.
Considering the risks of the AI tool being misused, the Chinese developer of ARTEX — Autumn-27 — on Thursday announced on code-hosting platform GitHub that it had converted it to a closed-source project and would no longer update it. ARTEX’s GitHub page has also been removed since then, media reports said. While transitioning to a closed-source model would make it harder for new users to create code, concerns persist that it would not prevent existing users from continuing to use downloaded copies. In other words, halting development alone is unlikely to fully block ARTEX-related cyberattacks.
This incident shows a real danger, as malign actors can dramatically accelerate the speed and scale of cyberattacks against high-value targets using agentic AI tools. According to CrowdStrike, the threat actor in the South Korean case acquired infrastructure at multiple IP addresses to establish command-and-control operations, meaning the person did not perform every technical step, but relied on AI assistance to search, organize, test and repeat the process multiple times. Broadly speaking, AI could enable cyberattacks to scale up, and more seriously, enable ordinary people to conduct cyberattacks like professional cyberwarfare outfits.
Using ARTEX or other autonomous AI agents for data breaches signals a new era of accelerated, intelligent cyberwarfare that challenges traditional security controls. Taiwan, like South Korea, is highly digitalized, with financial institutions, e-commerce platforms, telecom operators, Internet portals, government agencies and third-party financial service providers that are highly interconnected.
The real vulnerability of Taiwan’s financial system might not lie in its core banking systems, but in its auxiliary infrastructure, such as internal employee systems, external software vendors, outsourced information technology services providers and mobile support portals, which often represent the weakest link in cybersecurity defenses and tend to be overlooked.
Financial institutions must guard against not only malicious IP addresses or embedded malware, but a whole set of AI-driven attack processes, as breaches by AI agents using ARTEX are active, autonomous and capable of unprecedented speed and scale. In this respect, local financial institutions must shift from periodic manual audits to continuous, automated AI-driven defense mechanisms. In short, the principle is using AI to counter AI threats.
Microsoft Corp’s latest digital defense report showed that Taiwan ranked fourth globally in terms of the severity of various cybersecurity threats in the first half of this year, behind only the US, Israel and Ukraine. Given Taiwan’s unique geopolitical position and China’s relentless cyberattacks, the issue of cybersecurity is no longer just a concept of technical defense, but a broader effort involving all walks of life.

A dominant Max Verstappen won the Singapore Grand Prix for the first time on Sunday, 24 hours after taking the checkered flag in the sprint race at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.
TECHNICAL ISSUES
For the second weekend in a row, software glitches on this year’s generation of cars caused problems.
Photo: Reuters
A week earlier in Malaysia the issue had occurred on a formation lap in the rain where several cars ground to a halt. In Singapore, an erroneous deployment of the “overtake” mode meant some cars in the first sprint qualifying session had more power available than others.
Verstappen is one driver clearly fed up with the difficulty of managing and driving the modern cars, which have a 50-50 split between electrical and internal combustion energy, and called for a return to a simpler life behind the wheel.
“It is very complex now. I just hope the new rule set [for 2027] is easier,” the four-time world champion said in an interview. “The problem is there’s a lot of software in the background that can make you not pull away or there is glitch on slow laps.”
“You have to make sure the battery pack is charging in the right place,” Verstappen said. “That’s not what racing should be about. You should be able to go out, have a brake pedal and a throttle pedal and that’s it.”
WOLFF’S WARPATH
Mercedes boss Toto Wolff had unkind words for the “brainless” critics hiding “behind their screens” who have said the team had favored Kimi Antonelli over George Russell this season.
Championship leader Antonelli, 20, is 102 points ahead of the luckless Russell and on the brink of becoming the youngest world champion in history.
Russel’s retirement in Malaysia a week ago and his consequent engine penalties, as well as crashing while he led the Singapore sprint race, have piled on the agony for the Englishman. Wolff hit back at critics.
“They’re brainless, whoever thinks that. I mean, it’s completely nonsensical. We’ve had it in the past with Lewis fans,” Wolff told reporters. “Do they think I have a button that says, ‘George — engine failure now’?”
“I guess this is maybe where social media goes today. People hide behind their screens and then they lash out,” Wolff said. “Sometimes I read what people write. I find it hilarious. These people really contribute to my own entertainment when they are abusing the team or myself. ‘I’m Satan,’ I’ve heard. So, yeah, overall it’s funny.”

The weekend saw the first time Singapore had hosted an F1 sprint, and drivers seemed to agree it should be the last — unless more overtaking opportunities can be introduced on the Marina Bay Street Circuit.
“I think we shouldn’t host a sprint where you can’t pass,” said double winner Verstappen after a processional weekend of racing on the tight city centre track, only enlivened by heavy rain before Saturday’s sprint.
“The track is great, but also the problem we have at the moment is with the overtake mode, it barely does anything here,” Verstappen said of the electrical boost available to drivers.
Sunday’s 62-lap GP was largely uneventful once the field settled after the start, with only Lewis Hamilton’s blunder on tire choice having an effect on the order of the top six on the grid.
Hamilton was one of many drivers calling for the circuit to be modified to allow more wheel-to-wheel racing.
“I think there’s some adjustments that can be made to make this 100 percent a great circuit,” the seven-time world champion said. “But whether they’re going to do that, I don’t know.”
“I think they need to change the track to maybe a longer straight somewhere in order to allow us to overtake for it to be truly a great racing circuit,” he added.

2026 Elections: Six media outlets invite Chiang and Shen to debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:10 UTC
01:42:10 KST

Six major news outlets including the Chinese-language Liberty Times (the Taipei Times’ sister paper) yesterday formally invited all Taipei mayoral candidates to discuss their policies in a televised debate.
In a joint statement, the Liberty Times, China Television, Taiwan Television, Formosa Television, Mirror TV and Chinese Television System said Taipei residents have the right to assess candidates’ policy proposals and commitments to accountability through open, rational debates.
The invitation comes after TVBS and SETN announced they have invited the candidates to hold a televised debate.
Photo: Taipei Times
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Democratic Progressive Party Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) have already agreed to that debate.
The broadcasters met with representatives of their campaigns yesterday to discuss the details and agreed to hold a second meeting.
Meanwhile, the six media outlets’ statement said that jointly hosting a debate would bring together diverse perspectives and broaden the scope of the discussion, urging the candidates to accept the invitation and enter the debate on equal terms.
The debate would focus on substantive issues facing the city, with questions examining the feasibility of candidates’ policies to help inform voters, it said.
The debate should embrace openness and inclusivity, as it is intended to foster a representative cross-media dialogue based on mutual trust, it said, adding that the news groups would negotiate the format to ensure a fair debate.
Shen said he had already signed an agreement to participate, adding that he hoped all parties would quickly negotiate the details and set a good example for municipal policy debates.
Asked by reporters whether he would participate in the six-outlet debate, Chiang declined to give a definitive answer.
“Right now, we have signed with TVBS, and both sides have reached a consensus,” Chiang said. “Based on our past coordination experience and conventions, the next step is to negotiate the time, location, format and other details for this event.”
Typically, one debate would be held alongside two policy presentations for candidates to exchange views on municipal affairs, he added.
KMT Legislator Lo Chih-chiang (羅智強), a campaign spokesman for Chiang, said the campaign welcomed media outlets organizing a debate and hoped additional outlets would join as cohosts.
The Chiang campaign disagrees with the Shen campaign’s proposal to settle the total number of debates before deciding on the date of the first one, Lo said.
Chiang’s campaign remained open to holding multiple debates and was willing to participate in debates jointly organized by several media outlets, he said.
However, discussions about the date and other arrangements for the first debate should continue alongside negotiations over the total number of debates to avoid delays, he said.
Additional reporting by Hou Chia-yu and Tung Kuan-yi

2026 Nobel Prizes:  From scientific discovery to human endeavor  2026年諾貝爾獎揭曉：從科學發現到人文關懷
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:10 UTC
01:42:10 KST

The 2026 Nobel Prize laureates were announced from Oct. 5 to yesterday across six categories: Physiology or Medicine, Physics, Chemistry, Literature, Peace and Economic Sciences. Their award-winning contributions span a broad range of fields, including neuroscience, astrophysics, molecular chemistry, literary innovation, international human rights and macroeconomic policy. Here is a brief overview of this year’s laureates and their achievements:
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to US scientist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their contributions to optogenetics. Combining genetic engineering with optical technology, optogenetics enables specific nerve cells to respond to light, allowing researchers to precisely control neural activity and investigate causal relationships between brain circuits and memory, emotions and behavior. The technology holds promise for research into neurological and psychiatric disorders, including depression, epilepsy and Parkinson’s disease.
Photo: Reuters 照片：路透
The Nobel Prize in Physics went to Belgian-American physicist Francis Halzen for his pioneering leadership in establishing the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica. Neutrinos, often called “ghost particles,” are fundamental particles that rarely interact with matter. IceCube uses deep Antarctic ice and thousands of optical sensors to detect high-energy neutrinos, providing scientists with a new way to investigate black holes and extreme cosmic phenomena beyond conventional optical observations. This breakthrough has helped advance the emerging field of multimessenger astronomy.
Photo: AP 照片：美聯社
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry was jointly awarded to French chemist Henri B. Kagan and Japanese chemist Kenso Soai for their research on nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis. Many molecules exhibit chirality, a property in which two structures are mirror images of each other but cannot be superimposed, much like human hands. Their research revealed how minute molecular asymmetries can be amplified through chemical reactions, with significant implications for pharmaceutical synthesis, asymmetric catalysis and research into the origins of life.
The Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded to Canadian poet, writer and classical scholar Anne Carson. Drawing on ancient Greek mythology, philosophy, poetry, prose and visual art, Carson explores themes such as love, desire, memory and loss. Her acclaimed work Autobiography of Red reimagines classical mythology as a contemporary novel in verse. By transcending conventional literary genres, her writing demonstrates innovative possibilities for literary expression and the construction of meaning.
The Nobel Peace Prize went to South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay in recognition of her longstanding commitment to international human rights, international justice and accountability for war crimes. Pillay has served as a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court, as well as United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. She has also participated in investigations into human rights issues involving Israel and the Palestinian territories. Her recognition underscores the importance of upholding international law, human rights and judicial independence amid ongoing global conflicts.
The Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences was jointly awarded to American economists Michael Woodford and Robert E. Hall for their contributions to the microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization. Their research has advanced economists’ understanding of how individual and business decisions shape broader economic fluctuations and how monetary and fiscal policies can help stabilize the economy. Woodford is particularly renowned for his work on monetary policy, inflation expectations and forward guidance, which examines how central banks can influence economic behavior by communicating their future policy intentions. Their contributions have strengthened the theoretical foundations of modern macroeconomic policymaking, offering important insights into managing inflation, unemployment and economic instability.(Lin Lee-kai, Taipei Times)
2026年諾貝爾獎，自10月5日至10月12陸續揭曉生理學或醫學獎、物理獎、化學獎、文學獎、和平獎、經濟學獎等六大獎項，獲獎研究涵蓋神經科學、宇宙探索、分子化學、文學創新、國際人權以及總體經濟政策等領域。以下簡介各獎項得主：
生理學或醫學獎
頒給美國科學家卡爾．戴瑟羅斯（Karl Deisseroth）及德國科學家彼得·赫格曼(Peter Hegemann)、葛歐克·內格爾（Georg Nagel），表彰他們對「光遺傳學」（Optogenetics）的貢獻。這項技術結合基因工程與光學，讓特定神經細胞對光產生反應，使研究人員得以精準控制神經活動，進一步探索大腦迴路與記憶、情緒與行為之間的因果關係。其應用潛力涵蓋憂鬱症、癲癇及帕金森氏症等神經疾病研究。
物理學獎
由比利時裔美國物理學家法蘭西斯·哈爾岑（Francis Halzen）獲得，肯定他領導在南極建設「冰立方微中子天文台」（IceCube）的成就。微中子是一種極少與物質產生交互作用的基本粒子，有「幽靈粒子」之稱。IceCube利用南極深層冰層及數千個光學感測器偵測高能微中子，使科學家能藉由不同於傳統光學觀測的方式，研究黑洞及宇宙極端高能現象，推動多信使天文學發展。
化學獎
由法國化學家亨利·B·卡甘（Henri B. Kagan）與日本化學家硤合憲三共同獲獎，表彰他們在不對稱有機合成中的非線性效應與自催化研究。許多分子具有「手性」（Chirality，又稱對掌性），如同左右手互為鏡像卻無法重疊。兩人的研究揭示微小的分子不對稱性如何在化學反應中被放大，對藥物合成、不對稱催化及生命起源研究具有重要意義。
文學獎
由加拿大詩人、作家及古典學者安妮·卡森（Anne Carson）摘下桂冠。她擅長結合古希臘神話、哲學、詩歌、散文與視覺藝術，探索愛、慾望、記憶及失落等主題。代表作《紅的自傳》（Autobiography of Red）以當代詩體小說重新詮釋古典神話。她的作品打破傳統文類界線，展現語言形式與意義建構的創新可能。
和平獎
得主為南非法律學者瓦妮瑟姆．「納薇」．皮萊（ Navanethem “Navi” Pillay），肯定她長期致力於國際人權、國際司法及戰爭罪責追究。她曾任盧安達問題國際刑事法庭法官、國際刑事法院法官及聯合國人權事務高級專員，並參與以色列與巴勒斯坦相關人權調查。在國際衝突持續之際，此獎凸顯維護國際法、人權與司法獨立的重要性。
經濟學獎
由美國經濟學家麥可．伍德福德（Michael Woodford）與羅伯特．霍爾（Robert E. Hall）共同獲得，表彰兩人在「總體經濟穩定政策的個體經濟基礎」方面的貢獻。他們的研究讓經濟學界更能理解個人與企業決策對整體經濟波動的影響，以及貨幣與財政政策如何穩定經濟。伍德福德尤其以貨幣政策、通膨預期及前瞻指引（forward guidance）研究聞名，探討中央銀行如何透過傳達未來政策方向，影響經濟行為。兩人的貢獻鞏固了現代總體經濟政策制定的理論基礎，並為因應通貨膨脹、失業及經濟不穩定等問題提供重要見解。
（台北時報林俐凱）

Drone firm executives held over China-chip claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:08 UTC
01:42:08 KST

Two executives of drone supplier Jiin Ming Industry Co have been detained and held incommunicado over the company’s alleged use of prohibited China-made chips and camera lenses in drones supplied under military contracts, the Taoyuan District Prosecutors’ Office said yesterday.
The prosecutors said in a statement that they raided the offices of Jiin Ming — headquartered in Taoyuan — as well as those of its subsidiaries and its suppliers on Thursday last week.
The raids followed a report that the company allegedly had breached its procurement contracts by putting the prohibited components into drones delivered to the military.
Photo: Yu Jui-jen, Taipei Times
During the raids, prosecutors summoned Jiin Ming vice chairman and president Chien Hao-ting (簡豪廷), business manager Chen Yang-cheng (陳揚澄), seven other people connected to the case and a witness for questioning. They also seized items as evidence.
After questioning, prosecutors said they suspected Chien and Chen of contravening the National Security Act (國家安全法) by knowingly supplying Chinese-made products under military procurement contracts.
The two are also suspected of submitting falsified business records and of aggravated fraud committed by three or more people under the Criminal Code, they said.
Prosecutors said that they considered the two at risk of committing further offenses or interfering with the investigation, and sought their detention.
The Taoyuan District Court cited the case’s national security implications and the possibility that others were involved, and said that Chien, who had given inconsistent statements, might collude with others on testimony or flee.
In Chen’s case, although he denied the allegations during questioning, he was still strongly suspected of involvement in the alleged crimes, prosecutors cited the court as saying.
The alleged number of transactions and the volume of sales between Chen and the military, as detailed in the detention application, suggested a risk of repeat offenses, it said.
The court ordered both men detained for two months from Friday and barred them from receiving visitors or communicating with others. The ruling can be appealed within 10 days of receiving the court documents.
The other suspects were released without bail, prosecutors said.
In a separate statement, Jiin Ming, which is listed on the Taipei Exchange’s over-the-counter market, confirmed Chien’s detention and said chairman Tsai Hsiang-feng (蔡翔峰) had assumed his duties.
The company said its operations were continuing as normal despite the case and that it would cooperate with the investigation.

Chiang’s past catching up with him
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:05 UTC
01:42:05 KST

A Facebook post by Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) earlier this month achieved record levels of engagement — although perhaps inadvertently. In it, he attacked Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) for an op-ed published in 2014 discussing drug harm reduction policies. In attempting to stir up fear with talk of community centers, drugs and needles, Chiang’s comment section exploded. More than 100,000 comments poured in within the first two hours; more than 330,000 after the first 12; and more than 400,000 by noon the following day.
Rather embarrassingly, many commenters made a point not of joining Chiang in criticizing Shen, but of posting records of Chiang’s own proposal as a legislator in 2021. The mayor himself, it turns out, had once supported methadone substitution treatments, improving access to rehabilitation resources and creating a more supportive environment for those undergoing treatment. The political shots aimed at Shen appear to have found their way back to Chiang himself, only five years back in time.
Politicians can, of course, change their minds. However, if Chiang believed that drug harm reduction policies were reasonable in 2021, he should still have a clear understanding that harm reduction and actively encouraging drug use — which were conflated in his Facebook post — are two fundamentally different things. Moreover, Taipei already has its own system for preventing and addressing drug-related harm, and as mayor, Chiang should be better versed in these policies than the average citizen.
The specific proposals Shen put forward in an article 12 years ago can certainly be scrutinized, and there is ample room for public debate over which approaches are suitable for Taiwan. However, reducing a complex public health policy to a few sensational keywords to insinuate that one’s opponent “supports drugs” is not policy debate; it is the politicization of a professional issue for electoral purposes. The backlash to this kind of political maneuvering has been borne out in the hundreds of thousands of comments demanding that Chiang explain his own legislative record.
Things escalated further with allegations that comments had been deleted. Some people and media outlets used screenshots and video recordings to question why certain images or comments had disappeared so quickly. Chiang’s response was “how anyone could delete hundreds of thousands of comments,” and said that he welcomed differing opinions. However, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) went further, alleging that the flood of comments involved online troll armies or bots.
There is insufficient evidence to conclude that all these hundreds of thousands of comments were organic, just as there is no basis for labeling them all as the work of a “green-camp troll army.” Yet one does not need a definitive comment count to know that the Legislative Yuan’s proposal records from 2021 are here to stay.
Perhaps what Chiang should really be concerned with is not the question of comment trolls on his Facebook dashboard, but his own legislative record. Online engagement can be artificially inflated, comments can be duplicated and support can be mobilized by political platforms.
However, records of legislative proposals do not change with the algorithm. If Chiang still believes in his earlier positions, he should acknowledge that drug prevention and treatment require professional expertise, rather than using harm reduction policies for electioneering and fearmongering purposes. If he believes his former position was wrong, he should publicly explain what was wrong with it.
What makes the more than 600,000 comments worth examining is not the number itself, but how they flipped a political offensive into an invitation for hundreds of thousands of people to revisit Chiang’s own political record. The mayor should take note.
Elliot Yao is a reviewer.

Hall and Woodford win Nobel prize in economics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:00 UTC
01:42:00 KST

US-born economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford yesterday won the Nobel memorial prize in economics for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, saying the winners were being honored “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization.”
“The laureates have helped us smooth out the economy’s peaks and troughs,” the academy said in a statement.
Photo: AFP
Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford with Columbia University in New York.
Woodford yesterday spoke to the committee by phone from New York, saying: “It’s a tremendous honor, it’s a surprise.”
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences chairman John Hassler said in a news release. “With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume.”
The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish arms manufacturer and chemist.
Nobel purists say that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death in 1896.

Taiwan’s nuclear restart faces an environmental review dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:41:58 UTC
01:41:58 KST

The Nuclear Safety Commission (NSC, 核安會) on Sept. 24 approved the re-operation plan that Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) filed in March for the Ma-anshan Nuclear Power Plant in Pingtung County, after three rounds of review and 589 comments. Taipower now has to carry out the work in the plan and its own inspections on ageing, radiation and seismic resistance, then report back to the commission for review and on-site checks. Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) has named 2028 as the earliest restart. The NSC has given no date.
THE DEBATE
No challenge has been identified as to whether Ma-anshan needs an environmental impact assessment (EIA) under the Environmental Impact Assessment Act (環境影響評估法) before it runs again. The Ministry of Environment says it does not. Environmental groups say it does. If a suit came after a licence, a judge would rule on the procedure once the inspections ended.
Photo: Tien Yu-hwa, Taipei Times
Article 29 of the act’s implementing criteria requires an assessment to build a nuclear plant, add units or decommission one, and does not mention license renewal. The ministry last amended the criteria on Feb. 5; the nuclear item still lists those three cases.
Minister of Environment Peng Chi-ming (彭?明) in May last year asked: “Why does a restart or a life extension need no EIA, when decommissioning needs one?” Peng said the act would undergo review. But on March 22 he said current law requires no assessment for a life extension and that the NSC’s substantive review already resembles one. NSC Chairperson Chen Ming-chen (陳明真) said in December last year that the commission already assessed the environmental effects of radiation and would “take full responsibility.”
In written answers on Oct. 5, Lin Chien-Yen (林正原), a researcher at the Green Citizens’ Action Alliance (綠色公民行動聯盟), said Article 5 of the act lists the development of nuclear and other energy among activities that require an assessment, and that the criteria’s silence does not take license renewal out of the system. He cited Article 6 of the Nuclear Reactor Facilities Regulation Act (核子反應器設施管制法), under which an operator wishing to resume after its license expires must obtain a replacement license, valid for up to 20 years. Lin wrote that a renewal goes through a new application and a new review, and that the law in force on the day of the application should decide whether it meets the EIA requirements.
Photo: TT file photo
Anton Ming-Zhi Gao (高銘志), a professor at National Tsing Hua University’s Institute of Law for Science and Technology, cites Asia Cement Corp. The Taipei High Administrative Court in 2019 revoked the 20-year extension of the company’s mining rights at a mountain in Hualien County’s Sincheng Township (新城) after four Truku residents sued. The Supreme Administrative Court on Sept. 16, 2021 made the revocation final (Interpretation No. 894). The Ministry of Economic Affairs had granted the extension without the consultation and consent that Article 21 of the Indigenous Peoples Basic Act (原住民族基本法) requires. The court ruled under the Mining Act (礦業法). Gao reads it as treating an extension as a new administrative decision, subject to the law in force on the date of application, and he applies that reasoning to the EIA Act.
Huang Ching-ting (黃靖庭), deputy secretary-general of Citizen of the Earth, Taiwan (地球公民基金會), notes that judgment 894 does not say whether an extension creates a new right or continues an old one. It applies the law in force at the time of the extension — in that case Article 21. Huang treats a nuclear license renewal as the approval of a new period of generation.
“Even decommissioning must go through an EIA,” she wrote. “Going by the meaning of the law, would extension or restart, a more intensive development than decommissioning, not need one?”
Gao said a license renewal already includes an assessment of environmental effects, outside the procedure that the EIA Act sets, and a court that found the act applicable might not accept it as a substitute. He expects any suit after the NSC issues a license, at the High Administrative Court, and leaves open who would have standing, whether a court would suspend the license and what remedy it could order. The alliance did not say whether it planned a challenge. It wrote that it would follow the authorities’ decision on the EIA and the licensing procedure.
The Court of Justice of the European Union in July 2019 ruled in Inter-Environnement Wallonie (Case C-411/17) that Belgium’s 10-year extension of the Doel 1 and 2 reactors required a prior environmental assessment. The same judgment allowed a national court to maintain the extension where electricity supply faced a genuine threat. Theodoros G. Iliopoulos and Daan Bijnens of Hasselt University wrote in 2020 in the Maastricht Journal of European and Comparative Law that the court had added electricity shortage to the grounds for regularizing a project after the fact, and that the ruling moved the dispute into a second phase.
In the referendum on Aug. 23 last year, 4.34 million people voted to restart Ma-anshan and 1.51 million voted against. The yes votes did not reach a quarter of the 20.02 million eligible voters and the proposal failed.
Another referendum, to be held alongside the nine-in-one local elections on Nov. 28, asks whether the government should use nuclear power to revive the economy and abolish the “nuclear-free homeland” policy. Neither result binds the NSC.
EXPERTS should WEIGH IN
Meanwhile, the Green Citizens’ Action Alliance, Citizen of the Earth and 32 other groups on Sept. 29 said nobody should read the outcome as permission to restart and asked for geologists, seismologists and emergency-medicine specialists to participate in a safety review. Gao sat on a Taiwan People’s Party expert group on nuclear power that broadly backed a careful restart, and split with it over the EIA.
Gao said fuel supply and the US-Taiwan nuclear cooperation agreement barely come up in the legal debate over Ma-anshan. On small modular reactors (SMRs), he said the law assumes Taipower as operator and sets liabilities too heavy for a private company running one beside a data center or a chip fab. The National Atomic Research Institute (國家原子能科技研究院) estimated in April that Taiwan’s first SMR electricity would come in 2035 at the earliest.
In a 2022 study published in Energy Strategy Reviews, Gao, Yeh Tsung-Kuang (葉宗洸) and Chen Jong-Shun (陳中舜) found that the electricity mix the government announced on May 25, 2016, which removed nuclear power from last year’s targets in favor of 50 percent gas, 30 percent coal and 20 percent renewables, had not gone through a strategic environmental assessment.
Gao calls the NSC the body with the greatest legal capacity to halt the process. He sees no sign that it intends to and expects Ma-anshan to pass on safety, given its operating record. Article 16 of the NSC’s license-review rules, which the commission last amended on Oct. 8 last year, lists six documents a renewal application must include, from an integrated ageing assessment to a seismic safety evaluation. Item six lets the competent authority designate other documents, and Lin said the commission could use it to ask for environmental assessment reports. Gao considers a licence decision more likely next year than this year. The alliance estimates two to five years of work by Taipower before the commission’s next review.
Both instruments exist today. The environment ministry can amend Article 29 of the EIA criteria to state whether it covers license renewal, in the review Peng announced in May last year. The NSC can invoke item six of Article 16 before it rules. Either step fits inside the inspection years still ahead, would fix the legal basis of the license before anyone asks a judge and would give the groups opposed to the restart a procedure to take part in.
In Belgium the question went to court after the extension.

Photo courtesy of the Green Citizens’ Action Alliance
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) of the Democratic Progressive Party signed the full pledge.
KMT’s Tainan mayoral candidate Hsieh Lung-chieh (謝龍介) signed part of the pledge, while KMT candidates Lee Shu-chuan (李四川) and Johnny Chiang (江啟臣), who are running in New Taipei City and Taichung respectively, have declined to sign, the groups said.
The pledge addresses governance issues such as urban disaster preparedness, energy resilience, transportation and protections for disadvantaged groups, the advocates said, adding that climate risks transcend party lines.
GCAA senior researcher Chen Shih-ting (陳詩婷) urged all mayoral candidates to equip community facilities such as schools, activity centers, long-term care centers and emergency shelters with solar power, energy storage systems and microgrids to ensure they can operate independently during disasters.
Local governments should incorporate heat adaptation into disaster preparedness and public health policies as extreme heat becomes more frequent and severe in Taiwan, TCAN research assistant Lee You-jen (利祐任) said.
He urged local governments to identify high-risk areas and vulnerable populations, prioritize shaded and cooling spaces in under-resourced communities, and improve insulation and ventilation in older homes to make them more heat-resistant and extend their lifespan.
Taiwan Rivers Network secretary-general Tsou Ming-hsuan (鄒明軒) told the news conference that torrential rainfall has become frequent in the past few years, with a single downpour sometimes exceeding the capacity of existing drainage systems.
He called for greater use of land and urban spaces to manage flooding, for nature-based solutions in river management, and for more resources to help communities and households prepare for floods and reduce damage.

NHRI finds genes linked to early schizophrenia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:41:57 UTC
01:41:57 KST

A National Health Research Institutes (NHRI) research team has identified four potential hub genes highly correlated with early-onset schizophrenia, which could explain how the disease develops and lead to new treatments, a researcher at the institute’s Center for Neuropsychiatric Research said yesterday.
Schizophrenia is a leading cause of disability worldwide, with a median lifetime prevalence of 6.35 per 1,000 people, researcher Jen Ya-wen (任雅文) said.
Schizophrenia is typically diagnosed in young adulthood, but about 8 percent of cases are classified as early-onset, meaning patients experience core symptoms such as delusions, hallucinations and cognitive decline before turning 18, she said.
Photo courtesy of the institute
Early-onset schizophrenia is associated with a higher genetic load than adult-onset forms, and linked to more severe neurodevelopmental disruption and higher rates of treatment resistance, Yen said, adding that they are a more challenging patient group in clinical practice and in need of new therapeutic strategies.
Although past genome-wide association studies have identified hundreds of disease-
associated DNA variants, most of these variants have limited individual effects and are predominantly located in gene regulatory regions that do not directly encode proteins, making it difficult to directly explain the pathogenesis, she said.
Although schizophrenia has an estimated heritability of 80 percent, genetics alone does not tell the whole story, she said.
Much of this genetic link remains a mystery, and researchers believe that how genes interact with the environment plays a major role in driving the disease, she added.
The research team led by Center for Neuropsychiatric Research director Chen Wei-jen (陳為堅), Lin Yan-yeng (林彥鋒), an attending physician at the center, and Yen, in collaboration with local and international academics, aimed to identify the key genes that drive the genetic regulation of the disease.
The team used genotype data from patients in multiplex families and simplex families, referenced large-scale international brain tissue transcriptome databases, and through transcriptome-wide association studies, estimated the genetically regulated expression levels of individual genes in the brain and established individual-level gene expression risk scores that more closely approximate true biological functions, the institute said.
Yen said they found that “Module 10,” consisting of 58 genes, is most significantly associated with early-onset schizophrenia, a result consistent with findings from two sets of family data.
The team found that for every 1-standard-deviation increase in Module 10’s GeRS, the risk of developing early-onset schizophrenia increases by 1.32-fold, she said.
Subsequently, the research team identified four hub genes from Module 10 — COPS6, MRPS7, RUVBL2, and PSMD2 — which are involved in functions such as protein clearance, DNA repair and cellular operations, Yen said.
These hub genes are primarily concentrated in the brain’s excitatory neurons, which amplify neural signals, and their activity gradually increases from late fetal development through adulthood, suggesting that early-onset schizophrenia might be linked to abnormal gene regulation during brain development, she said.
The team believes the hub genes might have clinical relevance, and future studies integrating pharmacogenomic data and longitudinal clinical measures might be able to determine whether these genes can serve as therapeutic entry points or biomarkers for early intervention, Yen said.
The study was published in the peer-reviewed scientific journal Molecular Psychiatry in July, the NHRI said.

Official reaffirms drug prevention policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:41:57 UTC
01:41:57 KST

Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) yesterday reiterated that the ministry has no plans to ask social workers to distribute illegal drugs in community centers as the government’s drug policy comes under scrutiny.
Heated debates on the government’s drug prevention policies were triggered by Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) re-election campaign team, who earlier this month questioned Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) drug stance, citing an op-ed article he wrote in 2014, when he was a doctoral student.
Chiang and his team accused Shen of supporting decriminalization of drugs and “giving out [illegal] drugs and clean needles in local communities.”
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
Shen said that the article was about drug prevention policies around the world, including needle and syringe programs and medication-assisted treatment, which are harm reduction policies.
At a meeting of the legislature’s Social Welfare and Environmental Hygiene Committee, Taiwan People’s Party Legislator Chiu Hui-ju (邱慧洳) said that Shen had mentioned that Taiwan can learn from other countries in “providing drug users drugs and clean needles at community centers,” and questioned whether the “drugs” he mentioned referred to “oral methadone” as his supporters claimed.
Shih said although the existing methadone maintenance therapy service offers oral methadone, it is implemented simultaneously with the needle and syringe program, which gives out sterile injecting equipment to prevent the transmission of blood-borne diseases, so they can be given together.
Methadone is classified as a Category 2 narcotic and a Category 2 controlled drug, he said, adding that Shen has repeatedly explained his stance and the ministry respects the author of the article.
Regarding Chiu’s repeated request that the ministry conduct an assessment report on the feasibility of “providing drugs in local communities,” Shih said that the harm reduction programs have already yielded significant results in reducing HIV and other blood-borne diseases, and there is no need to change them.
The ministry’s stance is clear — it will not provide drugs at community centers and does not need to conduct a feasibility study on distributing them in local communities, he said.
Meanwhile, a claim by Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Lee Yen-hsiu (李彥秀) — a spokesperson for Chiang’s election campaign — last week that social workers would be distributing drugs in local communities prompted social workers to stage a protest in front of her office yesterday, demanding that she apologize.
Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Lin Yueh-chin (林月琴) said many frontline social workers and health professionals have expressed concerns that messages like this could undermine the government’s harm reduction program, smearing social workers as drug enablers and making drug users afraid to ask for help.
Shih said there is no such thing as social workers giving out drugs and that they are not “drug providers,” adding that harm reduction policies do not encourage drug use.
Aside from preventing stigmatization and protecting privacy to ensure the harm reduction services operate without interference, the easy accessibility of the services is another critical factor in the program’s success, he said.
The program is an interdisciplinary collaboration that includes physicians, nurses, pharmacists and social workers, Shih said.
Social workers play a vital role in providing case management, family support and community resource linkage, while helping drug users reintegrate into society, but they are not involved in “giving out drugs,” he stressed.
A Ministry of Health and Welfare’s report states that, to prevent HIV transmission among drug users, the accessible sterile needle and syringe service covers 770 health counseling stations, 388 automated vending machines and 575 needle disposal boxes.

====================================================================================================

Why Putin says Russia could ‘cease to exist’ if it loses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:41:57 UTC
01:41:57 KST

Ever since things in Ukraine first went sideways for Russian President Vladimir Putin back in the spring of 2022, he and his officials have said that, not only were they fighting Nazis and responding to NATO aggression, but that the stakes of the conflict were so high that Russia may cease to exist should they fail.
That claim has always been puzzling, because it seems so absurd, and yet such a belief would help explain the extent to which the Kremlin is ramping up attacks on Ukraine, expanding its campaign of hybrid warfare in Europe and — by announcing massive budget transfers from nondefense to military spending — risking discontent at home.
Putin touched on the idea yet again earlier this month in his annual address to the Valdai Club conference of foreign policy and Russia analysts. Harping on a 2022 comment from then-US permanent representative to NATO Ambassador Julianne Smith that the US sought Russia’s “strategic defeat,” Putin said this put his nation’s “very right to exist” in question.
What Smith intended must be seen in the context of the ultimatums Putin sent to the US and NATO before the war, in the form of two draft treaty proposals. These described his subsequent war aims and went far beyond requiring Ukraine’s neutrality. They also demanded the removal of all alliance troops, weapons and bases from Central and Eastern Europe, and all US nuclear weapons from any foreign base, significantly reducing the credibility of the nuclear umbrella Washington could offer its allies.
So, strategic defeat meant putting an end to Putin’s project to reimpose control over Moscow’s so-called historical zone of interest by stopping his forces in Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region.
Allow him to take Ukraine and the only question would be: Where next? It is still a valid concern, but use of the term “strategic defeat” has proved a gift that never stops giving to Putin’s victimhood narrative. “This is the way it was all articulated,” he recalled in his Oct. 1 address. “No one forgot this. At least, we did not forget this.”
How would losing in Ukraine pose a threat to Russia’s existence? Even in the unlikely event that Kyiv should win the war by pushing Russia’s troops all the way back to their internationally recognized borders — a true and humiliating defeat for Putin — Russia would not disappear. It would just continue to exist in the form it had until 2013. If the front lines were frozen where they are today, Russia would have gained about 20 percent of Ukrainian territory.
Whatever they might say, Russia’s leaders know their opponents bear no resemblance to the invading armies of Nazi Germany (1941), Napoleonic France (1812) or the Polish Lithuanian forces that occupied the capital in 1610. Nobody is marching on Moscow.
Indeed, the US has effectively moved to the sidelines. Having halted American aid to Ukraine last year, US President Donald Trump is doing more to help Moscow than Kyiv, calling for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy to unilaterally halt attacks on Russian oil refineries. When he refused, Trump lifted a ban on the purchase of diesel exports and called for Zelenskiy to resign.
Political expediency explains some of Moscow’s inflated rhetoric. Putin wants Russians to perceive a critical threat, because he is asking them to make new levels of sacrifice. He is boosting the country’s already large defense budget for next year by 27 percent, paid for in part by cutting further into education, healthcare and welfare spending, while printing money at the central bank. That would hit living standards.
He would also need to recruit more soldiers, whose average life expectancy at the line of contact the Ukrainian and US intelligence services now estimate at about 30 minutes. So, it helps for the cause to appear existential — as it could well be for Putin personally, and for the system he has built around him, should he be perceived to fail.
Hyping the threat also supports his efforts to persuade Europeans that by continuing to back Ukraine, their governments are inviting all-out war — perhaps even nuclear war — with Russia.
There is more at work here than cynical manipulation. There is also real paranoia among the crop of current and former KGB officers who run Russia, starting with Putin himself. Not only did their training and careers program them to assume threats all around, but they already saw one seemingly immortal great power (the former Soviet Union) collapse around them to the joy of the West. Why not the Russian Federation, too?
Putin and those of his ilk half believe it when they say they are re-enacting World War II, because they see the gains the Soviet Union made in Europe at the end of that conflict — and lost after 1991 — as what is at stake. They also genuinely think Ukraine is not a real country, but rather a Frankenstein state whose creation required ripping out Russia’s historic heartland. This history is wrong, but it is sincerely believed.
Just as for ex-KGB officials the distinction between war and peace is blurred, so too is the question of what Russia is and where it ends.
This is essential to understand. It affects what is and is not negotiable with the Kremlin, what the true purpose of any peace offer Putin makes might be and what is meant by the apparently ludicrous claim that Russia is being attacked in Ukraine. Western leaders should accept none of it, but they need to grasp the mentality to avoid unnecessary escalation or being gas lit into chasing settlements that cannot be had.
The Russia Putin talks about is quite simply bigger than the one on maps. It is also defined by keeping its place at the table of great powers, by an idea that it is a civilizational state that spills across borders and by a historical inheritance whose expanse that now, as always, had to be gained and held by force.
“Multiplying one’s heritage,” Putin told his Valdai audience, is the best way for nations to avoid becoming “a vintage collectible.”
To the president and his entourage, this would appear to be the worst of all fates — and it is certainly how they see the UK. Russian Minister of Foreign Affairs Sergei Lavrov oozed contempt when he described the UK as “diminished to the utmost degree” and no longer worthy of its permanent seat in the UN Security Council.
It is this potential future that Putin and others foresee with dread when they talk about their country ceasing to exist. The attempt to restore not necessarily the USSR or Russian Empire, but the idea of Russia as a great power supersedes all other Kremlin concerns, including for the economy, welfare or popular approval.
Putin would abandon his vision only if he becomes convinced it cannot be achieved, and that to continue in the attempt is more dangerous to him personally than to settle. This question would be decided by force, even if it ends in a negotiated ceasefire, because Russia’s now sovereign neighbors have their own ideas of history and heritage. They, too, want to exist.
Marc Champion is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Europe, Russia and the Middle East. He was previously Istanbul bureau chief for the Wall Street Journal. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Dozens killed in airstrike on gold mine in Sudan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:41:55 UTC
01:41:55 KST

At least 72 workers were killed by airstrikes on a gold mine on the Sudan-Egypt border, a Sudanese rights group said on Sunday, after survivors described scenes of chaos in the mountainous region.
The Emergency Lawyers rights organization accused the Egyptian air force of carrying out the attack. Agence France-Presse could not independently confirm the account and Egypt has issued no official comment.
The attack on Saturday was the second this year on Jabal al-Uqaydat, after airstrikes, reportedly by Egypt, killed 23 workers in the informal gold mining site in June.
Photo: Reuters
The Egyptian army did not claim the strikes, but said at the time that it had conducted a “large-scale operation” against illegal gold mining within its borders.
The border between Sudan and Egypt is disputed, with both countries claiming the resource-rich Halayeb triangle. However, Cairo is a key ally of Sudan’s army, at war with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The attack on Saturday “resulted in the deaths of 72 civilian miners, according to preliminary information, while efforts to document and verify the casualty toll are ongoing,” said the Emergency Lawyers, which documents atrocities in Sudan’s war.
Two survivors described their harrowing escape from the mine.
Miner Abdelaziz Youssef said a jet appeared overhead at about 8am on Saturday and “struck five times, many people were killed.”
“We ran up the mountain terrified of another strike,” he said.
Another survivor, Sharaf Ali, said there were thousands of people working at the remote site when it was hit.
“After the airstrike people scattered, some people came to al-Ansary market, others went in the other direction, that’s why no one knows how many exactly were killed,” he said from the gold market, just south of the Halayeb triangle.
Both survivors said they saw bodies on the ground as they fled, with many more feared trapped under the rubble, hours away from any urban center.
Since April 2023, the conflict has killed more than 200,000 people and created a deep humanitarian crisis that has pushed many into the dangerous gold mining industry, which fuels both sides’ war efforts.

Lin Yun-ju loses China Smash nailbiter

Taiwan’s Lin Yun-ju finished second in the men’s singles at the World Table Tennis (WTT) China Smash on Sunday in the final against world No. 1 Sora Matsushima of Japan.
Lin, the world No. 6, recovered from a loss in the first two games to take a 3-2 lead, but was overtaken by Matsushima, who won the match 4-3.
In the 55-minute final at Shougang Park in Beijing, Lin finished as the runner-up, with game scores of 7-11, 9-11, 11-7, 11-8, 11-5, 7-11, 9-11.
Photo: WTT Web site
Lin entered Sunday’s final with a 6-1 career record against Matsushima, although the Japanese player had won their previous encounter, a seven-game semi-final at this year’s International Table Tennis Federation World Cup.
Matsushima took the two opening games before Lin changed the tempo, using his trademark backhand flick and varying placement to win three straight games.
The Japanese player forced a decider after pulling away from a 6-6 tie in the sixth game. Lin then fell behind 6-0 in the seventh and could not make a comeback.
It was Lin’s second singles runner-up finish at a WTT Smash this year, after the Singapore Smash in February.
He was eliminated in the opening round of the inaugural China Smash in 2024 and in the round of 32 last year.
Last Friday, Lin also finished runner-up in the mixed doubles alongside Cheng I-ching, in the final against the world No. 1 pair Lim Jonghoon and Shin Yubin of South Korea.
The Taiwanese duo lost 3-2, with game scores of 14-12, 9-11, 18-16, 11-13, 8-11, after failing to convert eight championship points.
It was their second five-game loss in three weeks to the Korean pair, following the mixed doubles quarter-finals at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Sept. 25.

Taiwan to start exporting breeding cattle to Manila
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:41:54 UTC
01:41:54 KST

After two years of negotiations, Taiwan is to export breeding cattle for the first time after the Philippines approved imports on Friday last week, the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Agency said yesterday.
The cattle are Holsteins, a dairy breed traditionally raised in temperate climates that Taiwan has selectively bred to thrive in hot, humid conditions while maintaining high milk production, the Livestock Research Institute said.
Originating in the Netherlands and the German-Danish border region, Holsteins are renowned for their high milk yields. In tropical parts of Asia, farmers have traditionally relied more on the indigenous cattle and heat-tolerant zebu breed, which generally produces less milk, but are better adapted to local conditions.
Photo: Taipei Times
Crossbreeding with specialized dairy breeds has helped improve milk production while retaining some heat tolerance.
Taiwan applied to export breeding cattle to the Philippines in 2024, and Philippine officials inspected local farms in November that year.
In May last year, Manila approved Mei-gui Ranch in Tainan and Ho-sheng Ranch in Changhua County for live cattle exports, Animal and Plant Health Inspection Agency Deputy Director-General Fu Hsueh-li (傅學理) said.
The two sides negotiated animal health requirements for export quarantine certificates, with assistance from the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in the Philippines, Fu said.
The Philippines, which produces less than 5 percent of its domestic milk needs, is seeking to develop its dairy industry and has looked to Taiwan for cattle suited to the hot, humid conditions shared by the two island economies, Livestock Research Institute Director Huang Chen-fang (黃振芳) said.
Taiwan’s success in adapting Holsteins to tropical conditions while maintaining milk production is a major milestone for its dairy industry, Huang said.
The institute also hopes to export automated equipment, including farm-management robots, to the Philippines, he added.

Taiwan resumes processing visa applications for Moroccans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:41:54 UTC
01:41:54 KST

Taiwan yesterday resumed accepting visa applications from Moroccan nationals, ending a months-long suspension imposed after the North African country abruptly halted visa applications from Taiwanese nationals in July.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement that it had made the decision after receiving official confirmation that Morocco had resumed accepting visa applications from Taiwanese nationals on Sept. 21.
The ministry said it welcomed the Moroccan government’s decision and would reciprocate by resuming the processing of visa applications from Moroccan nationals.
Photo: Reuters
The visa dispute began when the Moroccan embassy in Japan, where Taiwanese travel agencies most frequently submit visa applications for travelers heading to the North African country, on July 23 suspended its review of visa confirmation letter (VCL) applications from Taiwanese without providing a reason.
Citing the principle of reciprocity, the ministry announced that it would stop processing visa applications from Moroccan nationals effective July 31, except for applicants involved in special projects approved by the Taiwan government.
The ministry at the time said that the Moroccan government’s suspension had seriously affected bilateral exchanges, as Taiwanese passport holders could obtain VCLs only through Moroccan embassies abroad and were not eligible for Moroccan e-visas.
Late last month, the ministry said that a staff member at its office in Tokyo had confirmed with the Moroccan embassy in Japan that it had resumed processing of VCL applications from Taiwanese travelers on Sept. 21.
However, the ministry said it was still seeking confirmation from Moroccan authorities on whether the resumption covered only tourism-related applications or also those for non-tourism purposes.
Therefore, the ministry had not yet resumed processing visa applications from Moroccan nationals at that time, it said.

Airport plan raises earthquake risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:41:53 UTC
01:41:53 KST

The relocation of Taipei International Airport (Songshan Airport), which Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) proposed on Thursday, has been debated for years. Mayoral candidates have previously advocated preserving the site as a park and green space, which I would have no objection to. However, plans for the site to undergo intensive development would risk overloading the land’s carrying capacity and seriously exacerbate the severity of potential earthquakes.
While a major offshore megathrust earthquake would severely affect Taipei and New Taipei City, movement along the Shanchiao Fault (山腳斷層) could mean an earthquake or subsidence event taking place right underneath the city, pushing the capital toward the point of destruction beyond repair.
As extensive land consolidation in low-lying areas contributes to fault risks, one cannot assume that the Shanchiao Fault would remain inactive. Consider the current state of the Taipei Basin: It has been 50 years since land consolidation began in the low-lying areas of New Taipei City’s Sinjhuang (新莊) and Wugu (五股) districts; plans have been made to raise the ground level across Shezidao (社子島); extensive filling is under way for the Wenzizun (塭仔圳) development project scheduled for completion next year; and large-scale land reclamation also lies ahead for Guandu Plain’s agricultural area. If a major development project follows the relocation of Songshan Airport, it would inevitably mean further land consolidation projects.
What is particularly concerning is that all these development projects are concentrated in areas with elevations close to sea level, which is precisely where movement along the Shanchiao Fault could cause the basin to subside. Here, extensive landfilling reaching the equivalent of two stories in height increases stress on the fault’s seismogenic zone by approximately 1.2kg per square centimeter.
For reference, the “stress drop” associated with the change is shear stress on a fault after each rupture usually only amounts to several to several dozen kilograms per square centimeter. The weight of vast quantities of fill and subsequent development could therefore be enough to destabilize the Shanchiao Fault, triggering a major earthquake directly beneath the city. At the very least, it could substantially shorten the fault’s recurrence interval, bringing the next earthquake forward.
The last earthquake along the Shanchiao Fault occurred in 1694. In its aftermath, the basin subsided and its northwestern half was inundated, forming a 5m-deep lake. This became known as the Kangxi Taipei Lake. If this were to happen again, today’s Taipei Basin could suffer severe soil liquefaction and ground deformation, damaging drainage systems, rupturing utility pipelines and causing buildings to collapse. Even underground MRT and high-speed rail tunnels could sustain serious damage, making post-disaster reconstruction exceptionally difficult.
Given these circumstances, the central government should act quickly to regulate or even ban large-scale land consolidation and development in the low-lying areas of the Taipei Basin. Particular care should be taken in deciding how the land would be used following the relocation of Songshan airport. Reckless urban expansion should not become a force that raises the risk of a devastating earthquake directly beneath the city.
Lee Chyi-ti is a professor at National Central University’s Graduate Institute of Applied Geology.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:41:52 UTC
01:41:52 KST

DRAM chipmaker Nanya Technology Corp (南亞科技) expects memory prices to remain on an upward trajectory this quarter due to an acute supply crunch and strong artificial intelligence (AI) demand, boosting the company’s gross margin outlook.
A 60 percent sequential surge in the average selling prices sent the company’s gross margin to 85.7 percent last quarter, an all-time high, Nanya Technology said.
Net profit skyrocketed to NT$87.63 billion (US$2.75 billion) from NT$1.56 billion in the same period last year, soaring 60.8 percent from NT$50.19 billion the previous quarter, the company said. Earnings per share advanced to NT$25.4 from NT$0.5 a year ago and NT$14.66 a quarter earlier, it said.
Photo: Lisa Wang, Taipei Times
“From our perspective, [average selling prices] will continue to increase in the fourth quarter... The DRAM supply crunch remains severe,” Nanya Technology president Lee Pei-ing (李培瑛) told a media briefing yesterday.
“The surging momentum of AI-related products has left a widening supply-demand gap,” Lee said. “Supply for conventional applications, such as PCs and smartphones, is also constrained due to capacity squeezes.”
Given the favorable price trend, the company anticipates further gross margin expansion this quarter, he said.
Nanya Technology expects AI-related DRAM to command a larger portion of its revenue through 2029, up from 20 percent last quarter, amid accelerating DRAM integration in AI infrastructure including AI servers, networking and storage, Lee said.
Market researcher TrendForce Corp (集邦科技) projected prices of standard DRAM chips would rise 10 percent to 15 percent sequentially this quarter on a contract basis.
Long-term agreements cover about 50 to 70 percent of Nanya Technology’s capacity, compared with 50 percent estimated three months ago, the company said. Numerous customers have requested to extend contracts from three months to three years or even longer, it said.
The company said capacity expansions across the industry would not avert supply constraints soon, as new capacity is designed to match long-term customer demand. Besides, longer tool lead times and advanced process technology migrations would keep supply-demand dynamics in check, it said.
Nanya Technology does not expect significant capacity growth by 2028, as its new plant is to ramp up production at the end of next year, the company said. The new plant’s installed capacity is expected to grow to 50,000 12-inch wafers a month in 2030 from 30,000 wafers in 2028, it said.
The company plans to build an advanced 3D wafer packaging and testing plant in Pingtung County for high-capacity and high-bandwidth memory modules used in AI-related chips, Nanya Technology said. The plan is expected to enter volume production in the second half of 2028, it said.
Rapid infrastructure development in Pingtung would allow for a faster production ramp-up than at other sites, Lee said.
The company plans to distribute larger third-quarter employee bonuses than in the second quarter due to strong performance in net profit and gross margin, Lee said. The company has implemented a policy for over 20 years that up to 12 percent of pre-tax profits can be distributed as employee bonuses on a quarterly basis, he said.

US nonprofit designates Lala Mountain a dark sky site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:41:51 UTC
01:41:51 KST

Lala Mountain (拉拉山) in Taoyuan has been designated an Urban Night Sky Place by DarkSky International, becoming the first site in Taiwan and the third in Asia to receive the recognition, the city’s Department of Tourism said yesterday.
The department said it was notified of the designation on Saturday by the US-based nonprofit, which is expected to formally announce it tomorrow.
The nonprofit works to protect the nighttime environment.
Photo courtesy of the Taoyuan City Government
An Urban Night Sky Place is a municipal park, open space, stargazing site or similar property in or near a heavily urbanized area, that promotes an authentic nighttime, DarkSky International said.
The designation recognizes sites that educate the public about responsible outdoor lighting that maintains public safety while reducing harm to the nighttime environment, the organization said.
DarkSky International lists 19 Urban Night Sky Places worldwide. The other two in Asia are Minami-Rokuroshi in Japan’s Fukui Prefecture and Zhangwu in China’s Zhejiang Province.
The department said applicants must meet several criteria, including being within 50km of a town with a population of more than 50,000, providing free public access and ensuring that more than two-thirds of outdoor lighting in the designated area complies with dark-sky lighting principles.
As the designated area at Lala Mountain includes indigenous communities and other residential areas, improving the lighting required extensive discussions with residents to balance dark-sky protection with road safety and daily needs, it said, adding that the city government also made adjustments to more than 400 streetlights.
The city hopes to combine ecological conservation with stargazing tourism to develop Lala Mountain as a nighttime travel destination, it said.
Separately, the Tourism Administration is seeking to attract more European visitors to Taiwan by launching a campaign in the Netherlands centered on Taiwan Travelogue (臺灣漫遊錄), an award-winning novel by Yang Shuang-zi (楊?子).
The Chinese-language novel was translated into English by Taiwanese-American translator Lin King (金翎), and Yang and Lin won the International Booker Prize earlier this year. The book had previously won the National Book Award for Translated Literature in 2024.
Yang’s book was also translated into more than 20 languages, with the Dutch edition published on Sept. 23. De Volkskrant, a national Dutch-language daily, also published a nearly three-page feature on Taiwan on Sept. 26, focusing on Taiwanese literature, history, culture and cuisine, as well as the cultural identity of Taiwanese.
Given the recent attention to Taiwanese culture in the Netherlands, the office worked with bookstore chain Relay and China Airlines (中華航空) to jointly launch a tourism campaign centered on the award-winning book.
The novel explores Taiwanese cuisine, culture and history through the story of a Japanese writer and her Taiwanese translator in the 1930s, when Taiwan was under Japanese colonial rule, office director Linda Lin (林毓珊) said.
“Through the recognition from international literary awards, the world now sees Taiwan’s creative energy. This also provides a prime opportunity to showcase Taiwan as an attractive overseas destination,” Lin said.
“We hope to transform this wave of immense interest and curiosity about Taiwan into motivation to visit Taiwan,” she added.
Lin said the tourism campaign, which is to continue until Oct. 29, would feature advertisements at Relay stores at major transportation hubs in Amsterdam, The Hague, Rotterdam, Breda and Eindhoven Airport, targeting commuters, shoppers and travelers.
Customers shopping at Relay stores can enter a free drawing for a chance to win a trip for two to Taiwan. In addition to flight tickets provided by China Airlines, the Tourism Administration will cover four nights of accommodation in Taipei, a one-day city tour, EasyCards, admission tickets to the National Palace Museum and a Dutch-language edition of Taiwan Travelogue.
The campaign will also launch the Web site “BeleefTaiwan.nl,” where people in the Netherlands can explore Taiwan’s cities, natural landscapes, culture and cuisine, as well as tours to Taiwan offered by Dutch travel agencies.

Boat capsizes off Djibouti, killing 139 migrants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:41:48 UTC
01:41:48 KST

At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying more than 300 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in east Africa, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Sunday.
That number only includes those buried by authorities in Djibouti. Others have been buried by the migrants themselves, but they will not be added to the official count until authorities can verify the bodies, IOM chief of mission in Djibouti Alexandre Coissac said.
“What is terrible is that they were buried with no names, in a common grave, like in a war situation,” Coissac said. “They all have a mother, a father, and we may never learn what happened.”
Photo: AP
He said the migrants boarded the ship in the evening of Thursday last week and that it sank very soon after, close to the shore, “mainly because it was overcrowded.”
“The local authorities did their best,” he said, adding that “they were overwhelmed with all the bodies that kept coming at once towards the shore.”
He said authorities were bringing the surviving migrants to the IOM rescue center in Obock where they receive medical assistance after swallowing sea water, and psychological support.
“They’re all in a state of shock,” said Coissac, who visited the area of the shipwreck on Saturday. “I tried to talk to some of them, but it’s very difficult.”
Some of the migrants in the IOM center are already aware that their family members died during the shipwreck. Others were given access to phones to call loved ones back home to notify them they are alive.
At least 84 people remained missing in one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular, but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations.
The boat was traveling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized on Thursday night or Friday morning, the IOM said.
More than 80 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals, it said.
The Geneva, Switzerland-based UN migration agency said the vessel had 305 people on board and warned that the death toll could still rise.
Personal items likely belonging to the migrants, including shoes, were seen on a beach in a video shared by IOM.
Rescue work continued as fears grew for the missing.
Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel every year through Djibouti and across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait toward Gulf countries in search of safety and economic opportunities, the IOM said in its statement.

The Persians return to Athens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:37:09 UTC
01:37:09 KST

The Persians return to Athens
MADRID - Standing before the Acropolis of Athens, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio traced the history of ancient Greece all the way to the rise of American industry in a speech delivered on Wednesday, in which he presented Western civilization as threatened by decline.
Rubio called for a return to the "classical conception of politics and the art of governing that the Trump Administration hopes to recover, not only for our country, but for our civilization as a whole."
This seemed to include a renewed claim to national pride, which, he said, the ancient Greeks had embraced, but which the West had abandoned upon feeling "ashamed that our achievements set us apart from the rest of the world."
The chosen setting is no accident: the pride he champions is anchored precisely in that foundational place. The West, understood as a discourse rather than a geographical location, is a historical sequence, the famous narrative running from Plato to NATO, in which classical Greece plays a foundational role.
Within this narrative, the Western refers to a developed, modern, secular and capitalist society, the result of a specific set of historical processes. Any society sharing these characteristics is considered part of the West. Discourses about the West produce and represent certain bodies in ways that are all too familiar to us. Civilized and barbarian, the West and the rest. The key to all of this is that the West cannot exist without its opposite: without that backward East, without that rest of the world it defines as such.
Finally, to be Western means to be democratic, though this claim conceals the impact of colonialism and racism in subverting any meaningful notion of democracy. In this case, its identity derives from the negation of despotism. The elements that constitute democracy acquire their meaning by being set against those considered constitutive of despotism a boundary with a long history.
According to the hegemonic view, democracy was born in Greece. The identification of democracy with the Greeks does not derive from an enumeration of the forms of government of the various Hellenic communities, but from the perception the Greeks themselves had of themselves as free, in contrast to the enslaved subjects of the Persian Great King. Greek freedom versus Persian slavery constitutes one of the earliest examples of a trope of Western political thought, reproduced as a variation on the theme of democracy versus Oriental despotism.
Later, many authors took this division seriously, to the point that the dichotomy has come to be regarded as one of the great dividing lines between the West and the non-Western world.
But as several scholars, such as Michael Mann, have pointed out, ancient Athens was a far more strictly disciplined society than the one subject to the Persian King of Kings. The King of Kings could command a permanent administration, a standing army, and resources drawn from regular tributes; yet in every case, the demands of imperial control required cooperating with local elites and depending on them. In other words, against the hegemonic idea that presents the West as the cradle of democracy, one could just as easily have presented Athens and, by extension, classical Greece as the cradle of totalitarianism.
Other traditions offer equally participatory models of government. Critical Muslim Studies, for example, formulate alternatives to the Eurocentric narrative that establishes a privileged relationship between the idea of the West and the democratic form. The government of the Prophet Muhammad is seen from this tradition as a manner of governing that was benevolent, just, and participatory. Another example is the government of Imam Ali, also characterized by its justice, benevolence, and attentiveness to the demands of the community.
This demonstrates that the supposed connection between democracy and "the West" is part of a narrative, not something natural. The same applies to the signifier "fanatic," used by Marco Rubio in his address to describe Iran's current leaders, whom he called "fanatics who lead a cult of death and use martyrdom as an instrument to achieve their political objectives."
The accusation of fanaticism directed at Muslims in general, and at the leaders of the Islamic Republic in particular, is once again part of Western discourse that creates a division between a supposed rational self and an "irrational and violent" Islamic other, with whom dialogue and agreement are impossible, and who therefore can only be subdued militarily.
By once again deploying a luminous West against a dark and dangerous East, represented by the Islamic Republic, Rubio's speech falls within a strategy aimed at justifying a possible new attack and presenting it as inevitable, given Iran's "irrational and violent" tendencies.
As Edward Said wrote in his book Orientalism: "Every European, in what he could say about the Orient, was consequently a racist, an imperialist, and almost totally ethnocentric."
The exact definition of Marco Rubio's speech.
