Iran pledges stronger deterrence, asserts sovereignty over Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:34:44 UTC
01:34:44 KST

Iran pledges stronger deterrence, asserts sovereignty over Strait of Hormuz
TEHRAN— Iranian military officials have reaffirmed the country’s determination to strengthen its defense capabilities, protect its maritime interests and oppose efforts to restore a US-dominated security order in West Asia, arguing that regional stability must be based on national sovereignty and cooperation among neighboring countries.
The statements by senior military figures and defense officials address several interconnected issues, including Iran’s military preparedness following recent hostilities, the strategic management of the Strait of Hormuz, the future of regional security arrangements and the growing controversy over Washington’s use of historical and civilizational rhetoric in its confrontation with Iran.
Military preparedness and deterrence
Iranian military officials say the country has drawn lessons from recent conflicts and strengthened its ability to respond to potential threats.
Rear Admiral Bemani, deputy commander of the Iranian Army’s Navy, said Iran had studied its adversaries’ weaknesses and developed new weapons and tactics considering recent military confrontations.
He said the Iranian Army’s Navy, working alongside Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy, had inflicted significant blows on US forces at certain stages of the fighting. According to Bemani, US forces are now operating farther from Iran’s maritime borders than in previous periods.
He warned that any renewed miscalculation would prompt a response from Iran’s Navy and could force hostile forces to move farther away from the country’s maritime borders.
Bemani also distinguished between the responsibilities of the armed forces and those of the government in addressing the US naval blockade. While the government handles its political and economic dimensions, he said, the military remains focused on resistance, defense preparedness and responding to threats.
Caretaker Defense Minister Brigadier General Majid Ebn al-Reza has likewise emphasized the importance of strengthening Iran’s scientific, industrial and defense capabilities. He said national security requires the means to defend the country’s sovereignty and ensure that the armed forces are adequately equipped to protect Iran.
The emphasis on domestic capabilities reflects the Iranian military leadership’s stated position that deterrence depends not only on weapons and operational readiness but also on scientific advancement, industrial capacity and the ability to adapt to evolving military threats.
Strait of Hormuz: Strategic management and maritime sovereignty
The Strait of Hormuz remains another central element of Iran’s security calculations, given its geographical position and importance to global energy supplies.
Major General Yahya Rahim Safavi, head of the Lt. Gen. Qassem Soleimani Research Institute of Sacred Defense Sciences and Teachings, has identified the strategic management of the waterway as a key component of Iran’s approach to countering the US naval blockade.
Safavi said Iran’s geographical position and rights as a coastal state underpin its authority to safeguard its interests in the strait and surrounding waters. He stressed that exercising sovereignty should not automatically be interpreted as an intention to escalate tensions.
He also distinguished between closing the waterway and managing maritime traffic, arguing that these are fundamentally different approaches. In his assessment, the transport of military equipment that directly threatens Iran’s national security could make the management or restriction of maritime traffic a strategic necessity.
Safavi added that alternative pipelines do not eliminate the Strait of Hormuz’s importance to international energy markets.
According to the US Energy Information Administration, approximately 20 million barrels of oil and petroleum liquids passed through the strait daily in 2022, accounting for roughly one-fifth of global petroleum liquids consumption. The waterway is also a major route for liquefied natural gas shipments, making its security a matter of international economic significance.
Iranian officials maintain that maritime security cannot be separated from the wider political and military circumstances in the region. From their perspective, the management of the strait must take account of Iran’s sovereignty, the security threats it faces and the need to protect vital national interests.
Safavi has also presented Iran’s approach as part of a broader response to maritime pressure and sanctions, while arguing that regional security should be pursued through the participation of countries in the area.
Tehran rejects a US-led security order
Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi, spokesperson for Iran’s Armed Forces, has said Iran will not allow the regional order envisaged by the United States and Israel to be restored in West Asia.
Shekarchi called on neighboring countries to reconsider their reliance on an ineffective US security umbrella. He argued that recent conflicts had demonstrated the risks of depending on Washington for regional protection.
He accused the United States of fuel smuggling, maritime theft and psychological warfare surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, adding that political statements and media messaging could not change realities on the ground. He also questioned Washington’s ability to guarantee regional security and urged neighboring governments not to base their security calculations on the policies of US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
 
Shekarchi said Iran’s armed forces were more capable than before and remained prepared to defend the country against threats.
The statements reflect Tehran’s long-standing emphasis on regional participation in security arrangements. Iranian officials argue that countries sharing West Asia’s geographical and strategic environment should play the leading role in maintaining its stability rather than relying on military structures dominated by outside powers.
In this view, regional cooperation is not merely a diplomatic preference, but a security requirement shaped by geography, shared interests and the consequences of military confrontation.
Civilizational confrontation and Washington’s historical rhetoric
Alongside the military and strategic debate, Iranian officials have strongly criticized the use of historical and civilizational references in contemporary political disputes.
Caretaker Defense Minister Ebn al-Reza condemned remarks by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Athens that invoked the ancient conflicts between Greece and Persia. He warned against turning historical and cultural differences into a basis for present-day political or military confrontation.
“Civilizational confrontation is playing with fire,” Ebn al-Reza said, cautioning that those who ignite such tensions may not be able to control their consequences.
He stressed that Iran possesses an ancient civilization and a distinct national identity that do not depend on external recognition. He also argued that the country must strengthen its scientific, industrial and defense capabilities to safeguard its independence.
Brigadier General Ali Balali, an adviser to the commander of the IRGC Aerospace Force, offered a broader ideological interpretation of the confrontation. He said the United States and Israel sought to exploit the wealth and resources of Eastern countries while preventing the emergence of a new Islamic civilization.
“Civilization belongs to the East, and they have no civilization of their own,” Balali said.
He urged neighboring Muslim countries to be aware of efforts by Washington and its allies to prevent the peoples of the East and the Muslim world from becoming more capable and prosperous. Balali also criticized the historical record of Western powers, citing the mass killing of Indigenous peoples in the Americas and violence against populations in Africa.
He maintained that Western powers would ultimately fail to prevent the emergence of a global order shaped by Islamic civilization.
The controversy has also drawn attention to Trump’s statements during the war against Iran. On April 1, he threatened to bombard Iran and said US forces would “bring them back to the stone ages,” while also threatening Iranian power plants and other infrastructure. On April 7, he warned that “a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again” if Iran failed to meet his demands.
The remarks have become part of the wider dispute over the language used to describe the conflict and its potential consequences. Iranian officials have argued that such rhetoric cannot be separated from threats against the country’s infrastructure, population and sovereignty.
The exchange has also revived historical references on both sides. Iranian political figures have invoked episodes from the country’s past, including the capture of Roman Emperor Valerian by the Sasanian king Shapur I in 260 AD, in response to Washington’s references to ancient Greco-Persian wars.
For Iranian officials, the issue extends beyond competing interpretations of history. They frame it as a broader question of who has the authority to define civilization, determine the political future of other societies and shape the emerging international order.
Taken together, the statements by Iran’s defense and military officials present a unified message: the country intends to strengthen its deterrent capabilities, safeguard its sovereign interests in strategically important waters and resist external efforts to determine the future of West Asia. In their assessment, lasting regional stability requires respect for national sovereignty and a greater role for regional countries in shaping their own security arrangements, rather than renewed dependence on outside military powers.

Record GMLRS rocket motor order goes to L3Harris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:34:25 UTC
01:34:25 KST

- L3Harris won a $250 million follow-on contract from Lockheed Martin for standard-range GMLRS rocket motors, the largest quantity in program history.
- The motors will be built at a new 60,000-square-foot plant in Camden, Arkansas, opening later this year; the quantity was not disclosed.
L3Harris Technologies has won a $250 million contract from Lockheed Martin to build solid rocket motors for standard-range Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System rockets, the largest quantity ordered in the program’s history, the company said Oct. 12.
The motors will be built at L3Harris’ new 60,000-square-foot (5,600-square-meter) plant in Camden, Arkansas, which the company says will open later this year and use automation and robotics across each stage of solid rocket motor production. L3Harris did not disclose how many motors the contract covers, the delivery schedule, or which customers will receive the finished rockets.
GMLRS is the guided rocket fired by the U.S. Army’s HIMARS and M270 launchers and by allied armies, including Ukraine’s. Each standard-range rocket can hit targets out to about 70 km (43 miles). Lockheed Martin is the prime contractor and assembles the rockets, also in Camden, while L3Harris supplies the motor that propels them, along with the electronic safe-and-arm device that keeps the warhead from detonating early and the proximity sensor that sets it off near the target.
“Securing this follow-on award at the highest quantity in program history demonstrates confidence in L3Harris’ missile propulsion expertise and our ability to deliver at scale,” said Scott Alexander, president of Propulsion Systems at L3Harris Missile Solutions. “With our investments to expand capacity ahead of need, we’re well-positioned to meet this surge while maintaining the quality our customers expect.”
L3Harris says it has doubled its GMLRS motor output in recent years through new manufacturing techniques. The company became a major solid rocket motor supplier when it bought Aerojet Rocketdyne in 2023, and the motor has long been one of the limits on how fast GMLRS rockets can be built. Demand has risen sharply since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, where HIMARS and GMLRS have been in heavy use, and as more countries buy HIMARS. Australia began building its own GMLRS rockets this year and test-fired the first Australian-made round from a HIMARS in April.
L3Harris named the Camden plant an “Arsenal of Freedom” facility, after the Department of War initiative to expand weapons production.

Faith, motherhood, and rock & roll: Three Israeli musicians reunite to form The Mothers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:29:00 UTC
01:29:00 KST

“Well, you’ve given up,” singer Sharon Rotter casually remarked to fellow musician Shiri Hadar during a conversation about their lives.
On the surface, the accusation was true: Rotter and Hadar were part of a generation of prominent female artists who seemed to walk away from the Tel Aviv indie scene at the height of their success in the early to mid 2000s, trading major record deals and mainstream stardom for family life and religious observance.
Rotter’s comment hit a nerve, exposing a deeper truth: While these women had given up the pursuit of commercial celebrity, they weren’t willing to give up on music itself.
But the sting of the remark acted as the sudden catalyst that sent Hadar, the former keyboardist for the indie-rock band Izabo, straight to her phone. “I said, ‘What?’ and immediately called Noa,” Hadar recalls.
The friend on the other end of the line was Noa Gino, a powerhouse vocalist who had spent years looking for a way back into a recording studio.
Gino had once been signed to the major label Hed Arzi and was the featured voice on Danny Sanderson’s Toldot HaMayim project, before her career paused.
Hadar’s phone call was the final piece of the puzzle. “I had wanted to form an all-female group for years,” Gino says. “My husband Ron and I thought of Shiri first. He knew Sharon, and I had met her during classes at a Tel Aviv Jewish heritage center.”
With that call, the three former indie icons were officially reunited, turning a shared sacrifice into a new, faith-based rock band. “We went full steam ahead,” says Hadar.
From Tel Aviv's indie rock scene to faith, family
Despite their shift toward religious lifestyles, all three women still carry the deep muscle memory of their rock & roll pasts.
They are no longer the secular indie icons who once dominated Tel Aviv’s airwaves, and today, they navigate vastly different personal realities:
Rotter lives on a moshav as a Breslov Hassid; Gino similarly chose a rural religious lifestyle with her family; while Hadar remains in secular central Tel Aviv, raising her children in an Anthroposophic school, while studying the inner dimensions of Torah and Kabbalah.
Yet, the creative link to their roots remains intact – evidenced by Rotter stepping back onto the stage last year at the Enav Center to perform her classic hit “Arutz Elecha” (“Run 2U”) with Berry Sakharof, Hadar writing songs in her home studio, and Gino penning new music from her abode.
The trio initially named their new project Ha’Imahot because their earliest rehearsal sessions were entirely dictated by childcare schedules.
“We used to schedule sessions, only for them to get canceled,” Hadar says.
When they finally committed to releasing music to the public, they swapped the name for the English version, The Mothers, aiming to reach a broader, global Jewish audience.
They have since released a debut single, “100%,” followed by their sophomore track, “Adon HaNiflaot,” which sets the traditional morning prayer blessing Yotzer Or to a chic, modern indie beat.
Inside The Mothers' creative process
The band now operates out of two home studios in central Tel Aviv, spaces shared by Hadar and her partner, Izabo frontman and producer Ran Shem-Tov. Inside the studio, their roles fell into place based on personality.
“Shiri has excellent taste and an original vision,” Rotter explains. “She always knows how to make things look unique, and she’s the boss in that realm.
“Noa is a gifted writer; she wrote most of the songs about motherhood. She’s the spirit of the group – bringing a deeply spiritual dimension.
“I’m the driving force – fast, efficient, and a pusher; I know how to handle production and keep things light.”
Hadar handles the primary music tracking in the house, working in the pockets of time left by their families.
“We’re waiting for the kids to grow up,” Rotter says with a laugh.
“When they were little, it was a time of survival, and music was at the bottom of the priority list because there was a more important kind of creation happening. Nowadays, the children no longer need me on a moment-to-moment, daily basis, so I can make time to return to things I loved – things that had been put on hold for 20 years.”
Hadar’s path to faith moved through Kundalini yoga before evolving into the study of Kabbalah and the teachings of Rav Kook. As a result, her own home exists in a delicate secular-religious balance.
“We know how to contain this situation within our complex reality,” Hadar says. “Ran hasn’t become religious, but he deeply respects my choice and my daughter’s choice. She is 15 and was with me throughout the entire process of becoming religious. For instance, on Shabbat, I don’t turn on the lights, but he does. Each of us does what we want, though there are things he won’t do. He wouldn’t turn on a burner in the kitchen, for instance.”
The lifestyle shift has fundamentally rewritten their lyric books.
“I once wanted to write only about what I felt was ‘right’ to write,” Gino says. “Back when I worked with Danny Sanderson, I wrote only about relationships and the search for love. Later, I went through a phase of writing only about the Almighty. Today, my lyrics focus on the inner workings of the soul and the world.”
Rotter views their distinct theological choices through a literary lens. “We started in the same place and headed down different paths – much like in Frost’s poem ‘The Road Not Taken.’ There are 70 faces to the Torah; each of us made a choice based on her specific situation... yet ultimately, it all comes down to the same thing.”
Different paths to Jewish spirituality
Operating as an all-female religious rock band presents unique halachic boundaries, particularly regarding kol isha – the Orthodox prohibition against men listening to female singing. To move forward, Gino sought out spiritual counsel before putting their music online.
“The rabbi gave me his approval because, essentially, men can choose whether or not to watch and listen,” Gino explains. “Those who observe the practice of not listening to women simply won’t listen. This approval allows us to work and release songs, because before that, we were really quite stuck.”
While their digital singles are streamed publicly, their upcoming live shows – funded by a grant from the Mifal Hapayis national lottery – will be open to female audiences only.
The rare setup occasionally draws comparisons to HaMechashefot (The Witches), Israel’s most famous all-female rock band, a connection that brings up personal memories for Rotter. “I moved in the same circles as the late Inbal Perlmuter, but sadly, we never actually met. I saw the film about her, and I cried through most of it. It’s a very sad story.”
Balancing religious observance with rock music
The reality of starting over from scratch after walking away from major label backing is a frequent topic of conversation among them.
“Yes, it definitely hurts,” Gino says openly. “Today, I make music and have to go out and find an audience – an audience that could have already been mine.
“My big break happened around the same time as Eviatar Banai’s; we were also signed to Hed Arzi. The label reps would come visit me and then drive down South to visit him. So, yes, it hurts – it hurt for years and used to make my stomach churn – but I’ve come to accept my own journey.”
Rotter measures the outcome differently. “There’s a small sense of a missed opportunity deep down, though I didn’t always feel that way... I make music because it’s part of who I am. I try not to focus so much on the outcome; what drives me is the joy of the journey itself. It’s enough if just one person’s heart opens up, or if we manage to bring someone a moment of happiness when they hear our music.”
Decades spent away from the professional grind have shifted their perspective on what defines a successful musical career. Rather than obsessing over industry metrics or mainstream validation, the bandmates actively practice personal growth and emotional resilience through their music. For them, the metric of success is no longer an industry standard, but a personal one.
“We’ve been working on our character traits for many years, and we realize that nothing is truly critical,” Rotter notes. “The main thing is just having fun together.”
For more, visit youtube.com/@THEMOTHERSIL

There is no neutrality in degradation, there is no balance in ignoring opposition to Zionists, there is no innocence in hosting Zionists.”
After Mohamied’s line manager reportedly asked her to consider deleting the posts, she refused and resigned in March 2024 before being referred to the Nursing and Midwifery Council and the Metropolitan Police under Prevent. Both referrals were dismissed, and her ongoing claim against her former employer continues.
NHS doctor accused of spreading antisemitic conspiracy theories
Another individual highlighted in the investigation is Dr. Mohamed Abdelaal Ragheb Elfarra, a general practitioner in the Accident and Emergency Department at St. James’s University Hospital in Leeds, which is part of the Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust.

Elfarra also shared posts claiming that the Rothschild family controls all the world’s money, as well as “Elon Musk is controlled by Zionists,” and wrote in April 2024 that “Zionists are the new Nazis of the last 100 years.”
A spokesperson for Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust said, “We are committed to creating an inclusive workplace where all colleagues feel safe, respected, and supported. The Trust has policies and procedures for appropriate staff conduct, and all allegations are investigated.”
NHS occupational therapist accused of sharing violent anti-Israel rhetoric
The investigation also identified occupational therapist Zaida Parveen Akhtar, who also works as a make-up artist and is known as Zee Zidane on Facebook. Akhtar was nominated for a Values in Practice Award by Birmingham Community Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust and works for University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust.
Akhtar shared a video in July 2025 concerning Netanyahu’s son, Avner Netanyahu, saying: “If you do see that face [...] Roadman, you know what to do. Sort out this waste.” She also told her followers to “get your jutiya off” – employing a Punjabi word meaning slipper or shoe, in an apparent reference calling for a beating, while also referring to Avner as the “son of the devil.”

In December 2025, she reposted a conspiracy theory video describing the Bondi Beach mass shooting as a “false flag” event.
Manchester-based registered psychiatrist Dr. Ahmed Sewehli, a member of Healthworkers for Palestine, was also named in the exposé after commenting in November 2024 that “Netanyahu should be dead, and then they wouldn’t have had to issue an arrest warrant for him either.” He replied to another social media post by Netanyahu in April 2025 with: “You need to be dead.”
Sewehli also wrote that “Zionism is the ideology of terror, mass murder, displacement, and depravity” and claimed that ISIS was learning new acts of depravity from the IDF.
NHS doctor suspended following complaints over social media posts
British-Jordanian A&E medic Dr. Nadeem Crowe was identified in the investigation after posting in July 2025 that there was “no doubt Israel is a terrorist octopus with its head in Israel and tentacles far reaching into every continent.”
In March 2025, he wrote: “Zionism is an insidious evil that is controlling every single one of us, internationally. There is an international ‘importance’ relating to ‘Israel’ that isn’t yet clear to the layman, but that means there is no option but to let it destroy all of us. I think the world knows that, if anyone takes any other stance, it will result in Armageddon, and that is a completely terrifying reality. I tend to believe most people are inherently good, but that there is a threat so powerful that even good has become evil.”
Crowe was suspended mid-shift from the Royal Free Hospital in August 2024 following colleague complaints regarding his online activity, and he is currently awaiting the outcome of a tribunal after alleging discrimination and harassment by the Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust.
A Royal Free London spokesperson said, “We cannot comment on ongoing legal cases. Our focus is always to ensure that our staff and everybody in our care feel safe and are treated equally, regardless of background or belief.”
NHS pledges zero tolerance as CAA demands action against antisemitism
CAA stated that the findings underscore an ongoing issue within public medical institutions. Stephen Silverman, director of investigations and enforcement at the CAA, said, “Our documentary on antisemitism in the NHS revealed how extremism is becoming rife in medicine, with employers and regulators failing to rein in radicalized doctors and nurses.”
He added, “These are yet more examples of the hate in healthcare that the authorities are doing nothing about. What is happening in British medicine is a national disgrace. Jewish people may be feeling the effects most keenly, but nobody wants to be treated by unhinged extremists. It’s past time that the authorities address the crisis.”
A Department for Health and Social Care spokesperson said, “We commissioned Lord Mann’s [government’s independent adviser on antisemitism] review to root out the cancer of antisemitism and other forms of racism from our health service. As well as the NHS implementing all of Lord Mann’s recommendations, we expect professional regulators to take the strongest possible action in individual cases wherever necessary.”
An NHS England spokesperson noted, “Any form of antisemitism and racism in the NHS is wholly unacceptable, and all local organizations must take a zero-tolerance approach, including police involvement and criminal prosecution where appropriate.”
“The NHS is implementing all recommendations from Lord Mann’s review to tackle antisemitism and other forms of racism in the NHS, including mandatory antisemitism training for all staff and strengthening accountability for senior leaders – and performance against new national standards will be reported and assessed,” the NHS England spokesperson said.
A General Medical Council spokesperson added, “We are very clear that antisemitism is completely unacceptable. Doctors and patients should have confidence that if a concern is raised with the GMC, it will be dealt with appropriately. We can and will investigate serious concerns that suggest patient safety or the public’s confidence in doctors may be at risk.”

====================================================================================================

Combating Israel's 'brain drain': Inside Hebrew University's new medical education center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:26:15 UTC
01:26:15 KST

Hebrew University of Jerusalem is launching a new Center for Advanced Medical Education, using a gift of $30 million from the family foundation of Steven H. Lavin, designed to revolutionize the way physicians are trained in Israel by incorporating new AI technology into education.
The new center aims to combat Israel's so-called 'brain drain', in which an increasing number of Israelis are receiving extensive education overseas and remain elsewhere just as Israel may need them the most. This has led to an increasing shortage of doctors in Israel, with the country projected to have only three doctors per 1,000 people by 2035.
Lavin told The Jerusalem Post that the October 7 massacre in 2023 highlighted the problem of this brain drain, specifically the element where highly qualified medical students are forced to go study abroad and often settle there just as Israel needs them the most.
"People are training abroad and staying abroad...they start to build their life, and they don't want to return," Lavin told the Post.
Lavin met up with a friend, Vice President of Hebrew University Ambassador Yossi Gal, with whom he discussed the problem, which led to the start of a concrete system to address the problem by partnering with Hebrew University to create a new system that would allow an increasing number of Israelis to study within Israel and begin to build their lives within the country.
In addition to retaining doctors within the country, Lavin stressed the benefit of having a generation of physicians trained in Israel, while immersed in the culture.
Professor Eli Pikarsky, Dean of the Faculty of Medicine at Hebrew University, underlined the importance of cultural immersion in patient care.
Pikarsky told the Post that the cultural preparedness of physicians and healthcare professionals will be an immensely important part of the program under development, as an essential, and yet one of the most difficult parts of the medical profession.
New training to utilize self-learning, group-learning systems to increase capacity
The system is designed to improve Israeli's medical education capacity without sacrificing the quality of education or the time and mentoring feedback from senior physicians.
Pikarsky explained that within the new system, a high proportion of the knowledge acquisition will be done using technology, both in self-learning and group learning. The new center envisions a future in which classes in large lecture halls can transition into modules that students will work individually and collaboratively to learn and work through.
Additionally, assessments of individual students will become more efficient, according to Pikarsky.
"Today, a physician, a mentor, meets a student next to a patient, and they do this simulated discussion of the patient case. They hear the patient, they examine the patient, and then this physician who is overworked, tired, has a family, has other obligations, and also wants a life has to sit at home at 10 o'clock at night and write the feedback. This is not the way to do it," he told the Post.
By using an automatic system during the discussion that will take notes and write a structured feedback outline for the mentor to use, the physician can then give more feedback sessions while also having an objective and online component.
Pikarsky said that the feedback itself will still come from the mentor, who will get an outline of what happened, suggested points for discussion with the student, and the general assessment.
"Then the mentor can then go over these and decide what he agrees with, what he doesn't agree with, and then provide that to the student," Pikarsky told the Post.
Pikarsky emphasized that the educational tools he'd described were just two of many under development.
Another tool Pikarsky suggested will use technology to assess medical students' ability to effectively communicate. While skill at communicating as a physician is one Pikarsky told the Post comes over time, the advantage that the system gives is the ability for students to strengthen their abilities without doing so in front of the patient.
They can then go over what happened, understand potential improvements, and implement them with another try in the system.
Tools will also be designed to help students collaborate and teach each other, which Pikarsky describes as an invaluable experience.
"It's really a very different way of learning something. And if all of our students had the opportunity to teach as part of their learning, they will learn more.
Embracing AI as the future of healthcare
Both Pikarsky and Lavin acknowledged that the idea of incorporating AI and additional technology into medical training concerns many who fear that this will lead to less personal connection within their education and then within patient care.
However, Lavin explained that while medical professionals will still be overseeing the work being done, tasks that are "inefficiently using highly trained people" will not have to be done by them.
Lavin told the Post that embracing these tools for training is the way forward to advance medicine and increase the quality of care.
"It's something that we will, as people have to adjust to. But I think that if we don't use the tools available to us for this training, we won't be getting the best medical service there is."
Pikarsky added on, explaining that contrary to the fear, the system is optimized to allow mentors more time to connect with students, observe them, discuss complex cases, and provide personal guidance without spending time on tasks students can complete with technological guidance.

All recent polls suggest that a bloc led by former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot would not be able to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition without support from Arab parties. But a Knesset speaker may be appointed by the Knesset even before a government is formed.
Asked if he would refuse to convene the Knesset for a vote to replace him, as his predecessor Yuli Edelstein did, Ohana declined, saying he would not allow the appointment process to reach the High Court of Justice again. "We are law-abiding, and we always have been," he said.
Edelstein, who also served as Knesset speaker on behalf of Likud, refused in March 2020 to convene the Knesset to elect a permanent speaker, despite 61 lawmakers – a majority in the Knesset – demanding a vote and supporting his replacement.
The incident took place during a tumultuous period in Israeli politics, following the third of five elections held over a four-year period.
Edelstein argued that a permanent speaker should not be elected until the composition of the next governing coalition was clear. But the High Court unanimously rejected his argument. Edelstein chose to resign rather than comply with the ruling, writing to the High Court justices that "my conscience does not allow me to comply with the ruling."
Ohana, who was justice minister at the time, encouraged Edelstein to defy the court even before the justices had ruled on the petition. When the High Court demanded that Edelstein say whether he would convene the plenum, Ohana said on X: "If I were the Knesset speaker, I would answer: No."
The Likud has long been running campaigns with messaging delegitimizing Arab parties and their supporters. The slogan "It's Bibi or Tibi," referring to Arab politician Ahmad Tibi, has been a focal point of campaigns for years.

ATHENS, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The Greek government presented a draft legislation on Monday that would ban children under 15 from accessing social media from Jan. 1, 2027.
The proposed law would require social media platforms to verify users' ages, Minister of State Akis Skertsos, Health Minister Adonis Georgiadis and Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence Minister Dimitris Papastergiou told a news conference in Athens.
The initial focus would be on Instagram, Facebook and TikTok, although the list of platforms covered could change, Papastergiou said.
According to the government, the proposed restrictions were intended to limit children's exposure to harmful content, cyberbullying and platform features that encourage excessive use, while preserving access to digital services needed for communication, education and everyday activities.
Skertsos said Greece aimed to become the first European country to introduce comparable legislation. He added that the proposal had been developed in consultation with relevant European authorities to ensure compatibility with the EU regulatory framework.
The legislation would be implemented under the European Union's Digital Services Act (DSA). Platforms found to be in breach of applicable rules could face fines of up to 6 percent of their global annual turnover, Papastergiou said.
The initiative comes as European policymakers consider broader measures to strengthen online protections for children. The proposed EU KIDS Act is still going through the EU legislative process.
The proposed social media ban follows other government measures to protect minors, including a ban on mobile phone use in schools and the development of digital tools to improve children's online safety. ■

The experience of Ningxia, such as viticulture in specific environments, investment in technology and knowledge, and a vision to create a well-known wine culture and tourism brand, offers important opportunities for international exchange and mutual learning, she said.
With the goal of building a new landscape for the wine industry, the president called for deepening cooperation with relevant authorities, institutions, experts and the wine industry in Ningxia and across China.
That cooperation will include Ningxia-based experts joining OIV's international network and expert groups, exchanges on grape growing, winemaking, climate adaptation and emerging technologies, plus ongoing alignment with international standards and best practices, she said.

Across OIV member states, the industry is deeply affected by climate change, economic pressures, changing social behavior and consumption patterns, geopolitical and trade uncertainties, and the rapid development of digital technologies, he said.

The congress, themed around building a new landscape for the global vine and wine industry, features an opening ceremony, a seminar on high-quality development of the Chinese vine and wine industry, a sci-tech sub-session, industry visits and a closing ceremony.
Over 400 academic papers from 35 countries will be on display at the sci-tech sub-session, introducing cutting-edge technologies that could help drive the transformation and upgrading of the vine and wine industry.
The 6th China (Ningxia) International Wine Culture and Tourism Expo opened alongside the congress, attracting 84 world-renowned wineries and enterprises from distinctive production areas in 16 countries. It has also drawn a total of 146 leading domestic wineries from Ningxia and other core production areas in China.

Namibia hosts first African nuclear test verification exercise

00:22:58 CST
01:22:58 KST

WINDHOEK, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Namibia is hosting the first Integrated Field Exercise in Africa, with about 250 international experts to test procedures and equipment used to investigate suspected nuclear test explosions.
In a statement issued on Monday, the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO) said the exercise, running from Oct. 10 to Nov. 20 in Namibia's Erongo Region, is designed to assess readiness to conduct on-site inspections under the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT).
Participants include surrogate inspectors nominated by signatory states, national technical experts, CTBTO staff and external evaluators, the organization said, adding that about 150 tonnes of technical and support equipment have been transported to Namibia by sea and air for the exercise.
Namibia's Minister of International Relations and Trade Selma Ashipala-Musavyi said hosting the exercise demonstrates the country's commitment to nuclear disarmament and contributes to strengthening the international on-site inspection system.
CTBTO Executive Secretary Robert Floyd said the exercise allows participants to test and refine the operational readiness needed to conduct inspections when questions about compliance with the treaty cannot be resolved through diplomatic or other technical means.
The scenario-based activities include establishing a temporary base of operations in Swakopmund and conducting field activities in a designated inspection area in the Erongo Region.
According to the CTBTO, an on-site inspection is a verification measure provided for under the CTBT. Once the treaty enters into force, a state party may request such an inspection to clarify whether a nuclear test explosion has taken place. The request would require approval by the CTBTO Executive Council.
Namibia hosts two certified facilities near Tsumeb that form part of the treaty's International Monitoring System.
The exercise follows similar integrated field exercises held in Kazakhstan in 2008 and Jordan in 2014, the CTBTO said. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- China announced on Monday that it will cut the value-added tax (VAT) export rebate rate for new energy vehicles (NEVs) to 9 percent from 13 percent starting April 1, 2027.
VAT export rebates for e-cigarette devices and related products will be scrapped from the same date, according to a statement jointly issued by the Ministry of Finance and the State Taxation Administration.
Export consumption tax policies for products subject to the tax will remain unchanged, with existing tax refund or exemption arrangements continuing to apply, the statement said.
The adjustment comes as China has continued to optimize export tax rebate policies.
The country scrapped VAT export rebates for photovoltaic products from April 1, 2026, while cutting the rebate rate for battery products to 6 percent from 9 percent on the same date. The rebates for battery products will be eliminated from Jan. 1, 2027.
China is the world's largest market for NEVs, a category that includes battery electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles. The sector has expanded rapidly in recent years, with automakers increasingly looking to overseas markets for growth.
Luo Zhiheng, chief economist at Yuekai Securities, told business news network Yicai that cutting export tax rebates can, to some extent, reduce rat race competition and encourage companies to shift from low-price competition to technology and brand-based competition.
"China's NEVs are highly competitive internationally. Against the backdrop of tight global supplies of traditional energy, NEVs have met the needs of residents in Europe and the United States. Even with a partial rebate cut, they can retain sufficient competitiveness," Luo said. "Objectively, this also plays a positive role in stabilizing the macro tax burden and can better support the development of domestic demand."
During the January-September period, China's auto exports totaled 8.205 million units, including over 4 million NEVs, more than double the level a year earlier, according to the latest data.
"Despite a complex and severe external environment, exports have continued to grow rapidly, demonstrating strong resilience, while domestic new growth drivers are being steadily unleashed and the share of NEV sales is rising steadily," said Chen Shihua, deputy secretary-general of the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers.
Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, the industry is expected to maintain steady operation, Chen said. ■

Uncrewed truck with anti-drone laser shown at AUSA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:22:20 UTC
01:22:20 KST

- Harbinger’s uncrewed Praesidia hybrid truck is powering an AeroVironment LOCUST X3 30-kW counter-drone laser at American Rheinmetall’s AUSA 2026 booth.
- The companies have not said whether the laser-armed configuration is tied to any U.S. Army contract or test.
An uncrewed hybrid truck built by California’s Harbinger is powering a 30-kilowatt AeroVironment counter-drone laser at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington this week, shown at American Rheinmetall’s booth.
Harbinger CEO John Henry Harris said in a LinkedIn post on Oct. 12 that the company’s Praesidia vehicle is supplying power to an AeroVironment LOCUST X3 laser weapon mounted on the truck, with autonomy software from Forterra.
The display is at Rheinmetall’s booth, No. 2285. Harris pitched the combination as cheap, mass-producible equipment with “unlimited magazine depth,” a reference to the fact that a laser keeps firing as long as it has electrical power rather than running out of missiles or rounds. He did not say whether the system has been tested together in the field, whether any U.S. Army unit plans to use it, or what it would cost.
The Praesidia is a militarized version of the plug-in hybrid chassis Harbinger builds for commercial delivery trucks. It has no cab, is driven by wire so autonomy kits can control steering, braking and acceleration, and combines a large battery pack with a gasoline engine that acts as a generator. Harbinger says the vehicle can travel more than 800 km (500 miles) on a full tank and full battery, or about 170 km (105 miles) on electric power alone, and can export up to 350 kW of power to equipment it carries. That power is what a laser weapon needs: a high-energy laser draws electricity continuously while firing, and the vehicle carrying it has to supply it.
AeroVironment’s LOCUST laser family came from BlueHalo, which AeroVironment acquired in 2025. The U.S. Army has tested earlier LOCUST lasers mounted on Joint Light Tactical Vehicles as part of its effort to shoot down small drones without spending missiles. AeroVironment has not published detailed specifications for the X3 version beyond the 30 kW power level Harris cited.
The truck at AUSA comes from a program already under contract. In August, the U.S. Army gave American Rheinmetall an 18-month deal to build autonomous supply vehicles under Project Sustainment, using Harbinger’s chassis, Forterra’s autonomy software and Primordial Labs’ Anura control interface. Those vehicles are meant to haul supplies to company-sized units without a driver. Harbinger has also said it is configuring the Praesidia for battlefield communications, troop transport, perimeter security and counter-drone missions, and the CIA-backed venture firm In-Q-Tel invested in the company in June.

Greenland lawmakers signal support for Trump security deal
COPENHAGEN, Oct 12 - A majority of Greenlandic lawmakers signalled support for the Arctic island's recent security agreement with US President Donald Trump in a debate on Monday, although some opposition party members questioned the deal's economic value.
The United States, Denmark and Greenland last month signed the agreement, aimed at ending tensions after Trump's repeated threats to take control of the strategically located and mineral-rich island.
The agreement is subject to a second reading in parliament before being put to a vote, with lawmakers expected to pass the legislation.
The deal expands the US military's role in Greenland, paving the way for two new military bases and Trump's "Golden Dome" missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination.
The chair of opposition party Naleraq, Pele Broberg, said many details still remained unclear on how the agreement would work in practice.
"The US is granted extensive rights in our country. The people of Greenland are not guaranteed any fixed payment for those rights," Broberg said in the parliamentary debate in Greenland's capital Nuuk.
The government parties, which have a majority of seats, defended the deal.
Former Foreign Minister Vivian Motzfeldt of the governing coalition's Demokraatit said Greenland had secured "massive" protection without having to pay for it, while winning recognition as an autonomous nation.
Foreign Minister Mute Egede said the deal was "a huge step forward" that could not be measured in terms of money.
Erik Jensen, chair of the Siumut party, said his party backed the deal.
"For several years, Siumut has been campaigning to ensure that agreements concerning Greenland are no longer concluded without Greenlandic participation... That is why we are satisfied," Jensen said. REUTERS

NEW DELHI: Ramlila Maidan, newly designated as one of the capital's three protest sites, is already booked for most of the next two-and-a-half months, leaving just three days available for reservations this year.Additionally, while a small section of the ground can be used for protests free of charge, booking the larger venue, which spans 12 acres and can accommodate up to 50,000 people, involves a daily fee and a refundable security deposit.Revealing that only December 29, 30 and 31 as the availiable dates, an official quoted by PTI said, "The booking rate for the ground is Rs 50,000 per day, plus a Rs 55,000 security deposit that is refundable. The initial outlay including taxes comes to Rs 1.21 lakh for a day's booking."However, officials clarified that a small portion of the ground, with space for around 150 people, remains available for protests and gatherings free of charge.Permission to use the larger ground must be obtained from the Municipal Corporation of Delhi's horticulture department, which processes bookings after applicants secure a no-objection certificate from Delhi Police.
The arrangement has drawn criticism from opposition leaders and protesters, who argue that the limited availability and high booking costs could make demonstrations difficult to organise.AAP Delhi president Saurabh Bharadwaj questioned the decision, pointing to events already scheduled at the venue. Govt. played another fraud with its citizens. The Ramleela Maidan is occupied with two Ramleelas," Bharadwaj wrote on X."How can one hold a protest here? Do they want to create chaos?" he asked.Protesters also highlighted the financial burden, noting that demonstrations at Jantar Mantar did not require comparable payments.Civic officials, however, pointed to the revenue implications of allowing unrestricted use of the ground. A BJP rally in 2014 reportedly caused traffic jams extending nearly four kilometres to ITO, despite being held on a Sunday.
The venue has been central to Delhi's political history for decades. Once a pond, the site was filled and levelled around 1930 to accommodate Ramlila performances, which began there in 1932. It subsequently hosted major political gatherings addressed by leaders including Jawaharlal Nehru, Indira Gandhi, Jayaprakash Narayan and Atal Bihari Vajpayee.On June 25, 1975, the day the Emergency was declared, Jayaprakash Narayan and Vajpayee addressed a rally at the ground. Relatively recently, Arvind Kejriwal took oath as Delhi chief minister there in 2013.The controversy follows an standing order issued by Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar, which removed Jantar Mantar from the list of designated protest venues and identified Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi as the three new locations for demonstrations. Police said a detailed, revised standard operating procedure for protests at these sites would be issued separately.

‘They played with the bomb’: Warning sign near deadly Israeli school trip blast raises questions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:19:06 UTC
01:19:06 KST

Students on a school trip near Israel's northern border reportedly picked up an unexploded munition, played with it and posed for photographs before it detonated, killing a 14-year-old boy and injuring 23 others. As investigators examine how the tragedy unfolded, new questions have emerged over a warning sign prohibiting entry to nearby woodland that had officially remained closed since May 2025.
The explosion occurred Monday near Mitzpe Pe'er in the Upper Galilee, during the first day of an annual excursion by eighth-grade students from the ORT Ma'alot-Tarshiha religious high school. Three students were seriously injured, 10 sustained moderate injuries and another 10 were lightly hurt.
Security officials increasingly believe the device was an old Hezbollah cluster munition left unexploded during the fighting along the Lebanese border. Police Commissioner Danny Levy said investigators were almost certain that cluster munitions were involved, although the weapon's precise origin and the circumstances of its detonation remain under investigation.
‘They were excited about it and took pictures’
About 50 students and teachers were participating in the excursion, which the Education Ministry said had received the necessary approval.
According to Eliyahu Galil, whose son was among the students, several boys discovered the unexploded device, handled it and photographed themselves with it before the blast.
"They were excited about it and took pictures. Apparently, one of the children put it in his bag, and it exploded when the bag was off to the side," Galil said.
He said his son, who escaped injury, sent him a photograph of the device after the explosion.
Galil described the object as resembling a cluster munition with a shaped charge, apparently belonging to Hezbollah.
"They were playing with it," he said, stressing that his account of how the explosion occurred was based on what he had learned from the students.
"This could have ended much worse," he added.
Although his son was physically unharmed, Galil said he had witnessed deeply distressing scenes as classmates lay injured around him.
"A lot of boys we know from the community and the surrounding area were injured. Shrapnel in the shoulder, in the eyes, all kinds of very unpleasant places," he said.
Police have not determined whether the boy who was killed was holding the munition when it detonated.
"We still don't know for certain whether the boy who was killed was holding the unexploded ordnance," Levy said. "We will collect testimony and investigate what happened."
A warning sign that remained in force
A separate question has emerged over the location of the excursion.
Near the explosion site stands a Jewish National Fund (KKL-JNF) sign warning that entry into forests and recreation areas is strictly prohibited.
According to the organization's website, the Naftali Mountains Forest cycling trail and scenic road have been closed since May 25, 2025, until further notice because of rehabilitation work following damage caused by the war.
Following an inquiry by ynet, KKL-JNF officials confirmed that the restriction remained in effect because of previous fires and the security situation.
They said the area had not been cleared of potential hazards.
The students' bus was photographed passing the warning sign, raising questions about the planning and authorization of the route.
However, KKL-JNF emphasized that it could not establish whether the explosion occurred within the specific forest areas under its jurisdiction where entry was prohibited. Its representatives had not been permitted to enter the blast site to make that determination.
KKL-JNF is also not the authority responsible for imposing security closures or restricting civilian access because of unexploded military ordnance. Those responsibilities fall to the police and military.
The distinction has become central to the investigation: A forest restriction was in place nearby, but it has not been established whether the school group entered an area that was officially closed to visitors.
The Education Ministry said its preliminary examination found that the excursion had been "organized in accordance with all procedures, under IDF supervision and instructions."
The military, however, is still examining whether permission had been granted for the students to travel along the specific route near Mitzpe Pe'er and, if so, whether that authorization passed through the required channels.
The site is extremely close to the Lebanese border, in an area previously used as a staging ground for IDF units and targeted by Hezbollah fire during the war.
‘The injured were scattered along the route’
Emergency responders described a chaotic scene as classmates tried to save one another in the moments after the explosion.
Tamir Duadi, a member of Kibbutz Manara's civilian emergency response squad, said he rushed to the site and was among the first to reach the wounded.
"I took out my first-aid kit to treat them and perform CPR," he recalled. Another responder from United Hatzalah joined him, while police and Magen David Adom ambulances were dispatched.
"I told myself that if I didn't take responsibility, I had no business being there," he said. "I stayed until the end, until I saw the last child evacuated."
MDA emergency medical technician David Radko, who arrived on a motorcycle, said he immediately recognized the scale of the disaster.
"The injured were scattered along the route. Some were holding and trying to help their wounded friends. Farther along, I saw the more seriously injured," he said.
He began sorting casualties according to the severity of their injuries and attempting to control bleeding.
Despite the shock, he said the students cooperated with rescuers and showed remarkable determination to help their classmates.
"Some had even applied tourniquets to their friends to stop the bleeding. I gave them instructions on how to help, and they listened and followed them," Radko said.
Paramedic Orly Ben Simon described shouting and confusion at the scene, where rescue teams found the 14-year-old unconscious and critically wounded.
"We immediately began prolonged and intensive resuscitation efforts," she said. "Unfortunately, his injuries were critical, and we had to pronounce him dead at the scene."
The injured were transported to Rambam Medical Center in Haifa, Ziv Medical Center in Safed and Galilee Medical Center in Nahariya.
Initial hospital reports indicated that 13 injured students had been admitted to Ziv, four to Rambam and six to Galilee Medical Center. Emergency crews also treated several people suffering from acute anxiety at the scene.
Police consider restrictions on school trips
At the scene, Commissioner Levy said police would examine the circumstances of the blast and consider further precautions to prevent similar incidents.
"Young children went out on a trip, and unfortunately there is one fatality and injuries of varying severity," he said.
"We will learn lessons to make sure things like this do not happen again."
Levy said investigators believed the explosion involved military ordnance left behind during the war, most likely a cluster munition.
He also suggested that authorities could temporarily restrict similar outdoor activities while the risks are reassessed.
"It may be that we will prohibit events like these for the coming period," he said.
Cluster munitions contain multiple smaller explosive devices designed to disperse across a wide area. When some of those devices fail to detonate on impact, they can remain dangerous long after fighting ends.
For the families of the students, the investigation now involves several painful questions: How did an unexploded munition remain accessible near a hiking route? Why were children allowed to handle it? And was the excursion properly cleared to pass through an area where warnings of wartime hazards were still in effect?
The authorities have yet to determine precisely where the students found the device, whether the fatal explosion occurred inside a restricted area or which body, if any, failed to prevent access to the hazard.

- The company has not released Specter’s speed, range or payload, and has introduced a maritime unit following its BlackSea Technologies acquisition.
AEVEX is showing a full-size model of Specter, its new jet-powered one-way attack drone, at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington this week, along with a maritime drone line built from its recent purchase of BlackSea Technologies.
The California-based company announced Specter on Sept. 23 as a high-speed, turbojet-powered autonomous strike platform under development with Divergent Technologies, a Los Angeles company that builds structures through additive manufacturing. AEVEX says Specter will come in ground-launched and air-launched versions and has a swappable nose section that can carry explosive warheads, electronic warfare equipment or surveillance sensors without redesigning the airframe.
The drone uses AEVEX’s CompassX autonomy software, which the company says is built to keep working when GPS and communications are jammed. AEVEX has not released Specter’s speed, range, size, payload weight, price or flight test schedule, and has not named a customer.
Divergent’s role is to make the drone easier to build in large numbers. Its DAPS production system designs and prints complex structural parts digitally, which AEVEX says lets it change the design quickly and plan for high-rate production from the start of engineering. The model at AUSA is the first time the company has shown Specter at full size.
AEVEX is best known for the Phoenix Ghost loitering munition, which the United States sent to Ukraine starting in 2022, and for larger Group 3 drones such as Disruptor. The company went public on the New York Stock Exchange this year. It also buys rocket-assisted takeoff motors for its drones from X-Bow Systems, which has delivered hundreds of them under a $12 million contract.
The company used AUSA to introduce AEVEX Maritime Systems, a new unit formed after it acquired BlackSea Technologies, a Baltimore-area maker of uncrewed surface and underwater vessels that supplies the U.S. Navy and other U.S. forces. The acquisition was valued at about $650 million. AEVEX says its portfolio now covers air, surface and subsurface drones, aimed at an army expecting to fight with jammed navigation, cut communications and supply lines under attack.

Zelenskyy: Ukraine skipped strikes on Russian energy
Unknown

- Zelenskyy said Ukraine did not strike Russian energy facilities overnight into Oct. 12 after Trump announced an energy ceasefire.
- He said Russia kept attacking Ukrainian gas and power infrastructure, and Moscow has not confirmed agreeing to the ceasefire.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine did not strike any energy facilities inside Russia overnight into Oct. 12, after President Donald Trump announced an immediate halt to attacks on energy targets, but that Russia kept hitting Ukraine’s gas and power infrastructure.
Zelenskyy made the comments in a live interview with Fox News on Monday. Trump said on Truth Social on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy facilities. Moscow has not confirmed accepting any such deal, and the exact scope of the proposal is still unclear.
“We didn’t attack any energy objects on the territory of Russia because President Trump said that there will be an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia. And we didn’t attack, but Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, infrastructure and other things,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
He said Kyiv was ready to observe the ceasefire but doubted Moscow was, describing the overnight strikes as Vladimir Putin’s answer to Trump and saying Russia had signaled it knew nothing about an energy ceasefire.
Ukraine’s charge d’affaires in Washington, Denys Sienik, said Russian forces hit a power plant in Kyiv, cutting electricity and water, and then struck a thermal power plant in Kharkiv after Trump’s announcement. Sienik said Russia had attacked electricity generation and transmission facilities more than 200 times over the past week. Russia has not commented on those claims.
A White House official told Axios that Trump’s proposal initially focused on stopping attacks on oil refineries, with a broader halt covering power plants and electrical grids possibly to follow. Ukraine’s long-range drone campaign against Russian refineries has been a point of friction with Washington, and Trump has argued the strikes push up fuel prices. Zelenskyy rejected a refinery-only arrangement, saying an energy ceasefire has to cover Ukraine’s power grid, and tied any pause on refinery strikes to Russia doing the same.
“If Russia will not attack our energy, we will not attack the energy,” said Zelenskyy.
He also disputed Trump’s view that Ukrainian strikes are behind higher diesel prices, pointing instead to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. On Friday, Trump announced a deal with Russia to release Russian diesel to the United States and global markets, which critics in Congress say gives Moscow more revenue for the war.
Zelenskyy also responded to Trump’s suggestion over the weekend that Ukraine needs a new president. He said he was ready to hold elections but that Ukraine would need at least 60 days of security for its infrastructure to prepare, given ongoing Russian drone and missile attacks. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov rejected the idea of a 60-day pause on Monday, arguing that European countries would use it to rearm Ukraine.
“I don’t think he deserves a respite,” Lavrov said, according to the BBC.
Zelenskyy said he last spoke with Trump in person at the U.N. General Assembly in New York in late September. Russia has not said whether it will stop striking Ukrainian energy facilities.

Musk has spent $366 million to help Republicans retain control of Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:10:32 UTC
01:10:32 KST

Inside Elon Musk’s US$276 million US midterm rescue mission for Republicans
Theodore Schleifer
NEW YORK - Elon Musk has quietly funnelled more than US$276 million (S$353 million) into Republican groups and his super political action committee since the start of July, building a huge turnout operation to help the party battle headwinds in the midterm elections.
The staggering amount of money makes Musk, the richest person in the world, by far the largest known donor in the midterms. Representatives for Musk supplied the previously unreported figures on his political giving to The New York Times before a federal filing deadline on Oct 8.
In an effort to save Republicans’ Senate majority, Musk gave a total of US$158 million this summer to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing the party’s candidates for the chamber, according to his team.
In sum, that is one of the largest political donations in American history, and more than the group’s Democratic rival raised from all of its donors that quarter.
Musk has also built a major Republican turnout operation through a super PAC he founded in 2024, America PAC. He donated over US$76 million this summer to the group, which in turn spent that much on building a sprawling canvassing programme to try to turn out hard-to-reach Republican voters.
The group is active in seven Senate battlegrounds and nearly three dozen House races.
Musk has already given far more money, about US$366 million, to federal committees during the 2025-26 election cycle than he did during the 2024 election, when he laid out roughly US$290 million to help return President Donald Trump and Republicans to power.
He has given even more in undisclosed donations during both elections, according to people briefed on the giving.
The latest torrent of spending has helped give the Republican Party a financial advantage in the midterms, as well-funded outside groups like Trump’s powerful super PAC flood the airwaves with advertising in the final weeks.
No Democratic billionaire is spending nearly as much as Musk, and money remains a central worry for the party in an otherwise favourable political environment.
The donations also clear up the mystery of how much staying power Musk wants to have in American politics.
“In terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future,” he said in May 2025.
Musk, who oversees a vast business empire that has benefited from enormous federal contracts, is famously unpredictable and often jumps from one project to another.
He has been far quieter about his political work since his dramatic blowup with Trump last year.
After months of wielding vast influence inside the White House and overseeing Trump’s government cost-cutting project, he raged against the president’s major domestic policy Bill and floated threats to start a third party.
But the two men have warmed back up, appearing together at three events in the last two weeks and praising each other.
Now Musk has donated more than a quarter-billion dollars to help Trump and Republicans in the midterms. The money signals his commitment to the right and sets him up as a potential player in the 2028 presidential election, when his super PAC says it intends to remain active – the first time it has confirmed such plans.
Beyond Musk’s donations to his super PAC and the Senate Leadership Fund, his representatives said that from July through September, he had given smaller but still substantial amounts to other conservative groups:
- US$20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the main super PAC for House Republicans
- US$10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group supporting Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for Senate in Texas
- US$10 million to the Republican Governors Association
- US$2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association
“If Democrats take control of Washington and win key gubernatorial and attorney general races this November, then America risks becoming a socialist, woke and borderless country,” said Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for America PAC.
“These robust investments have allowed the GOP apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history.”
Pushing for Paxton
On voters’ doors across Texas, the campaign literature carries a stark warning: “Radical Democrat socialists are winning elections all across America. Could Texas be next?”
The hanging door cards are the work of Musk’s voter-turnout operation, which deployed nearly 3,000 paid canvassers last week around the country, according to America PAC officials.
The group has devoted most of its more than US$76 million in midterm spending so far to this canvassing programme, shelling out smaller amounts on advertising, mail, phone calls and text messages. Much of the messaging targets Democrats, sometimes in misleading or overheated ways.
This spring, Trump’s political advisers asked Musk to reprise America PAC’s 2024 field programme, a person familiar with the conversation said. Despite the challenging environment for Republicans, some party strategists believe that a field programme can make the difference in particularly tight races.
America PAC relies on a few voter-canvassing firms that compete aggressively with one another for work and for staffing, according to people briefed on the operation.
Turnover in the canvassing industry is high. One canvasser who worked for America PAC told the Times that he was paid between US$1.50 and US$3.00 for each door he knocked on across Texas in the heat. America PAC says it has knocked on about 6.5 million doors across the country so far.
Musk and his operation, people close to them say, have been particularly focused on the Texas Senate race.
The group has unloaded over a third of its disclosed spending in that expensive race, more than in any other. It is uncommon to run an extensive field campaign in large states like Texas, where television ads are more often used to reach voters.
Musk, a resident of Austin, has extensive business interests and property holdings in Texas. Paxton, the state attorney-general, has investigated Musk’s opponents, including Media Matters, a liberal group.
Musk’s US$10 million donation to Paxton’s super PAC came at a critical time, when the Republican candidate was being badly outspent.
And Musk’s US$158 million in donations to the Senate Leadership Fund, the most the super PAC has ever received from a single donor in a quarter, may have made it possible for that group to suddenly spend big for Paxton after months of reluctance.
That is because Musk’s donations preceded the decision in late August by the super PAC, led by allies of Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the majority leader, to start what has become a US$149 million pro-Paxton ad campaign.
A focus on transgender issues
As it did in 2024, Musk’s operation is focused not on persuading swing voters, but on registering and turning out voters with conservative beliefs – especially “low-propensity” ones who are less likely to cast a ballot.
This is a lot harder for Republicans in a midterm election, without Trump at the top of the ballot.
To do it, Musk’s super PAC is leaning hard into the culture wars, especially transgender issues. (Musk’s daughter, who is transgender, has spoken about their clashes over her identity, and he has suggested that this led to his increased political engagement.)
At voters’ doors in Texas, canvassers are told to target Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate for governor, over her record on transgender issues, according to parts of a script reviewed by the Times.
Similarly, the Musk operation is leaving literature on doors that claims that James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, has a “radical trans agenda.” And America PAC’s top ad in the state, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact, denounces Talarico over his past comments suggesting that “God is nonbinary.”
The Musk group is also targeting other Democratic Senate candidates over transgender issues, including Josh Turek, the party’s nominee in Iowa. Nationally, one of the super PAC’s most visible ads on Facebook features a man in makeup and reads: “He made his plan to vote. Did you? Don’t stay home while crazies elect radicals.”
The group is running ads and sending mail on a broad range of topics, but socialism is a core theme.
The Musk super PAC regularly attacks Democrats as socialist and ties them to figures such as New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, according to 48 pieces of direct mail shared by Mintt, a mail-tracking firm.
Online, it is even running personalised messaging that invokes a voter’s first name. For example, in a video showing smiling Democrats: “Why are they smiling? Because Christopher hasn’t made a plan to vote yet.”
Much of this outreach points voters to an America PAC website where conservatives can learn how to register to vote. The super PAC is pushing what it calls an “America Pass,” a digital card on Apple or Google wallets on voters’ phones that lists their registration information, along with election dates and deadlines in their home state.
A big spender with a backseat role
While Musk is spending big again and using some tactics that are similar to those he deployed two years ago, this is not 2024 anymore.
He is in a different place politically. While he and Trump appear to be on good terms again – “our modern-day Thomas Edison,” the president called him on Oct 8 – Musk is taking a hands-off approach this election and does not appear as personally passionate.
He has not brought up the midterm elections or the Trump presidency much in private conversations with friends, according to people who have spoken to him in recent months.
He is focused on his businesses, these people say, and he and his business lieutenants have taken a less active role in America PAC’s operations, entrusting major decisions to Chris Young, his top adviser.
And on the social platform X, a semi-reliable indicator of where the billionaire’s mind is, Musk has written just seven direct posts in 2026 about candidates in competitive midterm races, according to a Times review, a far cry from his relentless calls throughout 2024 to elect Trump.
Five of those posts focused on Talarico – and one appeared critical of Senator Susan Collins, a vulnerable Republican in Maine.
Gone, too, are Musk’s barnstorming campaign stops, such as the ones he did in Pennsylvania in October 2024 or a Wisconsin judicial election in the spring of 2025.
There are no more sweepstakes where he personally hands an oversize check of US$1 million to those who register voters or sign a petition, a gambit that drew legal challenges.
Musk has not evidently grown infatuated with candidates this time around, as he did with Trump.
The closest he came was a US$10 million donation for a long-shot Republican running for the US Senate in Kentucky – an investment that went poorly.
The US$276 million figure is, of course, just what is publicly known. Musk has also made some seven-figure donations to support midterm candidates through groups that are not required to disclose their donors, according to a person with knowledge of the matter. NYTIMES

Lockheed unveils longer-range Patriot missile, PAC-3 Edge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:09:32 UTC
01:09:32 KST

- Lockheed Martin unveiled PAC-3 Edge, a longer-range, higher-altitude Patriot interceptor, as its entry in the U.S. Army’s Future Interceptor competition.
- Lockheed says the U.S. Army advanced it to the next stage and it is working toward an early operational capability by 2031.
Lockheed Martin has unveiled PAC-3 Edge, a new Patriot interceptor designed to reach higher, fly farther and maneuver harder than the PAC-3 MSE now in service. It is the company’s entry in the U.S. Army’s Future Interceptor competition.
The company debuted the missile on Oct. 12 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington. Lockheed says the U.S. Army has moved it into the next stage of the competition and that it is working toward what the service calls a residual operational capability by 2031, meaning a small number of missiles ready for emergency use before full fielding. The company did not release range, altitude, speed or cost figures, and did not name the other competitors.
PAC-3 Edge builds on the PAC-3 MSE, the hit-to-kill missile that destroys targets by striking them directly and has been used heavily against Russian missiles in Ukraine and Iranian missiles in the Middle East. Lockheed says the new version adds a new seeker, an upgraded propulsion system and improved flight controls. The seeker was designed by the company’s Strigo Product Center, which Lockheed says it funded with $250 million of its own money.
The company says the missile is meant to counter a wide range of aircraft, missiles and hypersonic weapons at higher altitudes and longer ranges than current Patriot interceptors. In the U.S. Army’s layered missile defense, it would sit between the PAC-3 MSE and the THAAD system, which intercepts ballistic missiles at much higher altitudes.
The U.S. Army has tried before to field a next-generation Patriot interceptor. It ran a Lower-Tier Future Interceptor competition between Lockheed and Raytheon, then announced in 2024 that it would cancel the effort before reviving the idea as the Future Interceptor program. The U.S. Army has not published the program’s budget, the number of missiles it plans to buy or when it will pick a winner.
PAC-3 Edge becomes the fourth missile in Lockheed’s Patriot family, alongside the older PAC-3 CRI, the PAC-3 MSE and the lower-cost PAC-3 ACE the company announced in July for European customers.
