From Diana to the ordinary citizen: How Britain lost its sense of duty - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:09:19 UTC
01:09:19 KST

In 1997, Princess Diana died in a Paris tunnel alongside Dodi al-Fayed, the son of an influential Egyptian businessman.
What followed was an extraordinary accusation: that Britain’s establishment had arranged her death because it feared that her relationship with a Muslim man – and the influence she wielded over millions – could change the country itself.
Dodi’s father, Mohamed al-Fayed, accused the royal establishment and British intelligence of orchestrating the crash. The allegations were investigated and rejected.
There was no established plot, and no proof Diana intended to convert to Islam. But the accusation mattered for what it alleged about the establishment’s priorities: that those at the top were prepared to sacrifice the mother of Britain’s future king rather than risk a profound change in British society.
Thirty years later, look at Britain.
A country once accused of being willing to sacrifice its crown jewel to stop a feared transformation now has leaders accused of refusing even the smallest political sacrifice to protect the ordinary citizen – the peasant.
That is the other side of the coin. The allegation then was that Britain would go too far to protect its identity. The indictment now is that its leaders have sold out the duty to protect it.
This is not a story about one demonstration, one election, or one religious community. It is about what happens when a government knows the dangers of extremism yet allows political calculation to outweigh its responsibility to confront them.
Britain was warned. Its own 2015 review described the influence of Muslim Brotherhood-associated organizations and recorded expressions of support for Hamas attacks among individuals linked to the movement. Islamist extremism was not a threat discovered yesterday. It was something Britain’s leaders had already examined in their own institutions.
Then came October 7. Hamas murdered civilians in Israel, and Gaza became a powerful force in British politics. Marches, campaigns and electoral pressure demanded a tougher posture toward Israel. Britain’s government made its own choices, and those choices – not the slogans on the street – are what its leaders must answer for.
In March 2026, London limited American use of British bases for offensive strikes against Iran, the regime that has armed and financed Hamas and Hezbollah.
US President Donald Trump publicly criticized the restriction. Britain later permitted specified defensive operations, but the dispute exposed how far London was prepared to distance itself from Washington on a central security issue.
Britain also imposed arms-export restrictions and sanctions relating to Israel, recognized Palestinian statehood and announced further measures involving Israeli settlements.
Israel closes Britain's Jerusalem consulate
The confrontation ended with Israel ordering the closure of Britain’s Jerusalem consulate. Its consular operations ceased in October, with 20 diplomats required to leave and a smaller British mission remaining.
No protester signed those orders. British ministers made those decisions. They may argue that each serves international law or British interests. They still owe their own citizens a convincing account of the priorities behind them – and of the consequences for the country’s security and alliances.
That is where the charge of a sellout comes from. Britain’s government has shown it can take hard positions when it chooses. Yet its critics see hesitation in confronting extremist intimidation at home, alongside a readiness to take measures against a democratic ally abroad.
British Jews face rising antisemitism; ordinary people are entitled to ask why protecting them is not met with the same resolve.
The controversy even reaches cultural partnerships. A Palestinian museum whose archives describe a perpetrator of the Coastal road massacre as a martyr has worked with British institutions.
That does not prove those institutions funded or endorsed the material. It does make the standards they apply a legitimate subject of scrutiny.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called Britain the “Islamic Republic of Britain.” It was a political rebuke, not a literal description of the country. But his words captured the anger at a Britain whose foreign-policy decisions appear, to its critics, increasingly remote from the instincts of its traditional Western allies.
The real failure is not that Britain’s population or religious life has changed. It is the accusation that its leaders have traded the courage to defend their people and principles for the comfort of avoiding political confrontation.
A government is not judged by how firmly it speaks of its heritage, but by what it protects when protection becomes costly.
Diana’s death was not justified, and the murder allegation was not proved. The contrast is about the extremes Britain was accused of contemplating then and the resolve its leaders are accused of lacking now.
Once, the alleged sacrifice was the princess – the highest symbol of the nation. Now, critics say, its leaders will not risk their political standing for the peasant – the ordinary person who depends on the government for security and freedom.
That is how a country loses its way: not when its people change, but when those entrusted with protecting them stop putting them first.
The writer is the founder and CEO of the Orthodox Jewish Chamber of Commerce.

Oct. 7 accusations and the manufactured crusade to bring down Netanyahu - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12

01:08:32 KST

The orchestrated storm of unconfirmed allegations surrounding Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s actions before and after the October 7 attacks has devolved into a transparent exercise in political warfare.
In recent weeks, the public square has been systematically flooded with self-serving leaks, retroactive warnings, and highly selective recollections. We are expected to blindly accept that United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ) magically warned Netanyahu of an impending offensive, and that Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel made a clandestine trip to deliver an identical alert.
Concurrently, a parade of defense and intelligence officials has stepped forward, audaciously claiming they systematically flagged a deteriorating security situation only to be ignored by the political echelon.
Attempts to sabotage Netanyahu, cover up military failures
Let’s inject some overdue reality into this narrative: The ongoing wave of unconfirmed accusations against Netanyahu is a desperate weaponization of institutional self-preservation and political timing, designed to cover up systemic military failures and sabotage his reelection.
To date, not a single one of these convenient external warning claims has been independently verified. More importantly, the forces peddling these assertions are far from neutral observers. The catastrophic failure of October 7 was, first and foremost, a colossal institutional collapse across Israel's military and intelligence apparatus. It is blindingly obvious that individuals within these very systems are highly motivated to leak curated narratives, shifting the blame from their own severe operational blind spots onto the prime minister.
Furthermore, the timing of these disclosures exposes their true intent. With shifting political horizons and the looming prospect of future elections, this sudden rush to air long-held grievances is a coordinated hit piece meant to destroy Netanyahu’s electoral viability. When accusations are deliberately timed to maximize political damage, their credibility evaporates entirely.
This pattern of selective narrative-building collapses under scrutiny, especially when examining the recent assertions made by Netanyahu’s former military secretary, Avi Gil. Gil claims that the prime minister bypassed critical "opportunities" to secure the release of hostages out of fear that his governing coalition would fall apart. This accusation completely divorces itself from reality. The American special presidential envoy for hostage affairs explicitly stated that during the time in question, Hamas was simply not interested in releasing any of the Israeli hostages.
This definitive assessment completely decimates the media's favorite lie that viable, realistic deals were sitting on Netanyahu's desk waiting to be signed.
The only "terms" Hamas ever seriously demanded centered on a total, permanent surrender – a comprehensive ceasefire and the mass release of high-profile security prisoners. Accepting these suicidal demands would have cemented Hamas's survival and rule in Gaza, delivering the terror group a total victory. Key coalition partners like Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich rightly vowed to leave the government if such a capitulation occurred.
While naive commentators argue that Netanyahu could have accepted Hamas's terms to return the hostages and subsequently wiped them out later, such a reckless gamble contradicts his historically cautious strategic doctrine. Confronted with a choice between political suicide or relying on a defense establishment hamstrung by decades of conceptual stagnation, the government faced an incredibly narrow operational path. The IDF’s initial challenges in securing a rapid, decisive victory point squarely to deeper institutional incompetence – including legacy doctrines associated with former chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot and restrictive rules of engagement that tied the army's hands – rather than simple political obstinacy.
Predictably, the mainstream media has completely buried alternative viewpoints that destroy their preferred anti-Bibi crusade. For instance, testimonies from hostage families revealing that Hamas was so heavily damaged that they were on the verge of cutting a deal far more advantageous to Israel have been met with total silence. Instead, it was the Israeli Left that rushed to Hamas's rescue, prioritizing an immediate hostage deal over the total destruction of the terror group, thereby granting Hamas vital strategic breathing room.
This disastrous approach was heavily championed by figures like Gadi Eisenkot, yet he and the other architects of this failure enjoy a striking lack of media accountability.
Instead, the media remains single-mindedly obsessed with Avi Gil’s baseless allegations. Yet Gil’s own credibility is entirely shot, given the glaring questions regarding his own failure to decisively alert the political leadership in the critical hours immediately preceding the October 7 assault.
As long as the national discourse relies on unverified leaks from desperate actors with everything to lose, the true history of this period will remain obscured by political warfare. It is time to look past the media consensus, ground ourselves in the external diplomatic reality that Hamas refused to deal, and reject this transparent hit job for what it is.

General Dynamics shows Wolf XM30 at AUSA 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:05:38 UTC
01:05:38 KST

- General Dynamics Land Systems displayed only a one-eighth-scale model of its Wolf XM30 at AUSA 2026, while its prototype undergoes U.S. Army testing.
- The U.S. Army expects to choose between the Wolf and American Rheinmetall’s Lynx in 2027 to replace the M2 Bradley.
General Dynamics Land Systems has brought its Wolf XM30 infantry fighting vehicle to the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, but only as a one-eighth-scale model, leaving the full-size vehicle out of public view while it undergoes U.S. Army testing.
The company is offering the Wolf as a replacement for the M2 Bradley Fighting Vehicle in the U.S. Army’s XM30 Mechanized Infantry Combat Vehicle competition.
In a social media post on Oct. 12, General Dynamics said the vehicle was designed from the start around the U.S. Army’s Modular Open Systems Approach, which uses common hardware and software interfaces so new sensors, weapons and electronics can be added without redesigning the vehicle. The company also said the Wolf was “born digital,” meaning its digital engineering model is used in testing, production and maintenance as well as design. It did not release new specifications, photos of the full-size vehicle or any test results.
General Dynamics delivered its first Wolf prototype to the U.S. Army at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, on Aug. 21. The only public photo since then has shown the vehicle wrapped in a black tarp on a flatbed trailer. The company has said seven more prototypes will go to the 1st Armored Brigade Combat Team, 1st Cavalry Division, at Fort Hood, Texas, where soldiers will put them through field trials. The Wolf is based on the company’s Griffin III demonstrator, itself derived from the ASCOD 2 infantry fighting vehicle, and its team includes GM Defense, AeroVironment and General Dynamics Mission Systems.
The other finalist, American Rheinmetall, is not showing its Lynx XM30 at AUSA at all. The company said its prototypes have gone straight to the U.S. Army for soldier evaluation. American Rheinmetall delivered the first of eight Lynx prototypes days after General Dynamics’ delivery in August.
The U.S. Army’s requirements for the XM30 call for an uncrewed turret armed with the XM913 50 mm cannon, a hybrid-electric drivetrain and room for six dismounted infantry soldiers. The vehicle would carry infantry squads and cavalry scouts into combat and support them with fire once they dismount, the same job the Bradley has done since the early 1980s.
The U.S. Army picked General Dynamics and American Rheinmetall as finalists in June 2023, with the design and prototype phase valued at about $1.6 billion between them. The U.S. Army expects to choose a winner in 2027, and its budget plans call for buying 108 vehicles by fiscal 2031 ahead of larger production later.

Federal agents raid anti-Israel US congresswoman's home amid reported immigration fraud probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:01:27 UTC
01:01:27 KST

Federal agents searched the Washington, D.C., home of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar on Monday as part of a federal criminal investigation reportedly involving immigration fraud allegations, in an extraordinary operation targeting one of President Donald Trump's most prominent political critics just three weeks before the US midterm elections.
The early morning search was carried out by agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the investigative arm of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The Justice Department confirmed that agents had executed a search warrant authorized by a judge, but did not publicly specify the nature of the investigation.
The department said the operation was part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation. Fox News reported that investigators were examining immigration documents completed by Omar's late father when she was a child. 
The search has attracted significant attention because Omar, a progressive Democrat representing Minnesota, has long been a target of attacks by Trump and other senior Republicans. Its timing, less than a month before congressional elections, has also raised questions about the Justice Department's longstanding practice of exercising particular caution when conducting politically sensitive investigations close to an election.
CNN described the operation as an unusually aggressive investigative step against a politician actively seeking reelection.
Immigration fraud allegations and claims Omar married her brother
Omar, who was born in Somalia, arrived in the United States at age 12 after her family spent time in a refugee camp in Kenya. She was elected to the House of Representatives in 2018, becoming, alongside Palestinian American Democrat Rashida Tlaib, one of the first two Muslim women elected to Congress.
Since then, she has won reelection three times and is now seeking a fifth term representing Minnesota's 5th Congressional District, which includes Minneapolis.
Republican politicians and conservative commentators have for years raised allegations about Omar's immigration history, including an unsubstantiated claim that she married her brother to help him obtain immigration status or student loans.
Omar married British citizen Ahmed Nur Said Elmi in 2009, and the couple divorced in 2017. She has repeatedly denied that Elmi is her brother, describing the allegations as "disgusting lies."
Republicans have also accused her of tax irregularities and suggested that she entered the United States in 1995 using a false name or different family identity to circumvent delays in refugee applications.
Those allegations have not been established as fact, and the Justice Department has not publicly confirmed whether they are directly connected to Monday's search.
Vance accused Omar of immigration fraud without presenting evidence
In May, Vice President JD Vance publicly accused Omar of immigration fraud, saying that he and Deputy White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller were exploring ways to investigate the Minnesota congresswoman.
"It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody's entitled to equal justice under the laws," Vance said at the time.
He said officials intended to examine the allegations and pursue prosecution if investigators found evidence of criminal wrongdoing.
In a separate interview with conservative podcast host Benny Johnson, Vance made a more categorical accusation, claiming without presenting evidence that Omar had committed immigration fraud against the United States.
Omar's office strongly rejected the accusations.
Her chief of staff, Connor McNutt, accused Vance of deliberately spreading falsehoods to distract attention from the administration's policies and political difficulties.
"This is rich coming from someone who literally said they were willing to 'create stories' to redirect the media," McNutt said.
He described the allegations as a ridiculous lie and an attempt to divert attention from the administration's war with Iran, rising gasoline prices and declining Republican polling numbers.
McNutt also used the phrase "pedophile protection party" in his criticism of Republicans, referring to allegations that the Trump administration had sought to prevent the release of documents connected to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Trump calls for Omar to be institutionalized
Omar has become one of Trump's most frequent targets, particularly over her progressive political positions, criticism of Israel and outspoken opposition to his immigration policies.
Trump and senior administration officials have also repeatedly criticized Minnesota's large Somali American community, of which Omar is a member.
Earlier this year, the administration launched a major immigration enforcement operation in the region involving ICE agents. Omar and her allies accused Trump of employing anti-Somali and anti-Muslim rhetoric, while the congresswoman described the president's repeated focus on her as a disturbing and unhealthy obsession.
The confrontation intensified in February, when Trump said Omar and Tlaib should be institutionalized and sent back to the places they came from.
The remarks followed criticism of the president by the two lawmakers during his State of the Union address, in which he praised his administration's restrictive immigration policies and enforcement operations.
Omar has repeatedly said that she and her family face death threats, which she attributes to hateful political rhetoric, particularly statements made by Trump.
The security concerns have also been accompanied by physical attacks.
Last month, a Minnesota man was sentenced to 14 months in prison after being convicted of spraying Omar with vinegar during a public appearance.
The attacker, Anthony James Kazmierczak, acknowledged that he targeted the congresswoman because he disagreed with her progressive political views.
An extraordinary raid weeks before US elections
The search comes at a particularly sensitive moment in American politics, with congressional midterm elections scheduled for November 3.
The Justice Department traditionally follows guidelines intended to prevent investigative actions from improperly influencing elections, particularly when candidates for public office are involved.
CNN noted that searching the residence of a sitting member of Congress just weeks before an election is an exceptionally unusual step.
The operation also follows renewed attacks by Trump on other Muslim Democrats who have criticized Israel.
Last week, the president targeted Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for Michigan's US Senate seat, while endorsing his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.
Trump described El-Sayed as a radical extremist and a sympathizer of terrorism. El-Sayed has also been an outspoken critic of Israel and has accused it of committing genocide in Gaza.
Omar's criticism of Israel and the 2019 entry ban
Omar has been among the most outspoken critics of Israel in the Democratic Party, taking positions that have repeatedly generated controversy both in Washington and Jerusalem.
Even before the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack and the subsequent war in Gaza, she supported the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, known as BDS, which campaigns for economic and political pressure on Israel.
She has also compared Israel's treatment of Palestinians to South Africa's former apartheid system and accused Israel of genocide in Gaza.
During her first term in Congress, Omar faced criticism from members of her own party over statements about American support for Israel that many interpreted as antisemitic.
One particularly contentious episode involved her suggestion that American politicians supported Israel because of financial contributions from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, known as AIPAC.
In 2019, Israel barred Omar and Tlaib from entering the country, a decision that drew criticism even from prominent supporters of Israel within the Democratic Party.
Monday's search now places Omar at the center of another major political confrontation. Federal authorities have confirmed that a criminal investigation is underway, but have not disclosed its precise scope or announced charges against the congresswoman.

Scientists uncover a possible trade-off in how the hippocampus replays new memories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:00:43 UTC
01:00:43 KST

When the brain rests after learning something new, it actively replays the recent experience to lock it into memory. A recent small study published in the Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience reveals that this mental replay involves a trade-off, where the brain prioritizes the general meaning of an event while weakening the memory of specific details. These biological adjustments suggest that false memories are a natural byproduct of how the mind extracts useful themes from the world.
Memory involves balancing two competing tasks. The brain must hold onto the specific details of a single event, but it also needs to find patterns across multiple events to predict what might happen in the future. If a person only remembers exact details, they might struggle to apply lessons from the past to new situations.
In traditional models of brain function, the hippocampus acts as a fast-acting recorder for new experiences. Over days and weeks, it slowly teaches these memories to the neocortex, the outer layer of the brain, which extracts statistical rules and overarching concepts. However, recent computational models suggest that this division of labor might also exist entirely within the hippocampus itself.
If the hippocampus manages both rapid recording and slow generalization, it must have a mechanism to edit memories shortly after they form. The biological principle of competitive plasticity suggests a possible method. When a person learns related concepts, the neural pathways sharing common features activate together and become stronger. Unique, isolated details that do not reactivate as often are competitively weakened.
To understand how the brain handles this balance, researchers Nicholas C. Hindy, Ryan Coleman, and Surya Rajan Meenakshi Selvam focused on specific sub-regions of the hippocampus. After a person experiences something, the hippocampus spontaneously reactivates the neural patterns associated with that event. The research team wanted to see if this reactivation process transforms a memory rather than just making a perfect copy of it.
They specifically looked at a sub-region called CA1. This area acts as a primary output hub, sending information to other parts of the brain. The structural position of CA1 allows it to resolve competition between specific episodic details and broader generalizations.
The experimental design aimed to see this competitive editing in action. The researchers conducted a small study with 24 adult participants using a classic psychological test known for reliably producing false memories. Participants heard word lists designed around a missing target concept. For example, a list might include the words bed, rest, and awake, but leave out the central theme word, sleep.
The words were read aloud by artificial voices, splitting the incoming information into two distinct channels. The semantic channel was the meaning of the words and their shared theme. The episodic channel was the specific sensory experience of hearing a male or female voice.
The research team used high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging to scan the participants. Standard brain scans often blur the tiny sub-regions of the hippocampus together. By using high-resolution techniques, the team could isolate the CA1 area, as well as neighboring regions known as CA3 and the dentate gyrus.
After listening to the words, participants spent 90 seconds performing a simple math task. This kept them distracted but allowed their brains to rest from active memorization. During this short rest period, the researchers used the brain scans to measure how often the hippocampus spontaneously replayed the neural patterns associated with the word lists.
Finally, the participants completed a memory test while still inside the brain scanner. They had to indicate whether they recognized words from the lists, and whether they falsely recognized lure words that fit the theme but were never actually played. They also had to recall which voice spoke the recognized words.
The researchers found that spontaneous brain reactivation during the rest period had opposing effects on the two types of memory. When the CA1 region replayed a memory more frequently, participants were more likely to confidently claim they had heard the lure words. At the same time, this increased reactivation predicted worse accuracy when participants tried to remember whether a male or female voice spoke a specific word.
This means the mental replay strengthened the overarching concept of the word list but weakened the memory of the exact sensory experience. The memory of the actual words that had been played remained unchanged by the reactivation process. The effect only influenced the broad themes and the specific voice details.
While the CA1 region showed the strongest evidence for a bidirectional trade-off, the other sub-regions displayed specialized roles. Reactivation in the CA3 area was linked exclusively to a higher rate of false memories for the overarching themes. Neuroscientists believe CA3 helps with pattern completion, a process where the brain rebuilds a full memory from a partial cue, which may naturally strengthen the broader concept.
Conversely, activity in the dentate gyrus was linked only to worse memory for the specific voices. The dentate gyrus is typically associated with pattern separation, the ability to tell similar experiences apart. When this region is forced to process overlapping themes, its ability to hold onto precise episodic details might be compromised.
The research team also noticed a spatial pattern along the length of the hippocampus. The front and middle sections of the structure were primarily linked to extracting general themes and falsely recognizing the related lure words. The rear section of the hippocampus was linked to the loss of specific source details, such as the voice of the speaker.
The study relies on correlational data, meaning the results show a relationship between brain activity and memory performance but cannot prove that the reactivation directly caused the memory changes. People might have processed the words differently while listening, which could influence both the brain replay and the later memory errors. The rest period was also very short, only capturing the earliest moments of memory formation.
The brain scans tracked activity linked to entire word lists rather than individual words. The researchers could not separate the replay of a single word from the general activity of the whole list. Future research will need to separate individual events with greater precision and track memories over longer periods to see how these trade-offs evolve.
The study, “Hippocampal Reactivation Trades Episodic Detail for Semantic Gist in Human Memory,” was authored by Nicholas C. Hindy, Ryan Coleman, and Surya Rajan Meenakshi Selvam.

Defence Readiness Bill to give government reserve powers
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:00:36 BST
01:00:36 KST

Legislation being developed to give ministers powers in reserve for escalation towards war will cover the Defence Nuclear Enterprise, and the government has committed to bring it forward within this Parliament, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what progress had been made on recommendation 33 of the 2025 Strategic Defence Review, which covers legislative reform that could direct industry to prioritise defence nuclear requirements in the sovereign supply chain, or enable compulsory acquisition of assets where necessary to protect national security.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State at the Ministry of Defence, said: “The Government has accepted the SDR recommendation to develop a ‘Defence Readiness Bill’ to ensure ‘the Government has powers in reserve to respond effectively in the event of escalation towards a war involving the UK or its allies’. Defence is working closely with the rest of government to develop detailed policy requirements, including for the Defence Nuclear Enterprise, and to establish what new legislation is required as part of the Government’s wider Home Defence programme.
“Defence Readiness legislation is being developed to ensure the Government has the powers it needs to keep the UK safe, both now and in times of heightened crisis or escalation towards war.”
The minister listed the measures under development as improving the ability to defend against sub-threshold threats; increasing industry preparedness, agility and resilience; expanding the supply of privately owned services to defence and access to and protection of critical national infrastructure; and strengthening the mobilisation of defence’s people, including the Reserves and civil servants.
Mr Pollard added: “The Government has committed to deliver this legislation within this Parliament. As is standard with the legislative process, any future legislation will be brought forward when parliamentary time allows.”
The answer does not say whether the powers to direct industry or compulsorily acquire assets that Mr Obese-Jecty asked about will appear in the Bill, and no date was given for its introduction.
A second question from the same member asked about progress on recommendation 30, which seeks to strengthen NATO and British led training and exercises addressing escalation and conflict scenarios with nuclear-armed states.
Louise Sandher-Jones, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Government is implementing the recommendations of the Strategic Defence Review 2025, including Recommendation 30, which seeks to strengthen coherence between the conventional and nuclear elements of NATO’s deterrence and defence posture.
“The Ministry of Defence continues to strengthen UK and NATO-led training and exercises through a programme of national and multinational activity that improves readiness, interoperability and the ability of Allied forces to operate across the full spectrum of conflict. This includes participation in NATO’s exercise programme, including the Alliance’s flagship STEADFAST exercise series, which tests collective defence plans and strengthens Allied deterrence and defence.
“Through these activities, we are working closely with Allies to ensure NATO is better prepared to deter, defend against and, if necessary, respond to threats from capable and nuclear-armed adversaries.”
The latest instalment of that series, the annual nuclear deterrence exercise Steadfast Noon, begins in Italy on Tuesday with seventeen nations taking part.

Moroccan navy vessels entered Spanish waters without permission during Ceuta crisis: Sanchez
MADRID - Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said on Oct 12 that Moroccan naval vessels entered Spanish waters off Ceuta without permission after late July’s mass migrant crossing into the North African enclave, state broadcaster TVE reported.
He played down the incidents, calling them isolated, and underscored the importance of relations with Morocco.
At the end of July, over 72,000 migrants crossed the border from Morocco into Ceuta, sparking a humanitarian and diplomatic crisis, which remains partially unresolved, stoking political tensions in Spain as it prepares for an early election on Nov 29.
El Pais newspaper reported on Oct 12, citing unnamed sources, that following the border rush, at least one frigate and several patrol boats from the Royal Moroccan Navy sailed through Spanish sovereign waters without seeking authorisation.
A Spanish frigate had to intercept Moroccan warships to repel them from Spanish waters, it said.
“We must acknowledge that, between two neighbouring countries, such isolated incidents do occur,” TVE quoted Sanchez as saying. It did not quote Sanchez addressing the specifics of the El Pais report.
“We are neighbours. Those were intense days, but cooperation between the navies remains smooth, regardless of that incident,” he added, saying relations with Morocco are “very important”.
The comments came on the eve of a visit by King Felipe and Queen Letizia to Ceuta on Oct 13 and 14 that could exacerbate tensions between Spain and Morocco. Rabat claims sovereignty over Ceuta and Spain’s other enclave, Melilla.
The government did not reply to a Reuters request for comment. The Moroccan foreign ministry could not be immediately reached for comment.
On Oct 9, Morocco’s King Mohammed said the cooperation model with Spain on migration had reached its limits, criticising Spanish court decisions impeding the repatriation of minors and asylum seekers as “obsolete”. While most migrants returned in the weeks after the crossing, thousands remained. REUTERS

Scarred blood vessels may be one clue to APOE4’s Alzheimer’s risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

Scarred blood vessels may be one clue to APOE4’s Alzheimer’s risk
The gene variant may alter cells that support the brain’s blood vessels
The gene APOE4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease. But it’s still something of a mystery to researchers.
Now, new work suggests one way the gene variant does its dirty work. It influences the production of scar tissue throughout vital vascular connections carrying blood to and from the brain, researchers report September 24 in Cell. This process may also contribute to the buildup of the protein amyloid-beta, which is thought to be one of the first signs of Alzheimer’s disease in the brain.
APOE4 is an allele, one of three slightly different, common forms of the APOE gene, which makes a protein that helps carry fats in the bloodstream. The variant is common among people who have Alzheimer’s disease. “If you had a room of 10 people with Alzheimer’s disease, and you asked how many of those people have the APOE4 allele, six of them would,” says neuroscientist Joel Blanchard of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City. Yet many people who carry APOE4 never develop the dementia-causing disease, leaving researchers trying to understand what the gene variant actually does to make the brain more vulnerable.
One clue came from people who seemed unusually resilient to that risk. In 2024, researchers examined more than 3,500 people, including some who carried two copies of APOE4 but had not developed Alzheimer’s. Genetic analysis showed that they had a mutation in their DNA that meant their blood vessels had far lower levels of a protein called fibronectin, a kind of cellular superglue that assists wound healing. The reserachers suggested that too much fibronectin could make it harder for the brain to clear amyloid-beta from the brain. A buildup of those plaques is a hallmark of the disease.
That result pushed Blanchard and his colleagues to look more closely at blood vessels. “The prevailing thought in the field is basically that the Alzheimer’s disease is so bad that the blood vessels break down,” Blanchard says. ”But we wanted to ask the question: Is it the other way around?”
Blanchard and his colleagues built an atlas that mapped gene expression — how DNA is read and converted into proteins — across the human brain vasculature at a cellular level. Stitching together data from three existing brainwide maps, their atlas represented 66,000 cells from 220 people. They team examined how this map differed in people with two copies of APOE4 compared with those with less harmful gene variants.
APOE4 carriers had fewer pericytes, starfish-shaped cells that wrap around and stabilize blood vessels. They also had higher numbers of myofibroblasts, cells normally formed during tissue injury that pump out fibronectin, the team found.
The map offered a snapshot, but it couldn’t show whether the missing pericytes were actually transforming into myofibroblasts. The researchers turned to 3-D models of human brain tissue grown from stem cells. In models carrying two copies of APOE4, pericytes began taking on the characteristics of scar-producing myofibroblasts. The transformation also offered a possible explanation for the earlier clue from resilient APOE4 carriers: Myofibroblasts produce large amounts of fibronectin. And when the researchers prevented cells in their models from producing fibronectin, amyloid accumulation dropped.
The researchers also found a possible trigger for the cellular switch. In the APOE4 models, signaling through the immune molecule TGF-beta helped drive pericytes toward the scar-producing state. Blocking that signaling in cell models and aged mice restored the proportion of blood vessels wrapped up by pericytes.
The TGF-beta data are “particularly interesting,” because inhibiting the protein reversed some of APOE4’s effects on pericytes, says Abdel Ali Belaidi, a neuroscientist at the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health in Parkville, Australia. But TGF-beta performs many jobs throughout the body, he says, making it a difficult molecule to target safely with a drug.
And damage to the brain’s blood vessels is only one of the many ways APOE4 has been linked to Alzheimer’s. Other studies have shown that the gene variant alters inflammation and interacts with another Alzheimer’s-linked protein, tau. How all these changes lock together to link APOE4 so strongly to Alzheimer’s disease is a greater mystery than one study can solve. ”As a field, we’re all progressing toward an answer,” Blanchard says.

Pakistan: Declaration of emergency must not be pretext to crackdown on human rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:53:34 UTC
00:53:34 KST

Responding to the declaration of a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, as well as the imposition of governor rule and the deployment of armed forces in the province, Babu Ram Pant, Amnesty International’s Deputy Director for South Asia, said:
“Reports of arbitrary detentions of key leaders – including the provincial chief minister – and internet disruptions across the province raise concerns about the proportionality of these emergency measures. While states may, in strictly limited circumstances, derogate from their human rights obligations to respond to a public emergency that threatens the existence of the nation, emergency measures are not a blank cheque to crack down on human rights, silence dissent, or concentrate power.
“Given the history of enforced disappearances and extrajudicial executions in counterterrorism operations by the armed forces, the deployment of the army further militarizes the province and could create conditions for unlawful use of force. Pakistani authorities must avoid using military personnel for ordinary policing tasks and ensure that military forces remain accountable and comply with international human rights law and standards.
Emergency measures are not a blank cheque to crack down on human rights, silence dissent, or concentrate power
Babu Ram Pant, Amnesty International’s Deputy Director for South Asia
“At this critical juncture, the federal authorities must ensure independent oversight of all actions taken under the emergency framework, and guarantee that any emergency measure is strictly necessary and proportionate to the situation.”
Background
President Asif Ali Zardari approved recommendations by the federal cabinet to impose a state of emergency and governor rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province under Articles 232 and 234 of Pakistan’s constitution respectively, citing an “unprecedented level of violent intensity of terrorist attacks” and a “breakdown of constitutional machinery” in the province on 11 October. A state of emergency allows the federal legislature (national assembly and senate) to pass laws regarding the province and allows the federal government to suspend fundamental rights such as the freedoms of assembly, association and expression.
The notification by the president stated that the powers of the provincial assembly will be exercised by the federal parliament and it was stated that the chief minister along with the provincial ministers, advisors, special assistants and advocate general would cease to hold office. Separately, the federal government deployed the Pakistan military “in aid of civil powers” in the province under article 245 of the constitution.
Former Prime Minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party has been in power in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province since 2013. PTI formed its latest government with a two-thirds majority after the 2024 general election.

Hackers heat French supermarket fridges, sparking fires and food losses
PARIS, Oct 12 - Hackers forced the temperature of many French supermarket fridges up to 50 degrees Celsius (122°F) overnight, causing fires and food losses at several hundred stores across the country in a major cyberattack.
The Paris prosecutor's office said a "large-scale" attack was "affecting connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France" and reported damage included "food losses and fires".
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu instructed France's National Cybersecurity Agency ANSSI to investigate, a person in his office said.
They said France "was coordinating with its European counterparts, as other countries may also be affected," while also investigating whether any other French firms were at risk.
Les Mousquetaires, which owns retailer Intermarche, said around 150 of its stores had been hit, with fridges heated up to 50 degrees Celsius for six hours. It had thrown all the food away to avoid any sanitary risks, a spokesperson said.
And Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher said his supermarket had also been hit by the attack.
"Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented," he wrote on X.
Carrefour said 80 of its supermarkets had been hit but that the vast majority of its 6,000 stores had not been affected.
Several other supermarket chains, including Monoprix, E.Leclerc and Auchan, did not respond to requests for comment.
DUTCH SECURITY ISSUE
Dutch supermarket operator Ahold Delhaize, which operates the Netherlands' largest supermarket chain Albert Heijn and has substantial operations in the United States, said it was also dealing with a "security issue" in its network, and had taken several systems offline to protect them.
A smartphone app for the retailer told clients that due to a "cybersecurity incident" it was unable to deliver groceries.
Online orders represent around 10% of sales for Albert Heijn. Physical stores remained open and Dutch news agency ANP reported that rivals had seen an influx of delivery orders.
It was not clear if there was any link between the French supermarket attack and the problems flagged by Ahold Delhaize.
Ahold is the fourth-largest grocery retailer in the US, where websites for its Stop & Shop, Giant, Hannaford and Food Lion stores all had notices saying "site temporarily down".
It was unclear if other operations were affected.
The source close to Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss.
Danfoss said it was "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems".
The affected units "were running outdated firmware", Danfoss said, adding that it had "long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions". REUTERS

The initiative was intended to strengthen Kerala's preparedness for future outbreaks of communicable and infectious diseases.
According to the minister, a Thrissur-based agency received the contract to construct the wards at an estimated cost of Rs 1.38 crore per facility. The Kerala medical services corporation limited (KMSCL) was assigned the responsibility of procuring equipment, with an estimated expenditure of Rs 44 lakh per ward.Only 55 wards completed, none fit to admit patientsAccording to the news agency PTI, the minister informed the assembly that construction had been completed at only 55 of the 88 proposed sites. The completed facilities were inaugurated in phases, he said.As of October 2026, 33 of the 55 completed wards had been handed over to hospitals, while the remaining 22 had been made operational with assistance from Kerala infrastructure investment fund consulting private limited (KIIFCON), Muraleedharan said.
However, he claimed that none of the 55 completed facilities was suitable for admitting or treating patients.The minister also pointed to several alleged deficiencies in the buildings, including the absence of air-conditioning and toilets, unfinished civil works and ceilings that could not accommodate fans.Despite an expenditure of around Rs 1.83 crore per ward, the completed facilities were not fit to house patients, he said.In view of the alleged shortcomings, the government has constituted an expert committee headed by the principal secretary, health, to investigate the matter, Muraleedharan added.

As in many European countries, Austria's judiciary is plagued by delays and backlogs as it struggles to cope with an ever growing number of cases. To draw attention to the problem, judges and prosecutors across the country have stopped handling non-urgent matters this week.
"Stop! We simply can't take this anymore," Anna-Maria Wukovits, vice president of the Austrian Prosecutors' Association, told a press conference marking the start of the protest week.
"Prosecutors cannot go on like this. We are at our limit," she added.
Austria's national judges' association estimates there is currently a shortage of more than 250 judges nationally, while Wukowits told national broadcaster ORF that for prosecutors the figure is around 70.
Workloads for prosecutors and judges have increased for various reasons, including ever more complex cases such as those involving cyber crimes, and many criminal complaints are now written using artificial intelligence but must then be reviewed manually by prosecutors, Wukowits said.
"Those often involve reams of pages that have to be read. One cannot ignore that," she said.
While the justice ministry has expressed sympathy with the prosecutors and judges, it has said the government's current priority is reducing the budget deficit, which came in last year at 4.1% of economic output, well beyond the EU limit of 3%.
"The rule of law cannot be maintained in the long term only because judges work unpaid overtime. For years, our colleagues have been making up for structural staff shortages by working on evenings, weekends and even on holiday," Austrian Judges' Association President Gerhard Karmuth said in a statement. Roundup: Bound by resolve, China and Lesotho mark national milestones, look to shared future
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
23:30:08 CST
00:30:08 KST

by Silence Charumbira
MASERU, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Two distant nations, vastly different in geography, size and historical trajectory, reached major national milestones within days of each other this month.
On Oct. 1, the People's Republic of China marked its 77th anniversary. Three days later, the Kingdom of Lesotho celebrated 60 years of independence.
Despite their physical distance and different sizes, a common thread runs through both anniversaries: an unyielding resolve to chart an independent path toward development and modernization.
"Our two countries have different national circumstances," Chinese Ambassador to Lesotho Yang Xiaokun said at a cultural event in Maseru on Friday. "But these anniversaries remind us of the determination of our peoples to shape our own future, pursue development, and build a better life."
Both nations embarked on modern state-building from arduous beginnings. In 1949, the New China emerged as a war-torn, agrarian society. In 1966, Lesotho gained independence as a poor, landlocked kingdom surrounded by apartheid South Africa.
Since independence, Lesotho has sought a development path suited to its own conditions, working to strengthen economic resilience and governance. China's own transformation into the world's second-largest economy has likewise rested on a path tailored to national realities, built on self-reliance and long-term planning.
"Modernization does not equate to Westernization, and there is no single model for development," Yang emphasized, affirming the right of African nations to chart their own course.
Lesotho's recent experience underscores why economic self-determination matters. The kingdom's vital garment industry has faced severe disruptions due to shifting global trade environments, leaving factories vulnerable.
Having navigated similar uncertainties during its own growth, China has consistently offered stability to its African partners. Under the frameworks of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation, China has extended zero-tariff treatment to all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic ties, including Lesotho.
Practical cooperation between the two nations continues to yield tangible results, ranging from debt relief and streamlined trade in agricultural exports like wool and mohair, to human resource development initiatives that sent over 270 Basotho professionals to China for training this year alone.
Progress extends beyond economics into cultural exchanges and global governance, where China advocates equal rights, equal opportunities and equal rules for all nations regardless of size. On Friday, a Chinese artistic troupe performed traditional Wu Opera in Maseru to mark Lesotho's diamond jubilee, celebrating mutual learning between distinct civilizations.
"Sixty years is not only a milestone; it is a new starting point," Ambassador Yang said, closing his address with Lesotho's national motto: "Khotso, Pula, Nala" (Peace, Rain, Prosperity).
Standing at this historic juncture, China and Lesotho are moving forward as equal partners, bound by a shared resolve to turn bilateral cooperation into lasting prosperity for both peoples. ■

====================================================================================================

On Columbus Day, remember Abraham Zacuto, the Jewish astronomer history forgot - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:17:37 UTC
00:17:37 KST

Every October, Christopher Columbus returns not only as history but as controversy. The voyages associated with his name transformed the world, but their legacy is inseparable from conquest, coercion and the destruction that followed European expansion.
Yet the same Iberian age also produced a quieter and far less controversial revolution: advances in astronomy, mathematics, cartography, instruments and practical navigation that made sustained oceanic voyaging possible. Its protagonists included scholars, translators, mapmakers, instrument makers and pilots whose names are far less familiar than those of the captains who commanded the ships.
Among them, one figure deserves particular remembrance on Columbus Day: Abraham Zacuto, a Jewish astronomer born in Salamanca around 1452. Zacuto belonged to the same Iberian world as Columbus, but experienced its monarchies very differently. In 1492, Columbus sailed west under the patronage of Ferdinand and Isabella. That same year, the Catholic monarchs ordered the Jews of their realms to convert or leave. Zacuto left Castile and continued his work in Portugal. The celebrated maritime discoveries and the expulsion of Iberian Jewry were therefore not distinct historical worlds; they unfolded under the same rulers, at the same moment, within the same culture of ambition, knowledge and power.
Zacuto stands out within that larger scientific story. He was a rabbi, astronomer, mathematician and historian whose astronomical work helped give oceanic navigation a new degree of precision and practicality. His contribution belongs not at the margins of the Age of Exploration but within the scientific infrastructure that made long-distance navigation increasingly systematic.
Around 1478, Zacuto completed his great Hebrew astronomical work, “Ha-Hibbur ha-Gadol,” the “Great Composition.” Working within a long scientific conversation that included Greek, Islamic, Jewish and Christian astronomy, he refined and organized astronomical calculations in forms of exceptional practical value.
After the expulsion from Spain, Zacuto entered Portugal at precisely the moment when the kingdom was pushing maritime exploration farther into the Atlantic and down the African coast. Zacuto’s pupil, José Vizinho, a Jewish adviser to Portuguese King John II, was associated with the practical Latin and Castilian presentation of Zacuto’s astronomical material. In 1496, Zacuto’s Almanach Perpetuum was printed at Leiria in four known issues - three with Latin preliminary matter and one with Castilian.
Zacuto's research proved incredibly useful
The importance of those tables was intensely practical. They supplied precise, ready-to-use values for the changing position of the sun through the year. For a pilot on the high seas in daylight, far from recognizable coastlines, this meant that a noon observation of the sun could be combined with solar-declination data to determine latitude - the ship’s north-south position. The difficult astronomical calculations had already been embodied in the tables. What remained aboard ship was an operational procedure: Observe the sun, consult the appropriate value and calculate latitude. That combination of precision and usability greatly facilitated daytime position-finding at sea. Solar tables derived from Zacuto’s work entered early Portuguese navigational manuals and became part of the practical scientific culture of oceanic travel.
The clearest measure of Zacuto’s importance may be what happened next. The Almanach did not remain a local Portuguese publication. Its tables were reprinted repeatedly in Venice in 1498, 1502, 1525 and 1528. A work first printed in Leiria moved into one of Europe’s great publishing centers and continued to circulate for decades. That publishing history alone tells us something about the standing Zacuto’s astronomy acquired.
Its reach extended farther still. Zacuto’s astronomical material was translated and adapted into Arabic. One Arabic version was produced, likely in Istanbul, in 1505-06; another, associated with Ahmad ibn Qasim al-Hajari in Morocco around 1624, survives in several manuscripts. The work of a Jewish astronomer writing in Hebrew in 15th-century Salamanca had crossed into Latin, Castilian and Arabic scientific cultures.
Zacuto’s name also became entwined with the memory of the great navigators. Accounts have long connected his tables with Columbus and Vasco da Gama, including the famous 1504 lunar eclipse in Jamaica. In this episode, Columbus intimidated Indigenous Jamaicans by predicting the disappearance of the moon, relying on Zacuto’s almanac, which he had on board. A manuscript connected with the Almanach also survives in Seville’s Biblioteca Colombina, the library created by Columbus’s son Hernando. Taken together, these associations reveal the stature Zacuto’s work acquired in the historical memory of the Age of Exploration.
Exiled from Portugal as a Jew
Perhaps the most striking part of Zacuto’s story is what happened to the man himself. Portugal valued the kind of expertise he represented. Yet in December 1496, King Manuel I ordered Portugal’s Jews to leave unless they converted, and in 1497 the crown subjected the Jewish population to mass forced conversion. Zacuto left Portugal as well.
Exile did not end either his travels or his scholarship. From Portugal he moved through North Africa, including Tunis, before eventually reaching Jerusalem. There, late in life, he returned once more to the astronomical work that had made his name known across the Mediterranean, recalculating and updating his earlier tables for the Jewish calendar and the meridian of Jerusalem. The strongest recent reconstruction of his life places his death in Jerusalem in Tevet 5274, or late 1513 or very early 1514 - commonly given as 1514.
Zacuto’s story is therefore larger than a footnote to Columbus. It joins two strands of Sephardic history too often told apart: persecution and exile, and the transmission of knowledge, texts and technologies across borders.
Zacuto’s own tables and 15th-century procedures are now obsolete, but their underlying navigational logic endures. Modern celestial navigation still determines position by combining observations of the sun, moon, planets or stars with authoritative astronomical data. The US Naval Academy requires all midshipmen to study navigation, and its current curriculum includes celestial navigation alongside electronic methods. The US Naval Observatory still describes celestial navigation as a critical independent backup to GPS and other electronic systems. And the Nautical Almanac, first published in 1855, remains the standard US Navy resource for marine celestial navigation. The instruments and calculations have changed, but the essential logic remains: Observe the heavens, consult reliable astronomical data and determine position.
Zacuto’s scientific reputation also survives in an unexpected place. In 1935, the International Astronomical Union formally adopted the name Zagut for a lunar crater honoring Abraham ben Shmuel Zacuto. Modern astronomy has, quite literally, written his name onto the Moon.
Columbus remains a household name because voyages leave dramatic images: ships, landfalls, encounters and conquest. The calculations, tables, instruments, translations and printed books that made such voyages possible are easier to forget. Remembering Zacuto widens the story: His tables brought greater precision and practicality to daytime navigation; his work crossed languages and continents; and his life traced the routes of Sephardic exile from Iberia to Jerusalem. The age of maritime discovery was also an age of scientific discovery, and some of the knowledge that carried Iberian ships across oceans was created by scholars whose communities those same monarchies expelled.

Federal authorities raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar on Monday morning as part of a criminal investigation of the Minnesota Democrat.

A person familiar with the situation, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the nonpublic investigation, told CNBC that the probe of the 44-year-old congresswoman is complex and has been going on for years.
MS NOW reported that a law enforcement source with direct knowledge of the raid — which comes weeks before November's midterm election — said the investigation into Omar is based on allegations of fraud.
Fox News, which first reported the raid, cited a source familiar with the probe as saying it is focused on her immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her father when she emigrated to the U.S. with him from Somalia as a child.
Homeland Security Investigations, a division of the Department of Homeland Security, conducted the raid. HSI investigators were seen outside Omar's home in the Northeast quadrant of Washington throughout the morning.
Omar, who is seeking reelection, has been a target of criticism by Trump for years. She heckled the president during his State of the Union address to Congress on Feb. 24, which came on the heels of aggressive immigration enforcement actions in Minneapolis by federal authorities.
Omar, who is deputy chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, blasted the raid and the investigation in a post on X on Monday.
"I'm ok," Omar wrote.
"Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation," she wrote.
"I will not be silenced."
Omar became a U.S. citizen in 2000 at 17. She was elected to Congress in November 2018 to represent Minnesota's 5th District, which includes all of Minneapolis.
She and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., became the first two Muslim women elected to Congress.
The Department of Justice, in a statement to CNBC when asked about the raid, said, "Today in the Washington, D.C., area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice."
"This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation," the DOJ said.

"There may be more to this, the whole family migration and possibly some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with," said Mullin. He said the investigation could end with deportations.
The DOJ, for years, has had a policy regarding the announcement and initiation of federal investigations and prosecutions close to elections. The policy discourages beginning an investigation, taking investigative steps, bringing criminal charges, or making public statements for the purpose of affecting an election or to give a candidate an advantage or disadvantage.
The person familiar with the raid on Omar's home told CNBC on Monday that the DOJ does not consider that action to violate the policy because the raid was not meant to be public.
Republican John Nagel is running against Omar in a race the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates "solid Democrat." The general election is just over three weeks away on Nov. 3.
The Democratic leadership of the House of Representatives blasted the Trump administration for the raid.
"The Trump administration's raid on Congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home is deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump's adversaries," said House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., and Rep. "Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family."

Delta planned to begin the route on Oct. 23, with an Airbus A350-900 wide-body plane, in what would have marked the first nonstop commercial flight between the U.S. and Saudi Arabia operated by a U.S. airline.
Since Thursday, more than 2,000 flights have been canceled to and from King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, according to FlightAware. The deadly attacks, claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, escalated Saturday, when a projectile struck a passenger terminal at the airport, officials said, killing at least 12 people and wounding more than 300.
King Khalid International Airport remains closed as of Monday.
"We remain in close contact with relevant government and aviation partners, including Saudia and Riyadh Air, as we monitor the situation," Delta said in a statement. "Saudi Arabia remains an important market for Delta, and we are committed to serving the Kingdom for the long-term."
Delta CEO Ed Bastian had told CNBC on Thursday that the airline hadn't yet decided whether to postpone the debut.
"Obviously, we were disappointed to see the news this week," he said. "Safety is going to make the call."
Delta's decision came after the Federal Aviation Administration on Sunday issued a warning for U.S. airlines.
The FAA said pilots should "exercise caution" in or around Saudi Arabia "due to safety-of-flight risks associated with ongoing military activities" and navigation systems. In the warning, which is in effect until Dec. 10, the agency said the threats could be a potential risk "to aircraft at all altitudes."
Airlines suspended flights to the airport, some for the rest of the week, while countries including the U.S. and Australia advised citizens against travel to the region.

Croatia Expands Probe Into Alleged Multi-Million-Euro Toxic Waste Scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:02:00 UTC
00:02:00 KST

Reported by
Croatia's anti-corruption office, USKOK, expanded its investigation into an alleged international illegal waste dumping ring, arresting and questioning five new suspects and three companies over the suspected criminal disposal of hazardous materials near the town of Benkovac and inside the Velebit Nature Park near Senj.
The suspects were released after questioning, as USKOK stated there were no legal grounds to request pre-trial detention. Friday's action marks the third expansion of the sweeping environmental crime probe, which now targets a total of 14 individuals and four companies suspected of severe environmental crimes and falsifying official documents within a criminal enterprise.
The investigation, supported by Europol and law enforcement from Italy and Slovenia, became public in February 2025 with the initial arrest of 13 people. Authorities dismantled an alleged criminal network that is accused of orchestrating the illegal import of hazardous waste from Germany, Italy, and Slovenia into Croatia.
According to Europol, instead of properly treating the materials, the network allegedly buried or dumped at least 35,000 tonnes of waste across at least three locations, generating an estimated 4 million euros ($4.5 million) in illicit profits. To execute the scheme, suspects allegedly generated hundreds of falsified waste tracking sheets and fake construction diaries to disguise hazardous materials as municipal waste cover or legitimate building materials.
The severe environmental toll of the scheme became clear in early August, when USKOK released an expert report from the University of Zagreb's Faculty of Geotechnical Engineering, which concluded the local habitat was "partially irreversibly destroyed." Testing at an illegal landfill in Gospić revealed critical levels of heavy metals—including copper, zinc, lead, and antimony—and "forever chemicals," synthetic compounds that do not easily break down in the environment or the human body.
The report noted that downstream water samples showed high concentrations of the chemicals while upstream samples were clear, proving the landfill was the source. Experts warned there is a "high probability of further deterioration" if the waste is not immediately removed.
The latest USKOK findings reveal the destruction extends further. Between 2020 and 2024, the network allegedly dumped nearly 2,900 tonnes of hazardous plastic and industrial waste at the Senj site, and almost 6,500 tonnes of waste laced with heavy metals and microplastics into an inactive mineral field in Benkovac. Prosecutors warned the microplastics serve as a permanent pollution source that could easily leach into groundwater and the local food chain.
The revelations of widespread contamination and potential long-term health impacts sparked mass outrage. In September, tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets of Zagreb to demand stronger environmental protections, while local communities demanded strict sanctions against those responsible for the ecological damage.
Seeking to manage the ongoing political fallout and reassure the public, Prime Minister Andrej Plenković announced following a meeting with a scientific council that the government is initiating urgent remediation efforts in Gospić. Plenković stated Monday on X that surface waste will be removed in large bags and buried toxins temporarily covered, insisting that recent air and water tests show no deviations from permitted limits and that the public water supply remains completely safe.

====================================================================================================

'Scary' dementia modelling shows how cases will surge by 2050
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:01:28 UTC
00:01:28 KST

Dementia cases to soar to 'scary' highs and women will face more risk, study reveals
By 2050 an estimated 24.7 million people will be diagnosed with dementia each year and women will be disproportionately affected, according to a landmark study.
The research found approximately 11.4 million people developed dementia globally in 2023 and that by 2050 that figure will double and demand for care will explode.
The study's authors said women's brain health needed to be prioritised and risk factors like hormonal changes and unequal education or job opportunities needed investigating.
"Understanding these differences is critical if we are to develop dementia prevention, diagnosis and care strategies that respond to the populations facing the greatest future risk," lead author Dr Ashleigh Vella said.
The research from the Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing (CHeBA) at the University of NSW analysed 38,418 people through population-based studies from 18 countries and territories.
It is one of the most comprehensive studies looking at the incidence rate of dementia. The study found cases were highest among women and people living in low income and middle income countries.
Nearly two thirds of dementia diagnoses in Australia are women and this has long been considered a symptom of their longer life expectancy but researchers said there may be more at play.
The paper, published in the Journal of the American Medical Association Neurology, suggested the higher prevalence could be caused by other factors such as:
- Menopause
- Disproportionate educational and occupational opportunities
- Cardiometabolic factors such as body mass index and physical activity
Co-director of the CHeBA and Senior Australia of the Year Professor, Henry Brodaty, said historically women had less access to education and fewer career opportunities which could lead to poorer cognitive resilience.
"[Studies have shown] people who are in more complex occupations, particularly where they have complexity in managing people, they have a lower rate of cognitive decline and dementia," he said.
"Education has its most benefit in childhood and early development through to young adulthood but you can still build up your cognitive reserve or buffer against pathology building up in the brain throughout your life."
Higher rates of depression, anxiety and obesity among women could also be contributing factors, Professor Brodaty said, and more research was needed on the role menopause might play.
"Perhaps stopping oestrogen production may play a role but it's not established … and there's been conflicting results about whether hormone replacement therapy makes a difference."
Leading dementia researcher Matthew Pase at Monash University said the research was ambitious and provided important comparisons on dementia rates between low income and high income countries.
He described the figures as "scary".
"To see what rates are projected to be in low-income countries is alarming because they are less equipped to deal with this … so any solutions need to be scalable and not just be available for people who can pay to see an academic at a medical centre in Sydney or Melbourne."
Reducing dementia risk
Professor Brodaty, whose father passed away with Alzheimer's at just 52, said having a clear idea of what was coming meant there must be more investment in diagnosis, care and prevention.
Almost half of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed by addressing 14 risk factors.
Professor Brodaty urged Australians to "embrace" brain health by:
- Engaging in at least half an hour of physical activity five days a week
- Staying socially connected and "stretching the brain" by learning new things
- Eating a diet rich in vegetables, legumes and extra olive oil aka the Mediterranean diet
- Talking to their GP about brain health when they have their subsidised health check between the ages of 45 and 49
Professor Pase said given the high cost of the two dementia drug therapies approved in Australia, which are not subsidised through the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, prevention was still key.

LONDON – British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Oct 12 that a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford air base in Britain was “highly likely” to have been coordinated in Iran, and almost certainly directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The RAF Fairfordbase in south-west England, which had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, became the focal point for a major security response after five British men were arrested nearby in the early hours of Sept 27 on suspected terrorism and explosive offences.
US officials have told Reuters that there had been a suspected plot involving Iran to launch a drone attack, and last week US President Donald Trump said a threat linked to Iran had prompted a decision to withdraw the bombers from the base.
“I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard (IRGC),” Burnham told Parliament.
Iran has rejected any connection with the Fairford incident.
“Tehran has had no involvement in this matter, and if the British government possesses any documents or evidence to support its claims, it should present them,” said Iran’s Ambassador to Britain, Seyed Ali Mousavi, according to Iran’s state news agency IRNA.
Fairford plot details sketchy
Details around the suspected plot remain thin. The five detained men were later released without charge on police bail “under stringent conditions”, and two other arrested men, including a British-Iranian national, have also been released.
Detectives have said petrol but no viable explosive had been found in vans seized along with the five men. However, both police and Burnham have pointed towards the involvement of a foreign state.
British interior minister Shabana Mahmood told parliament a known individual, whom she did not name, who was based in Iran was believed to be behind what had happened.
“We will not tolerate these threats on our soil,” Burnham said. “We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm.”
Foreign ministries from almost 30 countries including the US, Canada, France and Germany issued a statement condemning “Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners”.
“The UK has also concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors,” the statement said.
The British authorities have for a number of years accused Iran of being involved in numerous plots and attempted assassinations in Britain using criminal networks and proxies, accusations Tehran has repeatedly denied.
In 2025, Britain said there had been 20 credible Iranian-backed threats to kill or kidnap individuals based in the UK.
In July, Britain used new powers to ban support for the IRGC and a linked group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which had claimed responsibility for seven attacks earlier in 2026 at locations linked to Jewish and Israeli communities, and Persian-language media.
British foreign minister Ed Miliband said he had summoned the Iranian ambassador while the ministry announced two Iranian nationals had been sanctioned.
The two men were Ruhollah Bazghandi, who Britain said was the IRGC’s Head of Counterespionage Operations, and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, a facilitator for the already sanctioned Zindashti criminal network which is accused of involvement in several plots against Iranian dissidents. REUTERS
