Is fatness a feminist issue?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:00:42 UTC
23:00:42 KST

Recent research published in Sex Roles suggests that while many fat women identify as feminists, they do not consistently view their body size as a feminist issue. The study highlights a divide in how women understand their bodies, with some pointing to gendered double standards and societal discrimination, while others view their weight as a matter of personal responsibility.
Anti-fatness refers to the systemic and interpersonal prejudice directed at people with larger bodies. Feminist scholars have often linked this anti-fat stigma to traditional gender roles and patriarchal beauty norms. This perspective argues that societal pressure to be thin falls especially hard on women, creating toxic environments that negatively impact their body image, mental health, and social standing.
“American society is often fixated on how women look,” lead author Breanne Fahs, a professor of women and gender studies at Arizona State University and author of Fat and Furious: Igniting Radical Fat Resistance, told PsyPost. “Women are often told to be young, pretty, and skinny by their parents, partners, classmates, and strangers. Psychological research has often shown the problems with ‘thin idealization’ and living for a male gaze. In particular, women are criticized about having defective bodies, and they consequently fear gaining weight, try dangerous diets, and/or loathe their own bodies.”
“In the 1970s, second wave feminists warned that the fixation on slender bodies seriously hurt women and the slogan of ‘fat is a feminist issue’ was born,” Fahs added. “In the last twenty years there has been a growth of social movements that challenged the sexist assumptions of fat stigma, with the group called National Association to Advance Fat Acceptance (NAAFA) leading the way.”
Research has shown that fat women generally face harsher social and economic consequences for their body size than fat men. In one study, fat women were 16 times more likely than fat men to report weight-related job discrimination, and other studies have found that fat women receive harsher judgments of their parenting and are more often denied loans, promotions, or apartments. Fat men, on the other hand, tend to face less stigma and fewer everyday indignities for similar body sizes.
Despite these documented disparities, it has remained an open question whether fat women themselves view their physical experiences through a political or feminist lens. Fahs and her colleague Eric Swank, a professor of social and cultural analysis at Arizona State University, sought to understand how fat women talk about this connection and whether they recognize the gendered dimensions of weight stigma that academics often discuss.
“Lots of research has looked at the causes and consequences of fat hatred among women of all body sizes,” Fahs explained. “Some studies have even looked at the reasons for being a fat activist, but the way fat women view feminism has mostly been overlooked.”
Fahs’s own work helped motivate the project. She has written about women’s dread of gaining weight, anti-fat bias in health care, and the relationships between fat therapists and fat patients. Her experience as both a professor and a practicing clinical psychologist left her curious about whether fat women see anti-fat stigma through a feminist lens.
To investigate this, the researchers interviewed 20 women living in the United States who self-identified as fat or overweight. The participants were recruited through local classified advertisements on Craigslist, allowing the research team to reach a geographically diverse group. The women ranged in age from 27 to 66, with an average age of 40. Half were women of color, 40 percent identified as bisexual or lesbian, and their body weights ranged from under 200 to over 300 pounds.
All 20 interviews were conducted by Fahs over video calls and lasted about 90 minutes each. She asked the women questions about their bodies, their social experiences, and their political perspectives. Two key questions guided the core of the analysis: whether the participants considered themselves feminists, and whether they believed fatness was a feminist issue. The researchers did not provide a definition of feminism, allowing each participant to respond according to her own understanding.
The participants’ responses pointed to a complex divide between personal identification and political frameworks. Thirteen women explicitly identified as feminists, three said they might use the label for certain issues, and four rejected it entirely. When asked if fatness was a feminist issue, the group was evenly split: eight said yes, four said maybe, and eight said no. Several self-identified feminists insisted that fatness was not a feminist issue, while one woman, identified in the study as Marge, firmly rejected the feminist label but still stated that it was.
The researchers identified six distinct themes in how the participants evaluated the issue. Three of the themes supported a connection between weight and feminism. Four women highlighted gendered double standards, observing that society readily accepts fat men as funny or relatable, while fat women face intense social disapproval for the same size. Three women described fatness as a central way women are judged, explaining that a woman’s social worth remains tied to physical appearance.
Overt discrimination, tied for the most common theme linking the two concepts, was raised by four participants. These women cited institutional obstacles in hiring, healthcare, and media representation as evidence of a broader feminist problem. When discussing these barriers, Fahs noted that participants “elaborated how workplaces, hospitals, schools, and families discriminate against women who are fat.”
The remaining three themes rejected the connection between body size and feminism. Three women stated that fatness has nothing to do with feminism, arguing that body weight is an individual matter of personal responsibility and lifestyle rather than gender politics. Two women maintained that fatness has nothing to do with gender, arguing that weight stigma affects people of all genders equally and should not be framed as a women’s issue.
In the final theme, three participants argued that fat women deserve ridicule, framing teasing as a natural consequence of body size or a motivator to lose weight.
Describing these women, Fahs said, “They thought fat women were supposed to be ‘made fun of by someone who is not fat’ and fat people ‘should lose weight’ if they do not want to be teased. This diversity of perspectives shows how fat resistance and feminist fat liberation perspectives still diverge from narratives of self-blame and ridicule.”
The findings point to an uneven alignment between feminist theory and the everyday perspectives of fat women. While some participants expressed an awareness of gender inequality, others expressed anti-fat attitudes, which the authors say could reflect internalized stigma or a form of anti-feminism, or viewed their struggles as entirely personal. The researchers noted that framing fatness through a political lens rather than individual failure could help people challenge anti-fat bias and reduce feelings of personal self-blame.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study relied on a small group of 20 women recruited through Craigslist during the COVID-19 pandemic, so the sample does not reflect the full population of fat women in the United States. In addition, the questions about feminism came after about an hour of discussion focused on fatness, which may have influenced the way participants answered.
The study also asked participants whether they identified as feminists rather than measuring specific feminist beliefs, and several women appeared to associate feminism primarily with the #MeToo movement or perceived extremes. Both researchers identify as fat feminists, and Fahs conducted all 20 interviews herself, which could have shaped how participants discussed sensitive topics. Future research using standardized surveys could help clarify how widespread these viewpoints are across the broader population.
The study, “Does Fatness Politicize Women? Fat Women’s Narratives on Whether Fatness is a Feminist Issue,” was authored by Breanne Fahs and Eric Swank.

Europe still divided on buying locally for defence, MBDA CEO says

Europe still divided on buying locally for defence, MBDA CEO says
Oct 12 - The head of European missile maker MBDA said on Monday that efforts to steer more defence spending towards European suppliers faced political hurdles, with EU governments still divided over how much to rely on US security guarantees.
Washington has been pressing European NATO allies to increase defence spending, while France has led calls to buy more European-made weapons amid questions over the US commitment to Europe's security.
"Do we want as Europeans to really take our own fate in our hands and then bring our European capabilities to the NATO alliance, or are we simply increasing our capabilities by buying outside?" MBDA CEO Eric Beranger asked the Warsaw Security Forum.
"There are some different attitudes between the various governments. I think the jury is still out," Beranger said, adding: "There is still some way to go".
DETERRENCE
Beranger, who steps down next month, was among several speakers debating European strategic autonomy at the forum, which is taking place amid heightened tensions over the war in Ukraine.
Several European countries, including conference host Poland, Germany and the Netherlands, have turned to US suppliers for equipment such as F-35 fighter jets.
"Limiting American defense industry in European procurement programs threatens that partnership and weakens our mutual security", the US mission to the European Union said in February.
Nuclear deterrence was also a focus of the discussion, with Russia recently renewing warnings that it could use nuclear weapons to defend itself.
"Of all the events at this conference that the Russians will be most interested in hearing ... it will be this one", former British defence minister Ben Wallace said, referring to Europe's ability to strengthen its nuclear and conventional deterrence.
"Deterrence is not only capabilities; deterrence is also perceptions. Do we believe our American allies will come? Does Russia believe our American allies will come?" said Claudia Major, senior vice president for transatlantic security at the German Marshall Fund.
"I don't say give up on the US. I just say don't blind ourselves", Major added, citing recent friction with the US over Greenland, Russia and Ukraine.
NATO members, including the US, reaffirmed their commitment to collective defence in the Ankara Summit Declaration in July, repeating that "an attack on one is an attack on all".
Stressing that credibility is central to deterrence, Beranger said Europe already had the industrial base it needed to strengthen its defences. REUTERS

“The size and scale of projects such as at RAF Waddington present many challenges, in both their planning and delivery. Air Infrastructure will continue to work closely with colleagues in DIO, at stations and with our industry partners to ensure the RAF remains ready to fly and fight by ensuring our airbases are able to operate at maximum efficiency.”
Pete Shaw, project manager at the Defence Infrastructure Organisation, said: “I am pleased to see work commencing on this vital refurbishment project at RAF Waddington. This work will enhance the resilience and reliability of the airfield, ensuring Service personnel have the facilities they need to train and operate effectively, helping Defence remain ready to respond.”
Robert Weston, project director at Lagan Aviation and Infrastructure Ltd, said: “We are delighted to be starting works on the refurbishment of the airfield at RAF Waddington on behalf of DIO. Over the course of the project, we will continue to work with our stakeholders, utilising our expertise and experience gained through past successful projects. We have planned the works collaboratively with the Station to ensure operations are not impacted during the construction works.”
Waddington serves as the hub of British ISTAR, which supplies British and NATO commanders with the information their decisions rest on, and it is also home to the RAF Aerobatic Team.
Completion is expected in summer 2028, and the work forms part of a wider programme of airfield infrastructure projects across the estate, among them the recently finished resurfacing of the runway intersection at RAF Marham, which came in three weeks ahead of an eight-week schedule.

When climate change brings the heat, what happens to a mighty redwood?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)
Towering coast redwoods are known for their resiliency, withstanding fire, fungus and rot to survive for centuries. But these ancient trees now may be vulnerable to a relatively recent foe: heat waves.
As temperatures climb, photosynthesis slows in these iconic trees, researchers report September 22 in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Biogeosciences. Lab experiments show the rate of the sunlight-driven food making process in its needles roughly halves when temperatures rise from 30° to 40° Celsius.
Such a change usually indicates “severe levels of stress,” says Lily Klinek, an ecophysiologist at the University of California, Davis. That vulnerability can cause tree deaths that may jeopardize one of California’s largest stores of carbon, a shield against climate change.
Coast redwoods (Sequoia sempervirens) live only in a narrow strip of coastal habitat from central California to southern Oregon, where temperatures are mild and fog is abundant. But recent heat waves have spiked temperatures in parts of their range to over 40° C.
The impact of heat waves on photosynthesis has been studied in other tree species, with some faring better than others. But this is the first study to investigate how coast redwoods respond to the heat, says Troy Magney, an ecophysiologist at the University of Montana in Missoula.
From July 2022 to October 2024, Klinek, Magney and colleagues repeatedly measured the performance of needles from redwoods in California’s Mendocino County. That period included two heat waves.
Typically, trees stay cool when small porelike openings called stomata allow water to evaporate, taking heat with it, similar to how sweat cools humans. But when conditions get too hot and dry, stomata close, retaining a plant’s moisture. Under extreme heat, the team found that needles reached up to 10 degrees C hotter than the surrounding air due to the dark needles absorbing ample sunlight. That suggests that the stomata were at least partially closed.
Those same pores are crucial for photosynthesis; it’s where the trees take in carbon dioxide — used to make food — and release oxygen. “They could essentially starve if they don’t have access to enough carbon,” Klinek says.
It’s hard to investigate the impact of heat on photosynthesis in the field, though. That would take building a “heat chamber around a real-life branch or wait[ing] for a heat event to happen,” Klinek says. Instead, she climbed onto the roof of her car with a pole pruner and collected samples from about five meters high, in the lower canopy.
In the lab, the researchers subjected the samples to increasing heat to match the heat waves seen in recent summers and measured the resulting photosynthesis rates. Even though the samples were submerged in water, so had their stomata open and had full access to the ingredients for photosynthesis, the rate still declined. “They weren’t slowing their photosynthesis because of carbon starvation,” Klinek says.
For practical reasons, the study focused on younger coast redwoods, not the old growth giants. It’s difficult to reach even the lowest branches on trees more than 100 meters tall. “There are just fundamental limitations on what you can sample if you don’t have a jetpack,” says Christopher Still, an ecophysiologist at Oregon State University in Corvallis who was not associated with the study. Even so, the team’s results show that coast redwoods are “really temperature sensitive. You don’t see this as much with other species necessarily,” Still says.
In the field, Klinek observed trees closing their stomata to preserve water. This suggests that in more realistic conditions, where a heat wave and drought hit simultaneously, lack of heat and water could make the slowdown “even more intense.” But more work needs to be done, she notes. “We still don’t know what the threshold is for irreversible damage.”

NEW DELHI: An explosion by a suspected improvised explosive device (IED) was heard in a forward village along the Line of Control in the Krishna Ghati sector of Jammu and Kashmir's Poonch district on Monday, triggering heightened security measures, officials said.The powerful blast reportedly took place in the Satwal-Naki area near the zero line while a group of people was moving along the Pakistani side of the LoC, officials said. PTI reported.Casualties were reported, but the exact number of people killed or injured was not immediately known, they added.Officials said it was unclear whether the group comprised suspected terrorists attempting to cross the LoC or Pakistani security personnel patrolling the area. The circumstances leading to the explosion were yet to be established.
Security heightened
Following the blast, security forces sounded an alert across the sector and stepped up vigilance along the LoC to assess the situation and prevent any potential security breach, officials said.
In a separate incident, Indian Army troops detected two rusted landmines near the border fence in the Basoni area of the Mendhar sector on Monday.The landmines were spotted during track construction at 8.25 am and 12.10 pm, respectively, officials said.
Both devices were subsequently destroyed by Army experts in controlled explosions.Around a dozen landmines have been detected and defused by the Army in the area over the past week.Forward areas along the LoC are dotted with landmines as part of an anti-infiltration system. However, heavy rainfall can sometimes wash the mines away, causing them to surface in areas where they could pose a potential risk.

Hurricane Simon crawls along Mexico's Pacific coast, bringing floods and evacuations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:55:46 UTC
22:55:46 KST

Hurricane Simon crawls along Mexico's Pacific coast, bringing floods and evacuations
MANZANILLO, Mexico, Oct 12 - Hurricane Simon crept northwest just off Mexico's Pacific coast on Monday, lashing western states with dangerous winds, heavy rain and flooding that put riverside communities on alert for possible evacuations.
The US National Hurricane Center said Simon was about 55 miles (90 km) west-southwest of Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco state at 8 a.m. (1400 GMT), packing maximum sustained winds of 110 mph (175 kph), making it a Category 2 hurricane.
Simon has weakened since Saturday when it was a Category 4 system.
"Simon is slowly losing wind intensity and could ultimately stall this week and never make a true landfall as an organized storm," said Alex DaSilva, a hurricane expert at private forecaster AccuWeather.
Simon is forecast to make landfall on Thursday in Mexico's Sinaloa state.
"The slower Simon moves, the more rain potential the storm carries, but right now most of that rain is offshore and to the south of the storm's center ultimately sparing the feet of rain we thought this storm could initially bring," said DaSilva.
Simon was moving northwest at just 3 mph (6 kph) and was expected to continue along that track before turning northeast and moving inland across west-central Mexico around midweek.
Authorities said that Simon could bring life-threatening flooding and mudslides to parts of the Pacific coast and nearby mountains.
The hurricane is forecast to dump an additional 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 cm) of rain across coastal areas of southwest and west-central Mexico, with isolated amounts of 6 to 8 inches (15 to 20 cm) in parts of Jalisco and Sinaloa. The National Hurricane Center said isolated storm totals could reach 30 inches (76 cm) in parts of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco.
The head of Mexico's civil protection agency, Laura Velazquez, said one person was reported to have died due to the storm in Guerrero state, home to the popular tourist destination of Acapulco.
In the coastal town of Cihuatlan in southwestern Jalisco, patrols warned residents to prepare for potential evacuation as the Marabasco River rose. Floodwater inundated streets and low-lying areas of the town overnight.
In the port city of Manzanillo in Colima state, residents waded through flooded homes and streets as navy personnel helped remove water.
"Everything got flooded," said resident Maria Elena Vazquez from inside her home, pants rolled up as the water came up to her ankles.
The National Hurricane Center said Simon was expected to produce dangerous storm surge and large destructive waves close to where it approaches the coast. Swells from the hurricane are also forecast to create life-threatening surf and rip current conditions along southwestern and west-central Mexico over the next few days.
Following weeks of storms that have battered Mexico, at least 10 people are missing in the state of Baja California and one minor was killed in the coastal city of Ensenada. REUTERS

Authorities launch probe after chillers were cranked to 50 degrees Celsius, causing tens of millions of euros in losses
Hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators and freezers at hundreds of French supermarkets to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 Fahrenheit) overnight, causing fires and spoiling food.

14-year-old killed in northern Israel school trip blast; police probe ordnance in student's bag
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:52:49 UTC
22:52:49 KST

A 14-year-old boy was killed, and about 24 other people were injured, three of them seriously and one moderately, in an explosion believed to have been caused by unexploded ordnance during a school hiking trip near Mitzpe Pe'er along Israel's northern border on Monday afternoon. Police are investigating whether one of the students found an explosive device and placed it in his bag, where it detonated while he was standing alongside his classmates on the trail.
The victims were members of a group of students and teachers from the ORT Yeshiva High School in Ma'alot-Tarshiha, who were taking part in the first day of their annual hike along the Israel National Trail.
The explosion occurred in an area near the Lebanese border that had previously served as a staging ground for Israeli military forces and had also been targeted by Hezbollah fire.
The IDF is investigating whether the school trip had received the necessary authorization to pass through the area and, if approval was granted, whether it had gone through the appropriate military channels.
Investigators are also working to identify the unexploded munition, including whether it was a cluster munition or another type of explosive device. The military is examining whether the ordnance was left behind by Israeli forces or fired by Hezbollah and remained unexploded until Monday's incident.
The theory that a student may have picked up the explosive and placed it in his bag remains under investigation. Authorities have not established what triggered the detonation.
Footage from the scene showed students' belongings scattered across the ground following the blast.
Military helicopters and bomb disposal teams dispatched
Fourteen ambulances were sent to the scene, while the IDF dispatched three Israeli Air Force helicopters, personnel from its elite Unit 669 search-and-rescue force, a battalion medical team, bomb disposal specialists from the Yahalom combat engineering unit and additional military personnel.
The IDF Spokesperson's Unit said the circumstances of the explosion remained under investigation.
Kiryat Shmona police station commander Elad Ben Lulu said police received a report of the incident through the 100 emergency hotline at approximately 3 p.m., prompting a large-scale response involving emergency and security personnel.
"Every available rescue force arrived at the scene," Ben Lulu said, adding that investigators were examining all aspects of the incident as specialized teams worked to determine what caused the explosion.
Asked whether the explosive appeared to have been a large or small munition, he said: "Probably small, but there's no way to know yet. The professional teams are examining the scene, and I hope we'll establish the full circumstances as quickly as possible."
He confirmed that all the injured had been evacuated after receiving emergency medical care, including lifesaving treatment at the scene.
Police urged the public to stay away from the area and allow emergency and security personnel to carry out their work. They also called on anyone encountering unexploded ordnance or suspicious objects to keep their distance and report them to the police emergency hotline at 100.
'I heard a huge explosion and we ran'
One student who was taking part in the trip described the moments after the blast.
"I heard a huge explosion and we ran. A lot of children were injured," he said.
Eliyahu, whose son was among the students on the hike, described the uncertainty among families as details of the explosion began to emerge.
"I spoke to my son. He was apparently just meters away from the explosion," he said. "We still don't know which class was hit. Everyone is under enormous stress, and nobody knows who was injured."
"It's a school trip along the Israel National Trail. They started today. Suddenly, they heard an explosion and he ran," Eliyahu said. "They're waiting there to be evacuated. The group my son was with wasn't hurt."
The Ma'alot-Tarshiha municipality confirmed that students and school staff had been injured. Mayor Moti Ben David and municipal teams immediately headed to the scene and began coordinating with emergency services, rescue personnel and education officials.
"At this stage, the details of the incident and the conditions of those injured are still being clarified," the municipality said. "We are working to establish a complete picture and will provide verified updates as they become available."
The municipality urged the public to respect the privacy of the students and their families and refrain from spreading unverified information.
'A complex incident'
Magen David Adom (MDA), Israel's national emergency medical service, said it received the initial report at 2:53 p.m. through its 101 emergency hotline.
Itzik Shoshan, head of MDA's Yarden region, said emergency teams rushed to the area in large numbers immediately after receiving the report.
"When we received the report of an explosion in an open area in the Upper Galilee Regional Council, we immediately dispatched large numbers of ambulances, mobile intensive care units and an MDA helicopter," Shoshan said.
"When we arrived, we found several casualties with injuries of varying severity. We immediately began providing medical treatment to eight people with serious and moderate injuries, as well as others who were lightly injured."
"This is a complex incident," he added. "We are continuing to provide medical treatment to the injured at the scene and evacuate them to hospital as quickly as possible."
The Education Ministry described the explosion as an extremely serious incident and said it was working closely with security forces and professional teams to support the students, teachers and their families.
"This is an extremely serious incident, and our thoughts are with the injured and their families," the ministry said. "We are working alongside security forces and all relevant professional bodies to provide assistance to the students, educational staff and their families."
The ministry also appealed to the public to act responsibly and avoid circulating unverified information while the circumstances of the explosion were still being established.
Netanyahu orders swift evacuation of injured
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was briefed on the explosion and spoke with MDA Director General Eli Bin, Education Minister Yoav Kisch and his military secretary, the Prime Minister's Office said.
"The prime minister asked to ensure that the injured are evacuated to hospitals as quickly as possible and continues to conduct ongoing situation assessments," his office said.
The investigation now centers on several questions, including whether a student handled unexploded ordnance before it detonated, whether the explosive originated from Israeli military activity or Hezbollah fire, and whether the school group had been authorized to hike through an area previously used by the IDF and exposed to cross-border attacks.

====================================================================================================

Number of disability pensioners under 40 falls for first time since 2020
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:52:34 UTC
22:52:34 KST

The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.
The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.

Wang Huning, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), attends a conference marking the 70th anniversary of the establishment of the All-China Federation of Returned Overseas Chinese (ACFROC) and delivers a speech in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 12, 2026. BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- China's top political advisor Wang Huning on Monday urged efforts to unite and guide overseas Chinese in contributing to building China into a modern socialist country in all respects.
Wang, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), made the remarks at a conference marking the 70th anniversary of the establishment of the All-China Federation of Returned Overseas Chinese (ACFROC).
Affairs relating to overseas Chinese are a long-term strategic undertaking of the Party and the state, and the ACFROC is a people's organization led by the CPC, serving as a bridge linking the Party and the government with returned overseas Chinese, their relatives and overseas Chinese nationals, Wang noted.
Over the past 70 years, the ACFROC has united and guided overseas Chinese in playing a unique role in advancing the cause of the Party and the state, Wang said.
The country's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) is crucial to basically realizing socialist modernization, and affairs relating to overseas Chinese face new circumstances and tasks, he said.
Wang called on the ACFROC to leverage its unique strengths to improve work related to overseas Chinese to better serve the country's overall development, and unite and guide overseas Chinese in contributing to building China into a modern socialist country in all respects and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation on all fronts.
He also asked Party committees and governments at all levels to support the federations of returned overseas Chinese in carrying out their work in accordance with the law and their charters, and provide strong guarantees for them to fulfill their various functions.
About 770 people attended the conference, including officials from relevant central Party and state organs and representatives of overseas Chinese communities at home and abroad.
The ACFROC is a national people's organization composed of returned overseas Chinese and their family members. It is a constituent organization of the National Committee of the CPPCC. Federations of returned overseas Chinese at all levels enjoy the same status as people's organizations at the corresponding levels, including trade unions, Communist Youth League organizations and women's federations. ■

The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.

TALLINN, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Estonia's newly elected President Ulle Madise was sworn into office on Monday afternoon at the Riigikogu building in the capital, Tallinn, succeeding Alar Karis as the country's head of state.
Madise was elected president on Sept. 2 after securing 71 votes in the Estonian parliament. Under Estonia's Constitution, a presidential candidate must receive the support of at least two-thirds of the 101-member parliament, or a minimum of 68 votes, to be elected.
Madise, 51, previously served as a legal adviser to the Estonian president and has held the post of Chancellor of Justice since 2015. She is Estonia's sixth president since the restoration of independence and the country's second female president.

She warned against allowing fear and pessimism to take hold, saying fear clouds judgment and leads to unwise decisions. She emphasized that the future is neither inherently bleak nor uncertain, but something people shape themselves, urging the public to recognize and wisely seize major opportunities in times of uncertainty.
The Riigikogu is the unicameral parliament of Estonia. It has 101 members, directly elected by the people every four years through proportional representation. ■

====================================================================================================

Xi Focus: Turning China's innovation moments into lasting momentum
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
21:51:50 CST
22:51:50 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- In June 2024, China's Chang'e-6 probe brought back humanity's first samples ever retrieved from the far side of the moon, an achievement hailed by global media as historic.
Seven months later, DeepSeek's R1 reasoning model drew worldwide attention to China's advances in artificial intelligence (AI), with a Silicon Valley venture capitalist calling it AI's "Sputnik moment."
The wave of innovation milestones carried into 2026. In March, China approved the market launch of an invasive brain-computer interface medical device by a Chinese company, indicating that the device has now entered the phase of clinical application. Last week, the journal Nature published a research article reporting that Chinese scientists had developed a nuclear clock capable of stable operation, marking a breakthrough in ultra-precise time measurement with potential applications in satellite navigation and deep-space exploration.
How to transform breakthroughs in individual fields into lasting gains in productivity across the economy? China has made headway in this regard, as it is pursuing "new quality productive forces," an innovation-centered major task put forward by President Xi Jinping.
During an inspection tour of northeast China's Heilongjiang Province in September 2023, Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, brought the concept of new quality productive forces to the public's attention, calling for better integration of sci-tech innovation resources and the development of strategic emerging and future industries.
At the Central Economic Work Conference that December, Xi urged efforts to drive industrial innovation through sci-tech innovation, particularly by leveraging disruptive and cutting-edge technologies to foster new industries, new models and new growth drivers, and to develop new quality productive forces.
The policy drive stepped up on Oct. 9, when the CPC Central Committee and the State Council issued guidelines setting out 19 key measures to accelerate the development of new quality productive forces.
INNOVATE TO WIN THE FUTURE
"Innovation drives development and innovation shapes the future," Xi has stressed.
Shifting toward innovation-driven growth is imperative for China. The country has built a complete industrial system covering all industrial categories in the United Nations classification, yet it is still grappling with major pressures from demographic shifts to resource and environment constraints. The fact that some of its key technologies remain dependent on other countries, along with intensifying technological revolution and competition, adds urgency to this shift.
Xi's expositions on this concept have provided guidance for the country's high-quality development as well as for Chinese modernization.
At a group study session of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee in January 2024, Xi said "developing new quality productive forces is an intrinsic requirement and an important focus of promoting high-quality development."
With innovation playing the leading role, new quality productive forces mean advanced productivity that is freed from traditional economic growth mode and productivity development paths, features high-tech, high efficiency and high quality, and comes in line with the new development philosophy, said Xi.
From quantum technology and new energy to AI and future industries, sci-tech innovation has been a recurring focus of the Political Bureau's group study sessions in recent years.
The emphasis on breaking new ground echoes a long-standing idea in Chinese philosophy. At a meeting on cultural inheritance and development in June 2023, Xi identified innovation as one of the five defining characteristics of Chinese civilization.
Acutely aware of what matters for an economy with a vast industrial base, Xi has stressed that developing new quality productive forces "does not mean neglecting or abandoning traditional industries." He also stressed that developing new quality productive forces should be tailored to local conditions, warning against both a headlong rush into new industries and the neglect of traditional industrial strengths.
The guidelines issued on Oct. 9 align with this approach, calling for measures tailored to local conditions and for "establishing the new before abolishing the old." An official with the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) said these principles are intended to correct problems seen in practice, including investment and planning divorced from reality, a rush into emerging and future industries, and neglect of upgrading traditional industries.
FROM DISCOVERY TO PRODUCTIVITY
The crucial link is turning knowledge into application. Addressing a national science and technology gathering in Beijing in July 2026, Xi summed up the relationship: sci-tech innovation should highlight an application-oriented approach, while industrial innovation should raise scientific questions.
The brain-computer interface device approved in March illustrates how this works in practice. By decoding neural signals and transmitting commands to a pneumatic glove, it helps eligible patients with cervical spinal cord injuries perform grasping movements. Its market approval marks an important step toward wider clinical use.
In manufacturing, the demand for better products can itself steer research. At Yangquan Valve Co., Ltd., a century-old manufacturer in north China's Shanxi Province, engineers have developed ball valves for hydrogen pipelines, opening possibilities beyond its traditional products.
During a visit to the factory in July 2025, Xi emphasized responding to market demand and using technological innovation to breathe new life into traditional industries.
During a November 2025 visit to south China's Guangdong Province, Xi reviewed progress in integrating sci-tech innovation with industrial innovation, and called for the building of an internationally competitive modern industrial system.
He also stressed the need to accelerate indigenous innovation, vigorously support the adoption of homegrown innovative products, and foster a favorable environment for their application.
China's large market, extensive supply chains and strong research capacity create opportunities to turn scientific advances into industrial applications.
In Guangdong, a manufacturing powerhouse, the value added of the province's 20 major industrial clusters accounted for 31.7 percent of its GDP in 2025. In east China's Anhui Province, an expanding network of vehicle manufacturers and suppliers brings together batteries, chips, materials and vehicle assembly, making it possible to build an entire new energy vehicle without leaving the province.
The broader shift is visible in national figures. In August 2026, value added by high-tech manufacturing enterprises above the designated size rose 16.7 percent year on year, compared with a 5.2 percent increase for industrial enterprises above the designated size overall. The green transition offers another marker: renewable energy accounted for 73.9 percent of all newly installed power generation capacity in the first half of 2026, according to the National Energy Administration.
These changes show the scale of the transformation under way. Making the gains durable, however, requires more than successful products or fast-growing sectors. It requires an innovation system that can generate, test, finance, and spread successive rounds of advances.
SUSTAINING INNOVATION, SHARING OPPORTUNITIES
Xi has repeatedly focused on what happens between an invention and its wider adoption. During a November 2024 visit to the Wuhan Institute of Industrial Innovation and Development in central China's Hubei Province, he asked about development timelines, cost reductions, international competitiveness and cooperation with enterprises -- practical questions about how technology reaches the market.
There is also a longer horizon. Xi has emphasized basic research, which may not yield immediate commercial returns but provides the discoveries on which future industries depend. At a symposium on basic research in Shanghai in April 2026, Xi said, "We must seize opportunities, rise to challenges, put basic research high on the agenda, advance it with sustained commitment, and strive for continuous achievements."
China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) places the development of new quality productive forces and greater self-reliance and strength in science and technology among its strategic priorities.
Liu Zhenzhong, a researcher at the Institute of Industrial and Technological Economics of the NDRC, noted that transformative technologies are changing how innovation is organized and how resources are allocated. Institutional reform, he said, is therefore needed to clear barriers to development.
Xi has charted a practical path for empowering new quality productive forces through reform. He called for efforts to deepen reform of economic and sci-tech systems to "remove bottlenecks and blockages that constrain the development of new quality productive forces." He also urged establishing a high-standard market system and developing new ways to allocate production factors.
Reform efforts include guidelines issued in April 2026 to deepen reform of the ChiNext board of the Shenzhen Stock Exchange, the country's Nasdaq-style board of growth enterprises; an initiative launched in 2024 to promote mutual recognition of data products across trading platforms; and measures aimed at improving market-access rules.
Xi has also emphasized that innovation is not confined within national borders. At the second session of the 32nd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting in November 2025, he stressed digital, smart and green development and called on Asia-Pacific economies to "move faster to nurture and promote new quality productive forces." He advocated deeper cooperation on open-source technologies and an open, competitive ecosystem for innovation.
The core technology behind the signature substrate product of Austrian semiconductor materials company AT&S was first commercialized in southwest China's Chongqing Municipality and has since been refined there. CEO Michael Mertin said China has long made it a priority to train scientists and engineers, and the new generation of Chinese engineers "not only possesses outstanding mathematical skills but is also increasingly creative."
"In today's digital age, no company, city or country can innovate in isolation," Mertin said. "High-tech progress depends on trusted global networks, cross-border collaboration, and the exchange of talent, expertise and ideas."
In the latest signal of openness and cooperation, the new guidelines call for allocating advanced factors of production globally, building global networks for innovation cooperation, and establishing efficient, convenient and secure mechanisms for cross-border data flows.
"The more complex the international environment, the more we should be open-minded and engage with the world. We should determine the right balance between opening up and security, and achieve greater strength and self-reliance in science and technology through international cooperation," Xi once said. ■

====================================================================================================

Interview: Long March spirit inspires modern governance, global solidarity: Kenyan media executive
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
21:51:41 CST
22:51:41 KST

NAIROBI, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Ninety years after the victory of the Long March, the historic journey continues to resonate beyond China because the perseverance, sacrifice, solidarity and hope it embodied remain relevant to societies confronting development challenges and an uncertain world, said Paul Ilado, editorial director of Kenya's Radio Africa Group.
This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March by the Chinese Workers' and Peasants' Red Army.
In a recent interview with Xinhua, Ilado described the Long March as a decisive political and historical turning point. The Red Army was under severe pressure when the march began in 1934, and its survival was crucial to the continuation of the Communist movement, he said.
Yet what struck him most was not the historical outcome alone but the human qualities the march revealed, Ilado said.
"There is courage, because people continued despite extraordinary danger. There is sacrifice, because the journey demanded an enormous human cost. There is hope, because people endure hardship differently when they believe that the future can be better than the present," he said, adding that solidarity was also essential "because survival depended not only on individual strength but on people carrying one another through difficult circumstances."
Coming from Kenya, where stories of resistance, sacrifice and liberation also occupy an important place in national memory, Ilado said the Long March resonated with Kenya's own historical memory.
China's Long March and Kenya's anti-colonial struggle took place under different historical circumstances and should not be treated as identical, he stressed. What they share, he said, is the experience of people enduring enormous pressure because they believe a different future is possible. "That is a story people can understand across cultures."
For Ilado, the significance of the Long March spirit also lies in its continuity. Though the historic march ended, the value system and sense of purpose behind it have been carried forward in China's efforts to develop the country and improve people's lives, he said.
His understanding of the Long March spirit deepened during a visit to northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. Having grown up on a farm, Ilado said he was struck by how sustained poverty alleviation and development efforts helped transform once-impoverished areas.
In his view, the changes he witnessed offered a contemporary expression of the perseverance, collective purpose and commitment to a better future embodied in the Long March spirit.
The experience led him to view the Long March not simply as a historical event, but also as a much longer national journey "from survival to poverty alleviation to development."
Asked about Kenya's own challenges, Ilado said governance was the most pressing. He said China's development experience highlights the importance of visionary and disciplined leadership, continuity in national direction and priorities, and putting people at the center of development.
The Long March spirit also remains relevant to a world facing growing competition and shared challenges. What remains important, Ilado said, is the belief that lasting progress requires collective effort rather than isolated action.
"If you want to succeed, walk with other people. Do not walk alone," he said. "After all, the world has become a small village."
He also noted that each generation faces different circumstances, but the values that sustained the Long March can continue to inform how societies pursue long-term development.
For today's generation, the task is "to maintain continuity and to ensure that the technology that drives us today, which wasn't there in the days of the Long March, is used positively to affect the lives of many people," he said. ■

China steps up crackdown on food safety crimes

22:51:35 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- China is intensifying its crackdown on food safety crimes and tightening oversight of online food sales and other emerging business models, according to a new guideline.
The guideline, issued by the Commission for Political and Legal Affairs of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, calls for tougher penalties for serious offenses and closer coordination between food safety regulators and criminal justice authorities.
A commission representative said on Monday that China's food safety situation remained generally stable, but authorities faced new challenges as food safety crimes became more sophisticated, increasingly exploited online platforms and spanned multiple stages of the supply chain.
The guideline identifies meat products, school meals, health foods, vegetables and fruit as top enforcement priorities. It also calls for tighter scrutiny of food production, online sales, catering services and imports.
To improve coordination between administrative enforcement and criminal proceedings, the guideline calls for clearer procedures for referring suspected criminal cases and better information sharing between agencies.
China also plans to expedite revisions to the food safety law to clarify the regulatory responsibilities of businesses involved in fresh food e-commerce, food delivery and livestream sales.
China's State Administration for Market Regulation on Saturday announced it was soliciting public comments on a draft revision to the country's Food Safety Law, which was enacted in 2009 and comprehensively revised in 2015.
The draft addresses several issues of public concern, including school catering and food products sold online. It requires food producers and distributors to install monitoring equipment at critical stages in their operations and connect live video feeds to the information systems of market regulation authorities.
The guideline also states that authorities should update lists of banned additives as investigations identify new illegal substances.
It further urges authorities to address food safety risks uncovered in individual cases and strengthen oversight across the supply chain.
According to China's National Health Commission, as of May this year, the commission has issued 1,750 food safety standards covering more than 340 food categories across the supply chain, from raw materials and production to transport and storage. ■

Jajarm offers budget-friendly rural escape, but rail links need improvement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:50:39 UTC
22:50:39 KST

Jajarm offers budget-friendly rural escape, but rail links need improvement
JAJARM, North Khorasan Province – With its quiet rural surroundings, historical railway station and proximity to protected natural areas, Jajarm has the potential to attract travelers seeking an affordable alternative to Iran’s busier tourist destinations. But poor railway facilities, limited train tickets and a shortage of visitor services remain major obstacles to turning that potential into a thriving tourism destination.
Situated about 165 kilometers from Bojnurd, the capital of North Khorasan province in northeastern Iran, Jajarm offers opportunities to experience rural life and a slower pace of travel without the costs often associated with more developed tourist centers.
One of the area's distinctive landmarks is Jajarm railway station, a historical building that has served as the province's only active passenger rail connection to Iran's national railway network. The station, whose origins date to 1930 according to its glazed brick tiles, was inscribed on Iran's national industrial heritage list in 2019.
Built during the early Pahlavi period, the approximately 33-by-15.9-meter structure features a stone facade and turquoise tilework. It once formed part of a larger railway workers' complex, of which only the station's administrative building and a water reservoir remain.
Beyond its architectural significance, the station could play a greater role in connecting visitors with the region's rural communities and natural attractions.
The nearby Railway Station Village, which takes its name from the railway facility, has experienced decades of population decline. Its population has fallen from around 800 people two to three decades ago to about 230 residents in 70 households, according to local figures. Many former railway workers and their families moved to cities such as Jajarm, Shahrud and Semnan after retirement, while some residents continue to travel between the village and larger urban centers.
Local efforts to develop tourism have recently offered a measure of hope for the settlement.
In August 2025, the Fanoos Kavir Abrisham ecotourism lodge opened after receiving its operating permit. It was described as the second licensed ecotourism accommodation in Jajarm county and has created direct employment opportunities for some villagers. Local initiatives to train residents and encourage small-scale tourism businesses have also helped stimulate interest in returning to the village.
Owners of Fanoos Kavir Abrisham ecotourism lodge, a middle-aged couple, welcome guests. (Photo: Saeed Fotouhi)
The lodge is intended to accommodate visitors arriving by train and those exploring the surrounding region. The village's location near Touran National Park and the Miandasht Protected Area, known as a habitat of the endangered Asiatic cheetah, also provides opportunities for nature-based tourism.
For travelers on a limited budget, such accommodation and locally run tourism services could provide a way to explore a less-visited part of northeastern Iran while supporting rural livelihoods. However, the availability of affordable accommodation alone is not enough to make the area an accessible destination.
Railway station struggles to meet basic needs
Despite its historical importance and tourism potential, Jajarm railway station faces serious infrastructure and service problems.
Field reports describe a badly deteriorated passenger platform, with sections of its concrete surface crumbling into sand and soil. The station building and equipment also require maintenance, while inadequate nighttime lighting and a lack of basic amenities, including a restaurant and shop, make waiting for trains inconvenient.
Ticket availability presents another major challenge. Passenger quotas are limited, and travelers may need to book one or two months in advance. Trains that pass through the station make only brief stops, restricting opportunities for visitors to plan trips around rail services.
Speaking to the Tehran Times, Ebrahim Akhavan, head of the Jajarm City Council, said the station lacked adequate passenger facilities and suitable waiting areas despite being the province's only active passenger rail connection to the national network.
A view of Jajarm railway station
Local officials and tourism advocates have also raised concerns about security around the station, including insufficient lighting and the lack of an adequately staffed police post.
The railway network's limited reach compounds the problem. Although other stations exist along the rail line, including those serving the areas of Esfarayen and Sankhvast, they do not provide comparable passenger access and services. Residents across North Khorasan therefore often have to travel by bus to Jajarm before boarding a train.
Local representatives are calling for repairs to the platform and station building, more available tickets, additional train stops and better lighting and security. They have also proposed facilities for food and refreshments, stalls selling local handicrafts and souvenirs, and a local rail service connecting Jajarm with Tehran and Mashhad.
Ancient cistern reflects traditional water management
Jajarm’s ancient underground cistern, locally known as an ab-anbar, offers a glimpse into the town’s traditional water management system, according to Akhavan, who spoke to the Tehran Times.
He said spring water was distributed through canals and channels to the cistern, public bathhouses, gardens and agricultural fields, connecting water storage with everyday urban life and farming.
Jajarm’s ancient underground cistern
The cistern features a large underground reservoir with walls built using sarooj, a traditional water-resistant mortar. According to Akhavan, the use of sarooj and lime helped reinforce the walls against water pressure and protect the stored water. The structure stands as an example of Jajarm’s architectural heritage and its historical approach to water storage and supply.
From transit point to tourism gateway
Improving the station could benefit both residents and prospective visitors. Better rail access would make it easier to plan short rural breaks, while additional stops and reliable ticket availability could help tour operators develop rail-based itineraries linking Jajarm's historic sites, villages and nearby natural areas.
Small improvements could also create opportunities for local businesses, from ecotourism accommodation and food services to handicraft sales and guided excursions.
Yet Jajarm's tourism prospects depend on more than railway repairs. Turning the area into a recognized destination will require coordinated planning, reliable transport, adequate visitor services and sustained cooperation between public authorities, local communities and private businesses.
For now, Jajarm remains an option for travelers willing to venture beyond established tourist routes, particularly those interested in rural experiences and a quieter atmosphere. Its historic station and surrounding natural assets provide a foundation for tourism development, but limited transport capacity and deteriorating infrastructure continue to stand between that promise and a more accessible destination.
With better rail services and modest investment in local facilities, Jajarm could become a practical, budget-conscious gateway to North Khorasan. Without them, the province risks missing an opportunity to turn its railway connection and rural character into lasting economic benefits for its communities.

Republicans Denounce Trump’s Diesel Deal With Russia’s Putin Amid Mounting Backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:49:38 UTC
22:49:38 KST

President Donald Trump on Monday defended his plan to import diesel from Russia amid mounting calls from within his own party to reverse course on the controversial deal. "I made the right choice for the American People—always America first," Trusmp said of the move.
Lawmakers across party aisles, however, argue that the deal goes against a 2022 law which banned Russian oil imports and is not in the best interests of the American public.
“Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine. Congress was clear: The U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO allies,” read a joint bipartisan statement released Sunday by four Republican Senators and three Democrats.
The lawmakers argued that Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. “runs directly counter to that law” and criticized the lack of congressional overview, insisting that the Administration had failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation over its decision. “The United States should not provide [Russian President Vladimir] Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they urged.
The statement was co-signed by GOP Senators Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Susan Collins of Maine, Thom Tillis of North Carolina, and John Curtis of Utah, alongside Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Ron Wyden of Oregon, and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut.
Trump said Friday he had reached an agreement with Putin for Moscow to "immediately" supply 300,000 tons of diesel to American and global markets. The move comes amid a renewed push by the Administration to lower energy prices for Americans, which have skyrocketed since the Iran war began in February. The increased diesel fuel prices have shaken the loyalties of some of Trump’s most ardent support groups, with farmers telling TIME their day-to-day operations are being severely impacted.
In the wake of the diesel supply deal, Trump on Sunday claimed Russia and Ukraine had “agreed” to an energy cease-fire “effective immediately.” However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday said Russian strikes overnight and into the morning had included attacks on energy facilities, with 33 people wounded across the country.
“So there were Russian violations of the energy cease-fire announced by President Trump,” said Zelensky. “For now, this is Putin’s answer to Trump—Russian attacks. But we are waiting. We are waiting for the details of the conversation between the Americans and the Russians. We are waiting to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take.” Trump over the weekend responded to Zelensky's initial criticism of the diesel deal by telling reporters "it's time for Ukraine to get a new President."
U.S. lawmakers pushing back against Trump’s Russia diesel plan had sternly warned against putting trust in Putin.
Sen. Tillis, during an appearance on NBC’s Meet the Press, expressed concern that the diesel deal could place American lives at risk. “These are bad people hanging out with bad people, putting American lives at risk—particularly our Special Operators and forward-deployed personnel,” Tillis said, insisting that Putin “cannot be trusted.”
He also doubled down on his argument that the President’s deal may violate the law passed by Congress four years ago, as it outright banned Russian oil imports unless specific criteria were met, including a full Russian withdrawal from Ukraine.
“I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the President’s not following the law,” Tillis said. “We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of [the] territory they occupied.”
Just three weeks ago, Trump signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill, intended to target the country's financial institutions and the energy industry, which has largely financed the assault on Ukraine. The bill was named after Sen. Lindsey O. Graham, the late Republican Senator who spent the final year of his life building support for the measure.
Some Republican lawmakers mentioned this legislation as they criticized the diesel plan. “The President should be using those authorities instead of allowing Russia to export diesel, rake in revenues, and continue its catastrophic war in Ukraine,” said Murkowski.
“I oppose President Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on the purchase of diesel from Russia,” said Collins. “I was a co-sponsor of the Russian sanctions law, which the President recently signed, but is now not following.”
TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania announced Saturday he plans to introduce a bipartisan bill intended to stop Trump from lifting sanctions on Russian oil.
“We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil. It will be called the ‘Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act,’” said Fitzpatrick.
Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, a Republican who has clashed with Trump on other high-profile issues, said he has already agreed to be a co-sponsor of the bill, insisting that “Congress must make a stand.”
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has defended the move, insisting the agreement with Russia will work through existing legal channels the U.S. has to help bring prices down.
“We’re doing it with all the legal authorities we have, so anyone in Congress who says that—whether it’s an old bill or the current Lindsey Graham bill—prohibits us from doing it, is wrong,” he told Fox News.
Republican Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming has also defended the diesel deal, telling CBS' Face the Nation that the President “has to make tough decisions.”
European leaders warn Trump's diesel deal could bolster Russia's war
Kaja Kallas, the E.U.'s foreign policy chief, announced Monday that during a Foreign Affairs Council Meeting in Luxembourg, European Foreign Ministers had adopted nearly 1,600 new sanctions targeting Russia's military-industrial complex, underscoring the contrast between Washington's decision and Europe's continued push to economically isolate Moscow.
Ahead of the sit-down, Lithuania's Kęstutis Budrys led the criticism of Trump's deal with Putin, saying it "doesn't help neither the price of oil products nor the unity of the transatlantic community" and insisting “it is not the European way.” Latvia's Baiba Braže said the bloc’s position has “not changed” and that there “is no other way, just pressure on Russia, [and] support to Ukraine.”
Ireland's Helen McEntee called Trump’s deal “concerning” and agreed that European countries need to "redouble [their] efforts" in keeping the pressure on Russia.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson led the initial response from Europe last week, expressing his “regret” over Trump's deal with Putin and warning that “energy revenues are central to the Russian war chest.” Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal similarly said the agreement was a “big miscalculation,” arguing that it “is opposite to the long-term activities of the western world to limit the flow of energy carriers to Putin.” Both Sweden and Estonia were among the top 10 countries providing aid to Ukraine as a share of their GDP between January 2022 and February 2026.
The U.K. has also opposed Trump's agreement. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said Sunday that Britain did not support the deal with Putin and would instead look to "strengthen sanctions” against Russia. Prime Minister Andy Burnham acknowledged that “the last 24 hours had been difficult for Ukraine and reiterated his complete solidarity” during a phone call with Zelensky.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also spoke with Zelensky on Sunday and expressed his view that the “agreement is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe.”

Stolen Renoir paintings found hidden behind cinder block wall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:43:20 UTC
22:43:20 KST

Stolen Renoir paintings found hidden, and damaged, behind cinder block wall: "Completely undetectable"
Two paintings by impressionist master Pierre-Auguste Renoir, stolen from a museum in southern France and later discovered hidden behind a wall, have sustained slight damage, prosecutors said on Monday.
In September, thieves broke into the museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer and escaped with two works by Renoir, abandoning two others as they fled.
The value of all four paintings had been estimated at $10 million.
On Friday, authorities announced that the two outstanding stolen works had been found.
They were a portrait titled "Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano" and a depiction of a woman at a well called "Young Woman at the Well."
Speaking to reporters in Paris, Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said the paintings were recovered last Thursday during a search of a home in the southern town of Clermont-l'Herault.
The discovery of the stolen works followed the arrest of six people, including a woman, last Wednesday, said Bessone.
"The paintings were hidden behind a solid cinder block wall. They were completely undetectable," Bessone said. "It was through interrogation work that investigators were able to get the receiver of the stolen goods to admit that he had indeed taken possession of the paintings."
A 29-year-old man seen as the main suspect was charged over the weekend after DNA evidence linked him to the theft.
The two paintings were "in relatively good condition," although "the two works showed signs of damage," Bessone said, speaking alongside the head of France's national judicial police, Christian Sainte.
The frame of "Young Woman at the Well" was slightly damaged, while "the canvas of 'Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano' had a tear," Bessone said.
 The tear was located "on the dress" in the portrait, the prosecutor said, adding that both paintings "will require restoration work."
String of recent heists
Culture Minister Catherine Pegard praised "the efficiency and determination of all those who made this outcome possible."
"Their commitment made it possible to recover these works in record time," the culture ministry said.
A spate of heists at French museums — including at the Louvre — has highlighted inadequate security in some cases and led to questions about whether criminal gangs see them as soft targets.
Crown jewels valued at around $100 million were stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris last year.
The suspected thieves have been arrested and charged, but none of the jewels have been recovered except for a crown that was dropped as the group escaped.
Other French museums have been targeted in recent months. In July, burglars stole millions of dollars worth of jewelry from the museum of French luxury glassmaker Lalique.
In October 2025, a woman was arrested and charged over the theft of gold from the Natural History Museum in Paris.
The month before that, thieves snatched three porcelain works worth millions of dollars and classed as national treasures in a heist at the Adrien Dubouche National Museum in Limoges in central France.

Nepal floods strand over 100 foreign trekkers, five villagers missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:36:36 UTC
22:36:36 KST

More than 100 foreign trekkers have been stranded in Nepal’s mountainous Gorkha district after flash floods swept away bridges and damaged trekking routes over the weekend.
Five villagers, including two women, remain missing after a landslide between Lokpa and Chumling blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, triggering floods downstream, local news outlet Online Khabar reported on Monday, citing local authorities.
Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said four army helicopters were conducting rescue operations, with at least 47 people evacuated so far. A total of 437 security personnel had been mobilised.
The floods destroyed several bridges and damaged houses, two telephone towers and 50 electricity poles, the authority said.
No electricity
Md Shahadat Hossain, a Bangladeshi trekker stranded in Jagat village, said that nine Bangladeshis were awaiting possible helicopter evacuation.
“We have been stranded in Jagat since yesterday. A flash flood came down from above the village and flowed through its lower part,” he said.
He said more than 200 trekkers, including Nepalis, were sheltering safely in the village, but supplies were dwindling.
“We are safe, but there has been no electricity since yesterday, communication with the outside world has been disrupted, and food supplies are gradually running short,” he added.
The Manaslu Circuit, near Nepal’s border with China, is a popular Himalayan trekking route, with October among its busiest months.

An unexploded ordnance blast near Israel's northern border with Lebanon killed at least one hiker and injured 19 others Monday, Israeli media reported.
