Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning’s Regular Press Conference on October 12, 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
21:31:27 CST
22:31:27 KST

Member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and Minister of Foreign Affairs Wang Yi will attend the Seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA) held in Baku, Azerbaijan on October 15 as Special Representative of President Xi Jinping, and visit Azerbaijan, Croatia, Montenegro and Bulgaria from October 14 to 20.
Beijing Daily: Today, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs put on its website the decision to take countermeasures against Paraguay’s Minister of Information and Communication Technologies Gustavo Emigdio Villate Samaniego and Belize Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Francis Fonseca. Could you share more information on that?
Mao Ning: The Taiwan question is a major issue of principle bearing on China’s sovereignty and national reunification. It is at the core of China’s core interests. Certain politicians in Paraguay and Belize willingly serve as chess pieces for the DPP authorities in their pursuit of independence by soliciting external support. Their visits to Taiwan and reception of “Taiwan independence” separatist forces in their countries constitute severe interference in China’s internal affairs. They also attacked and smeared China by spreading the “Chinese cyber attack” disinformation, causing egregious impact in the world.
In response to these moves and in accordance with the Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law of the People’s Republic of China, China announced in the form of MFA decree countermeasures as an action of warning and deterrence.
China News Service: Foreign Minister Wang Yi will attend the Seventh CICA Summit as Special Representative of President Xi Jinping and visit Azerbaijan. What’s China’s expectation of the visit?
Mao Ning: CICA is an important mechanism for security dialogue and cooperation in Asia. Since its inception, CICA has been committed to enhancing interaction and confidence-building among countries and made important contribution to security, stability and development in the region.
With growing complexity and volatility in the international and regional landscapes, Asian countries are increasingly keen to ensure peace and tranquility and promote economic growth. At the upcoming summit, China will engage in extensive dialogue and consultation with various parties to practice multilateralism, actively implement the four global initiatives, and enhance Asian governance, so as to make new contribution to building an Asian community with a shared future.
China and Azerbaijan are comprehensive strategic partners. In recent years, under the strategic planning and guidance of President Xi Jinping and President Ilham Aliyev, China-Azerbaijan relations have maintained strong momentum of growth, with ever-deepening political mutual trust, steady progress in Belt and Road cooperation and fruitful collaboration on international affairs. This will be Foreign Minister Wang Yi’s first official visit to Azerbaijan in seven years. He will hold talks with Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov. We believe the visit will help fully implement the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state and deliver new outcomes for bilateral cooperation across various fields.
AFP: U.S. President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia on Sunday. The ceasefire was met with surprise from Kiev and silence from Moscow and appeared shaky as Russia appeared to strike multiple Ukrainian power plants on Sunday. Does the foreign ministry have a comment on this “energy ceasefire”?
Mao Ning: China’s position on the Ukraine crisis is consistent and clear. We believe that dialogue and negotiation is the only viable way out, and support all efforts conducive to peace.
Reuters: The U.S. State Department last week said China’s maritime activities off Taiwan’s east coast are “deeply destabilizing.” What is the foreign ministry’s comment on that?
Mao Ning: China has on multiple occasions made clear its position on this. China has exclusive economic zone and continental shelf in waters east of the Taiwan island. It is fully within China’s sovereign rights and jurisdiction, therefore legitimate, lawful and beyond reproach, for China to carry out activities in these waters. The party that instigates troubles and disrupts stability in this part of waters has never been the Chinese side.
The Taiwan question is China’s internal affair that brooks no external interference. The U.S. needs to abide by the one-China principle and the three China-U.S. joint communiqués, handle the Taiwan question prudently, and take concrete actions to uphold the overall China-U.S. relations and peace and stability in the region.
Xinhua News Agency: On October 10, leader of the Taiwan region Lai Ching-te made a speech in which he again solicited external support for “Taiwan independence,” and smeared Chinese mainland. What’s your comment?
Mao Ning: There is but one China in the world. Taiwan is an inalienable part of China’s territory, and the Government of the People’s Republic of China is the sole legal government representing the whole of China. To uphold the one-China principle, reject “Taiwan independence” separatist activities and support China’s reunification is where international public opinion trends.
Lai Ching-te’s so-called “democracy” cannot hide his “Taiwan independence” separatist nature. Taiwan’s return to China is an integral part of the outcome of WWII victory and the postwar international order. The real status quo across the Taiwan Strait is that both sides of the Strait belong to one and the same China. Whatever Lai Ching-te says or does, it does not change the fact backed by history and law that Taiwan belongs to China or the doomed failure of “Taiwan independence,” and will by no means stop China’s ultimate reunification.
CGTN: Could you elaborate on the program and China’s expectation of Foreign Minister Wang Yi’s visit to Croatia, Montenegro and Bulgaria?
Mao Ning: Croatia, Montenegro and Bulgaria are China’s important cooperation partners in Southeastern Europe. In recent years, China has maintained close exchanges with the three countries. Notable results have been achieved in cooperation on economy and trade, investment, tourism and infrastructure. There is extensive common ground on safeguarding multilateralism, tackling global challenges, growing China-Europe relations and other topics. During the visit, Foreign Minister Wang Yi will hold talks with the foreign ministers of the three countries and have in-depth exchange of views with their leaders.
Croatia is China’s important partner in the EU. The Chinese-built Pelješac Bridge is a landmark project of China-Croatia and China-EU cooperation. The two countries have enjoyed a more mature and stable partnership of comprehensive cooperation. Through the visit, China looks to better synergize development strategies and expand practical cooperation with Croatia, so as to promote the steady and sustained growth of bilateral ties.
This year marks the 20th anniversary of China’s diplomatic relations with Montenegro. Throughout those two decades, the two sides have always treated each other with respect and as equals. Together, the two countries have built a series of landmark projects, such as the South-North Expressway in Montenegro. China hopes that through the Chinese foreign minister’s first visit, the two sides will expand the breadth and depth of mutually beneficial cooperation, carry forward the traditional friendship, and inject new impetus into bilateral relations for the next 20 years.
Bulgaria is the second country in the entire world to establish diplomatic relations with New China. Police swooped on Renoir theft suspects fearing second museum heist, prosecutor says
NANTERRE, France, Oct 12 - French police accelerated the arrest of suspects in a theft of two Renoir paintings after one of the alleged thieves visited another museum, raising fears of an imminent second theft, Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said on Monday.
Police arrested six suspects earlier this month and four men have since been charged. The two men suspected of carrying out the theft were charged with organised theft and other offences.
A third man, accused of hiding the paintings, was charged with organised handling of stolen goods. A fourth suspect, who investigators say was approached about buying the artworks, was charged with handling stolen goods and taking part in a criminal conspiracy.
PAINTINGS WORTH MORE THAN €4 MILLION
The stolen works, "Madame Colonna Romano" and "Young Woman at the Well" by Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, were valued at about €4.2 million ($4.7 million), Bessone said.
The theft took place on September 8 at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, on the French Riviera. According to investigators, the thieves entered the museum grounds through a hole cut in a garden fence and got inside through a window.
The paintings were later found hidden behind a false wall in a house.
Both works were damaged and will need restoration. One of the paintings, "Madame Colonna Romano", had been torn.
The recovery came almost exactly one month after the theft, following an investigation that used DNA evidence, mobile phone geolocation data and surveillance footage.
Bessone said the suspects had denied planning a second museum raid, but he added that he did "not believe the principal suspect visited that museum simply out of a love of art".
The thieves also attempted to steal two other Renoir paintings, "Madame Pichon" and "Coco Reading", which depicts Renoir's young son Claude. They abandoned those works in the museum gardens while fleeing police who had arrived at the scene. ($1 = 0.8945 euros) REUTERS

‘The Sixty-Year Mission’ Brings the Legacy of ‘Star Trek’ to a New Generation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

William Shatner wasn’t sure if the audience would approve of his new documentary or not.
When the 95-year-old star took the stage at the Regal Times Square theater for the New York premiere of The Sixty-Year Mission: How Star Trek Changed Television and the World he said “maybe you’ll like it, maybe you won’t.” But, the Captain Kirk actor declared, “you’re going to see a lovely film made by people who cared.”
Focusing on the original Star Trek series, which ran from 1966 to 1969, The Sixty-Year Mission is written and directed by Mark A. Altman, creator of the Inglorious Treksperts podcast. The documentary, which screened during New York Comic Con and hit select theaters this weekend, explores the show’s cultural impact and legacy, and also demonstrates how much it was a product of the political climate of the era in which it was made.
“I think audiences are pleasantly surprised that Sixty-Year Mission shows how the ‘60s shaped Star Trek,” Altman explains. For the film, Altman interviewed dozens of prominent fans and stars, from Shatner and Simon Pegg to Star Trek: The Next Generation stars Jonathan Frakes and Brent Spiner. The president’s niece—and Trek fan—Mary L. Trump praises the show’s pioneering representation, specifically Nichelle Nichols’ Lieutenant Uhura. George Takei, who played Sulu, gives a harrowing account of his time in an internment camp for Japanese Americans during World War II. Others discuss how characters like Spock became heroes for queer fans.
As has been well-documented, these considerations were important for Gene Roddenberry, the show’s creator, who died in 1991. He was a WWII veteran with a progressive bent despite years spent in traditionally conservative spaces like the US Army and the Los Angeles Police Department. Altman insists that “Captain Kirk was ‘JFK: Space Captain,’” and that President Kennedy’s idea of a New Frontier was the final frontier that Trek sought to explore.
Shatner, however, didn’t initially see the show that way at all. “I didn't think in those terms when they offered me the role,” says Shatner, who served as executive producer on Sixty-Year Mission. “I thought, ‘I got a regular paid job.’ Only later did the magic of Star Trek happen.”
Part of that magic, Shatner adds, is how “Star Trek had an effect on people’s lives.” Those people come from many backgrounds, and the show remained accessible because of the very special tension that existed within its politics, Altman explains. “Roddenberry was liberal on social issues but hard-nosed on defense, and that is absolutely what Star Trek is,” he says. “We need our phasers to defeat the Klingons, but we believe in a diverse crew.”
Karim Diané, who plays Jay-Den Kraag on Star Trek: Starfleet Academy, notes that as the person playing the first openly gay Klingon character in the franchise, he’s playing someone who means a lot to viewers. “I wish I could release the DMs because the love I've gotten is overwhelming,” Diané says.
Trek even had a point of view on AI that feels incredibly relevant in 2026 as Trump and Silicon Valley leaders talk about a new era of “superintelligence.” The franchise’s most recognizable AI—the android Data from Next Generation—was an ideal version of the technology. In that series Data consistently struggled to be understood, as both smarter than humans and incapable of emotional intelligence. One episode, “The Measure of a Man,” even addressed whether Data was his own being or merely property.
For Spiner, who played Data, AI’s modern incarnation is far from the thoughtful machine he portrayed. “If only AI could be what Data was: responsible, truly concerned about humanity, considering what serves humans best as opposed to what serves profit best,” he says.

The Mystery of Kyrgyzstan’s Newly Launched Satellite(s)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:29:00 UTC
22:29:00 KST

On October 1, Kyrgyzstan reportedly joined Central Asia’s other spacefaring nations, successfully launching a domestically designed and produced nanosatellite aboard a SpaceX rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California
According to Kyrgyzstan’s government, the unnamed, loaf-of-bread-sized spacecraft weighs 5 kilograms, cost around $130,0000, was equipped with high-resolution cameras, and was — nearly exclusively — the product of domestic innovation.
The satellite was assembled by two local companies, Kyrgyz Asman and Kyrgyz Electronics, Bishkek stated. The latter company’s director Ilya Cherny did admit that the technology behind the satellite was largely Russian, but pointed out that the team behind its production consisted of 10 homegrown engineers.
The government also said the satellite would help advance Kyrgyzstan’s top agricultural, environmental, and strategic priorities over its purported 15-year lifespan.
In a statement published on September 24, the country’s Ministry of Water Resources, Agriculture and Processing Industry stated the satellite’s data would track crop conditions, detect early signs of drought, and monitor glaciers.
Speaking from California on launch day, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov said that the country had previously had to pay to obtain this kind of data from other countries, no matter whether it was “information on 100 hectares, 1,000 hectares, or the weather.”
Japarov suggested that the satellite would allow “every square meter” of Kyrgyzstan’s land to be studied to determine its potential arability, while touting the launch as an achievement in national self-sufficiency.
“We did not have our own satellite before… now we will no longer be dependent on [other countries],” Japarov added. “We will control it ourselves 100 percent from Bishkek.”
Cosmically Large Scandal
At first glance, the story of Kyrgyzstan’s satellite launch seemed like a genuine achievement. The country had joined Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, and – as of this August – Uzbekistan in the ranks of Central Asia’s spacefarers, largely thanks to its own ingenuity.
The success had been extensively covered in domestic, regional, and international media. And then came a confusing development.
On October 2, the day after launch, news reports began to include a previously unmentioned detail: the satellite was a joint effort between Kyrgyzstan and the United Arab Emirates.
Three days later, a Kyrgyz news site published a notice that Kyrgyzstan had established a new space monitoring center to receive, process, and utilize data transmitted from the newly launched Altair satellite.
This was striking for two reasons. First, the name “Altair” had been missing from earlier government press releases. Second – and more importantly – it said the monitoring center would be “provided” data coming from the “UAE-operated” satellite by a body called the Abu Dhabi Maritime Academy.
Suddenly, Japarov’s claims that Kyrgyzstan would be “no longer dependent” on other countries began to ring hollow.
Not only had Russian technology supposedly been used to design the satellite, but the UAE was apparently going to operate the craft, with Kyrgyzstan merely receiving “access” to its data.
It also didn’t help that Gulf-focused news sites were calling Altair the “first satellite developed and built by UAE engineers,” without even mentioning Bishkek’s involvement in the project.
What, then, had happened on October 1? Had Kyrgyzstan really launched a satellite of its own making? If so, in what ways were other countries involved? And if the craft launched from California was primarily an Emirati initiative, would Bishkek walk back its claims of national self-sufficiency?
A Second Satellite?
So far, none of the above questions have been definitively answered. And the matter, described by one prominent regional commentator as a “scandal of cosmic proportions,” has prompted a growing number of increasingly conspiratorial explanations.
Local news outlet Kaktus Media, for example, suggested that two satellites were likely launched on October 1, one developed by the UAE and one with Russian assistance. (It also noted that Kyrgyzstan’s first satellite initiative, launched in 2019 by a team of all-female engineers, seemed not to be involved, having been wound down previously with no details about the project’s completion.)
Tandyr Media, meanwhile, an independent media outlet known for its popular YouTube channel, drew attention in its video covering the launch to a series of Threads posts by an individual named Dima Balakirev, who claimed to have been personally involved in the satellite project’s development.
In his post, Balakirev appeared to depict himself standing next to a different — much larger — satellite than had been shown in the government’s earlier press releases. Incidentally, the photo also clearly showed a line of text reading “Made in UAE” on one side of the satellite.
According to Balakirev, the spacecraft was a joint project with the UAE, entirely funded “by grants and the Abu Dhabi government,” and was an Earth Remote Sensing satellite – that is, likely the satellite that Japarov was referring to when he was talking about Kyrgyzstan’s newfound capacity to survey itself from above. (Subsequent reporting from government-affiliated sources mentioning the Altair satellite likewise suggested that its data would be used in agricultural planning, water resource management, and environmental monitoring.)
Notably, when questioned by Threads users citing the government’s original (smaller) size specifications, Balakirev insisted that national news outlets had confused two different projects:
“The first is a satellite for Kyrgyzstan, which was assembled in Abu Dhabi. This is a joint project with the UAE, and the Emirates are covering the entire cost. The second is a satellite being built by the team at Kyrgyz Electronics. This is a separate project with its own objectives. The figure of 5 kg and 10–12 million soms [$114,350 – $137,200] refers specifically to this one.”
Although Balakirev’s exact title and position are unknown, as Tandyr Media pointed out, the self-described “entrepreneur and techie” appeared to have been present in California alongside Japarov, and shared Instagram stories from the event.
Bishkek, Do We Have a Problem?
Given all that, as Tandyr host Dmitriy Lozhnikov himself concluded, what is left now is a substantially muddied picture.
According to one possible version of events, Kyrgyzstan did launch its smaller, unnamed bread-loaf-sized satellite, whose function is not entirely clear, on October 1. On the same day, meanwhile, the larger, UAE-designed Altair satellite also launched from California – data from which Bishkek has confirmed it is now paying to access.
In another plausible version, proposed by emigre political scientist Aidarbek Raev, the Kyrgyz-designed nanosatellite might not have been launched at all, which would mean that reports of Kyrgyzstan’s national technological achievements have been greatly exaggerated.
The government, meanwhile, has commented little on the affair since the satellite’s supposed launch day. But in any case, it appears the country’s leadership has further cosmic ambitions.
“If there is stability and peace in our country and Central Asia, in the next five to ten years, depending on our readiness, the day will come when we launch a [telecommunications] satellite as well,” Japarov said on October 1.

Peace in the Middle East? Kurdish PKK leader discusses regional ‘third world war’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:27:16 UTC
22:27:16 KST

The Middle East is at a crossroads. It is also in the midst of a “Third World War,” Kurdistan Workers’ Party’s (PKK) Murat Karayilan said in an interview published on October 12. “This war is in essence a global war. A Third World War; however, these make it into a regional war. War between Shias and Sunnis. War between Iran and the Arab Gulf States. This comes from a supremacist plan and mentality. A supremacist mentality, regarding how to design the region, how to control it, and how to govern it. It is such a plan,” he told Kamal Chomani from The Amargi news outlet. This is an important interview that puts a spotlight on Kurdish issues and the region. It comes at a unique time as the PKK is moving toward disarmament.
Kamal Chomani, a PhD student at the University of Leipzig in Germany, published an important and exclusive interview with Murat Karayilan, who co-founded the PKK and who is its key leader today.
Chomani notes in the introduction to his interview, posted on X, that “I spent 10 days in the PKK headquarters and caves before finally reaching Murat Karayilan, for this exclusive interview with The Amargi.” He noted, “We begin with the wars reshaping the Middle East and then break down the peace process, in which Mr. Karayilan clearly calls on the Turkish state to end policies of denial and annihilation, and on Kurds to abandon rebellion and work toward establishing a democratic state.” He also noted that the PKK leader has not spoken to an external media outlet for 12 years.
The interview comes at a crucial time in the region when many are at a crossroads, including the Kurds. The PKK, since its founding in 1978, has been one of the key Kurdish movements in the region. The other major Kurdish movement is primarily linked to parties and groups associated with the Kurdistan Democratic Party. The PKK’s main role has been in Turkey, where there was a long conflict with the Turkish government costing thousands of lives. The most recent round of that war restarted in 2015. The PKK also has had branches and influence in Syria, Iran, and Iraq among Kurds. In Syria, the main group was the People’s Defense Units (YPG), and in Iran it is the Kurdish Free Life Party (PJAK).
As the PKK and the Turkish government have appeared to move toward a peace deal that will see the PKK dissolved and disarmed in Turkey, and in other areas, there are a lot of questions about what comes next. The interview may provide a window into this and appears to show how the PKK wants to get its message out today. The party is often opaque and complex to analyze because of the devotion of its members, many of whom join when they are young.
PKK leader discusses regional changes and the movement's future strategy
In the hour-long interview, which is on YouTube and also translated to English from Kurdish by The Amargi, the PKK leader discusses the current changes in the region. Although this part of the interview is actually the shortest part, it is also the most interesting for our purposes. The PKK's internal ideology and choices, and how it views Turkey today or its concepts of democratic confederalism, may be important, but it is the pragmatic choices made by the PKK these days that matter the most.
Karayilan discusses the recent changes in the region. He is asked about how the wars caused by the Hamas October 7 attack have changed the region, and also how changes in Syria, Libya, Iraq, and other places are shaping the region. The interview took place after US forces left Iraq on September 30. It also took place more than eight months after the US left Syria and after the US-backed Syrian Democratic Forces agreed to a deal to integrate with the Syrian government. The Syrian Democratic Forces’ (SDF) largest armed component was the YPG, which is linked to the PKK.
PKK leader says global powers are competing for dominance in the Middle East
“The Third World War emerged over time. It differs from the First and Second World Wars in its methods. It’s not a single event; it emerged over time, spread, and continues to this day. It’s a global war among capitalist forces competing for hegemony. It’s between forces that seek global dominance. You’ve mentioned the Middle East, but there is also the Ukraine-Russia conflict, and Ukraine is supported by NATO states,” the PKK leader says. “The Third World War continues with various methods. The primary objective is to establish dominance in the Middle East. The global capitalist actors led by the US are afraid of China.”
The ideology and worldview that Karayilan mentions views the current conflict as a global war that is between “capitalist forces” fighting for dominance. This is not just between NATO backing Ukraine and the Russian invasion. This is also about the Middle East. He mentions AI and also new technology and the struggle for control of rare earth elements necessary for solar panels and chips. As such, he suggests that one goal of the US and the West is to weaken Russia and block China’s ambitions.
“They’re trying to build a line from Egypt to Kazakhstan to stop China’s advance. This is not openly stated, but it is the core objective. Energy sources are very important to capitalist forces. Then there are rare earth minerals used to produce chips and solar panels. Then there is uranium, as an important energy source,” he says. The conflict has spread, not just to Iran but also to the Gulf and Yemen.
The PKK leader stresses that today war is not a solution. War does not serve the interests of the people. He argues that his movement presents a third way of supporting democracy. He stresses this in discussing Turkey today and the region. He also stresses how US allies, such as Greece, Turkey, and Israel, do not all agree on strategy, or may even be against each other. Greece and Israel today are closely aligned.
“Tensions exist between the US and NATO partners – they are not all united. So, Iran, on one side, wants to represent the Shia line, but then you’ve got Turkey and Israel as two other sides. There are also conflicts between them. It is true that two days ago the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that they do not allow contradictions between their allies to escalate into war. He was referring to the conflict between Greece and Turkey.”
PKK disarmament raises questions over Turkey's political future
The challenge for the PKK today is that while it has this regional outlook, it continues to stress the need for greater democracy in Turkey. It wants its leader Abdullah Ocalan, who has been in prison for decades, released. The PKK calls Ocalan “Apo,” and Karayilan speaks about how he must administer disarmament. This creates challenges ahead. So far, Ankara has appeared flexible; however, there are questions about what happens next. Will the ruling party use the deal with the PKK to divide the opposition or get votes from Kurds? The Justice and Development Party (AKP) has received Kurdish votes in the past, and it is important for them if they want to stay in power after around two decades of rule.
The interview also delved into the details of the current issues in northern Iraq where the PKK has bases. Turkey has sent forces into the Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq because of this. “We pulled our forces out. They were hidden, but we got them out, some using vehicles, some on the roads. So we pulled out our forces. This year they say ‘Metina too.’ They are next door to each other – Zap and Metina. So they tell us you must pull out from Metina too. We say, ‘Why? Why just us taking steps?,’” Karayilan says. “Finally, after a lot of dialogue and internal discussions, we took the decision to also pull out of Metina. Two days ago. Today is October 10. So on the 8th, our final forces pulled out of the tunnels of Metina. Since then, we have had no one in Metina.” What this shows is how the PKK is not just focused on large ideas about its version of democracy and what it sees as a struggle for world order in the region, but also on its bases and operations that continue to be sticking points in peace with Ankara. Chomani’s interview represents a rare glimpse into the PKK’s current views and helps shed light on what may come next in the region.

Iran spread anti-Israel, US disinformation to global media through fake journalists, OpenAI says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:26:38 UTC
22:26:38 KST

Iran used artificial intelligence to generate social media comments, create at least seven fake journalist personas, and pitch long-form articles to global media outlets as part of a covert influence operation, OpenAI confirmed in an announcement released on Thursday.
OpenAI said it had disrupted two influence operations, one originating in Russia and the other in Iran, that abused its technology to create “false front entities” to promote their narratives about the Russia-Ukraine and US/Israel-Iran wars. The company said both campaigns used “questionable or outright deceitful methodologies to exaggerate the operators’ effectiveness.”
Although influence operations predate the advancement of AI, OpenAI acknowledged that the technology has made them easier to conduct. It noted that Iran's fake journalists closely resembled “Alice Donovan,” a fictitious journalist created as part of a Russian influence campaign in 2017.
OpenAI rated the Iranian campaign a four on its six-point Influence Operation scale, with one representing the lowest level and six the highest. The rating reflected the campaign's success in placing content in mainstream media outlets. Referring to the 30 covert operations it had uncovered over the previous two and a half years, the company said such campaigns aim to get social media posts and other content published by legitimate media outlets to expand their reach and impact.
AI used to disseminate false information through fake authors
Beyond helping operators place content before wider audiences, OpenAI said AI enabled malicious actors to conduct operations with greater scale, efficiency, linguistic fluency, and editorial ability.
According to OpenAI, a cluster of ChatGPT accounts originating in Iran was used to generate content in both Persian and English. The actors reportedly accessed ChatGPT through a VPN and used the model to improve long-form articles and editorial pitches published under fabricated bylines.
The fake bylines belonged to Ervin B. Hoskins, Noah Lamington, Sophia Gonzalez, Michael Harrison, Ericka Feusier, Jenny Williams, and Alice Johnson. All were presented as Western journalists focusing on international politics, the Middle East, human rights, or conflict.
The Jerusalem Post located an article by “Noah Lamington” published in International Policy Digest that sought to portray political insecurity in Israel. The article was headlined “The Knesset Revolt Netanyahu Couldn’t Prevent.”
An article by “Sophia Gonzalez” was also found in the News Register under the headline “Sophia Gonzalez: When diplomacy becomes another weapon of war.” Meanwhile, “Ericka Feusier” appeared to have published extensively on insecurity in Iraq and American unemployment on websites including Eurasia Review, Common Dreams, and the IA Forum.
The articles focused primarily on the US-Iran war, while a smaller proportion of the generated comments addressed US domestic politics. OpenAI identified nearly 100 articles produced by the operation that appeared in syndicated publications and small and medium-sized media outlets around the world.
The earliest article identified by OpenAI was published in July 2025, while the latest appeared in October 2026. The volume of content increased following the outbreak of the US-Iran conflict.
Online outlets shared the AI articles to millions of social media followers
One online outlet that published articles from the influence campaign had nearly two million Facebook followers, approximately 355,000 followers on X/Twitter, and more than 544,000 on Instagram as of August 2026.
Several of the fictitious journalists also maintained social media accounts on X, Facebook, Instagram, or Threads. However, further investigation found that the accounts were operated from within Iran or elsewhere in West Asia.
Despite the campaign's success in placing articles in media outlets, OpenAI noted that none of the generated social media comments attracted substantial engagement.
In July, for example, the campaign produced several X posts claiming that the US was preparing a “large-scale assault” on Iran, followed by a burst of comments posted within a 10-to-13-minute window. Some comments included screenshots of articles generated as part of the campaign, promoting them in an apparent attempt to make the content appear popular.
Based on the operation's overall activity, OpenAI suggested that those behind it were likely commercial actors running a for-hire influence campaign.

Israel, Kurdistan, and the hopes for a strong political alliance - opinion
Unknown

As the Kurdish journalist and researcher Suzan Quitaz put it recently: “Standing with Jewish people in the face of antisemitism is the opposite of being racist.
“It is about standing up against hatred, discrimination, and violence toward people because of their religion or ethnicity. It is standing up against one of the oldest and strongest forms of racism: antisemitism.”
In a twisted way, the closer Kurds and Jews get, and the more visible that becomes, the more people start seeing Kurds as another kind of Jew. Not in a way that changes those people’s attitude toward Kurds, because we were alone in our struggle anyway, but in how they frame the Kurdish political struggle.
Those same people, on the global Left and on the libertarian American Right alike, were always antisemitic, and always on the side of Ankara and Tehran in the name of anti-Americanism (which they veil with the term anti-imperialism).
They stand with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s Ankara and the mullahs’ Tehran; they sided with Saddam’s Baghdad and Assad’s Damascus, and never with the Kurds.
Now they cannot openly side with Ankara or Tehran, but they can present themselves as against American interventionism, against the Gaza genocide.
With Kurds, they have a difficulty: they cannot frame Kurds as imperialist interventionists or Gaza genociders.
In an interview, the American right-wing commentator Tucker Carlson called the Kurds “the most brutal people” he had ever met.
This is the opposite of the truth of Kurdish armed struggles: with exceptions, which the Kurdish movements themselves apologized for and corrected, Kurdish armed struggle has never become uncontrolled violence.
The Kurdish struggle has always taken its legitimacy from its demands for recognition, equality, and self-rule.
On the other side, Saddam Hussein’s Anfal campaign of 1988 murdered (or disappeared) between 50,000 and 182,000 Kurdish civilians.
In September 1979, two weeks after Khomeini declared holy war on the Kurds, Revolutionary Guards entered the unarmed village of Qarna and slaughtered dozens of civilians, children and the elderly among them.
In March 2004, when Kurdish spectators were attacked at a football match in Qamishli, former Syrian president Bashar al-Assad’s security forces opened fire on the Kurdish crowd, and some 30 people were killed in the days that followed.
And Turkey, having successfully labeled Kurdish fighters terrorists, respected none of the rights that any human law would otherwise have protected.
There is a historical connection between treating Kurds this way and antisemitism in its various forms. Charles Dickens hardly needed to name the villain of Oliver Twist; “the Jew” was good enough to describe him.
Hitler and his allies all over Europe needed nothing other than anti-Jewish rhetoric to mass-murder Jews.
Together, we can be a strong alliance
The same can be seen in how people handle suffering in the Middle East. The same people who defend the right of Palestinians to go to their homes never mention the hundreds of thousands of Jews who had to leave Yemen, Iraq, or Syria.
They never mention the depopulation of Kurds in Turkey, Syria, or Iraq in the same way. Antisemitism is not seeing what Jews suffer, and the same formula applies to Kurds today.
This gives the Kurds, my people, the chance to review how they see the world. People do not take sides because of their “beliefs”. Not even the most educated, those we sometimes admire. The litmus paper is our own struggle.
How can they side with Ankara, Moscow, or Tehran, but not with us?
If Israel is so bad, if US interventionism is so bad, how come we benefit from their actions in our region?
The no-fly zone of 1991. The air support at Kobani in 2014. Israel’s public backing of the 2017 independence referendum, when no other state would give it.
Not that American support has ever been more than tactical, but we have lived the fact that these interventions saved our lives and our habitat.
Israel’s rising rhetoric may also be what the moment requires of Israel, in answer to Turkey’s adversarial politics in the region. But it also shows that Kurds have enough argument to build their own representative political organs and to build on those.
These are perfect times, in my opinion. We Kurds are learning what realpolitik is about. Not pity but power struggle.
And there is one way to win: make allies, become stronger, and instead of begging for pity, make your point in a way that forces them to choose sides.
Israel has legitimacy because it is a sovereign country. Kurds have legitimacy because we are imprisoned by outsiders on our own ancestral lands, denied our identity.
Let’s raise our flags together. It means working together in the diaspora.
Jews have the advantage of having been settled in these communities for centuries. Kurds have the advantage of both numbers and an unshakeable legitimacy to live sovereign on our ancestral land.
Combined, this forms one of the strongest aligned diaspora coalitions. We both offer something, and we both benefit. It is a loop that feeds itself and grows stronger.
Let them choose to be on the wrong side. By standing together, we break their perverted “non-legitimacy and oppression” rhetoric.
The writer, based in Vancouver, is a commentator on Kurdish affairs, Kurdistan, and international politics.

Tracking the electioneering vagaries of the parties in the run-up to the October 27 polling day for the 26th Knesset is not an easy task.
With all the latest possibilities available to publicize party messages, whether touting your own platform or attacking your opponent, there are many pictures, clips, memes, speeches, and interviews.
On the other hand, every election campaign has its quiet side. Or even a silent side. Some things are avoided or even suppressed.
Prime Minister Benyamin Netanyahu will probably not refer to the term “responsibility” in his campaign. On the other hand, I am not sure there is anything National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir will not say.
As for Netanyahu’s opposition leaders, issues are being avoided. The media is also muting its references to those issues, if not ignoring them, since they do not help the cause.
One example is the renewed sessions of the Netanyahu trials. In the past month, one witness, former MK Eitan Cabel, basically undermined Case 2000. In it, Netanyahu is charged with criminal corruption for allegedly exchanging favors with Yediot Aharonot.
His testimony also affected Case 4000, the Bezeq-Walla affair. Prosecutors alleged that Netanyahu traded state regulatory benefits for favorable media coverage.
In June 2023, the three judges told the parties they saw “difficulties” in proving the bribery offense and suggested that the prosecution consider withdrawing that count. In June 2026, they repeated their earlier assessment and made clear it had not changed.
A tantalizing media spin-off resulting from that trial was the revelation that in November 2015, prominent journalist Ben Caspit, a foe of Netanyahu, met with police investigator Eran Kamin.
Irregularly, Caspit urged Kamin to open Netanyahu’s baggage at the airport, and that of his wife, as evidence of embezzlement would be found. That development is absent from mainstream media coverage.
There is quiet regarding why the investigation into former military advocate-general Yifat Tomer-Yerushalmi, a second example, has stalled with no prosecution entered.
Now dismissed from service but still receiving financial benefits, she perpetrated the illegal disclosure of the Sde Teiman security-camera video to Channel 12. The person who edited it so maliciously is still unknown. Afterward, she also misled the High Court and other officials about the source of the leak.
The most senior IDF officer in the army’s justice corps is suspected of obstruction of justice, fraud, breach of trust, and abuse of office, too. Since last February, the case has gone nowhere, and we still do not know whether Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara or people in her office were involved.
A third matter that has gone very quiet is Qatargate with its overlapping Bild classified-document leak connection. That was highly publicized even as a matter of national treachery.
It also seems to be meriting the quiet treatment, and the media is not relating to the matter. High-profile figures close to Netanyahu were presented to the public as arch criminals.
These included Yonatan Urich, Netanyahu’s close media adviser; Eli Feldstein, a former Prime Minister’s Office spokesman; Srulik Einhorn, long-time Likud campaign strategist; and even Tzachi Braverman, Netanyahu’s chief of staff and current ambassador-designate to the United Kingdom.
Why is there quiet?
With all those figures, why is there quiet? Could it be that there really isn’t anything to make noise over?
One possible reason is that the former Mossad chief David Barnea said in April 2026 that he had not identified damage to Israeli national security or to the hostage negotiations resulting from Qatargate.
The 2024 unauthorized transfer of a highly classified Israeli intelligence document to the German newspaper Bild by some of those same Netanyahu advisors is also under the radar.
We are still waiting for the full report on Brig.-Gen. (res.) Oren Solomon’s internal inquiry into the IDF’s actions and failures during October and his accusation that senior military leadership tried to suppress his critical findings.
To remind us, that article (printed in Israel Hayom with the censor’s approval, incidentally) indicated that Yahya Sinwar and Hamas were deliberately preventing a hostage agreement, including by using the hostages to pressure Israel.
The anti-Bibists fulminated, and the media loudly accused the Netanyahu clique of manipulating public opinion.
However, with now-former White House coordinator for the Middle East Brett McGurk’s admission that “the idea that Hamas just was ready to release all the hostages is complete bulls***,” the Bild leak is in its proper proportion.
McGurk said Israel repeatedly agreed to proposals while Hamas resisted.
In other words, the extremely loud campaign in Hostage Square that the government was preventing any deal was unsupported by the facts.
Actually, now the tables are turned, and the role of the Kaplan Camp in the Hamas decision to go ahead with its invasion plans should be highlighted. Did their activities encourage the idea that Israeli society was imploding? Why is the media silent?
There is quiet because the public relations principle is: if an item serves your goal, quash it and ignore it. Don’t even mention it.
This is true especially if it turns out your own source goes on television to contradict and disavow the fairytale you spread.
Of course, there are two more weeks in the campaign, and I am not a prophet; nor do I suggest any one side is unblemished.
I think it fair that the public be reminded that the many media storms we have experienced over the last few years have either been proven wrong or led nowhere.
If the media goes silent on a hot story and lets it peter out, that may be a sign that something was wrong in the first place, or that the media is supporting one of the sides.

Saudi Arabia faces new missile and drone fire after major attacks on airports
RIYADH, Oct 12 - Saudi Arabia said it was facing a new barrage of incoming fire on Monday and that Riyadh airport would remain shut for now, days after Saturday's deadly missile strike on a departure terminal that was claimed by Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.
Incoming drones and missiles were reported by the Saudi-led coalition backing government forces in Yemen, though there was no immediate news of whether they were intercepted.
The Houthis have been attacking Saudi airports and oil facilities since last week as part of a rapidly escalating conflict that has spilled over from the wider regional conflagration between the United States and Iran.
Those attacks have shut down parts of Saudi airspace, suspending operations at Riyadh airport, and largely emptying the skies over the capital even as the city hosts a major energy conference.
Saudi Arabia now faces a nightmare predicament, having re-entered Yemen's civil war to push the Houthis from the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait oil route and stop the group making further gains after its sudden advances in September.
With the Yemeni forces Riyadh supports having made some gains against the Houthis around Bab el-Mandeb but still on the back foot on other fronts, Yemeni military sources said, any pressure on the Houthis could take time to pay off.
Saudi Arabia's long-time regional rival Iran offered to mediate between its Houthi allies and the kingdom. "We have repeatedly expressed our readiness to help facilitate dialogue between the parties," foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday.
Meanwhile, despite intensified Saudi airstrikes against the group, including what Yemeni television said were hits on al-Jawf province on Monday, the Houthis show no sign of letting up their own barrage of attacks on Saudi infrastructure.
The group has repeatedly threatened to target airports and airspace, as well as Saudi oil installations that provide the engine for the kingdom's economy and its ambitious development plans.
UAE CALLS FOR JOINT GULF ACTION
Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said at Monday's conference that the kingdom would stay focused on bringing in investment as part of its wider economic development goals.
"The development of our energy system and industrial capability continues," he said.
Saudi Arabia's neighbour the United Arab Emirates on Monday called for a revival of joint Gulf action on security and defence in response to the attacks. UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said the targeting of Saudi Arabia undermined the security of all Gulf states and added that the neglect of collective Gulf security had "emboldened others" to overreach against regional states.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE had been partners in the Yemen conflict for years, but they backed different forces within the Yemeni military coalition supporting the government and fell out last winter.
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that Washington was considering joining Saudi Arabia in strikes on the Houthis, but there has been no sign yet of any US action. REUTERS

Israel's Finance Ministry is preparing to seek parliamentary approval for emergency across-the-board cuts to government spending just two weeks before the October 27 election, in an unusual move aimed at securing urgent defense funding that could help revive a failed $1 billion deal to purchase 12 Apache attack helicopters from the United States.
The ministry is expected to request a special session of the Knesset, Israel's parliament, to approve cuts affecting all government ministries without exception. However, the proposal remains subject to a decision by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, with officials considering reductions totaling between 1 billion and 3 billion shekels.
One possibility being examined is redirecting funds from civilian ministries to rescue the Apache helicopter deal, which collapsed in recent days after Israel failed to sign the purchase agreement and transfer the required funding before the final deadline.
The deal fell through despite three extensions granted by U.S. aerospace manufacturer Boeing, as the Finance and Defense ministries remained at odds over funding equivalent to nearly 1 billion shekels.
The final deadline expired on October 7. With no signed contract or payment from Israel, Boeing informed Israeli officials that the helicopters would be offered to other customers waiting to purchase them.
The state budget currently contains no allocation for the helicopters, meaning that emergency spending cuts would be required if officials determine that the deal can still be salvaged.
The planned purchase, estimated at approximately $1 billion, had been in preparation for more than a year before collapsing amid the unresolved budget dispute.
The Finance Ministry is now awaiting Netanyahu's decision on the scope of the proposed cuts, as well as legal authorization to pursue such a measure so close to a national election.
"We are now waiting for the prime minister's approval and legal authorization to carry out cuts across all government ministries just days before the election," a senior Finance Ministry official said.
Two major questions remain unresolved: whether the Knesset can approve an across-the-board spending reduction so close to the election, and whether the government can secure a parliamentary majority to support it.
It also remains unclear whether the proposed cuts would cover only an initial payment required to revive the helicopter purchase or the full cost of the deal, estimated at approximately $1 billion.
Political opposition could complicate the effort. Several ministers have recently warned that their departments have already exhausted their capacity to absorb further reductions without affecting essential public services.
"We have reached a point where further cuts to our ministry's budget would seriously harm citizens," ministers have said.
That resistance could make securing approval particularly difficult, especially among ministers whose positions on party lists leave them unlikely to return to the Knesset after the election.
The government must now determine whether it can secure both the funding and parliamentary support needed to revive the Apache purchase, after the missed deadline put Israel's planned acquisition of the helicopters in jeopardy.

Australia’s Billionaire Problem and the ‘Corruption of the Democratic Process’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:17:00 UTC
22:17:00 KST

Mining magnate Gina Rinehart and close associates have reportedly gifted over AU$3 million to the One Nation Party in the last financial year, in cash and even an entire aircraft. “Reportedly,” as none of this has to be declared publicly until February 2027.
Clive Palmer splurged over AU$260 million on electioneering at the last three national polls, and then some. The land of the “fair go” has never been as egalitarian as it thinks. As long as billionaires dress down and speak rough, they can speak with a loud hailer and burn money to inflate their interests.
Yet even before the billionaires, Australia had a money-in-electoral-politics problem.
The two parties of government, Labor and Liberal, have been running business “forums” or “networks” and charging over AU$100,000 for membership, permitting access to front-benchers at regular gatherings. The electoral commission even held, bafflingly, that these sums were not disclosable “gifts,” because they bought something of value. That is the very form of privileged access that most citizens believe corrupts the democratic process.
Current national laws are laissez-faire, by world standards. Disclosure, as noted, is rooted in an untimely model from the paper-and-pen era of the 1980s. And it only applies to “gifts” over AU$17,300 per annum. Unlike the majority of states, there have been no caps on donations – aside from recent bans on “foreign source” donations, inspired by fears of Chinese influence. Nor have there been caps on national electioneering spending.
Hence the Rinehart, Palmer, and party network examples have all been lawful. And parties at the national level have long enjoyed public funding – “clean money,” but it has been extra cream rather than compensation for any limits.
That legal permissiveness is set to change, from sometime next year. For the first time, party and lobby group electioneering at national elections will be capped. So too will donations. Disclosure of donations will be at a lower level, and closer to “real time.” The change has been a long time coming.
The new laws – around 250 pages, including transitional rules – were the result of protracted negotiations across 2024. They passed in early 2025 with support from the Coalition. One upside of this is that buy-in, from both major parties, means the principles underlying caps and transparency are accepted for the foreseeable future.
This doesn’t mean the laws are ideal. The Greens support the principles, but (rightly) decry that the caps are too generous. The headline cap prevents donations of more than AU$50,000 to one political entity. But that obscures the ability to donate that amount to each division of a nationally organized party, several of its candidates and even a couple of sympathetic lobby groups. The effective cap is more like AU$1.6 million per annum.
The spending cap will be AU$90 million for a national party. That’s roughly at the Palmer level, which in his hands was both a record and a turnoff for voters. Within that total cap, there is a limit of AU$800,000 per targeted, marginal seat campaign. The “Teal” independents say that all the caps need redrafting, alleging unfairness to them. Party candidates benefit from the nationwide spending of their party, promoting its brand, policies, and leadership. Also, parties can fund that wider campaign with multiple donations from a single source, something independents cannot. There is a legitimate concern that rules shouldn’t artificially shield established parties, at a time when party politics is realigning.
Lobby groups will face an AU$11.25 million “electioneering” cap. So sugar daddies of the Teals will be able to do background electioneering supporting them. Interest groups will also still be able to mount unlimited single interest campaigns, providing they just promote their policy interests rather than boosting or attacking parties or candidates.
All-in-all, the new laws are better than nothing, if far from ideal. First, the limits are exceedingly generous. No one wants parties to be starved of resources. Party democracy beats billionaires directly campaigning – like Bloomberg and Musk in the U.S. party machines, however derided, have an ongoing interest in their long-term reputation. Channeling donations through parties, in the Australian way, insulates against corruption. It is far easier to buy a self-interested individual politician, as U.S. experience also shows.
The new laws will dampen the ability of incumbent and business friendly parties to rely on mega-donations, from corporations or unions, into their campaign budgets. In return, the regime will ramp up public funding to AU$5 per vote – or AU$10 per elector given we have House and Senate votes. In addition, mimicking state practice, parties (and independent MPs) will get a second flow of subsidies. In the form of “administrative” assistance, paid at a metric based on the number of Commonwealth MPs they have.
Second, the new laws are unduly complex. Admittedly, regulating the flow of money is hard. There are waterbed effects. So, to mix metaphors, regulation engages in a cat-and-mouse game. But these laws numb my brain, and I’ve spent 30 years studying the area. Parties, especially small or new ones, rely on volunteers at ground level. Not all can afford legal advice. The electoral commission will do well to focus not on missteps by small fry, but on lurks by the well-to-do and well-advised.
Finally, why is there a two-year delay for the new restraints and obligations to come into effect? The official explanation is that the commission needs time to gear up the new disclosure portal and educate itself and others as to the new complexities. One doesn’t have to be too cynical, though, to suspect another motive. Seeing Rinehart shower big money on One Nation – and its explosion in the polls – the major parties want time to catch up, to fill their election coffers ahead of a late 2027 or early 2028 poll. As St. Augustine quipped, “Lord make me chaste; just not yet.”
One thing to watch for is unintended effects. Will big money just reappear in other guises? Palmer, capped in what he can give to his own party, may just run more oblique campaigns directly through a corporate vehicle. Unions and business groups too may campaign more nakedly to help Labor and the Coalition. Astro-turfed groups may appear to strain the law.
Ultimately, there is no perfect regime of regulating money in electoral politics. Integrity values, the ideals of political equality and liberty, and the pragmatic need for fair party resourcing, have to be accommodated. Being part of a cat-and-mouse game, the new laws will inevitably be revisited by the end of the decade.

Americans Hall and Woodford win economics Nobel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:13:25 UTC
22:13:25 KST

Portraits of Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford are displayed on a screen after they were announced as this year’s Nobel economics prize laureates. (AP Photo)
American economists Robert Hall and Michael Woodford were awarded the Nobel economics prize on Oct. 12 for their work on how monetary and fiscal policy can help stabilise fluctuations in the economy.
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” the jury at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said in a statement.
“With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” John Hassler, chair of the prize committee, said in the statement.
During the oil crises in the 1970s, the existing Keynesian models long used to determine when and how measures should be implemented to tackle recessions or other economic fluctuations no longer worked.
That prompted Hall and Woodford to develop new tools for understanding which policy responses could be the most effective.
“Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation,” the academy jury said.
The economics prize is the only Nobel not among the original five created. It was created instead through a donation from the Swedish central bank in 1968.
Like the other Nobels, the economics prize consists of a diploma, a gold medal and a $1.2 million cheque.
The laureates will receive their prizes at formal ceremonies on Dec. 10, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of scientist Alfred Nobel, who created the prizes in his will.

South Korea decided on October 8 to recall Ambassador Park Ki-chang from Ukraine. It’s Seoul’s first ambassador recall since 2008, when South Korea withdrew its envoy from Japan over a territorial claim to the Dokdo islets.
The decision came 15 days after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea in a speech to the United Nations General Assembly. Seoul says the two governments had agreed to keep the transfer confidential. However, Kyiv first denied any such agreement before its Foreign Ministry attributed the dispute to differing interpretations.
The two soldiers at the center of the dispute were captured in January 2025 in the Kursk region of Russia. North Korea had sent troops there to support the Russian invasion of Ukraine. The captured soldiers arrived in South Korea in mid-September after saying they wished to settle there.
Zelenskyy’s public announcement of their arrival drew a response from South Korean President Lee Jae-myung on September 24 in a post on the social platform X. He called the disclosure deeply regrettable. Lee also cited the problems that disclosure could cause.
Kyiv rejected that account the next day. Dmytro Lytvyn, a communications adviser to Zelenskyy, denied that any confidentiality agreement existed.
The South Korean presidential office voiced strong regret over the disclosure and Ukraine’s denial on September 27. It demanded an official explanation and apology. It also signaled that additional measures were under consideration. Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said that Ukraine’s had sought the secrecy itself. He added that Kyiv had cited possible criticism at home for giving up a chance to swap the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners held by Russia.
The next day, First Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo summoned Andrii Vieshkin, who is Ukraine’s acting ambassador in Seoul. The vice minister repeated the demands to him.
Still, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the dispute on October 1 as a diplomatic misunderstanding. Sybiha did not offer the public apology that Seoul had demanded.
In a post on X the next day, Lee wrote that Ukraine had made the South Korean head of state a “liar” by denying the agreement. He also warned of further measures unless Kyiv publicly apologized.
Lee also broadened his criticism to remarks by Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Ukrainian presidential office. Budanov had warned in an interview on September 27 that tension along the inter-Korean border was rising by the day. Days earlier, suspected North Korean mines had exploded inside the Demilitarized Zone between the two Koreas and wounded three South Korean soldiers. So Lee accused Kyiv of speaking of an imminent clash between the two Koreas as if wishing for war.
On October 6, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told lawmakers that a message from Ukraine had included words of apology. However, he said it fell somewhat short of the expectations of Seoul.
Kyiv characterized the message differently. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said on October 7 that Ukraine had expressed regret over the public criticism between the two countries. The spokesperson also attributed the dispute to differing interpretations of the confidentiality arrangement.
A separate dispute surfaced in the same week. Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the presidential commissioner of Ukraine for sanctions policy, said on October 6 that fuel shipments from South Korean ports had helped Russia offset refinery losses caused by Ukrainian strikes. The South Korean presidential office rejected the claim on October 7.
In the announcement recalling Ambassador Park the next day, the South’s Foreign Ministry said it hoped to settle pending issues through continued consultations with Ukraine.
The Foreign Ministry of Ukraine responded that diplomacy should prevail over emotions. Tykhyi added that diplomatic efforts were underway through private channels.
Park returned home on October 10.
Seoul had good reasons to want the transfer kept quiet. According to Seoul, the families of the two men remain in North Korea, where they could face reprisals over their relatives’ decision to defect.
The National Intelligence Service also told lawmakers on September 30 that the disclosure appeared aimed at building public support in South Korea for arms supplies to Ukraine. Seoul has supported Ukraine with financial and humanitarian aid but not with lethal weapons, even after North Korea began sending tens of thousands of soldiers to fight for Russia.
If Ukraine’s government was hoping to bolster its image with South Koreans, it badly miscalculated. Instead, Kyiv has lost the trust of Seoul, and the harm cannot be repaired in private. Because the disclosure was public, a message passed between ministers cannot solve the problem.
Meanwhile another Ukrainian official opened a second dispute. Vlasiuk raised the fuel claim on October 6 while Seoul was still waiting for an apology. The South Korean government says petroleum products are not on its list of controlled exports. Whatever the merits, the claim muddied a dispute that Kyiv had started. The fuel question belongs in a separate channel on sanctions compliance.
With that question set aside, Seoul has demanded three things. Kyiv should acknowledge that a confidentiality agreement existed. The Ukrainian government should offer an official, public apology. And Kyiv should commit to steps that prevent a recurrence.
Park may return to Kyiv only after Ukraine does all three.

French supermarket chains say cyberattack forced refrigerator shutdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:10:00 UTC
22:10:00 KST

French supermarkets suffer refrigerator shutdown after ‘unprecedented’ cyberattack
- French supermarket chains were hit by an “unprecedented” cyberattack that remotely defrosted refrigerators in hundreds of stores, spoiling fresh and frozen food.
- E. Leclerc, Intermarche and Cooperative U confirmed damage, while Paris prosecutors opened an investigation into the large-scale attack and related fire outbreaks.
- Officials said the attack exposed food security risks and showed the danger of connected industrial equipment, with teams working to restore systems and prevent wider spread.
AI generated
PARIS – Major French supermarket chains on Oct 12 said they had been hit by a cyberattack that caused their refrigerators to defrost in hundreds of stores, forcing spoilt food to be thrown away and raising concerns about food security.
Top retailers E. Leclerc, Intermarche and Cooperative U confirmed to AFP they had been hit by the cyberattack that Cooperative U’s chief executive described as “unprecedented”.
“Food security requires more attention at all levels,” said the EU’s food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen on X, condemning the attack and saying such “exploitation of food” was now a “reality”.
At least 300 shops of Intermarche or its Netto brand were targeted, along with over 100 Cooperative U outlets, and several E. Leclerc stores, the retailers told AFP in separate statements.
Paris prosecutors confirmed the attack, which reportedly also hit other major chains, and also indicated it had prompted outbreaks of fire.
BFM TV said hackers “managed to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores”.
Those branches that were affected will have to “throw away all of the products” that are fresh and frozen, Intermarche told AFP.
Specialist French retail sector news website Je Bosse en Grande Distribution said other retail giants Carrefour Market and Monoprix were affected but the companies have yet to confirm this.
E. Leclerc confirmed to AFP “that a cyberattack affected one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers”, resulting in “repercussions on the operation of refrigeration systems in several stores”.
According to a source close to the issue, the refrigeration control systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss were targeted.
Danfoss told AFP in a statement that most of the affected equipment were “legacy” products which “no longer receive software or security updates”.
It said its AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 fridge regulator systems were notably affected, with a version of the former using “outdated firmware”.
It added that it had long advised supermarkets to update from those models. Danfoss gave no figures of how many systems were affected.
‘Unprecedented’
A person close to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said France’s cybersecurity agency had already identified “a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and has contacted the vendor”.
“It is liaising with its European counterparts, as other countries may be affected,” and is seeking “to identify other French companies involved in order to alert them” and “prevent the spread”, the source added.
The chief executive of Cooperative U, Dominique Schelcher, described the attack as “unprecedented” and confirmed the cyberattack had affected refrigeration systems since night-time on Oct 11.
“Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable,” he wrote on X.
He added that the company’s teams are “fully mobilised” to restore the situation as quickly as possible.
“An investigation will be necessary to shed full light on this attack,” he added.
The office of the Paris prosecutor confirmed to AFP that an investigation has been opened into “the large-scale cyberattack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France”.
The probe will help “identify the victims and establish the link with the damage they reported in terms of foodstuff losses and the outbreak of fires”, the prosecutor’s office said.
Intermarche condemned the food waste and financial losses resulting from the attack, without providing figures, and warned there could be issues with insurance policies which do not “cover this type” of in-store incident.
BFM TV said temperatures were “altered remotely, resulting in the destruction of stocks of fresh and frozen products”.
‘A level of sophistication’
The incident comes against the background of growing concern over the potential havoc that can be caused in Europe in all sectors by cyberattacks by malicious actors.
President Emmanuel Macron, a strong supporter of Ukraine in its fight against the Russian invasion, in September ordered measures to protect France’s critical infrastructure from Russian “hybrid attacks”.
Industrial equipment such as refrigeration units, long isolated from the internet, are now connected via sensors or remote monitoring systems, Antoine Hautin of cybersecurity consultancy Almond told AFP.
By likely affecting hundreds of units simultaneously, the attack demonstrated “a certain level of sophistication”, he added. AFP

UN rapporteur joins weekly hunger strike over Iran's execution surge and protest crackdown

Gina Romero Rodríguez, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly and of Association (FoAA), is to join a weekly hunger strike on Tuesday to protest the Islamic Republic’s ongoing human rights violations and use of the death penalty to suppress dissent, she announced on X/Twitter on Monday.
Though Rodriguez did not respond to a request for comment from The Jerusalem Post, in a video statement on social media, she confirmed that she would be joining the longstanding weekly “no-execution Tuesday hunger strike” against both the use of the death penalty and the continued denial of the right to free assembly in Iran.
“The death penalty is being used against people for exercising the rights of freedom of assembly, association, and expression, as well as their political rights,” she said, recalling how in January the Islamic regime’s security forces brutally murdered tens of thousands of protesters and have since continued to execute those detained in connection with the demonstrations.
While human rights groups have said upward of 30,000 were killed, Iran’s internet blackout and continued suppression efforts have prevented international groups from reaching an exact figure on those killed. Rodriguez also noted that at least 46 political prisoners and protesters have been executed since March 19.
“This is the highest concentration of political executions in Iran in nearly 40 years. Protesters have been unlawfully detained, and their cases have been riddled with procedural unfairness and underlying gross human rights violations, including torture, enforced disappearances, sexual violence, coerced confessions, and denial of access to lawyers of their choosing,” she said.
“The execution and planned executions of young people, including students and athletes, show how protests and peaceful political associations are being turned into capital offenses and used to stifle dissent.”
Rodgriguez urges international community to join hunger strike
Urging the international community to join her in the hunger strike, she said she wanted to express solidarity with the protesters killed in Iran, including Alireza Sepahi, 24; Alireza Raisi, 21; Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi [age unknown]; Ali Hemmati, 21; and Majid Nik-Andish, 25; as well as 26-year-old law graduate Mehdi Khanaki.
Rodriguez also hoped to draw international attention to the cases of former boxing champion Mohammad Javad Vafaie Sani, 30, 18-year-old Shervin Bagherian, and brothers Hamidreza and Abdolreza Fathi [ages unknown], all of whom are on death row.
Sani, whose request for a retrial was rejected in December last year, was arrested in 2020 for taking part in nationwide democracy protests in 2019 and for allegedly supporting the opposition group the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran.
Bagherian was sentenced to death on the charge of moharebeh (“enmity against God”) in connection with the Alikhani Square case, in which dozens were arrested over clashes with security forces in Tehran during the January protests. He turned 18 only days before he was arrested at his home and tortured into confessing on state television.
Corruption on earth, enmity against God
The Fathi brothers were sentenced by the Shiraz Revolutionary court to death on charges of “corruption on earth” over allegations of involvement in the death of a Basij member and damage to public property. According to Hengaw, both brothers were tortured into confessing, leaving one of them with a broken arm.
According to a report released by the Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) on Friday, at least 2,003 people were executed in Iran between October 10, 2025, and October 8, 2026, including at least four juvenile offenders. During the same period, at least 230 additional people were sentenced to death.
The majority of the documented executions, 95%, were carried out without any announcement from authorities. Nine of the executions were carried out in public.
HRANA’s documentation found that 57.56% of those executed had been convicted of murder and 36.25% of drug-related offenses. Political and security-related charges of moharebeh or baghi (“armed rebellion”) accounted for 2.4% of executions, while 1.1% involved other or unknown charges.
A further 0.9% were executed on security-related charges, including espionage, assassination, or bombing; 0.8% for rape; 0.8% for non-political moharebeh; and 0.15% for corruption on Earth.
Of 69 people executed on political and security-related charges over the past year, 35 were killed in connection with the January 2026 protests.
