14-year-old shoots principal and teacher at French school after bringing shotgun in guitar case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:07:36 UTC
22:07:36 KST

A 14-year-old boy opened fire Monday morning at a school in Aubagne, near Marseille in southern France, lightly wounding the principal and a teacher. The teenager arrived at the middle school armed with a shotgun that was reportedly concealed inside a guitar case and fired several shots at staff members. The principal was wounded in his thighs and the teacher was also struck in the thigh, but neither suffered life-threatening injuries. A staff member overpowered and disarmed the teenager, who was subsequently arrested by police. His motive remains unclear.
The shooting occurred at Joseph Lakanal college, which has approximately 700 students. According to local media reports, the teenager entered the school carrying a 12-gauge shotgun concealed in a guitar case.
Jacques Witkowski, a government official who arrived at the scene, told AFP that "the suspect, for reasons that remain unknown, fired at the principal, who was struck in the thighs by a spray of shotgun pellets."
"He then fired a second shot at a teacher, who was struck by a pellet in her thigh, and fired a third shot in a hallway before a staff member overpowered him," Witkowski said.
The 53-year-old principal and 37-year-old teacher received medical treatment and were taken to hospitals in the area. Authorities said neither suffered life-threatening injuries and no students were hurt.
The person who stopped the gunman was a school staff member responsible for extracurricular activities. According to reports, he rushed at the teenager, overpowered him and took away his weapon before police arrived. The teenager was arrested and taken in for questioning.
The shooting sparked panic at the school, with many students calling their parents after hearing gunfire and witnessing disturbing scenes. Worried parents rushed to the school to pick up their children, and many remained outside into the afternoon as police and emergency responders worked at the scene.
Maryline, the mother of a student at the school, told AFP about the phone call she received from her daughter shortly after the shooting.
"She called me in a panic. She said there was blood everywhere and that it was an attack. I left work and tried to calm her down. When I arrived, I was told the boy had been arrested," she said.
Local authorities established an emergency response center at the school and arranged psychological support for students and staff who witnessed the incident. Security forces cordoned off the area, and the municipality urged residents to stay away from the school to allow emergency crews to work without interference.
Police are investigating what prompted the teenager to open fire, how he obtained the shotgun and how he managed to bring it into the school.
According to Witkowski, the suspect is a ninth-grade student who had not previously come to the attention of authorities for criminal activity or extremism.
"He is a student at the school, in ninth grade, with no known history of criminal behavior or radicalization," the official said.
He stressed that investigators had yet to determine what motivated the teenager to shoot at school staff.
Aubagne Mayor Jean-Pierre Squillari said the suspect had been described as a quiet teenager. He added that the boy's father had recently requested a meeting with teaching staff, although it was unclear whether that request had any connection to the shooting.
The incident came amid a wave of protests by high school students in France over issues including the state of the education system and learning conditions. Some demonstrations have involved clashes with police and incidents of violence, but authorities were quick to clarify that there was no indication of a connection between the protests and the Aubagne shooting.
"The middle school was not affected by the high school student protest movement," local police said.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu instructed Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez and Education Minister Édouard Geffray to visit the scene. Sabrina Roubache, the minister responsible for education and vocational training, was also expected to visit the school.
The education minister condemned the attack, saying it reflected the spread of violence in French society, and called for a collective effort to combat the problem.
Knife attacks more common at French schools
School shootings are relatively rare in France, but numerous knife attacks have occurred at educational institutions in recent years.
In April, a high school student was seriously wounded in a stabbing in Ancenis, western France. Two months earlier, in February, a 14-year-old student stabbed an art teacher at a school in Sanary-sur-Mer in southern France, leaving her seriously injured. According to authorities, the teenager stabbed the teacher several times during class in front of other students.
In September 2025, a former student entered a horticultural high school in Antibes, southern France, and stabbed a teacher and a student.
In June 2025, a particularly serious attack occurred in Nogent, eastern France, when a 14-year-old student stabbed a 31-year-old school staff member to death during a police inspection of students' bags at the school entrance. The killing shocked the country and prompted calls for tighter controls to prevent weapons from being brought into educational institutions.
Two months earlier, in April 2025, a knife-wielding high school student killed a 15-year-old girl and wounded three other people at a school in Nantes, western France.
The attack reignited public debate in France over the safety of students and teachers, violence among young people and the need to strengthen security measures at schools.

The state is suing a former IDF company commander for more than NIS one million to recover benefits paid and expected to be paid following sexual offenses he committed against soldiers under his command, the prosecution announced Monday.
The lawsuit, filed on behalf of the Defense Ministry in Nazareth Magistrate’s Court, seeks to hold former captain Ofir Menachem financially responsible for the public cost of the harm he caused. Menachem was convicted after pleading guilty to offenses involving two female subordinates, sentenced to imprisonment and demoted to private. Prosecutors described the civil claim as the first of its kind.
In the lawsuit, the state argues that Menachem’s position as a commander placed him under a heightened duty to protect his subordinates and uphold their trust. Instead, prosecutors say, he used his rank and authority to exploit them, breaching both his obligations toward the subordinate women and public trust in the IDF.
The military appeals judgment describes how Menachem mixed sexual advances with discussions about the soldiers’ service and requests for leave.
According to the judgment, one soldier approached Menachem in May 2022 seeking permission for regular evenings at home because of personal circumstances. During their conversation, he made sexual comments and asked questions of a sexual nature. The soldier felt obliged to participate in the conversation so that he would approve her requests, the judgment recounts.
Former IDF commander exploited authority over female subordinates
Menachem subsequently invited her to his room and repeatedly approached her about meeting with him. She put him off with excuses and feared how he would treat her as her commander if she rejected him. The judgment also describes him telling the two women that they were competing for the same position.
The original indictment was filed in September 2023. Following mediation, Menachem pleaded guilty to an amended indictment in July 2024. His convictions included sexual offenses involving exploitation of authority in military service, sexual harassment through abuse of that authority, and conduct unbecoming.
In February 2025, the military court sentenced him to 22 months in prison, imposed suspended prison terms, demoted him to private, and ordered him to pay the victims a total of NIS 38,000 in compensation.
Military appeals court reduces former IDF commander's prison sentence to 18 months
A military appeals court reduced his prison sentence to 18 months in May 2025. In explaining the reduction, the judges cited the need for gradual increases in sentencing severity and his guilty plea, which spared the women from testifying to establish his guilt. The remaining penalties were unchanged.
The civil claim draws on the criminal findings. The state argues that it may exercise the injured woman’s right to seek compensation to recover the benefits it has paid and expects to pay because of Menachem’s conduct. Any money recovered through this lawsuit would return to the public treasury.

PM-SETU has a total outlay of Rs 60,000 crore and aims to upgrade 1,000 government ITIs and strengthen five National Skill Training Institutes. Its broader funding framework provides for Rs 30,000 crore from the Centre, Rs 20,000 crore from states and Rs 10,000 crore from industry.
NEW DELHI: A Rs 440-crore overhaul will put a steelmaker at the helm of nine government Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) in Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh, giving industry a direct role in shaping what students learn and how they train. ArcelorMittal Nippon Steel India (AM/NS India) will hold a 51% stake in the entities that will manage the institutes under PM-SETU.The skill development ministry on Monday announced the signing of shareholders’ agreements covering five ITIs in Surat and four in Visakhapatnam. Of the approved investment, Rs 240 crore is earmarked for the Surat cluster and Rs 200 crore for Visakhapatnam. Citing India’s recent top-10 finish at WorldSkills in Shanghai, she also called for the upgraded institutions to nurture future champions.Dedicated entities, called special purpose vehicles, will now be established to manage the modernisation and operations of the two clusters.
Alongside AM/NS India’s majority stake, the Centre and the respective state government will hold 24.5% equity each.The agreements clear the way for implementing investment plans already approved under the scheme. While the steelmaker will bring manufacturing expertise, NAMTECH will support curriculum changes, teaching methods and faculty development.
PM-SETU has a total outlay of Rs 60,000 crore and aims to upgrade 1,000 government ITIs and strengthen five National Skill Training Institutes. Its broader funding framework provides for Rs 30,000 crore from the Centre, Rs 20,000 crore from states and Rs 10,000 crore from industry.
Manash Pratim Gohain is a seasoned journalist with over two decades at The Times of India, where he has built a rich body of work spanning education policy, politics, and governance. Renowned for his incisive coverage of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, accreditation reforms, and skilling initiatives, he has also reported on student politics, urban policy, and social movements. His political reportage—both reflective and news-driven—adds depth to his writing, bridging policy with public impact. Through his 2,500 articles and related outlets, he has emerged as a trusted voice in national discourse, particularly in linking education reform to broader societal change.

14:00:52 BST

NATO’s annual nuclear deterrence exercise begins on Tuesday and is being hosted by Italy this year, with seventeen nations taking part, according to the alliance.
Steadfast Noon is described as a long-planned, routine training activity, part of the effort to maintain readiness and test the procedures that contribute to deterrence and defence. The overall scale is in line with previous iterations, and no live weapons are used at any point.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said: “NATO is a defensive Alliance. This exercise helps us ensure a safe, secure, effective, and credible capability to preserve peace, prevent coercion and deter aggression. It also sends a clear message of unity and resolve.”
The alliance adds that the exercise is not linked to current world events and is not directed against any country.
Flying is expected to run from Aviano in Pordenone province and Ghedi in Brescia province, along with other locations across the area of responsibility, over roughly ten days, according to Il Sole 24 Ore. Aviano hosts United States Air Force units, and Ghedi is an Italian Air Force base operating the F-35A.
Seventeen participating nations is an increase on the fourteen that took part last year and the thirteen the year before. France does not take part, having never joined NATO’s Nuclear Planning Group, and the United States contributes flight crews and maintenance personnel.
Last year’s edition was led by the Netherlands from Volkel, supported by Kleine Brogel in Belgium and RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk, and drew around seventy aircraft from fourteen allied nations across a mix of conventional and dual-capable types. Italy has hosted the exercise six times before, in 2010, 2013, 2014, 2018, 2021 and 2023.
The Italian Air Force has said that no live ammunition is to be used.

====================================================================================================

Patience with life’s small annoyances is linked to lower anxiety, but it doesn’t buffer spiritual struggles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:00:34 UTC
22:00:34 KST

A recent study reveals that while religious and spiritual struggles are linked to higher anxiety in college students, developing patience for daily annoyances can predict a reduction in general anxiety over time. The research, published in Psychology of Religion and Spirituality, suggests that patience improves mental health independently rather than shielding students from the specific stress of existential doubts.
Religion and spirituality often provide a sense of meaning and social support. Yet these belief systems are not uniformly beneficial for psychological well-being. Many people experience profound tensions, doubts, and negative emotions related to their faith. Psychologists refer to these experiences as religious and spiritual struggles.
These struggles can take many forms. They might involve anger toward a divine figure, conflicts with members of a religious community, or deep concerns about moral failures. Previous research links these faith-based tensions to higher anxiety and depressive symptoms. The college years are a particularly common time for these struggles to emerge, as emerging adults frequently question inherited beliefs and explore new frameworks of meaning.
Laura Upenieks, a sociologist at Baylor University, and her colleagues wanted to understand which psychological traits might help people navigate these difficulties. They focused on the virtue of patience. In psychological terms, patience is an active coping skill that involves emotional regulation and the ability to endure hardship without acting impulsively.
The researchers looked at three distinct types of patience. Interpersonal patience involves managing frustration with other people. Life hardship patience reflects the capacity to endure major life difficulties. Daily hassles patience is the ability to tolerate everyday irritations, such as waiting in a long line or sitting in heavy traffic.
The research team suspected that patience might protect individuals from the anxiety associated with spiritual turmoil. They theorized that a patient person might have the emotional stability to process deep existential questions without becoming overwhelmed by fear or stress.
To test this, the researchers examined data from 274 undergraduate students attending a large Christian university in the southern United States. They tracked the students across their college careers. The students completed surveys during their first semester and again during their senior year.
The surveys asked students to rate how often they experienced struggles related to religion or spirituality over the past year. The students also completed a questionnaire designed to measure their generalized anxiety symptoms over the past week. A separate section of the survey measured their levels across the three different types of patience.
The researchers used a technique called latent change score modeling. This statistical approach allowed them to evaluate the starting baseline levels of each trait while simultaneously tracking how those traits evolved and influenced one another over the four-year period. By separating the initial states from the changes over time, the researchers could better isolate the direction of the associations.
At the beginning of college, students who reported more frequent spiritual struggles also reported higher levels of anxiety. This pattern held true over time. Students whose spiritual struggles increased over the four years were likely to experience an increase in their anxiety symptoms as well.
The researchers then looked at whether patience acted as a buffer against this anxiety. They expected that highly patient students would be less affected by the stress of spiritual doubts. The data did not support this hypothesis. The statistical interaction between patience and spiritual struggles was not statistically significant. Patience did not change the trajectory of how spiritual struggles fueled anxiety.
Spiritual struggles often challenge the core belief system that a person uses to understand the world. Because these struggles strike at the foundation of how someone finds meaning, emotional endurance alone is likely not enough to eliminate the resulting distress. The anxiety generated by a crisis of identity or a fear of divine abandonment might simply bypass the regulatory mechanisms of patience.
However, patience still operated as an independent predictor of mental health. During their first semester, students with high levels of interpersonal patience and life hardship patience exhibited lower initial levels of anxiety. Being able to endure major setbacks and tolerate difficult people provided a distinct mental health benefit from the start.
When looking at changes over the four-year period, a different pattern emerged. Changes in interpersonal and life hardship patience did not predict changes in anxiety. Instead, students who developed more daily hassles patience over time showed a notable decrease in anxiety symptoms by their senior year.
This suggests that learning to tolerate everyday annoyances might relieve a general accumulation of stress. Preventing minor irritations from escalating could create the emotional space needed for better overall mental health. Patience seems to set a baseline of emotional stability, even if it does not solve the specific existential crises associated with religious doubt.
The study has a few methodological limitations. The sample consisted entirely of students at a religiously affiliated university. The experiences of these students might not reflect the experiences of individuals at secular institutions or the broader public. The shared religious environment on campus could make spiritual struggles more visible and prominent, as theological commitments are heavily integrated into the academic and social life of the school.
Additionally, the researchers measured religious and spiritual struggles using a single survey question. This broad approach captures the general frequency of distress, but it cannot differentiate between specific types of issues. A person arguing with their pastor might experience a very different type of anxiety than someone secretly doubting the existence of a deity.
The study also relied on self-reported data, which can introduce bias if participants answer in ways they think are socially desirable. The analytical models used in the study are highly complex for a sample of 274 individuals. Replicating the analysis with larger and more diverse populations would help verify the results.
Future research could explore behavioral interventions based on these findings. Training people to manage their reactions to minor daily inconveniences might offer an accessible way to lower generalized anxiety. At the same time, addressing the root causes of spiritual struggles may require entirely different support systems, such as community conversations or pastoral care.
The study, “Religious/Spiritual Struggles, Patience, and Anxiety: A Longitudinal Examination of Virtue and Vulnerability,” was authored by Laura Upenieks, Hiroki Matsuo, Kevin D. Dougherty, Perry L. Glanzer, and Sarah A. Schnitker.

Stolen Renoir paintings found behind wall in France, says prosecutor

Stolen Renoir paintings found behind wall in France, says prosecutor
PARIS – Two paintings by impressionist master Pierre-Auguste Renoir, stolen from a museum in southern France and later discovered hidden behind a wall, have sustained slight damage, prosecutors said on Oct 12.
In September, thieves broke into the museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer and escaped with two works by Renoir, abandoning two others as they fled.
The value of all four paintings had been estimated at €9 million (S$12.9 million).
On Oct 9, the authorities announced that the two outstanding stolen works had been found.
They were a portrait titled Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano and a depiction of a woman at a well called Young Woman at the Well.
Speaking to reporters in Paris, Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said the paintings were recovered on Oct 8 during a search of a home in the southern town of Clermont-l’Herault.
The discovery of the stolen works followed the arrest of six people, including a woman, on Oct 7, said Bessone.
“The paintings were hidden behind a solid cinderblock wall. They were completely undetectable,” Bessone said.
“It was through interrogation work that investigators were able to get the receiver of the stolen goods to admit that he had indeed taken possession of the paintings.”
A 29-year-old man seen as the main suspect was charged at the weekend after DNA evidence linked him to the theft.
The two paintings were “in relatively good condition”, although “the two works showed signs of damage,” Bessone said, speaking alongside the head of France’s national judicial police, Christian Sainte.
The frame of Young Woman at the Well was slightly damaged, while “the canvas of Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano had a tear,” Bessone said.
The tear was located “on the dress” in the portrait, the prosecutor said, adding that both paintings “will require restoration work”.
Latest heist
Culture Minister Catherine Pegard praised “the efficiency and determination of all those who made this outcome possible”.
“Their commitment made it possible to recover these works in record time,” the culture ministry said.
A spate of heists at French museums – including at the Louvre – has highlighted inadequate security in some cases and led to questions about whether criminal gangs see them as soft targets.
Crown jewels valued at around US$100 million were stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris in 2025.
While the four suspected Louvre robbers were arrested, the jewels they are accused of grabbing in the seven-minute heist have still not been found. AFP

Google Fitbit Edge: Specs, Features, Price, Release Date
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Google’s screenless Fitbit Air made a splash, but it’s been three years since the company updated its display-equipped Charge 6. That older tracker is showing its age, lacking newer automatic workout detection, deeper health metrics, and an IP68 rating. That's where the new Fitbit Edge comes in.
Announced on Monday, it is the successor fitness tracker fans with a screen preference have been waiting for. It sits in a sweet spot at $180—not as costly as a Google Pixel Watch but offering a similar experience in a slimmer, pill-shaped design. And unlike the Pixel Watch, it's compatible with Android and iPhones via the Google Health app. Preorders are available now, and it goes on sale on October 27.
The Fixable Fitbit
The Edge has a user-replaceable battery, a Fitbit first, aligning with Google’s efforts to make its Pixel Watch more repairable. (Likely also due to new battery regulations set to take effect next year in the European Union.) Repair options will vary by region and availability.
If you find the Pixel Watch’s round face too bulky, the Edge's capsule-shaped alternative might suit smaller wrists better. If the Charge 6’s 1.04-inch display was too small, the Edge upgrades it to a larger 1.34-inch screen. The difference is noticeable, and that extra real estate could make a real impact when glancing at your metrics mid-workout.
The Edge borrows a few more attributes from the Pixel Watch, including an altimeter that uses atmospheric pressure to measure elevation changes. That means it can record elevation gain and loss during outdoor activities, track floors climbed, and add more context to your outdoor stats. It also has a far-field skin temperature sensor, replacing the standard device temperature sensor found in other Fitbits. By bringing some of the Pixel Watch’s more advanced hardware to a fitness-first wearable, Google is giving the Edge a compelling middle-ground position in its lineup at a Fitbit-friendly price.
The Edge inherits the Fitbit Air’s improvements while restoring several Charge 6 features the screenless tracker lacks, including built-in GPS and electrical sensors that work with the electrocardiogram (ECG) app. You can also control music playback on a connected Bluetooth device, as you could with the Charge 6, and Google Maps turn-by-turn directions will arrive later this year.
Google also announced more advanced automatic activity tracking for the Edge, using Gemini Intelligence to identify up to 100 workout types. It can track more than 50 exercise modes, up from 40 on its predecessor. Google will also roll out these features to the Pixel Watch 5 and Air. If they work as promised, it means users won't have to log every activity manually.
With a Google Health Premium subscription, the Edge can track blood pressure trends without manual calibration and insulin resistance trends without requiring a blood draw. Google first announced these capabilities alongside the Pixel Watch 5's debut, but they only became available at the end of September. They’re also available on the Air, keeping Google’s screenless tracker up to date as its lineup expands.
The seven-day battery life remains unchanged, but it’s one of the Edge’s biggest advantages over the Pixel Watch. Like the Air, it takes about 90 minutes to fully charge, which is half an hour less than the Charge 6.
One odd omission is a near-field communication (NFC) sensor, which means the Edge doesn’t support contactless payments through Google Wallet. That’s a downgrade from the Charge 6 and a strange function to lose on a fitness tracker that Google is pitching as a step up from its basic Fitbits.
Dressed for Every Occasion
The Edge introduces new digital and analog clock faces, and the Canyon band color returns from the Pixel Watch 5, alongside five other band styles (Active Band, Active Sport Band, Performance Loop Band, Magnet Band, and Metal Links Band). The Stephen Curry collaboration ($220), which also appeared with the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 5, is back in the same brown-orange color.
Alongside the Edge, Google is also giving the screenless Fitbit Air a visual upgrade with a new Metal Mesh band. It’s an even dressier strap than the polyurethane Elevated Modern Band. The Air may have initially been designed to disappear on your wrist, but the new band makes it a statement accessory.
If you’re all in on the screenless Fitbit Air, the Edge won’t change your mind. But if you’re not ready to give up a display, the Edge might be a compelling and affordable alternative for both iPhone and Android users. Stay tuned for our review.

China's first batch of national parks delivers notable ecological progress
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:59:15 CST
21:59:15 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- China's first batch of national parks has achieved substantial results since the official designation of five such parks in 2021, the National Forestry and Grassland Administration said on Monday.
Over the past five years, a national park system with Chinese characteristics has taken basic shape, the quality of natural ecosystems in key areas has continued to improve, and populations of flagship species have grown steadily, according to the administration.
In 2021, China established its first national parks: the Sanjiangyuan National Park, the Giant Panda National Park, the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park, the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park and the Wuyishan National Park.
The five national parks cover a total area of 230,000 square kilometers and incorporate more than 120 nature reserves of various types and levels.
By implementing a series of measures like habitat restoration, ecological corridor connectivity, and regulation of human activities, the five national parks have delivered notable ecological successes over the past five years.
For instance, as "the water tower of China," the Sanjiangyuan National Park has significantly enhanced its water conservation capacity, channeling an average of 80 billion cubic meters of high-quality water downstream annually. The Giant Panda National Park has opened up 13 ecological corridors linking isolated wild giant panda populations, greatly improving habitat connectivity.
In terms of flagship species protection, the Tibetan antelope population in the Sanjiangyuan National Park has recovered to more than 70,000. In the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park, the number of wild Amur tigers has increased from 27 to 72, and that of wild Amur leopards from 42 to 115.
Meanwhile, national park construction has coordinated ecological protection with livelihood improvement. Nearly 50,000 local residents have been hired as ecological rangers, earning annual wages of 12,000 yuan (around 1,782 U.S. dollars) to 21,000 yuan per person.
China has also implemented the national park law and revised regulations on nature reserves, marking a new stage of law-based and standardized development for the nature reserve system with national parks as the main body.
During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), China will continue to promote high-quality national park development and establish new national parks in an orderly manner, the administration added. ■

Across China: Fishing tourism on the rise in historic south China port
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:59:12 CST
21:59:12 KST

This undated photo shows a wooden recreational fishing boat operated by Yang Liguo's team. (Xinhua)
HAIKOU, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- A fishing boat laden with tourists and angling gear eased away from the port in Tanmen Township of the city of Qionghai, south China's Hainan Province, setting off on a leisurely sea-angling trip.
Standing by the rail with his wife and son, a tourist surnamed Cheng from southwest China's Yunnan Province took in the coastal scenery.
"It's my first time fishing at sea, and I'm looking forward to seeing what we'll catch," he said.
The sea angling trip was part of an activity launched in Tanmen during the recent National Day holiday, inviting visitors to spend a day as a fisherman in Tanmen. Tourists boarded boats and cast their lines under the guidance of local fishermen. Many said the experience had given them a real taste of life at sea.
At nightfall, as the boats returned to shore, the seafood street along Fugang Road in Tanmen came alive, with seafood dining offering another way for visitors to experience local fishing culture. After dinner, some tourists settled in for the night at one of more than a dozen traditional fishermen's homestays in nearby Paigang Village.
From sea-angling trips to seafood dinners and fishermen's homestays, Tanmen is seeking to connect different parts of the visitor experience and encourage tourists to spend more time and money in the town.
During the National Day holiday earlier this month, Tanmen received about 89,600 tourist visits and generated approximately 3.08 million yuan (around 457,564 U.S. dollars) in tourism revenue, according to local statistics.
Behind these experiences lies a broader effort to diversify the economy of a town long shaped by fishing. Tanmen, notably, has preserved much of its traditional fishing-village landscape, while generations of seafaring experience, port infrastructure and maritime heritage have laid the foundation for the development of recreational fisheries.
In recent years, Tanmen has explored new business models combining leisure activities, fishermen's homestays, seafood sales and educational tours.
Yang Liguo, from Beijing, is one of those working in Tanmen's recreational fishing sector.
"My work gave me a deep affection for the sea. On a random sea-angling trip in Hainan, I began thinking about having my own recreational fishing boat," Yang said.
In 2025, Yang invested more than 3 million yuan to convert a 205-tonne wooden fishing boat into a recreational sea-angling vessel, which retains an all-wood structure. Its cabin preserves traditional maritime tools, including a compass and old fishing nets, while modern rescue equipment has been installed.
For Yang, the appeal of Tanmen extends beyond its fishing grounds. The town's maritime culture, passed down through generations, was another major reason he chose to operate there.
"We invite veteran local captains aboard to share stories about Tanmen fishermen's voyages, allowing visitors to experience the history of the Maritime Silk Road and the culture of Geng Lu Bu, traditional handwritten sailing-route manuals used by local fishermen," he said.
Since the vessel began operating in May 2025, it has hosted educational tours involving over 2,500 participants, Yang noted.
According to official statistics, Qionghai's recreational fishery output value reached 284 million yuan last year. From January through August 2026, meanwhile, Tanmen received 1.33 million tourist visits and generated tourism revenue of 47.8 million yuan.
The government also plans to develop Tanmen into a recreational fishing hub, upgrade its recreational fishing pier, improve supporting facilities such as tourism service complexes, and provide more tourism products in sightseeing, cultural experiences, accommodation and science education.
Li Zhi, Party chief of Tanmen Township, recently inspected the renovation of Tanmen's central fishing port. The town has also taken the port renovation as an opportunity to develop facilities for recreational fishing.
"The first phase has been completed, and work on the second phase is underway. The port upgrade is intended to serve traditional fishing as well as the emerging recreational fishing sector," Li said.
The upgraded port is set to include a 310-meter pier dedicated to recreational fishing, with capacity for up to 19 recreational fishing boats, as well as a beach, an observation lighthouse and a seafood market.
"Both traditional fishing and recreational fishing need to develop well. That is how local people can improve their livelihoods and fishermen can enjoy better lives," Li said. ■

Erdoğan says access to safe food is matter of national security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:52:29 UTC
21:52:29 KST

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan sent a video message to the opening ceremony of World Food Forum.
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has said access to safe food is a fundamental component of national security, calling for greater efforts to combat food waste and ensure a sustainable future for coming generations.
“We cannot speak of peace, tranquility or prosperity in a world where we witness millions struggling to survive without even dry bread on the one hand, while food waste continues to increase on the other,” Erdoğan said in a video message sent to the opening ceremony of the World Food Forum.
The president said Türkiye was contributing to efforts to leave a livable world for future generations, particularly in areas such as climate change, environmental protection and food security.
“Acting on this premise, we view access to safe food not merely as a matter of supply, but as a fundamental element of our national security, and we are taking steps accordingly,” he said.
“According to global reports, the largest share of food waste — 60 percent — occurs in households, that is, at the consumer stage... Around 1.5 billion tons of food produced worldwide is lost or wasted each year.”
Erdoğan also called for support for Türkiye’s candidate, Mehdi Eker, in the election for director-general of the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization.
A veterinarian and agricultural economist by training, Eker served as Türkiye’s minister of food, agriculture and livestock from 2005 to 2015. He was elected to parliament in 2002, 2007, 2011 and 2018.

‘This deal doesn’t help’: Europe slams Trump’s plan to buy Russian diesel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:52:02 UTC
21:52:02 KST

European governments rebuked U.S. President Donald Trump’s plan to import hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel, and vowed to keep isolating Moscow and supporting Ukraine as it heads into a brutal wartime winter.
Trump said over the weekend he would import 300,000 tons of Russian diesel, weeks ahead of U.S. midterm elections in which the Republicans are polling badly and in which energy prices and cost-of-living concerns are expected to play a major role.
“This deal doesn't help neither the price of oil products nor the unity of the transatlantic community,” Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said at a gathering of the bloc’s foreign ministers on Monday morning, adding “it is not the European way.”
Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee called Trump’s announcement of a deal with Moscow “concerning,” while German Minister of State for Europe Gunther Krichbaum said every dollar spent on Russian energy funded the purchase of weapons used against Kyiv.
The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, reminded Washington that “Russia has started this war. We should not forget this.”
On Monday, Zelenskyy suggested that Washington had other motives for pursuing an energy agreement with Moscow, arguing that the Russian fuel involved would make little difference to global supplies.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Zelenskyy said proposed Russian diesel deliveries were insignificant compared with global monthly consumption of roughly 120 million tons.
"I don't think that this will have a tangible impact," Zelenskyy said. "I believe that there are different rationales behind this decision."
Advertisement
Zelenskyy also suggested Washington should consider an alternative arrangement with Kyiv. "Why doesn't America then conclude a diesel deal with Ukraine?" he asked. "Let's propose a diesel deal with Ukraine."
He also revealed that Kyiv had not been informed beforehand of Trump's announcement that he had secured an energy ceasefire. "No, we did not know about that," Zelenskyy said. "We've learned that from the media as well."
On their way into their meeting, the EU's foreign ministers remained united in their insistence that increasing pressure on Moscow was the only way forward.
“Obviously our position has not changed — pressure on Russia, sanctions, support to Ukraine, Russia’s isolation is the way to peace,” Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said.
The British Foreign Office’s minister of state Stephen Doughty said London was “not planning to follow suit with” purchasing Russian energy and would ratchet up “economic pressure” on Moscow.
“Pressure, pressure, pressure on Russia,” Lithuania’s Budrys said.
Advertisement
What ceasefire?
Trump’s claim that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” drew confusion from Kyiv and its allies over the weekend, with Zelenskyy saying the truce and its terms were “news” to him but that he would support it nonetheless — provided Moscow followed suit.
Just hours after Trump’s announcement, however, Russian bombs fell on Ukrainian power plants, causing widespread blackouts.
Kyiv is bracing for its fifth winter since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, which Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said last month could prove “tragically critical” for Ukraine due to Russia’s near-constant strikes on infrastructure.
At the opening session of the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Tusk slammed "anyone who is trying to introduce any symmetries, who suggests it is Ukraine responsible for the war," saying doing so "gives a valuable present, gift, to the aggressor, to Putin."
Kallas said any ceasefire shouldn’t “only apply to the refineries, where Ukraine has one and Russia has plenty,” adding that would “definitely [be] in the benefit of the Russians.”
She also called on Washington to join Brussels and London in imposing harsh sanctions on Russia. “Of course the U.S. is our biggest ally,” she said, “but our message is clear: If we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is putting more pressure on Russia.”
Advertisement
Ukraine’s financial needs are set to come up at a meeting of European heads of state and government on Thursday in Brussels. The IMF estimated that Kyiv will face a financing gap of $30 billion to $35 billion next year.
"Ukraine will be front and center at this week's European Council," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement Sunday night after a phone call with Zelenskyy, adding the war was entering a "new, grimmer phase."

Fiji Criticized in U.S. Trafficking Report Over Failure to Tackle Grace Road Cult
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:48:00 UTC
21:48:00 KST

Reported by
Fiji has been granted a one-year reprieve from a potential downgrade that could lead to U.S. aid cuts, amid concerns over its efforts to combat human trafficking, including its response to the Korean doomsday sect the Grace Road Group, according to a U.S. State Department report released last week.
This year’s Trafficking in Persons (TIP) report kept Fiji on its “Tier 2 Watchlist” of countries that do not fully meet the State Department’s minimum standards for combating human trafficking, noting that the Pacific island nation had failed to secure a trafficking conviction for three years running.
“Official complicity and corruption undermined anti-trafficking efforts and allowed traffickers to operate with impunity” in Fiji, the Oct. 8 report found.
However, the State Department granted Fiji a one-year waiver sparing it from being automatically downgraded to Tier 3, a designation that would have put it alongside countries including Iran and Afghanistan and could result in restrictions on U.S. non-humanitarian assistance.
Fiji, a country of just under a million people, has been on the Tier 2 Watchlist since 2024, but last year’s TIP report was the first to single out Grace Road.
Previous OCCRP reporting has revealed how Grace Road has become one of Fiji’s largest conglomerates, with businesses including supermarkets, beauty salons, and restaurants. The group has built ties with members of the country’s elite, despite consistent allegations that members are beaten and subjected to slave-like work conditions. The group’s leader, Shin Ok-joo, is currently imprisoned in Korea and other leading group members in Fiji are wanted by Korean law enforcement.
“Foreign nationals, including from the Republic of Korea and the United States, who are members of a religious organization, the Grace Road Group, experience conditions indicative of human trafficking,” this year’s TIP report said. “Victims associated with the organization have reported being forced to work excessive hours with no rest days, physical violence, passport confiscation, extortion, and unpaid wages.”
While the report said that Fijian police continue to investigate trafficking allegations involving members of the Grace Road Group, it also said that the government “continued to inadequately respond to INTERPOL red notices for leaders of the organization associated with related allegations, leading to further concerns of official complicity.”
“Despite public reporting on suspected forced labor in this organization since at least 2018, the government has never prosecuted or convicted any offenders associated with the allegations,” the report said.
Earlier this year, two American women who escaped Grace Road told OCCRP that they were ready to return to Fiji to testify against the group.
Grace Road Group denied the allegations in the TIP report, saying in a statement that they were “not findings by any Fiji court and should not be reported as established facts.”
“Grace Road Group’s businesses in Fiji are lawful commercial operations,” it said.
The TIP report also noted other alleged trafficking operations in Fiji.
“Traffickers exploit foreign victims, including from Thailand and China, as well as Fijian women and children in sex trafficking, using commercial sex establishments, hotels, private homes, massage parlors, websites and cell phone applications to facilitate the exploitation of sex trafficking victims,” it said.
A nation on the Watchlist that has failed to improve after two years normally would be relegated to Tier 3. However, Fiji was given a one-time waiver because it had “devoted sufficient resources to a written plan that, if implemented, would constitute significant efforts to meet the minimum standards, the report said.
The waiver gives Fiji until next year to make clear progress or be downgraded.

US embassy renews Saudi airport security alert for third consecutive day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:47:44 UTC
21:47:44 KST

The US Embassy in Saudi Arabia renewed its security alert for the third consecutive day on Monday, warning American citizens of heightened risks following a series of reported attacks by Houthi militia targeting airports across the kingdom.
The latest notice, issued on October 12, cited additional attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and a targeted attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Sunday.
The embassy had issued similar alerts on October 10 and 11 as security concerns mounted around Saudi Arabia’s aviation hubs.
Americans urged to prepare for travel disruptions
The US mission advised American citizens to exercise “extreme caution” when using major airports in the kingdom, warning that flight cancellations, airspace closures and other disruptions could affect travel plans.
It urged travellers to check flight information directly with airlines and airports and consider private cars, trains and buses as alternatives where appropriate.
US government employees in Saudi Arabia must obtain special authorisation to use King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and airports in Jeddah and Dammam, according to the embassy.
The mission also advised Americans to remain alert, monitor local media and follow instructions issued by Saudi authorities in the event of an aerial attack.
Restrictions tightened in high-risk areas
The embassy said US government employees were prohibited from travelling within 32 kilometres (20 miles) of the border with Yemen because of security risks.
Special authorisation is also required for official travel to the provinces of Jizan, Asir and Najran, as well as the cities of Qatif, Yanbu and Taif.
The warning follows a series of attacks on Saudi civilian airports that the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government has blamed on the Houthi militias.
According to figures cited in the supplied report from Saudi authorities and diplomatic sources, weekend attacks on Riyadh’s airport killed 14 people and injured 320 others.
The coalition has vowed a firm response to the attacks, raising concerns about further escalation and the potential impact on civilian infrastructure and regional travel.

'Gods would be aghast': SC seeks balance between faith and public health in firecracker debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:42:49 UTC
21:42:49 KST

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday stressed the need to balance religious sentiments with public health concerns while considering restrictions on firecrackers in Delhi-NCR. It said a greater public awareness and voluntary adoption of less polluting practices could offer a way forward.A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said it was not inclined to hurt religious sentiments but emphasised that citizens should be encouraged to celebrate festivals in ways that minimise air and noise pollution."We will not hurt religious sentiments but at the same time, people should themselves come forward and opt for it. The whole exercise should involve a balancing approach," the Chief Justice said, according to news agency PTI.The bench was hearing suo motu proceedings concerning air pollution in the National Capital Region, covering issues including firecrackers, stubble burning and solid waste management.During the hearing, Justice Bagchi questioned the religious basis for bursting firecrackers, asking, "What is religious about bursting crackers?"Senior advocate Aparajita Singh, who is assisting the bench as amicus curiae, highlighted the health risks associated with air pollution, particularly for children, elderly people and those with existing health vulnerabilities.
"Gods would be aghast if they knew that children were suffering and getting sick in their name," Singh said, responding to arguments linking firecrackers with religious practices, PTI reported.She also flagged difficulties in enforcing restrictions on the duration of firecracker use, arguing that limits on the number of hours allowed would have little impact without effective implementation.
"It sounds really nice in court, that it is only two hours or one hour. But the court also knows that it is not implemented. It is impossible for police officers to be on every street all the time," Singh said.The amicus suggested referring the issue to the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM), the statutory body responsible for air quality management in the region, so that it could examine the available material and associated medical concerns.The bench, however, cautioned against issuing directions that might be difficult to implement on the ground."We have to be extremely careful in passing an order unless we are in a position to make it manageable and enforceable," the Chief Justice said, adding that restrictive directions were often perceived as coercive.

====================================================================================================

The China-EU Trade Truce Buys Time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:37:00 UTC
21:37:00 KST

Like last month’s summit between the U.S. and Chinese presidents, the China-EU Trade and Investment Consultations in Beijing were primarily about stabilization rather than a breakthrough. EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao closed a handful of agreements and confirmed that neither side wants a trade war. However, the structural issues remain unresolved. What both sides gained is time.
For the European Union, the choice is increasingly difficult: secure real concessions from Beijing to address structural trade imbalances or deploy stronger unilateral measures to protect its industrial base. Compounding this dilemma is Europe’s risk of becoming an adjustment variable in the China-U.S. strategic competition, absorbing diverted Chinese exports when tensions escalate while losing market opportunities and negotiating leverage when Washington and Beijing strike bilateral deals. Washington holds the technology lever, while Beijing controls critical minerals and key nodes of global supply chains. Europe depends on both.
The most concrete outcome of the talks concerns the automotive sector. Under a preliminary deal, Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the EU could be curbed more than half against projected levels over the next four years. The stakes are high. In 2025, the EU imported more than 1 million Chinese-made cars, worth $15.5 billion (13.7 billion euros) and up 30 percent in volume on 2024. Hybrids tell the story best: 659 Chinese hybrids sold in the EU in 2022, versus more than 160,000 in the first seven months of 2026, plus almost 218,000 plug-in hybrids.
Chinese brands now hold almost 12 percent of Europe’s new-car market, up from 1 percent five years ago, and roughly a third of plug-in hybrid sales. In the United States, Chinese cars are absent. Washington has effectively shut Chinese electric vehicles out of its market through 100 percent tariffs, while Europe remains far more exposed to Chinese automotive imports. The U.S., a market of 16.2 million new vehicles, bought fewer than 90,000 China-made vehicles in 2024, almost all of them Western brands built in China.
The rapid expansion of Chinese carmakers has intensified competitive pressures on European manufacturers, particularly in Germany and France, which had pushed for tougher trade measures. The proposed 50 percent reduction in Chinese hybrid exports is a step forward, but it is measured against projected growth, not current volumes.
China’s hybrid expansion accelerated after the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese battery-electric vehicles in 2024. Manufacturers shifted toward hybrids, which were exempt from those duties. While Washington imposed steep barriers to Chinese electric vehicles, Brussels left a significant loophole. The hybrid cars deal is therefore less a breakthrough than an attempt to correct a weakness in Europe’s trade policy.
As for whether the deal will work, much will depend on enforcement. Effective restrictions could give European automakers time to adjust. Weak implementation would allow Chinese exports to expand further, forcing Brussels to consider tougher measures and risking retaliation that could disrupt supply chains and investment on both sides. Meanwhile, Chinese automakers are increasingly moving from exports to manufacturing inside Europe. The strategic question is no longer simply how many Chinese cars are imported in the European market, but where industrial value is created, who controls the technology, and where the jobs are located.
The second result concerns market access and trade rebalancing. Brussels and Beijing agreed to cut tariffs on a range of EU products to the most-favored-nation (MFN) rates set under WTO rules. The goods covered, from car parts to olive oil and footwear, account for nearly $4.7 billion in exports. If implemented, the measure would save European exporters at least $260 million in duties.
Set against the trade figures, however, it is a small gain. In her State of the Union speech, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the EU’s deficit with China “unsustainable.” It now runs at more than 1 billion euros a day. The goods deficit rose from 306 billion euros in 2024 to 360 billion euros in 2025 and could reach 400 billion euros ($470 billion) this year, according to Eurostat.
The United States, meanwhile, moved in the opposite direction. In 2025, its goods deficit with China fell by almost a third to $202 billion, the lowest in two decades, as imports from China dropped 30 percent. China’s share of U.S. imports fell to about 9 percent, the lowest since it joined the WTO in 2001. The EU’s goods deficit with China is now twice America’s. What Washington kept out with tariffs, Europe increasingly absorbs.
Sefcovic defended the new deal with China as the result of an intense negotiation, noting that Washington had needed far more rounds to get its own deal. But he warned against complacency.
The third result concerns critical raw materials, above all rare earths and permanent magnets. This is where Europe depends on China most – 98 percent of EU demand for rare earth magnets is met by Chinese imports. Beijing will ease export licensing for European companies through a green channel. That matters for carmakers, renewables, and defense. But Beijing keeps control of the licenses, and with it the power to turn supplies on and off.
Washington got more. At the Busan summit in October 2025, the United States secured a one-year suspension of China’s new export restrictions and general licenses for its companies. The White House summit in September 2026 extended that suspension until January 10, 2027. Brussels obtained faster procedures for licenses that remain individual and revocable. Washington negotiated with tariffs and semiconductor controls on the table. Europe only trade-defense tools it has yet to use.
The industrial strategies differ as well. The United States has stepped up directly, with the Pentagon taking a stake in MP Materials and Washington forging minerals deals with Australia and Japan. Europe is relying on the Critical Raw Materials Act and RESourceEU, a sound framework but slower and less funded. Faster licenses make Europe’s supplies more predictable, but they do not make it less dependent.
That’s not to say Europe has no leverage. Four days before the talks, France and Germany jointly called for stronger trade defense instruments against Chinese overcapacity, subsidies, and market distortions. Beijing got the message. In response, official Beijing urged Paris and Berlin not to push the EU toward protectionist tools. Germany’s position carried the most weight. The European Commission went to Beijing with more leverage than before.
EU leaders will discuss the deal at the European Council on October 15–16. They will find a difficult balance in it. The hybrid agreement limits Chinese exports that hurt European carmakers. The rare earth agreement eases Chinese exports that the same carmakers rely on. Europe wants fewer of some Chinese goods and a steady supply of others, and on both counts the decision rests with Beijing. The recent truce calms the relationship but leaves the imbalances in place.
What Europe does with the next few months will matter more than the deal itself. If it invests in competitiveness, innovation and economic security, it can negotiate from strength next time. If it doesn’t, it will remain the adjustment variable in a rivalry it does not control.

Taiwan’s Nanya Technology sees DRAM prices rising in Q4
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:31:46 UTC
21:31:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Nanya Technology expects DRAM prices and its gross margin to rise further in Q4 as severe supply shortages persist, company President Li Pei-ying (李培瑛) said Monday.
At an online investor conference, the company reported Q3 revenue of NT$133.649 billion (US$4.19 billion), up 61.9% from the previous quarter, as the average selling price of DRAM rose more than 60%, per CNA. Sales volume fell 4% to 6% as inventory was largely depleted.
Gross margin rose 6.2 percentage points from Q2 to 85.7%, while net profit totaled NT$87.627 billion, or NT$25.40 per share. Net profit for the first nine months reached NT$163.877 billion, with earnings per share of NT$49.28.
Li said the expiration of long-term contracts at the end of June and the adoption of new prices in July drove the sharp increase in Q3 gross margin, per Liberty Times. With DRAM still in short supply, prices are expected to rise further in Q4, potentially lifting gross margin again, though increases will vary by product.
Growing AI use is driving demand for higher-capacity, higher-bandwidth, and customized memory, Li said. AI infrastructure, including servers, networking, storage, and system management, accounts for more than 20% of revenue, a share expected to grow. Strong DDR4 demand, meanwhile, means the company plans to keep DDR5 at around 10% of revenue in the short term.
Equipment installation at Nanya Technology’s new 5A fab is scheduled to begin in Q1 2027, with monthly capacity targeted at 30,000 wafers by the end of 2028 and 50,000 by the end of 2030. Li said customer validation of the 1C process is expected to begin in early 2027, while development of newer processes remains on schedule.

Taiwan secures first breeding cattle export market in Philippines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:31:21 UTC
21:31:21 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Philippines has approved imports of breeding cattle from Taiwan, opening the country’s first overseas market for the animals after two years of negotiations, the agriculture ministry said Monday.
CNA reported that the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Agency received confirmation of the approval on Friday through Taiwan’s representative office in the Philippines. Breeding cattle can now be exported if they meet Philippine import and quarantine requirements.
Taiwan applied for export approval in 2024, and Philippine officials visited that November to inspect cattle farms. In May 2025, the Philippines approved Meigui Farm in Tainan and Hesheng Farm in Changhua County as eligible exporters.
However, exports could not begin until both sides agreed on quarantine rules and animal health certificate requirements. Further talks, supported by Taiwan’s representative office in the Philippines, led to final approval ahead of the National Day holiday, per Liberty Times.
The agency said the agreement marks a milestone for the domestic livestock industry, which already exports breeding pigs, per CTS News. It is the first time Taiwan has gained approval to export breeding cattle.
The deal allows the two approved farms to enter the Philippine market and creates new business opportunities for local cattle breeders. It also marks a step toward expanding Taiwan’s livestock exports beyond its existing markets, per CTEE.
The agency said it would continue working with agricultural and veterinary research institutes to maintain animal health and meet export standards. It also plans to seek access to more overseas markets to strengthen the livestock industry’s competitiveness.

Taiwan university develops recycled shotcrete to protect coastal slopes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:31:16 UTC
21:31:16 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ocean Affairs Council said Thursday that National Kaohsiung University of Science and Technology has developed shotcrete reinforced with recycled ocean waste to protect coastal slopes, according to a press release.
The council subsidized the university’s development of structural fibers made from discarded fishing nets and plastic bottles. Mixed directly into shotcrete, the fibers replace steel wire mesh, which is vulnerable to rust in coastal environments. The university also used sensors to monitor changes in the slopes.
NKUST Civil Engineering Professor Chen Sung-ching (陳松靖) led the project to protect the country’s fragile southern badlands coastline. The team turned recycled fishing nets and bottles into structural fibers mixed with green shotcrete to replace rusting steel wire mesh.
Shotcrete uses compressed air to spray concrete onto surfaces. The high velocity helps the concrete adhere to the target area.
The council said the university extracted threads from fishing nets and pressed them into thick, structural-grade fibers mixed with concrete as a building material. It added that the material is safer and easier to deploy than steel wire mesh and can reinforce slopes against earthquakes or rockslides.
The council said each cubic meter of shotcrete uses 6 to 10 kilograms of ocean waste while reducing carbon emissions by 27 kilograms. It estimates that the material could protect coastal slopes for more than 12 years and reduce lifecycle maintenance costs by more than 20%.
The team also sprayed sensors onto the slopes with the shotcrete. The sensors use a wide-area connection to relay slope data around the clock.

CNA reported that the Taipei Social Workers Union accused Lee of misrepresenting social workers’ role in addiction treatment. The union said her comments could stigmatize vulnerable groups and undermine public health efforts to reduce drug-related harm.
The dispute began after Lee warned that public spaces used for exercise and community activities could become places where social workers distribute drugs or medication to people with addiction. She questioned the risks such arrangements could pose to neighborhood safety.
The union rejected her remarks, saying social workers help people access treatment and support services rather than distribute drugs. Protesters carried signs demanding an apology and accusing Lee of using social workers for political purposes, per SETN.
Lee defended her position, saying her criticism was directed at an earlier proposal by DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Shen Po-yang (沈伯洋). She said Shen had suggested establishing community centers that would provide drugs and clean needles to people who use drugs, with social workers involved in providing assistance, per CTS News.
Lee said she opposed the proposal because it could undermine community safety and misrepresent the responsibilities of social workers. She argued that addiction treatment should follow existing medical procedures, including methadone treatment administered under professional supervision at health care facilities.
Lee also said she respects social workers and recognizes the pressures they face, including long hours, heavy workloads, and poor working conditions. She maintained that their professional role and rights should not become tools for political attacks.
DPP Spokesperson Wu Cheng (吳崢) accused Lee of refusing to acknowledge the harm caused by her comments. He also criticized Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) for defending Lee and called on both politicians to apologize to social workers, per Liberty Times.

Kurdish PKK militants quit some camps in north Iraq, Turkish sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:30:43 UTC
21:30:43 KST

Kurdish PKK militants quit some camps in north Iraq, Turkish sources say
ANKARA, Oct 12 - Militants from the outlawed Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) have withdrawn from four camps in northern Iraq in the first step of an intended disbandment, Turkish security sources said on Monday.
Turkey's parliament in August passed a law to set out parameters for the PKK's dissolution as part of a peace process hoped to end a decades-old conflict that has killed tens of thousands and ravaged the mainly Kurdish southeast.
The legislation provides protections for many former militants who have not committed specific crimes and facilitates the suspension of sentences for some convicted of PKK membership, paving the way for their reintegration into society.
The security sources said the PKK had from last Thursday withdrawn from the Hebat, Yajk, Sabri and Sason camps in the Baze district of Iraq's Metina region in evidence that the peace process was pressing ahead.
Once it ceased all activities, PKK members could join social integration programmes in education, economic and other areas as part of the legal framework for disbandment, the sources added.
The peace process between Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army, and the PKK began in late 2024, but came to a near standstill earlier this year due to the Iran war and concerns about regional instability.
There was no immediate comment from Iraq or the PKK on the withdrawals.
The PKK is designated a terrorist organisation by Turkey, the United States and the European Union. It launched its insurgency in 1984 and initially sought an independent Kurdish state in southeast Turkey, but later refocused on seeking autonomy and Kurdish political rights.
Last month, Turkey agreed to gradually hand over a military camp for its forces in northern Iraq to the Baghdad government, as part of a recalibration of security threats amid the peace process. REUTERS

Some 13 wounded in explosion of unknown ordnance near Lebanese border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:30:20 UTC
21:30:20 KST

A 14-year-old boy was killed, and 24 people were injured in an explosion involving an unexploded Hezbollah cluster munition between Kibbutz Manara and Kibbutz Yiftah in northern Israel on Monday, the IDF reported. The military has declared the incident a mass-casualty event.
Students and staff members from the ORT Ma’alot Yeshiva High School were among the victims, according to a statement by the local municipality. Haifa’s Rambam Health Care Campus said it admitted three teenagers and one adult to the trauma unit after evacuating them from the scene, while Safed’s Ziv Medical Center is treating 14 injured victims in total. Nahariya’s Galilee Medical Center is treating an additional six victims, one of whom was seriously injured.
The municipality noted that the students were in the area on an annual field trip, with the Israel Fire and Rescue Authority saying that a preliminary investigation showed evidence that one of the students put the Hezbollah cluster munition into his bag, which later detonated. According to Magen David Adom, two of those seriously injured were 14 years old, with eight of those moderately injured being children, as well as 12 of those with minor injuries.
IDF, rescue helicopters, bomb disposal teams, MDA paramedics respond
Northern District police officers and bomb disposal experts responded to the incident, as well as IDF and Hatzalah helicopters and MDA paramedics.
Israel Police Commissioner Daniel Levi and Northern District Commander Meir Eliyahu also arrived on scene to assess the situation, with the commissioner later noting that the field trip “received approval from the relevant authorities” to the best of his knowledge.
Parents of victim: Children were praying together when explosion occured
Parents of several of the victims said that the students were in the middle of praying together when the explosion occured, which contributed to the large number of casualties.
"My son called first, and we guided him on how to apply a tourniquet to himself," said Dvir Klein, father to victim Itay Klein, who suffered a leg injury. "The boys showed amazing responsibility."
"I believe the war of the past three years has prepared both the medical teams and us, the civilians," he added. "This includes the awareness shown by the teenagers, who took responsibility in an amazing way."
Klein noted that, while his son told him one of the students had touched the unexploded ordnance, he believed "it is right for the accurate, true facts to be known, rather than just my son's account."
"I think it is appropriate for those who have the full, correct information to share it with the families and the injured, not me," he emphasized.
MDA personnel recount experiences at scene of explosion
An MDA medical technician at the scene of the explosion said he witnessed children holding and assisting their injured friends when he arrived.
“Everyone tried to help their friends as best they could,” he said. “Some even applied tourniquets to their friends to stop the bleeding.”
MDA paramedics described the chaos on scene, with one noting the variety of injuries among the victims.
“There was a great deal of commotion and shouting at the scene,” he recalled. “We found several casualties with varying degrees of injury lying on the access path from the main road, while others were walking around the area.”
An operations center staffed by social workers and psychologists has been set up in the area “to provide care for the students,” Ma’alot Mayor Moti Ben-David told Army Radio later on Monday. A bus was sent to collect non-injured students at the scene.
An additional site to treat victims suffering from shock was set up at Ziv Medical Center, including a dedicated team for the treatment of children and teenagers, according to the Health Ministry.
Beterem CEO: Parents should speak to children about danger of unexploded ordnance
Orly Silvinger, CEO of the child safety organization Beterem, said the incident calls attention to the danger unexploded ordnance poses to children and that parents must teach them not to touch, or even go near, suspicious objects.
“To a child, unexploded ordnance may look like an intriguing, harmless object, but it can be deadly,” she emphasized.
“Parents, do not assume, ‘It won’t happen to us.’ Make it clear to children of all ages, including teenagers, that if they see a suspicious object, they must not approach, touch, or try to move it. They should move away, tell an adult immediately, and call 100 to report it to the police. A simple, clear conversation with children can save lives.”
According to data compiled by the organization, three children were killed, and 10 were injured in incidents involving landmines, explosives, or unexploded ordnance between 2016 and 2026.
Meit Asher Regional Council head Moshe Davidovitz reiterated the call for citizens to be “vigilant on trips,” asking them not to approach unexploded ordnance and to report any sightings to the authorities.

US launches immigration raid of Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home

Democratic lawmaker and Trump critic Ilhan Omar’s home raided in immigration fraud probe
- US authorities raided Democrat Ilhan Omar’s Washington-area home at dawn on Oct 12 in an ongoing immigration fraud probe.
- The case centres on immigration paperwork filled out by Omar’s late father when she was a child, according to Fox News Digital sources and a Justice Department spokesman.
- The raid came before the Nov 3 midterm elections, as Trump kept attacking Omar and other Muslim lawmakers, drawing criticism for anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim rhetoric.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Federal officials conducted a predawn raid on Oct 12 on the Washington-area home of Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, an outspoken critic of Donald Trump who has been the target of political insults by the Republican president, as part of an ongoing investigation.
A person familiar with the investigation said it is related to alleged immigration fraud, and part of the probe concerns the Somali-born lawmaker’s immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child.
“Today in the Washington, D.C. area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorised search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation,” a department spokesman said in an e-mail.
Homeland Security Investigations is part of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE.
Tom Homan, the Trump administration’s border czar, told Fox Business Network that the Justice Department is leading the investigation with the Department of Homeland Security. Homan declined to get into the specifics of an ongoing criminal investigation.
The raid came a little more than three weeks before the Nov 3 midterm elections, when President Donald Trump’s Republicans will be trying to defend their thin majorities in the US Congress.
Omar, a prominent progressive who is running for re-election, represents a safe Democratic district. She was re-elected in 2024 by a margin of 50 percentage points.
Minnesota Democrats condemned the raid.
“Americans see this for what it is,” Minnesota governor Tim Walz, a Democrat, wrote on social media. “President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election.”
Justice Department policy bars federal prosecutors and agents from timing any action to affect the outcome of any election or benefiting a candidate or political party. The department has historically avoided taking investigative steps against political candidates within about 60 days of an election.
During Trump’s second term in office, the Justice Department has investigated and brought charges against a range of his perceived political enemies.
It has charged former FBI Director James Comey, New York state Attorney-General Letitia James and Trump’s former national security adviser turned critic John Bolton.
It also has investigated Democratic lawmakers who urged the US military not to follow illegal orders, Democratic Senator Adam Schiff and Federal Reserve officials Jerome Powell and Lisa Cook.
The case against James and one of two brought against Comey were thrown out by a federal judge. Bolton pleaded guilty and is scheduled to be sentenced later in October. Grand juries and federal judges have stymied several other probes.
Omar, who has been a frequent target of Trump’s political insults, called his focus on her an “unhealthy and creepy obsession”. He has also cast the Somali American community as a threat to Minnesota in a burst of anti-Somali and anti-Muslim rhetoric.
Last week, he called Democratic candidate for US Senate from Michigan Abdul El-Sayed, who is Muslim, a “RADICAL Extremist” and “Terrorist Sympathizer”, while offering support for the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers.
Civil rights advocates have criticised his rhetoric towards minorities and immigrants, including when he previously called Somalis “garbage”.
In February, he said Omar and Democratic Representative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, who is also Muslim, should be “institutionalised” and sent back to “where they came from”.
Both lawmakers criticised Trump during his State of the Union address as he touted his administration’s hard-line immigration crackdown and its immigration enforcement actions.
Omar has repeatedly said she and her family have faced death threats, which she attributes to “hateful political rhetoric”, especially from Trump.
In September, a Minnesota man who squirted vinegar on Omar was sentenced to one year and two months in prison after pleading guilty to assaulting a federal official.
Anthony James Kazmierczak admitted to attacking Omar because he disagreed with her progressive political views. REUTERS

Manchester City scandal a test of Britain’s commitment to rule of law
After backlash to Burnham’s response, unravelling the tangled web of this sorry affair is no longer just a question of sporting integrity
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
 Listen
A journalist for more than 30 years, Cliff Buddle began his career as a court reporter in London and moved to Hong Kong in 1994 to join the SCMP. 
The visit by star-studded Manchester City, the most successful English football team of recent times, was a highlight of Hong Kong’s football festival this summer. Supporters, sporting the club’s colours, flocked to Kai Tak Stadium, turning it into a sea of blue.
Now, the club has plumbed the depths, found guilty by an independent tribunal of systematic breaches of the English Premier League’s financial rules over almost a decade.
The affair has, with justification, been described as one of the biggest sporting scandals ever. But it transcends football. The controversy has diplomatic and economic implications for the United Kingdom – and has become a problem for Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
City are appealing against the decision and strenuously deny any wrongdoing. The club has been majority owned, since 2008, by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, an Emirati royal and vice-president of the United Arab Emirates. The UAE is an important economic partner and ally of the UK.
