A 14-year-old Israeli boy was killed and 24 people were wounded Monday when unexploded ordnance left over from the Israel-Hezbollah war exploded during a school trip near Israel's border with Lebanon, police said.
The wounded included students in seventh through ninth grades and staff members from ORT Ma'alot's religious high school, with two teenagers in serious condition, according to Israel's Magen David Adom emergency service. An initial police investigation found that a student had put the ordnance in his backpack before it detonated.
MDA added that two adults and eight teenagers were moderately wounded and another 12 teenagers sustained light injuries.
A student injured on a school trip told investigators that another student picked up an unexploded munition along the trail and put it in his backpack. "He played with it a little. Some kids told him to leave it alone, but no one thought it had explosives inside," he recalled. "At a certain stage they stopped to pray the afternoon prayer. After prayers, he played with it again, put it in the bag and then there was a tremendous boom."
The police and Education Ministry are considering suspending school trips to northern Israel in the coming days following the explosion. Additional school trips to the area are scheduled for Tuesday, but the ministry has yet to decide whether they will proceed as planned or be canceled until inspections of the area are completed.
The IDF said an initial inquiry indicated that the explosion was likely caused by a part of a Hezbollah cluster rocket that had remained in the area and detonated, adding that the incident was still under investigation.
The Israeli army is investigating whether the trip received the required approvals before it was authorized to take place. At all sites and along all routes opened to the general public, the IDF is required to inspect the area and clear any unexploded ordnance beforehand.
The IDF said that its forces were at the scene to provide assistance and that Air Force helicopters were on their way. It added that the circumstances of the incident were being investigated.
A source in the Education Ministry said the trip had received the required approvals. The ministry has yet to officially confirm this and is checking whether the route taken by the students was the one approved by its situation room. The mayor of Ma'alot-Tarshiha, the town where the wounded students' school is located, also said the trip had been approved by the ministry.
During the war that began in February, Iran and Hezbollah fired cluster missiles and rockets on several documented occasions at the Ramim Ridge and the area around Metula. Such munitions leave behind large numbers of unexploded bomblets. The bomblets from Iranian cluster munitions were relatively large, while those left behind by Hezbollah rockets were smaller.
Mayor Moti Ben David said unexploded ordnance had been a constant concern since the start of the war, and that the municipality was trying to determine how it exploded.
During the war, Iran and Hezbollah fired cluster rockets on several documented occasions toward the Ramim ridge and the area around Metula in northern Israel. Cluster munitions leave behind large numbers of unexploded submunitions. While the bomblets released by Iranian cluster munitions were relatively large, those released by rockets were smaller.
The use of cluster munitions poses significant challenges for rescue and recovery forces, as many unexploded submunitions are left behind. These can remain in the field for months or even years and may detonate if touched. The high rate of unexploded submunitions is one of the main reasons for an international convention banning cluster munitions. Neither Iran nor Israel is a signatory to the convention.
Dvir Klein, the father of one of the injured children, said his son was wounded in the leg and would need surgery. He said his understanding was that everyone was together for prayer when the explosion happened, which is why so many people were wounded. "He called me right away," he said of his son. "We called in the army and MDA, and we explained to him how to do a tourniquet," which he said his son did for himself. He added he considered it a serious matter that a child had picked up ordnance.
Education Minister Yoav Kish said his ministry was working to provide assistance to the students, teaching staff and their families. "We ask that everyone act responsibly and avoid spreading unverified information at a time when details of the incident are still being clarified."
In August, six foreign workers were wounded in an unexploded ordnance blast in an agricultural area near Metula in northern Israel. Three of the workers, two seriously wounded and one moderately wounded, were taken by helicopter to a hospital in Haifa, and the others were transferred to a hospital in Safed, medical sources said.
During the period when northern Israel's civilian security squads were called up for reserve duty, one of their roles was to search the area for as many unexploded ordnance items as possible to prevent casualties.
However, locating unexploded ordnance in open areas is more difficult because, unlike built-up areas, fewer eyewitnesses can report them. "It's easier to locate ordnance that exploded, even if the blast itself wasn't captured on cameras or seen by people, because you can identify vegetation or even trees that were burned in the immediate vicinity of the impact," a security source told Haaretz. According to the source, "if a piece of ordnance did not explode, it's much harder to locate, especially if it's a very small bomblet."

====================================================================================================

How diesel became the new geopolitical battleground, and what it means for the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:22:54 UTC
21:22:54 KST

Access to diesel, the fuel that powers global economic activity, has become the latest geopolitical battleground amid two raging wars, setting off a domino effect across nations and hitting the Global South hardest.
Diesel prices are going through the roof in most of the world. Even in the US, which retains the capacity to subsidise retail consumers as the world’s richest country, the diesel price has gone up 70 percent since it attacked Iran on February 28.
But the diesel crisis is far worse in the Global South, where poorer countries lack emergency stockpiles or massive cash reserves to protect consumers from an existential threat to basic food supply chains, transport, and critical infrastructure.
Some countries, like the Philippines, have declared national energy emergencies, while others, such as Sri Lanka, have rationed fuel supplies. In some African countries, fuel prices have surged by up to 150 percent.
In Pakistan, the government has adopted a daily price revision mechanism for diesel, which is now 40 percent more expensive than it was at the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran.
Analysts point out that unlike previous price shocks driven mainly by crude constraints, the current upswing in diesel prices is partly due to a deficit in refinery capacity.
Drone and missile attacks by Iran and its allies have targeted large crude processing plants in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Bahrain.
Russian refineries have also come under a spate of attacks by Ukraine in what is being described as the ‘energy war’; Russian refineries are now operating at 60 percent of capacity.
The price of diesel has increased more than the price of petrol — used mostly by passenger cars — for two main reasons. One, diesel supplies were already tighter than those of gasoline, even before the start of the Iran war.
And two, refineries in the Gulf countries that came under fire produced more diesel than petrol. No other countries had the idle capacity that could be tapped immediately to make up for the production loss.
As a result, millions of barrels of Middle Eastern and Russian diesel have disappeared from the global market.
To counter the shortage, the US has struck a deal with Russia to buy diesel, even though heavy sanctions otherwise restrict Moscow's ability to sell energy worldwide.
Separately, US President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine on October 11, even though Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was still waiting to see the deal's details.
Resource nationalism rears its head
Analysts say the global diesel crisis has unleashed a wave of ‘resource nationalism’ in which top producers limit supplies, driving global ‘crack spreads’, or refining margins, to historic highs.
Last month, Moscow extended a strict ban on diesel exports through the summer and autumn, stating shipments would not fully return until Western sanctions were lifted.
Likewise, Beijing temporarily paused fuel exports to prioritise its domestic inventory.
Before striking a diesel import deal with Russia, the US aggressively pressured European allies to release strategic reserves or face a US diesel export ban, setting off a global alarm.
Baris Alpaslan, an economist and chief adviser at IC Holding – a Turkish conglomerate with energy production and distribution businesses – makes a distinction between resource sovereignty and resource nationalism.
“I think we need to distinguish between the legitimate exercise of resource sovereignty and the broader consequences of resource nationalism,” he tells TRT World.
Protecting domestic supply is a real duty, particularly during a major crisis, he says.
But the problem arises when many countries do it all at once.
“(Export bans) may shift part of the economic cost of a geopolitical crisis onto countries that had little or no role in causing it, particularly poorer, fuel-importing economies in Africa, Asia and Latin America,” he says.
Higher diesel prices quickly feed into transport costs, food prices, and broader inflation, he says.
“The frustration in the Global South is understandable. Many of these countries are price takers in global energy markets, with limited fiscal capacity to cushion their populations against external price shocks,” he says.
The collective result can be a deeper global shortage, with the poorest and most import-dependent economies often bearing a disproportionate share of the cost, he says.
New battle lines
Yasar Sari, director of the Haydar Aliyev Centre for Eurasian Studies at Ibn Haldun University, tells TRT World that access to diesel is already pushing countries to “form alliances around fuel supplies, rather than ideology”.
He points to India’s import dependence – more than 80 percent of its crude requirement – and the strain of balancing outside diplomacy with negotiations inside BRICS, a group of emerging economies mostly from the Global South.
The May BRICS summit produced no joint statement and referred only to “differing views among some members” of the bloc, which includes both Iran and the UAE as full members.
The absence of a joint statement indicated that energy security issues are eroding regional cohesion, he notes.
China’s heavy inventories, estimated to be 1.49 billion barrels and described as mostly crude, still give Beijing leverage to hold product at home, he adds.
European countries hold the largest emergency diesel reserves, with France and Germany together accounting for more than a third of the EU’s strategic stocks, he says.
American public stocks provide a regional cushion at best, not a global store, he notes.
This is the reason the US has pressed France and Germany to draw those stocks down, with restrictions on US diesel exports held out as leverage ahead of the US midterms planned for the first week of November.
Sari refers to the 1973 Arab oil embargo, when producers from the Gulf cut supply to states that had backed Israel.
But he highlights the difference between then and now: “(Fuel) weaponisation is less about producers withholding supply and more about importers hoarding it – a reverse embargo in which vulnerable nations scramble to secure what remains,” he says.
According to Alpaslan, energy access is increasingly becoming a source of geopolitical leverage.
A government short of diesel for farms, freight or power may be more receptive to a supplier that can offer reliable deliveries or favourable financing, he says.
His concern is that energy insecurity can narrow the foreign-policy choices available to poorer countries.
“The real test is whether access to essential fuel remains governed primarily by reliable trade and commercial considerations, or increasingly becomes an instrument of political pressure,” he says.
Survival beyond wars
Sari says China and South Korea can shield home markets and limit exports. Indonesia, the Philippines, Bangladesh and Ethiopia cannot.
“Fuel access isn’t causing a clean geopolitical split, but it is accelerating fragmentation, with each nation’s survival strategy shaped by its reserves and ability to pay,” he says.
How long can that be managed?
Sari says the window to manage the crisis without triggering catastrophic damage to the global economy is narrow – likely measured in weeks, not months.
Even a political settlement would not quickly restore normalcy, he notes.
He describes the G7’s 100-million-barrel release as a gesture that only buys time.
Ending both wars today will end the war premium almost at once, he says.
“But physical supply recovery would take months to years because of damaged refineries, disrupted shipping, and structural changes in trade flows,” he says.

12:21:58 UTC

A Turkish court on Oct. 12 acquitted 44 people who faced legal proceedings over protests that erupted following the March 2025 arrest of Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu.
The ruling came in the case, which was brought against young protesters who took to the streets after İmamoğlu was detained on March 19, 2025, as part of a corruption investigation involving the Istanbul Municipality.
The court acquitted 44 of the 45 defendants standing trial over the demonstrations in Saraçhane, the area outside Istanbul City Hall that became a focal point of the protests.
The remaining defendant was sentenced to seven months and 15 days in prison on charges of inciting the commission of a crime over a social media post.
The court, however, ruled to defer the announcement of the verdict, a measure under Turkish law that can allow a conviction to be annulled if the defendant meets certain conditions during a specified period.
Mass demonstrations broke out across Türkiye following İmamoğlu’s arrest on corruption allegations last year, with hundreds of people detained in connection with the protests.
İmamoğlu, a prominent opposition figure, went on trial on March 9, nearly a year after his imprisonment. The proceedings remain ongoing, and no final verdict has yet been delivered in his case.

‘Inconvenient truth’: Man City case spotlights realities of UK-UAE ties
Analysts point to a much deeper network of high-stakes diplomacy and geopolitical economics between London and Abu Dhabi
When Liverpool fans greeted Manchester City at Anfield on Sunday with jeers and banners demanding the Abu Dhabi-owned football club be relegated, they took aim at what critics have long dubbed “sportswashing” – the practice of using high-profile sports investments to launder a tarnished international reputation.
Focusing solely on public relations, however, obscures a much deeper network of high-stakes diplomacy and geopolitical economics between London and Abu Dhabi.

Rather than buying influence through sport, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan’s 2008 takeover was the result of “intense diplomacy” that subsequently helped London navigate the global financial crisis that struck later that year, Chadwick said.

Saudis vow firm response to attacks testing country's resilience

2026-10-12
12:20:00 UTC
21:20:00 KST

Saudi Arabia's energy minister vowed a firm response Monday following a series of deadly Houthi attacks, acknowledging that the kingdom’s infrastructure and resilience have been tested.
The Houthi attacks over the weekend marked a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Saudi Arabia has long supported the internationally recognized government.
On Sunday, a strike hit Riyadh's international airport, killing one person, just hours after another Houthi-claimed attack on the same site killed 13 people and left hundreds of others wounded, forcing authorities to suspend operations there.
The attacks on Saudi Arabia, a regional powerhouse and the world's top oil exporter which has poured billions of dollars into its military, were the deadliest to hit the kingdom in a decade.
"For Saudi Arabia, these circumstances have tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience. They have also tested decisions made long before present crises, because resilience is built before crises begin," Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said.
"Energy security can't be taken for granted," he told a high-profile conference in Riyadh. "The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious."
The Houthis on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the last 24 hours, including on the airport, and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom's transit hubs, calling them "a theater of operations for our forces."
Hours later, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group reported that a projectile struck the capital's King Khalid International Airport, sparking a fire.
Air defenses also intercepted a missile nearby, it added. Journalists and locals reported hearing multiple blasts in the city Sunday.
"The whole house shook," said one resident of the Al-Aarid neighborhood in the city's north.
Authorities extended the suspension of operations at the airport, even as Saudi Arabia's high-profile convention and entertainment season kicks off this month.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
The airport was not the only one in the country to be targeted: the civil aviation authority also reported another attack on Dammam airport in the east.
The Saudi-led coalition said Monday it had also "intercepted and destroyed" a Houthi ballistic missile heading for the southern city of Khamis Mushait, home to a major military base.
Although Saudi Arabia has poured billions into its military, Houthi attacks continue to slip through.
"Saudi air defenses have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it's simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves," said Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University.
The anti-Houthi coalition called Saturday's attack a "full-fledged war crime" and vowed to "respond decisively."
Houthi media reported two Saudi strikes in Yemen's Houthi-controlled Sanaa governorate Sunday.
A spokesperson for the Houthi-run Health Ministry said on X that one of the strikes killed a civilian and wounded five others.
Saturday's attack on Riyadh drew condemnation from the United Nations and leaders around the world, including U.S. President Donald Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
Iran, which backs the Houthis, said Monday it was "deeply concerned" over the escalation.
Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed, the civil aviation authority said, with 309 people wounded.
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia also said one of its citizens died Sunday after being wounded the day before.
Witnesses to Saturday's strike described chaos in the aftermath.
"Some had lost a hand or an arm. People were running while carrying injured people, covered in blood," a 32-year-old Riyadh resident told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
The U.S., Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh airport.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen's government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.
Ottawa University's Juneau said the Houthis now "want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them."
On the ground in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing in their counteroffensive against the Houthis around the Bab el-Mandeb strait, a key shipping route, military sources said Saturday.
The Houthis claimed to have repelled them.
Claims by both sides have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

Anduril bets on mass-produced missile interceptors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:18:58 UTC
21:18:58 KST

- Anduril unveiled Steelfin, a family of two-stage surface-to-air interceptors aimed at cruise, ballistic and hypersonic missiles, with flight tests planned next year.
- The company plans to build several thousand a year and says Steelfin will fit existing launchers including Patriot, Mk 41 and Typhon.
Anduril Industries has unveiled Steelfin, a family of surface-to-air interceptor missiles designed to shoot down cruise, ballistic and hypersonic missiles at a fraction of the cost of today’s interceptors, with flight tests set to begin next year.
The company announced Steelfin on Oct. 12, the first day of the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington. Anduril says it plans to build on the order of several thousand Steelfin missiles a year in the short term. It did not give a unit price, name a customer or say which U.S. service is backing the program, saying only that it has been developing Steelfin for years while investing alongside multiple customers. The company has completed ballistic testing with representative air vehicles but has not yet flown a Steelfin missile.
The first stage is a solid rocket booster that can be swapped for different motors depending on how far and how fast the missile needs to fly, and how tightly it must pack into a launcher. The second stage is a common “terminal interceptor” that carries the airframe, electronics, software and flight controls shared across the family, with open interfaces so Anduril can drop in different seekers and mission systems without redesigning the missile.
Anduril says the approach lets it build versions for every layer of air and missile defense, from short-range point defense of a single site to upper-tier ballistic missile defense, while aiming for a fraction of the cost of current interceptors in each class. The company did not say what those benchmark costs are, but a single Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptor costs about $4 million, and the Missile Defense Agency is pursuing a separate low-cost interceptor effort with a target price below $750,000 per round.
Because the variants share parts, Anduril says they can run down the same production line with the same tooling and workers, letting it shift output to whichever version is in demand. The company also says the common interfaces let it buy commercial components and use multiple suppliers.
Steelfin is designed to fire from launchers the U.S. military already fields, including the M903A2 launcher used by the Patriot air defense system, the U.S. Navy’s Mk 41 Vertical Launch System aboard cruisers and destroyers, the U.S. Army’s Typhon mid-range missile launcher, and newer containerized launchers. Anduril says it will work with existing fire control systems such as the U.S. Navy’s Aegis and the U.S. Army’s Integrated Battle Command System, known as IBCS, rather than requiring a new command network.
The launch comes as U.S. air defense stocks have been drawn down by combat in the Middle East. This month alone, Raytheon received contracts worth up to $6.3 billion for SM-3 Block IB interceptors and up to $24.4 billion for SM-6 missiles to replenish U.S. Navy inventories. Anduril already makes smaller counter-drone interceptors such as Roadrunner and Anvil, but Steelfin is its first family aimed at cruise and ballistic missiles.

====================================================================================================

The next generation of Israeli entrepreneurs is in defense tech - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:11:08 UTC
21:11:08 KST

For decades, Israel's technology story has been defined by its ability to turn military experience into commercial innovation. Cybersecurity is perhaps the clearest example. Young Israelis left elite military units with technological expertise, identified problems that extended far beyond the battlefield, and built companies that became global leaders.
Today, we are witnessing the beginning of another shift. Some of Israel's most ambitious entrepreneurs are no longer looking only to cybersecurity, enterprise software, or consumer technology for their next venture. Increasingly, they are choosing defense tech.
This is not simply a consequence of October 7, nor is it a temporary response to war. It reflects a broader transformation in the global technology industry and in how the next generation of Israeli entrepreneurs thinks about the problems worth solving.
From cyber to the battlefield
Five or 10 years ago, launching a defense start-up was far from an obvious choice for an Israeli entrepreneur. Defense markets were considered difficult to enter. Procurement cycles were long, customers were governments, regulation was complex, and venture capital investors often preferred the scalability and speed of software businesses. Many talented engineers and military veterans naturally gravitated toward cybersecurity, cloud computing, and enterprise software instead.
That calculation is changing.
The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have exposed new technological needs at extraordinary speed. At the same time, rising geopolitical tensions have pushed governments across Europe, the United States, and elsewhere to rethink defense spending and technological preparedness.
The result is a market that looks very different from the one entrepreneurs faced only a few years ago.
But perhaps the most important change is not the amount of capital entering the sector. It is the people entering it. We are seeing entrepreneurs and early employees who combine operational military experience with backgrounds in artificial intelligence, cloud computing, software, and other areas that historically sat outside the traditional defense industry. We are also seeing experienced executives from Israel's defense companies who have spent years managing complex technological programs choose to build their own companies. This combination is particularly powerful.
Israel's unique advantage
Defense technology is different from conventional software. Understanding the technology is not enough. Founders need to understand how a product will actually be used under operational conditions, how military customers think, and what problems genuinely need to be solved.
Israel has an unusually deep pool of people with exactly that experience.
At the same time, it has one of the world's most mature start-up ecosystems. Engineers and entrepreneurs who understand AI, cloud infrastructure, and software can work alongside people who have spent years dealing with operational challenges in the field.
The convergence of these two worlds is difficult to replicate elsewhere.
Because it is already influencing the technologies being developed. Autonomous systems, counter-drone technologies, advanced sensing, cutting-edge artificial intelligence, and new forms of maritime and aerial defense are increasingly being approached with the speed and mindset of the technology industry rather than solely through traditional defense development cycles.
That distinction matters. The technological requirements of modern warfare are evolving too quickly for innovation to take years.
The start-up model enters defense
The traditional defense industry will remain essential. Building complex military platforms at scale requires enormous engineering, manufacturing, and integration capabilities.
Start-ups serve a different role.
They can focus on a single problem, experiment quickly, take technological risks, and adapt their products as operational needs evolve. The most interesting question, therefore, is not whether start-ups will replace traditional defense companies. They will not.
The question is what becomes possible when start-up speed is combined with the capabilities of established defense industries and the needs of military customers.
This is also why international collaboration will become increasingly important. No Israeli defense tech start-up should be built with Israel as its only market.
The challenges these companies are addressing are global. European countries are increasing defense investment, the United States is looking for ways to accelerate defense innovation, and militaries around the world are confronting many of the same challenges.
For Israeli entrepreneurs, the opportunity is therefore significantly larger than the domestic market. Building relationships with international investors, defense companies, governments, and military customers early will be critical to creating the next generation of global companies.
A new generation of Israeli technology companies
Israel has reinvented its technology ecosystem before.
The country's cybersecurity industry did not become a global powerhouse overnight. It emerged because a unique concentration of talent, experience, capital, and market demand came together at the right moment.
Defense tech may now be approaching a similar moment. There is capital entering the sector. There is global demand. Technological breakthroughs in AI, autonomy, robotics, and sensing are changing what is possible. Most importantly, a generation of Israeli entrepreneurs increasingly sees defense not as an old industry, but as one of the most consequential technological challenges of their careers.
For many of them, the motivation also differs from previous startup cycles. Recent events have made the problems they are trying to solve tangible and immediate. Building technology that protects soldiers, civilians and critical infrastructure is no longer an abstract market opportunity.
That sense of purpose should not be underestimated.
The next great Israeli technology company may still be a cybersecurity company, a fintech platform or an enterprise software business. Israel will continue to produce all of them.
But when we look at where some of the country's most ambitious engineers, experienced executives and returning entrepreneurs are choosing to spend the next decade of their lives, a new direction is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.
The next generation of Israeli entrepreneurship is already taking shape. A significant part of it will be built in defense tech.
The author is a founding partner of Kinetica Ventures and an experienced investor in defense tech and cybersecurity, with a background spanning venture capital and the US Department of Defense.

European Union foreign ministers agreed on Monday to establish a new support mission in Lebanon aimed at advising and training the country's military and internal security forces.
The mission "will advise and assist the Lebanese Armed Forces and Internal Security Forces to strengthen territorial control, border security, and internal security," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in a statement, adding that "Europe is invested in Lebanon's future."
The Council of the EU said the mission would have an initial mandate of three years and include both a civilian and military pillar.
"The military pillar will provide advisory support and training to strengthen the capabilities of the Lebanese Armed Forces, for border security and maritime security," it said, while the civilian pillar would provide training for Lebanon's Internal Security Forces in areas such as cybercrime and anti-smuggling.
Kallas said last month that more than 10 EU members were willing to contribute resources and people to the mission.
Personnel may be deployed in coming months as UNIFIL mandate expires
More operational planning is expected before the bloc makes a decision to launch the mission's work. An EU official said on Monday that the bloc hoped to deploy personnel under the new mission in the coming months.
The mission stems from the EU studying ways to strengthen Lebanese forces to help free up the Lebanese army to focus on disarming the terrorist group Hezbollah.
The mandate of the UN Interim Force in Lebanon is set to expire at the end of 2026, when it is expected to begin a year-long drawdown and withdrawal.

Throughout the interview, Abu Shahab glorified the fida’i (Palestinian fighter) and portrayed past terrorist operations in a positive light, particularly Fatah’s abduction of Israeli watchman Shmuel Rosenwasser in 1969.
Nostalgia for Fatah abductions, attacks

He was held captive for over a year in Jordan before being released in March 1971 in exchange for Mahmoud Hijazi, a Fatah terrorist serving a life sentence in an Israeli prison.
“The first Fatah operation involving the capture of Israeli soldiers took place in that area (Metula), led by the late Abu Ali Iyad, one of the Palestinian figures associated with the movement,” Abu Shahab said, speaking about how he was still able to look over the Israeli town from the Wazzani area. “You can see your village right in front of you, yet you cannot do anything to return to it.”

Fatah invests in improving Palestinians' image in Lebanon

Shahab said Fatah had invested in improving Palestinians’ image in Lebanon by funding Siraj al-Awda, a 133-member folk dance troupe that he said had “enabled us to enter areas that we could not otherwise have visited because of political sensitivities, including Kfar Shuba (a Sunni Muslim village) and other places.”
“Some Lebanese groups regard Palestinians as occupiers, but we were able to return to the embrace of the communities that had once welcomed the Palestinian revolution,” he said.
Shahab said that although Fatah can “operate” on Lebanese territory, the security situation has prevented it from holding a high-ranking meeting of the Palestinian National Council in Lebanon.
He also warned against individuals seeking to “exploit divisions” and “turn people against members of the Fatah movement.”
To counter these efforts, he said that Fatah members should refrain from criticizing their leader, “even if you believe that he does not possess all the qualities a leader should have,” arguing that unity was essential to strengthening the movement.
“The road ahead of you is difficult. You must always understand that you are being targeted,” Shahab told Fatah members.
“There is a saying in popular culture: when the arrows are directed at you, know that you are on the right path… God has protected [Fatah]. And why has God protected us? Because of the blood of the martyrs and the souls of those who sacrificed their lives. Their presence and their sacrifices continue to protect the Fatah movement.”

Pakistani physics gold medalist’s death sparks fraud investigation over fake US scholarship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:10:52 UTC
21:10:52 KST

[ISLAMABAD] The death of a 24-year-old Pakistani physics gold medalist who dreamed of becoming a scientist has sparked a national outcry and prompted a federal investigation into an alleged education consultancy fraud that cost her family millions of rupees.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Laiba Ejaz, from Sargodha in Pakistan’s Punjab province, was found dead on Friday, October 9, at a weekly market in Islamabad’s G-10 sector. Police said her body was found hanging from a tree, with a traditional scarf tied around her neck.
Investigators are examining allegations that two suspects defrauded Ejaz and her family of 9.3 million Pakistani rupees (around $34,000) by promising to secure her admission to Harvard University, along with a scholarship and a US visa. The suspects allegedly supplied forged admission letters, scholarship documents, and payment receipts.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ordered a thorough investigation, describing Ejaz’s death as “extremely tragic” and instructing Islamabad Police to arrest those responsible and ensure “exemplary punishment,” according to a statement from the Prime Minister’s Office.
Following his directive, Pakistani Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi and State for Interior Minister Talal Chaudhry visited the bereaved family on Saturday. Islamabad Police and the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) launched investigations into the circumstances surrounding her death and the alleged fraud.
According to preliminary findings obtained by The Media Line, 2.9 million rupees were transferred through Ejaz’s bank account, while the remainder was paid in cash. Investigators believe the alleged deception caused severe psychological distress before her death.
Ejaz had earned a gold medal in physics from the International Islamic University Islamabad and hoped to continue her education in the United States before pursuing a scientific career.
Her family said she had been searching for an overseas education consultant when she met Muhammad Nauman, who claimed he could arrange her university admission, scholarship, and visa.
After receiving payments from the family, Nauman allegedly produced a forged Harvard admission letter. According to officials, the document was rejected when Ejaz appeared for a visa interview at the US Embassy in Islamabad.
Her family said she became increasingly distressed as questions emerged about the authenticity of the documents and the whereabouts of the money.
The financial sacrifice behind her academic ambitions was considerable.
Her father, Ejaz, has sold milk and yogurt on the streets of Islamabad since 1994. Although he did not complete primary school, he was determined that his four daughters would receive an education through the master’s degree level.
Laiba, the youngest of his seven children, hoped to follow her eldest sister, who received a scholarship to study in China and now works as a translator for a major Chinese company in Lahore.
To finance Laiba’s plans, her father sold a plot of land he had purchased to build a family home. Her mother pawned her jewelry to help meet the consultant’s financial demands, according to relatives.
The family said Ejaz had previously been offered a scholarship to study in Saudi Arabia through her university but declined because she was determined to pursue higher education in the United States.
On Saturday, the FIA registered a criminal case against Nauman and an alleged female accomplice, Fatima Sarwar, following a complaint filed by Ejaz’s maternal uncle, Amjad Ur Rehman.
A copy of the first information report (FIR) obtained by The Media Line alleges that the pair, acting with other individuals, deceived the family through the fraudulent scholarship and visa arrangement. In Pakistan, an FIR is a formal police record of an alleged crime that sets the criminal investigation in motion.
Law enforcement sources told The Media Line that Nauman was arrested during a late-night raid in Islamabad’s H-13 sector, where he had reportedly been staying in a rented room to avoid detection.
Investigators reportedly recovered material from his mobile phone suggesting possible involvement in other online fraud schemes and the blackmail of women. Those allegations remain under investigation.
Sources also alleged that Nauman had previously been dismissed from his position with the Anti-Corruption Department in Quetta over accusations of fraudulent activities.
Case is impersonation scam, says FIA director
FIA Director Gen. Usman Anwar characterized the case as an impersonation scam rather than a conventional education consultancy fraud. He said the alleged female accomplice had falsely presented herself as Nauman’s contact in the United States.
Rehman, a lawyer and the complainant in the case, told The Media Line that Nauman had claimed to have access to scholarship and financial sponsorship documents through a woman named Aiza, purportedly based in the United States.
Believing those assurances, the family proceeded with the application process. However, as Nauman’s conduct became increasingly suspicious, relatives began checking the authenticity of the documents.
Rehman said the family contacted Harvard University directly and made inquiries through its own contacts at the US Embassy in Islamabad. Neither institution could verify the documents supplied to Ejaz, he said.
Zaid bin Afzal, Ejaz’s brother-in-law, told The Media Line that Nauman had repeatedly postponed her visa interview. On three or four occasions, he allegedly contacted her the night before a scheduled appointment to inform her that it had been canceled.
During his final conversation with Ejaz, Nauman reportedly claimed that another interview had been scheduled for October 12 and demanded payment of the remaining 2.2 million rupees before that date.
By then, Afzal said, Ejaz had discovered the alleged deception and was deeply distressed.
On October 9, she left home without informing her family where she was going. Before leaving, she had been online with her elder sister, Afzal’s wife, while her laptop remained at home.
Afzal said Ejaz contacted him shortly before her death and pleaded with him not to reveal the alleged fraud to her father.
“Don’t tell my father about the fraud committed against me; otherwise, he will die,” she said, according to Afzal.
He said Ejaz had concealed Nauman’s final demand for money from other family members.
Afzal later went to the market in Islamabad’s G-10 sector, where he said he discovered her body. He alerted police, who removed the body and transported it to a hospital.
The case has renewed concerns about fraudulent consultants targeting Pakistani families seeking educational opportunities abroad.
FIA has previously investigated similar cases
Pakistan’s FIA has investigated several cases involving forged university admission letters, scholarship documents, visas, and other paperwork used to exploit prospective students and their families.
In a separate recent investigation, the agency’s Anti-Corruption Circle raided education consultancy and courier offices in Islamabad and arrested 22 people, including six officials from the Pakistani Foreign Affairs Ministry.
The suspects allegedly produced or used counterfeit apostille stickers, forged stamps, and fraudulent documents while charging substantial fees for expedited services and paying bribes to facilitate the process. Authorities said the counterfeit authentication stickers had circulated across Pakistan, potentially causing financial losses to the national treasury.
Media reports have also alleged that unofficial channels collected approximately 12 billion rupees ($43 million) over one year to process roughly 800,000 documents, raising further questions about oversight of document authentication and overseas application services.
Bilal Ranjha, an education consultant based in Lahore, told The Media Line that many young Pakistanis seeking opportunities at Western universities turn to questionable intermediaries in the hope of bypassing standard admission requirements.
He said the desire for shortcuts had created opportunities for fraudulent and unqualified consultants to charge exorbitant fees for forged documents and promises they could not fulfill.
Ranjha estimated that 90% of young people who seek such shortcuts resort to falsified paperwork, although he did not provide supporting data for that estimate.
He also alleged that some individuals involved in fraudulent operations had connections to embassy employees, either through direct employment or personal contacts. The allegations were not independently verified.
Ranjha emphasized that legitimate applicants seeking admission to universities in the United States and Europe can use established procedures without relying on questionable intermediaries. Universities generally communicate admission decisions and send official documents directly to applicants, he said, allowing students to verify offers through recognized institutional channels.
Naheed Khan, an Islamabad-based youth rights activist, told The Media Line that Ejaz’s death should be understood in the context of Pakistan’s wider economic and institutional difficulties rather than viewed solely as the alleged misconduct of one consultant.
Khan said poverty, unemployment, and limited opportunities at home were putting increasing pressure on young Pakistanis, many of whom see overseas education and employment as a path toward financial security and a better future.
She called for stronger enforcement of existing laws, more effective regulation of overseas education consultants, and public policies aimed at protecting students and their families from exploitation.
Khan also questioned whether the institutions responsible for overseeing education consultancy services were providing adequate safeguards for young people pursuing opportunities abroad.

ISIS, though, has been considerably weakened and generally only consists of scattered cells in very rural areas. Iraq appears to be trying to send a message that it will not allow ISIS to exploit the situation.
ISIS rose in Iraq in 2014 during a time of sectarian tension and chaos. The United States had left Iraq in 2011. Under Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki, it was not a strong state. Maliki, who was very pro-Iran, was seen as an abusive prime minister by Iraqi Sunnis. The large Arab cities resented his rule. When ISIS appeared as an alternative, sweeping into Iraq from Syria, many backed it in places such as Mosul, Ramadi, and Fallujah.
ISIS was able to defeat two Iraqi army divisions and take most of the equipment from the depots of the units. That move gave it a lot of strength.
Today, ISIS no longer has such strength or any of the influence that gave it power in the past. It consists of aging fighters or a few young recruits and it is scattered in various areas.
However, it has pockets that have never been defeated. One is in the Hamrin Mountains and areas near the Hawija district. Some of these cells have connections further north in the area of Mount Qarachogh, where ISIS has exploited the vacuum in power between the Kurdistan Regional Government and the Iraqi federal forces.
F-16 Airstrikes destroy ISIS elements in Iraqi territory
On Sunday, Iraq’s Security Media Cell, which posts official statements on the Iraqi security forces, said that it had carried out strikes against ISIS.
It said that “based on intensive field monitoring to track terrorist elements, and relying on precise and confirmed intelligence provided by the Military Intelligence Directorate, and in joint coordination with the Aerial Reconnaissance and Surveillance Center in the Office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, F-16 aircraft carried out two airstrikes targeting a hideout belonging to remnants of ISIS elements in the Nareen area within the Diyala Operations Command sector, resulting in its complete destruction.” The statement didn’t name Islamic State, but it was clear it was the target.
Iraq is worried about ISIS activity west of Kirkuk. It sent Brig.- Gen. Abdul Amir Al-Shammari, director of the Office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, to chair a meeting with the Deputy Chief of Staff of the Army for Operations and the Commander of Kirkuk Operations.
“The director of the office listened to a detailed briefing from the commanders regarding the plans for the deployment of units and their openness within the sector of responsibility of the Kirkuk Operations Command,” Iraq’s Security Media Cell said.
“The meeting witnessed in-depth discussions regarding the enhancement of security measures and the securing of borders and villages within the sector, and the attendees concluded with a number of important recommendations that emphasized the importance of intensifying intelligence efforts and coordinating efforts among the various security units to ensure security stability and protect citizens in the province.”
Further reports discussed the threat of ISIS in Iraq.
Shafaq News noted that “ISIS militants struck the same village in Kirkuk’s Hawija district twice in less than 24 hours, and both times they went after the cameras. The attacks disabled thermal imaging equipment that Iraqi forces use to watch open farmland and valleys at night. They have also renewed attention on stretches of northern Iraq that local commanders concede are not fully covered.”
Iraqi, Kurdish forces fighting ISIS for decades
It also noted how Hawija, west of Kirkuk, has been an ISIS hotbed for years.
During the war on ISIS, there was a line of hills overlooking the valley near Hawija. The Kurdish Peshmerga held this line at the time. During most of the war the Peshmerga looked down on the ISIS-held areas in the desert around Hawija. It remained an Islamic State holdout until October 2017, when the Iraqi federal government finally conquered it.
Shafaq said that “on the evening of October 5, militants attacked a position held by the 3rd Battalion of the Federal Police’s 9th Brigade in al-Bargliya, in Hawija’s al-Danadish sector. One officer was killed, four were wounded, and several thermal cameras at the site were destroyed.”
Meanwhile, Arab Weekly noted that “Iraqi security forces carried out an airborne assault on six suspected Islamic State hideouts in Kirkuk province on Monday, highlighting Baghdad’s continuing campaign to eliminate the group’s remaining cells nearly nine years after declaring victory over the militants.”
Iraq’s Joint Operations Command said they had sent forces by helicopter into Zghaitun.
Rudaw, a Kurdish media outlet, wrote that “Iraqi F-16 fighter jets carried out two airstrikes targeting an alleged Islamic State (ISIS) hideout in Diyala province late Sunday, destroying the site as concerns grow over the group’s movements in areas where security gaps persist between Iraqi forces and Kurdish Peshmerga.”
Meanwhile, in nearby Kirkuk, there is a meeting taking place as candidates seek out the office of governor. According to Shafaq, several Turkmen candidates are running.
In another development, Shafaq noted, “Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair is heading to Saudi Arabia to prepare for Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s upcoming visit, with discussions expected to focus on reviving a long-idle oil pipeline linking Iraq to the Saudi Red Sea port of Yanbu, a government source told Shafaq News on Monday.”
The pipeline stretches from the Zubair oilfield in Iraq’s southern Basra province to Yanbu and was built in the 1980s.
“Operations ceased in 1990, following Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait, while Saudi Arabia repurposed sections on its territory in 2001 to connect with its East-West pipeline, which provides an alternative export route bypassing the Strait of Hormuz,” Shafaq noted.

IDF probes suspected negligence after officer killed in Humvee accident in southern Lebanon

2026-10-12

21:10:35 KST

The IDF is investigating allegations that commanders in the Combat Engineering Corps' 603rd Battalion and the 7th Brigade failed to follow operational procedures during an accident in Lebanon last Thursday that killed Capt. Eliav Haim Tzapalamus, 21, from Haifa.
Tzapalamus's family said Sunday morning that their son might have been saved had military procedures been followed.
According to the family, only one Humvee was sent on the mission, despite operational orders requiring at least two vehicles to travel together in Lebanese territory.
The family claims that after the Humvee overturned, Tzapalamus remained trapped beneath it for approximately 20 to 30 minutes. The other soldiers, who were injured in the accident, were unable to call for help because the radio communication system had stopped working.
The soldiers also struggled to turn the overturned vehicle upright, which the family believes contributed to Tzapalamus's death.
His relatives maintain that a second vehicle could have allowed the soldiers to summon help sooner, right the Humvee more quickly, and provide lifesaving medical treatment.
The IDF's Northern Command is investigating the circumstances of the accident, including whether the force complied with operational orders governing vehicle movements in Lebanon.
IDF examines what caused Humvee to overturn
Maariv has learned that the Humvee was heading toward Israeli territory to transport soldiers when the accident occurred.
The vehicle overturned on a road near the Litani River in the eastern sector of southern Lebanon.
Although the road is paved in the area where the accident occurred, the route presents several driving challenges, including steep descents, winding sections, sharp inclines, and stretches of damaged or unpaved road.
The IDF is examining what caused the Humvee to overturn, particularly given that the vehicle is designed to maintain strong traction on both paved roads and rough terrain.
Preliminary findings suggest that the driver had undergone the required training and was experienced in operating the vehicle.
Investigators also believe the Humvee was traveling at a reasonable speed, although they are examining whether it was moving too quickly for the road conditions along the section where the accident occurred.
Investigators are also examining whether a rock on the road caused the driver to lose control, leading the Humvee to overturn onto its right side.
Three other IDF soldiers were lightly wounded in the accident. They were evacuated to a hospital for medical treatment, and their families were notified.
In a separate incident earlier that day, two soldiers were lightly wounded following the improper use of ammunition.
Katz pays tribute to fallen officer
Defense Minister Israel Katz paid tribute to Tzapalamus following his death.
"At this difficult time, my heart is with the family of the late Capt. Eliav Haim Tzapalamus, a combat officer in the 7th Brigade, who fell during operational activity in southern Lebanon," Katz said. "On behalf of the entire defense establishment, I share in the family's profound grief and offer strength to his commanders and comrades."
"I wish a speedy and full recovery to the soldiers wounded in this difficult incident. May his memory be blessed."
The IDF offered its condolences and support to Tzapalamus' family.
"The IDF shares in the sorrow of the bereaved family and the wounded and will continue to support them," it said. "The matter is under investigation and has not yet been presented to the bereaved family. Once the investigation is concluded, its findings will be presented to the family with full transparency."

Hungarian Ad Agency Got Millions From Firm Owned by Orban’s Billionaire Friend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:07:00 UTC
21:07:00 KST

Just a few years after launching in 2020, Megafon Digital Incubator Center had become one of Hungary’s most influential political advertising agencies, mainly running social media campaigns in support of the ruling party and its leader, Viktor Orbán.
But Megafon appears to have lost its sense of purpose since Orbán was swept from power in national elections this past April. Four months after that stunning loss, its website was taken offline.
Now, internal documents from a firm called V-Híd Zrt reveal the source of much of Megafon’s income. Around $12 million in donations came from that company, which is owned by Lőrinc Mészáros, Orbán’s childhood friend.
Mészáros became fabulously wealthy during Orbán’s 16 years in power, building a business empire spanning sectors from construction to banking and energy. Mészáros’ companies won seven percent of all public procurement contracts — together worth about $2 billion — between 2018 and 2020 alone, according to Transparency International.
József Péter Martin, executive director of Transparency International’s Hungarian chapter, said the relationship between Megafon and Mészáros illustrates how Orbán and his Fidesz party relied on affluent elites and friendly media — and how those allies benefited in turn.
“It’s a vicious cycle,” Martin told OCCRP’s member center, Direkt36.
“Mészáros’s company wins the public procurement contract and gets rich as a result. He uses that money to fund a private company that works to keep Fidesz in power by spreading propaganda,” he said.
Research groups like the Rule of Law Lab at New York University have documented in detail how Orbán and Fidesz co-opted the media to maintain power.
Public broadcasters became government mouthpieces, while there was a “consolidation of private outlets under allied ownership,” the Rule of Law Lab said in a report early this year. Eventually, the report noted, Mészáros “became Hungary’s largest media owner.”
Mészáros did not own Megafon, but his company’s money was key to its operations, according to the documents obtained by Direkt36. They show that payments from V-Híd amounted to one third of Megafon’s total revenue from 2022 to 2024. The funding grew year-by-year, accounting for more than half of Megafon’s entire income in 2024.
The payments from V-Híd were referenced in the documents as “donations.”
Neither V-Híd nor Megafon responded to requests for comment. Mészáros did not respond to requests for comment.
Communications included among the documents show a cordial relationship between the two companies. In one February 2023 exchange, Megafon’s founder, István Kovács, wrote to V-Híd to express gratitude for the donations his company had received — and to say the company was open to more funding.
“On behalf of the entire Megafon team, I would like to once again thank you for your previous support,” Kovács wrote in an email.
A week later, a V-Híd executive issued an internal order: “Please transfer the 500 million to Megafon now!”
That amount — worth about $1.4 million at the time — was sent by V-Híd the same day, according to a transfer receipt included in the documents. In July 2023, V-Híd made another transfer of about $1 million.
Funds from V-Híd helped Megafon pump out a steady stream of pro-Fidesz messages on social media. These included videos posted before the 2024 municipal elections accusing the opposition of trying to drag Hungary into war by supporting Ukraine in its fight against Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
Megafon kept campaigning in the run-up to the vote this year, organizing an event featuring Orbán, and posting pro-Fidesz messages on social media.
But the advertising agency’s fortunes were about to change.
After winning elections in April, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar pledged to stop state advertising being funneled into pro-Fidesz media — including almost 500 outlets that had been consolidated as part of the Central European Press and Media Foundation (KESMA).
Some outlets reportedly stopped publishing and others downsized, including Mediaworks, which was owned by Mészáros and folded into KESMA. Mediaworks announced in mid-June that it would undertake a restructuring process that would involve “changes in staff numbers.”
Megafon appears to have suffered a similar fate. A document from a company that provides Hungarian business intelligence and commercial registry data shows that the Megafon had 72 employees in April. By August, the company was down to three staff members, and its website was taken offline.

Southeast Asia Has a Serious Drug Problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:07:00 UTC
21:07:00 KST

Southeast Asia is awash in meth.
In June 2025, anti-drug police in Thailand descended on a small tourist boat moored at a pier in Rayong, a seaside town south of Bangkok. Aboard the ship, inside plastic bags disguised as corn flour packages, they found an alarming cargo: 2.4 metric tons of crystal methamphetamine. This one shipment, bound for overseas markets, was bigger than the entire annual total of meth seizures that Thailand made in 2016. An official from the Department of Special Investigation later told the press that the shipment was worth an estimated $9.15 million – and would sell for ten times that once it hit foreign shores.
Thailand’s meth bust was just the tip of the iceberg. Just a few weeks before that, authorities in Indonesia seized a cargo ship near Batam Island, just south of Singapore. On board they found a similar haul: 2.1 tons of crystal meth. It was the largest drug confiscation in Indonesia’s history.
There were more mega-seizures in late 2025 and early 2026. In September 2025, authorities in Yangon confiscated 1.8 metric tons of crystal meth and 4 million methamphetamine tablets, which authorities said were set to be smuggled to Malaysia. In February 2026, Malaysia confiscated 76 sacks of crystal meth, totaling around 1.5 tons, from two vessels off the east coast of peninsular Malaysia. Two months after that, Thai authorities confiscated 2 metric tons hidden in a pickup truck en route to a port in eastern Thailand.
According to experts, all of these meth shipments originated in the Golden Triangle, the rugged region where Thailand’s borders converge with those of Myanmar and Laos. For decades the Golden Triangle has been associated with narcotics – initially heroin, synthesized from the poppies that grow well in the region’s cool upland climate.
But over the past decade, the Southeast Asian drug trade has shifted decisively toward synthetic drugs – particularly methamphetamine. These are cheaper to make, easier to transport, and not dependent on the weather for a good harvest.
Southeast Asia’s drug labs are now pumping out unprecedented amounts of meth. According to the U.N. Office on Drugs and Crime – or UNODC – regional seizures of methamphetamine hit a new record of 349 tons in 2025, up from 236 tons the year before. In 2015, regional seizures captured just 65 tons. And these drugs are being sold all around the world.
The UNODC says that last year, Southeast Asia accounted for around 94 percent of all the methamphetamine seizures in the entire world. The UN agency reported an “immense volume of methamphetamine trafficked through land-based and maritime routes.”
Everybody knows that drug seizures represent only a small fraction of the total amount of drugs being trafficked through the region. Southeast Asia is facing down the biggest drug crisis in its history.

On Feb. 28, Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and U.S. bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.
A ceasefire was achieved between the warring parties on April 8. On June 18, Iran and the United States signed the MoU on ending the war in the region on all fronts.

Six Turkish drones cross into Greek airspace over Aegean
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:02:27 UTC
21:02:27 KST

- Greece says six Turkish drones made eight air traffic infringements and five violations of Greek national airspace over the Aegean on Oct. 10.
- Greek forces intercepted the drones, which flew over the northeastern, central and southeastern Aegean, the general staff said.
Six Turkish military drones flew into Greek-claimed airspace over the Aegean Sea on Oct. 10, Greece’s Hellenic National Defense General Staff said, the latest in a run of near-daily incidents this month.
The Greek military recorded eight infringements of air traffic rules inside the Athens Flight Information Region and five violations of Greek national airspace by the drones. The flights took place over the northeastern, central and southeastern Aegean. Greek forces detected, identified and intercepted the drones in line with international rules and standard procedure, the general staff said. It did not say which Turkish drone types were involved, how long they stayed in the area or what aircraft Greece used to intercept them.
An infringement means a Turkish military aircraft entered the Athens Flight Information Region, the area where Greece manages air traffic, without filing a flight plan with Greek controllers. A violation means the aircraft crossed into what Greece considers its national airspace, which it sets at 10 nautical miles (about 18.5 km) from its coastline. Turkey recognizes only 6 nautical miles, matching the width of Greek territorial waters, and does not accept that its military flights need to file plans with Athens. Ankara regards the flights as taking place in international airspace.
The Oct. 10 incidents followed several similar days. On Oct. 6, the general staff reported seven Turkish aircraft over the Aegean, including two armed F-16 fighters, a CN-235 maritime patrol plane and four drones, which together logged 10 infringements and 15 violations. On Oct. 8, five Turkish drones and an ATR-72 maritime patrol aircraft recorded five violations and seven infringements.
The flights came days after U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited Athens, where he described Greece as a key strategic partner of the United States and NATO ally. Greece and Turkey are both NATO members but have long disputed airspace limits, maritime boundaries and the demilitarization of Greek islands near the Turkish coast. Mock dogfights between Greek and Turkish fighters were common for years before the two governments improved ties in 2023, and in recent years Turkish drones have made up a growing share of the recorded incidents.

Kuwait buys British-built air defence system worth millions
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:00:51 BST
21:00:51 KST

Kuwait has bought an air defence system built in Britain under a £370 million contract that will create a hundred jobs in the United Kingdom, according to the Ministry of Defence.
The contract with MARSS Systems Limited, an EOS company, covers skilled engineering and manufacturing roles, and the work will expand the company’s British offices with production based in Bristol.
MARSS will provide and integrate the system for Kuwait, bringing together jammers, radars and interceptors with its NiDAR platform, an AI-enabled command and control centre, to improve the country’s ability to detect, deter and defeat airborne threats.
The deal forms part of Taskforce Sabre, the British effort that brings government and industry together to help Gulf states secure systems and weapons quickly, and it follows Iranian missile and drone attacks in the region.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard said: “This deal is a clear demonstration of the UK delivering on its promise to support our regional partners.
“By backing Kuwait with world-leading British technology, we’re not just strengthening a vital ally’s defences against real and growing threats. We’re creating skilled jobs here at home and proving that UK industry can deliver when it matters most.”
Johannes Pinl, chief executive of MARSS, said: “Countering drones and aerial threats is not about any single system, it is about an intelligent, layered architecture that detects, decides and defeats within seconds, and MARSS has built exactly that.
“Through 2027, MARSS will integrate the sensors and effectors that protect Kuwait’s people, critical infrastructure and national assets, backed by British engineering and new skilled jobs here in the UK.”
Britain has already supported Kuwait with Rapid Sentry, a ground-based air defence missile system, and the Royal Air Force’s ORCUS counter-drone system is operating in the country, helping personnel detect drones early and act on what they find.
The Ministry of Defence describes the latest contract as building on that existing support and cementing Britain’s role as a defence partner to Kuwait and the wider Gulf region.

When women share a husband, physical fights between co-wives are common across cultures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:00:33 UTC
21:00:33 KST

A cross-cultural analysis of ethnographic records suggests that when women share a husband in polygynous marriages, physical fights between co-wives are common. Physical aggression was documented in most of the 19 cultures examined, providing evidence that women’s competition can include direct confrontation when the stakes are high, in contrast to the prevailing view that female rivalry is mostly indirect. The research was published in Evolution and Human Behavior.
What drives competition among women? Evolutionary theories have suggested that women avoid physical fights to protect their survival and the lives of their children, relying instead on indirect social tactics. For example, a theory called the “staying alive” hypothesis, proposed by psychologist Anne Campbell in a 1999 paper, suggested that natural selection favored risk-averse strategies in women because physical injury could severely harm the survival chances of their highly dependent infants.
Building on this idea, a 2013 review summarized the prevailing scientific view that women primarily compete for mates through indirect aggression, such as gossip and social exclusion, rather than physical fights. This aligns with a study covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that women reported more envy toward well-off same-sex peers than men did and were more likely to engage in indirect competition such as gossip and spreading rumors.
However, anthropological surveys of polygynous marriages, in which a man has more than one wife at the same time, indicate a different pattern. When high-stakes resources and partners are on the line, direct physical conflict between women appears common. For instance, a 2005 cross-cultural study of polygynous societies found that co-wives routinely experience intense jealousy and often resort to verbal and physical violence when competing for their shared husband.
Maryanne L. Fisher of Saint Mary’s University in Canada set out to examine this dynamic systematically. She notes that much of the evidence for indirect competition comes from laboratory and survey studies of young women in Western countries competing over low or hypothetical stakes with rivals they did not know. In Fisher’s reading, the staying alive hypothesis was always conditional: women weigh the costs of physical risk more heavily than men, but direct aggression should become more likely when the payoff is high enough. She used co-wife arrangements as a test case, since co-wives compete repeatedly, over years, for resources that bear on their reproductive success and their children’s survival.
To explore how co-wives compete, Fisher analyzed ethnographic records, which are detailed written accounts by anthropologists and other observers who studied or lived among particular communities. The records came from the eHRAF World Cultures database, a comprehensive collection of cultural texts. She examined records from 19 distinct cultures spanning five major world regions (Africa, the Middle East, North America, South America, and Oceania), ranging from hunter-gatherer groups to intensive agricultural communities. Fisher coded the historical and cultural texts using a four-part system focused on the causes of co-wife competition, the modes of competition used, how conflicts were resolved, and what strategies were used to prevent disputes in the first place.
Fisher searched the database for records combining polygamy and wives with terms such as aggression, violent, and fight, and kept only records that directly described competition or conflict between co-wives. Three cultures turned up in the search but were excluded because their records described peaceful relations or no conflict between co-wives. Each remaining culture was coded for whether a given behavior was documented at all, so the percentages below reflect the share of cultures where a behavior appeared in the records, not how often it occurred. A second, independent coder applied the same scheme, and the two refined their definitions until they fully agreed.
The analysis indicates that competition for the husband’s sexual and emotional attention was the primary cause of conflict, documented in 14 of the 19 cultures (73.7 percent). This included jealousy over sleeping arrangements, fear of being replaced, and competition for general affection. Competition over material resources, such as food, garden plots, livestock, and unequal distribution of resources to children, was the second most frequent cause, present in 7 of the 19 cultures (36.8 percent). Status competition, such as rivalry over who is senior wife, was a third cause, identified in 5 cultures (26.3 percent).
When looking at how women competed, direct physical aggression was the most frequently documented method. Fisher found explicit accounts of physical fighting in 12 of the 19 cultures (63.2 percent). This low-level direct combat included behaviors like hitting, biting, hair-pulling, and occasionally the use of objects like sticks or paddles, though a few accounts were more severe, including one in which a woman was knocked senseless and others describing fights that caused injury. Verbal aggression, such as face-to-face shouting matches, direct insults, and arguments, was documented in 10 cultures (52.6 percent).
Covert hostility, where women maintained an icy or deliberately hostile atmosphere without open fighting, appeared in 6 cultures (31.6 percent). Less common strategies included the use of supernatural means, such as curses or food pollution rituals, which were noted in 4 cultures (21.1 percent). Gossip and social exclusion, often considered classic indirect tactics, appeared in only 2 cultures. In a few cultures, competition took the form of property destruction, such as tearing a rival’s belongings or deliberately ruining her prepared food.
Because indirect tactics were split into many separate categories, Fisher also grouped them into a single category for a fairer comparison. Combined indirect aggression appeared in 9 to 11 of the 19 cultures (47 to 58 percent), depending on how broadly it was defined, compared with 12 cultures for physical aggression. Direct confrontation of any kind, physical or verbal, was documented in 14 cultures (73.7 percent).
The findings suggest that physical confrontation is a common element of co-wife rivalry, occurring alongside indirect strategies rather than replacing them.
The study also looked at how disputes between co-wives were handled. The most common resolutions, each documented in 9 of the 19 cultures (47.4 percent), were the husband intervening to arbitrate or separate the wives and the permanent dissolution of the relationship, such as a wife fleeing or being expelled. Less frequently, conflicts were arbitrated by community members, such as in-laws or neighbors, which happened in 8 cultures (42.1 percent). Only rarely were co-wives documented resolving a conflict through quiet negotiation among themselves.
Many societies also had arrangements that kept co-wives apart or reduced friction between them. The most common preventative measure was the spatial separation of wives, documented in 11 cultures (57.9 percent). This involved housing wives in separate dwellings, assigning them different cooking fires, or even placing them in completely different settlements, which Fisher interprets as a way of managing co-wife conflict.
Another common preventative strategy, found in 7 cultures (36.8 percent), was a cultural preference for marrying sisters, known as sororal polygyny. Ethnographic records often stated that men preferred sisters as co-wives because they tended to fight less than unrelated women. Evolutionary theory suggests that individuals are less likely to harm close genetic relatives because they share many of the same genes, meaning a sister’s reproductive success indirectly benefits the other sister. Fisher argues that the cross-cultural prevalence of this arrangement suggests societies implicitly recognize the volatility of non-kin co-wives and organize households to deter anticipated conflict.
“This study provides a valuable cross-cultural perspective by reviewing 19 different cultures, challenging the lab-based view that women’s competition is always indirect,” said Farid Pazhoohi, an interdisciplinary psychologist and researcher at the University of Plymouth who was not involved in the research.
Pazhoohi noted that the results should be viewed in their specific context. “[W]hile readers might mistakenly interpret this as proof that women are universally violent, the findings instead point to a flexible strategy where women use direct aggression when the stakes are high enough to outweigh the risks,” he told PsyPost.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on a sample of 19 cultures, which limits how broadly the prevalence estimates can be generalized. Fisher also notes that the contrast with laboratory studies is suggestive rather than a direct test, since those studies differ from ethnographic records in their populations and methods. The sample was uneven as well: 13 of the 19 cultures were in the Americas, while Africa was represented by a single culture.
Pazhoohi also pointed out limitations in the study’s design. “Because it relies on second-hand ethnographic records, observational secondary data is inherently less informative for pinning down strict causal relationships. While we can spot broad patterns, we cannot isolate direct cause-and-effect or rule out hidden confounders,” he said, referring to other factors that could explain the pattern.
“Furthermore, reducing complex cultural behaviors down to summary percentages and binary metrics (such as noting whether a behavior is simply present or absent) can conceal individual variations and local context,” Pazhoohi added. “Historical field notes are prone to reporting biases, meaning dramatic physical fights are much easier for ethnographers to record than covert hostility or quieter tensions.”
Fisher acknowledges this issue as well, noting that her search terms were geared toward overt conflict, so the prevalence of indirect tactics should be read as a minimum. The data also captured whether conflict occurred but not its intensity or duration. Future longitudinal research could show how verbal disputes escalate into physical fights and when these conflicts are successfully interrupted.
The study, “The battle of the brides: Co-wife competition and aggression across 19 cultures,” was authored by Maryanne L. Fisher.
