UN aid operation underway in Nepal following fresh floods
The United Nations has rushed to assist Nepal following new flash floods in the central Gorkha district on Sunday that swept away homes and bridges just weeks after catastrophic flooding in the north.
At least five people are missing and 95 have been rescued, according to the authorities. Hundreds are affected.
It is believed the disaster was caused by a landslide that blocked the Budhi Gandaki River.
‘We stand with Nepal’
“Our hearts are with every family affected by the Budhi Gandaki floods,” the UN Country Team said on social media. “We stand with Nepal.”
The UN is supporting the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) in getting food to those who lost their homes.
The World Food Programme (WFP) said on Sunday that three trucks carrying ready-to-eat food and relief supplies were on the way to help meet the immediate needs of affected communities.
Food security at risk
The “devastating” floods have damaged key roads, crops and livestock, threatening local food security, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said in a post on social media.
The UN Country Team said FAO drones and satellite imagery by the UN humanitarian affairs office OCHA are being used to “map damage in places roads can’t reach.”
Families in need
The raging flood waters disrupted essential services that children and families rely on, including water supply, education and healthcare. Displaced families now require safe shelter, clean drinking water, child protection and psychosocial support
UN children’s agency UNICEF is supporting rapid assessments to identify impacts and to determine priorities for the immediate response.
UNICEF also has stocks of emergency supplies pre-positioned and ready for deployment, including hygiene kits, water treatment supplies, dignity kits, winter clothing, education materials and psychosocial support services.
Communities in Nepal are still reeling from the impact of flooding in late August that was triggered by a glacier collapse in the Himalayas. At least 1,400 people were killed and more than 5,000 are still missing.

‘Efficiency has limits’: UNHCR chief warns refugee protection is buckling under cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

‘Efficiency has limits’: UNHCR chief warns refugee protection is buckling under cuts
The money is running out faster than needs are growing: with 117 million men, women and children now forced from their homes, the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) has received just $3 billion of the $8.5 billion it needs this year – and its chief, Barham Salih, warns that the global support system for asylum-seekers risks buckling.
Protection at risk
UNHCR was created after the Second World War with the pledge that people fleeing persecution should be protected and not sent back to places where they might be in danger. Today, that pledge is under strain as deep funding cuts take effect.
In his first keynote address to UNHCR’s Executive Committee meeting in Geneva on Monday, Mr. Salih stressed that the world’s most vulnerable are going without the help they need.
“There is…a difference between doing more with less and being asked to do the impossible,” he said, while also highlighting the “exceptionally difficult year” at the agency, marked by the departure of 8,000 staff since 2024.
Cost of cuts in Sudan, Chad and beyond
He added: “In Sudan, insufficient funding threatens specialised medical care, legal assistance and psychological support for more than 50,000 survivors of conflict-related sexual violence. In Chad, services for thousands of unaccompanied and separated children and children with specific protection needs are at risk.”
In Ethiopia, meanwhile, refugee registration has been halted for tens of thousands of people arriving from South Sudan and Eritrea, while hundreds of thousands more are awaiting verification and integration into the national identification system.
Worldwide crisis
Conflicts are uprooting people faster than governments and aid agencies can help them.
So far in 2026, UNHCR has responded to 22 emergencies in 18 countries, from Yemen to the Horn of Africa and from Sudan to the Sahel.
Despite growing humanitarian needs, the agency has received less than one third of its funding requirement for this year.
Mr. Salih warned that countries that have hosted refugees for decades are frustrated at the lack of international solidarity, while refugees themselves are increasingly afraid for their safety, amid deep cuts to assistance.
The result is that women and girls are more exposed to violence and exploitation, children are losing years of education and persons with disabilities face protection barriers, the High Commissioner said, in an appeal for greater support.
“Efficiency has limits. There comes a point when greater efficiency cannot compensate for fewer resources. When funding falls below that point, the consequences are not abstract, they are borne by people who depend on it,” he insisted.
Inhumane treatment
At the end of last month, Mr. Salih – a former Kurdish politician and President of Iraq – told the Security Council that the situation for refugees today was “genuinely, truly, inhumane”.
Speaking in Geneva, the UNHCR chief highlighted an initiative launched earlier this year that aims to halve the number of refugees living in protracted displacement and depending on humanitarian assistance by 2035.
Nearly 14.5 million refugees in low and middle-income countries currently rely on aid to meet their basic requirements, he said.
“We cannot claim success simply because assistance has been reduced or responsibility has been transferred to host countries,” he added.
“Success is measured by whether people’s lives have genuinely improved and whether they have become self-reliant and active contributors to their communities. For those who still require humanitarian support, our responsibility remains.”
Mr. Salih urged solidarity and empathy with asylum-seekers, whose long-standing plight and hardship remains unresolved around the world. “When we speak about refugees and displacement, we should do so with humility,” he said.
“None of us knows who may be forced to flee tomorrow, or who may be called upon to offer refuge.”

Colombia peace deal must endure as insecurity grows, Security Council hears
Nearly 10 years after Colombia signed a historic peace agreement to end a decades-long insurgency, the deal is under strain from growing insecurity – and the UN’s top official in the country says it cannot be allowed to falter.
Miroslav Jenča told the Security Council on Monday that the 2016 accord must be implemented in full, with proper funding, better coordination between institutions and protection for former combatants.
He pointed to real gains: rural development, and mechanisms for transitional justice and reparation for victims. But he admitted that implementation has had “many shortcomings” and that much remains to be done.
Security policy and the peace agreement should reinforce each other, Mr. Jenča said, and the accord should be carried out comprehensively.
“We look forward to the further definition of its policies, and we stand ready to support the Government in this regard,” he said, offering the experience gained by the UN Verification Mission over almost a decade of supporting implementation.
Violence stalks communities
Communities in conflict-affected regions remain exposed to armed groups, geographical isolation and limited access to public services. Child recruitment, particularly among ethnic communities, and threats and attacks against women remain major concerns, ambassadors heard.
Government data presented to legislators show that illegal armed groups grew from around 15,000 members in 2022 to approximately 28,000 today.
Mr. Jenča also condemned the killings of civil society leaders María Ovidia Palechor and James Flor in Cauca on 1 September, highlighting the risks faced by rights defenders.
He said expanding economic opportunities, improving public services and strengthening local institutions were essential to reducing violence.
Reintegration commitment
Despite these challenges, more than 11,000 former members of the FARC-EP rebel group remain committed to reintegration.
With State and international support, they have developed around 6,000 productive projects and 300 cooperatives in sectors including agriculture, tourism, trade and textiles.
Mr. Jenča highlighted tourism initiatives involving former combatants and victims, aimed at stimulating local economies and job markets.
However, economic sustainability and security remain significant challenges. Since the agreement was signed in 2016, 501 former combatants have been killed, most recently on 22 September in Cesar.
The Special Representative reaffirmed the UN mission's readiness to continue supporting implementation and highlighted its value on the ground, noting that over almost a decade it had built relationships of trust in some of regions most impacted by continuing violence.
Colombia had entered “a new political chapter, with wide ranging challenges ahead,” Mr. Jenča said, calling for “sustained international engagement in order to overcome remaining obstacles.”

Sudan: Drought and war push Darfur and Kordofan towards famine

Sudan: Drought and war push Darfur and Kordofan towards famine
The risk of famine is growing in parts of Sudan already torn apart by war, as a severe El Niño drought makes life even harder in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan, the UN-backed global hunger monitor warned on Monday.
In a new alert, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) said fresh evidence shows malnutrition getting worse in several hotspots. Aid is not keeping up, held back by a severe lack of funding, insecurity and restricted access.
The IPC food insecurity alert index is a global partnership that includes the UN emergency food agency WFP and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).
Read our UN News explainer here
In Eastern Jebel Marra, South Darfur, a survey of two camps for displaced people found acute malnutrition among children at 38 and 30.8 per cent – above the threshold for famine. Hunger was severe and death rates were high.
Across Greater Darfur, 13 of the 17 nutrition surveys carried out since January found critical levels of acute malnutrition.
In Nyala, the share of children seeking nutrition help who needed treatment for severe acute malnutrition more than doubled between January and August, from five to 11 per cent.
Drought on top of war
Drought now covers more than half of Sudan, wiping out crops in some areas and leaving families without food or income.
In North Darfur, 64 per cent of cropland is showing poor plant growth.
Rains arrived in late September, too late to save most cereal crops, the alert said, and cereal prices are very likely to keep rising.
Greater Kordofan, described in the alert as the epicentre of Sudan’s conflict, has seen more than 300,000 people forced from their homes since October 2025. Markets have been hit by more than 170 airstrikes, looting incidents or armed clashes this year.
Aid workers face extreme danger. Two trucks contracted by WFP came under fire on 2 and 3 October, killing at least one person.
Children are going without treatment. As of August, only 26 per cent of those expected to need care for severe acute malnutrition with medical complications had received it. Without treatment, as many as two thirds of them could die.
As of 8 October, less than half of the humanitarian appeal for Sudan had been funded.
‘A humanitarian catastrophe’
The IPC’s Famine Review Committee said there is not enough survey data for a full analysis, but the evidence points to a rapidly worsening situation.
“Famine is the collapse of systems,” the committee said. “We are witnessing a humanitarian catastrophe, already of historic proportions.”
The alert called for an end to the fighting, safe and sustained access for aid agencies – especially in North and West Kordofan – and flexible funding on a large scale. Without a major increase in help, it warned, more lives will be at risk.

General Assembly adopts pandemic declaration, but not by consensus

General Assembly adopts pandemic declaration, but not by consensus
The General Assembly on Monday adopted a political declaration on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response, by 153 in favour to three against (Argentina, Israel and United States) with two abstentions (New Zealand and Paraguay).
The text was due to be approved by consensus at a high-level meeting on 25 September.
Objections from the United States and a few other States blocked that, pushing the issue back to the assembly.
Read the full political declaration here.
Chile’s representative summed up one prevailing view, saying that “no country, no matter how big it might be or how prepared it might be, can alone address a threat that knows no borders.”
The declaration is political and non-binding. It calls for stronger national, regional and international cooperation, guided by science, equity and respect for human rights, and it welcomes last year’s landmark adoption of the World Health Organization (WHO) Pandemic Agreement.
“WHO welcomes this strong commitment by UN Member States to continue working together on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response,” said World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.
“The world has come a long way since COVID-19. We urge countries to now fulfil the commitments they have made – especially to finalize negotiations on the Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing system (PABS) annex, so the WHO Pandemic Agreement can be opened for signature, begin the process of ratification and enter into force as international law.”
Unfinished annex
The agreement cannot be opened for signature until Member States complete the annex on pathogen access and benefit-sharing – the system by which countries would share samples and genetic data.
Those that do so would receive a share of any resulting vaccines, treatments and diagnostics.
Talks have stalled amid a standoff between developing countries and some high-income European nations together with the US.
The World Health Assembly – comprising the WHO’s 194 members – is due to return to the annex next May.
The US representative had previously cited “divisive ideologies that lack definitional consensus” as well as the declaration’s references to the continuing annex negotiations.
More action in the General Assembly
In addition to adopting the pandemic declaration, the 193-member world body had a number of items on its agenda on Monday, including the consideration of draft resolutions on the UN Declaration on Sea Level Rise and a political declaration of the high-level meeting to mark the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the anti-racism Durban Declaration and Programme of Action.
Read a summary of the meeting here.
WHO aims to spot new outbreaks within 24 hours
The World Health Organization (WHO) on Monday launched a five-year strategy for its Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence, with the goal of detecting emerging health threats within 24 hours.
Set up in 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic, the hub wants every country to be able to identify and understand new threats quickly, so outbreaks can be contained before they become epidemics or spread internationally.

Is a “Hardwired Pause” of AI Possible?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:55:59 UTC
20:55:59 KST

Various parties concerned about the risks that artificial intelligence (AI) pose to humanity have called for a pause in its development. But such a call faces a difficult collective action problem.
Can it be solved?
I have been skeptical (and suggested an alternate type of approach to AI safety here). But a new report argues that a pause is indeed possible.
Drafted by the Working Group on AI Pause Feasibility, an interdisciplinary group led by statistician William Fithian and philosopher Wesley H. Holliday (both of Berkeley), the report‘s focus is:
a scenario in which world leaders would prefer pausing to not pausing if they could be confident that others were also pausing or that defections from a pause would be detected within a reasonable timeframe. In such a pause-willing scenario, is a pause for at least a decade feasible?
Their answer is that a “hardwired pause” is feasible. What is a hardwired pause?
A hardwired pause would stop the production of training-capable AI chips, which are needed to develop more powerful AI models. Over time a hardwired pause would also phase out most or all of the pre-pause stock of such chips. It would replace them with inference-only AI chips, which are capable of fast, energy-efficient AI inference on approved models but are not practically useful for training new frontier AI models, even if stolen or seized, due to the way the chips are constructed.
Such a pause is feasible, they argue, mainly because of two sets of facts. The first concerns chip production:
The supply chain for AI chips is highly concentrated with several chokepoints, bolstering governments’ abilities to enforce rules on the production of such chips. In addition, bypassing existing supply chains is extraordinarily difficult.
The second concerns the demands of training new models:
Because training new models requires large numbers of training-capable chips, the feasibility of verification is an inherently quantitative question: while it is next to impossible to detect an evader who is using a single computer to train a small AI model, it is far easier to detect an evader who is training a frontier-scale AI model using hundreds of thousands or millions of chips... To research and train a new model that would significantly advance the frontier after a hardwired pause, absent an unforeseen methodological breakthrough, an evader would need to marshal a significant fraction of the world’s total computing capacity for months or years at a time.
The above quotes are from the executive summary of the report. The full report is here, and a press release from Berkeley about it is here.
Discussion welcome.
(via Wesley Holliday)

Chinese-owned rental cars recorded Norwegian military drill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:55:48 UTC
20:55:48 KST

- Chinese-owned rental cars used in a Norwegian Home Guard exercise stored video of soldiers, their movements and codes entered at military gates, a participating officer said.
- The recordings were deleted afterward, but it is not known whether the data stayed only on the cars; Volvo Cars denies any security risk.
Rental cars used by Norway’s Home Guard during a large exercise in September recorded video of soldiers, their routes and the codes they typed into military gates, according to a soldier who took part, Norwegian business daily Dagens Næringsliv reported.
The cars were rented by the Norwegian Armed Forces from Hertz in Norway, which belongs to Volvo Cars and, through Volvo, to China’s Geely group. At least two of them were electric cars from Deepal, a brand of Chinese automaker Changan, according to Norwegian media. Soldiers discovered during Exercise Hovedstad, or “Capital,” that the vehicles had a recording function no one had asked for or told them about. The unit kept using the cars for the rest of the exercise because few other vehicles were available.
Lt. Fredrik Blanck, who took part in the exercise, told the newspaper that the stored video showed who got in and out of the cars, where they drove, who they picked up and how long they stayed at different locations. He said the recordings also captured the access codes soldiers entered to open military gates and doors, and that it was unclear whether the data stayed in the car or went anywhere else. Two other unnamed sources confirmed the account to Dagens Næringsliv, and newspaper VG said a separate source told it the recordings were raised during the exercise.
The recordings were deleted from the cars after the exercise, according to Norwegian media, but it is not known whether the data was stored only on the vehicles. Volvo Cars rejected the idea that Chinese ownership poses a security risk and said no data can be shared with Geely without a legal basis. The Norwegian Armed Forces had not publicly explained why the cars were rented or whether it will review the use of such vehicles.
Exercise Hovedstad ran from Sept. 14 to 18 and was the Home Guard’s largest exercise of the year. About 5,000 soldiers from the Oslo and Akershus Home Guard District trained across the capital region, including around the parliament and government buildings. Part of the exercise focused on protecting Oslo Airport, Gardermoen, in wartime. The Home Guard is Norway’s territorial defense force, made up mostly of reservists who guard key infrastructure at home.
Modern cars carry cameras for parking, driver monitoring and dashcam-style recording, along with GPS and internet connections that can send data back to the manufacturer. That has raised concerns about Chinese-made vehicles in several Western countries. In Norway, Oslo’s public transport operator Ruter said last year that tests found the Chinese bus maker Yutong had remote access to the software of electric buses it had supplied, which in theory could allow them to be stopped.
It is not clear whether the Deepal cars were set to record by default, whether the video was ever uploaded, or whether the Norwegian Armed Forces will bar Chinese-owned or Chinese-built vehicles from future exercises.

Israel has reportedly introduced restrictions barring foreign airline pilots and cabin crew who hold citizenship in countries without diplomatic relations with Israel from serving on flights entering its airspace, with United Airlines and Air France reportedly adjusting their crew assignments in response.
The new security measures come after the attempted hijacking of a Flydubai flight to Tel Aviv last month by an Omani co-pilot. The incident raised concerns about Israel's screening of foreign flight crews and prompted Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to order a review of aviation security.
On Thursday, Israel's Kan public broadcaster reported that the Transportation Ministry's Aviation Security Operations Center had issued a series of new and updated directives following the Flydubai incident. According to Kan, the guidelines bar pilots and flight attendants who hold citizenship in countries that lack diplomatic relations with Israel, including dual nationals.
"The airline is exclusively responsible for ensuring that all flight crew members do not hold citizenship, or are not dual nationals, of countries that do not have official diplomatic relations with the State of Israel," the directive reportedly says.
On Saturday, Live and Let's Fly, an aviation blog, reported that United Airlines had notified its pilots and flight attendants of the new policy, asking affected crew members scheduled to fly to Tel Aviv to contact the airline's scheduling department.
"Our teams will work with you to make any necessary scheduling adjustments," the airline told employees, according to an internal memo that the blog did not publish.
The same day, French investigative website Mediapart reported that Air France had issued a similar memo to its pilots and flight attendants, informing them of the new restrictions and their implications for crew scheduling.
Both outlets published lists of countries whose nationals are barred from serving on flights entering Israeli airspace. The lists include Saudi Arabia, Iran, Malaysia, Venezuela and Pakistan, as well as Oman, the home country of the Flydubai co-pilot involved in the attempted hijacking.
Live and Let's Fly reported that the restrictions apply to nationals of 29 countries, while Mediapart listed 31, adding Nicaragua and Colombia.
Business Insider Africa reported on Monday, citing the United Airlines memo, that ten African countries are also included: Algeria, Comoros, Djibouti, Libya, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Somalia, Sudan and Tunisia.
Both Nicaragua and Colombia severed diplomatic ties with Israel in recent years over the war in Gaza. However, Colombia's new president has pledged to strengthen ties, and Bogota's embassy in Jerusalem is expected to officially open later this week.
Netanyahu ordered a review of security procedures for foreign civil aviation four days after the Flydubai incident. He instructed National Security Council chief Shmuel Ben Ezra to appoint an examiner to conduct a thorough review of aviation security. Haaretz previously reported that the National Security Council had warned of shortcomings in the Transportation Ministry's screening of foreign flights.
Haaretz has contacted both United Airlines and Air France for comment.
On September 30, Flydubai Flight 1073 was traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv when its Omani co-pilot, later identified as Hamam al-Hammami, attacked the captain in an attempt to seize control of the aircraft. Despite his injuries, the captain, Indian national Smit Machchhar, managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew members to intervene. Two other pilots and several Israeli passengers subdued al-Hammami, and the plane landed safely in Saudi Arabia.
Last Friday, the United Arab Emirates' attorney general confirmed earlier reports that al-Hammami, inspired by the September 11 attacks, had planned to crash the plane into Ben-Gurion Airport, Israel's largest airport, according to state-run news agency WAM.

Love blooms on a hostile colony world in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:55:02 UTC
20:55:02 KST

One of science fiction’s oldest themes is its insistence that the future isn’t inevitable. Few contemporary authors embody that idea more than Becky Chambers, whose stories imagine alternative futures—not through grand revolutions or galaxy-spanning battles but through ordinary people trying to care for one another.
As a defining voice of the “hopepunk” genre, Chambers has built a reputation for science fiction that prizes empathy as much as imagination. Her latest novel, As You Wake, Break the Shell, brings us to the hostile, unpredictable world of Fortune, where acid rain falls and billowing volcanoes shroud the horizon. The story follows a reclusive botanist and a spacefaring pilot across alternating timelines as they search for connection and purpose, attempting to navigate a life where Fortune has never favored the bold.
We caught up with Chambers to discuss a toxic planet’s world-building, scientific accuracy in storytelling and the motivational merits of unrelenting spite.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
[An edited transcript of the interview follows.]
This story spends a lot of time on a colony planet with a poisonous atmosphere. What does designing an ecosystem teach you about designing a civilization?
Everything. It’s really important for me to start with what the environmental conditions are because that’s going to affect everything from what we’re eating, what we’re building houses out of, what kind of clothes we have—and all of those things, in turn, affect culture. There is so much about our values, our personalities, that are actually molded by the physical environments we exist in, both natural and constructed.
Starting from [the questions] “what do we have” and “what do we not have” is really important for me. Suppose someone’s eating a sandwich. What’s in the sandwich? It’s a throwaway line that seems like it doesn’t matter, but it’s actually really important to say whether or not there’s lettuce in this sandwich, because that does communicate a lot of information about how this world works.
For this book, I had a really big table of crops [to reference], what are we growing, how are we growing it, what’s available and what’s not?
Those are details I spend a lot of time sussing out before I really get into the thick of drafting the story.
What specific ideas inspired the scientific foundation for this story?
Botany is the big one. I have always had an appreciation for plants but not any actual sort of technical knowledge about what it is that I’m looking at. So I did a lot of research for this book into how plants work, and specifically into seeds, which is a topic I have become fascinated by the more I learn about it. Seeds are a big part of this book, as are plants and the way they communicate with each other.
How does scientific accuracy influence your storytelling? Do you often find yourself molding the plot to fit the science, or vice versa?
I look at science as partially a foundation but more of a tool that I use to color the world that I’m in. I want it to feel tangible and possible, but I’m very willing to take some liberties here and there for the sake of getting the feeling across.
I tend to think of what I’m doing as more like impressionism than photorealism. If you think of something like Monet’s Water Lilies, for example, it doesn’t look like a real pond, right? But it feels like a real pond. And I often use a similar approach with my work. I am not necessarily painting you a picture of the cosmos as it actually exists, but what I’m trying to communicate is the sense of wonder and awe that I feel when I’m experiencing those things in the real world. So it’s a matter of getting the emotional quality of discovery across, and sometimes that does mean taking shortcuts.
With As You Wake Break the Shell, I kept it within the realm of “with sufficient technology, this could be possible.” Is it probable? Probably not. There are a lot of things that I gloss over because they’re not things that everyday people outside of science would know about or understand. We know [in the reality of the story] that there are giant space-dwelling creatures out there. We don’t need to know how it is that they evolved or what kind of world it is that they came from. Those are questions that interest me as a person who is into real science, but they don’t serve the story.
This book has a knack for taking the unknown and making it feel familiar while making the familiar feel unknown, simply by showing it from a new perspective—for instance, that of an enormous, cargo-toting space behemoth. How do you get into the headspace of examining humanity from the outside?
It’s a highly technical process that involves me sitting in my armchair and just staring at the ceiling and thinking about what it would be like to have a body other than mine, and just sort of deconstructing everything that makes me down to the raw components and trying to figure out what it is that’s necessary and what’s not.
I take a lot of inspiration from the natural world. I have a really keen interest in invertebrate life and in deep-sea life, and I have a real interest in animal intelligence that exists in nonmammalian creatures.
What would it mean to communicate through color? What would it mean to communicate through pheromones? What does the world feel like if you don’t have a sense of sight like we do? I just love taking any one of those traits and then expanding it to make something that we would recognize as a person, regardless of whether they physically look like us or not. How does that make you think about yourself? How does that make you think about existence?
As You Wake, Break the Shell is a love story as much as a space story. What did pairing those genres let you explore that you couldn’t do with either one on their own?
It allowed me the freedom to not segment any of the things I was thinking of into separate boxes. This was a really personal book for me in that I’m writing about everything I care about in this one. I’m writing about the natural world, I’m writing about society, and I am also writing about love, romantic love, and these are all things that are extremely important to me in my everyday life.
We have a bazillion stories about “and then they lived happily ever after,” but I actually want to see what that looks like because it’s never that simple.I feel that the most interesting parts of a relationship are what happens “after,” and so that was what drove a large part of my decision to have [the book] be a split timeline, where it’s very clear from the jump that they’re going to be together a long time and we’re going to see all these different stages in what makes them them, because I do think that that’s an area that is underexplored.
You’ve said before that you write the stories that you need to hear. What did you need to hear from this book?
I wanted to see a relationship that matched my own. Queer representation in media is better than ever in a lot of ways, and yet it’s still very rare to see anybody over their 20s.
By the time we started getting more stories about coming of age or people falling in love when they’re young, I was already too old for those stories. I was feeling a real frustration in not finding love stories that spoke to me where I am now in my life. It was one of those things of, “I guess I’ll just have to write it myself.”
Your work has been described as “wholesome,” “thoughtful” and “heartwarming.” How much of your inspiration and motivation actually comes from spite?
[Maniacal cackling] So much! I’m so happy you asked this question because so many people come at it from, like, “How do you maintain hope? How do you maintain the sense of coziness?” And the answer is that I am so pissed off all the time about everything. And honestly, so much of it does come from a place of looking at so many of the directions we are headed in the real world, so many of the decisions we are making about technology, about the environment, about how we organize ourselves as a society, feeling the crushing, overwhelming despair that I know we all feel and then just flipping that off and saying, “I’m sorry, I don’t accept that this is all there is and that it has to be like this.”

"This could involve sabotage attacks on the territory of a NATO member state against a facility connected to aid for Ukraine, a drone or missile attack on a weapons depot intended for Ukraine, or, in an extreme case, even a limited military action against one of the neighbouring member states of the Alliance," Koudelka said.

According to the intelligence chief, Moscow's hybrid operations, which can include sabotage, cyberattacks and other disruptive activities, are designed to undermine cohesion within NATO and weaken the alliance's collective response to Russia's war in Ukraine.
His assessment comes amid growing concerns over the possibility that Russia could expand its confrontation with Western countries beyond Ukraine without launching a full-scale military attack against NATO.

AI boom could widen income inequality, Labor MP warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:45:08 UTC
20:45:08 KST

AI boom could widen income inequality, with only a handful of 'toll collectors' benefiting
In short:
Labor MP Andrew Leigh says artificial intelligence (AI) could see wage gaps shrink but he is concerned overall income inequality could rise.
He warns that a handful of AI companies could end up being the main economic beneficiaries.
What's next?
This week a Senate committee looking into AI guardrails will table their interim findings to the government.
If a handful of artificial intelligence (AI) companies become "toll collectors" for the rest of the economy, overall income inequality could rise even as wage gaps shrink, an MP is warning.
The assistant minister for productivity, competition, charities and treasury, Andrew Leigh, will make a case for whether AI increases inequality, during a speech to JPMorgan AI Conference tomorrow.
In an advance excerpt of his speech, Mr Leigh will argue that the biggest gains from AI may flow to those who own the technology, rather than those who use it.
"If a handful of AI companies become toll collectors for the rest of the economy, overall income inequality could rise even as wage gaps shrink," he will say.
Mr Leigh will make the link that while AI makes a junior worker more productive, it could reduce the number of junior workers a firm needs.
He will say the employment scoreboard currently reads: some concerning signals for young Americans, much less movement in Denmark, and Australian entry-level outcomes that remain solid.
It is possible that the US is atypical, or that effects there are driven primarily by the shift towards working from home. But it is also possible that the US is experiencing the impact of AI a year or two earlier than the rest of the advanced world.
He will argue if the junior accountant catches up with the senior accountant, the wage premium attached to education and experience falls and wage inequality could decline.
"Yet total income inequality could still rise. The reason is ownership," Mr Leigh will outline.
"It is quite possible for the first to become more equal while the second becomes more unequal. That could occur if pay packets equalise but the economy tilts in favour of capital."
He will highlight that AI can be a huge driver of productivity and economic benefit for Australia, but first people have to be able to trust that the technology is working for them, and not the other way around.
As assistant minister for competition, he says he is now "thinking hard about the effects of market structure".
He argues if every bank, law firm, retailer and manufacturer relies on a small number of upstream AI systems, then the model provider begins to resemble a toll road sitting across a growing share of the economy.
"The economic question is the size of the toll."
Mr Leigh will warn that a business may achieve a productivity improvement, yet retain only part of it if suppliers possess pricing power and competitors quickly copy the innovation.
Conversely, an AI provider with market power may collect rents across downstream industries.
Therefore the risk of AI on inequality is not primarily through its effect on the wage distribution but on who gets hired, who owns the productive assets, and how much of the surplus is captured by firms with market power.
"AI could narrow the gap between the novice and the expert, but at the same time, it could widen the gap between people who earn mainly from their work and people who earn heavily from owning productive capital."
Mr Leigh will state that AI will boost productivity but distributing the benefits fairly is the real challenge.
"Our government will apply the enduring values of fairness to make AI work for Australians."
Bipartisan agreement on AI guardrails within reach
The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence will this week table their interim findings to the government on AI guardrails.
Chair and Labor MP Jo Briskey joined Afternoon Briefing with the committee's deputy chair and Liberal senator Jonno Duniam to reveal they had come to an agreement about the direction the country should take on AI.
The committee was established to examine the opportunities and risks of AI, and the barriers to adopting the technology.
The federal government is trying to break a months-long gridlock over reforms to copyright laws, as AI companies seek to train their technology on creative content.
Ms Briskey said she sees a pathway to a bipartisan deal that will ensure creatives remain in control of their work.
"That's the key principle for us when negotiating the outcome, but as the study said, we have to get it right for Australia's interest and AI working for us, not the other way around," Ms Briskey said.
Senator Duniam said there needs to be a recognition of Australia's sovereignty and right for people who own copyright to be recompensed for the work they produce.
"I believe there is an opportunity for us to build our own sovereignty under our laws on our terms, our benefit," he said.

Peace must remain at the heart of UNESCO’s mission: Iran

Peace must remain at the heart of UNESCO’s mission: Iran
TEHRAN –Secretary-General of Iran’s National Commission for UNESCO Hassan Fartousi has underlined the importance of preserving peace at the heart of UNESCO’s mission, and urged National Commissions for UNESCO to play a more active and responsible role in sustaining lasting regional and global peace while delivering a talk at the Traditional Meeting of UNESCO National Commissions.
The meeting took place on October 8 and 9, at UNESCO Headquarters in Paris, France, on the sidelines of the 225th Session of the Executive Board. Fartousi addressed the meeting online, IRNA reported.
Referring to the devastating impacts of war in Iran, the official said that wars affect education, scientific cooperation, and common heritage of humanity. He also highlighted that UNESCO’s fundamental vision is to build lasting peace in the minds of women and men through education, culture, science, communication, and dialogue.
Hence, UNESCO and its national commissions bear a great responsibility for fostering regional peace, Fartousi noted.
Underscoring the unparalleled role of national commissions in aligning UNESCO’s global priorities with national realities and capacities, the official said strengthening national cooperation with UNESCO and its National Commissions is among the top priorities of the Iranian National Commission.
The Traditional Meeting of UNESCO National Commissions was opened by UNESCO Director-General Khaled El-Enany and Assistant Director-General for Africa Priority and External Relations Lidia Brito.
The discussions centered on reaffirming the role of National Commissions as a bridge between UNESCO and Member States, enhancing intersectoral cooperation, and increasing field office synergy.
Iran urges UNESCO to help restore scientific infrastructure damaged in war
On October 1, the head of the National Committee for Management of Social Transformations (MOST) called for UNESCO to play an effective role in safeguarding knowledge, ensuring uninterrupted access to learning, and rebuilding academic centers damaged during the US-Israeli imposed war against the country.
Highlighting the destructive impact of conflicts on educational institutions and human capacities, Seyyed Ziae Hashemi said the international community needs to pay close attention to these outcomes, IRNA reported.
The official made the remarks while addressing the extraordinary session of the Intergovernmental Council of MOST Program, which took place at UNESCO headquarters on October 1 in Paris; the official and the Secretary General of Iran’s National Commission for UNESCO attended the session online.
Referring to the impacts of the US-Israeli war against Iran, and the damage inflicted on certain educational and scientific institutions, cultural heritage and civilian infrastructures, he called for UNESCO to utilize its capacities for rebuilding scientific and educational capacities, strengthening international cooperation, and supporting sustainable development.
“International responses must be tailored to the specific circumstances of each crisis, while simultaneously placing the fundamental principles of protecting human lives, safeguarding knowledge, and ensuring the continuity of learning at the heart of these efforts,” he added.
“The catastrophic dimensions of war in Gaza have inflicted irreparable damage on civilians, educational centers, cultural and scientific activities; the international bodies have to make it clear what they can do within the frameworks of BRIDGES and MOST to protect knowledge, sustain education and research,” he added.
The restoration of the right to education for Afghan girls and women was another issue raised by the official.
Fartousi, for his part, emphasized that science is not merely a driver of industry or technology, but an essential part of human life and a factor that enhances our understanding of the world. Access to knowledge, equal learning opportunities, and universal participation in research are fundamental rights in human society.
Referring to UNESCO’s approach to open science, he called for the establishment of specific mechanisms that prevent the monopolization of knowledge, ensure the free flow of knowledge, and strike a balance between supporting researchers and universal access to science.
Highlighting the challenges faced by researchers due to unilateral and coercive measures, the official noted that BRIDGES frame work needs to propose practical solutions to remove barriers to scientific cooperation, prevent concentration of knowledge and power, and consolidate the concept of knowledge as a shared heritage and asset of humanity.
The Intergovernmental Council (IGC) of the MOST Program was established by UNESCO Member States in 1994. It is composed of 35 Member States elected by the General Conference, whose representatives meet every two years to guide and oversee the planning and implementation of the MOST Program. The IGC defines the MOST Program’s broad priorities, reviews its activities and achievements, and helps strengthen the link between social and human sciences research and public policy.
Through its work, the IGC provides a platform for Member States to exchange on contemporary social transformations and to promote more inclusive, evidence-based policies aligned with national priorities.

Çiftçi has embarked on a series of visits to countries where members of Turkish criminal networks are believed to have sought refuge to evade legal proceedings at home.

Speaking to local broadcaster KonTV over the weekend, Çiftçi vowed to intensify the crackdown on organized crime, warning fugitives against assuming they could evade justice by fleeing abroad.
He said his upcoming visits to Germany and Italy would help strengthen cooperation to track down and repatriate suspects wanted in Türkiye.
Turkish gang leader Barış Boyun was arrested in Italy in May 2024 during a joint operation and is currently held at L’Aquila prison under the 41-bis regime, a stringent detention system that severely restricts contact with the outside world.
Italy has rejected Türkiye’s requests concerning Boyun’s extradition and asylum.
In Germany, meanwhile, numerous members of Turkish criminal gangs, specifically Daltons, are known to operate.
Türkiye has increasingly focused on so-called “next-generation gangs,” which have expanded their activities in recent years.
Unlike traditional Turkish mafia groups, these networks frequently recruit minors and teenagers to carry out crimes ranging from extortion to murder. They also use social media to publicize their activities, glorify criminal behavior and attract new recruits.
“As of the end of September, we had conducted 1,741 operations targeting 625 criminal organizations as part of our campaign against next-generation gangs. The total reflects repeated operations against certain groups. These efforts resulted in 8,170 people being arrested and remanded in custody,” Çiftçi said.
He stressed that the groups operate beyond Türkiye’s borders, with members often fleeing overseas when they come under pressure from law enforcement.
“Next-generation criminal organizations do not confine their activities to Türkiye. When they get into trouble, their members immediately flee abroad. I visited Bulgaria in recent months to address this issue, followed by Georgia, where I met with the interior minister. On Thursday [Oct. 8], I was in Greece, holding separate talks with the ministers responsible for citizen protection and migration and asylum,” he said.
Çiftçi said the meetings focused on security cooperation, the activities of emerging criminal networks and the countries in which their members seek shelter.
Türkiye secured the extradition of 736 people from abroad during the first nine months of the year, according to Çiftçi. He said the individuals had committed crimes in Türkiye before fleeing overseas in an attempt to escape prosecution.
“We will increase that number through our upcoming visits and continued security diplomacy. We will pursue every one of them and bring them back to Türkiye,” he added.

UN official: Environmental protection must be integral to post-war recovery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:41:43 UTC
20:41:43 KST

UN official: Environmental protection must be integral to post-war recovery
TEHRAN – UN Resident Coordinator in Iran Christine Weigand has stressed the far-reaching and long-term environmental consequences of war, saying environmental protection must be incorporated into both emergency response measures and long-term recovery plans, as protecting the environment ultimately means safeguarding human health, livelihoods and the future.
Weigand made the remarks in Tehran on Sunday at a conference on the environmental consequences of war and human rights.
Referring to the loss of human lives, the displacement of families and the destruction of homes and infrastructure, she said the environment and valuable ecosystems were also among the victims of war, warning that the damage inflicted on them could persist for generations.
Conflicts and environmental degradation, she noted, reinforce one another, deepening human suffering, undermining livelihoods and food security, and making reconstruction and the achievement of sustainable development more difficult.
Weigand also referred to the United Nations’ designation of November 6 as the International Day for Preventing the Exploitation of the Environment in War and Armed Conflict in 2001. She noted that contaminated water resources, damaged agricultural land and degraded ecosystems have consequences that extend far beyond the immediate destruction caused by war, undermining communities’ ability to rebuild their lives.
Citing examples of environmental damage in the conflicts in Gaza and Ukraine, the UN official addressed the consequences of attacks on oil facilities and water infrastructure in Iran. She said attacks on oil facilities had released smoke containing hazardous substances into Tehran’s atmosphere, while damage to a desalination facility on Qeshm Island had reportedly disrupted water supplies to more than 25 villages.
Weigand also warned of the possibility of oil pollution reaching the mangrove forests on Qeshm Island, emphasizing that such contamination could threaten sensitive coastal ecosystems along the Persian Gulf.
Recalling her own experience of air pollution in Tehran following the attacks on oil facilities, she said that, for millions of people, the issue was not merely an environmental concern but one that directly affected the air they breathed every day.
The UN Resident Coordinator cautioned that the disappearance of visible smoke does not necessarily mean the danger has passed. Burning oil can release hazardous compounds, she explained, and the resulting pollution can contaminate soil and water, affect agricultural produce and threaten human health. These consequences may persist long after a conflict ends, with children and future generations particularly vulnerable.
Emphasizing that investment in environmental protection is an investment in people and their future, Weigand said healthy ecosystems sustain community livelihoods, provide clean water and safe food, and strengthen societies’ resilience to crises. Conversely, the degradation of these systems increases vulnerability and makes recovery more difficult.
She identified evidence-based assessments, stronger national environmental management capacities, cooperation among different sectors and national and international institutions, and investment in climate change adaptation as essential measures for protecting and restoring the environment in conflict-affected countries.
Weigand also highlighted the longstanding cooperation between the UN Country Team in Iran and national partners in areas including climate resilience, sustainable water resource management, biodiversity conservation and pollution reduction. She reaffirmed the UN’s commitment to continuing this cooperation and its readiness to support national efforts to address emerging environmental needs.
Concluding her remarks, the UN official stressed that commitment to protecting and restoring nature must remain unwavering in the face of global environmental challenges.
“Our shared responsibility is to protect what remains, restore what has been damaged, and invest in building a more sustainable and peaceful future for all,” she said.

Mustafa Prize laureate donates award money to support young scientists

Mustafa Prize laureate donates award money to support young scientists
TEHRAN – Turkish Professor Mehmet Toner, a 2025 laureate of the Mustafa Prize, has pledged his share of the prize money to support the development of the Rasul Medal and provide research grants for young scientists.
Toner was named one of three laureates of the Mustafa Prize in 2025. Under the prize’s regulations, the $500,000 cash award was divided among the three recipients.
The biomedical engineering scientist has now pledged his share of the award to jointly support young scientists through the Rasul Medal and fund research grants for early-career researchers.
Before Toner, Professors Ugur Sahin, Omid Farokhzad, and Wahab Mirrokni, laureates of the Mustafa Prize in 2019, 2023, and 2025, respectively, had also donated their prize money to establish and sustain the Rasul (PBUH) Medal.
Born in 1958, Toner is a professor of biomedical engineering at Harvard Medical School. He received the sixth Mustafa Prize in 2025 for developing nanomicrofluidic systems. The technology isolates circulating tumor cells from the bloodstream, enabling earlier disease detection, monitoring of treatment progress, and the development of more precise therapies.
The Rasul Medal is presented alongside the Mustafa Prize to young scientists from the Islamic world under the age of 40.
The initial list of nominees for the second edition of the Rasul Medal, has been finalized.
The shortlist comprises four nominees in engineering sciences, four in mathematics, four in computer science, eight in biological and medical sciences, two in chemistry, and two in physics. The award ceremony for the final winners is scheduled to be held in December.
The initial list considered for the Rasul Medal included more than 100,000 candidates across seven scientific fields. The biological and medical sciences category accounted for 55,878 candidates, followed by 4,675 in physics, 7,897 in chemistry, 1,965 in mathematics, 5,589 in computer science, and 26,377 in engineering sciences. In addition, 14 candidates in the field of nanotechnology met the required criteria to be included in the initial list.
In order to appreciate prominent scientists and provide the ground for scientific cooperation and development worldwide, the Mustafa Prize was established in 2012 as a symbol of scientific excellence at the international level.
The Mustafa Prize, a top science and technology award, is granted biennially to the top researchers and scientists of the Islamic world in three categories: “Life and Medical Science and Technology”, “Information and Communication Science and Technology”, and “Basic and Engineering Sciences”.
The Prize is granted to works deemed to have improved human life, have made tangible and cutting-edge innovations on the boundaries of science, or have presented new scientific methodology.
One of the objectives of the Mustafa Prize Foundation is to establish a scientific network. The goal is not merely to introduce the prize laureates, but also to connect scientists, enabling them to be identified while creating an environment conducive to synergy, collaboration and mutual scientific exchange.

Israel's war on Nobel Laureate Navi Pillay is a war on international law itself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:36:40 UTC
20:36:40 KST

The announcement that South African human rights lawyer Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize apparently knocked off balance the Israeli Foreign Ministry's social media staffer.
"If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn't just be a contender. She'd be a frontrunner," the ministry wrote on the day the prize was awarded. It added: "Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell."
Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, also raised the dead when he wrote that Menachem Begin, Henry Kissinger and Martin Luther King were turning in their graves.
These reactions reflect the chasm that has opened in the last decade between Israel on one side and UN agencies and the mainstream of international law on the other. The relationship with Pillay, which has mostly seen downturns since 2011, is a mainstay of this chasm that will largely shape Israel's relations with the world in the coming decades.
Pillay went from a state visit to Israel in 2011 to severe criticism of the occupation and Israeli human rights violations in the West Bank. Heading a UN commission of inquiry, she went from lambasting Hamas' crimes on October 7 to harsh reports on suspected Israeli war crimes in Gaza, even concluding that Israel's actions amounted to genocide.
In her reports, Israelis can find not only detailed documentation of crimes by both sides but also evidence and conclusions on Israel's failure to protect its citizens. To some extent, Pillay also entered the vacuum created by the government's refusal to form a state commission of inquiry.
Pillay, 85, has served as an anti-apartheid activist, the UN human rights commissioner, the first non-white woman justice on South Africa's Supreme Court, and a member of the tribunal that prosecuted the perpetrators of the Rwandan genocide. So her opinion can't be easily dismissed. The detailed reports she heads are packed with facts and legal analyses.
In 2011, when she served as UN human rights commissioner, she was the last person in that office to visit Israel. She met with senior officials at the time including President Shimon Peres and Supreme Court President Dorit Beinisch. She even visited Yad Vashem.
Such a trip has now become unimaginable, after Israel's radicalization and distancing from the UN and international law. All commissioners after Pillay have been boycotted by Israel, which ceased cooperation with the UN Human Rights Council.
In 2021, the council held a special session following the events of May that year – an air war between Israel and Gaza and Jewish-Arab violence in Israel. The council appointed an independent commission of inquiry for the region and put Pillay at its helm. With some justification, Israel argued that the commission enjoyed a broad mandate compared to similar UN committees. Its brief included not only the West Bank and East Jerusalem but also Israel itself and even the right to investigate the "roots of the conflict."
The commission's mandate also does not require periodic renewal but renews automatically. All told, the wide mandate and Pillay's stature made her reports crucial in shaping the international legal discourse on Israel.
In October 2022, the commission recommended that the UN General Assembly request an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice in The Hague on the legality of the occupation. The opinion handed down two years later was unequivocal: Israel violates international law and its control of the West Bank is illegal. The opinion, approved by the General Assembly, became a milestone in how the international community views Israel and the occupation. For example, recent decisions by European countries to boycott products from the settlements are largely based on this decision.
In May 2023, the commission published a report on civil society in Israel and the parts of the West Bank governed by the Palestinian Authority. The report was highly critical of both sides, addressing Israel's restrictions on journalists and rights activists, as well as infringements on freedom of expression and restrictions on civil society organizations and journalists in PA territory and Hamas-ruled Gaza.
Later that year, the commission began investigating the events of October 7. Its basic rule was that an event was verified when there was supporting information from at least "two independent and reliable sources." In cases of sexual violence or torture, where verification of testimony can be particularly difficult, a single reliable primary source or consistency with a pattern of similar events may suffice.
On this basis, the commission published two reports in June 2024. The first dealt with the events of October 7, and the wide mandate it received three years earlier allowed it to address Hamas crimes' in Israel.
The report on October 7 spans 59 pages and includes close analyses of the main sites including kibbutzim, army bases, Zikim Beach and Sderot. In fact, in the absence of a state commission of inquiry, the UN report is a broader and more detailed document than any published by the Israeli government on the events of October 7. (The Israeli army has published detailed investigations into most of the major events, but Israelis have still not received a comprehensive report on what happened in the Gaza border communities.)
The commission determined that Hamas committed a long list of war crimes including murder, abductions, torture, beheadings, the desecration of bodies, the burning of bodies and sexual violence. But according to the panel, the Israeli authorities failed to protect the citizens, security forces were not deployed quickly enough, and the activation of the so-called Hannibal Directive, which allows "all means" to prevent the capturing of soldiers – caused the deaths of at least 14 civilians.
Lacking a state commission of inquiry's conclusions, Israelis can at least be content that a commission headed by a Nobel Peace Prize laureate determined that the authorities abandoned the citizens. Immediately after this report was published, a second document addressed Israel's response to Hamas' attack and included harsh criticism of the bombings and harm to innocent civilians in Gaza.
As evidence mounted of possible war crimes by Israel, Pillay's reports became increasingly harsh. Throughout 2024 and 2025, she published reports on systematic sexual violence against Palestinian detainees and civilians and the destruction of Gaza's healthcare system. In September 2025, the commission published its most scathing report, declaring that Israel had committed genocide.
The commission determined that the Israeli army and other security forces committed four out of five acts considered genocide under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention: killing members of a group, causing serious bodily or mental harm, deliberately inflicting conditions of life designed to physically destroy the group in whole or in part, and imposing measures intended to prevent births in the group. The fifth act, of which Israel was not accused, is "forcibly transferring children of the group to another group."
"It is clear there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the Genocide Convention. The responsibility for these atrocity crimes lies with Israeli authorities at the highest echelons who have orchestrated a genocidal campaign for almost two years now with the specific intent to destroy the Palestinian group in Gaza," Pillay said. The report joined numerous others by rights groups and petitions by legal scholars.
Due to Pillay's standing and the commission's meticulous investigation, the panel has special status in the world of international law. Israel, of course, angrily rejected the report and berated its authors and conclusions. But the chasm that has opened between Israel and the doyens of international law can no longer be bridged.
International law doesn't behave like domestic law. It is heavily influenced by the political balance of power, and the backing of the Trump administration has so far allowed Israel to keep ignoring it. The wheels of international justice grind even slower than the judges in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's corruption trial.
But they do grind, and, as Pillay's reports show, the chasm that has opened between Israel and international norms will shape Israel's image for the foreseeable future.

BIG stacks floating terraces above green public space in tirana
a translucent facade, slender columns, and an open ground plane shape a proposal that brings public space, community facilities, and the surrounding landscape into a single architectural framework.
BIG raises cloud-like building above public park in albania
Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) wins the Fountain Plaza Tirana international design competition with a proposal that raises the building above a park-like public realm in Tirana, Albania. The project combines elevated building volumes, a translucent facade, and a network of slender columns to create an architecture that remains open to the landscape. BIG approaches the site as a continuous public environment, integrating an open-access library, community facilities, and a covered public auditorium with the surrounding greenery.
The proposal rests on the idea that the building and landscape should operate as one. A dense field of slender, cane-like columns lifts the structure above ground level, leaving space for public activity and allowing pedestrians to move through the footprint. The jury particularly praised this permeability, describing the scheme as one of the most generous park experiences among the competition entries.
The upper floors are set back to bring natural light into the covered auditorium and make room for planting. Vegetation and public spaces extend beneath and around the building, while the structure provides shade and shelter. Its translucent facade contrasts with the slender supporting columns, giving the building a light, layered appearance.
Fountain Plaza Tirana connects public space, water, and urban life
An open-access library and integrated community facilities are intended to make the ground level an active social destination rather than a residual space beneath a large building. The covered auditorium adds another public program, creating an area for collective gatherings within the elevated structure. This emphasis on shared space also informs the relationship of the project with its wider urban context. According to the jury, BIG’s proposal considers the possibility of pedestrianizing the adjacent traffic road and extending the park toward the neighboring area. These moves suggest an approach that reaches beyond the immediate footprint of the building, treating the competition as an opportunity to reconsider how pedestrians, green space, and surrounding infrastructure might connect. The jury highlighted the integration of the adjacent canal as an active component of the team’s design, linking the waterway to the environmental and microclimatic conditions of the site.

Iran to expand nuclear technology applications in healthcare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:34:49 UTC
20:34:49 KST

Iran to expand nuclear technology applications in healthcare
TEHRAN – The Ministry of Health and the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) have signed a memorandum of understanding to expand the application of nuclear technology in the healthcare sector.
Health Minister Mohammad-Reza Zafarqandi and AEOI chief Mohammad Eslami signed the agreement, which primarily aims to control Aedes mosquito populations and combat dengue, chikungunya, and Zika viruses through the sterile insect technique (SIT), IRNA reported.
The initiative is an environmentally friendly pest control method; male mosquitoes are mass-reared and sterilized using irradiation. The release of sterilized male insects significantly declines the insect population.
Accordingly, both parties will utilize the scientific, research, and technological capacities of the country to launch a center for Aedes aegypti mass-rearing, and conduct pilot and field studies to evaluate the effectiveness of the technology.
The AEOI will help supply gamma or X-ray irradiation equipment, train personnel, provide specialists in the fields of irradiation and dosimetry, and guarantee the performance and maintenance of the delivered equipment.
Mosquitoes only need a small amount of water to lay eggs. Bowls, cups, fountains, tires, barrels, vases, and any other container storing water make a great nursery.
Dengue is a viral infection transmitted to humans through the bite of infected mosquitoes. The disease is transmitted through the bite of Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. These mosquitoes also transmit the Zika and Chikungunya viruses, making them a significant threat to public health.
Dengue disease has different infectious phases, including the fever phase, critical phase, and recovery phase.
Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus have been recorded in the country. Aedes aegypti is a more invasive mosquito that is more common in Iran. Due to the physiology of this mosquito, people in contaminated areas are told to wear clothes that cover most parts of their bodies for the first two hours of the morning and two hours before evening.
Transmission occurs two days before symptoms and two days after the fever. The disease can spread from mosquitoes to humans, from humans to mosquitoes, and from humans to humans through blood transfusion, organ transplant, and mother to child in pregnancy.
The lifespan of Aedes mosquitoes is between one and 4 weeks; they take blood meals every 1 – 2 hours, accounting for 40 to 50 meals throughout their lifespan.
About 40 to 80 percent of patients with dengue have mild or no symptoms. By adhering to sanitation practices, dengue fever cases can be reduced by 70 percent.
Aedes aegypti was first reported in Hormozgan province in 2019. Now, the mosquito is found in Hormozgan, Sistan-Baluchestan (Chabahar and Konarak), Bushehr, and Fars provinces.
The other species, Aedes albopictus, has been observed in the northern and northwestern provinces, including Gilan, Mazandaran, Ardabil, East Azerbaijan, and Zanjan.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), about half of the world’s population is now at risk of dengue, with an estimated 100–400 million infections occurring each year.
Prevention and control of dengue rely on vector control. There is no specific treatment for dengue/severe dengue, and early detection and access to proper medical care greatly lower fatality rates of severe dengue.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s machinery exports reached NT$109.24 billion (US$3.44 billion) in September, up 35.8% from a year earlier and extending their year-on-year growth streak to 20 months, the Taiwan Association of Machinery Industry (TAMI) said Monday.
Exports totaled NT$888.34 billion in the first nine months, up 22.5% from a year earlier, per CNA. With overseas orders remaining strong, TAMI said exports and annual output could reach record highs this year, although supply chain disruptions remain a risk.
Demand from the semiconductor and AI server industries has helped drive growth, with electronic equipment exports exceeding NT$22 billion in September, up 61% year on year. Electronic equipment exports totaled NT$176.8 billion in the first nine months, up 46.1%, while electronic equipment and testing and measurement equipment together accounted for 37.6% of machinery exports.
TAMI warned that conflict in the Middle East continues to affect energy and raw material prices, while geopolitical tensions and export controls on high-tech goods and rare earths could disrupt global supply chains, per RTI. As the machinery industry relies heavily on overseas markets, longer lead times and difficulties sourcing key components could affect orders and exports, it said.
The machine tool sector remained weaker, with exports totaling NT$5.32 billion in September, down 1.8% from a year earlier, according to the Taiwan Machine Tool and Accessory Builders’ Association, per CNA. Exports in the first nine months fell 1.9% to NT$47.42 billion, while imports rose 15.8% to NT$15.83 billion.
The association said the sector showed diverging trends, as exports of key components rose 13.1% in the first three quarters despite declining finished-machine shipments. Component exports to Italy, India, and Vietnam grew, while demand for machine tools was strong in India, Vietnam, and Malaysia.
TAMI said the weaker Japanese yen and South Korean won continued to weigh on the competitiveness of machine tools. The US was the largest destination for machinery exports in the first nine months, accounting for 26%, followed by China at 21.1% and Singapore at 7.6%.

Gunmen in Nigeria kill 20 people heading to market
ABUJA, Oct 12 - Gunmen ambushed a convoy of traders travelling to a market under military escort and killed at least 20 people in Nigeria's northwestern Zamfara state, a witness and a military source said on Monday.
• Local resident Musa Danladi told Reuters the attack occurred around 2 p.m. on Saturday with the convoy en route to Nasarawa market in Bukkuyum district from Gwashi
• Danladi, who helped retrieve the bodies, said four soldiers, three policemen and a Nigerian civil defence corps officer were among those killed, along with 12 civilians
• Northwestern Nigeria has seen a surge in attacks by heavily armed gangs, known as bandits, who raid villages, abduct residents for ransom and rustle livestock
• A military source confirmed the attack and said 19 people were also wounded
• Military and police authorities did not immediately respond to requests for comment REUTERS
