How Trump’s Policies Are Testing Farmers’ Loyalty Ahead of Midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:28:27 UTC
20:28:27 KST

Rising diesel and fertilizer costs, coupled with President Donald Trump’s shifting tariff policies, have made it harder for Oklahoma farmer Brent Rendel to plan future crops. Over the past few months, he says, the political mood among fellow farmers—traditionally some of the President’s most reliable supporters—has begun to shift.
“From my discussions with other farmers, there is a higher level of dissatisfaction with what's going on with the [Trump] Administration,” says Rendel. “You didn't used to really see that, but now we're seeing it and hearing it.”
That dissatisfaction could pose a political problem for Trump and Republicans ahead of the pivotal midterm elections. Trump won 69% of the rural vote in 2024, but an AP-KFF poll, conducted in August, found that 57% of rural voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of the economy. Among rural Republican voters, around one-quarter (27%) disapproved of his handling of the economy—and that group was "substantially less likely" than those who approved to say they were certain to vote in November.
Three-quarters of rural voters described the cost of living in their communities as “fair” or “poor.” A Reuters/Ipsos poll, conducted in June, had already put Trump's approval rating among rural Americans dropped at a new low of 50%, with just 31% approving of his handling of economic issues.
The findings come as Democrats poll competitively in some traditionally Republican states such as Texas, Iowa, and Kansas. Democratic leaders are also addressing farmers' economic frustrations in their policy proposals. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Amy Klobuchar, ranking member of the Senate Agriculture Committee, last month unveiled a bill intended to lay the groundwork for “America’s first-ever fertilizer reserve.” American farmers are “getting crushed from all sides by this Administration,” Schumer said as he introduced the Strategic Fertilizer Reserve Act with endorsements from the National Farmers Union and New York Farm Bureau.
Farmers and agricultural experts interviewed by TIME described four overlapping pressures: Trump’s expansion of low-tariff beef imports, rising fertilizer and diesel costs stemming from a global energy crisis triggered by the Iran war, and tariffs that have increased some production costs while provoking retaliation against American exports.
The impact has been felt by consumers, who have seen a steady climb in grocery prices. In one September AP-NORC poll, 64% of Americans said Trump has “gone too far” on imposing new tariffs on other countries. Trump’s latest tariff row with Canada has prompted further economic concern, particularly in rural states such as Montana, which listed Canada as its largest export market in 2025.
In response, White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told TIME that Trump “has repeatedly affirmed his support for America’s great farmers and ranchers.”
She added: “While the President has been clear about temporary disruptions as a result of the conflict in Iran, the Administration continues to implement the proven Trump agenda of tax cuts, deregulation, and energy abundance to keep America on a solid economic trajectory.”
Trump campaigned on promises to keep the U.S. out of foreign wars and focus on prosperity at home.
The farmers who spoke to TIME say the economic consequences of his policies are now reaching their day-to-day operations.
Beef imports
The average price of ground beef in the U.S. has risen sharply since the end of 2020. It climbed from $5.58 per pound in August 2024 to $6.92 in August 2026, according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data. Shrinking cattle herd sizes, drought and strong demand have all contributed to the increases. At the start of this year, the U.S. cattle inventory hit a 75-year low.
The price surge has created a political challenge for Trump.
“A major part of [Trump’s] campaign to households around the U.S. two years ago, was the fact that they could keep inflation low,” says Joe Glauber, a research fellow at the International Food Policy Research Institute, noting that many rural Americans and farmers are concerned that this hasn’t materialized.
Trump’s 90-day scheme to suspend tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of imported foreign beef to ease the strain on grocery bills went into effect on Sept. 1. The stated intention was for the imported beef to be sold at 25% lower than market price.
But the American Farm Bureau Federation (AFBF), an agriculture lobbying group, has urged Trump to reverse course, citing its own analysis that found the increased imports have not lowered prices for consumers. The AFBF tracked daily prices of 80% lean ground beef at 41 grocery stores in 22 states, starting the day after the proclamation went into effect. In 30 of those 41 stores, ground beef prices cost relatively the same on Sep. 23 as they did on Sep. 2.
Incumbent Texas Commissioner for Agriculture Sid Miller, an eighth-generation farmer and rancher, says farmers have felt the effects of the fallout of the beef import scheme.
“I haven't talked to one rancher that's not upset about it,” says Miller. “Just the packers and the processors are reaping the benefits, not the consumer or the cattle rancher. Calves that are going to market now are bringing $300-500 a head less.”
Derrell Peel, a professor of agricultural economics at Oklahoma State University who specializes in livestock and cattle markets, says ground beef has become the “poster child for higher food prices,” making it a focus of the political debate.
“Cattle producers increasingly feel that Trump is willing to throw them under the bus to try to get lower beef prices before the election,” Peel tells TIME. “None of the political actions have had any significant impact on beef prices and there is no quick solution to high beef prices.”
In Florida, Kansas, Kentucky, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Dakota, and Texas—10 major beef-producing states—Trump has seen a decline in approval rating, according to Civiqs polling data collected between Aug. 21-Sep. 21.
“For Republicans, as a rule, our strongest voting bloc is the rural areas of the United States,” says Miller.
“I think we're going to lose some statewide races in Texas because of multiple things,” he adds, listing tariffs, diesel fuel costs, and fertilizer prices as other key concerns. “It's like death from 1000 cuts.”
Recent ICE raids targeting meatpacking plants across Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas are also causing concern and placing further strain on the U.S. beef supply chain.
“ICE [recently] raided workers from packing plants in Kansas, shutting the packing plants down,” says Miller. “That lowers prices for the cattlemen because the cattle back up, they can't get processed, and it raises prices for the consumer, because there's less beef on the market.”
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Sept. 25 disputed the nature of the raids and said “ICE is not conducting worksite operations in Kansas.” Industry groups said worker absences nevertheless forced some plants to close temporarily.
Fertilizer
Steve Sheffels, a wheat farmer who serves as president of the Montana Grain Growers Association, says that around 40% of his expenses go towards buying fertilizer. He says that outlook could become “dire” if prices continue to rise.
Rising fertilizer costs, combined with extreme weather in Montana over the past year, has led Sheffels to conclude that “we are not able to produce our crops and make money doing it.”
Sheffels highlights a specific example of how his costs have risen since the onset of the Iran war.
“We just got done seeding this fall, and the cost of starter fertilizer, which has a lot of potassium in it, was just under $1,000 a ton,” he says. “Last year, it was $600 a ton.”
The rise of fertilizer costs is a major concern as crops such as corn and wheat heavily rely on nitrogen fertilizer. Natural gas is key in the production of nitrogen-based fertilizers, including urea and anhydrous ammonia. Exports of liquified natural gas from Gulf countries have been severely disrupted by the war and shipping disruptions have continued.
The shipping of natural gas exports via the Strait of Hormuz “remained effectively suspended” through August, according to data published last month, while other fertilizer product exports “remained sporadic and subdued” across the month.
In April, 94% of farmers responding to a Farmer & Rancher Policy Sentiment survey said the Iran war had impacted their business by raising fertilizer costs, energy costs, or both. While the survey came amid a sharp spike in fertilizer prices across April to June, concerns remain.
The price of anhydrous ammonia was up 9.3% as of late September compared to late February, before the onset of the war. The price of urea is up 7.9% for the same period, according to data from analytics company DTN.
Diesel fuel
In the U.S., the price of diesel hit record highs last month, sitting at a national average of over $6.52 per gallon on Sept. 22, according to the American Automobile Association.
Trump signed an Executive Order last week to waive the off-road requirement for a specific type of tax-free diesel fuel primarily used by the agriculture industry. Temporarily allowing highway use of red-dyed diesel “will put money directly back in the pockets of American farmers, truckers, and workers,” the White House said. While it may help lessen the costs associated with the transportation of harvested goods, Rendel says it “won’t be the solution for our farm economy woes.”
Days later, the President also announced that Russia had agreed to supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the American and global marketplace.
Prior to these efforts, Trump floated the possibility of a diesel export ban. But he ruled out the idea on Oct. 2 as the G7 group of nations committed to a co-ordinated release of 100 million barrels of diesel alongside other reserves through the International Energy Agency (IEA), in an effort to stabilise world energy markets.
In the meantime, farmers continue to grapple with increased prices.
“Diesel directly affects farm production costs for field operations, planting, harvesting, and for shipping both inputs and outputs,” says Peel. “The impact [when prices are increased] is very immediate.”
In the August AP/KFF poll, 67% of rural voters said they were “very or somewhat” worried about gasoline or other transportation costs.
Rendel is already feeling the impact. Last month, he explains, he had diesel delivered to his farm that cost him over $5 a gallon.
“I know in a lot of the world, that's probably not ridiculous, but for farm diesel, which is subjected to a lower tax rate in the U.S., that is ridiculous,” he says. “Anytime it goes over $4, it gets painful, and now we're already over five.”
“Fuel is a real strong pain point for everyone. As long as the war is going on, there's really not going to be any significant relief available,” he adds.
Crop farmers in particular rely on heavy, diesel-fueled machinery to sow and harvest.
“If fertilizer prices rise, which they have risen over the past year or so, you can really look at your soil fertility and make decisions that can save you some money. When seed prices go up, you can shop around and maybe find less expensive seed or reduce your seeding rates,” Rendel says. “But fuel's not that way. My combine, when I'm harvesting soybeans, uses about 200 gallons of fuel per day, and that doesn't change.”
Diesel is also essential for transporting goods once they are harvested. “I’ve got to deliver the grain to the buyer. The fuel is a very inflexible expense,” Rendel says, citing a lack of alternatives.
Sheffels is feeling the impact of transport costs as a result of diesel fuel prices, too. “We're having to pay more to get our grain moved around in the short term,” he says. “In the long term, it's going to have a huge [financial] impact because of the distances.”
The renewed trade war with Canada has added to concerns for farmers in the U.S., after negotiations between the two countries collapsed in August. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods took effect last month, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matching the levies imposed by the Trump Administration. Canada's counter tariffs apply to products covering $27.6 billion in imports from the U.S., focusing on sectors such as steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, among other products.
“The U.S. and Canadian economies are highly integrated,” says Peel. “There are no winners in trade wars in general and especially in this one with so many components that will be impacted.”
Overall, tariffs on key production inputs have imposed roughly $2.6 billion in additional costs on crop farmers from February 2025 through July 2026, according to data from the Association of Equipment Manufacturers.
Following Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the White House in late September, Beijing agreed to drop tariffs on various U.S. agricultural products. However, soybeans were excluded from the list, and will remain subjected to 10% tariffs, offering little relief to farmers like Rendel.
Soybeans remained the top U.S. agricultural export to China in 2025, even as shipments fell by roughly three-quarters between 2024 and 2025 amid Trump’s implementation of wide ranging tariffs on Beijing.
For farmers already facing higher diesel and fertilizer costs, shrinking export markets create pressure at both ends of the supply chain. “You're hitting people at both levels, at the input level, and then look at the prices they get for their commodity if they're not able to export it,” says Glauber, from the International Food Policy Research Institute.
Sheffels says the repeated policy shifts are disruptive for farmers across America.
“The level of uncertainty that we've had to live with is completely unacceptable,” he says. “It's impossible to make investment decisions when you don't know what the rules are going to be five minutes from now, let alone in six months.”
With the midterms fast approaching, the question for Republicans is whether that frustration will change how some farmers vote—or whether they vote at all.

Rise in poverty is ‘a wake-up call for the world’, UN development chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:28:07 UTC
20:28:07 KST

Rise in poverty is ‘a wake-up call for the world’, UN development chief says
The number of people living in “multidimensional” poverty has risen for the first time in 15 years, reaching 1.2 billion, as families struggle to meet their basic needs.
The finding comes in the 2026 update of the global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) published by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and Oxford University, which measures overlapping hardship across health, education and standard of living.
The 1.2 billion figure represents 51.5 million more people than in the 2025 update. Of this number, more than half are children – 617 million – and 83 per cent live in rural areas.
‘This is unacceptable’
“The rise in poverty should be a wake-up call for the world,” said UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo.
“Behind these figures are 1.2 billion people facing hardships that reinforce one another: hunger, missed schooling and a lack of clean water or electricity. This is unacceptable.”
The index was developed in 2010 to measure poverty beyond what people earn.
Overlapping deprivations
It examines 10 indicators of health, education and standard of living, such as nutrition and child mortality, years of schooling, and access to electricity, drinking water and sanitation.
A person is considered “multidimensionally poor” if they are deprived in one-third or more of the indicators.
Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia account for the overwhelming majority of deprivations across every indicator.
Mixed picture, fragile success
The 2026 update – which covers 108 countries, representing some 78 per cent of the global population – reveals that the increase in poverty is partly due to population growth outpacing efforts to improve living standards.
In 95 countries where no new survey data was available, updated population estimates increased the number of people counted as poor by nearly 16 million.
The remainder of the increase comes from 13 countries where data was gathered, reflecting the genuine change in poverty incidence and the associated demographic change, as well as differences in indicator coverage.
The updated surveys also revealed a mixed picture on the ground. Five of these countries – Egypt, Nepal, Tajikistan, Angola and Zambia – have reduced the share of people living in multidimensional poverty, however population growth outpaced poverty reduction in both Angola and Zambia, meaning that the total number of people living in poverty still increased.
Meanwhile, Nigeria provides an example of how fragile progress in tackling poverty can be. Although the country made significant reductions in multidimensional poverty in the 2010s, both the poverty rate and the number of people struggling to make ends meet have increased.
‘Progress is possible’
The international community has pledged to reduce the proportion of people living in poverty by at least half before the end of this decade, in line with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
The authors of the 2026 MPI update believe that this target is achievable.
“We know progress is possible,” Mr. De Croo insisted. “Countries that have tackled these challenges together, rather than in isolation, have shown what determined action can achieve.”
UNDP reported that 33 countries have halved their MPI value in fewer than 15 years, including six in sub-Saharan Africa. In Eswatini, the share of people living in multidimensional poverty has fallen from nearly 39 per cent to eight per cent.
Meanwhile, China recorded the fastest reduction among countries with available data by halving its MPI value from 9.5 per cent to 4.2 per cent in just four years (2010-2014).
The shows that many countries continue to make progress, with some reducing poverty rapidly and at scale, underscoring both the urgency of renewed action and the possibility of success, the agency said.

Hong Kong steps up Russia arrival checks after Siberian lab worker’s death
Unknown

Hong Kong steps up Russia arrival checks after Siberian lab worker’s death
Health officials order expanded surveillance at airport after researcher at anti-plague institute in Siberia dies from pneumonia of unknown origin
Hong Kong will step up health surveillance measures for arrivals after a laboratory worker at an anti-plague research institute in Russia died from pneumonia, but authorities have stressed the risk to residents remains low.
According to World Health Organization (WHO) information provided by Russian authorities, there was no evidence of ongoing transmission, the Centre for Health Protection (CHP) said on Monday.
Russian authorities previously stated that the worker at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute in Siberia had died from pneumonia, but that the origin of the infection had yet to be determined.
The centre said it had not received any reports of residents or travellers arriving in Hong Kong from Russia with cases of pneumonia of unknown origin in recent months.

UN refugee agency's funding shortfall is impacting refugees worldwide, its chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:20:19 UTC
20:20:19 KST

Asked to ‘do the impossible’: UN refugee chief warns aid cuts threaten vital lifelines
- UNHCR chief Barham Salih warned that deep funding cuts are forcing painful global aid reductions. The agency has only US$3 billion (S$3.8 billion), or 35%, of the US$8.5 billion it needs for 2026.
- UNHCR has cut staff from 20,000 in 2024 to just under 12,000. Salih said “protection has a floor”, and warned the crisis is already harming refugees and partners.
- Aid cuts are threatening key work in Chad, Ethiopia and the Americas. The Americas face a 32% budget cut in 2027, while displaced people there may rise to 24.5 million.
AI generated
GENEVA – Deep funding shortfalls are forcing the UN refugee agency (UNCHR) to make painful cuts across its humanitarian operations worldwide, and there are limits to how much restructuring can offset shrinking donor support, its chief warned on Oct 12.
UNHCR has secured only US$3 billion (S$3.8 billion), or 35%, of the US$8.5 billion in funding it requires for 2026, High Commissioner Barham Salih told the agency’s executive committee at a meeting in Geneva.
The shortfall follows aid cuts by countries, including the United States under President Donald Trump, at a time of record global displacement.
Funding for 2026 remains uncertain although the expected figure of around US$2.68 billion could improve after a UNHCR donor pledging conference in December, Salih said.
UNHCR has launched one of its largest restructurings in its history because of the budget squeeze, with Salih saying its workforce has been reduced since 2024 from 20,000 employees to just under 12,000.
“Protection has a floor. Below it, the system does not simply become smaller. The protection we can provide begins to fail,” he said.
Salih cautioned that restructuring could not compensate indefinitely for lower funding, and that the funding crisis is already having tangible consequences for refugees and humanitarian partners.
“There is a difference between doing more with less and being asked to do the impossible,” he said.
UNHCR is seeking to preserve frontline operations by cutting jobs at its Geneva headquarters and worldwide regional offices, with 88% of staff remaining outside headquarters, Salih said.
About 95% of the staff doing protection work, such as registering refugees and providing legal assistance, and helping refugees find longer-term solutions, such as returning home safely, have been retained in field locations, he said.
He cited several examples of programmes under threat.
In Chad, he said, insufficient funding risks disrupting specialised medical care and legal assistance for more than 50,000 survivors of conflict-related sexual violence who fled neighbouring Sudan.
In Ethiopia, refugee registration has been suspended for tens of thousands of refugees from South Sudan and Eritrea, he said.
Colombia has raised concerns on behalf of Latin American countries that their region is being disproportionately impacted.
The Americas, which include the US, Canada, Latin America and the Caribbean, face a budget reduction of 32% in 2027 compared to 2026, or about US$485 million – the largest budget reduction of any region – while the number of forcibly displaced and stateless people in the Americas is projected to increase by 4% to about 24.5 million people in 2027, Salih said. REUTERS

2026 Nobel Prize in Economics goes to Robert E. Hall, Michael Woodford
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:17:13 CST
20:17:13 KST

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics is announced in Stockholm, Sweden, Oct. 12, 2026. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced Monday that the 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel has been awarded to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford for "microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization." (Patrik Lundin/Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences/Handout via Xinhua)
STOCKHOLM, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced Monday that the 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel has been awarded to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford for "microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization."
The academy said the laureates have developed macroeconomic models that have significantly improved the ability to implement effective stabilization policies. Based on these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can help smooth economic fluctuations.
"The laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," said John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.
Both laureates were born in the United States. Hall is a professor at Stanford University, while Woodford is affiliated with Columbia University. ■

PARIS, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Chinese automakers are becoming more visible in the European market, with their product offerings becoming more structured and their technological level continuing to improve, said Serge Gachot, director of the Paris Motor Show.
In a recent interview with Xinhua ahead of the 2026 Paris Motor Show, Gachot said the biennial event would bring together more than 60 automakers and over 100 exhibitors from Europe, America and Asia, with Chinese automakers having a more visible presence than at the previous edition.
"The content of the automobile itself is evolving," Gachot said, adding that electrification, software, artificial intelligence, connectivity and automated driving are playing an increasingly important role.
"The Paris Motor Show thus showcases an automobile that is no longer limited to the powertrain and the vehicle itself, but increasingly integrates various technologies and new uses," he said.
Speaking about Chinese automakers, Gachot said their product offerings had become more structured. "They no longer come only with competitively priced electric vehicles, but with broader ranges, mainstream and high-end positioning, and greater attention to design, onboard technologies and the digital experience," he said.
Gachot also noted that the technological level of Chinese automakers had continued to improve, particularly in batteries, driving range, connectivity and driver-assistance systems. "This evolution is driving a growing commercial presence of Chinese automakers in Europe," he said.
On the localization of Chinese automakers in Europe, Gachot said Chinese automakers are also beginning to localize part of their activities in Europe, including production, research and distribution, adding that it would strengthen their integration into the European automotive industry.
"By investing in production, research or local supply chains, they become directly involved in this ecosystem," he said.
He said such localization would strengthen competition, while cooperation would also increase.
"Intelligent driving is a good illustration: it requires combining automotive expertise, software, sensors, data and artificial intelligence. No single player necessarily masters the entire chain alone," he noted.
On the European market for electrified vehicles, Gachot said the transition was already well underway.
"In France, electric vehicles represented 30 percent of new car sales as of the end of August 2026, compared with 20 percent for the whole of 2025. In Germany, they reached 26 percent, compared with 19 percent a year earlier," he said.
The price remains a key factor in consumers' choice of a vehicle, Gachot said, but it needs to be considered alongside the cost of use, driving range, ease of charging and available infrastructure, as well as comfort, digital features and the software experience, which are playing an increasingly important role.
Gachot also recalled his visit to Auto China 2026 in Beijing in April, which left a strong impression on him.
He said the automobile was also being redesigned around the passenger experience, with new formats, including SUV-style multi-purpose vehicles, placing greater emphasis on space, comfort and connectivity.
"As the car takes on an increasing share of driving, value is also shifting toward what people can do inside: relax, work, communicate or entertain themselves," he said.
"We are witnessing not only the rapid progress of an industry, but also an evolution in the very conception of the automobile." ■

China-EU consensus on vehicle trade averts escalation of trade frictions: commerce ministry

BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The consensus reached between China and the European Union (EU) on hybrid and electric vehicle trade has helped prevent an escalation of trade frictions, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce said on Monday.
The spokesperson made the remarks in response to speculation by some foreign media outlets over details of the trade arrangements, particularly those concerning hybrid vehicles, following the latest meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism in Beijing.
The spokesperson said China and the EU had engaged in sustained dialogue under the mechanism and reached consensus on a number of outcomes, helping maintain a stable and balanced relationship between these two key trading partners.
Guided by the principles of mutual respect and equal consultation, the two sides held intensive talks on hybrid and electric vehicle trade, addressing economic and trade differences and each other's concerns in a balanced manner, the spokesperson noted.
Regarding hybrid vehicles, the two sides emphasized and confirmed three basic principles: respect for facts, non-discrimination and compliance with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules.
Citing Eurostat data, the spokesperson said the EU imported 107,000 hybrid vehicles from China in 2024 and 302,000 in 2025.
Building on the 2025 level, the two sides reached an arrangement allowing for further increases, ensuring room for Chinese enterprises to maintain exports and achieve steady growth while taking into account the legitimate concerns of industries on both sides based on actual conditions, the spokesperson said.
Under the principle of non-discrimination, no measures will specifically target Chinese products, let alone discriminate against Chinese enterprises. The quota allocated to China will be no lower than that granted by the EU to any other source of imports, according to the spokesperson.
The two sides also confirmed that the trade arrangement should comply with WTO rules. China reserves all its rights under the WTO framework, including the right to resort to dispute settlement and seek trade compensation, the spokesperson said.
Regarding electric vehicles, the spokesperson said China and the EU achieved a "soft landing" in the EU's anti-subsidy case in January this year, with the bloc issuing a general guidance document on price undertakings. The EU will continue to advance relevant procedures concerning price undertakings by companies involved in the case, as well as other review procedures, the spokesperson added.
The spokesperson stressed that the consensus, reached on the basis of reciprocity and mutual benefit, has effectively safeguarded the interests of Chinese enterprises, prevented an escalation of China-EU trade frictions, and provided a stable, predictable and sustainable environment for bilateral trade and investment, contributing to the stable, balanced and sound development of China-EU economic and trade relations. ■

====================================================================================================

How Apple Puts Indigenous Languages on the iPhone Keyboard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:15:00 UTC
20:15:00 KST

Chuck Hoskin Jr. fondly recalls watching a room full of Cherokee immersion students crowd around a screen to watch How to Train Your Dragon. Except Hiccup and Astrid weren't speaking English—the protagonists were speaking Cherokee, dubbed by voices from the local community.
“They're hearing it in our mother tongue—that didn't happen a generation ago,” Hoskin Jr., principal chief of the Cherokee Nation, tells WIRED. “We're a long way, thankfully, from rote classroom instruction and memorization to a world where kids can see the sort of creativity that sparks imagination and helps every kid become more articulate and literate.”
The Cherokee Nation has around 1,500 active speakers left, and most are over 70. Hoskin Jr. says the community is rapidly losing that generation, which is why it has spent time training up second-language learners. It even has a baby immersion program, hoping their first words are Cherokee.
“The foes we’ve had historically are the so-called Age of Discovery, colonization, the displacement of our people economically and geographically, boarding schools,” he says. “But it's nothing compared to the mathematics we’re up against now. Which is why we’re filled with this urgency every day to do all we can to find partners that can help us accelerate what we want to do.”
One of those accelerants is Apple. The Cherokee Nation has long collaborated with the iPhone maker, and Cherokee was the first Native American language included in iOS in 2010. Today, Apple says its iOS keyboard supports more than 200 languages and language variants, with a handful added last year in iOS 26, like Haitian Creole and Nez Perce. In iOS 27, it expanded support for Indigenous languages to include other Native American languages like Blackfoot, Comanche, and Northern East Cree.
The goal is to meet young people where they already spend much of their waking hours: phone screens. Hoskin Jr. says that to revitalize and save a language, it has to become accessible. Apple says the effort isn't as simple as translating words. It’s a multi-year endeavor that requires deep research, and the company leans on community members for their expertise.
But the process doesn’t start in Cupertino. It actually begins with Unicode. You may have heard of the name—it’s the organization that approves and standardizes the new emoji that appear on your smartphone every year. It also handles time zone localization, currency names, imperial versus metric, and so on.
Before you can type or read a character on a smartphone screen, it needs to exist as a recognized character in the Unicode Standard. “Everything does start with Unicode in terms of a language, but it actually starts with characters and scripts,” says Unicode CEO Toral Cowieson. “We now have more than 157,000 characters that are included.”
Cowieson calls Unicode a kind of digital Switzerland—a neutral consortium where rivals like Apple, Microsoft, and Google sit at the same table as linguists and volunteer contributors. (Cowieson told WIRED earlier this year that Unicode had only four full-time employees.) Proposing a language, verifying it, and then encoding the character set can take three to five years.
After a script is encoded, platforms like Apple and Google need to add font support. Without this step, a character could appear as an empty box—often called “tofu.” Next is orthography: a set of rules and systems for writing a language. Often, languages have a well-defined orthography, but when it’s not standardized, communities use ad hoc replacements because historically available keyboards don't support it.
Take the glottal stop—the speech sound made in the throat between the syllables when you say, “uh-oh.” Some languages have distinct characters for glottal stops, but as some keyboards don’t support them, many indigenous cultures use alternatives, like a question mark, to represent the sound. That's when Apple connects with the community to figure out the best way to represent the sounds in digital text.
That brings us to the keyboard layout. When a community already has an established physical keyboard layout—like Osage—Apple adapts it directly to the software keyboard. Some cultures prefer the QWERTY layouts people are already familiar with.
Other languages need more custom approaches. For example, Nez Perce, or Nimipuutímt, does not use capital letters. Rather than having the Shift key toggle traditional uppercase letters, Apple repurposed it to reveal an accented secondary layer, so users don’t have to hold down individual keys to see those characters, which can slow typing. In the Cherokee language, each character mostly represents a consonant combined with a vowel sound, a form known as syllabary. Apple added adaptive vowel keys on the bottom row, so when a user types a consonant, these keys change to show the vowel combinations they can make.
That’s a newer change to the Cherokee keyboard—one Apple approached the community about, meaning building a keyboard for a language isn’t a one-and-done project.
But digitizing an indigenous culture’s language hasn't always been harmless. Genner Llanes-Ortiz, a Maya scholar and researcher at Bishop's University, studies how Indigenous people use digital technologies to reclaim language heritage. He recalls how Māori speakers rejected proposals to sell their language to tech companies.
“There’s a historical memory about the ways of dispossession that Indigenous peoples have experienced in the world,” Llanes-Ortiz says. “Māori working in their own revitalization efforts have been very firm in protecting access and storage of their linguistic materials because they have been exploited. They have experienced extraction of knowledge in the past.”
Language sovereignty and data ownership are top of mind, according to Chirasree Mandal, an Apple software engineer. “We don’t own anything, and we make it very clear that we are not trying to silo any data that we gain from this process,” she says. “It’s about making sure that the best choice for representing someone’s language is being made on our platform so they feel good using it.”
For its part, a Google spokesperson tells WIRED it has a long history of bringing lesser-known and Indigenous languages to its platforms so people can communicate, pointing to collaborations to integrate languages like Manx and Māori. Google also says it’s exploring how generative AI can simplify the coding and research required for new languages, but “successful integrations require direct participation from native speakers” for the keyboard to meet the community’s needs.
Hoskin Jr. says that writing in syllabary is seen as a badge of honor for young Cherokee speakers. People type their names in Cherokee on Facebook—that’s empowering. But he sees that progress as vulnerable to broader political rhetoric in the US that pushes a monolithic, English-speaking America, which he says bypasses several chapters, including Native American history.
“The greatest enemy we have right now for saving the Cherokee language is the passage of time and the fragility of human life,” Hoskin Jr. says. “Time is precious to everyone, but particularly precious to us in this mission.”

Cuba denies involvement with island-bound fuel shipments seized by US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:10:33 UTC
20:10:33 KST

Cuba denies involvement with island-bound fuel shipments seized by US
HAVANA, Oct 12 - Cuba's top energy official denied any link between the nation's communist-run government and shipments of Cuba-bound biodiesel seized in September by US authorities, rejecting US claims that the island nation was involved in those deals.
The US said last week that it had seized 90 separate shipments of biodiesel worth nearly $3 million under contracts involving a sanctioned Cuban state energy trader known as ENETEC, part of a crackdown on what the US alleges are illegal shipments of fuel to the island.
Cuban Minister of Energy and Mines Vicente de la O Levy said he had no knowledge of any of the shipments intercepted by the US Department of Homeland Security.
"We can assure you that there was no contract of any kind with ENETEC S.A.," de la O Levy told Reuters in an exclusive interview at his Havana office. "No Cuban state-owned company has managed to secure a fuel contract, whether for small or large quantities."
The oil blockade imposed by the US — initiated following the detention of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January — have vastly worsened Cuba's existing energy crisis. Fuel, water and electricity shortages, combined with soaring prices, have brought the island to the brink of a humanitarian crisis.
The US has since early this year allowed fuel exporters to ship gasoline and diesel to the island's nascent private sector but prohibits any such shipments to Cuba's government. Imports of fuel from US companies have soared in recent months but remain a fraction of what the island's economy needs, de la O Levy said.
“I would venture to say that the amount entering the country doesn't even cover 3% of its fuel needs,” he said.
Cuba and the United Nations have called US efforts to limit fuel shipments to Cuba "illegal" and contrary to international law.
The US has openly said it is seeking to topple Cuba's government.
COBALT AND NICKEL
De la O Levy said that the island government intends to remain in the business of nickel and cobalt mining, but that significant barriers remain to restarting production due to stiffened US sanctions.
Cuba is a top global producer of cobalt, according to the US Geological Survey, and has significant reserves of nickel, both essential in the production of batteries and automobiles.
Canada's Sherritt International Corp has for more than 30 years participated in a joint venture with the Cuban government at Cuba's largest mine, at Moa, but announced earlier this year that it would suspend operations due to US sanctions.
The Canadian mining company later said it had signed a non-binding agreement in May with Gillon Capital LLC, a Dallas-based development firm, to sell a stake in its Cuban mining business. Gillon's vice chairman is Ray Washburne, a longtime backer of US President Donald Trump.
De la O Levy said any purchase involving the joint venture would involve shares in the Canadian company, not a direct acquisition of the joint venture with the Cuban government.
"We have always made it clear that what the US company would be buying are shares in Sherritt, not in the joint venture," he stated. "The Canadian company is publicly traded, and any investor has the right to buy its shares."
Cuba said it would be willing to continue operating under the joint venture's existing rules should a deal be inked.
“But any restart would require discussions on how to supply fuel and spare parts, as well as how to handle payments for exports and production inputs,” de la O Levy said. “If the intention is to resume nickel production, all those issues would need to be resolved.”
Neither Sherritt nor Gillon immediately responded to a request for comment on the minister's statements.
RENEWABLE ENERGY
De la O Levy said Cuba was pushing ahead with its planned transition to renewable energy.
He said 144 solar farms with a combined capacity of 1,418 megawatts have been installed over the past several years, assuring baseline daytime production of electricity despite the US fuel blockade.
The island's domestic crude oil production remains stable, he said, but is almost entirely allocated to thermoelectric power plants.
Around 40% of Cuba's electricity comes from domestic oil.
Electric transport has also expanded, with the country now boasting over a million motorcycles and tricycles, while renewable energy sources have been installed at all of the country's small health clinics, maternity homes, nursing homes and funeral homes, he said.
"We are moving forward with our solutions little by little, though not as fast as we would like," the official stated. REUTERS

Smaller firms still having issues getting into defence
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:00:44 BST
20:00:44 KST

Companies trying to break new ground in defence still find it very difficult to get into the government market, a former senior Royal Air Force officer who now advises across the industry told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday.
Air Vice-Marshal (Retired) Gary Waterfall, senior defence advisor at Clarion Defence and Security, speaks into DSEI UK and also runs a portfolio business of around ten companies, none of which he would describe as being on the front line in the way some of his fellow panellists are.
He placed himself deliberately outside the part of the market that is currently getting all the attention, and did it with some relish. “I’m very much sat in the rear echelon, from primes through SMEs into small businesses, all of which are trying to get a worthwhile foothold in the market without having maybe the lure of the sexy dish of the day, very much in that drone environment, yet with a lot to contribute,” he said.
Recent work with a private equity company has sharpened the point for him, and he said the gap between the rhetoric about private investment and what actually happens is wide. “Defence talks about intended growth. Let’s go out, let’s get some private investment in to actually get the gears moving and working,” he said. “The reality is, when you’re trying to break new ground, it’s very difficult to get into government and defence in terms of marketplace. So I see that from an investor perspective. I also see that across all of the SMEs that I’m working with.”
His second argument was that defence companies have more to learn from outside the sector than they generally admit, and he reached for motorsport to make it. “Formula One technology is a real classic, where they raced last weekend, they’re racing next weekend, and they’re going to win, and they’re iterating through rapid cycles the whole time,” he said. “I’m involved with one of those companies, and it’s fascinating to watch them outstrip the pace of defence thinking, as they’re always thirsty for information.”
He also asked the panel to look further ahead than the current reaction cycle. “What we’ve heard is a lot of reacting to what the threat’s doing, and then iterating away. But let’s think beyond that. Let’s think beyond to where we might be going with degrees of certainty, the further out you go, and look at how you best advocate your technologies to meet that threat,” he said.
In Ukraine the loop is closed and innovation is happening in contact, he said, and companies there are doing an extraordinary job of it. The harder question is what firms outside that fight are doing to make themselves better at innovating, and his answer was that defence-based companies still have a great deal to learn.
Air Vice-Marshal Waterfall retired from the Royal Air Force before moving into advisory and investment work, which gives him a view of the industry from both the customer and the supplier sides. The panel was chaired by Lieutenant General (Retired) Stuart Skeates, chairman of Apex Europe.

Brain injury triggers unexpected hormone release in progenitor cells
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:00:27 UTC
20:00:27 KST

Following a brain injury, specific progenitor cells produce a neuropeptide to prevent their neighboring cells from maturing too quickly, a process that aids in tissue repair. This regulatory mechanism also guides myelin formation in the developing and adult brain under healthy conditions. The findings were published in the journal Cell Reports.
The central nervous system relies on myelin, an insulating layer that forms around nerves. This protective sheath allows electrical impulses to transmit quickly and efficiently along nerve networks. Oligodendrocytes are the specialized cells responsible for producing this vital myelin.
When the brain is injured or developing, it needs to generate new oligodendrocytes. These mature cells arise from oligodendrocyte progenitor cells, which migrate to where they are needed and transform into their final, myelin-producing state. This maturation process requires strict regulation to ensure the cells survive and function properly.
Neuropeptides are small protein-like molecules that brain cells use to communicate. Unlike classical neurotransmitters that cross tiny gaps between two specific cells, neuropeptides are released in large amounts and wash over a broader area. This localized broadcasting process is known as volume transmission.
Corticotropin-releasing hormone is one of the most heavily studied neuropeptides in biology. It is primarily known for coordinating the body’s response to stress by interacting with its main cellular receptor, CRHR1. Researchers Clemens Ries, Jan M. Deussing, and their colleagues at the Max Planck Institute of Psychiatry sought to understand how this hormone might act outside of traditional stress pathways.
The research team used genetically modified mice that produce a fluorescent red marker whenever a cell expresses the corticotropin-releasing hormone. In a small study involving brain injuries like tiny stab wounds, the researchers tracked the cellular response. They observed that cells producing the hormone aggregated around the injury sites, with the first such cells detectable as early as twelve hours after injury.
By applying specific chemical stains to the brain tissue, they identified these glowing cells. The cells were not neurons, as one might normally expect for this specific hormone, but rather oligodendrocyte progenitor cells. This marked an early and unusual secretory response by these progenitor cells to physical brain trauma.
To understand the ultimate fate of these specific progenitor cells, the researchers tracked them for over four months. They found that these cells multiplied heavily in the days immediately following the initial injury. Over the following weeks, they reliably transformed into mature oligodendrocytes.
These newly formed oligodendrocytes successfully integrated into the healing brain tissue. They extended their physical processes to form myelin sheaths around local nerve fibers. Once established, the cells survived for the entire duration of the four-month observation period.
Because neuropeptides operate by binding to specific receptors, the team searched for cells in the injury area equipped with the CRHR1 receptor. Using a different strain of genetically modified mice, they highlighted the receptor’s exact location. They discovered a completely separate group of oligodendrocyte progenitor cells expressing this receptor.
This finding established a potential communication network in the damaged tissue. One group of progenitor cells was releasing the hormone in response to injury, while a distinct neighboring group was equipped to receive that signal. The researchers then designed experiments to see what information the signal carried.
The researchers tested what happens when this communication is disrupted. They bred mice lacking the ability to produce the hormone in progenitor cells, as well as mice completely lacking the CRHR1 receptor. After inducing brain injuries, they compared these altered mice to regular mice.
In the altered mice, the progenitor cells equipped with the receptor matured into myelin-producing cells much faster than normal. Under typical conditions, the hormone acts as a brake, forcing the cells to delay their maturation. Removing the signal removed the brake.
While maturing faster might sound beneficial for wound healing, it proved detrimental in cases of larger brain injuries. The rapid maturation led to a noticeable drop in the number of oligodendrocytes that survived long-term. The researchers suspect that the injured environment contains high levels of oxidative stress.
The hormone-induced delay likely helps the cells wait for these harsh conditions to subside before completing their vulnerable final transformation. Moving beyond injury models, the team investigated whether this signaling network operates in healthy, uninjured brains. They counted the receptor-equipped progenitor cells in mice at various ages.
The team noted that these specific progenitor cells naturally increase in number as the mice grow into adulthood. To test the network’s role in healthy development, they examined postnatal mice lacking the CRHR1 receptor. In these young mice, oligodendrocytes formed earlier than usual in the brain’s white matter.
This confirmed that the hormone system also prevents premature cellular maturation during normal brain development. The researchers then evaluated how this early developmental shift affected the adult brain’s physical structure. They analyzed the brains of adult mice lacking the receptor using magnetic resonance imaging.
The researchers utilized a specialized imaging technique that detects the density of myelin by measuring how protons interact with surrounding macromolecules. The imaging revealed that mice lacking the receptor possessed a higher overall myelin content across multiple brain regions, including the corpus callosum. To see the microscopic details, the team employed electron microscopy.
Using the electron microscope, they measured the mathematical relationship between the radius of the inner nerve axon and the radius of the entire myelinated fiber. A lower ratio indicates a thicker myelin sheath relative to the nerve size. The microscopic analysis showed a structural shift in how myelin was distributed across the nerve fibers.
Smaller nerve fibers received thicker myelin sheaths than usual. In contrast, the myelin sheaths on larger nerve fibers were unusually thin. This suggests the hormone network helps ensure myelin is distributed in the correct proportions based on nerve fiber size.
Readers should exercise caution when interpreting these results in the context of psychological stress. While corticotropin-releasing hormone is heavily involved in emotional stress responses, this study focuses strictly on localized tissue signaling after physical trauma or during baseline cellular development. The results do not imply that psychological stress directly alters myelin through this specific pathway.
The study features limitations regarding the genetic models used in the experiments. The primary mouse model lacking the receptor had it deleted globally, meaning the receptor was missing in neurons as well as progenitor cells. This systemic absence could indirectly influence the behavior of the brain’s glial cells.
Future investigations will need to use genetic models that delete the receptor exclusively in oligodendrocyte progenitor cells. Additional studies could also explore how this hormone network responds to diseases that actively destroy myelin.
The study, “Neuropeptide CRH prevents premature differentiation of OPCs following CNS injury and in early postnatal development,” was authored by Clemens Ries, Tibor Stark, Benoit Boulat, Torben Ruhwedel, Jan Philipp Delling, Antonio Miralles Infante, Julia T. von Poblotzki, Alessandro Ulivi, Iven-Alex von Mücke-Heim, Simon Chang, Kenji Sakimura, Keiichi Itoi, Dennis B. Nestvogel, Alessio Attardo, Michael Czisch, Klaus-Armin Nave, Wiebke Möbius, Leda Dimou, and Jan M. Deussing.

Feds Got Warrants to Use Fake Cell Towers to Hunt Down Don Lemon’s Producer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

US law enforcement agents obtained authorization to use a controversial surveillance device capable of intercepting cell phone signals to find and arrest a 21-year-old college student who helped produce journalist Don Lemon’s coverage of an anti-ICE protest, court filings show.
The former student, Jerome Richardson, who has since graduated from Temple University, is among 39 people charged with conspiring to violate worshippers’ civil rights and interfering with religious worship at Cities Church in St. Paul, Minnesota, in January. Protesters said they targeted the church’s January 18 service because one of its pastors, David Easterwood, also led ICE’s St. Paul field office. Those charged include journalists Georgia Fort and Lemon, a former CNN host, who say they were there to cover the demonstration.
Twelve days after the protest, judges in two states began signing warrants authorizing agents to use so-called cell-site simulators, commonly known as Stingrays or IMSI catchers, to target Richardson’s phone: one in Minnesota on January 30 and another in Pennsylvania the next day. The purpose, his lawyers wrote in a motion seeking to exclude the tracking evidence, was “locating and arresting him.”
Agents also applied for cell-site simulator warrants targeting the phones of Fort and Jamael Lundy, then a Minnesota State Senate candidate. They separately sought pen register orders, which can log the numbers a phone contacts, for Fort and a number WIRED traced to Lemon. It's unclear whether a judge approved any of those applications.
The records reviewed by WIRED do not establish whether investigators actually deployed a cell-site simulator to locate Richardson or whether judges approved the applications targeting Fort and Lundy. In a July letter filed in court, Fort’s lawyers said prosecutors “did not know” whether the surveillance applications had been authorized or had yielded evidence.
Cell-site simulators impersonate cell phone towers to locate a target’s phone. In doing so, they can also collect identifying information from any nearby cellular device, including those belonging to people who aren’t suspected of a crime. That indiscriminate collection has made the devices controversial among privacy advocates, who describe them as dragnet surveillance tools.
The use of cell-site simulators has long been shrouded in secrecy. FBI records released in 2023 showed that police borrowing its simulators had to agree to keep details of their use secret, even in court. Privacy advocates have long warned that the devices could be turned against protesters and journalists.
“Using an advanced surveillance capability such as a cell-site simulator against members of the free press for reporting stories that are unfavorable to the president is an appalling attack on the First Amendment,” says Cooper Quintin, senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a tech-focused civil liberties nonprofit. Quintin has spent years researching the devices and developing tools to help people detect them. Using EFF’s detection software, WIRED found evidence suggesting a cell-site simulator was deployed near the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, though who operated it and for what purpose remain unknown.
Attorneys for Lemon, Lundy, and Fort did not respond to requests for comment. Richardson’s attorneys declined to comment on the record.
The previously unreported warrants are a product of a campaign of contentious investigative tactics waged by federal agents in pursuit of people connected to the protest at Cities Church. According to court records, the Department of Homeland Security demanded journalists’ telephone and YouTube records under a customs authority that requires no prior judicial approval. Agents also sought records identifying everyone who had purchased a particular beanie at REI in the Minneapolis–St. Paul area over a period of more than two years. Defense attorneys have identified 92 customs summonses and are challenging the government’s authority to issue them.
The cell-site simulator warrants raise serious questions about both the accuracy of the information investigators presented to judges in their effort to obtain authorization for surveillance tool’s use, as well as why they sought such intrusive tracking to find Richardson in the first place.
The affidavits supporting the applications to track Richardson claimed video showed Fort, Lemon, Richardson, and others “chanting with agitators.” Prosecutors have since conceded that Lemon and Fort did not chant. According to her lawyers, the government acknowledged that the false claim appeared in at least 15 warrant affidavits.
DHS policy says cell-site simulators are deployed only “in the fraction of cases in which the capability is best suited to achieve specific public safety objectives,” but it’s unclear what specific public safety reason justified its use in this case. Investigators obtained a second simulator warrant to locate Richardson, then a senior at Temple University, two days before he walked up to a federal courthouse in Philadelphia and voluntarily surrendered. He was released on bond that afternoon.
The Justice Department responded to WIRED’s request for comment by writing in an email that the department “speaks through its court filings.” DHS declined to discuss ongoing investigations or investigative methods and referred questions to the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Minnesota, which did not respond to a request for comment.
The warrant was signed January 31, the same day Richardson posted a YouTube video saying he expected to enter federal custody “in the coming days,” suggesting he had no intention of fleeing. It is unclear whether the warrant preceded the video, leaving questions about why investigators sought such an intrusive tool to find someone who was publicly anticipating his arrest and whom prosecutors agreed to release the day he surrendered.
While Richardson’s suppression motion asks to suppress evidence obtained from the phone tracking, it does not specify whether agents used a simulator or obtained evidence through either.
A former federal prosecutor who spent a decade working on counterterrorism cases says using a simulator to locate someone is not necessarily unusual. But based on the court records they reviewed about Richardson’s case, they called the government's tactics aggressive: “I don’t understand why it would be at all necessary.” They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record
Richardson, a St. Paul native, had led an NAACP chapter at 16 and served as executive director of Minnesota Teen Activists, according to his fundraiser’s organizer. He described his work for Lemon as handling logistics and connecting him with local contacts. He drove the journalist to Cities Church, where Lemon livestreamed the demonstration and interviewed protesters and churchgoers. Prosecutors allege Richardson joined chants and obstructed congregants.
In his video, Richardson defended his role. “I was proud to support his work,” he said of Lemon. “This is the price of being unapologetic about humanity and love of Christ.”
The government’s initial effort to obtain arrest warrants met resistance from judges. A magistrate judge refused five of eight warrants, and after an appeals court rejected the Justice Department's bid to override that decision, the department withdrew its request. In a filing with the appeals court, the chief judge wrote that two of the five “were not protestors at all; instead, they were a journalist and his producer” and that there was “no evidence that those two engaged in any criminal behavior.” Prosecutors later secured a grand jury indictment on January 29.
The way the government chose to arrest some defendants has also drawn objections from defense lawyers. Lemon’s attorneys say in court filings that prosecutors rejected their offer to arrange his surrender; agents instead arrested him shortly before midnight at a Beverly Hills hotel while he was covering the Grammy Awards. Fort’s lawyers say agents arrested her at home rather than allowing her to turn herself in.

Lettuce engineered to produce meat proteins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:59:28 UTC
19:59:28 KST

Perhaps you enjoy a burger in a lettuce wrap once in a while—but what if greens were also crucial to the patty? That’s the ultimate promise of new research showing lettuce can be engineered to produce myoglobin, a protein found in meat.
Myoglobin (and its better-known relative hemoglobin) contains the compound heme, the red pigment in blood. Adding heme can give plant-based meat alternatives a meaty flavor and the ability to “bleed.” For example, Impossible Foods uses a compound called leghemoglobin (a heme protein derived from soybeans) to flavor its meat alternatives. But using myoglobin, which is found in animal tissue, could lead to vegetarian products that not only look and bleed like red meat but smell more like it, too.
In the study, published in Frontiers in Plant Science, the researchers describe how they got lettuce and tobacco plants to produce myoglobin for the first time, says lead author Alexia Groff, who worked on the project as a Ph.D. student at Imperial College London. The team engineered the plants’ photosynthesizing chloroplasts—the cell structures that typically turn sunlight into food—to make them do the job.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In previous attempts to make myoglobin using nonanimal sources such as yeast, the protein-production directions were placed in the nucleus’s genome, but Groff and her colleagues found that adding them to the chloroplast genome instead could yield more of it—perhaps producing myoglobin even more efficiently than animals do.
Right now yeast fermentation is the standard method of producing heme (as leghemoglobin), but the sterile environment and industrial equipment necessary for manufacturing can be pricey. Plants are much easier to grow. “Row-crop protein production would likely be faster than fermentation-derived production,” says Adam Leman, a principal scientist at the Good Food Institute, who was not involved in the study. “If existing crop-processing equipment can be used, costs for isolating and purifying a myoglobin-rich fraction could be quite low.”
Lettuce is especially promising: the medium itself is edible, meaning lettuce-produced myoglobin could move more easily through the regulatory steps that can slow down the path from laboratory to market. A more streamlined process could also mean less money spent in production—and far less energy use.
The meat industry is a voracious energy consumer: 60 percent of agricultural energy use comes from farming and transporting animal products. Making meat substitutes less resource-intensive is a step toward more sustainable food systems—even if it means making meat proteins in a vegetable.
“In science, there were things that we used to think were impossible that now are an everyday occurrence,” Groff says. “I’m very excited for what the future of this sector is going to look like.”

Light-controlled cells, multimessenger astronomy and lessons from an old turtle on aging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:59:16 UTC
19:59:16 KST

Rachel Feltman: Happy Monday, listeners! For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. You’re listening to our weekly science news roundup.
Some of the biggest stories in science last week were the announcement of the Nobel Prize awards in Chemistry, Physics, and Physiology or Medicine. So we’re going to focus on those groundbreaking research topics today—with a fun little animal story at the end to send us off, of course.
Let’s start with the prize for physiology or medicine, which was announced last Monday. This year’s award went to Karl Deisseroth at Stanford University, Peter Hegemann at Humboldt University of Berlin, and Georg Nagel at the University of Wurzburg in Germany. They were recognized for their discoveries around light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Optogenetics allows scientists to switch individual brain cells on and off. Because neurons use electrical signals to communicate with one another, scientists realized almost a century ago that they could use electrical stimulation to activate brain cells. Optogenetics combines this idea with genetic engineering to allow for more targeted, less invasive, safer cell stimulation than used to be possible. After genetically modifying neurons to make proteins that react to light, researchers can control those cells with a flash of light instead of an electrode.
Hegemann and Nagel contributed to the field by studying a single-celled alga that swims toward light, which they found had to do with a particular protein that opened up pores in the cell membrane when exposed to light. Deisseroth took those findings and applied them to experiments in living mammals.
We spoke to him about his win last week. Here he is explaining the impact of his discovery:
Karl Deisseroth: You know, once you know what matters for function, you can ask: How can dysfunction be addressed? You know, are there cells that cause dysfunction? Are there cells that can counteract dysfunction in a precise way? And what we're doing now is—and many others as well—is we're seeing: how can we leverage this precision to find new treatments, new medications, new neuromodulator approaches that build on this foundation of causality?
You know, this brings an opportunity that might help me communicate more with the public and to share the excitement of science, how discovery happens, how unlikely things get nurtured and that it takes time and it takes risk but that the outcome can be amazing if we’re willing to take the time and the risk.
Feltman: Last Tuesday saw Francis Halzen from the University of Wisconsin–Madison secure a rare solo award in Physics for the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of extraterrestrial origin. Here to tell us more about his contributions to the field is Joseph Howlett, a senior reporter at Scientific American and our resident physics expert. Tell us about those neutrinos, Joe!
Joseph Howlett: So neutrinos are my personal favorite fundamental particle. Of the 17 that we know about, the neutrinos are the ones we know the least. And that's why they've netted five times the Nobel Prize in Physics now.
The main thing that makes neutrinos different from other particles is that they pass through regular matter almost all the time without interacting. So there's neutrinos coming from space, from faraway black holes where super violent things are happening, like supernova and accretion, and these send out these very high-energy neutrinos. They make it all the way to Earth, but almost all the time they pass right through. We never notice that they're here. They're actually passing through us all the time. Neutrinos from the sun go right through our bodies without interacting.
It's really hard to build a detector that can catch a neutrino. And Halzen had this super ambitious idea to do so at the South Pole. He spearheaded the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. They chose Antarctica because it's a place with a lot of ice, and ice is great because when a neutrino interacts with ice, the light shines right through. It can go right through the ice like it's not there, all the way to whatever cameras you've buried inside.
So that was Halzen's great idea was that the Earth built this natural detector for us, right? All we have to do is put the cameras there to capture the light. So they bored these mile-deep holes with hot water jets and then lowered these strings of expensive cameras into each of them.
They span like a cubic kilometer of ice. And when a neutrino passes through that ice, usually it goes right through, but very rarely it will interact with one of the water molecules and produce a shower of light. And because the cameras are there, they can capture that light and say where that neutrino came from and how much energy it has.
So for the first time, we're able to see these neutrinos from these very, very faraway galaxies.
And actually, IceCube was the first experiment to see neutrinos from outer space, from outside of our solar system with this super high energy. So we've learned a lot about the universe thanks to this one experiment. It's also heralded this new era that astronomers call multimessenger astronomy. Basically, we've been looking at the sky with telescopes for hundreds of years, right? Measuring the light from faraway galaxies, from stars, X-rays even from black holes. But neutrinos are a whole new thing. They're not light. We're able to see the universe through a different lens. And when you combine this with the light measurements from all the telescopes in space and across the world, and you combine them additionally with gravitational wave detectors, which are another new technology that's won a Nobel Prize recently, now we have these three lenses that together can look at the same faraway objects and teach us all kinds of new things about them.
The thing about the multimessenger era is that it's just beginning. IceCube's only been operating for 16 years, and it's got a lot of life left to live, so we're gonna continue to learn all kinds of new things about the universe thanks to neutrinos, especially combined with these other experiments measuring light and gravitational waves.
Feltman: Thanks for breaking that down for us, Joe.
Last but not least is the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, which this year honored Henri Kagan of Paris-Sud University and Kenso Soai of the Tokyo University of Science for their pioneering research on autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis. Try saying that one five times fast!
Many molecules come in two versions that are mirror images of each other. They can’t be superimposed over one another, the same way you couldn’t lay your right and left hands on top of each other and get them to line up. That’s called chirality, which happens to be one of my favorite words. When chemists create chiral molecules in the lab, they typically end up with equal amounts of each version. But that's not ideal, because the proteins in your cells—and in the natural world in general—are made from only one of those mirror images. Kagan and Soai figured out how to create just one of those mirror images at a time.
We’ll wrap up today’s news roundup with a story about a very, very old tortoise. The oldest tortoise, in fact. And not just the oldest tortoise, but the oldest terrestrial animal known to man. His name? Jonathan.
Giant tortoises are known generally for their long lifespans, but at around 190 years old, Jonathan is at least a century older than seems to be standard for his kind. And yeah, he is definitely that old. Photographs have confirmed that he was fully mature when he was brought to the island of Saint Helena in 1882, which means he had to have been at least 50 at the time.
A study published last week in Science Advances aims to explain how Jonathan is still alive and kicking all these years later. Genetic analysis of the tortoise compared with four of his peers apparently revealed mutations associated with DNA repair, cancer, telomere maintenance, mitochondrial health, insulin regulation, and other pathways associated with aging.
The researchers also took a look at the methylation of Jonathan’s genome. Methylation is when a small chemical tag gets added to DNA, which generally serves to turn a gene off. One sign of aging is a process called methylation entropy, which is where random patterns of methylation start to become more common. In other words, your body gets worse at targeting the right genes to switch off, which makes it more likely that some important protein won’t get made the way it’s supposed to.
In Johnathan’s genome, methylation entropy was unusually low in gene regions associated with mitochondrial function, RNA processing, and genome repair. That could give scientists some clues about what genes to target if they want to increase lifespan for other animals.
Speaking of longevity: We’ll be back on Wednesday to talk about why there’s so much shoddy science in this very buzzy field of research.

Marielle Issa and Aaron Shattuck fact-check our show. Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. Have a great week!
