A unique shape, a 3D einstein tile, has been discovered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:58:54 UTC
19:58:54 KST

It may look like a child’s Lego creation, but it’s a mathematical marvel. Researchers have just discovered a three-dimensional “einstein” tile—a special shape with unique capabilities.
The finding follows a major announcement from 2023, when a new hat-shaped tile called an “einstein” rocked the popular mathematics world. David Smith, an amateur mathematician, discovered that shape. In an article later published in Combinatorial Theory, he and three other researchers—Joseph Samuel Myers, Craig Kaplan and Chaim Goodman-Strauss—proved that “the hat” was the first known example of a two-dimensional aperiodic monotile, also called an “einstein” (ein Stein roughly translates to “one shape” in German). In other words, the hat is a shape that can infinitely tile, or cover, a 2D surface without ever creating a repeating pattern. These building-block hats can be placed next to one another to create bigger and bigger shapes that also look like the hat. But each individual hat will be situated in a nonrepeating pattern that continues to change no matter how large the overall tiling is.
Now a researcher has taken this concept into the third dimension with a 3D shape dubbed the Chair44 monotile. Chair44 can infinitely tile a three-dimensional space by covering it without gaps or overlapping shapes. Moreover, that tiling is aperiodic, meaning that the pattern is never repeated. The finding was announced by Ioannis Tsiokos, director of Automorph, which he describes as an AI research lab.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“I’m not a mathematician myself,” says Tsiokos, who is the sole human author of the preprint announcing Chair44. Tsiokos says he used Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 artificial intelligence model to write the paper and the OpenAI model ChatGPT-6 Astra to search for a 3D monotile, including to verify that the Chair44 monotile met the criteria for an einstein.
Chair44 isn’t exactly the first example of such a monotile in three dimensions, according to Kaplan, a computer scientist whose research focuses on the intersection of mathematics and art. “For decades, we’ve known of an aperiodic monotile in 3D: a shape known as the Schmitt-Conway-Danzer biprism,” Kaplan says. That biprism, however—a kind of convex polyhedron—“obeys the letter of the law of aperiodicity but not the spirit,” making it weakly aperiodic, he notes. The Chair44 discovery, on the other hand, fulfills a decades-long quest to find a strong example.
“I’m pleased that we have the solution to what was, until recently, a nagging open problem in tiling theory,” Kaplan says. “We can also hope that this discovery will generate renewed excitement in the mathematics of tilings and encourage more young people to play around with geometry.”
Propagating the Chair
To understand the geometric intuition behind the Chair44 shape, Tsiokos says, imagine a large cube composed of eight tiny cubes that are joined together. Next, remove just one cube. “Now you have a seven-cube chair,” he says.
The next goal on this journey is to create a bigger “chair” shape. That larger shape can be constructed by connecting four of these smaller chairs. To create a full tiling, just repeat this process over and over again, ad infinitum.
As you build bigger and bigger chairs, however, you must arrange the smaller chairs in a nonrepeating pattern so that the resulting tiling will be aperiodic.
“The trick” to ensuring an aperiodic tiling “is that you need to grow the chair in such a way that the behavior of the chair grows with it,” Tsiokos says. “To have this iterative, recursive building of chairs” requires making sure “that there are some sort of key locks between the chairs so that they form bigger and bigger chairs” that are made from a nonrepeating tiling pattern.
Experts Respond
When the hat monotile was discovered, it was so lauded that five researchers organized a two-day Hatfest celebration at the University of Oxford. Time will tell if Chair44 inspires its own celebration. For now, the reception to the finding has been mixed, largely because of Tsiokos’s significant use of generative AI in the proof.
“There was a lot of human work that went into what went into Astra to do this,” Tsiokos says.
Chaim Goodman-Strauss, one of the mathematicians behind the hat proof and an outreach mathematician at the National Museum of Mathematics, wrote a preprint reacting to the Chair44 results. In it, he described Tsiokos’s paper as having “hallmarks of an LLM-driven research paper,” including “so much irrelevant puff to push through.” Goodman-Strauss is one of at least two researchers who have now presented their own human-written proofs demonstrating that Chair44 is an aperiodic monotile.
Tiling problems have been “a big part of my career,” Goodman-Strauss says. He has studied the shape that Tsiokos calls Chair44 for more than 30 years, he says, and is used to calling it “the L.”
To explain how tiling with the shape works, Goodman-Strauss begins with an L-shaped building block. “You can make a bigger version of it out of eight little copies,” he says. “The problem is, that shape can also do all kinds of other crazy stuff,” he says. But because you can build a tiling from increasingly larger L shapes made up of smaller ones that are organized without repeating a pattern, each tile exists within what he calls “a supertile” that’s arranged in a unique configuration out of the smaller tiles.
Hence, Chair44 or the L is an aperiodic monotile in 3D.
Felix Flicker, a theoretical physicist at the University of Bristol in England, was one of Hatfest’s organizers. “I know a lot of mathematicians are unhappy with how the tile was discovered,” Flicker says. “The positive take is that we have a new important result.” The announcement comes after a summer in which AI models have repeatedly conquered many of math’s longstanding open challenges, including one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems. “The risk is that our jobs get reduced to sifting through AI slop in search of nuggets of gold,” Flicker says.
Flicker also wrote a Chair44 preprint, which he says aims to “provide the first human-written, human-readable, and therefore referee-able and defensible proof that Chair44 is a strongly aperiodic monotile.” (Even Flicker noted in his paper that he used Claude for coding and discussions in his study.)
Tsiokos’s Chair44 paper “is just the first example of something that we’re going to be encountering a lot of” in terms of generative AI usage, Goodman-Strauss says. “One of the big lessons here in the age of LLMs is that we should remember all the [math] questions we asked before that were difficult to deal with.” Perhaps some of those problems can now be solved through the use of LLMs as a mathematician’s tool—although those technologies aren’t a substitute for human reasoning, he notes.
The use of generative AI to find new potential math research results isn’t going away. “It’s just that we have got to come to terms with what’s expected in terms of communication” of those results, Goodman-Strauss says.

citroën revives the iconic 2 CV as a compact electric concept with a roll-up fabric roof
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

citroën revives the iconic 2 CV as a compact electric concept with a roll-up fabric roof
unveiled at the 2026 paris motor show, citroën's 2 cv concept reinterprets the 1948 classic as a compact electric car measuring just 3.76 metres.
CITROËN 2 CV CONCEPT REIMAGINES THE 1948 CLASSIC
At the 2026 Paris Motor Show, Citroën is bringing the 2 CV back to the drawing board — and this time, it runs on electricity. The 2 CV Concept revisits the French manufacturer’s most recognisable small car, first unveiled at the same event in 1948, with an emphasis on lightness, affordability and everyday practicality. Rather than simply reproducing a familiar silhouette, Citroën is exploring the ingredients for a new electric model that it plans to introduce by 2028, preserving the original’s philosophy of making mobility accessible without sacrificing personality.
At just 3.76 metres long, the concept is actually shorter than its predecessor, a rather unusual achievement in an automotive industry accustomed to making everything bigger. Its silhouette retains the original’s rounded proportions, vertical windscreen and flowing roofline, while introducing a more contemporary expression. Circular LED headlights appear to float beside the sculpted bonnet, 18-inch steel wheels reinterpret the classic design, and the bright Infra Red bodywork shifts between orange, yellow and red tones depending on the light. The manually retractable fabric roof is another familiar touch, bringing the original’s open-air character into the electric era.
PLAYFUL TECHNOLOGY SHAPE THE ELECTRIC CAR INTERIOR
Inside, the Citroën 2 CV Concept takes a similarly unconventional approach. A cylindrical structure replaces the traditional dashboard, bringing together a single-spoke steering wheel, simplified controls and an eight-inch square touchscreen featuring comic-book-inspired graphics by Belgian illustrator Jean-Luc Delvaux. Essential driving information appears through the Smart Vision display, positioned within the driver’s field of vision. The cabin also combines yellow tartan upholstery with beige details inspired by the Bakelite components of earlier models, creating an interior that feels deliberately cheerful rather than technologically intimidating.
Practicality comes with a few surprises. The front bench seat can be removed and used outdoors during a picnic, while a detachable Radioën unit doubles as a portable speaker. Instead of a central console, passengers get a removable storage basket made from wood and bio-based plastic using 3D printing, and flexible fabric straps replace conventional door handles. Above, the roll-up fabric roof opens the cabin to daylight, while a string of lights suspended from the headlining introduces an unexpected festive touch. Apparently, even a short drive deserves a little atmosphere.
CITROËN’S ELECTRIC 2 CV LOOKS TO SIMPLICITY FOR THE ROAD AHEAD
Some of the smallest details carry the strongest references to the original. The accelerator and brake pedals feature illustrations of a hare and a tortoise, while the door compartments are designed to accommodate eggs, recalling the famously practical specifications of the first 2 CV. Numbers printed on the windscreen mark 1948, the original launch; 1990, the end of production; and 2026, the concept’s debut. Even the horn and start-up sound echo those of the historic model. These playful gestures turn automotive heritage into something that can be experienced rather than simply admired.
Beyond nostalgia, Citroën is proposing a different approach to affordable electric mobility. The future European-built production model is targeting a starting price of around €15,000, while the concept’s engineering aims for a weight close to one tonne, reduced manufacturing complexity and easier repairs through independently replaceable bumpers. A collaboration with Michelin also explores digital tyre-monitoring technology that uses vehicle data instead of dedicated tyre sensors. ‘Reinventing the 2 CV isn’t about replicating a car from the past,’ says Citroën CEO Xavier Chardon. Whether the eventual production car can retain this same balance of simplicity, ingenuity and character remains the more interesting question.

name: 2 CV Concept
designer: Citroën Design Team
brand: Citroën | @citroen
Location: Paris, France (2026 Paris Motor Show)

Tyeb Mehta’s ‘Rickshaw Puller’ fetches record Rs 69.1 crore at Volte Una auction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:54:08 UTC
19:54:08 KST

Tushar Jiwarajka, Founder of Volte Una, with the Tyeb painting.
For much of his life, artist Tyeb Mehta lived in a cramped one-room Bombay apartment that doubled as a studio by day and a bedroom at night.It was only in the 1990s that he and his wife Sakina could afford to move into a two-bedroom apartment in Lokhandwala. Today, his paintings command staggering sums. The latest is Rickshaw Puller, which sold for Rs 69.1 crore at Volte Una’s inaugural auction, setting a world auction record for the artist.The sale surpassed the previous record of Rs 61.8 crore, set by Trussed Bull in April 2025, and makes Rickshaw Puller the fourth-most expensive Indian work of art ever sold at auction.Painted in 2002, during the final decade of Mehta’s career, the acrylic on canvas depicts the rickshaw puller, a figure he returned to in his later work. The painting attracted multiple bidders in the final minutes before the auction closed.
The record is particularly striking for an artist known for his exacting standards, who routinely destroyed works he considered unworthy. It also marks a significant debut for Volte Una, a new auction house built around an unusual premise: selling one major work at a time rather than offering multiple lots in a single sale.The single-lot format is designed to give collectors time to engage closely with each artwork before bidding, with an emphasis on privacy and discretion.“We are thrilled that we were able to respect Tyeb Mehta’s painting by exposing it to the most serious and discreet collectors globally in private settings,” said Tushar Jiwarajka, Founder of Volte Una. “And we have introduced a business model that allows the traditional buyer’s premium to be significantly reduced, putting that money back in the pockets of consignors and successful bidders.”Volte Una’s next auction, scheduled for the end of November, will feature a work by M F Husain from the renowned Herwitz Collection.

French high school students Monday were planning a new stage of their campaign for improved conditions and launch wave of demonstrations to maintain momentum.
The new protests, scheduled for Tuesday, could be a turning point in the movement, launched in mid-September, which the government hopes is already winding down.
On Friday, the government noted a dramatic drop in the number of blockades and meetings outside the country's lycees, where students – most between 15 and 18 – complete their high school education.
More than 96% were opening Friday, said the Education Ministry.
The authorities are all the more keen to see the student protests end given that online activists have called for demonstrations next Saturday to protest the cost of living.
For President Emmanuel Macron's administration, that brings back troubling memories of the grassroots Yellow Vest movement.
Their protests, launched in 2018 over a planned fuel tax rise, saw massive demonstrations and clashes between police and protesters that shook the presidency during Macron's first term in office.
The government is still counting the cost of the high school protests.
A government source told journalists last week that the cost for damage caused by the demonstrations was "at least 30 million euros."
On Friday, the justice ministry said more than 6,800 people had been detained since the demonstrations started, 86% of them minors.
After clashes between some protesters and riot police left some students severely injured, sparking criticism of police tactics, the government suspended the use of stun grenades that cost one student his hand.
Police are investigating 18 alleged cases of misconduct within their ranks.
Last week, the government came up with concrete proposals to try to address the students' demands.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced late Thursday that some 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu Sunday promised to make changes to the planned budget 2027 to respond to some demands set out in an online platform the government set up to gather students' views.
The student organizations behind the protests are yet to be convinced, however.
The Union of High School students described the initial announcements last week as "crumbs." They are maintaining their demand for an extra 10 million euros to be invested in the country's lycees.
France's 10,000 medical students, however, are beginning to express concern at the effect any continued school blockades could have on exams starting Monday that help determine their eventual speciality.
They do not want to see the students' action disrupt such a crucial stage of their education.
Last Thursday's student demonstrations mobilized tens of thousands of people across France: 71,500 according to Interior Ministry figures.
Nearly 256,000 took part in last Tuesday's day of action.
And one poll, carried out by Ipsos-BVA and published Sunday, said 54% of respondents backed the high school student protests.
They had the most sympathy with student complaints about the excessive size of classes and with the need to renovate the country's crumbling schools.

No public funds for bank liquidations, says VP Yılmaz
Unknown

2026-10-12

19:51:09 KST

Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz spoke on a live broadcast by Anadolu Agency, Oct. 12, 2026. (AA Photo)
Investigations into the troubled funds are continuing, Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz has said, adding that no public money will be used in the liquidations of those funds.
“Investigations are continuing regarding people who obtained very high returns or unfair gains through illegal transactions,” Yılmaz said on Oct. 12 during a live broadcast by Anadolu Agency.
Addressing the process following the return of unlawful gains, Yılmaz said legal responsibilities would remain in force.
“If there has been an unlawful transaction, responsibilities do not disappear,” he said.
Yılmaz said authorities moved quickly to prevent the incident from spreading to the broader fund market and damaging the overall financial system.
“The problematic funds were, in a sense, placed under quarantine. Measures were imposed on seven companies and 131 funds under them,” he said.
He added that a judicial process is underway.
“Many people are currently under arrest, in custody or under investigation, and many have given statements. Asset freezes have been imposed and travel bans have been introduced,” Yılmaz said.
According to Yilmaz, the Fund Coordination Board established during the process has held four meetings and adopted key principles.
He also said the State Supervisory Council had launched a broad-based field investigation involving around 15 inspectors and auditors covering all relevant institutions.
“Independent financial authorities and all of these institutions will be examined and investigated. Administrative shortcomings and individual responsibilities will be revealed through this process,” he said.
“There are seven companies and 131 problematic funds. These funds account for 4.6 percent of all funds and 7.7 percent of the total fund portfolio. More than 455,000 investors are involved in these funds,” he said.
He noted that three of the seven companies had accepted ordinary liquidation procedures and were liquidated as of Oct. 8.
“Payments have been made to nearly 44,000 citizens, and 17 funds have consequently exited the system,” Yilmaz said.
He added that more than 2,000 investors were involved in closed-end funds managed by the three entities undergoing ordinary liquidation, and that those funds would be liquidated according to their own structures and characteristics.
Yilmaz stressed that neither ordinary nor extraordinary liquidation would involve the use of public resources.
“There will be no use of public funds in either ordinary or extraordinary liquidation,” he said.
Explaining the reason, Yilmaz said the state does not provide guarantees for capital markets and investment funds.
“There is no state guarantee in fund markets or capital markets. In the banking system there is a state guarantee up to a certain amount, but such a guarantee does not exist in capital markets,” he said.

carsten höller’s goggles turn the world upside down to challenge perception
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:50:54 UTC
19:50:54 KST

carsten höller’s goggles turn the world upside down to challenge perception
inspired by a 19th-century psychology experiment, the wearable artwork turns familiar surroundings into an unsettling test of perception and movement.
carsten höller’s goggles disrupt our sense of orientation
‘The dream is the confusion machine I didn’t have to build,’ Carsten Höller told designboom in our interview back in April, describing his fascination with experiences that interrupt our usual sense of control. For the artist, dreams represent an extraordinary disruption of reality when the mind generates an environment that feels entirely convincing, even as perception becomes unstable and voluntary movement disappears. Höller explores a related uncertainty through his installations, from slides that induce physical vertigo to rotating beds and wearable devices that interfere with how we experience our surroundings.
Höller’s Upside-Down Goggles, first presented in 1994, invert the wearer’s field of vision, making familiar surroundings appear upside down. Simple gestures, such as walking through a room or reaching for an object, suddenly require a different kind of attention. The space may remain the same but moving through it is no longer intuitive.
seeing the world upside-down
Back to the 1890s, American psychologist George M. Stratton wanted to understand how we perceive the world as upright when the image projected onto the retina is inverted. To investigate, he constructed an optical apparatus that reversed his visual field, allowing him to observe how his perception and movements responded to this unfamiliar arrangement. In his first experiment, published in 1896, Stratton wore the apparatus for 21.5 hours over three days. He followed this with a longer investigation in 1897, wearing it for 87 hours over eight days.
As he moved around his garden and through the surrounding village, he recorded the difficulties of coordinating his movements with what he saw. Spatial relationships became unfamiliar, forcing him to rethink how what he could perceive through his sight related to his bodily experience. Stratton’s observations helped establish visual adaptation as a subject of psychological research. His experiment suggested that perception involves more than the passive reception of images and is shaped by the relationship between sight, movement, and experience.
an experiment in perception
Höller describes noticing a slight shift in perception after only five minutes of wearing the goggles. The experience changes considerably when the subject wearing the pair begins to move. Forms seem to slide into one another, while objects appear unexpectedly close or far away. The visual inversion is only part of the effect, as movement alters the apparent relationships between things and makes the surrounding space harder to read.
These observations bring the work back to the relationship between vision and physical experience. We rarely have to think about how we judge a distance, reach for a glass, or step around a chair. Such actions depend on an ongoing coordination between what we see and how we move. The goggles interrupt that coordination, turning familiar gestures into uncertain ones. There is also a difference between adapting to an unfamiliar image and feeling at ease within the world it presents.
Stratton’s experiments explore the changes that could occur over extended periods of inverted vision. Höller’s observations, by contrast, begin with minutes of wearing the device, when perception may start to shift but movement remains unfamiliar. The wearer must act within a world that looks recognizable in its details but no longer behaves as expected. Höller’s goggles make the act of navigating an ordinary space feel newly uncertain. What usually passes unnoticed, the coordination of sight, distance, and movement, becomes the central experience of the work.

IMF chief warns AI could disrupt jobs, widen Asia's economic divide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:44:34 UTC
19:44:34 KST

Artificial intelligence could help offset the economic drag from Asia's ageing populations, but the technology also threatens to disrupt jobs and widen the gap between advanced and developing economies unless governments act quickly to prepare workers, the International Monetary Fund head said on Monday.
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva described AI as a “slow-moving tsunami” at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, warning that it would have profound consequences for jobs, growth, education and even how governments generate revenue through taxation, given the expected shift from labour to capital.
The IMF estimates that AI could lead to 40 percent of jobs being augmented, downgraded or eliminated, over time, she said. An initial study showed that 10 percent of jobs in the US already required AI skills.
While routine, repetitive jobs were shrinking, low-paying jobs were increasing in two lower-paying sectors, construction and data centres.
"It is a transformative technology. It so completely changes how we work, how we live," she said, noting that an AI assistant now gave her a 30-second message about her schedule each day.
The US, China and India are the most important producers in the AI supply chain, but many of the firms building the needed infrastructure are in Asia, Georgieva said, referencing Thailand, host of this year's annual meetings.
Who gains from AI?
“We cannot imagine today what the world of work will look like five years from now,” Georgieva said, urging policymakers to study the changes and act on the lessons they provide.
The stakes are particularly high in Asia, where ageing populations are expected to shrink the workforce in major economies. China, Japan and South Korea could lose nearly a quarter of their working-age populations by 2050, according to findings presented in an IMF book on the region's economic challenges and opportunities.
AI-driven productivity gains could more than offset some of that demographic pressure. The IMF estimates that AI could lift growth in advanced Asian economies by between 0.5 and 1 percentage point.
But the benefits are unlikely to be evenly distributed.
Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific department, said advanced economies were more exposed to AI but better positioned to capture its gains, while emerging markets faced a greater risk of falling behind.
“What matters is whether AI augments workers or automates jobs,” Srinivasan said, adding that reforms to improve skills and productivity could accelerate adoption in emerging economies by a decade or more.
AI impact on entry-level jobs
World Bank President Ajay Banga, who has made jobs a central focus of his presidency, said the development bank was focused on leveraging "small AI", which is not dependent on large language models, to generate enormous productivity gains for farmers, healthcare systems, educators and others in emerging markets.
Singapore's President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking at the same event, said governments should address how AI was reducing job opportunities for graduates.
"There is a particular problem that we have to address very soon ... and that is that, the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," he said.
He said the world should also guard against AI resulting in a "new divergence" in growth and job creation between developing and advanced economies.
"AI is going to widen the divergence if we are too passive about it," he said. "So we've got to do everything we can to first use AI to create good jobs and to create jobs that can be done well by human beings, can allow them to ride up a career ladder despite AI."

19:42:19 KST

- The U.S. Army received its first Hanwha-built Mobile Tactical Cannon prototype, a wheeled K9-based howitzer meant to replace the towed M777.
- The deal covers six prototypes with options for 12 more, worth up to about $263 million, with fielding targeted by 2031.
The U.S. Army has received its first Mobile Tactical Cannon, a wheeled 155 mm howitzer built by Hanwha Defense USA that the service is testing as a replacement for the towed M777, less than a year after it first asked industry for proposals.
Brig. Gen. Robert “RJ” Mikesh Jr., the Army’s portfolio management executive for offensive fires, told reporters on Oct. 8 ahead of the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting that the cannon had been on display at an “Army Modernization Day” on Capitol Hill earlier this month, Military Times reported.
“We’re excited to have that and get ready to test it,” said Mikesh. “And get that soldier feedback, that we think is so important.”
The Army picked Hanwha in August under an Other Transaction Authority agreement, a faster contracting route for prototypes. The four-year deal is worth about $100.3 million to start and up to roughly $263 million if all options are used. It calls for six prototypes to be delivered quickly, with options for 12 more, for testing and experiments with soldiers. Hanwha beat a crowded field that included BAE Systems, General Dynamics Land Systems, American Rheinmetall, a Leonardo DRS and KNDS team, and an Elbit Systems of America, Anduril and Oshkosh team.
The Mobile Tactical Cannon is Hanwha’s K9 Mobile Howitzer, an eight-wheeled version of the tracked K9 that has served with the South Korean Army since 1999. K9 variants are now used by about 10 other countries, and Hanwha says more than 2,500 have been fielded worldwide. The company is building an integration and test site in Opelika, Alabama, to develop and deliver the howitzers in the United States.
“What enabled that was this close partnership under the PAE construct and trying new and novel ways of contracting,” said Mikesh. “In this case, we were not going after a clean-sheet design; we were looking for mature and available technologies. We opened our aperture for companies around the world, knowing that they’d have to onshore production within two years. That howitzer is now on contract.”
The new gun is meant to give units more range and protection than the M777, a lightweight towed howitzer the Army has used since 2005 that must be hitched to a truck and set up by its crew. The M777 can hit targets out to about 24 km (15 miles) with standard rounds and about 40 km (25 miles) with the Excalibur guided shell. The K9’s longer 52-caliber barrel can reach more than 60 km (37 miles), and a self-propelled gun can fire and move before counter-battery fire arrives.
The Army plans to field the cannon first to Stryker brigade combat teams, then to Mobile and Infantry brigade combat teams. It also wants to use the prototypes in its 155mm Artillery Propulsion Modernization project, which is testing new propellants, charges and ignition systems to hit targets out to 70 km (43 miles). In late August the Army issued a separate solicitation for a tracked version of the Mobile Tactical Cannon, which Hanwha has said it will also pursue.
Army leaders want a ready version of the Mobile Tactical Cannon fielded by 2031.

Changhua County targets illegal farm wastewater with smart monitoring
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:40:49 UTC
19:40:49 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Changhua County is using smart monitoring technology and legal measures to tackle years of pollution in the Dongluo River, a waterway affected by illegal wastewater discharges.
Business Today reported that the river, often called Changhua’s “mother river,” has long been polluted by wastewater from livestock farms and households, as well as illegally dumped garbage. The county is home to 595 livestock farms and is a major supplier of milk, eggs and meat in Taiwan.
Livestock wastewater is a major source of pollution, but illegal discharges are difficult to catch. Some operators release untreated wastewater at night or during off-peak hours, making it harder for authorities to collect evidence and issue fines.
To address the problem, the Changhua County Environmental Protection Bureau introduced what it calls Taiwan’s first data-driven smart water monitoring network. The system tracks water conditions and helps officials identify possible pollution incidents.
In 2022, the bureau worked with the Changhua District Prosecutors Office to investigate illegal wastewater discharges involving 19 livestock farms. The case led authorities to combine legal enforcement with measures to prevent further pollution.
Prosecutors agreed to defer prosecution if the operators invested in a livestock wastewater treatment center. The arrangement allowed the farms to avoid immediate prosecution while requiring them to help fund improvements to wastewater treatment.
Changhua County Environmental Protection Bureau Director Chiang Pei-ken (江培根) said wastewater pollution remains a major challenge for the county. The monitoring network and cooperation with prosecutors aim to improve river conditions while allowing the livestock industry to continue operating.
The initiative goes beyond fines by requiring polluters to contribute to long-term wastewater treatment. It also gives authorities additional tools to detect illegal discharges and prevent further damage to the river.

139 people dead, including 15 children, after migrant boat capsizes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:39:22 UTC
19:39:22 KST

139 people dead, including 15 children, after migrant boat capsizes off Africa: "Overwhelmed with all the bodies"
At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying more than 300 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in east Africa, the International Organization for Migration said Sunday.
"This is a devastating loss of life. Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives," Alexandre Coissac, IOM chief of mission in Djibouti, said in a statement.
That number only includes those buried by authorities in Djibouti. Others have been buried by the migrants themselves, but they won't be added to the official count until authorities can verify the bodies, Coissac told the AP via the phone.
"What is terrible is that they were buried with no names, in a common grave, like in a war situation," Coissac said. "They all have a mother, a father, and we may never learn what happened."
Coissac said the migrants boarded the ship in the evening of Oct. 8 and that it sank very soon after, close to the shore, "mainly because it was overcrowded."
"The local authorities did their best," Coissac said, "but they were overwhelmed with all the bodies that kept coming at once towards the shore."
The IOM said among the bodies recovered were nine girls and six boys. More than 80 people survived the shipwreck, all Ethiopian nationals. IOM released video of the aftermath of the wreck, showing the capsized vessel and victims' clothes on the shore.
He said authorities were bringing the surviving migrants to the IOM rescue center in Obock where they receive medical assistance after swallowing sea water, and psychological support.
"They're all in a state of shock," said Coissac, who visited the area of the shipwreck Saturday. "I tried to talk to some of them but it's very difficult."
Some of the migrants in the IOM center are already aware that their family members died during the shipwreck. Others were given access to phones to call loved ones back home to notify them they are alive.
At least 84 people remained missing in one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations.
The boat was traveling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized on Thursday night or Friday morning, according to the IOM. More than 80 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals, it said.
The Geneva-based U.N. migration agency said the vessel had 305 people on board and warned that the death toll could still rise.
Personal items likely belonging to the migrants, including shoes, were seen on a beach in a video shared by IOM. Rescue work continued as fears grew for the missing.
Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel every year through Djibouti and across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait toward Gulf countries in search of safety and economic opportunities, the IOM said in its statement.
That movement has continued despite newly escalating fighting in Yemen, on the other side of the strait.
"This is a devastating loss of life," said Coissac. "This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities."
In recent weeks, at least 2,000 Yemenis have received aid in Djibouti as the fighting has escalated in Yemen between the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels.
That's the opposite direction from the movement of the migrants who died in the shipwreck and the typical migration patterns of recent years: The tens of thousands who cross from eastern Africa toward Yemen each year have typically been looking for work in places like Saudi Arabia.
More than 900 migrants died or went missing along the route last year, according to IOM's Missing Migrants Project, while the number undertaking the journey increased by 18%.
Earlier this year, IOM said 53 people were dead or missing after a boat capsized in the Mediterranean Sea off the Libyan coast. Only two survivors were rescued.
"No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way," IOM Director-General Amy Pope said. "We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down."

More than 700 computer science professionals and students attended the national computer science conference on Thursday to discuss the field's future amid the changes brought about by artificial intelligence.
Organized by the Ben-Gurion University of the Negev's Stein Faculty of Computer and Information Science, the conference also marked the faculty's one-year anniversary, established in 2025.
The conference also featured the launch of the Israeli Computer Science Association, which aims to establish a national framework for Israel's academic and professional computer science community.
The association seeks to strengthen ties between institutions, promote conferences and community initiatives, and develop position papers on issues affecting the future of computer science in Israel.
For its first two years, the association will be managed by Ben-Gurion University. Its leadership is then expected to rotate among Israeli universities.
The conference also featured the presentation of the association's first awards for outstanding research achievements.
The awards committee, chaired by Prof. Yuval Filmus, selected four recipients, including Dr. Haggai Maron of the Technion-Israel Institute of Technology, Dr. Oded Padon of the Weizmann Institute of Science, Dr. Yuval Dagan of Tel Aviv University, and Dr. Liat Peterfreund of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
Mobileye CEO Prof. Amnon Shashua also attended the conference and delivered a guest lecture on the development of machine intelligence and its impact on scientists, researchers, and experts.
AI doesn't make computers obsolete, Israeli expert says
"Artificial intelligence does not make computer science obsolete. It is ushering in the golden age of the field," said Prof. Shakhar Smorodinsky, head of the Institute for the Theory of Computing at Ben-Gurion University's Stein Faculty of Computer and Information Science and chairman of the Israeli Computer Science Association.
"Writing code is only one part of computer science. As AI tools become better at writing code, the ability to define problems, develop algorithms, design systems, verify correctness and safety, and understand the limitations of the models themselves becomes increasingly important," Smorodinsky said.
"It is precisely in the age of artificial intelligence that Israel needs greater scientific depth, not less."
Smorodinsky also emphasized the need to establish a shared framework for Israel's computer science community.
"The establishment of the association provides Israel's computer science community with a shared framework for cooperation and for expressing a professional voice on issues relating to research, teaching, and national policy. We want to connect researchers from all institutions, identify shared needs, and promote initiatives that the entire community can benefit from," he said.
"We believe that the new association and the conference we established will strengthen the modern understanding of computer science as a broad, diverse, and dynamic field, and we intend to make this event a tradition," said Prof. Ariel Felner, conference organizer and deputy dean of Ben-Gurion University's Faculty of Computer and Information Science.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday that Russia continues to strike Ukraine's energy facilities, despite President Donald Trump's claim a day earlier that both nations had agreed to an energy cease-fire.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had learned through media reports that Trump had secured an energy cease-fire deal with Russia which would involve a mutual pause in strikes on energy sites. Zelenskyy said he would be willing to honor such an agreement, if Moscow did the same.
"We support it, but I have not heard approval of this proposal from the Russian side," Zelenskyy said.
Trump's brief social media post Sunday claiming the purported agreement offered few details but said that the energy cease-fire took effect immediately, adding: "Do not break it!"
Yet Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been "horribly surprised" that following Trump's "sudden but very important post," Russia had struck numerous energy facilities including a power plant in the northeastern city of Kharkiv, as well as a gas production facility and a civilian gas station.
"It was clear that (Russian President Vladimir) Putin does not read Truth Social," Zelenskyy said, referring to Trump's social media platform.
Trump previously announced a similar agreement on ceasing energy strikes that did not come to fruition. In a social media post on Sept. 14, he said both countries had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure, but offered no details on that proposal either.
Russia has used attacks on energy facilities in order to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as "weaponizing winter," and fear Russia could ramp up such attacks as cold weather approaches.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has leveled strikes against Russian energy sites like oil refineries, sometimes deep within Russian territory, prompting Trump to blame Zelenskyy for high diesel prices on world markets.
On Friday, Trump struck a deal with Putin to import Russian diesel in an attempt to address high fuel prices just weeks ahead of U.S. midterm elections.
On Monday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to comply with Trump's requests to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine's energy system, and asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree. He added that if Moscow does not agree to an energy cease-fire this winter, "we will respond."
"We are waiting for the details of the conversation between the Americans and the Russians, and we are waiting to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take," he said. "This energy cease-fire can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war."
The European Union's top diplomat Monday welcomed the prospect of a pause in energy strikes in Ukraine, particularly as winter approaches, but said she sees no sign that Russia would be willing to respect it.
"We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said at a meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers in Luxembourg.
"Personally, I would also welcome that the cease-fire would include people not being killed, not only energy," she added.
Ukrainian and European officials reacted with dismay to Trump's diesel deal with Putin, saying it will help fund Russia's war effort.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna told reporters in Luxembourg Monday that he doesn't believe the deal "is actually going to change anything" in terms of fuel prices and that it is "much more connected to the domestic situation in the U.S."
Kallas, the EU's foreign policy chief, also pushed back on Trump's comments on Saturday that it was time for Ukraine to get a new president and that Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war. She said that now is not the time to hold elections in Ukraine, at least not without a cease-fire.
On Monday, Zelenskyy said holding elections in Ukraine was impossible during war time, especially with new Russian tactics involving attacks during both the day and night.
"Under such circumstances, it's impossible to hold elections," he said, but added that he would be ready to work toward doing so if Ukraine secured a full cease-fire lasting at least 60 days.
A Russian drone attack on the village of Pisochyn in the Kharkiv district on Sunday evening killed three people and injured nine others, including children, according to the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office.
Investigators said the attack occurred at approximately 7:25 p.m., striking a densely populated area near apartment buildings and grocery stores and sparking a fire.
Ukrainian air defense forces shot down or suppressed 89 of 121 Russian drones overnight Monday, Ukraine's Air Force said in a Telegram post.
The attack involved one Kh-59 guided air-to-surface missile and 121 drones, including 76 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, the statement said.
Strikes were recorded at 15 locations in Ukraine, while debris from downed drones fell at four locations.
The Russian Defense Ministry Monday said its air defenses overnight intercepted 151 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions as well as the illegally annexed Crimea and the waters of the Black Sea.
In a separate statement, the ministry said its forces overnight carried out drone strikes on Ukraine's unspecified port infrastructure and a bulk carrier heading to Ukraine's port city of Odesa with military cargo on board.

How Jantar Mantar became Delhi's designated protest site and what changes now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:34:39 UTC
19:34:39 KST

Jantar Mantar’s changing role in Delhi’s history of dissent.
NEW DELHI: Jantar Mantar, one of Delhi's best-known protest venues, has lost its status as a designated site for demonstrations. On October 12, Delhi Police de-notified the site and named three alternatives: Ramlila Ground, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi.The decision follows recommendations from a committee constituted by the ministry of home affairs (MHA) to examine alternative venues for protests and demonstrations.
For several decades, Jantar Mantar has been synonymous with protests in the national capital, a place where farmers, students, workers and political organisations have gathered to raise their demands. More recently, it became the centre of youth-led protests over the NEET paper leak, with demonstrators demanding reforms to the examination system and the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
Jantar Mantar’s legacy: A landmark site of dissent faces a shift
However, Delhi's address for protests has not always been Jantar Mantar. Before it emerged as a prominent hub for demonstrations, the sprawling lawns around India Gate and the Boat Club, close to Parliament and the government's principal offices, were among the capital's most important spaces for political mobilisation.The latest decision marks another chapter in the history of how authorities have regulated where citizens can assemble to make their voices heard.
Before Jantar Mantar, there was Boat Club
For decades after Independence, the Boat Club lawns near India Gate were an important venue for political rallies.The lawns near modern-day Central Vista gave demonstrators proximity to Parliament, the government's principal offices and other institutions at the centre of national power.The scale of the gatherings, however, also presented challenges for the authorities.One of the defining episodes came in 1988, when farmer leader Mahendra Singh Tikait led a massive agitation in Delhi. Farmers gathered at the Boat Club and surrounding lawns to press their demands, bringing a large mobilisation into the heart of the capital.The episode became a turning point in the debate over whether such prominent public spaces should remain open to large demonstrations.Authorities increasingly sought to regulate gatherings in central Delhi, citing concerns around security, traffic and public order.READ ALSO: SC permits Congress delegation to file petition within premises as Rahul leads INDIA bloc march
When Rajpath became a protest ground
In 'India After Gandhi: The History of the World's Largest Democracy', historian Ramachandra Guha recounts how the lawns along present-day Kartavya Path, formerly Rajpath and known as Kingsway during British rule, became a prominent site of political dissent in the early 1990s.The book recalls tents occupied by people from different parts of the country, representing causes ranging from demands for a separate state and better prices for agricultural produce to recognition for regional languages.Other groups included industrial workers, Tibetan refugees seeking Indian citizenship and Hindu religious organisations campaigning on cow slaughter.The lawns near the country's most prominent government buildings in Lutyens' Delhi became a temporary home for movements that wanted their demands to be seen and heard.But the encampments did not last. Guha writes that the tents were dismantled in the early 1990s, with the government concerned about the impression created by visible demonstrations near the ceremonial heart of the capital.Protesters subsequently regrouped near Jantar Mantar, where they remained visible to people passing through the busy commercial district.The restrictions on gatherings around Boat Club and Rajpath helped set the stage for Jantar Mantar's emergence as a prominent location for demonstrations.Live Updates: Delhi SIR Protest: Crowd swells as police stop Rahul, INDIA bloc leaders marching towards SC
How Jantar Mantar became Delhi's protest address
Built by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in the 18th century, Delhi's Jantar Mantar is an open-air astronomical observatory designed to track celestial movements.Over time, the area around the historic site evolved into a major hub for protest movements, offering demonstrators a prominent public platform while remaining easier to manage than larger, more central locations.Located close to busy Connaught Place and within reach of Parliament and government offices, it allowed demonstrators to bring their demands into public view without occupying the expansive lawns around India Gate.The site hosted protests involving workers, farmers, civil society groups and citizens campaigning on a range of social and political issues.Its prominence grew further during the anti-corruption movement led by social activist Anna Hazare in 2011, when demonstrations demanding a stronger Lokpal mechanism brought corruption and accountability to the centre of national political debate.As the movement grew, Ramlila Maidan became the venue for larger gatherings and Hazare's prolonged fast. The two locations demonstrated how different sites in Delhi could accommodate protests of different scales.The significance of Jantar Mantar was not simply a matter of geography. It became an established public address for people seeking to draw the attention of political leaders, government officials and the media to their grievances.Over the years, Jantar Mantar has witnessed protests on a range of issues, from Anna Hazare's campaign for a Lokpal Bill and the 2017 Tamil Nadu farmers' agitation to demonstrations against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act and the wrestlers' protests against Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh in 2023.More recently, it became the centre of demonstrations by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) over the NEET paper leak and demands for the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.However, its status as a designated protest venue did not mean that demonstrations could take place without restrictions. Police permissions, public-order measures and court directions continued to determine how the site could be used.ALSO READ: 'Resign': Congress Keralam unit to 'dear' CJI Surya Kant, draws BJP fire
When the right to protest reached the Supreme Court
In October 2017, the National Green Tribunal (NGT) ordered an end to protests at Jantar Mantar following complaints about noise, sanitation and disruption to residents.The restrictions were subsequently challenged before the Supreme Court.In its July 23, 2018, judgment in Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v Union of India, the Supreme Court examined restrictions on protests at Jantar Mantar and the Boat Club, including the effects of demonstrations on residents and public spaces.The court recognised peaceful assembly and protest as fundamental rights under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) of the Constitution. At the same time, it acknowledged that the exercise of these rights could be regulated to protect public order and the interests of other citizens.ALSO READ: FIR against Kejriwal, AAP leaders for 'chaos' at Bangla Sahib during CEC protestThe judgment addressed the competing claims of demonstrators and residents, making clear that one group's rights could not simply extinguish those of another.It called for a balance between the right to protest and the need to prevent unreasonable disruption.The constitutional basis for that balance is set out in Article 19. Article 19(1)(b) guarantees citizens the right to assemble peacefully and without arms, while Article 19(3) permits reasonable restrictions in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order.
The latest decision comes amid protests by opposition parties and the youth-led CJP against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged electoral irregularities and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The proposed CJP protest on October 10 was met with extensive security arrangements, detentions and restrictions on movement in parts of Delhi.Under the new arrangement, Jantar Mantar will no longer be a designated protest venue. Ramlila Ground, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi have been identified as alternatives.Delhi Police has said a detailed and revised standard operating procedure for demonstrations at these three venues will be issued separately.The decision changes where organisers can hold demonstrations under the designated-venue system. However, de-notification should not be confused with a blanket prohibition on all peaceful assembly, which remains subject to constitutional protections and lawful restrictions.
Why the location of a protest matters
The significance of the decision extends beyond the physical relocation of demonstrations. The location of a protest affects its visibility, the ease with which people can reach it and its proximity to the institutions being addressed.A venue in central Delhi offers demonstrators a different kind of access and public visibility from a ground farther away from the corridors of power.For organisers, the choice of location can therefore be an important part of how a protest communicates its message.
Among the newly designated venues, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi are farther from the central government district than Jantar Mantar.At the same time, large demonstrations in central Delhi can create challenges for traffic management, security and the daily movement of residents.The October 10 protests, for instance, were accompanied by extensive security arrangements and disruptions to movement across parts of the city.The latest decision once again brings into focus a question that has shaped Delhi's protest history for decades: how to balance the right to peaceful demonstrations with security, public order and the functioning of the national capital.

“If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond,” Zelensky told the Warsaw Security Forum via videolink.
Trump sowed confusion when he announced an energy ceasefire between the two warring countries without providing details, sparking astonishment in Kiev, silence from Moscow and support from Ukraine’s Western allies.
“We are waiting for the details of the conversation between the Americans and the Russians, and we are waiting to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take,” Zelensky said.
Trump’s announcement on Oct. 11 came two days after he declared a temporary easing of U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel, prompting outrage by European allies and Kiev, who said it would only embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people,” Zelensky said.
Trump has previously taken to his Truth Social account to announce truces or other arrangements before either Kiev or Moscow confirmed them.
“An energy ceasefire and other steps to reduce escalation and guarantee security are truly needed here in reality, not just on Truth Social,” Zelensky said.
"We don't want a ceasefire, we want long-term peace," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters, saying President Vladimir Putin would only order his troops to cease fire on election day itself.
"I do not think he (Zelensky) deserves a respite," added Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.
Also speaking on Oct. 12 at the Warsaw Security Forum, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that all western countries should be more decisive in containing Russia, as the invasion of Ukraine enters a fifth winter.
“This is the moment when the entire West, Europe, the United States, should show Russia and Putin that it is ready to pursue a policy of containing Russia by even more decisive means,” he said, adding he was primarily referring to sanctions.
“That is why I will go to Brussels to persuade all our European partners to seriously consider increasing sanctions against Russia,” he added, ahead of a summit planned later this week.
The European Union, on the other hand, Oct. 12 formally added almost 1,600 new individuals and entities to its sanctions blacklist over Russia’s war on Ukraine, in a bid to keep pressure on Moscow.
“This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas wrote online.
“Europe is again showing a united front. More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles,” she said.
“We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians,” she added.
Ukraine says Erdoğan could mediate Zelensky-Putin talks
In an interview published on Oct. 12, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has said that Zelensky could meet Putin through President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s mediation,
Sybiha also raised the possibility of Trump participating in a meeting between the two leaders.
He said Kiev remained ready to resume trilateral talks with Russia and the United States.
“We would like it to take place as soon as possible. We will use every opportunity, even the smallest, to bring peace closer,” Sybiha said.
The minister said direct talks between Zelensky and Putin would offer the best prospect of advancing efforts to end the war. He identified a ceasefire, prisoner exchanges and the return of children as potential outcomes of such a meeting.

AlterMe Review: Fitness Built Around My DNA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:34:00 UTC
19:34:00 KST

Easy-to-follow workouts based on my DNA and readiness score. Variety of chill yoga or breathwork sessions plus more intense strength, dance, and cardio workouts. The app tracks nutrition and sleep and analyzes meals.
TIRED
Workouts are short—ranging from five to 40 minutes. DNA results are interesting, but there’s no quick fix to fitness. Premium price.
When I was asked to review AlterMe’s fitness system that claims to use DNA and biometric data to create a personalized fitness, nutrition, and recovery program, I was intrigued. I’ve used some of the best fitness trackers before, but have never tried a system that combines DNA testing, personalized workouts, nutrition insight, and its own smart wearable all within a single ecosystem.
I’m someone who needs constant fitness motivation to stay on track. Rather than push myself through strenuous weights and cardio, I prefer feel-good Pilates and an ice bath at my local David Lloyd gym. But in an effort to step out of my comfort zone and try something a little more challenging, I decided to give AlterMe a go.
I’ve used numerous fitness apps over the years, such as Bala and Freeletics, but not one that suggests specific fitness workouts based on my DNA testing results. AlterMe combines guidance across exercise, nutrition, sleep, and recovery, going beyond simply reporting on your DNA and biometric data to suggest small, manageable actions to drive behavioral change over time.
There’s no denying that it comes at a premium price, but having workouts and nutrition guidance in one place helped me build better habits—even if the DNA insights weren’t particularly revelatory.
Getting Set Up
Photograph: Emily Peck
AlterMe’s all-in-one health and fitness program is built around a DNA test and a smart ring that measures data and provides insights and workouts in the app. It’s convenient, but this is an expensive offering. The entry-level AlterMe Essential plan is $1,299, and the AlterMe Advanced plan is $1,899. Both offer biometric tracking, nutrition insights, and fitness workouts accessible from the app, but the Advanced plan gives you a more in-depth DNA analysis and lifetime membership as opposed to the Essential’s three-year membership.
Upon signing up and answering questions on my weight-loss goals, height, weight, and general fitness levels, I was sent both a DNA cheek-swab kit and a ring sizing kit. I emailed AlterMe to confirm my ring size and sent the DNA swab back in the mail. Within two weeks, I received my AlterMe smart ring and had booked in a date to talk over my Fitness and Wellness Genetic report with an AlterMe representative. I’ve been diving in and out of the app and following the fitness workouts for over six months now.
A Tailored Fitness and Wellness Genetic Report
AlterMe app via Emily Peck
Research into genetic influence on athletic performance is still developing, and AlterMe acknowledges that its genetic findings reported through DNA testing have not been clinically validated. However, the company conducts its own research to produce a personalized Fitness and Wellness Genetic Report. It says it uses “a rigorous genetic interpretation process that adheres to strict scientific standards” with “scientific integrity” and “robust research.” AlterMe also states that saliva samples are processed in the US in a CLIA- and CAP-certified lab that meets local regulations.
With this in mind, I approached the DNA test report with equal measures of skepticism and intrigue, as should anyone curious to get more insight into their health and well-being.
The report claimed to use my DNA to reveal how my body responds to different types of exercise, nutrition, recovery, and stress. It suggested types of exercise to suit me and how I could approach training and recovery. Strength training, for example, was identified as the best fit for my genetic profile, while my genetic response to carbohydrates was rated as “lower than average.”
Perhaps not surprisingly, the report told me that I’m “externally motivated to exercise,” suggesting I may not naturally enjoy physical activity just for the sake of it. That certainly felt familiar.
Representatives at AlterMe explained how these assessments are determined: “Our assessment looks at markers associated with several traits, including how body composition changed during exercise interventions. For cardio-related body composition response, the markers in our scientific review are ADRB2 rs1042713 and LPL rs328. For resistance training, the model draws on a set of obesity and body composition markers, including variants near FTO, GNPDA2, NEGR1, and SLC39A8.”
So far, everything was sounding on point. But despite the personalized insights, I hadn’t discovered anything particularly groundbreaking.
Smart Ring Bling
Photograph: Emily Peck
AlterMe has its own smart ring wearable, designed to provide health insights and work alongside the app. The ring uses PPG sensors to monitor metrics such as heart rate and blood oxygen, alongside a temperature sensor and an accelerometer to track activity. It then uses data including my HRV, resting heart rate, sleep, and recent activity load to turn the raw measurements into a “Readiness score” from 0 to 100, before suggesting a workout tailored to my current state and my DNA insight.
This type of health tracking is similar to what you get with Oura's Ring 5 offering. The key difference is that AlterMe is a more closed ecosystem, combining its wearable data with its own genetic insights to generate an AI-powered workout plan every day based on my biometrics.
Oura, meanwhile, provides detailed sleep, activity, readiness, and broader health insights as well as guided fitness content within its app and integration with services such as Apple Health. Its primary focus, however, remains tracking and interpreting your health and activity data, whereas AlterMe puts more emphasis on the personalized workouts it prescribes.
The ring has a titanium outer frame and comes in either a gold finish, silver, or Stealth black. My gold finish has picked up some scuff marks over the couple of months I’ve been wearing it. While the gold finish looks good, I found the ring quite bulky—and thicker than the sleek Oura Ring 5—which means it sometimes gets in the way when I’m lifting weights.
Tailored Workouts Depending on ‘Readiness’ Score
Within the stats section of the app, I was able to view my daily calorie burn, step count, distance covered, sleep duration, and readiness score—all data the ring was providing. The app then provides a daily workout to follow. The workouts can be as low-key or as challenging as I want, depending on how I am feeling. I could choose from stretch, strength, cardio, yoga, or combat-style sessions, so there’s no excuse to skip a workout. As AlterMe representatives told me, the biometric data collected can help make a recommendation, but it can’t capture every detail about how I feel—soreness, illness, stress, injury, or demands of the day may change what feels right, for example—which is why you get the option to choose your level.
“Giving you a choice is also an intentional part of the AlterMe experience,” say AlterMe representatives. “Without choice, it’s hard for you to stay consistent. We want to offer useful guidance while leaving you in control of your effort. Your choice adds context and makes the plan easier to fit into real life.”
On the days I had poor sleep the night before, the app recommended a lighter workout or recovery session—the 15-minute breathwork session has become a particular favorite. On the days I’d slept well, I was tasked with a more strenuous session depending on my current level, from beginner to level 6.
While the workouts are easy to access and follow, I found them short—20 minutes was the average workout time, with 40 minutes being the longest session I tried. But it is possible to stack the workouts if you want to push yourself further. There’s also a way to track activities such as a run or group workout outside the guided library of workouts.
I trust that the app was recommending workouts to suit my health stats and genetic traits, and I mostly felt good when following them. But there were some days when I was feeling terrible due to poor sleep, and the app was telling me that my readiness score was high, which left me feeling a little confused. But I dutifully obliged with the suggested workout—even if I did opt for a shorter 20-minute session. On the days I had forgotten to wear my ring to bed the night before, the app would ask me to self-score from 1 to 10 on how I was feeling before a workout was suggested.
AI Nutrition Coach and Body Scanning
Exercise is just one piece of the fitness puzzle, and one of the pros of the AlterMe app is that it has a nutrition tracker. Rather than having it provide a single diet plan, I like the way the app can generate meal and snack ideas by referencing my DNA to keep me hitting my macro targets. You can generate a recipe and then log it if you decide to make it. Simply by clicking “generate recipe” I could get breakfast, lunch, dinner, and snack ideas in under 20 seconds. The recipes are pretty enticing too—Zesty Lemon Herb Grilled Chicken Qith Roasted Green Beans and Quinoa was one I tried. But I found the snack ideas most helpful, as I’m always thinking about snacks—Roasted Edamame With Smoked Paprika and Sea Salt is a particular favorite.
In the Nutrition tab of the app, I could access personalized calorie and nutrition guidance based on my DNA results, weight, BMI, activity level, and weight-loss goals. My DNA report suggested I have an average response to protein and a low response to carbs and fats. I like how easy it is to log food in the Nutrition tab in the app and instantly see whether I’d hit my protein, fat, and carb macro goals. I often forgot to track everything I ate, but on the days I remembered to do so, I found it easy to track my calorie intake and meals.
AlterMe app via Emily Peck
The app also has a 3D/body composition scanning feature to analyze body shape and provide stats on things like BMI, estimated body-fat percentage, and lean mass.
You do need to put in your height and weight when you sign up, but this feature adds more. As AlterMe told me, BMI is calculated from height and weight, but the scan provides a much fuller view by creating a standardized 3D model and estimating body-fat percentage, lean mass, body shape, and body part circumferences. Repeated scans help show whether and where the body is changing, giving members a clearer way to compare their progress with their goals. You need to use your phone camera to capture a picture of your body shape, but turning as it takes photos. I found this feature a little intrusive, as I didn’t really want to take photos of myself to put on the app. But if this doesn’t bother you, I think this is a compelling extra.
Is the AlterMe App Worth It?
There are numerous workout apps and wearables that can track your health data, but this personalized program that combines DNA testing, a smart ring wearable, and on-demand workouts in one ecosystem is a unique offering. It’s convenient, but pricey, and it's important to note that while the DNA testing can be insightful, it hasn’t been clinically validated. There are also understandable privacy concerns around handing over DNA data, although AlterMe notes on its site that it destroys samples after testing and extracted DNA is retained for just 45 days for quality assurance.
My journey with AlterMe has generally been positive, but it hasn’t altered me. It has made me more aware of what I eat and made me feel physically stronger due to the regularity of my training sessions. I like wearing the ring and having an app that suggests an optimum workout based on my biometrics. Having a tailored workout to follow has made me feel good—particularly on the days that I haven’t felt like training. When I feel stuck in the gym and not sure which exercises to do, I take out the app and simply follow a workout. It makes me feel like I have a personal trainer in my pocket, ready to bark orders at me whenever I need a little push. I think if you’re willing to follow the workouts and track your nutrition, AlterMe can be a helpful tool for building positive habits and improving fitness. You could, alternatively, use the money and invest in a good personal trainer—whatever you decide, it’s always nice to have options.

How China and the EU pressed pause on trade war – and what it took to get there

Weeks of high-wire negotiations between China and the EU culminated in a surprise trade deal that will, among other measures, impose strict quotas on Chinese hybrid car exports to the bloc and slash Chinese tariffs on a variety of European goods.
The deal, unveiled on Friday, takes some of the heat out of searing bilateral trade tensions and temporarily averts the prospect of a bruising trade war.
Beijing agreed not to retaliate against Brussels’ move to curb imports of Chinese hybrid cars, which will see shipments capped at 350,000 units per year, rising at 6 per cent annually. This will leave exports at less than half the 800,000 vehicles the EU has projected will be shipped in 2026.
Asked on Monday how Beijing grew to accept the concessions – after Chinese officials spent weeks rejecting the prospect of voluntarily limiting auto shipments – Brussels framed its position with a time-worn business maxim: “The customer is always right.”

South Korea tests drone wingman concept with FA-50 light fighter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:33:31 UTC
19:33:31 KST

- KAI flew its FA-50 light combat aircraft in formation with its AAP jet drone for 20 minutes on Oct. 8, holding 9 to 30 meters apart.
- KAI plans further tests with the FA-50 pilot controlling the drone in flight and multi-drone formations flown by an AI pilot.
Korea Aerospace Industries has flown its FA-50 light combat aircraft in formation with a jet-powered drone for the first time, a test the company says is the first real manned-unmanned formation flight in South Korea.
The flight took place on Oct. 8 over the sea south of Goheung, in South Jeolla Province, KAI said on Oct. 12. The FA-50 and the company’s Adaptable Aerial Platform, or AAP, flew side by side for 20 minutes at about 2,100 meters (7,000 feet), holding a distance of 9 to 30 meters (30 to 100 feet) between them. They flew at 360 km/h (224 mph), a speed KAI chose for stability and safety. KAI did not say whether the drone was flying autonomously, under remote control or with input from the FA-50 pilot during the test.
The AAP is a small jet drone weighing about 150 kg (330 pounds), 3.1 meters (10 feet) long with a 2.2-meter (7-foot) wingspan, and a top speed of 790 km/h (490 mph), according to KAI. The company has developed it with its own money since 2024, and the drone first flew in October 2025. KAI is training it with an artificial intelligence pilot the company calls KAILOT.
KAI designed the AAP to fly ahead of crewed fighters into heavily defended areas and carry out reconnaissance, electronic jamming, decoy and strike missions. This kind of pairing, known as manned-unmanned teaming, lets a pilot send cheaper drones into the most dangerous part of a mission.
KAI said it will gradually raise the drone’s speed toward its maximum and widen its operating range. Next, it plans tests in which the FA-50 pilot controls the AAP’s mission in flight, and formation flights with several drones flown by the AI pilot. The company says the work will feed into a future South Korean unmanned combat aircraft.
KAI laid out a three-phase plan for the effort in 2024. The second phase, running from 2025 to 2028, is meant to end with a demonstration of an FA-50 controlling up to four drones at once. The third phase, through 2037, would move the technology to a two-seat version of the KF-21 fighter.
The FA-50 is a supersonic light fighter developed from KAI’s T-50 trainer. Beyond South Korea, it is flown or on order in Poland, the Philippines, Malaysia, Indonesia, Iraq and Thailand, and KAI has said it hopes existing operators will add drone-teaming capabilities to their jets. KAI showed a scale model of an FA-50 flying with AAP drones at the World Defense Show in Riyadh in February.
