What to Know About the Controversy Surrounding Kimberly Guilfoyle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:00:10 UTC
19:00:10 KST

President Donald Trump is reportedly considering dismissing the U.S. ambassador to Greece, former Fox News host and ex-fiancée of Donald Trump Jr. Kimberly Guilfoyle, following reports of alleged misconduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
“We’re looking at it,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday. “We’re not happy.”
The Associated Press and CNN, citing unnamed sources, said that a decision on Guilfoyle is expected soon. A senior U.S. official told the AP on Sunday that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely assess future action after the Monday U.S. holiday.
The controversy emerged in late September, when the Wall Street Journal began publishing a series of reports about Guilfoyle’s questionable activities—including promoting a Greek construction firm, bragging about luxury trips paid for by businessmen, and asking a Trump donor to pay a $100,000 credit card bill in exchange for getting the attention of the Trump Administration.
The State Department’s inspector general is looking into the allegations, the AP and the Journal reported.
In a statement to the AP late Sunday, Guilfoyle’s lawyers denied any wrongdoing by the ambassador, claiming that the money she requested from the Trump donor was payment for earlier unpaid services and disputing other allegations of impropriety.
The reports surfaced around Rubio’s multiple-day visit to Europe last week, when the Secretary of State boasted about the Trump Administration’s achievements and Guilfoyle attended most of his events in Athens. When asked about the reports on Oct. 8, Rubio at first appeared incredulous, telling journalists: “I don’t even know if what you’re reporting is true. You guys somehow walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me.”
As the reports emerged, Trump did not defend Guilfoyle, who was in a relationship with his eldest son between 2018 and 2024. “I just heard about it—too bad,” the President told reporters on Friday. “I mean, I don’t know. She’s an ambassador. I just heard a little bit about it. I don’t know too much. She was always very nice.”
Vice President J.D. Vance reserved comment on the reporting around Guilfoyle, though he said Thursday that he does not like “anybody selling access to another government official, certainly a high-level government official,” and added the next day that “if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences for it.”
Here’s what to know.
Who is Kimberly Guilfoyle?
Trump announced he would nominate Guilfoyle to be the U.S. ambassador to Greece in December 2024, just before the start of his second term and amid reports of her split with Trump Jr. She was sworn in in September 2025, becoming the first woman in the role.
The 57-year-old Guilfoyle was a former prosecutor in the San Francisco and Los Angeles District Attorney’s Offices and was appointed Assistant District Attorney in San Francisco in 2000. She gained fame as a co-host of the Fox News’ conservative political talk show The Five, which she joined in 2011 and left in 2018.
Besides Guilfoyle’s legal and media work, she also helped raise funds for Trump’s presidential campaign in 2020. Guilfoyle was also a witness to the events leading up to the Jan. 6, 2021 U.S. Capitol attack, and met with the House committee investigating the insurrection in 2022.
From 2001 to 2006, Guilfoyle was married to Gavin Newsom, then a San Francisco supervisor and later mayor and now California’s governor who’s widely seen as a Democratic presidential contender.
What has been reported about Guilfoyle?
On Sept. 25, the Journal published a report on Guilfoyle promoting the Greek construction firm Aktor Group and having the company’s lobbyist, Christos Marafatsos, attend diplomatic meetings across Balkan states. Guilfoyle reportedly encouraged governments from Bulgaria to Albania to work with Aktor Group.
The Sept. 25 report also detailed Guilfoyle’s alleged behavior with Greek government officials. According to the Journal report, during a March dinner, Guilfoyle told attendees, including the country’s energy minister, that the U.S. could influence political changes in other countries, which the minister balked at.
Per the Journal, Guilfoyle’s lawyer disputed how the dinner unfolded. The Greek government also denied the threat, adding: “Such a thing would never be tolerated.” Marafatsos’s lawyer also contested the Journal’s reporting. Lawyers for Aktor Group denied allegations that Guilfoyle acted improperly in promoting its business interests.
Then, on Oct. 7, the Journal reported, citing Guilfoyle’s text messages ahead of her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025, that she asked businessman and Trump donor Eric Deters to wire $100,000 to clear her American Express credit card debt in exchange for access to the Trump Administration.
Deters, who did not pay Guilfoyle, told the paper that he had transactions with Guilfoyle dating back to 2020. The Journal reported that Deters promised Guilfoyle as much $1 million if she succeeded in helping him connect with the Trump Administration, and that she reportedly offered to use her links as Trump Jr.’s former fiancée. Guilfoyle also reportedly asked Deters to stop creating a paper trail of their dealings.
Jesse Binnall, Guilfoyle’s lawyer, told the Journal that the ambassador disputes the messages’ authenticity. He also said that Guilfoyle was paid for events before her nomination and that the ambassador “was owed a balance for traveling to and supporting these patriotic events.”
Three days later, the Journal published another report, this time on how Guilfoyle flaunted luxury trips financed by several businessmen, through an audio recording that the paper reviewed. She reportedly acknowledged in the recording that she flew to the January 2026 World Economic Forum on a private jet with Aktor Group’s CEO Alexandros Exarchou. Guilfoyle also reportedly said in the recording that she planned to travel with a Greek shipping magnate, who reportedly also paid for her accommodations.
Responding to the Journal’s latest report, a spokesperson for the U.S. Embassy in Athens said that Guilfoyle has “faithfully followed State Department ethics and gift reporting guidelines.”
How are lawmakers reacting?
Guilfoyle and the allegations surrounding her add to other issues hounding the Trump Administration heading into the November midterms, where Republicans are hoping to defend their majorities in Congress.
Some Democrats have called for her removal. In a Sept. 30 letter to Rubio, Rep. Gregory Meeks (D, N.Y.), the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, sought answers about the allegations. Meeks said in a statement that the reports about Guilfoyle’s actions were “deeply concerning and suggest potentially corrupt influences on U.S. foreign policy,” adding that if found true, she should be “removed from her position.”
Rep. Robert Garcia (D, Calif.), the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, wrote to Guilfoyle on Oct. 8 that her reported conduct with Deters “raises serious public corruption and national security concerns.” Garcia requested she hand over financial and communications records related to the controversy.
Even some top Republicans are concerned: GOP Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso of Wyoming called the reports about Guilfoyle “very troubling.”
“I’m sure there’s going to be an investigation,” Barrasso told CBS News Sunday. “I know that the Senate Foreign Relations Committee will have oversight and look into that as well. But I think the public has a right to know what is found, and it is quite a bit of concern.”

China accounts for about 5 per cent of the equipment and materials directly supplied to the US chip industry when measured by country of manufacture, but its grip on certain rare earths needed for chipmaking is over 90 per cent, according to the Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA).

The Case for Shifting Mental Health Care From Institutions to Communities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

In recent decades, many countries have made meaningful progress in developing community-based mental health services. Moreover, rights-based approaches have gained traction as people with lived experience increasingly have a voice in shaping mental health policy and services. These developments have shown that people living with mental health conditions can flourish in their communities when given the right support.
Yet, around the world, very large numbers of people with mental health conditions live behind closed doors in psychiatric hospitals and social care institutions. Some have been there for months; others for decades. According to the World Health Organization’s Mental Health Atlas, about half were brought in against their will, stripped of basic daily choices like what to wear or when to eat, and cut off from the outside world.
We think of institutional mental health care as an outdated model. But it is far more than that. It is a human rights issue hiding in plain sight. Many countries still rely heavily on standalone psychiatric institutions. Across the world, we estimate that nearly half of all public mental health funding is spent on maintaining these large facilities, while access to community-based mental health care, including in general hospitals, for millions of people remains underfunded and overlooked.
Sri Lanka embraced mental healthcare reform by replacing isolated institutions with community-based services. Guided by the country’s mental health policies over the past 20 years, Sri Lanka has made significant progress in transforming the mental health system from an asylum-based model to a decentralized network of district and community services. Today, mental health care in Sri Lanka is delivered through inpatient and outpatient units in general hospitals, outreach clinics, intermediate rehabilitation units, and child mental health clinics throughout the country.
Facilities that uphold human rights, dignity, and personal autonomy promote recovery. However, when care is characterized by coercion, rigid control, or social isolation, it risks becoming a form of confinement rather than care.
Deinstitutionalization is not simply about reducing hospital beds. It is about creating the conditions for people to live independently and participate fully in society, with access to appropriate housing, education, employment, social protection, and person-centered mental and physical health care. This is the foundation of recovery, inclusion and human rights-based mental health care.
Scaling back psychiatric hospital beds must go hand in hand with building up local services and practical supports—housing, community mental health care, peer support, social connection, education and employment, legal support, and support for families. No one should be discharged without continuity of care. People should be welcomed into services and communities that are ready for them.
Countries worldwide are proving that advancing deinstitutionalization is achievable across all income levels, from changing care practices and expanding alternatives to psychiatric hospitals to establishing comprehensive networks of community-based services. Deinstitutionalization is a cultural shift that requires the meaningful involvement of people with lived experience, health service providers, and the whole of society.
To support this transition, the World Health Organization has released new, practical guidance to help health leaders navigate each step. Every country begins from a different position, with different resources, laws, service systems and community networks. Implementers need to identify feasible, high-impact actions that are appropriate to their own context.
We must ensure that people receive the support they need in environments that promote dignity, autonomy, relationships and inclusion. We call on governments, health and social care systems to make this a priority, with people with lived experience as partners throughout the transition.

We Need to Bring Back Matchmaking Our Friends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

Last year, I started hosting monthly house parties. When I saw two friends get on really well, I set them up on a date. “You two should go out sometime,” I casually said. “I think you’d have a lot in common.”
Turns out, they did.
So far, there have been three dates among people who met at my house parties. Little did I know, my unintentional matchmaking efforts may have a higher success rate than dating apps.
In my view, one sad side effect of the rise of dating apps has been a noticeable decline in matchmaking. Whatever happened to setting friends up on a blind date? Or even just recommending that two people you love give it a shot of finding love themselves?
And in our modern moment of isolation, polarization, and loneliness, it is clear to me that now is a crucial time for us to bring back matchmaking for our friends. When one of my friends called me after her date to get more insight about my other friend, I was able to answer all her concerns. That couldn’t have happened if she had met a stranger on a dating app.
Dating apps have made meeting someone feel increasingly detached from the people and communities we already belong to. We swipe through strangers based on a handful of photographs and prompts, often with very little context about who they are beyond what they have chosen to present.
A friend, on the other hand, can tell you things an algorithm never could: what someone is actually like, how they treat people, whether they are kind, funny, or reliable, and whether they are compatible with you.
“Friends, especially long-term friends, know literally every nuance of who we are that an algorithm or app cannot capture. Digital mechanisms capture factual data,” says Blythe Landry, a trauma and relationship therapist. “Friends carry history, trauma narratives, inside jokes, the way our nose wrinkles when we laugh, and our favorite order at Starbucks.”
Our nearest and dearest know our likes from the inside out and, perhaps most importantly, they know we can sometimes be totally blind to our patterns in choosing romantic partners. Many of us have the experience a year after a breakup when a best friend says, “I knew that was never going to work! I just didn’t say anything because it was important for you to see that for yourself.”
Friends also know our limitations and what we can and cannot bring to a partner. They are more likely to be brutally honest with us than an app that matches us with someone in our area. Once, I had to tell a friend of mine that the person she met at my house party and went on a date with might not be compatible with her financially. Ultimately, she agreed.
Too often, we underestimate the value of this kind of social knowledge. I remember being annoyed at my friend when she casually told me that she has three brothers. I am not saying I wanted to get with any of the brothers, but surely those brothers have big friend groups and she could have set me up with someone? My friend herself has been in a relationship over the last few years and had no idea that I would prefer her help over the multiple dating app options I have at my disposal. “Why would you want to meet any of my stupid brothers’ friends when you have the whole world at your fingertips?” She asked me innocently.
When we erase community and friendships from the dating experience, dating becomes strategic in the most unpleasant of ways, says Landry. “Because we are now in a time where every single thing we do is online, there are simply way too many ways to ‘not engage’ with someone online, even if offline they could be our perfect match.”
Landry’s best friend died in 2021 of cancer, but years before her death, she had the great pleasure of introducing her to the absolute love of her life. “It was my one and only setup, and it was literally like I momentarily became a professional matchmaker.” Both of her friends had been single for a decade. “One day, I was at coffee with my friend, and he ordered his tea the exact same way my other friend ordered hers.” At that moment, time stood still and out of her mouth came, “You should really meet my friend.” They both protested. Both told Landry that they had nothing in common and had no interest in the other. Just weeks later, they were living together.
“While I will always miss my friend, I will forever be so happy she got to find true love with someone,” she says. “And, point being, no app could have ever caught that ‘match’ moment like a best friend could.”
There is something reassuring about being set up by someone who knows both people involved. It also changes the stakes of dating: you aren’t meeting a complete stranger who exists entirely outside your social world, but someone who already has a connection to it.
Perhaps this is why we also need to bring back house parties, hosting a casual dinner, and planned drinks with friends. But no matter the form, this is why we need to bring back matchmaking. When dating is mediated by apps, we have fewer opportunities to organically meet the friends of our friends. House parties create the kind of low-pressure social environment where those connections can happen without anyone having to announce that they are “looking for love.”
My three successful matches are obviously not scientific evidence that dinner parties can replace dating apps. But they have made me wonder whether we have outsourced too much of our romantic lives to technology and whether our friends, who already know us better than any algorithm, should have a bigger role in helping us find someone.
The return of matchmaking among friends could offer an antidote to the impersonal nature of app dating. I believe that the energy you put out there is the energy you get back, so I am hoping that while I play cupid for my friends, they too, at some point in the future, will decide to set me up with someone suitable.

They War-Gamed Dimming the Sun. It Went Even Worse Than You Think
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

When it comes to deciding the fate of the planet, Colleen Golja always thought science and reason would have a seat at the table. That was until one morning last September in London, when the climate researcher took part in the first in a series of war games. The goal: to prevent an uncontrolled global race to develop a technology aimed at cooling the planet but that comes with vast, unknown risks that could reshape life on Earth.
“I thought that would be such an easy thing. Like, we can all agree to do ethical research and make sure it's for the better of all humans,” she told WIRED. “And boy, was I wrong.”
The simulation, titled Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies, saw a couple dozen foreign-relations experts, scientists, military personnel, and former government officials from across the world convene in a meeting room at Queen Mary University of London. After making introductions over coffee and little yogurts, they sat at tables arranged in a square with the name of the country or organization each person was playing: national governments, climate NGOs and nonprofits, indigenous groups, and tech companies. Golja was assigned to provide technical advice to help participants make scientifically literate decisions.
The point of the game was to stress-test the world’s response to a group of prospective technologies known collectively as solar radiation modification. These technologies promise to reverse global warming by reflecting away a portion of the sunlight reaching Earth, for example by spraying particles of sulphur dioxide or some other manufactured substance into the atmosphere. The cooling effect of this kind of solar geoengineering is widely accepted. It would mimic the well-known impacts of large volcanic eruptions, which temporarily cool the planet by half a degree or more. But the fallout is less certain—and less equal. Some regions will suffer: Models predict drying in sub-Saharan Africa and more intense tropical storms in the Atlantic. The cooling effect would also last only as long as the geoengineering continued; after that the global temperature could shoot back up with wild and hard-to-predict effects.
Until recently, the idea of solar radiation modification was a speculative niche of climate science. That has changed fast. Private firms are exploring solar geoengineering as a commercial opportunity: Last year, a US-Israeli startup called Stardust Solutions raised $60 million, and in May it released details of a suite of new inventions it claims would give humans the ability to dial down the global temperature as desired. In August, Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX might be a candidate for delivering geoengineering interventions, threw his voice behind solar geoengineering, writing on X: “Space satellites to control temperature and massive geo-engineering will be needed or it will be game over.”
The world is going to have to make decisions about how to govern this technology much sooner than most policymakers imagine, Cynthia Scharf, a former UN advisor, told WIRED. “It's not 15 years from now; it's in the next decade, easily.”
It was against this backdrop that Danielle Young, an assistant professor in international relations at Leeds University, arranged the war game. Its setting was a hastily convened UN committee charged with coordinating the international response to developments in solar geoengineering. The game unfolded over simulated meetings set at three points in time: the present, September 2027, and September 2028. Each step ratcheted up the stakes, with the game creators introducing new advances in sunlight-reflecting technology. As in real life, no one knew all the facts, and players had to respond to events that were bringing the world closer to a full-scale attempt at deploying solar geoengineering tech, even when they may not have a full picture of what had truly occurred—or what any of the others were up to.
The first session set the tone. Distrust and disinformation dominated. As participants discussed rules governing outdoor experiments in an attempt to agree an international deal, players representing both the US and China told the group they could not sign a deal that constrained their pursuit of research considered to be in their “national interest.” Nor could they accept a deal that would see their superpower rival taking the lead technologically. Speaking to WIRED, Jeffrey Nielsen, a major in the US Army who played the role of a US national security attaché, summarized the position as “worse than no deal at all is any deal that favors China.”
Tensions escalated when the team running the simulation handed the Russian delegates an “intelligence report” indicating they had found a plane near the Bering Strait believed to be involved in a US geoengineering research program. The US team—which was indeed flying research missions—accused Russia of disinformation.
Meanwhile, the US became convinced China was also conducting research and developing its own program. Beijing’s representatives had tried to insert language into a mooted deal that would ensure no retroactive punishment for past experiments. Then, China approached a player representing SpaceX to float the idea of a technology-sharing program. In a private discussion away from the group, the SpaceX player immediately reported the Chinese approach to the US team. The US demanded an international investigation. The finger-pointing continued, and countries abandoned the talks. The Canadian representative called it a “humiliating defeat.”
At the end of the session, Nielsen was pumped. He’d busted China and derailed any prospect of a global deal. In the context of the game, he told WIRED, it was a “humungous victory” for the Americans. But Young, the researcher who designed the scenario, said the Chinese were not, in fact, conducting experiments in the game. Mutual suspicion meant all parties left the room believing the others were moving as quickly as possible to build their own geoengineering capability.
What played out in the first session reflected “the likelihood, in my opinion, of the geoengineering arms race,” says Nielsen, who clarified he was speaking to WIRED in a private capacity and not representing the views of the actual US government. Most experts agree it would take a superpower’s reach to ensure the safe passage of planes needed to deliver payloads of dust to the stratosphere in a geoengineering exercise. But neither the US nor China would lightly cede control over the global thermostat, says Nielsen, and distrust and poor communication are a significant risk: “Any action related to the issue by one actor can be perceived as malintent by the other.”
The threat of falling behind a rival is “a very strong driver of research and development of capability,” a former British diplomat with a background in national security told WIRED. “But that's not at all the same thing as deployment.” There are similarities with nuclear arms dynamics—though solar radiation management, unlike nukes, has more obvious benefits as well as downsides, many of which are poorly understood. “There is an interdependence here,” says the former diplomat, who was not involved in the game and spoke on condition of anonymity to preserve relationships. “It's not an inherently zero-sum game.”
Scharf, who represented the US government alongside Nielsen in the game, told WIRED a “scientifically transparent international collaboration” between China and the US “might be the best we can do in terms of fending off a very dangerous competition between the two. But I certainly cannot imagine that happening under the Trump administration.”
Compounding the problem is a lack of information. Geoengineering has historically been viewed with suspicion and often ignored by the scientific mainstream. One researcher told WIRED he’d experienced ostracization and barriers to academic progression owing to his interest in the technology; he no longer works in the field.
This lack of scientific interest greatly frustrated Golja, who spent much of the game watching as a bystander while political posturing dominated. Given the low level of knowledge around solar radiation modification and its side effects, she was one of very few experts who could help the participants understand the climate impacts of what they were discussing—yet she was largely ignored.“I was just so surprised about how little anyone actually cared about the science,” she says.
In the next sessions, the organizers tried in vain to nudge the talks back toward the realities of climate change. The participants received frequent notifications of climate disasters. These barely registered. Golja had prepared an “emulator,” a real-world demonstration of the best available science on how solar radiation management might affect weather patterns in different regions. It was ignored. If country representatives asked her anything, it was usually a leading question looking for data that would serve their ends or frame a rival’s proposal as reckless.
Then, during the last day, players were trying to find a way to respond to reports that a major plume of aerosols had been detected. In the game, this had been caused by a joint US-Saudi test of Stardust’s technology, though not everyone knew this. Finally, scientific advice was at a premium. Countries needed to know how to establish a monitoring network of satellites and other observational tools in order to prevent tests like this from happening in secret. A player representing an NGO called the Climate Futures Cooperative approached Golja, offering her money to fund such a scheme.
“Great. Fabulous. Why wouldn't I do that?” she recalls thinking.
But it soon came out that the Climate Futures Cooperative was actually backed by the fossil fuel industry. The organizers had recognized that fossil fuel companies and major producing countries like the US and Saudi Arabia would have a clear interest in removing barriers from the development of a technology that could combat climate change without having to immediately stop burning coal, oil, and gas. The shadowy NGO spent the game subtly wrecking the vibe and carping about process—though mostly they just sat back and let it burn. Some players—Russia, the US, SpaceX and Stardust—figured out the CFC was not what it seemed, says Young. “But they assessed it was to their benefit and didn’t draw attention to it.” Then the CFC chose its moment to offer money to Golja, only to crater her credibility, isolating and fragmenting the voice of science in the room.
“It was a whole mess,” says Golja.
That final lesson in fossil fuel realpolitik was about all Golja could endure. By the end of the last day, she was in tears.
At no point did the countries in the game agree to a deal, despite multiple proposals being put forward. European countries and Canada tried to build support for safeguards and open scientific research, but the talks constantly got bogged down by delay tactics and veered into tense showdowns over duelling strategic interests. In their final report, the researchers running the simulation—whose work was sponsored by the UK government-funded Advanced Research and Invention Agency—concluded that “strategic competition and state sovereignty drove the simulations, not climate concerns.”
Simulations like this one are not supposed to predict the future. The outcomes depend on the design of the game and the relative personalities and experience of the players. Many of those in the room lacked first-hand diplomatic and national security experience. The UN forum, which organizers selected as the game’s setting, may also not be as effective as talks between smaller groups of major countries. But the experiment in London echoed and refracted through the real world, during and after the months it was running.
In March, two papers from conservative US think tanks urged the Trump administration to take the lead on solar radiation modification and counter China’s threat. One memorably invoked a new, MAGA-coded term: “Weather sovereignty.” This month, the Observer newspaper in London revealed that the UK Ministry of Defense had paid a deep tech security consultancy to conduct research into sunlight reflection. Then, last week, the British government released its first official policy paper on the field, backing further research but stating firmly that it did not support deployment and “does not plan to do so.” Stardust has continued its lobbying of the US and governments around the world; CEO Yanai Yedvab told WIRED its job was getting easier as, unlike before, “the majority of policymakers … are already aware of this technology.”
Stardust has always maintained that it will not conduct large-scale outdoor experiments, let alone full deployment, before global governance is in place. “We are developing a very powerful tool,” Yedvab says. “When you develop this kind of powerful technology—and you have many precedents—national interests will play out. We're not naive about it.”
Meanwhile, drivers of the climate crisis are intensifying. During the time span of the game, efforts to curtail the use of fossil fuels were being undermined by rising energy costs and political hostility. Week after week, an incredible summer of drought and heat pounded Europe. In the final week of August, the collapse of a glacier on the Tibet-Nepal border fulfilled the prophecies of decades of climate scientists, killing more than 1,450 people.
In the months since the simulation ended, Golja has reevaluated many things. On a corkboard behind her desk, she has pinned up a note to herself, laying out a vision for life in a world ruled by narrow geopolitical self-interest rather than science, evidence, and reason. Her answer: She plans to return to the small coastal town where she grew up in Connecticut and use her expertise to help local climate groups build the seawalls and coastal erosion buffers they will need to cope with the inevitable. “To try and make a difference where it feels like I actually have traction,” she says. After what she saw, pursuing science in the hope of informing global decisions no longer held as much appeal. “Now it feels a little bit more personal.”

Is everything conscious?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
29 minute listen
When an explanation makes a fact intelligible, the mystery goes out of it. We understand it so well that we can hardly conceive of things being otherwise. Consider the simple mathematical fact that one plus one equals two. Once we understand elementary arithmetic, we no longer feel the urge to ask why one plus one equals two. That one plus one equals two strikes us as not merely true but unavoidable; we cannot even coherently imagine its falsity. Much of philosophy aims to bring other fundamental features of reality into a similar light, to make them appear not arbitrary but inevitable and, thus, intelligible.
This aspiration that philosophy render the world intelligible is best expressed by the German polymath Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz and the Dutch philosopher Baruch Spinoza. According to Leibniz: ‘we can find no true or existent fact … without there being a sufficient reason why it is thus and not otherwise.’ And, as Spinoza wrote: ‘For each thing there must be assigned a cause or reason, both for its existence and for its nonexistence.’ What’s being expressed here, in the words of the US philosopher Michael Della Rocca, is the desire ‘to make the world and our place in it intelligible’. To grasp the kinds of reasons or explanations sought by Leibniz and Spinoza ‘is the perennial hope and promise of philosophy’.
The demand for intelligibility can lead to some extraordinary places. For Leibniz, the demand led him to propose that reality is ultimately made up of a multiplicity of monads: indivisible, infinitesimally small units of substance, each of which is a causally isolated, self-contained universe. Spinoza’s resolute commitment to universal intelligibility led him to conclude that reality is, instead, a single infinite substance that he called God or nature. As we will see, the demand for intelligibility can also lead into the strange and fascinating world of panpsychism.
Panpsychism is an increasingly popular view about consciousness. You are conscious, you feel pleasures, pains and all manner of other experiences. At every waking moment, and even when you dream, there is something that it is like to be you. The same goes for other humans and animals, and this accounts for moral status: thumping a fist on a desk in frustration is morally permissible in a way that hitting a conscious person or animal is not. Desks, chairs, rocks and so on are not conscious – and are therefore without moral status – whereas humans, bonobos, dogs and so on are conscious, and deserving of at least some moral recognition. But panpsychism rejects this division into conscious and non-conscious things. It is the view that consciousness is a fundamental property of matter, so everything from electrons and protons to tables and planets, and, of course, humans and dogs, has consciousness to some degree.
Panpsychism is a remarkable thesis, motivated by the ‘perennial hope’ that the world is ultimately intelligible. To investigate whether panpsychism truly can make the world intelligible, we will explore three different arguments, each of which is grounded in a principle that crystallises the ambitious aim of universal intelligibility: the principle of sufficient reason (PSR). This simple and plausible principle of philosophical enquiry – that there exist satisfying explanations for everything – can lead to a whole new understanding of the nature of reality. And, though I’m sceptical about the availability or even desirability of explanations that dissolve all the world’s mysteries, there is exceptional value in the mere contemplation of such projects.
If you come home from work to find a bouquet of flowers on your doorstep, there will be a reason for this. Maybe it’s a birthday present, a congratulations on a new job, a thank you for some good deed. If your car dashboard shows a warning light, you’d be wise to assume that there is some reason for this, such as a problem with the engine, fluids or tyres. The Chicxulub crater, 200 km wide and 1 km deep, in the Yucatán peninsula in Mexico, cries out for scientific explanation, which is precisely what the hypothesis of an extinction-level asteroid impact millions of years ago provides.
But is there really a reason for everything? The mass of a proton is 1.672 × 10-27 kg. What’s the reason for this? What’s the reason for a particular radioactive decay event to which our best scientific theory on the issue, quantum mechanics, assigns only a probability? According to the PSR, there is indeed a reason for everything. For any way the world is, from the flowers on your doorstep to the mass of a proton, there is some reason why it is this way and not some other way. All facts have a reason, and – according to the PSR in its strongest form, as defended by Spinoza – that reason makes them intelligible and necessary, and their contrary inconceivable.
Though the PSR found its fullest expression in Leibniz’s work – ‘The fundamental principle of reasoning,’ Leibniz wrote, ‘is that there is nothing without a reason’ – its lineage is far greater. As Della Rocca showed in his book Spinoza (2008): ‘Versions of [the PSR] go way back in philosophy and can be found in philosophers such as Parmenides, the Stoics, [and] Aquinas.’ And the principle is not restricted to Western European philosophy. It occupies a key position in the metaphysical system of the Islamic philosopher Ibn Sīnā (also known in Europe as Avicenna), who used it to argue that things that exist merely contingently – that is, things whose existence is not necessary – must have a cause outside themselves. Versions of the principle have also been defended in contemporary metaphysics and philosophy of physics. Shamik Dasgupta has argued that every substantive fact has a metaphysical grounding that makes it necessary. And Eddy Keming Chen has developed a physical model of the Universe according to which every single fact (from the number of hairs on your head at 2 pm this afternoon, to the mass of the electron) is entailed and thus explained by the laws of nature.
The PSR is so alluring because it would seem that the very activity of enquiry – whether philosophical, scientific, or the first ‘Why?’ question of a young child – is premised on there being an explanation, a reason, for everything. To endorse the PSR is to adopt an attitude of optimism that the world and our place in it are intelligible and infused with reason and meaning. If anything were unexplainable, there’d be a grave risk that human enquiry is ultimately futile. The falsity of the PSR would constitute a fundamental mismatch between our inquisitive nature and the world in which we find ourselves; it would imply that the world is unintelligible.
The optimistic attachment to intelligibility and reason comes at a significant cost
Intelligibility and meaningfulness are two sides of the same coin. When, on reflection, we can find no good reason for our personal and professional pursuits (lining the boss’s pockets won’t generally satisfy us!), when these things seem absurd or unintelligible, it’s natural to express the predicament in terms of a lack of meaning in life. Analogously, failure to uncover satisfying answers to questions about the nature of reality can lead to deep philosophical worries that the world itself is ultimately meaningless.
But this is not to say that the PSR is universally accepted among philosophers. It is controversial because it seems to entail necessitarianism – the thesis that everything is necessary. You are currently reading an essay about the PSR and panpsychism, but you could have been doing something else. If the PSR is true, however, then there is a sufficient reason why you are currently reading this essay, which makes it necessary that you are currently reading this essay and hence impossible that you could be doing anything else. Since the PSR applies to everything, it seems to entail the necessity of everything, and many find this unpalatable because it threatens free will and the seemingly obvious fact that all manner of things could have been different in all sorts of ways.
Contemporary philosophers who describe themselves as ‘Humean’, that is, as influenced by the Scottish Enlightenment philosopher David Hume, are explicit in their rejection of necessity and ultimate explanations. David Lewis, perhaps the most prominent Humean of the past century, maintained that ‘all there is to the world is a vast mosaic of local matters of particular fact, just one little thing and then another.’ That is to say, there are no reasons, and no necessity for what goes on in the world. In a similar spirit, the Dutch American philosopher Bas van Fraassen consistently challenges the need for a metaphysical explanatory structure. This manifests itself in the rejection of robust laws of nature that necessitate events in the Universe. Science, according to Van Fraassen, can get along just fine without deep explanations that make things necessary.
So, the optimistic attachment to intelligibility and reason comes at a significant cost: it demands a commitment to widespread necessity. There are, however, ways of mitigating this cost. Various authors, including Leibniz himself, have argued that the PSR is at least consistent with a sense in which things could have been different, and this will correspond to weaker senses of explanation. The strongest explanations, those that yield necessity, can be demonstrated in a finite number of steps; prime examples include mathematical and geometrical demonstrations. Other explanations are not finitely demonstrable, though they can be perceived by the infinite mind of God. But the fact that some explanatory connections cannot be grasped by our limited human intellect suffices, according to Leibniz, for contingency.
Alternatively, one could embrace necessitarianism, as Spinoza does, and see it as just another positive facet of the interconnectedness and intelligibility of all things – this seems the way to go if one is to maintain the courage of one’s conviction as a philosophical optimist. But necessitarianism is not the only controversial upshot of the PSR. It can also motivate panpsychism.
Perhaps the most elusive question in all of science and philosophy concerns the nature of conscious experience. Why are the arrangements of matter that constitute human beings and other animals accompanied by conscious experience? Why is there something that it is like to be you? Why are some physical states, but not others, conscious? However completely we describe the physical arrangements of matter that make up a conscious being, that description leaves out the very thing we’re trying to explain: what it feels like from the inside. This challenge to provide an explanation that bridges the gap between third-person scientific descriptions of matter and first-person conscious experience is what the Australian philosopher David Chalmers dubbed the ‘hard problem of consciousness’.
The question is so fiendishly hard because it does not seem amenable to scientific methods of enquiry. The operation of a mill, for example, can be explained by its components: water flow rotates a wheel, which drives gears connected to millstones, which grind wheat into flour. The whole operation of the mill and its output (flour) can be made intelligible to us. If we ask ‘Why does the mill produce flour?’ a fully satisfying answer can be given. No mystery remains.
The mill example is illustrative of scientific explanation in general. The boiling point of water is explained in terms of the hydrogen-bonding of H2O molecules, and the path of light around a massive celestial body is explained in terms of the curvature of spacetime described by Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity. These cases take more work to understand, but the principle is the same as in the mill case.
If consciousness is a fundamental property of matter, then the problem of explaining consciousness does not arise
However closely we look at the physical matter that makes up conscious beings, we get no closer to understanding how consciousness arises. Leibniz encouraged us to imagine increasing the size of the human brain to the size of a mill so that we can walk around inside it and observe all its working parts in meticulous detail. If we did this, at no point would we observe conscious experience. Conscious experience, by its very nature, is private, first-personal. Since scientific methods can yield knowledge only of the objective, third-person-accessible facts regarding matter in motion, there is an essential mystery concerning the origin of consciousness. The question of why some physical states, but not others, are conscious seems unanswerable.
Unanswerable questions do not sit comfortably with our inquisitive human nature. If consciousness cannot be explained in principle, this would be a particularly egregious violation of the PSR. However, it is worth considering our options for explaining consciousness and, thus, upholding the PSR once we accept that reductive scientific explanation is not up to the task.
One option is to understand consciousness in terms of a new substance entirely, one fully distinct from physical matter. On this view, reality is bifurcated into physical substance characterised by spatial extension, and mental substance characterised by thought, where the latter accounts for consciousness. This is called dualism. The most influential champion of dualism was the French philosopher René Descartes. But Descartes ultimately failed to uphold the PSR, since he couldn’t say why there are two substances as opposed to just one.
Alternatively, we could question the seemingly obvious assumption that fundamental physical matter isn’t conscious. The mystery arises because there is no way to understand how non-conscious physical matter, arranged in space and time, can give rise to consciousness. But why must we think that fundamental physical matter is not conscious? This assumption is not mandatory. If consciousness is a fundamental property of matter, then the problem of explaining consciousness, as formulated above, does not arise. So, in the interest of avoiding this in-principle obstacle to explaining consciousness, many are inclined to believe that consciousness is a fundamental property of matter, that panpsychism is true.
The hypothesis that fundamental matter is physical and non-conscious blocks the possibility of an intelligible explanation – in terms of the fundamental ‘bits’ of matter – of why creatures like us are conscious. If consciousness is absent at the fundamental level, there will always be an explanatory gap between the physical and the mental. What this means is that, for any arrangement of physical matter constitutive of a conscious being, it always seems possible that consciousness was absent; no arrangement of matter seems to be necessarily connected with, and hence able to explain, consciousness. But if consciousness is introduced at the fundamental level, this obstacle is removed. According to panpsychism, we no longer need to bridge the gap from non-conscious fundamental matter to consciousness at higher levels of organisation, since consciousness is present all the way down.
There is still significant work to be done to explain how fundamental consciousness combines to create human-level consciousness. But, at the very least, panpsychism offers a way of avoiding what would otherwise appear to be a potentially devastating violation of the PSR. If consciousness is already present at the fundamental level, there is no longer the same pervasive explanatory gap between wholly non-conscious matter and conscious beings at higher levels.
There is another route to panpsychism via the PSR. The Norwegian philosopher Hedda Hassel Mørch argues that fundamental consciousness is required to properly explain the basic motions of matter, documented by fundamental physics. Science tells us plenty about how matter behaves and what different subatomic particles such as protons, electrons and neutrons do. But it does not tell us what matter is. This is evident from the way in which science characterises matter. The electron, for example, is characterised in terms of its properties: mass, charge and quantum spin. And these properties, in turn, are understood in terms of how they dispose the electron to behave. What is absent from this scientific description of the world is an account of what physical properties are like in themselves, and hence why they have the power to dispose matter to behave in certain ways.
Why do the properties of an electron dispose it towards certain behaviours? How can this be rendered intelligible as per the demands of the PSR? Consider pain. If you are in pain, this mental property disposes you to avoid the thing that’s painful: accidentally touch a hot radiator, and you’ll instantly remove your hand. As Mørch puts it: ‘In the absence of any interfering motives, it seems pain always makes subjects try to avoid it, and [it is] difficult to conceive otherwise.’ If we ask why someone withdrew their hand from the radiator, it is a perfect explanation to say that the heat caused them pain. The explanation renders the action fully intelligible because part of what it is to be in pain is to try to avoid the painful source. Mental properties are special in that they are the only properties with this ability to provide intelligible explanations of behaviour. As Mørch writes:
The only fundamentally dispositional properties we know or can positively conceive of are phenomenal properties – in particular, phenomenal properties associated with agency, intention and/or motivation.
Other properties, such as negative charge, could, for all we know, have disposed things to behave very differently or in no systematic way at all. But it is inconceivable that pain disposed us to do anything besides avoid the source of pain. ‘It does not,’ Mørch writes, ‘seem conceivable that pain makes subjects try to do anything else than avoid it in virtue of its intrinsic character alone.’ This raises a fascinating prospect. In the interest of rendering the behaviour of matter intelligible, we should take those properties responsible for that behaviour to be conscious mental properties. That is to say: all paradigm physical properties such as charge, mass and quantum spin are conscious mental properties. This move provides an answer to the question of what matter fundamentally is, which, in turn, explains why matter does what it does. The fundamental properties of matter are properties of consciousness. By their very nature, they dispose the matter of which they are properties towards certain behaviours. This plugs the explanatory gap left by the scientific method alone. Again, the primary motive in this argument is the desire for intelligible explanations of the world, as per the PSR.
For Spinoza, if things depend on properties because properties individuate things, then it follows that properties are more fundamental than things
There is a third way that a commitment to the PSR leads us to panpsychism. Spinoza is perhaps most famous for his pantheism, the idea that God is nature. On this view, God is not a separate entity that is an external cause of nature; rather, God is coterminous with nature. It turns out that the argument for pantheism also works well as an argument for panpsychism. And, crucially, Spinoza’s argument depends on a truly unwavering commitment to the intelligibility of nature.
If asked ‘How many things exist?’ we’d probably say that there are a great many things indeed – a cat here, a house there, some protons, electrons, and so on – one might even think that there are infinitely many things. But Spinoza argues that there is just one thing. If we hold that there exists more than one thing, we must say something about what each of these things is like. So, we might say ‘This cat is black,’ ‘That house is made of brick,’ ‘Socrates is wise’ and so on. Crucially, for the advocate of the PSR, the different things that exist cannot have all the same properties. If two things, this table and that table, for example, are distinct, there must be some explanation of their distinctness that appeals to some difference between them, some difference in their properties (eg, one is square, the other oval).
Distinct things are individuated by their properties. But this relation of individuation is what philosophers call a dependence relation. For example, the fact that this is an essay on panpsychism, intelligibility and the aim of philosophy depends on the fact that there are words arranged in the appropriate way. This relation of dependence induces an ordering of fundamentality: the words are more fundamental than the essay because the latter depends on the former.
But, for Spinoza, if things depend on properties because properties individuate things, then it follows that properties are more fundamental than things. This result, however, is not acceptable. Things – or ‘substances’, as Spinoza would say – are supposed to be absolutely fundamental. What it is to be a substance, a distinct thing that exists, is to be independent of everything else, completely self-sustaining. It seems odd to say that properties occupy the fundamental level. Is the redness of an apple more fundamental than the apple itself? Surely not, since the apple, the thing, is required to exist before redness can be instantiated. So, we must find another way to explain why there are multiple distinct things. Doing so in terms of properties won’t cut it.
Instead of maintaining that different things merely have different properties, perhaps we ought to say that they are radically different in their essential attributes. What are ‘essential attributes’? Recall that, according to dualism, reality is bifurcated into mental substance with the essential attribute of thought, and physical substance with the essential attribute of extension. In other words, the mental and the physical have radically different essential attributes. But this raises a new question: why is mental substance not extended, and why is physical substance not thinking? The PSR demands an explanation. One might think that the nature of mental substance excludes being extended, and vice versa. But Spinoza objects that this violates the independence of substance, since it entails a mutual dependence of mental and physical substance to explain the fact that they exclude one another. Ultimately, Spinoza thinks there is no reason why substances would differ from each other and, since there is no reason, they do not differ. There is, then, just one substance, one thing, and this thing has all properties, and is both extended and thinking, because there is no reason that it should lack any properties or essential attributes.
A single thing with all properties and essential attributes fits the bill of both God and nature, hence Spinoza’s argument, that only one thing exists, is an argument for pantheism. But this can also be cast as an argument for panpsychism. The single existing substance is, according to Spinoza, both extended and thinking. Hence, thought is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of reality. There is, however, scope for debate about whether the fundamentality and ubiquity of thought amounts to panpsychism since there is reason to believe that not all thought is conscious thought, in Spinoza’s system. But, at the very least, mentality is a fundamental property of matter, for Spinoza, and many are happy to equate this with consciousness and, thus, categorise Spinoza as a panpsychist. The US philosopher Martin Lin, for example, writes: ‘Spinoza is a panpsychist. For him, mentality is a pervasive and fundamental feature of the natural world.’
This argument for panpsychism (and pantheism) results from leaving no stone unturned in the application of the PSR, and, in particular, from the demand to explain the idea that there are multiple distinct substances with different properties or attributes. Ultimately, Spinoza concludes that this demand cannot be met, which leads to the conclusion that there is a single fundamental substance with all properties and with both essential attributes of thought and extension. This conclusion can be cast in pantheist terms: to maintain that there exists just a single substance with all properties and attributes invites the identification of this substance with both God and nature. It can also be cast in panpsychist terms: the single fundamental substance is essentially a conscious, thinking thing. Hence consciousness is a fundamental property of reality.
Pursuing the demand for intelligibility leads to unexpected and thought-provoking places. If panpsychism doesn’t resonate with you, it’s worth asking if there truly is a reason for everything – if the world is ultimately intelligible after all. On the other hand, if you consider the PSR indispensable, panpsychism may seem inevitable.
But does this latter path offer a deeper sense of meaningful existence? I’m not so sure. In fact, uncertainty about ultimate meaning fuels the arts, which, at their most powerful, embrace and celebrate the unintelligibility and absurdity of life. On the other hand, it seems legitimate to criticise art when its meaning is too obvious, its message too on the nose. So, just as clear and unambiguous meaning is far from the supreme aesthetic goal, it’s not clear that rendering reality fully intelligible, providing the ‘meaning of life’, is a desirable or realistic aim for philosophy.
Dissatisfaction in life, a crisis in meaning, may originate when we can find no good reason for our personal and professional pursuits, and, analogously, philosophical dissatisfaction may stem from an inability to render the world intelligible. But it is far from clear that this sort of dissatisfaction can ever really be remedied by the provision of better reasons.
A messy, unintelligible world doesn’t preclude the construction of highly orderly philosophical edifices
A more prestigious or better-paid job may constitute a reason to get out of bed in the morning. But deep questions about value and meaning will remain untouched. The absurd is not so easily vanquished. Similarly, the promise of a philosophical system built on the PSR, such as Spinoza’s, may appeal to the extent that we want to ‘solve’ philosophy by providing an answer to any possible question. But we may equally take an explanation of everything as an explanation of nothing.
Instead of seeking perfect reasons for all our pursuits, perhaps we ought to just embrace what we do, whatever it may be, for what it is. As the French philosopher and writer Albert Camus reflected, solace for Sisyphus can only come from positively embracing his situation: ‘The struggle itself towards the heights is enough to fill a man’s heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy.’
Perhaps it’s misguided to expect to render the world intelligible, and we ought instead to just enjoy the process of contemplating its messy unintelligible glory, of pushing our philosophical boulder up the mountain. One way of engaging with this contemplative project is in the development and exploration of systematic philosophical theories. A messy, unintelligible world doesn’t preclude the construction of highly orderly philosophical edifices. But it would be a mistake to think these capable, even in principle, of definitively dissolving life’s mysteries. Philosophical theories such as panpsychism are better thought of as providing new and enriching perspectives on these mysteries, and we should remain open to the possibility of their collapse and replacement.
By giving up the all-encompassing demand for intelligibility and, instead, conceiving of philosophy as providing different perspectives on our condition, we can better understand what it is to make progress in philosophy. Widespread philosophical disagreement should not be taken as evidence that philosophy is degenerate compared with, say, the natural sciences. Rather, we should celebrate the fact that opposing views such as dualism, physicalism and panpsychism exist to provide us with richly diverse perspectives on life’s most tantalising mysteries.
Can panpsychism make the world intelligible? I’m not sure that anything can, or that it even makes sense to pursue supreme reasons. But there is still plenty of joy to be had in the contemplation of panpsychism as a response to the deep mystery of consciousness, and I doubt we could ask any more of a philosophical theory.

KYIV – Waves of Russian strikes on Ukraine overnight and into Oct 12 killed several people and wounded dozens, including attacks on energy facilities that Kyiv called a violation of a ceasefire on such targets announced by US President Donald Trump.
Under pressure over high energy prices ahead of US midterm elections in November, Trump had blindsided Ukraine and its European allies by announcing that Kyiv and Moscow had agreed not to hit each other’s energy systems.
Trump has also unveiled a deal to buy diesel from Russia, and called on Ukrainians to replace their wartime leader, President Volodymyr Zelensky, in elections.
Ukraine’s European allies voiced scepticism over any such energy ceasefire and urged the US to keep pressure on Moscow, while the European Union approved its own largest set of sanctions since the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Zelensky, who has said he learnt of Trump’s purported energy ceasefire only from the media, said a Russian jet-powered drone had hit a gas production facility in Ukraine at midnight, and a petrol station had been struck by several drones.
“There were Russian violations of the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump,” Zelensky told a conference in Warsaw via video link.
“This energy ceasefire, it can work, and it can become a major step towards ending the war if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect it.
“We are waiting for the details of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, and we are waiting to see one specific step the Americans are ready to take.”
He said Ukraine had carried out no attacks on Russian refineries overnight, but he made clear that if Russia wanted Kyiv to suspend these attacks, it must stop hitting Ukraine’s energy system.
He also said elections, suspended during wartime, could be held if Moscow agreed to a full ceasefire for 60 days.
Russia, for its part, said talks were ongoing about a possible energy ceasefire, and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said further information would be revealed in due course.
But he also rejected Zelensky’s proposal for a 60-day truce.
“In the Kremlin, both President (Vladimir) Putin and officials at other levels have repeatedly stated that we do not want a ceasefire,” said Peskov.
“We want long-term peace and are prepared to do everything possible to achieve it.”
Body among wreckage
In Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-biggest city, rescue workers picked through wreckage of shattered buildings. The body of a civilian in jeans and white sneakers lay beneath debris, lit up by floodlights in the night-time darkness.
Nataliia Minka said she had just made it to a shelter when a missile struck nearby. She and her child had seen what they believed to be a missile hitting a nearby power station.
“Ten minutes had passed since they promised they wouldn’t target energy facilities,” she said.
“It’s so hard to describe how a child was lying there, already covered up, and the father was running around her, crying and screaming.
“It’s so terrifying – it’s impossible to get through something like this.”
After night-time attacks killed at least three people in the city, further strikes took place in the morning, hitting residential buildings and wounding at least 22 more people, municipal officials said.
At least three other people were reported killed on Oct 11 in the western city of Ivano-Frankivsk.
Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire appeared similar to one he announced a month ago, which neither side ever confirmed.
The EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said she would prefer a ceasefire “which includes people not being killed” and that it was not clear whether Russia would stick to it.
“We would call the US to get the sanctions in place so that we could actually finish the war,” she said at a meeting of foreign ministers in Luxembourg.
To maintain pressure on Moscow, EU ministers adopted nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex, Kallas said.
“More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles,” she said in a post on X.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Moscow “will only negotiate seriously under pressure, which is why we are sticking to our sanctions against Russia.
“Following Moscow’s ruthless attacks on Ukraine’s civilian energy infrastructure, we must actually tighten them further”.
Trump grows impatient
In recent months, Ukraine has increasingly been targeting Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs, its answer to 4½ years of relentless Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities, including a persistent campaign to knock out Ukrainian heat and power particularly in the winter.
Trump has become increasingly impatient, blaming Kyiv’s attacks on Russian refineries for the surge in costs for fuel, especially diesel, to record levels since he launched his military campaign against Iran.
On Oct 10, he said Zelensky had “better damn well stop” attacking Russian refineries.

District heating prices set to rise for thousands of Danish customers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:54:40 UTC
18:54:40 KST

The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.
The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.

“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Navy will assist the Coast Guard if Chinese maritime militia vessels engage in military operations near Taiwan, Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) said Monday, following reports that a Chinese militia ship had appeared off the country’s east coast for the first time.
Koo told the Legislative Yuan that the military and Coast Guard were monitoring Chinese maritime militia vessels at sea using joint intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capabilities, per Rti. He said the vessels, like Chinese coast guard ships, are considered part of China’s armed forces.
“If these militia fishing boats cross any boundaries, the Coast Guard will be the primary law enforcement agency responsible for driving them away, just as it is for Chinese coast guard vessels,” Koo said. “The Navy will provide assistance in accordance with our support agreement with the Coast Guard.”
Reuters reported Thursday that the Chinese maritime militia fishing vessel Minfudingyu 07902 appeared off Taiwan’s east coast in mid-August, operating alongside Chinese coast guard cutter 2502 and the research ship Xiangyanghong 3. It was reportedly the first known appearance of a Chinese maritime militia vessel in waters off eastern Taiwan.
The US State Department on Thursday described China’s activities off Taiwan’s east coast as “deeply destabilizing” and called on Beijing to stop pressuring Taiwan and engage in meaningful dialogue with Taipei, per Reuters. The reported deployment has raised concerns that Beijing could use maritime militia vessels to expand its gray-zone operations beyond Taiwan’s western approaches.
Separately, a July-August public opinion survey by the Japan Press Research Institute found that 76.7% of Japanese respondents felt a sense of crisis over a potential Taiwan contingency, but only 9.9% supported the Self-Defense Forces fighting alongside the US military if China attacked Taiwan. More than 80% opposed Japanese military participation, with respondents favoring options ranging from no military involvement to logistical support for US forces without Japanese troops engaging in combat.
Asked about the findings, Koo said the Defense Ministry does not comment on how other democracies with shared values might respond to a Taiwan contingency, Rti reported. He said the military is focused on building its own defense capabilities and maintaining its determination to fight independently to ensure national security.

We will examine it," Justice Bagchi said, according to LiveLaw.The Chief Justice cautioned lawyers against reading too much into the court's observations, saying, "Don't pick up words like this ..."The bench agreed to issue notice on the petition and listed the matter for October 27 along with connected petitions concerning Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Iran maintains indirect comms as it weighs US' Hormuz plan reply
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:43:00 UTC
18:43:00 KST

Iran continues to review a U.S. response to its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and will reply through intermediaries once the review is complete, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday.
Baghaei also told a press conference that Iran continues to exchange messages via intermediaries, without elaborating. Qatar and Pakistan, among others, have acted as mediators in efforts to end the war that began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28.
"The exchange of messages between Iran and the U.S. through mediators continues," Baghaei said.
"We are reviewing the Americans’ proposals for negotiations. Iran’s preconditions must be observed for any negotiations," he added.
After a June interim cease-fire crumbled and on-off strikes resumed, Iran presented its proposal in mid-September and later confirmed receipt of a U.S. response.
However, the process has since stalled, with Iran’s security chief saying Sunday that Washington’s response did not sufficiently address Tehran’s seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and returning to negotiations.
A central point of disagreement has been Washington’s insistence on addressing Iran's nuclear program from the outset.
Tehran says negotiations should initially focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war carried about a fifth of the global trade in oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) and restoring security in the waterway.
Baqhaei added that Russia also continues to play a "constructive" role regarding Iran’s nuclear file, pointing to Moscow’s involvement in the 2015 nuclear agreement.
He said Iranian and Russian relations are based on mutual trust and that Tehran welcomes supportive efforts by friendly countries, but stressed that, "technically and precisely," mediation between Iran and the U.S. remains in the hands of countries such as Pakistan and Qatar.
Turning to the Strait of Hormuz, Baqhaei said developments there were a direct consequence of U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran and rejected suggestions that Tehran’s actions were intended to create negotiating leverage.
"What we have seen in the Strait of Hormuz since Feb. 28 was the direct result of the U.S. and the Israeli regime's attack on Iran," he said.
"With the current U.S. approach, security will not return," he added.
Baqhaei rejected U.S. assertions that Iran had lost its leverage, saying such claims did not correspond with realities on the ground.
"They can say Iran has lost its leverage, but we are doing our work," he said, arguing that energy markets were not responding to Washington’s assertions.
Baqhaei also said that Iran was "deeply concerned" by escalating attacks between Yemen's Tehran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia, after 14 people died in two days of strikes on Riyadh's airport.
"We are deeply concerned about the developments taking place in the Arabian Peninsula," he said, adding that Tehran was ready "to help facilitate dialogue between the parties."
A Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on Sunday killed one person and wounded 11 others, a day after 13 died in the deadliest strike on Saudi soil in more than a decade.
"We absolutely do not want hostilities and war to continue between two Islamic countries," Baqhaei said, urging the parties to resolve the situation "through dialogue and engagement."
The Houthis are part of the Iran-backed "Axis of Resistance," a network of groups opposed to Israel that also includes Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iraqi Shiite armed groups.
