Pope Leo sticks to busy schedule before surgery to remove lung nodule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:40:52 UTC
18:40:52 KST

Pope Leo to be hospitalised on Tuesday ahead of surgery, Vatican says
VATICAN CITY, Oct 12 - Pope Leo will go into hospital on Tuesday before surgery to remove a small growth found on one of his lungs, the Vatican said, as the pontiff kept up a busy schedule on Monday, holding seven previously planned meetings in the morning.
Leo, 71, said on Sunday that the growth, a small nodule, had been found on a recent check-up, was "well-contained" and had been spotted early.
The nodule was found during a routine health check, the Vatican press office told journalists earlier on Monday, before confirming that the pope is expected to be hospitalised late on Tuesday morning, ahead of his surgery.
It did not say when the actual operation would take place.
A regular advisory on the pope's daily schedule, issued at noon (1000 GMT) on Monday, said he met that morning with visiting bishops from Argentina, Nicaragua and the United States, among others.
In a meeting at the Vatican with members of a Rome-based charity group on Monday, the pope spoke in a strong, clear voice, thanking them for their work.
COMPLICATION RATE FOR NODULE REMOVAL LOW
Leo, elected pope by the world's cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had health issues previously.
The Vatican has said the pope's recovery is expected to take about a week.
A nodule on the lung is a small, localised lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than 5% of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although risk rises with age, size, and other factors such as smoking.
Dr. Federico Venuto, chief of thoracic surgery at Rome's Policlinico Umberto I hospital, said surgeries to remove lung nodules are usually minimally invasive, and can sometimes involve use of a thin camera tube called a thoracoscope.
"The complication rate is extremely low," he told Reuters.
POPE'S TRANSPARENCY ABOUT HEALTH UNUSUAL
Leo's decision to discuss his upcoming surgery publicly on Sunday marked a contrast with his predecessor, the late Pope Francis, who died in April 2025 at age 88.
Francis was hospitalised several times as he grew frail in his later years and did not usually announce his hospital visits in advance, sometimes sparking a media frenzy over his health.
Canadian Cardinal Gérald Lacroix said on Monday that he was grateful for Leo's transparency.
"I really appreciated yesterday ... (that) he himself said, 'This is what's going on,' very transparent, and asked for prayers," said Lacroix. "I like that."
Leo, the leader of the 1.4-billion-member Church, had several public appointments on his calendar for this week, including a Mass in St. Peter's Square on Wednesday morning.
The Vatican said the Mass would now be led by Filipino Cardinal Luis Tagle, a Vatican official whom Leo last week approved as the dean of the Church's college of cardinals, in the first selection of an Asian cleric to the elite role.
In the event of a papal death or resignation, the dean of the cardinals is responsible for organizing the secret conclave to elect his successor.
The pope is the final earthly authority for the world's Catholics and does not have a deputy who steps in when he is sick. When a pope is incapacitated, the business of the Vatican's vast bureaucracy carries on as usual, holding off on any decisions that require papal approval. REUTERS

Against that backdrop, Energy Minister Abdulaziz bin Salman, one of the most senior Saudi officials to speak publicly in the wake of the strikes, sought to project resilience, telling oil industry executives that the kingdom remained committed to providing energy security.

The attacks on Saudi Arabia, a regional powerhouse and the world’s top oil exporter which has poured billions of dollars into its military, were the deadliest to hit the kingdom in a decade.
‘Full-fledged war crime’
Although Saudi Arabia has poured billions into its military, Houthi attacks continue to slip through.

Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen’s government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.

On the ground in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing in their counter-offensive against the Houthis around the Bab el-Mandeb strait, a key shipping route, military sources said on Oct 10. The Houthis claimed to have repelled them.

Why CJI declined to meet Rahul Gandhi, Kharge amid protests against Gyanesh Kumar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:32:33 UTC
18:32:33 KST

CJI Suryakant, Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge
NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant had declined a request from Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi and Rajya Sabha leader of opposition Mallikarjun Kharge for a meeting to discuss issues arising from the ongoing protests in Delhi.He said the matters are already pending before the Supreme Court and discussing them administratively would violate the principle of separation of powers.
In a letter dated October 11, the CJI advised the two Opposition leaders to approach the Supreme Court through the judicial process instead of submitting a memorandum on the administrative side. He also assured them that any petition filed on the issues would be heard at the earliest possible opportunity in accordance with the law.The request concerned allegations of irregularities involving the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and the Election Commission of India, alleged arbitrary arrests of students, the closure of metro stations and the cancellation of trains amid protests in the national capital.READ ALSO: How Jantar Mantar became Delhi's designated protest site and what changes nowExplaining his decision, CJI Surya Kant said the issues raised by Gandhi and Kharge were “already sub judice before the Supreme Court of India.”“Therefore, convening a meeting to discuss pending cases would wholly contravene the principle of Separation of Powers, an intrinsic facet of the basic structure doctrine of the Constitution of India, and would be incompatible with the established ethics and judicial propriety,” the CJI said.
He also clarified that the Supreme Court did not have administrative powers to address the concerns raised in their letter, but could examine them through its judicial jurisdiction.“However, in the exercise of our jurisdiction under Article 32 of our Constitution, along with other plenary powers, including that of judicial review, we are duty-bound to consider on the judicial side the gravamen of issues affecting the citizens of India,” he said.The CJI reiterated the Supreme Court’s commitment to protecting citizens’ fundamental rights and said they could seek their enforcement through the legal process.“Supreme Court of India reiterates its commitment to preserve and protect the Fundamental Rights of every citizen of India and they are entitled to seek enforcement of such rights at all hours through the procedure known in law. It would thus be more appropriate on your part to invoke the judicial powers of the Supreme Court of India, instead of submitting a memorandum on the administrative side,” he said.Pointing to the court’s schedule, CJI Surya Kant said matters involving similar issues were listed for hearing on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. He invited the Opposition leaders to file a petition on Monday, either physically or through the court’s e-filing facility.“If so advised, you may submit your petition on Monday, either physically at the Supreme Court of India, between 10:30 A.M. and 04:30 P.M., or alternatively, by utilising the e-filing option, which permits filing at any time and on any day. You have my assurance that any such petition shall be heard at the earliest possible opportunity, in accordance with the law,” he said.Gandhi and Kharge had sought an appointment with the CJI amid Opposition protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of electoral irregularities, including what Congress has described as “vote chori”.
Kharge said in a social media post on Sunday that the Opposition would continue its fight and that he and Gandhi had written to the CJI seeking a meeting.“We will continue our fight. Tomorrow, we are also going to meet CJI. I have written a letter, and Rahul Gandhi has also written a letter. We have scheduled a meeting between 4-5pm, during which we will apprise him of the situation... Chaos is being created in the country by home minister and PM, and everywhere an undeclared emergency is imposed,” Kharge said.The CJI’s response leaves the Opposition leaders free to pursue their concerns through a formal petition, with the court indicating that related matters could be taken up through judicial proceedings.

Trump turns to Russian diesel ahead of midterms, but analysts see little price relief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:31:22 UTC
18:31:22 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump's latest geopolitical dealmaking effort to ease a diesel supply crunch ahead of November's midterm elections is unlikely to make a dent in prices, according to analysts.
Trump's declaration of an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday surprised policymakers across the world — not least in Kyiv — and prompted oil prices to fall on Monday, despite Russia striking a power plant shortly after the announcement. Oil later rose.
The president's declaration comes after he announced a deal for Russia to release 300,000 metric tons to the U.S. and global markets immediately, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons after that. Moscow will then deliver another 3 million tons of diesel based on the condition of Russia's refineries, Trump said.
Trump has sought to tame inflation ahead of the congressional midterms in November, when his Republican Party is at risk of losing both houses.
According to the Pew Research Center, 84% of registered voters say the economy is "very important" to their vote.
Diesel prices hit a record high average of $6.5276 a gallon in late September, according to AAA, as the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East took their toll on supply.
"Trump is exploring all avenues to bring down diesel prices before the mid-terms," Mohit Kumar, chief European economist at Jefferies, said in a note on Monday.
"The deal with Russia has drawn opposition both from within the US and from European leaders, as it would be bypassing the Russian sanctions in place," he added.
"While more supply of diesel would ... ease some pressure on diesel prices, the volumes agreed are unlikely to make a substantial difference."
Russia's 'mystery' diesel supply
The U.S. Treasury has issued a temporary license easing sanctions on Russian diesel to facilitate the deal Trump announced Friday.
Lombard Odier analysts said in a Monday note that the agreement, in addition to Chinese plans to resume refined-fuel exports, are "potentially significant because diesel shortages have amplified the inflationary consequences of disrupted energy supply, particularly through transportation, agriculture and industrial production."
But they cautioned that "announced shipments are not equivalent to delivered supply," and "neither agreement immediately restores damaged infrastructure or normalizes maritime transportation."
Neil Atkinson, former head of the Oil Division at the International Energy Agency, was less optimistic, telling CNBC in a note: "Where the volumes to supply the Trump deal come from is a mystery, unless it comes from domestic supply, which will cripple the Russian economy."
Atkinson noted that the G7 recently authorized the release of 50 million barrels of oil products, mainly diesel, but "it has made almost zero difference to the underlying diesel market tightness" due to lack of clarity over how much will be released, or when and where.
"The same will be true of the new US/Russian deal to allow exports from Russia," he said. "Even if the initial 300 kt (about 70 kb/d over a month) were available tomorrow it would have little impact.
"The lack of impact is because the US uses 3.7 million barrels a day of diesel. The world uses 29 million barrels a day of diesel. The US is sitting on 105 million barrels of commercial diesel stocks," Atkinson added.
"Pre-war, the Middle East Gulf exported nearly 1 million barrels a day of diesel. This is still largely lost due to damage to refineries and the difficulty of exporting products by ship."
Deal to 'fail economically' — and embolden Putin
In a Monday note to clients, analysts at Singapore's Quantum Strategy outlined a particularly pessimistic outcome.
"We expect this deal to fail economically. We remain long distillates and crude. We remain short US assets," they wrote.
"We expect Putin to read the deal as an open invitation to escalate his gray-zone warfare in Europe to a much higher level. The effects would be negative for the Euro and for EU sovereign debt, as European powers scramble to ensure their defense."

China steps up crackdown on food safety crimes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:25:52 CST
18:25:52 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- China is intensifying its crackdown on food safety crimes and tightening oversight of online food sales and other emerging business models, according to a new guideline.
The guideline, issued by the Commission for Political and Legal Affairs of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, calls for tougher penalties for serious offenses and closer coordination between food safety regulators and criminal justice authorities.
A commission representative said on Monday that China's food safety situation remained generally stable, but authorities faced new challenges as food safety crimes became more sophisticated, increasingly exploited online platforms and spanned multiple stages of the supply chain.
The guideline identifies meat products, school meals, health foods, vegetables and fruit as top enforcement priorities. It also calls for tighter scrutiny of food production, online sales, catering services and imports.
To improve coordination between administrative enforcement and criminal proceedings, the guideline calls for clearer procedures for referring suspected criminal cases and better information sharing between agencies.
China also plans to expedite revisions to the food safety law to clarify the regulatory responsibilities of businesses involved in fresh food e-commerce, food delivery and livestream sales.
The guideline also calls for authorities to update lists of banned additives as investigations identify new illegal substances.
It further urges authorities to address food safety risks uncovered in individual cases and strengthen oversight across the supply chain. ■

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: China rolls out "token factories" to drive AI economy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:25:49 CST
18:25:49 KST

This photo provided by iSoftStone Information Technology (Group) Co., Ltd. shows a scene inside a token factory at the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 21, 2026. (Xinhua)
BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- As AI applications gain momentum, China is accelerating the rollout of "token factories" in a bid to build an economic order suited to the AI era.
Every time a user prompts an AI model to generate code, images or video, tokens are consumed behind the scenes. In March, China adopted "ciyuan" as the official Chinese term for "token," giving its AI services a standard unit for measuring, settling and tracking usage -- similar to how electricity is measured in kilowatt-hours.
In late September, Beijing unveiled an action plan to accelerate the development of the token economy for 2026-2028. "This is the first provincial-level policy in China specifically dedicated to the token economy," said Zhang Jinrui, an official with the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Economy and Information Technology.
"With the rollout of Beijing's new policy, tokens are no longer just a technical term associated with large models. The token economy has officially entered a stage of industrial application and institutional development," said Liu Yong, president of the Beijing-based Zhongguancun Internet Finance Institute.
The Beijing action plan calls for building world-class token factories and establishing tiered evaluation standards, with throughput capacity, time to first token, PUE (power usage effectiveness) and cache hit rate as core metrics, to ensure the large-scale supply of high-quality tokens.
A token factory can be thought of as the AI era's equivalent of a power plant. It integrates electricity, chips, data and models to directly produce tokens. Unlike traditional data centers that only rent out computing cards, customers no longer need to deploy models or optimize inference themselves -- they simply pay for the tokens they use.
In the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area, the Chinese capital's first token factory is now in operation, with a daily capacity of up to 1.4 trillion tokens in its first phase.
The plan also designates token distribution platforms as part of the city's new infrastructure layout, exploring market-based pricing and circulation mechanisms for tokens, so that tokens can truly be measured and traded as an economic factor.
On the application side, the new policy encourages the development of general-purpose and industry-specific AI agents, bringing token capabilities into sectors such as industry, research and government affairs.
Chen Guangming, an official with the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Economy and Information Technology, said token consumption is currently growing fastest in AI-generated content and programming, and more vertical industries will become potential growth drivers for token consumption in the future.
"In the internet era, competition was all about traffic and user attention. In the AI era, the logic has shifted -- what matters now is the quality and efficiency of outputting effective tokens," Liu said, adding that the shift from a traffic economy -- one built on user visits and attention -- to a token economy represents a new trend in China's economic development.
Data from China's National Data Administration shows that by June, the country's average daily token calls had surpassed 500 trillion. "More than half of those calls were made in Beijing," Zhang said, noting that the city has so far registered 242 large models for public use.
Beijing's early push is aimed not merely at building a series of token factories, but at exploring institutional rules suited to the token economy, making the city a testing ground for the industry's development, according to local authorities.
Elsewhere, localities across China are developing token economies tailored to their own strengths, as part of efforts to implement the State Council's guidelines on the "AI Plus" initiative. The guidelines aim to build a systematic support framework for AI covering models, data, computing power, applications, open-source development, talent, policies and regulations, and security.
In May, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, drawing on its green computing resources, launched a token trading platform integrating model calls, token matching and transaction settlement. Nanning, capital of south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, is exploring new models such as cross-border data compliance and remote model inference delivery, helping domestic computing power and large-model capabilities reach ASEAN markets as standardized token services. East China's Anhui Province, meanwhile, encourages banks to offer "token loans" as a financial tool for the token economy.
Industry observers generally agree that the global token economy remains in its early stage but holds vast potential. A research report by CICC, a Chinese investment bank, sees "token factories" as one of the fastest-growing and most commercially promising business models for large-model developers in the near term. JPMorgan predicts that China's AI inference token consumption will grow about 370-fold between 2025 and 2030.
China's three major telecom operators rolled out token packages in May for individual users as well as government and enterprise clients, bringing token commercialization further into reach for individual consumers.
Li Lingran, an engineer at an internet company in Beijing, says using large AI models at work has become as essential as water. He now spends more than 200 yuan (about 30 U.S. dollars) a month on tokens, even more than his traditional mobile phone bill. "This is a shift you can't ignore," he said. ■
This photo provided by iSoftStone Information Technology (Group) Co., Ltd. shows a scene inside a token factory at the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 21, 2026. (Xinhua)

Housing costs push 456,000 Western Australians into poverty: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:25:44 CST
18:25:44 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- An estimated 456,000 people in the Australian state of Western Australia, including almost 99,000 children, are living in poverty in 2026 as rising housing costs and inadequate household incomes deepen financial hardship, according to a new report.
The 2026 Poverty Snapshot, released by the Bankwest Curtin Economics Center, found that 15.1 percent of the state's population lived in poverty, up from 11.8 percent in 2021. The number has increased by about 145,000, or 47 percent, over five years, according to a statement released Monday by Australia's Curtin University.
The report estimated that around 180,000 Western Australians were living in deep poverty, while more than 650,000 had incomes below 60 percent of the national median after housing costs.
The state capital Perth's median weekly rent reached 720 Australian dollars (about 502 U.S. dollars) in June 2026, having more than doubled since June 2020. More than one in four private renters in the state were living in poverty, the report found.
Children faced particularly severe hardship, with almost half of those living in poverty in deep poverty, compared with about one in four in 2021. Children in poverty faced an average household income shortfall of 224 Australian dollars a week.
The report called for expanded social and affordable housing, stronger support for households experiencing rental stress and measures to ensure incomes keep pace with living costs. ■

Analysis: Four things we learn in Spain's Matchday 8
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:25:39 CST
18:25:39 KST

MADRID, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Barcelona continued its perfect start to the La Liga season after the international break, while controversy surrounding Vinicius Junior overshadowed Real Madrid's narrow home victory over Villarreal. Here are four things we learned from the weekend's action in Spain.
1. No Raphinha, no problem for Barcelona
Barcelona's leading scorer Raphinha missed Saturday's 3-0 win over Getafe with a thigh injury, but Gabriel Jesus stepped up to show he can lead the attack in the Brazilian's absence.
The result was rarely in doubt after Anthony Gordon opened the scoring in the second minute against a Getafe side that managed just 20 percent possession.
Barcelona has now won all eight of its league matches this season at an average of more than three goals per game.
Saturday's comfortable victory underlined the attacking options available to coach Hansi Flick, even without one of his most influential players.
2. Vinicius remains a headache for Real Madrid
Vinicius Junior's new contract with Real Madrid this summer was expected to help ease tensions between the Brazilian and the club's supporters, but his relationship with sections of the Santiago Bernabeu crowd remains strained.
Despite his talent, Vinicius continues to attract boos from some home fans, and Saturday's 1-0 win over Villarreal brought another controversy.
The Brazilian had a goal disallowed after a VAR review showed he had pulled the hair of Villarreal defender Nathan Saliba, an incident that also resulted in his dismissal.
Vinicius reacted angrily and had to be restrained by teammates. He now faces a possible suspension, with the length of any ban yet to be determined.
The incident has raised fresh questions about his discipline and his uneasy relationship with Real Madrid's supporters.
3. Encouraging signs for Aguirre despite Valencia draw
Javier Aguirre had to wait less than two minutes for the first goal of his tenure as Valencia coach, with Dani Raba putting his side ahead away to Racing Santander on Sunday.
Although Valencia eventually settled for a 2-2 draw at El Sardinero, there were encouraging signs for the new coach.
Valencia played with greater intensity and aggression, showing the determination it will need to climb away from the relegation places.
Aguirre will be disappointed not to have secured all three points, but the performance offered reasons for optimism as he looks to improve results and restore confidence among supporters at Mestalla.
4. Vallecas protest understandable but counterproductive
Saturday's match between Rayo Vallecano and Athletic Bilbao was abandoned after home supporters repeatedly threw small plastic balls and paper airplanes onto the field at the Estadio de Vallecas.
The protest reflected growing frustration among Rayo fans, whose team was forced to play its first three league matches of the season away from home because of safety concerns at the stadium.
Some supporters blame club president Raul Martin Presa for the problems and fear he wants to move Rayo away from its traditional home.
Their anger is understandable, given the importance of Vallecas to the club's identity, but disrupting matches risks making the situation worse.
Rayo could face a stadium closure of between one and three matches, according to reports, potentially depriving the team of home support just as it has returned to its own ground. ■

China Focus: China's school autumn breaks take shape as cities roll out local plans
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:25:16 CST
18:25:16 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- China is turning a national policy initiative for school spring and autumn breaks into local arrangements, as cities across the country announce autumn holidays for students.
The breaks are designed to enrich students' social experiences and promote their all-round development. They also give families more time for leisure and can help spread tourism spending more evenly throughout the year.
In the latest example, the education bureau of Shenzhen, in south China's Guangdong Province, said on Oct. 9 that all schools providing compulsory education in the city, including private schools, would have a four-day autumn break from Nov. 17 to 20, 2026, and a two-day spring break on April 1-2, 2027. Kindergartens may follow the same arrangement, while high schools can set their own schedules based on their circumstances. The city said it would not require make-up school days after either break.
Local arrangements vary. In Sichuan Province in southwest China, Chengdu will let districts and schools schedule a three-day autumn break over the last three days of the second week of November, linked to the weekend. Zigong has fixed its break for Nov. 16-18, creating a five-day break with the preceding weekend.
In Fuzhou, in the eastern province of Fujian, different districts and county-level areas have different dates. Ningbo, in east China's Zhejiang Province, will schedule its break for Nov. 25-27. Guizhou Province in southwest China has issued guidance setting the autumn break at three days in general, with mid-November as the suggested time.
The moves come about seven months after China's 2026 government work report called for introducing spring and autumn breaks for primary and secondary school students in areas where conditions permit, along with a system of staggered paid leave.
Beyond providing students a break from classroom routines, the new arrangements could also encourage families to travel during less busy periods, potentially benefiting tourism and related businesses.
An earlier pilot in Sichuan provided an indication of the possible impact on tourism. During a five-day autumn break in November 2025, ticket bookings for scenic spots in the province more than quadrupled from the same period a year earlier, while bookings for flights departing Chengdu rose 22 percent from the previous week, local media reported.
While social media users generally welcomed the introduction of spring and autumn breaks, some raised practical questions. One user from Guangdong asked who would care for primary school children when parents were working.
Local authorities are working to address childcare needs. Measures in local guidance include school-provided care, study camps and group activities for students whose parents cannot take leave.
In Altay, in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, the three-day "snow break" scheduled for Dec. 16-18 will be combined with the following weekend to create a five-day holiday.
Authorities there plan to organize activities using local winter resources, including ice-and-snow study trips, winter sports and cultural experiences. Schools will reduce written homework and encourage practical assignments related to winter sports and local ice-and-snow culture. Free school-provided care will be available during the break for students who cannot join study trips.
The arrangements show how school holidays can be adapted to local conditions to extend learning beyond the classroom while giving families more flexibility.
Making the breaks work for families also requires coordination between school calendars and workplace arrangements. Lu Ming, a national political advisor and a professor of economics at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, said in March that employers should allow greater flexibility during school breaks so parents could adjust shifts or take leave to spend time with their children. Where parents cannot take time off, he said, schools and community organizations could organize activities with government support.
In China, autumn school breaks are tailored to local conditions rather than set under a uniform national system. Their longer-term success will depend not only on school calendars but also on parents' access to leave and the availability of school-provided or community-based care for children whose parents cannot take time off. ■

Accused of raping two girls, Louisiana man set to become police chief after opponent quits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:21:35 UTC
18:21:35 KST

Christopher Paul, 48, who was arrested last month on suspicion of raping two 13-year-old girls nearly 20 years ago, is poised to become police chief of the small Louisiana town of Elizabeth, despite facing two criminal charges of second-degree rape. With his only opponent having withdrawn from the race, Paul is now the sole candidate for the position, and Louisiana law does not prevent him from taking office while the charges remain unresolved.
The extraordinary situation has sparked criticism in Elizabeth, a town of approximately 400 residents. Local officials are already considering changing how the police chief is selected, as the prospect grows that a man awaiting trial on serious sexual assault charges could soon be responsible for enforcing the law.
Paul, a Republican, registered as a candidate for police chief on August 6. About a month later, he was arrested over allegations that he raped two girls, both 13 at the time, in 2005 and 2006. He faces two counts of second-degree rape and was released on $60,000 bail.
According to Allen Parish Sheriff Doug Hebert, the investigation began in early August after police received a complaint concerning alleged assaults dating back approximately two decades. Detectives interviewed the complainants and additional witnesses before obtaining an arrest warrant. Paul surrendered to authorities on September 8 and was taken into custody.
Paul initially faced another candidate, Zachary LaCaze, who intended to run as an independent in the November 3 election. However, LaCaze announced on September 23 that he was withdrawing after discovering that his federal government employment prevented him from continuing his campaign.
LaCaze works at the Fort Polk military installation and said he was initially told he could run for office provided he did not identify himself with a political party. He later learned that because his opponent was running as a Republican, his candidacy was subject to restrictions under the federal Hatch Act, which limits certain political activities by government employees.
Faced with a choice between keeping his job and continuing his campaign for police chief, LaCaze decided to withdraw.
Speaking to local television station KPLC, LaCaze acknowledged the consequences of his decision.
"I have a lot of concerns if it happens, but it's out of my hands," he said when asked about the possibility that his withdrawal would effectively hand Paul the position.
LaCaze withdrew after the official deadline for new candidates had passed, leaving Paul without an opponent and positioning him to take office without a contested election.
According to Louisiana election authorities, LaCaze's name may still appear on ballots because of the late withdrawal, but notices will be posted at polling locations explaining that the race has been canceled following his departure.
Mayor: ‘We have no authority to change the ballots’
The unusual circumstances have left local officials facing a legal dilemma. Under Louisiana law, a felony conviction can disqualify someone from holding public office, but pending criminal charges alone do not prevent a candidate from running or serving.
Unless Paul is convicted of an offense that would make him ineligible, he remains legally entitled to assume the position. The new police chief's term is scheduled to begin January 1, 2027.
Elizabeth Mayor Mandy Leo Green issued a statement to residents amid the controversy, stressing that neither she nor the town council has the authority to remove Paul from the race.
"Charges are allegations, not a conviction," she emphasized.
"The candidate in question has been arrested and charged, but has not been convicted of any crime. Under the law, anyone accused of a crime is presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law. This is an important part of our justice system."
Green added that the local administration and town council cannot alter the ballots despite concerns surrounding the election. She invited residents to attend a council meeting scheduled for Monday, October 12, to express their views.
Meanwhile, the Youth Peace & Justice Foundation, an American organization dedicated to preventing violence against children, has called on Paul to voluntarily withdraw his candidacy until the criminal proceedings against him are resolved.
Paul declined to comment on the allegations when approached by local media but made clear that he intends to remain in the race.
In response to the situation, the Elizabeth town council has approved a special ballot measure for December 12, allowing residents to decide whether to change the process for selecting their police chief.
Under the proposal, the position would no longer be filled through direct elections. Instead, the police chief would be appointed with the approval of the town council.
According to council documents, the vote will take place about a month after the November election in which Paul is expected to be declared the winner, and less than three weeks before the new police chief's term begins.
It remains unclear when the proposed change would take effect if approved and whether it could have any impact on Paul's anticipated term. The official documents also do not explicitly state whether the decision to hold the vote was prompted by the criminal case.
Residents have another possible option under Louisiana law: a recall procedure aimed at removing an elected official from office.
In a community the size of Elizabeth, initiating such a process would require signatures from 40% of eligible voters, according to state rules.
For now, with only weeks remaining before the November election, the small Louisiana town faces an extraordinary prospect: its next police chief, the person responsible for enforcing the law, could be a man awaiting the outcome of two serious charges involving the alleged rape of underage girls.

Airbus Valkyrie combat drone completes first European flight
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:15:58 BST
18:15:58 KST

Airbus and Kratos have completed the first European flight of the U740 Valkyrie uncrewed combat aircraft, with the demonstrator reaching Mach 0.8 during a test campaign intended to support development of a European Collaborative Combat Aircraft capability by 2029, according to Airbus.
The flight took place at a test facility in northern Europe on 29 September and included a rocket-assisted launch, manoeuvres at several altitudes and speeds, and changes to a pre-planned route while the aircraft was airborne. Airbus said all objectives for the first flight were achieved.
Speaking during a media briefing on the programme, Hendrik Zippel, Airbus Head of CCA Collaboration and Development, described the flight as “picture-perfect” and said preparations began at 6am before the aircraft was moved from its hangar to the launch position.
The Valkyrie took off at around 10.30am using rocket boosters, which separated after approximately two seconds. Zippel said the aircraft initially flew a diamond-shaped pattern before entering a longer racetrack profile used to test different flight conditions.
“We then entered into a longer racetrack pattern where we flew at several flight levels, 10,000, 20,000, 30,000 feet, with several acceleration and deceleration phases,” he said.
“We went up to 0.8 Mach, and also tried out the reconfiguration of a pre-planned route, and all of this went very successfully.”
The flight also tested the procedures required to recover the aircraft at the end of the mission, with Airbus saying the vehicle came down inside the planned recovery area. Zippel said the actual landing point was substantially inside the boundary established before the test.
The aircraft flown in September is based on Kratos’ Valkyrie platform, which Airbus intends to combine with its own Multi-platform Autonomous Reconfigurable and Secure mission system, known as MARS.
Airbus describes MARS as the mission-system layer that will provide control over mission applications, software, data and hardware, while adding autonomous functions and the ability to coordinate multiple aircraft. The company says a human will remain within the command hierarchy for critical decisions.
The next flight-test campaign is planned for the middle of 2027 and is expected to include the first increment of the MARS mission system integrated into the aircraft.
Zippel said: “After flight test is before the flight test. The next flight tests are planned mid of next year. We plan to then have already integrated into the birds, into the aircrafts, the first increment of our MARS mission system.”
Airbus is aiming to offer the resulting system as a Collaborative Combat Aircraft that could operate autonomously or under the direction of crewed fighters, including the Eurofighter.
According to an Airbus news update, Mike Schoellhorn, CEO of Airbus Defence and Space, said: “In an increasingly complex and contested threat environment, air forces require affordable combat mass.”
He added: “By pairing Kratos’ proven airframe as a ‘program of record’ with Airbus’ sovereign European mission system, we are able to offer a robust, sovereign, affordable, and combat-ready CCA system by the end of the decade.”
Airbus says the U740 Valkyrie is 9.1 metres long with a wingspan of 8.2 metres and has a maximum take-off weight of approximately three tonnes. The aircraft has an internal weapons bay as well as external payload stations beneath the wings, while the company quotes a range exceeding 5,000 kilometres and a service ceiling of 45,000 feet.
The aircraft can use rocket-assisted launch equipment rather than depending on a conventional runway, although Airbus says runway take-off and landing remain available as an alternative. The company sees that flexibility as a way of dispersing uncrewed combat aircraft away from established airbases.
Eric DeMarco, President and CEO of Kratos, said: “First flights typically include plenty of learning opportunities, but with the maturity of the Valkyrie system and the well-integrated Airbus and Kratos team, this flight was an amazing success.”
Airbus and Kratos are now moving towards more complex flight testing in which the European mission system will begin to be introduced into the aircraft, with the companies continuing to target a combat-ready CCA capability by 2029.

In pictures: Gaza's olive harvest shrinks as war damage, Israeli access restrictions hit farmers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:12:34 UTC
18:12:34 KST

Palestinian farmers in Gaza are facing a difficult olive harvest this year as production declines, large areas of agricultural land remain damaged and many groves are inaccessible because they lie in areas controlled by the Israeli army or beyond the so-called “yellow line.”
On accessible farmland, farmers continue picking olives and separating them from leaves and branches despite shortages of fertiliser, irrigation water and agricultural supplies, as well as higher labour, transportation and pressing costs.
The pressures have left many families unable to store their usual annual supplies of olive oil and olives.
On July 13, Gaza’s agriculture ministry estimated losses to the sector from Israel’s genocidal war, which began on October 8, 2023, at more than $3 billion, including $1.49 billion in direct damage and $1.59 billion in indirect losses.
Kamel Baraka, a farmer from Deir al Balah in central Gaza, said olive tree yields had fallen significantly.
“A tree that produced around 100 kilograms (220.4 pounds) of olives before the war now produces no more than 20 (44 pounds) to 30 kilograms (66 pounds),” Baraka told Anadolu.
That represents a decline of around 70 percent to 80 percent, he added.
“A season that once provided an important source of income for farmers, traders and workers now barely meets the needs of some families because of current conditions and shortages of essential agricultural supplies,” Baraka said.
“Olive cultivation requires constant care, fertiliser, irrigation and other inputs that have become increasingly difficult to obtain,” he added.
Massive damage
Damage to farmland and restrictions on access have also directly reduced the harvest.
“Large areas of olive groves in eastern parts of central Gaza lie in zones farmers cannot reach, particularly east of Salah al-Din Street and around the ‘yellow line,’” Baraka said.
The “yellow line” is a notional line inside Gaza to which the Israeli army withdrew under the first phase of US President Donald Trump’s plan to end the war, under which a ceasefire deal took effect on October 10, 2025. It separates areas in eastern Gaza that remain under Israeli army control from areas west of the line where Palestinians are allowed to move.
“Farmers in Deir al-Balah, Bureij and Maghazi face difficulty reaching agricultural land that had been a major source of olive production,” Baraka said.
He said available farmland west of Salah al-Din Street is insufficient to meet residents’ needs for olive oil and olives.
Before the war, preparations for the harvest began about a month in advance, with farmers arranging workers and preparing equipment for picking and transport, while families stored olives and oil for the year ahead.
Those preparations have declined as production falls and costs rise, with some farmers now collecting only enough olives for household consumption and limited quantities for sale.
Costs triple
Farmers are also struggling with sharply higher transportation and pressing costs, as well as shortages of containers needed to store olive oil.
“The cost of pressing olives has risen to around three times what it was before the war,” Baraka said, adding that the increase has placed further pressure on farmers whose incomes have already fallen because of lower production.
“Before the war, olive press owners often transported harvests from farms to pressing facilities, while farmers now struggle to find transportation even for small quantities,” he added.
Higher costs for pumping water and irrigating trees, combined with shortages of fertiliser, labour and storage containers, have made preserving the harvest and storing oil increasingly difficult, particularly for families that depend on farming for their food needs.
“The olive season, once an opportunity for farmers to improve their livelihoods and secure food supplies for the year, has become an exhausting season that provides many of them with only a fraction of what they need,” Baraka said.
Since Israel’s genocidal war began on October 8, 2023, Gaza’s agricultural sector has sustained widespread damage, according to the agriculture ministry.
The ministry said 158,909 dunams (39,267 acres) of agricultural land have been damaged out of a total 182,247 dunams (45,033 acres), or around 87 percent, sharply reducing crop production and the capacity to provide food.
The genocidal war also has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, according to Palestinian figures, also destroying about 90 percent of the besieged enclave's infrastructure.

OMA adapts historic houston coffee plant into music and arts academy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:11:28 UTC
18:11:28 KST

OMA adapts historic houston coffee plant into music and arts academy
inspired by montessori principles, the adaptive reuse project organizes classrooms, libraries, and performance spaces into a connected learning environment, giving new life to an industrial landmark.
OMA reimagines a Houston coffee plant as a school
OMA transforms Houston’s historic 1930s J.A. Folger & Co. coffee plant into the Frank Liu Jr. Academy for Music and Arts (FLAMA), a tuition-free public charter school designed around music, creative learning, and community. Led by OMA partner Jason Long and project architect Salome Nikuradze, the 6,050-square-meter project sits along Houston’s Buffalo Bayou East corridor, across from the future Turkey Bend development. Now under construction, the school combines the adaptive reuse of an industrial building with a spatial approach that treats education as a collective cultural experience.
FLAMA organizes learning around shared spaces
The architects at OMA organize FLAMA across three stories, arranging its programs according to the developmental stages of its students, with younger children occupying the lower levels and older students moving upward. Drawing on Montessori principles, the design supports independence, openness, and collaborative learning through a series of shared spaces that OMA calls ‘neighborhoods.’
Each floor is organized around two central gathering areas, or ‘cymbals,’ with classrooms, practice rooms, and academic programs arranged around them. Rather than treating circulation as a means of moving between enclosed classrooms, the design makes shared space an integral part of the educational experience. These commons accommodate informal gatherings, independent study, project work, and performances, allowing everyday activities to overlap.
music shapes the architecture
At ground level of FLAMA, the youngest students share an intimate common area for play, movement, and drum circles, reflecting the Montessori emphasis on physical development. Nearby, students in grades one and two gather around a larger open space, where a sculptural staircase curves like a French horn and provides a setting for informal performances. On the upper floors, the shared spaces shift toward reading, collaboration, and more focused study. Students in grades three through five use an open library with flexible furniture that accommodates group projects and after-school activities.
Above, a second library commons serves grades six through eight, with more concentrated areas for independent work. The two libraries connect through an opening in the floor shaped like the letter ‘f.’ The form references the forte symbol in musical notation, the f-shaped sound holes found on string instruments, and the academy’s own name. Beyond its visual reference, the opening establishes a connection between floors that allows light and sound to pass between the two learning environments. At the center of the school, a double-height cafetorium brings students together for lunch, assemblies, and performances. A large circular opening and curved auditorium staircase recall the body of a banjo, transforming a space for daily meals into a setting for collective gathering and musical expression.
bringing daylight into an industrial structure
One of the main challenges in turning the former coffee plant into a school is bringing natural light into the building. OMA places classrooms along the exterior walls to give them access to daylight, while new circular skylights bring light into the central shared spaces. The team also preserves elements of the building’s industrial past. The original windows along the street facades are restored and upgraded to meet current energy standards. Inside, a landscaped courtyard introduces a more playful approach, with colorful geometric window divisions that give the historic building a new identity. The courtyard connects the industrial history of the building with its new role as a school.
project info:
 name: Frank Liu Jr. Academy for Music and Arts (FLAMA)
architect: OMA New York | @omanewyork
location: Houston, Texas, United States
area: 6,050 sqm (65,120 sq ft)
 partner: Jason Long
project architect: Salome Nikuradze
client: Lovett Commercial
architect of record: RDLR Architects
landscape architect: SWA Group
structural engineer: IMEG
MEP: DBR Engineering
acoustics: Salas O’Brien

Unknown

09:06:49 UTC
18:06:49 KST

The Population and Immigration Authority rejected German journalist Serena Bilanceri's work visa application in Israel on Sunday, blocking her appointment as the permanent Israel correspondent for the German newspaper Die Tageszeitung (taz).
The decision followed an official recommendation from Avi Cohen Scali, director-general of the Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Ministry, submitted to the Population and Immigration Authority.
The recommendation was made under Amendment 40 to the Entry into Israel Law, which allows authorities to deny entry and visas to individuals acting against the state. It was also issued under an agreement between the ministries to share information and recommendations in such cases.
Bilanceri, 43, a German journalist of Italian descent who covers the regional conflict from Jordan, Syria, and Israel, published several prominent opinion articles over the past year accusing Israel of "apartheid" and calling on the international community to take strong measures against it.
Boycott under the guise of journalism
An official letter sent by the Diaspora Affairs Ministry to Amnon Shmueli, head of the Ben-Gurion Airport division, outlined the statements that led to the recommendation.
In an article published in November 2025, titled "Sanctions Against Israel," Bilanceri argued that settler violence was part of a "radical expulsion strategy" and called on the US, Germany, and other European countries to impose economic and military sanctions on Israel. She also adopted Amnesty International's characterization of Israel as an "apartheid state."
In an article published in September 2025, titled "The European Union Must Act Together Now," Bilanceri criticized Germany for opposing a European Commission proposal to impose sanctions on Israel over the fighting in Gaza. She called on European countries to coordinate their efforts to impose sanctions and, if necessary, tighten them.
Scali commented on the decision, stating that "Anti-Israel actors and those who slander Israel should not set foot in the country."
"We will not tolerate calls for a boycott of Israel under the guise of professional journalism," he said.
The decision was made under the authority granted to the interior minister by Section 2(d)(1) of the Entry into Israel Law.
It follows a series of regulatory measures recently taken by Israeli security and government authorities against foreign activists and journalists who advocate boycotts and sanctions against Israel.

Türkiye’s overall trade sales volume increased by 0.6 percent year-on-year in August, while the retail sales volume index jumped by 10.1 percent, data from the Turkish Statisticial Institute (TÜİK) showed on Oct. 12.

Mail orders and internet sales volume increased by 17.9 percent year-on-year.
Electronic goods and furniture was the only retail sub-sector to experience an annual decline, dropping by 3.1 percent.
Food, drinks, and tobacco sales volume grew by 5.3 percent compared to the same month of the previous year.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taoyuan’s Lalashan will soon receive certification as an Urban Night Sky Place, becoming the first site in Taiwan and the third in Asia to earn the designation, according to the Taoyuan City Government.
The official announcement and certification ceremony is scheduled for Wednesday at National Taiwan University’s Chee-Chun Leung Cosmology Hall in Taipei. Attendees are expected to include Taoyuan Mayor Chang San-cheng (張善政), DarkSky International President Nalayini Brito-Davies, CEO Ruskin Hartley, and Taiwan Dark Sky Association President Lin Cheng-hsiu (林正修), per UDN.
The designation recognizes efforts to reduce light pollution while protecting the natural nighttime environment and promoting responsible stargazing tourism. Taoyuan’s Tourism Administration said the project combines forest ecology, Atayal Indigenous culture, and astronomy-based tourism to establish Lalashan as an international ecotourism destination.
The city government has improved more than 400 public streetlights by installing shields or adjusting their angles to reduce light pollution. It has also worked with dozens of local accommodation operators to sign dark-sky management commitments and introduced municipal guidelines on light pollution prevention, per CNA.
Officials said the process required extensive consultation with Indigenous communities and residents in the certification area. Lighting improvements had to meet international standards without compromising road safety or the daily needs of local communities.
The city government organized local briefings, lighting-improvement workshops, astronomy guide training, and dark-sky activities, alongside coordination among government departments. Taoyuan plans to work with travel agencies to develop stargazing tours along the Northern Cross-Island Highway, linking nighttime tourism with local businesses and community development.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei’s two-Michelin-star restaurant Nobuo has launched a new seasonal tasting menu featuring ingredients from Taiwan and Japan.
Tucked away in a quiet alley in Taipei’s Dongmen neighborhood, the 14-seat restaurant has embraced the concept of home since opening in 2024.
Upholding its core philosophy of simplicity, purity and honesty, Nobuo earned a Michelin star in its inaugural year and was awarded two stars in the Michelin Guide Taiwan 2026.
Chef-owner Nobu Lee (李信男) stays grounded in his culinary roots with the new menu. Avoiding superficial presentation, Lee uses three guiding principles — reveal, retain and restrain — to highlight ingredients at their seasonal peak. For Lee, every dish begins with the raw material itself, and knowing when to stop is essential to showing culinary depth.
Starters include Hokkaido surf clams with Kyoto mizuna and arugula pesto, thinly sliced Sanxia green bamboo shoots with fresh mountain pepper, and smoked scallop alongside a warm scallop mousse.
The main courses draw on ingredients from Taiwan and abroad. Prawns from Penghu are lightly seared and cooked in spiced olive oil with local bitter melon and sakura shrimp. Line-caught red bream from eastern Taiwan is steamed and paired with coconut broth foam, morel mushrooms and a sake-infused asparagus sauce. Quail is brushed with Hatcho miso and wild mountain pepper before grilling.
The centerpiece features New Zealand veal tenderloin and Australian veal sweetbreads, paired with abalone and rare cockscomb simmered in a sukiyaki reduction. Rich in collagen and tender in texture, the cockscomb is balanced with a romaine-spinach sauce and cashew puree.
A special off-menu curry rice, created in memory of Lee’s late close friend, follows. Refined with subtle flavor adjustments, the slow-cooked dish offers deeper complexity and serves as a poignant part of the meal.
Dessert features sake-poached peaches with stracciatella cheese, followed by Japanese ginger sorbet with citrus and kudzu starch spheres.
Beyond the food, beverage pairings play a central role. Nobuo collaborates with a local tea brand to create a cold-brew white tea smoked with dried straw for 24 hours.
A highlight of the wine list is “La Perle Shiro 2025,” an exclusive white wine made for Nobuo by Taiwanese winery Weightstone. With only 360 bottles produced, its crisp acidity pairs with the menu’s herbal notes.
Despite its two-star status, Nobuo maintains the intimate feel of a neighborhood restaurant. Kitchen chefs personally serve and explain each dish, bridging the gap between kitchen and table.
Nobuo offers tasting menus starting at NT$4,680 (US$146), with lunch sets starting at NT$3,280.
*Do not drink and drive. Excessive drinking is harmful to health.

Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana urges Herzog to pardon Netanyahu in letter with no formal legal basis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:06:34 UTC
18:06:34 KST

Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana sent a letter on Sunday urging President Isaac Herzog to grant Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s pardon request, saying former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit’s testimony “exposed failures and violations of the law.”
Ohana’s letter is a political appeal, not a formal step in the clemency process, as he lacks the legal authority to issue such a request.
“I was shocked to learn from the former attorney-general’s testimony that even the remaining charges - after the panel of judges twice suggested that prosecutors withdraw the bribery charge, thus indicating, in their view, that no such bribery ever took place - are based on unlawful investigative actions conducted without his knowledge or approval,” Ohana wrote.
“This conduct, which exposes a series of omissions, failures and violations of the law, cannot end merely with dramatic reports across the media. It must also lead you to reach a decision on the prime minister’s pardon request.”
Ohana, himself a lawyer, said one of the “chronic failings” of Israel’s justice system is “the dragging out of proceedings,” and called on the president to make the “just, courageous, and appropriate decision” to pardon Netanyahu.
Netanyahu submitted a formal pardon request in November 2025, which has since gone through the Justice Ministry’s Pardons Department and been forwarded to Herzog. The president has the authority to grant a pardon; Ohana’s letter does not give him a role in that process or change the status of the request. Israeli law allows any individual to submit a clemency request, so the letter is not meaningless, but it has no independent legal effect.
Mandelblit told court investigators took steps without his approval
Ohana’s characterization of Mandelblit’s testimony goes beyond what has been established in court. Mandelblit told the Jerusalem District Court on Sunday that investigators took some serious steps without his approval, but also testified that he authorized the investigations and did not have to approve every police action.
The prosecution disputes the defense’s account, as the trial continues in the defense stage.
In 2021, the judges rejected a defense request to dismiss the indictment over the authorization issue, while criticizing the lack of separate written approvals.
Netanyahu asked Herzog for a pardon more than five years after his trial began in 2020, while the proceedings were still underway and before any verdict. The President’s Office says clemency requests are generally considered only after legal proceedings have ended.
Although the Supreme Court has upheld the president’s authority to grant a pardon before indictment in rare circumstances, Netanyahu’s request to end an active trial is unprecedented and raises questions about the boundary between presidential clemency and the courts’ role.
Sarah Ben-Nun and Yonah Jeremy Bob contributed to this report.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — ProLogium Technology is expanding into AI data centers and aviation as weak EV demand and high costs slow the commercialization of all-solid-state batteries, Nikkei Asia reported Sunday.
ProLogium CEO Yang Ssu-nan (楊思枏) said non-automotive uses are expected to account for 40% of the company’s production capacity by 2032. The company began mass-producing automotive batteries in Taiwan in 2024 and plans to invest NT$185.75 billion (US$5.82 billion) in a French factory, potentially raising its annual global capacity to 14 GWh by 2032.
The company sees data centers as a key market, with generative AI driving demand for emergency power supplies, per CommonWealth Magazine. It believes its batteries’ high output and lower fire risk make them suitable for use near servers and aims to begin sales for these applications around 2028.
ProLogium is also developing batteries for aviation, per Nikkei Asia. In June, it began research with Dutch electric aircraft startup Elysian Aircraft on batteries for planes with a range of about 1,000 kilometers, while partnerships in unmanned aviation could lead to deployment around 2027. Yang said non-automotive applications generally command higher prices.
The move comes amid intensifying competition in the EV battery market. US EV sales have fallen since the Trump administration ended purchase subsidies in September last year, while Chinese manufacturers, which hold about 70% of the global battery market, have expanded output and improved conventional lithium-ion technology.
The average price of lithium-ion batteries fell 40% per kilowatt-hour from 2020 to 2025, according to the International Energy Agency. Automakers are also adopting cheaper batteries that use fewer rare metals, while solid-state alternatives remain costly because of expensive electrolytes and the investment needed for production facilities.
Other manufacturers are pursuing non-automotive markets as well. US-based QuantumScape, a partner of Volkswagen and Honda Motor, announced plans to diversify this year and established business units for data centers, aviation, and defense over the summer.
Japanese automakers continue to target solid-state batteries for EVs. Toyota Motor is working with Idemitsu Kosan and Sumitomo Metal Mining toward commercialization in 2027 or 2028, while Nissan Motor aims to develop mass-production technology in fiscal 2028.
Nagoya University visiting professor Sato Noboru said solid-state batteries are unlikely to exceed 10% market share until electrolyte costs fall and other technical improvements are made, per Nikkei Asia. He expects widespread adoption no earlier than 2035.

Taiwan health minister opposes legalizing marijuana

18:06:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Health Minister Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said Monday that he opposes legalizing marijuana and that the health ministry will not introduce community drug supply programs, CNA reported.
Shih said the health ministry supports measures to reduce the health risks of drug use but opposes programs that provide drugs directly to users. Some legislators had suggested reviewing overseas approaches, including supervised injection facilities in Canada, to assess whether they could work in Taiwan.
UDN reported that Taiwan introduced harm reduction programs in 2005 after HIV infections rose among people who shared needles. The measures include providing clean needles to prevent infections and methadone treatment to help people manage drug dependence.
The programs now operate across all 22 cities and counties, with 163 drug treatment facilities nationwide. Many offer methadone therapy as part of addiction treatment.
Shih also distinguished between illegal drugs and medicines. He said some controlled substances have medical uses but require strict oversight because of the risks of misuse and addiction, per Liberty Times.
On drug testing in schools, Shih said screening students at higher risk could help detect drug use early. However, inaccurate results could lead to students being wrongly identified as drug users or cases going undetected.
He said testing must be accompanied by counseling, referrals, and follow-up care. Schools must also protect students’ rights and avoid stigmatizing those who test positive.

Taiwan police warn of rise in scam calls using North American dialing code
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:06:08 UTC
18:06:08 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Calls displaying numbers with North America’s +1 dialing code are on the rise in Taiwan, with scammers impersonating the 165 anti-fraud hotline or telecommunications providers, the Criminal Investigation Bureau (CIB) said Monday.
An analysis of Whoscall’s database and CIB intelligence identified nearly 200,000 calls from suspicious +1 numbers in August and September, according to a press release.
Whoscall is a mobile app developed by Taiwanese cybersecurity firm Gogolook that identifies unknown callers and filters fraudulent messages. The company said scammers have been switching between different dialing codes every two to three weeks to evade detection.
In August alone, Gogolook identified about 260,000 scam calls beginning with +422, accounting for 55.8% of calls displaying overseas numbers.
The International Telecommunication Union has not assigned +422 as a country calling code. Scammers can make calls appear to come from such numbers by altering the caller ID.
Calls beginning with +1800 and +1953 picked up in September, with more than 20,000 recorded from each prefix.
The analysis also found that scammers impersonated government agencies, including the National Communications Commission and Financial Supervisory Commission, to obtain personal information.
The CIB urged the public to heed the warnings in Mandarin and Taiwanese played before international calls: “This is an international call. Beware of scams.”
Taiwanese government agencies and the 165 anti-fraud hotline will never call from numbers beginning with “+,” the bureau added.

Taichung Suncake Culture Festival to take place Oct 17
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:06:04 UTC
18:06:04 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taichung City Government Economic Development Bureau Director Chang Feng-yuan (張峯源) announced Monday that the 2026 Taichung Suncake Culture Festival will take place at Wenxin Forest Park on Saturday.
Chang said the 21st festival will bring together more than 80 pastry makers and souvenir brands at the park, offering discounted products and coupons, per CNA. He said the festival has expanded beyond traditional pastries to include other foods and merchandise that represent the city.
Chang added that the 2027 festival would expand further, bringing together neighboring municipalities and major cities around the world.
Suncakes, one of Taichung’s most iconic treats, date back to the Qing dynasty and Japanese colonial era, per Liberty Times. Local history researcher Lin Liang-che (林良哲) suggested that the pastry originated from flaky butter pastries that were made smaller after customers complained about their size.
A suncake pastry chef said the pastry was initially known as maltose cake, per TVBS. Tai Yang Tang, a pastry shop on Ziyou Road, became so well known for its maltose cakes that people began referring to the pastry by the shop’s name. Tai yang means “sun” in Mandarin.
Other local legends offer different explanations for the name. Some say the pastry was used as an offering to the gods during a solar eclipse, while others attribute its invention to a pastry apprentice seeking to win the favor of his master’s daughter. Another theory holds that the red stamp in the center of the cake resembles the sun.
Pastry chef Wei Ching-hai (魏清海) is credited with refining the suncake into its modern form, with local legends identifying him as its inventor. Wei’s pastry shop, Chuan An Tang, has since been converted into the Taiwan Museum of Suncake, which showcases the pastry’s history and offers hands-on suncake-making courses, per Mirror Media.
The National Museum of Taiwan History featured a suncake in a 2019 exhibition on Taiwan’s social movements, per ETtoday. After then Deputy Secretary-General of the Cabinet Hsiao Chia-chi (蕭家淇) complained that Sunflower Movement protesters had allegedly eaten his suncake, protesters began buying suncakes in bulk in response.

Kindle Aluminum Review (2026): Gorgeous, but Expensive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:04:00 UTC
18:04:00 KST

Nice compact size for smaller hands or reading on the go. Aluminum back makes the e-reader heavier, but not so heavy it's uncomfortable. Colors are beautiful. Double the storage of the plastic version. Compatible with new Kindle Click remote. Aluminum is ad-free (plastic version can be ad-free if you pay extra).
TIRED
Expensive for the least amount of features in a Kindle. No warm light, and no auto-adjusting light like you'll get on the aluminum version of other Kindles. Not compatible with Kindle Page Turn Cover.
The Kindle Aluminum has no right to be this beautiful.
Amazon announced a new Kindle lineup at the start of the month, with new versions of the Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and Kindle Colorsoft. The base Kindle is the first one available, with both a plastic version and an aluminum version. It's simply named the Kindle Aluminum, while the aluminum versions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft are now the new Signature Editions with extra features (like wireless charging, an auto-adjusting front light, and a couple AI features).
The Kindle Aluminum only offers the AI features compared to the Signature Editions, while also including a different body, 32 GB of storage, and no lock screen ads. It's not really enough to validate the price change, yet still I find myself loving it.
Notably, it comes in two colors, Seaglass Green and Alpine Sky. The latter is currently sitting just a few inches away from me as I write this, glinting in the sunlight. It's the shade of blue I had hoped the MacBooks would be when Apple released its Sky Blue color in 2025, and every single reader friend I've shown it to has said they want it for the color alone. Even my editor, who strongly prefers physical books (which is hilarious given that she edits my ever-growing list of e-reader reviews, including this one), said just looking at my photos made her want one.
It's a smart move on Amazon's part. There's little reason to upgrade your Kindle if you already have one, but most generations only came in black. The last generation just had one color for the Kindle and one for the Paperwhite. Now, with the base Kindle, you have two colors of the plastic version (the classic black and Ube purple) and the aforementioned green or blue aluminum—these options could have plenty of existing Kindle owners champing at the bit to upgrade.
But it's hard to say it's worth it just for the color, since you could always buy a case instead. It's not a bad device, and there are some improvements—just not enough to justify the price tag.
New Body, Same System
The 12th-generation Kindle still has the same 6-inch screen, but the device's overall form factor has changed. The screen is flush with the rest of the body now, rather than sitting indented, and the new Kindle body is actually a quarter of an inch shorter than the 2024 Kindle's. That sounds like a small increment (and it is!), but having both devices side-by-side, it was easy to spot. The new Kindle also felt like it fit better in my palm, perhaps due to the smoother aluminum backing.
It's also heavier, thanks to the backing. Amazon says the Kindle Aluminum is 5.7 ounces, while the plastic 2026 Kindle is 4.9 ounces. (The 2024 plastic Kindle is 5.56 ounces.) Despite the tiny difference in weight between the 2024 Kindle and the new aluminum version, the aluminum felt palpably heavier to me—almost as if felt like my hand was putting more effort into holding it up. I double-checked on my kitchen scale, and it really is only a 0.2-ounce difference. I had my husband try both models, and he agreed that the aluminum felt heavier and was surprised at how small the difference really was. I think the smaller frame makes the weight sit a little differently.
Opening the 2026 Kindle Aluminum sends you to the same interface as any other Kindle. You'll have a homepage and your library page, and the same set of menus by tapping the right-hand corner dots or swiping down from the top of the page. I did find that while the page-turn speed seemed nearly identical, the new Kindle opened up books much faster than the 2024 Kindle. On the latter, I always had to wait a handful of seconds for my latest Kindle Unlimited read to open (I'll own up to it currently being Verity, my first and very likely last Colleen Hoover book), but the 2026 Kindle near-instantly opened it each time.
The other difference turned out to be the front lights. While neither model has a warm-color front light, the Kindle Aluminum's light tone seemed a touch warmer than the bright-blue tinge of the 2024 Kindle. It was still too blue to comfortably read in dark mode before bed, but side by side, I could see an improvement. It's hard to tell in my photo below, but I know I'm not hallucinating after seeing multiple similar photos already uploaded to the Kindle's Amazon reviews.
Colorful Cost
Ultimately, you don't need this Kindle if you already have one, and $190 is a steep price to pay for a model that doesn't even have a warm option for the front light. The real draw here remains the color body, and Amazon has done a good job with this. My TikTok feed is full of e-reader fans talking about the Ube shade, while the shine of the Alpine Sky is one I would've been eyeing had I not ended up reviewing it. I also like that the aluminum body really does feel like an upgrade when I hold it in my hands.
Amazon might be trying to take a page from Apple's playbook for the iPhone, encouraging you to upgrade your Kindle every two years for the new colors, the way superfans update their smartphones. While Kindle has a much lower cost of entry, that's because a smartphone comes with many more features and upgrades. The Kindle will always have one use: as an e-reader that shows you books. Unlike the second- to third-gen Kindle Scribe update, Kindle isn't providing a new homepage experience, though you will get two of the AI-powered features the Scribes have (Story So Far, to recap where you left off in a story, and Ask This Book—coming soon, to ask about a story). You aren't even getting the auto-adjusting light that aluminum versions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft will have.
It's a good gift for Christmas for someone who already has everything, or an excuse to finally upgrade your own Kindle if it's starting to lag. But you might also want to wait and see if the Paperwhite or Colorsoft Signature Editions are the way to go instead, especially since only those two models will be compatible with the new Kindle Page Turn Cover ($80) that will give you on-device page-turn buttons. Neither the 2026 Kindle Aluminum nor the plastic version will be compatible with this accessory, making it even harder to justify upgrading, but they will at least work with the Kindle Click remote ($35).
Again, this isn't a bad Kindle. The faster book openings and slightly warmer (though still not actually warm) front light, and double the storage make it a legitimate upgrade to the 2024 model. If you don't already have a Kindle, it's not a bad choice if you want to get one of the prettiest models available. It's up to you if that's worth spending almost $200 on.
You'll likely be just as happy with the plastic Ube version and spend between $20 and $40 less, depending on whether you want ads or not (though it does have half the storage of the aluminum model, at 16 GB). Still, this is a much higher price than these basic Kindles used to be available for. Hopefully we will see these Kindles on sale for Black Friday, but I wouldn't hold my breath for any good sales this year.
