WARSAW – A mass deployment of police to Polish schools has helped calm tensions, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Oct 12, after three recent stabbing attacks in four days sparked fears of copycat violence.
The authorities have dismissed rumours that the attacks were linked to an online challenge or organised group.
However, the government says the glorification of violence online is harming young people and it is fast-tracking legislation to make it easier to remove harmful content.
“Our actions and probably the passage of time have led to a significant reduction in online tension and risky situations,” Tusk told a crisis meeting.
“We will continue as long as we observe situations that give cause for concern,” he said.
Police launched the mass security operation late last week after rumours spread online of a planned “Bloody Friday” wave of knife attacks following violence at schools on Oct 7 and 8.
Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said around 20,000 police officers were deployed to schools on Monday, equivalent to roughly one-fifth of the national force.
Dozens of arrests
The operation has led to 135 arrests, authorities said, as police cracked down on threats and online posts linked to the unrest.
Police Commander-in-Chief Marek Boron said the offenders were mainly young people inspired by last week’s attacks trying to get attention with online pranks, while others were inspired by computer games or Nazi subcultures.
In one incident, police said a boy created a model of his school in the Roblox game and simulated attacks on students. He was found to possess a firearm, ammunition and knives.
On Oct 12, prosecutors in the south-eastern city of Lublin said police detained a 21-year-old Ukrainian citizen on suspicion of planning to “murder a stranger using a knife, driven by racial hatred” as part of “Bloody Friday”.
The latest stabbing occurred on Oct 10, when three people were injured at a further education college in Warsaw.
It followed an attack on Oct 8 in Leszczydol-Nowiny, north-east of the capital, where a 15-year-old former pupil wearing a helmet-mounted camera killed a school caretaker and wounded two teachers.
On Oct 7, a 19-year-old injured 10 people, including himself, at a school in Ostroleka, north of the capital.
‘Grim trend of violence’
Tusk on Oct 11 condemned what he called a “grim trend of violence” fuelled by the glorification of extremist ideologies and violent criminals online.
Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said the authorities were monitoring online activity around the clock and had detected increased activity by Russian bots linked to the security situation.
Russia has repeatedly denied using online disinformation to destabilise European countries. REUTERS

Marham runway repairs done three weeks ahead of plan
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:00:29 BST
18:00:29 KST

Resurfacing work at RAF Marham has been completed in five weeks against an eight-week programme, and Lightning Force operations ran from a taxiway while all three runways were out of use, according to the Defence Infrastructure Organisation.
The £3.5 million project covered 28,000 square metres of the runway intersection, last resurfaced in 2018, and dealt with deterioration below the surface as well, with just over 4,000 square metres of underlying pavement needing repair before the new surface could go down. A further 675 square metres was resurfaced on Runway 05.
Because the work sat at the intersection, every runway was unavailable at once. Contractor movements were coordinated with air traffic control and the airfield manager so the taxiway could carry Lightning Force flying with as little disruption as possible.
Tim Fenton, the organisation’s project delivery manager, said: “Completing these essential repairs is an important investment in the resilience of RAF Marham’s airfield infrastructure. By working closely with the Station and our delivery partners, we were able to tackle the immediate deterioration while also taking the opportunity to address additional requirements as part of the same programme of work. This has reduced the need for future intervention and helped ensure the airfield can continue to support Lightning Force operations.”
Flight Lieutenant Steve Southward of RAF Central Region said the scope had been extended through collaboration between the station, the organisation, VIVO and Air Infrastructure to take in further repairs while contractors were already on site.
VIVO carried out the work with sub-contractor Allied and four specialist sub-contractors. Alongside the £3.5 million spent, the team recorded a £3.8 million saving by adopting an approach that removed the need for an on-site concrete batching plant.
Marham is the main operating base for the F-35B Lightning force and home to 617 Squadron and 207 Squadron, the operational conversion unit for the type.
Infrastructure of this kind has been a persistent weak point across the estate, and the Ministry of Defence has acknowledged a substantial maintenance backlog across its airfields and accommodation.

The United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding on navigation through Hormuz in June, but the arrangement broke down amid renewed fighting and disputes over security in the strait.

Wind power could save Türkiye $4 Billion a Year in gas imports, Industry group says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:56:45 UTC
17:56:45 KST

(AP Photo)
Türkiye’s current wind power capacity could help the country save nearly $4 billion annually in natural gas imports, according to İbrahim Erden, chairman of the Turkish Wind Energy Association (TÜREB).
Erden said that every 1,000 megawatts of installed wind power capacity reduces natural gas imports by about $250 million per year based on current energy prices.
“Türkiye’s wind power capacity, which exceeds 16 gigawatts, provides the opportunity to save nearly $4 billion annually in natural gas imports at current energy prices,” he said.
Erden noted that renewable energy sources have accounted for more than 40 percent of Türkiye’s electricity generation in recent years, with the share exceeding 60 percent in the first eight months of this year.
He also said global wind power installations increased by 165,000 megawatts last year, of which 2,000 megawatts were added in Türkiye.
Recalling that Türkiye raised its combined wind and solar installed capacity target for 2035 to 120 gigawatts in 2024, Erden said TÜREB aims for wind power to account for 48 gigawatts of that total.
According to Erden, Türkiye needs to add around 8,000 megawatts of new wind and solar capacity annually to reach the 120-gigawatt target by 2035.
He added that if the country’s wind power capacity reaches the 48-gigawatt level targeted by TÜREB, electricity generation from wind would roughly triple, and the reduction in natural gas imports could reach approximately $10 billion to $12 billion per year under current price and production assumptions.

Bolat will also attend the Türkiye-EU Business Summit, organized by the Foreign Economic Relations Board (DEIK) and the European Business Summit (EBS), where he and Sefcovic will address business representatives from both sides. Penny Wong urges Palestinian Authority to hold elections 'without delay'
In short:
Penny Wong has urged the Palestinian Authority to hold elections after they were postponed.
The Opposition and pro-Israel groups have called on the government to hold Palestine "accountable" after statehood recognition.
What's next?
The Palestinian Authority says general elections will be held in September 2027.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong has labelled the Palestinian Authority's (PA) decision to postpone general elections as "deeply disappointing", as the Coalition accused Labor of "prematurely" recognising Palestinian statehood.
President Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday postponed what would have been the first Palestinian elections in 20 years, scheduled for November, until September 2027, citing changed conditions.
"We call on the Palestinian Authority to ensure elections take place without delay," Ms Wong said.
"Credible elections are an important element of the Palestinian Authority's commitment to the international community on reform, democratic renewal and accountable governance.
"Continuing to delay elections undermines the prospects of a two-state solution."
The Executive Committee of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) cited ongoing Israeli attacks in the occupied West Bank, continued strikes on Gaza, and Israel's refusal to allow election materials or international observers to enter Gaza as key factors for the delay.
"These conditions prevent the establishment of an appropriate environment for elections and undermine guarantees for the safety of voters, candidates and electoral workers," the PLO said in a statement.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar on X accused the Palestinian Authority of "once again deceiving the international community".
"[Mr Abbas's] attempt to drag Israel into this, falsely claiming that Israel imposed obstacles to holding elections, is yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability," Mr Sa'ar wrote.
Israeli outlet, the Jerusalem Post, has separately reported Israel's elections, scheduled for October 27, could be postponed if Israel returned to war with Iran within the next three weeks.
Pro-Israel group demands PA accountability
Australia last year joined 156 other UN member states in recognising Palestinian statehood, with "clear requirements" set out by the international community.
At the time of the decision, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Mr Abbas gave "direct undertakings to Australia" including commitments to hold democratic elections.
Australia/Israel & Jewish Affairs Council (AIJAC) executive director Colin Rubenstein has called on the government "to hold the PA accountable for breaking yet another key commitment underpinning Australia's recognition of a Palestinian state".
"Recognition of Palestinian statehood by Australia, however premature and counterproductive it was, should not remain a blank cheque.
"The Albanese government must explain what consequences will follow for the PA's repeated refusal to abide by the very commitments upon which recognition was based."
Coalition blasts 'premature' recognition
Shadow Foreign Minister Ted O'Brien on Monday joined AIJAC in calling on the prime minister to "explain" what actions the government would take if elections were not held next year.
"The promise of democratic elections gave Labor's premature recognition of Palestine a veneer of legitimacy, and now that veneer has been stripped away," Mr O'Brien said.
"The Australian government should be pressing for that decision to be reversed."
France's government has urged the Palestinian Authority to reverse its election delay, which the French foreign ministry said would "deprive the Palestinian people of their right to democratically express themselves" for the first time in two decades.
Ms Wong has not gone that far.
"We look forward to the Palestinian Authority making progress on the commitments it has made to Australia and the international community, so that next steps like diplomatic relations and the opening of embassies can proceed," she said.

Corruption watchdog abandons Bruce Lehrmann submarine secrets probe
In short:
The NACC has abandoned a probe into ex-political staffer Bruce Lehrmann, who was accused of taking classified material from his former boss's office.
The 31-year-old sued the special minister of state and the then-head of the NACC, who he accused of abusing their power.
Those proceedings are ongoing.
Bruce Lehrmann is no longer under investigation for allegedly using secrets about French submarines for his own ends.
The ex-political staffer got the reprieve on Monday after a letter from the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC) informed him it had abandoned the probe.
The notification ends part of a saga that began with officials raiding the 31-year-old's home in June 2024 over allegations he swiped secret documents from the office of former defence minister Linda Reynolds five years earlier.
The sweep, conducted under an operation dubbed "Ivanhoe", included seizing a blue moleskin diary, which the government claimed contained eight pages of classified security information.
"The former commissioner decided to take no further action concerning the investigation in Operation Ivanhoe," the corruption watchdog's letter reads.
Mr Lehrmann then sued Special Minister of State Don Farrell and then-NACC commissioner Paul Brereton, saying the raids were an abuse of the watchdog's power.
He also alleges he was unlawfully forced to give evidence at two secret hearings in October 2024 in Hobart, where he resides, and described the agency's investigation as driven by "frivolous, James Bond-like allegations".
His legal skirmishes with Mr Farrell and Mr Brereton are ongoing.
"The NACC has been a colossal waste of taxpayer money," Mr Lehrmann said in response to the watchdog's letter on Monday.
"Over two years the former commissioner used his powers to personally advance a conspiracy that I was a spy and traitor to the nation, selling defence secrets to foreign countries.
"The NACC needs to be abolished and replaced with nothing."
Mr Lehrmann was accused of foraging for the classified information on the French submarines days after he allegedly raped his colleague Brittany Higgins in then-senator Reynolds's parliament house office, in March 2019.
The rape allegations were found to be proven, on the balance of probabilities, by Federal Court Justice Michael Lee in 2024.
That finding was upheld twice by the Full Federal Court and the High Court.
Mr Lehrmann has denied the sexual assault claims, which remain untested in a criminal court.
The ex-Liberal staffer remains party to a second anti-corruption investigation, Operation Greenough, into whether federal police misused information during their probe into Ms Higgins's alleged sexual assault.

'Blaming Jews has become the default mode,' President Herzog addresses a delegation of French Jewish leaders
Herzog said boycotts and sanctions harm the Palestinians first and absolve Hamas leadership of responsibility
"What we are seeing in Europe today is that blaming the Jews has become, once again, the default mode, the easiest solution, a cathartic and satisfying disguise for the anger and disappointment over Europe’s own failings and fears." This is what Israeli President Isaac Herzog said to a visiting delegation of the Consistoire, the central religious institution of French Jewry.
The delegation of community leaders and public officials from across France was led by Consistoire President Élie Korchia and included the Chief Rabbi of France Haïm Korsia.
Herzog began by acknowledging how the community was feeling. "I know that it has not been an easy time to be a Jew in the world. It certainly has not been an easy time to be a Jew in France," he said. He then described what that has meant for Jewish communities, alluding to the antisemitism in Europe during the 20th century which led to the Holocaust.
"In a Europe that not so long ago turned on its Jews and on itself, today Israel is demonized, while its Jewish communities contract in fear, forced, once again, into a defensive posture between two identities, and denied, once again, simple, safe belonging."
Herzog drew a line between criticism and what he sees now. "Disagreeing with Israel on its strategy or on its political venue is legitimate debate," Herzog said. "But that is not what's going on in Europe and in France. What we are seeing in Europe today is pure scapegoating."
The President called the blanket rejection of Israel and attempts to isolate it "a grave error."
Suggested articles
On boycotts and sanctions, Herzog was blunt. "Calling for boycotts and sanctions is not simply morally wrong. It reflects a deep alienation from Europe's own intellectual inheritance while speaking to the darkest shadows of its past." He said, adding, "Boycotts and sanctions harm, first and foremost, the Palestinians, robbing them of jobs and income. At the same time, they absolve corrupt Hamas leadership of any responsibility for their rabid antisemitism or for their crimes against their own people."
Herzog closed on a hopeful note about the two countries. "I would like to see Israeli and French entrepreneurs and scientists, artists and teachers, investors, and companies doing far more together," he said. "I believe in this with my whole heart."

Supermarket chains Albert Heijn and Delhaize hit by IT woes
The problem began on Sunday afternoon. “We took immediate measures to protect our IT environment. Part of this involves the preventative temporary shutdown of a number of systems,” said Albert Heijn.
Customer service and logistics systems have also been temporarily shut down, meaning that groceries ordered online cannot be delivered.
The shops remain open, but last week’s promotional prices are still visible on the electronic labels in the racks. “These are the prices for last week’s promotions, a lower price may therefore be shown on labels in the racks and a higher price at the check-out.”
It is not clear whether any customer data has been leaked. “We are investigating the incident and working to restore our services. Protecting the data of our customers, staff and partners is our top priority,” the company said in a statement.
Impact on Delhaize
Delhaize has also taken immediate steps to protect its IT systems. “All our shops in Belgium and Luxembourg remain open and customers can continue to do their shopping as normal,” Delhaize assures us. The company is doing everything it can to get the systems up and running again as quickly as possible.
For the time being, customers cannot place orders for this week. Due to the IT incident, customer services are temporarily unavailable, although the app and website remain accessible.
“Protecting the data of our customers, staff and partners is our absolute priority. We are currently unable to say when all our systems will be available again,” the company states.

Feature: China-Central Asia archaeological cooperation extends exchanges along Silk Road
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:31:37 CST
17:31:37 KST

TASHKENT/BISHKEK, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Archaeological finds are being sorted and examined at a laboratory in Bukhara Region, Uzbekistan, and Wang Shujing is working there for the joint study of an ancient burial site along the Silk Road.
The slope of the burial passage, the arrangement of human remains -- thanks to 3D modelling technology -- the original layout of the Gamkhurd I burial site gradually takes shape on the computer screen.
Wang, from the School of Archaeology and Museology of Peking University, is the leader on the Chinese side of a Sino-Uzbek archaeological expedition, which started in August 2025 with the Samarkand Archaeological Institute.
The team's work includes field excavations of the Gamkhurd I burial ground, where the Bukhara oasis and the desert steppe join in Navoi Region.
Based on burial structures and the characteristics of those unearthed, the joint archaeological team tentatively dated the burial ground to between the 2nd century BC and the 2nd century AD -- a period coinciding with major migrations across the Eurasian steppes and intensified interactions among civilizations along the ancient trade route of the Silk Road.
The team incorporates Chinese specialists in natural sciences and modern material analysis techniques, enabling in-depth research work. Djamal Mirzaakhmedov, who heads the Uzbek side, noted that the collaborative study also makes a significant contribution to the study of the history of Uzbek nomadic and agrarian tribes and peoples.
While filling gaps in the study of regional ancient history, the cooperation, evidently, also carries on the legacy of mutual learning among civilizations along the Silk Road.
Similar cooperation is also seen in Kyrgyzstan, in another aspect of archaeology.
At the Ak-Beshim archaeological site in Chui Oblast, known to Chinese people as the ancient city of Suyab, Bai Yushu, a cultural heritage conservation expert from the Dunhuang Academy in Northwest China, is scrutinizing the ruins alongside fellow researchers to identify signs of structural deterioration.
"Currently, this archaeological site is suffering the erosion of wall foundations, flaking, structural cracking, and the formation of erosion gullies," Bai said, noting that without timely, effective interventions, the damage could become irreversible.
Trying to help, Chinese specialists constructed an experimental wall in an open space nearby with similar environmental conditions and soil properties. They replicated ancient construction techniques, and monitored the changes inside and outside the wall to document the progression of structural deterioration.
The specialists are also conducting reinforcement trials on the wall to assess various conservation techniques. Proven methods are expected to be applied more widely at the Ak-Beshim site in efforts to keep its original appearance as faithfully as possible.
Aisin Duishanalieva, an official for the protection of historical and cultural monuments under the Kyrgyz culture ministry, highlighted the modern scientific methods employed by the Chinese specialists, and expressed hope that the cooperation on conservation work will continue.
The staff from the Dunhuang Academy have the experience of doing conservation work on the ruins of the Beiting Ancient City in Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, which, like Ak-Beshim, is located on the northern side of the Tianshan Mountains and is severely affected by the regional microclimate.
Like in Ak-Beshim, their conservation methods and techniques may also be used elsewhere in Central Asian countries.
The archaeological cooperation between China and Central Asian countries is not only of academic significance, but the joint finds also help revisit the history of development and prosperity along the Silk Road, with traces seen of exchanges, mutual learning among civilizations, as well as their enrichment and advancement. ■

Global vine, wine congress kicks off in northwest China's Ningxia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:31:20 CST
17:31:20 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 12, 2026 shows an exterior view of the venue of the opening ceremony of the 47th World Congress of Vine and Wine in Yinchuan, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Wang Peng)
YINCHUAN, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The 47th World Congress of Vine and Wine opened on Monday in Yinchuan, capital of northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, China's top wine-producing area.
This is the first time the congress, held alongside the 24th General Assembly of the International Organization of Vine and Wine (OIV), has been hosted in Asia since its launch in 1924.
The event has drawn more than 800 participants, including delegates from 51 OIV member states, diplomatic envoys to China from 25 countries, representatives from 47 countries and international organizations, leading experts and scholars in the wine sector from at home and abroad, as well as heads of domestic business associations and leading enterprises.
Themed around building a new landscape for the global vine and wine industry, the congress features an opening ceremony, a seminar on high-quality development of the Chinese vine and wine industry, a sci-tech sub-session, industry visits and a closing ceremony.
Over 400 academic papers from 35 countries will be showcased at the sci-tech sub-session, introducing cutting-edge global wine technologies and helping drive the transformation and upgrading of China's vine and wine industry.
The 6th China (Ningxia) International Wine Culture and Tourism Expo opened alongside the congress, attracting 84 world-renowned wineries and enterprises from distinctive production areas in 16 countries. It has also drawn a total of 146 leading domestic wineries from Ningxia and other core production areas in China.
The eastern foot of Helan Mountain in Ningxia has become China's largest contiguous wine grape production area. This region has 607,000 mu, or about 40,467 hectares, dedicated to wine grape cultivation and development, accounting for nearly 42 percent of China's total.
Ningxia, home to 261 wine enterprises, including 130 wineries, produces 140 million bottles of wine annually.
The local wine industry has also become a driver of tourism. Wineries in Ningxia receive more than 3.7 million tourist visits each year, generating combined benefits of over 50 billion yuan (around 7.4 billion U.S. dollars). ■

With his reformist credentials battered by coalition compromises and a looming general election, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has used his 2027 budget to launch a fresh wave of anti-corruption measures.

Skies over Saudi capital Riyadh largely empty after deadly Houthi strikes on airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:25:24 UTC
17:25:24 KST

Saudi capital’s airport to remain shut this week as airlines cancel services
RIYADH - The authorities have extended the closure of Riyadh’s international airport until Oct 17 and airlines scrapped flights after continuing attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis emptied the skies over Saudi Arabia’s capital.
Operations at King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia’s second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended to “allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport’s facilities”, the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement.
Late on Oct 12, the Houthis said they had attacked the airport with a ballistic missile, shortly after Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the group towards Riyadh.
The Houthis also said in a statement that they targeted an airbase in Khamis Mushait in the kingdom’s south-west with a drone. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation.
A Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) issued later in the day showed that the airport will stay closed until 9pm GMT on Oct 17 (5am on Oct 18, Singapore time).
The airport has been shut since an attack on Oct 10 that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Sunday, another attack killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.
The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi aviation in years, adding to pressures on an industry already grappling with conflict across the Middle East and with higher jet fuel prices that are eating into profits.
They have also raised worries over civil aviation becoming a target in armed conflict.
“This level of sustained intense attack on civil aviation is unprecedented,” said Mark Zee, founder of OPSGROUP, a membership-based organisation that provides aviation safety advice.
“I think this requires us to rethink how we view the current risk picture, and tread very carefully,” he said.
Air traffic tracker Flightradar24 showed planes avoiding the city on Oct 12, though jets were crossing Saudi airspace and landing at top hub Jeddah on the country’s west coast.
Cancellations across all Saudi airports reached 46.4%, aviation analytics firm Cirium said.
Crisis overshadows Saudi business outlook
The disruption has forced airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services, while the Federal Aviation Administration advised US carriers on Oct 11 to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia.
EU aviation body EASA widened a Saudi airspace warning on Oct 9, citing missile and drone attacks.
“The impact goes beyond Saudi Arabia to the wider region and to its global connections,” said aviation analyst John Strickland.
OPSGROUP advised airlines to avoid the southern aviation corridor over the Middle East altogether, and take a route from Europe to Asia over central Asia.
That adds “extensive distance” for some routes and “closes off options for getting into Dubai, Abu Dhabi for most western carriers,” Zee said.
On Oct 13, Etihad Airways said it had cancelled flights between Abu Dhabi and Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam due to “regional disruption”. 
All flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh have been cancelled until Oct 19, it said.
Lufthansa Group has cancelled all flights to Riyadh until Oct 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a suspension to and from Riyadh until the end of the month. Abu Dhabi’s Etihad Airways also extended cancellations.
Delta Air Lines said it was delaying planned services from Atlanta to Riyadh, initially due to start on Oct 23, until March 2027.
The escalation with the Houthis has raised concerns over the broader economic impact. Saudi Arabia’s real GDP is projected to contract by 3.6% in 2026, reflecting a combination of factors including lower oil activity.
The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh in October under pressure, including the kingdom’s flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the programme. REUTERS

Rail operator NMBS
3 out of 10 InterCity trains will not be running Belgium’s state-owned rail operator NMBS says. It has drawn up an alternative timetable. The rail strike runs from 10.00 pm Sunday until last trains on Monday.
This means that 7 out of 10 IC trains are running today. In addition, 1 in 2 Local and Suburban trains are running. Few P or commuter trains are running; these are the trains that normally provide extra services during the morning and evening rush hours.

Across Flanders as a whole, an average of 61 per cent of all buses and trams will be running, but there are differences between the regions.
Like NMBS, De Lijn has drawn up an alternative service based on the staff available.
De Lijn advises passengers to always check its route planner via the website or app before setting off. “Services that are cancelled will not appear in the route planner,” it states. The bus stop and route pages indicate cancelled services with the message ‘not running’.
Brussels local transport company MIVB
The MIVB says all bus and metro lines are operating at a reduced capacity. Some tram lines are also operating.
Passengers can visit the website or use the app for the most up-to-date information. The transport company does, however, expect “significant disruption”.
Education
Disruption extends to schools. Socialist union ACOD Education has given notice of a strike. Traditionally, ACOD has a stronger presence in the GO! official education network.
Flemish public broadcaster VRT
VRT 1 TV will only be showing archive programmes, abridged news bulletins and an episode of VRT NWS Terzake. VRT Canvas, the second channel, will be showing the same content as VRT 1. Ketnet, the channel for youngsters, will only be showing pre-scheduled programmes.
No scheduled programmes will be broadcast on the radio. The radio stations will only be playing music. There is a news bulletin every hour but there is no regional news.
Visual banners and audio messages will be shown regularly on television and radio. In this way, the trade unions are making it clear that a strike is underway.
Other sectors
The strike may also affect household waste collection, which could be disrupted in many towns and municipalities.
For example, Net Brussel is urging residents not to put out their bin bags today. Waste collection may also be disrupted in Ghent, amongst other places.
The strike may also cause disruption in prisons and detention centres, as well as at postal services provider Bpost.

US Marines to deploy missile systems on Japan island near Taiwan for first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:17:45 UTC
17:17:45 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The US Marine Corps plans to deploy anti-ship and air-defense systems to Japan’s Yonaguni Island, about 110 kilometers from Taiwan, for the first time during a military exercise later this month.
In an article published Saturday by The National Interest, defense analyst Harrison Kass described the planned deployment as part of a “significant transformation in Marine Corps strategy.” The shift emphasizes small, mobile missile units across the Pacific rather than traditional amphibious assault operations.
The deployment is planned for the biennial Keen Sword exercise, scheduled for Oct. 19–29, involving Japan’s Self-Defense Forces and the US military. The Marine Corps plans to bring its Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS) and Marine Air Defense Integrated System (MADIS) to Yonaguni.
Yonaguni is Japan’s westernmost inhabited island, near maritime routes connecting the East China Sea and the Pacific. In a Taiwan Strait conflict, “the waters near Yonaguni would become one of the most crucial operating areas in the world,” Kass said, adding that anti-ship missiles could “complicate” Chinese naval movements.
Japan established radar and surveillance facilities on Yonaguni in 2016 as regional security concerns grew, per Defense News. During Chinese military exercises around Taiwan in August 2022, a Chinese ballistic missile landed in waters about 80 kilometers from the island.
NMESIS combines an unmanned ground vehicle with a launcher capable of carrying two Naval Strike Missiles, Kass said. The sea-skimming cruise missiles have a publicly reported range of about 185 kilometers, potentially putting waters off northeastern Taiwan within reach from Yonaguni.
MADIS provides short-range air defense using vehicle-mounted sensors and weapons to counter drones, helicopters, and low-flying aircraft. While NMESIS provides anti-ship firepower, MADIS is designed to protect deployed Marines and missile units from aerial threats.
The systems are part of the Marine Corps’ Force Design modernization initiative, which shifts away from some traditional heavy equipment, such as tanks, toward mobile expeditionary units, precision missiles, drones, and reconnaissance capabilities in contested coastal areas.
Japan is also expanding its missile defenses in the southwestern island chain. Japanese Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro said in February that Japan plans to deploy a Type 03 surface-to-air missile unit on Yonaguni by 2030.
The Type 03 system has a reported range of about 50 kilometers and can track up to 100 targets simultaneously while engaging as many as 12, per UDN. Koizumi described the planned deployment as a measure to strengthen Japan’s southwestern island defenses.
During this year’s Keen Sword exercise, Japan’s Ground Self-Defense Force is expected to train with its Type 25 anti-ship missile system, which has a reported range of 1,000 kilometers, UDN reported. It will also use the Type 88 anti-ship missile system, which has a range of about 180 kilometers.

The new protests, scheduled for Oct 13, could be a turning point in the movement, launched in mid-September, which the government hopes is already winding down.
On Oct 9, the government noted a dramatic drop in the number of blockades and meetings outside the country’s lycees, where students – most between 15 and 18 – complete their high school education.

For President Emmanuel Macron’s administration, that brings back troubling memories of the grassroots Yellow Vest movement.

They do not want to see the students’ action disrupt such a crucial stage of their education.
The Oct 8 student demonstrations mobilised tens of thousands of people across France: 71,500 according to interior ministry figures.

She holds no official position at Kfar Saba City Hall, but investigators suspect Meital Saar, wife of Mayor Rafi Saar, played a central role in an alleged corruption network that steered municipal contracts to businesspeople in exchange for cash bribes. Police sources described her as a "dominant figure" who "had a hand in everything," alleging that businesspeople seeking lucrative city projects approached her directly and paid her bundles of cash.
The allegations emerged Monday as police arrested 17 suspects, including the mayor and his wife, in a sweeping municipal tender-rigging investigation. Rafi Saar has since temporarily suspended himself from office, while employees at City Hall struggle to absorb the revelations. Some remain convinced the mayor will emerge from the investigation unscathed, but police sources have painted a different picture of his wife's influence over municipal affairs.
"He is an elected official, she holds no public office, but she had a hand in everything," sources in the National Fraud Investigations Unit said, describing Meital Saar's alleged involvement in helping businesspeople secure major tenders, from renovations of educational institutions to cleaning services and the placement of food trucks.
One source described the suspected corruption in particularly stark terms. "This was a city that was sold, nothing less than that," he said, adding that there had long been widespread talk suggesting the mayor's wife "held the key to running the city."
Investigators from Lahav 433 remained inside Kfar Saba City Hall on Monday, examining computers and seizing documents in an effort to substantiate the allegations. "It's a complete shock. We never imagined there was anything criminal going on inside this building," one municipal employee told ynet. "I believe he'll get through this easily because he's an honest man."
Some employees who arrived at the municipal building in the city center early Monday morning were surprised to find police investigators already at work.
The investigation is continuing at both City Hall and the municipal economic development company, with detectives collecting documents and examining computer records.
"There are quite a few police officers inside," another municipal employee said. "They're not asking many questions. They're mainly collecting documents and checking computers." During searches at the mayor's home, investigators also found luxury watches and handbags.
Déjà vu at City Hall: ‘Unfortunately, we know the protocol’
For some municipal employees, the investigation has revived uncomfortable memories. Kfar Saba's previous mayor, Yehuda Ben Hamo, was convicted in a corruption case and sentenced to 24 months in prison in April 2022.
"We're all relatively calm here," one employee said. "Unfortunately, most of us were here the last time something like this happened, so we know the protocol."
This time, however, the municipal economic development company is also implicated in the investigation. Employees describe it as an entity operating separately from the municipality. Its CEO, attorney Sagi Chen, was among those arrested on suspicion of offenses involving public corruption, bribery, fraud and breach of trust, money laundering and tax violations.
At the center of the case are Rafi and Meital Saar, who investigators suspect worked together to promote the interests of businesspeople and associates, including individuals with alleged criminal connections, in exchange for cash bribes.
Police conducted searches at approximately 30 locations as the investigation became public. The undercover operation began about a year and a half ago, following dozens of intelligence reports raising suspicions of widespread corruption within the municipality.
According to information collected by investigators, the couple allegedly worked to direct municipal tenders, properties and projects to associates, businesspeople and individuals with financial interests, some of whom are known to police for criminal activity.
In return, investigators suspect Meital Saar received bundles of cash from those individuals, with whom she maintained direct contact.
How the mayor's wife allegedly steered municipal tenders
According to investigators, the suspected scheme revolved around Meital Saar's contacts with businesspeople seeking municipal contracts. Those interested in securing projects allegedly approached the mayor's wife, established quid pro quo arrangements and relied on her assistance to win tenders.
Police suspect that, to conceal preferential treatment of certain businesspeople and the alleged manipulation of tenders, municipal projects were transferred from City Hall to the economic development company.
Investigators believe the couple coordinated with the company's CEO, who allegedly knew in advance which bidder was supposed to win each tender brought before him.
Sources familiar with the investigation said that, in some cases, obstacles were allegedly placed in the way of competing bidders until they were forced to withdraw. The projects were then allegedly awarded to businesspeople whose connections with the couple were suspected of benefiting them.
The allegations cover almost every area of municipal operations, including school renovations, food trucks, the opening of businesses, leisure and entertainment complexes, sports projects, transportation, traffic lights, street lighting and cleaning services.
Another central aspect of the investigation concerns the couple's lifestyle and their allegedly extensive use of cash.
According to National Fraud Investigations Unit sources, Rafi and Meital Saar maintained a lavish lifestyle, paying numerous expenses in cash, including overseas travel, jewelry, clothing and handbags.
"We're not investigating a technical violation involving the use of cash. If that were the issue, we would find a great many offenses of that kind," investigators explained, emphasizing that the transactions were being examined as part of the suspected bribery scheme.
During the police raids, including searches of municipal offices, investigators discovered large quantities of cash, packaged and concealed in locations where detectives had anticipated finding it.
Expensive jewelry, luxury watches and evidence of overseas flights and shopping trips were also found in the couple's possession. During their most recent return to Israel, customs officials at Ben Gurion Airport discovered 20,000 shekels in cash in Meital Saar's possession, and she was questioned at the scene.
The couple also drove expensive, recently purchased vehicles.
A separate line of investigation concerns suspected connections between the mayor, his wife and criminal figures operating in the Sharon region. According to intelligence obtained by police, individuals known to Central District police for criminal activity allegedly assisted Saar during the local election campaign.
Investigators suspect those individuals pressured political candidates running against Saar in an effort to influence the election. Police are examining the nature of the relationships between the alleged criminal figures and the couple, as well as suspicions that those same individuals subsequently exerted pressure on the mayor and his wife.

IMF chief alarmed at ‘slow-moving tsunami’ of AI for jobs

- She said AI is already cutting demand for routine human work, hurting young job seekers, and may widen inequality as gains stay with a narrow group.
- Georgieva also warned AI could weaken tax revenues, but said it may lift growth by up to one percentage point in advanced Asian economies, which could offset ageing costs.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned of the disruptive threat from artificial intelligence to the labour market and taxation, urging policymakers to rethink education and act now to help society adapt.
“It is a slow-moving tsunami, but tsunami nonetheless,” managing director Kristalina Georgieva said on Oct 12 during her first appearance at the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok.
Speaking at a session on AI’s impact on employment, she said the technology is already hollowing out demand for many human workers by taking over routine, repetitive tasks. At the same time, it is increasing low-paying jobs in sectors like construction, which she said is “not a story to celebrate”.
It is a transformation with far-reaching consequences for public finances, Georgieva said.
The risk is that AI strains government revenues by tilting the economy towards capital and away from labour – traditionally the main source of tax income.
The comments are the latest warning about the potential shock from AI on jobs and the global economy.
Young workers in AI-exposed fields have already seen a slowdown in hiring, leaving new entry-level applicants far more vulnerable. Concern is also growing that the technology will widen inequality, with its gains so far concentrated among a narrow set of workers and economies despite a global investment supercycle.
“We cannot today imagine what exactly the world of work will be five years from now,” she said. “But we can be disciplined and carefully assess what is happening, and then draw lessons, but – most importantly – act on them now.”
Despite the employment headwinds, the technology can ultimately prove a positive for growth overall. The IMF estimates the spread of AI can add up to a percentage point to growth in advanced Asian economies.
Such a growth boost “is a very big deal”, Georgieva said, adding that it will “more than offset” the drag from ageing in rich countries across the region. BLOOMBERG

- Russia says brown bear numbers have more than doubled to 308,000 in 30 years. Officials are drawing up urgent measures after at least 22 deaths since spring.
- Residents say they live in fear as bears enter homes, parks and gardens. They want the animals controlled, but worry hungry bears may stay active even in winter.
AI generated
PODTESOVO, Russia – A brown bear bounds across the Siberian taiga before two hunters close in on their prey. Three shots ring out and the bear quickly drops dead in the long grass.
Cradling his rifle as he rests his hand on the dead animal’s fur, hunter Mikhail Kondakov says he and others have heeded requests from residents in the nearby settlement of Podtesovo after a fatal bear attack on local women.
“The bear situation in the settlement is very difficult at the moment,” Kondakov told Reuters.
“Bears have increasingly been coming directly into the settlement. This year we had a tragedy – two women who went mushroom picking were killed by a man-eating bear. We decided to start hunting bears because there are so many of them.”
Bear population has spiralled out of control
The problem is nationwide. The Russian government said in September it was drawing up urgent measures to control the population of brown bears that has spiralled out of control in some regions, with at least 22 people killed in attacks since this spring, according to state media.
The population of brown bears has more than doubled in the last three decades to 308,000 according to government data, in part due to shorter and milder winters.
Experts cited in Russian media have said bears have been forced to look further afield for food in 2026 because an early and dry spring meant there was a lack of berries for them to feed on.
People have also been blamed for leaving food waste out in the open where it attracts bears and for ignoring safety rules.
In Krasnoyarsk, the Siberian region where Kondakov is hunting and which is home to nearly 27,000 bears, investigators said in September that they had opened a criminal case into the local environment ministry, accusing it of failing to keep bear numbers under control, negligence which they said had led to the deaths of seven people in that month alone.
In Podtesovo, a settlement of around 3,500 people perched on the right bank of the River Yenisei, a simple wooden cross stands on the grave of Zoya Gubanova along with a colour photograph of the late pensioner.
Gubanova, 67, was killed on Aug 31 in a bear attack while out gathering mushrooms, a popular Russian pastime.
Chatting outside her wooden house, Yulia Markova, a local resident, says the situation has become intolerable.
“We have been living in fear for almost two months now, we cannot even go out for a walk in the evening. People are afraid to let their children go out alone. This is not a cuddly toy, it is not some soft, harmless teddy bear. It is a wild animal. And who knows what its intentions are, what kind of mood it is in when it comes here. Maybe it is simply curious, or maybe it is looking for its next victim,” she said.
Markova said that locals, like bear attack victim Gubanova, had not fully understood the danger posed by bears and that people had initially felt sorry for them because they clearly did not have enough nuts and berries to eat in 2026.
But she said hearts had hardened after the bears started coming into the settlement in large numbers.
“We have never seen an invasion like this before,” said Markova.
Bears coming into parks where children play
Watching her daughter relax at the local playground, pregnant mother Valeriya Efremova said heightened bear activity had changed locals’ lives.
“When the bears started coming out of the forest, we restricted outings as much as possible, even to the park. It was really frightening because bears were even coming into the park where children play. Going out after dark was absolutely out of the question. Even now, although the number of sightings seems to have fallen, at least according to the information we have, you still walk around looking over your shoulder,” she said.
Nikolai Zhilinsky, another local, said people were waiting for the weather to get colder and for the bears to hibernate, but he said people would still be worried even when that happened.
“We are not sure that all of the bears will hibernate. There are too many of them and they are hungry,” he said. He was afraid to go fishing in his boat in case he was attacked by a bear, he added.
Vladimir Vagin, another local, said people feared they could be attacked in their own gardens. He pointed to an area near a raspberry bush in his own garden where he believed a bear had been.
Driving through the settlement after dark, he noted how empty the streets were.
“People don’t go out because they are afraid,” he said. REUTERS

A quarter-century ago, an advertising campaign presented the two-wheeler as a symbol of “Naye Bharat ki Nayi Tasveer”. But is the India of 2026 still commuting mainly on two-wheelers, has it moved to cars, or are more people walking? The answer depends a great deal on which states people live in, whether they are in a village or a city, and on their gender. All three, in varying degrees, shape how people get around and how much they pay for it.Among some of the extremes featured in India’s National Household Travel Survey, in Puducherry, 92.7% of workers use a two-wheeler as their primary mode. In Nagaland, more than seven in ten walk. West Bengal has the highest published bicycle share, Ladakh stands out for buses, and Sikkim for cars. Conducted from July 2025 to June 2026, the survey covered 4,92,023 households and 18,44,179 people aged six and above.At the national level, the old two-wheeler image still rings true, though the averages hide big regional differences. Among workers who travel at least 1km to work, 42.6% mainly use a two-wheeler, 28.3% walk and 10.7% cycle. The average one-way trip to a fixed workplace takes 25 minutes, and travel costs about ₹785 a month per worker.
India on the move
Rural-urban divide
Between India and Bharat, the numbers shift substantially. In rural India, workers are split almost evenly between two-wheelers at 37.1% and walking at 36.6%.
In cities, the balance tips firmly towards the engine, presumably because of longer distances. Two-wheelers rise to 52.3% and walking falls to 13.5%. Autos, buses and cars all carry a bigger share too.The metro and local-train story is overwhelmingly urban. The survey’s Train/Monorail/Tram category, which includes metro rail and suburban or local trains, carries 5% of urban workers but just 0.4% of rural ones. In urban Maharashtra, home to Mumbai’s suburban railway, the share is 20.7%. It is 16.5% in urban West Bengal and 14.4% in Delhi, known for its metro network.The survey reports Rail separately. That category accounts for just 0.2% of workers nationally, 0.2% in rural India and 0.3% in urban India.
Two Indias, Two Ways to Travel
Students take the bus, workers take the bike
Students and workers commute very differently. In villages, 40.5% of students walk and 18.9% cycle. In cities, buses at 33.7% and autos at 14.4% play a bigger role. Nationally, 37% of students walk, 29.5% take a bus and 15.8% cycle, while only 6.7% use a two-wheeler. Among workers, buses account for just 6.7%, exactly the share two-wheelers have among students.The contrast is sharpest in Kerala, where buses carry 72% of students but 24.9% of workers. Age changes the picture too. Students aged 15 to 29 walk far less than those aged 6 to 14, 22.2% against 47.3%, and cycle more, 21.4% against 11.9%.
Men ride, women walk
Among workers, 47.1% of men use a two-wheeler to get to work. Among women, it is 18.4%. About half of female workers, 50.6%, walk, against 24.1% of men. Women are also much more likely to take the bus, 14% against 5.3%.It would be easy to put this down to rural India, where more people walk. But the divide holds in cities too. There, 57% of male workers use two-wheelers, against 25.8% of women, while women are twice as likely as men to walk, 24% against 11.6%. The bicycle divide is even starker in relative terms. Among workers, 12.3% of men cycle to work but only 1.7% of women do.
The Gender Divide in India’s Commute
Yet among students, the sexes are much closer. Some 17.7% of male students cycle, against 13.4% of female students. Odisha makes the contrast particularly striking. Female students there cycle almost as often as male students, 32.8% against 34%. Among workers, though, the Odisha gap opens up. Some 25.5% of men cycle to work, against 5.8% of women.
Short commutes, steeper city bills
Most work commutes are under half an hour. Some 83.4% of workers travelling to a fixed workplace get there within 30 minutes. Students do even better, with 87.6% reaching school or college within half an hour.However, travelling in cities is much costlier. The average urban trip to work takes 27 minutes, just four more than in villages, but costs ₹1,044 a month against ₹612, about 71% more. Urban students pay about 71% more too, even though their average trip is a shade shorter, 22 minutes against 23 in villages.Even within cities, there are stark differences. Workers in urban West Bengal and urban Delhi spend about the same time getting to work, 36 and 35 minutes on average. But the urban West Bengal worker spends about ₹825 a month, while the urban Delhi worker spends about ₹2,081, roughly two and a half times as much.Urban West Bengal also has a much bigger long-commute tail. Some 13% need over an hour to commute, against 4.1% across urban India. Hence, lower monthly spending there does not necessarily mean a quicker journey.
City Travel Comes at a Price
The work clock
Across India, 56.5% leave for work between 8am and 10am. In Mizoram and Ladakh, some 97.1% and 95.1% of commuters leave between 8am and 10am.Evenings vary even more. Across India, 31.1% leave work at 6pm or later. In Tamil Nadu it is nearly half, 48.9%, with Gujarat at 45.2% and Delhi at 44.6%. Men are more than twice as likely as women to be leaving that late, 34.1% against 16%.Take work and study out of the picture and far fewer people step out at all. On a given day, 18.7% of people aged six and above travelled at least 1km for some other reason, 23.8% of males and 13.3% of females.They also get there differently. Among men making such trips, 40.1% use a two-wheeler, against 17.6% of women. Among women, 30.4% take an auto or e-rickshaw, against 12.7% of men. For women, autos and e-rickshaws play much the same role that two-wheelers do for men.
For long trips, the bus still rules
In the 28 travel days before the survey, 11.3% of households made an overnight trip of 50km or more that kept a member away from home for more than 24 hours. More than half of these households, 55.8%, used the bus as their primary mode.The separately reported Rail category comes next at 17.7%. Cars account for 15.1% and two-wheelers 8.8%. Another 3.3% fall under Train/Monorail/Tram. Just 0.6% travelled by air.
Few of these trips were about work. Some 70.2% of households making overnight trips travelled for socialising, communication or religious purposes.How far are people travelling? The answer is not provided in the details released so far. The survey collected trip distances, as well as information on licences, household vehicles and bus or rail passes, but none of these appears in the released estimate tables.A quarter-century after the “Naya Bharat” pitch, the two-wheeler still leads the national picture. But the survey shows how much that picture hides, and the big missing piece is how far India travels. At a time when there is demand for metros in every Tier 2 city and road and rail connectivity is better than ever, the full data, when released, will help policymakers make more informed decisions about how to prioritise India’s transport needs.

HMS Dragon went from dry dock to deployment in a week
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:00:18 BST
17:00:18 KST

A Type 45 destroyer sent from maintenance to the eastern Mediterranean in seven days has returned to Portsmouth after 214 days away, having shielded the British bases in Cyprus from drone and missile attack, according to the Royal Navy.
HMS Dragon was in dry dock when she was activated as part of the British response to the conflict in the Middle East, which had brought the sovereign base areas on Cyprus under attack. Working alongside Army and Royal Air Force capabilities, the destroyer formed part of the shield against air attack over the island.
General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord and Chief of Naval Staff, said: “HMS Dragon’s seven-month deployment has shown the Royal Navy at its best.
“Deployed at short notice, her crew have protected our bases on the island of Cyprus, safeguarded shipping and worked closely with our allies across the Mediterranean and Middle East. They have operated in some of the world’s most dangerous waters with skill and professionalism. Every member of Dragon’s crew should return home proud. And to the families who supported them throughout, thank you for the sacrifices you have made.”
The ship was later sent east of Suez to provide air defence for a proposed international mission to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, sailing through the Bab el Mandeb Strait at the foot of the Red Sea, where Houthi forces in Yemen have been firing missiles and drones at shipping since 2023. Dragon also ran maritime security patrols in the Indian Ocean and spent a period attached to the French carrier strike group led by FS Charles de Gaulle.
Around 950 friends and family met the ship at Portsmouth Naval Base and along the harbour walls.
Vice Admiral Steve Moorhouse, the Fleet Commander, said: “The resilience, professionalism and fighting spirit of Dragon’s ship’s company throughout the last seven months have been outstanding. In an increasingly uncertain world, we need a warfighting ready Navy that can respond at pace wherever the nation requires. Dragon has shown exactly what that looks like. To the friends, families and loved ones who have supported the ship’s company throughout this challenging deployment, thank you, your contribution has underpinned Dragon’s success.”
Dragon is the third of six Type 45 destroyers, all based at Portsmouth, and the class is the fleet’s first line of defence against aircraft, missiles and drones.

Berlin shopkeeper attacked after displaying posters against antisemitism for Oct. 7 anniversary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:58:51 UTC
16:58:51 KST

A 67-year-old shopkeeper who uses a wheelchair was repeatedly attacked by groups of youths in Berlin's Kreuzberg district after displaying posters opposing antisemitism to mark the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre, Berlin police said on Saturday.
The shopkeeper, Hans-Georg Lindenau, called police to his store on Falckensteinstrasse on Friday evening and reported a series of attacks that began on Wednesday, October 7, according to a police statement.
At approximately 7:20 p.m. on Wednesday, a group of about six youths entered the store, verbally abused Lindenau, and sprayed him with pepper spray.
On Thursday, at around 7 p.m., a group of up to six youths returned to the store and again sprayed him with pepper spray. Lindenau cried out for help, prompting the youths to flee.
However, the suspects returned shortly afterward as Lindenau was preparing to close the shop. According to police, they again sprayed him with pepper spray and beat him. Following the assault, Lindenau complained of pain in his face.
The harassment continued on Friday. Several eyewitnesses told police they saw a group of up to eight youths arrive at the store on electric scooters, punch and kick the entrance door, and then flee. The door was damaged in the incident.
Lindenau runs M99, a store selling literature, posters, and accessories associated with left-wing protest movements.
Speaking to the German newspaper Bild, Lindenau estimated that the attackers were between 10 and 15 years old and said they had asked him whether he was Jewish. He also said that during one of the attacks, the assailants struck him with a starter pistol.
Berlin police said the investigation had been transferred to the State Security Division of the city's criminal police, which is examining a possible antisemitic motive. No arrests were reported.
Over 2,000 antisemitic offenses recorded in Berlin in 2025
The attacks come amid a wave of antisemitism in Berlin since the October 7, 2023, Hamas massacre.
According to Berlin police figures, 2,268 antisemitic offenses were recorded in the city in 2025, an increase of 24.3% compared with the previous year and more than six times the number recorded in 2022.
RIAS, an organization that monitors antisemitic incidents, documented 2,197 incidents in Berlin in 2025, an average of approximately six per day.
Although that represented a decline from the 2,521 incidents recorded in 2024, the figure remained significantly higher than in the years preceding the war.
Last week, ahead of the third anniversary of the massacre, RIAS warned that antisemitism remained widespread in Berlin in 2026.
The organization said Jewish residents were avoiding certain locations and reducing their presence in public spaces because of concerns for their personal safety.

Gaza BoP expects progress after elections, rejects 'Telegraph' conflict-of-interest claims -report

07:58:42 UTC
16:58:42 KST

The Gazan Board of Peace expects the "very substantial groundwork" laid for the establishment of post-war governance and reconstruction in the Gaza Strip to transition into full-scale execution after the US midterms, according to a Saturday report by The Telegraph.
Little progress was expected to be made prior to the October 27 Israeli elections and the subsequent midterm elections in the US in early November, the Telegraph reported citing "well-placed" sources.
“It’s not like we’re not moving. There is movement. There’s a lot going on, but maybe nothing that can be seen from the outside as ‘major movement’ before the elections,” a source was quoted as saying.
The report, which was published as an investigation into alleged conflicts of interest within the organization, said that "extensive planning" and "detailed groundwork" have been established over the past six months in preparation for the rebuilding of Gaza.
Board officials insist political obstacles remain the main challenge
The Telegraph report identified overlapping financial interests involving several senior figures in the initiative, including Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, US special envoy Steve Witkoff, and billionaire financier Marc Rowan, raising questions about the relationship between their private business activities and their roles in shaping Gaza's future.
At the center of the investigation is Affinity Partners, the private equity firm founded by Kushner, which has attracted billions of dollars in investments from Gulf sovereign wealth funds, including those associated with Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the UAE.
According to The Telegraph, Phoenix was the largest institutional shareholder in Smart Shooter, an Israeli defense technology company that recently secured a US military contract worth up to $150 million.
The company manufactures artificial intelligence-assisted rifle sights and other weapons systems, including remotely operated gun platforms and armed drones. Its technology has been used by the IDF during operations in the Gaza Strip.
Despite the concerns raised by the investigation, officials involved in the Board of Peace rejected suggestions that financial interests were influencing its decisions.
Concerns over conflicts of interest were “bull----”, one of the sources told The Telegraph. “We literally have never had a single discussion at any point about business interests.”
Two people familiar with the board's operations told The Telegraph that the principal obstacles to implementing the Gaza plan were political rather than economic.
They said substantial preparations had been completed for a new Palestinian administration, an international stabilization force, and the establishment of a Palestinian police force.
The Telegraph investigation comes as the implementation of Trump's Gaza peace plan remains stalled, despite the ceasefire agreement that entered into effect on October 10, 2025.
Although the initial agreement facilitated the release of the remaining Israeli hostages, Hamas's disarmament, the establishment of new security arrangements, and major reconstruction efforts remain unresolved.
The Board of Peace's implementation roadmap calls for the transfer of Gaza's civilian governance to a Palestinian technocratic administration, alongside security arrangements intended to prevent armed groups from retaining control of the enclave.
A source within the board recently insisted that the organization was continuing to advance its plans, despite limited visible progress ahead of the Israeli election.
Kushner also marked the first anniversary of Trump's peace initiative on Friday, highlighting achievements including the return of the hostages while acknowledging the challenges remaining in Hamas's disarmament.
The latest investigation adds a further issue for the board to address as it attempts to translate months of diplomatic planning into concrete changes on the ground.
While its members maintain that private financial interests have not influenced their diplomatic work, questions surrounding their investments could complicate efforts to establish public confidence in the international body tasked with overseeing Gaza's reconstruction.
Board of Peace: Telegraph publishes 'sensationalization' with little substance
The Board of Peace responded to The Telegraph report. In a statement posted by the organization on X/Twitter, it said the investigation is manufacturing conflict while failing "to identify a single Board of Peace contract, procurement decision, or diplomatic action influenced by the commercial interests it describes. There’s a whole lot of insinuation and very little substance conveniently wrapped into a sensationalized headline."
The statement also pushed back on the report's account of Kushner's private equity firm, Affinity.
"Affinity owns a minority stake in Phoenix, one of Israel's largest publicly traded, highly regulated financial institutions, managing approximately $220 billion across thousands of investments. Through its managed portfolios, Phoenix held shares in a small defense company that later won a *U.S. government* contract, not a Board of Peace contract...There was no Board of Peace involvement, no Board of Peace decision, and zero demonstrated personal benefit."
The Board of Peace statement went on to defend its progress in Gaza.
"Hamas has accepted a disarmament plan, the International Stabilization Force and Gaza’s transitional administration are preparing to deploy, and initial police recruits have been selected. Of course, significant challenges remain, and there is hard work ahead of us, but a year ago none of this architecture existed," the statements read. "These accomplishments would have made for a worthwhile story given the enormous positive consequences for the region."
The statement concluded by saying the bottom line is that the Board of Peace is committed solely to peace. It argued that too many people have become invested in perpetuating conflict - not just terrorists - but also members of an "international architecture" that they claim is invested in continuing a cycle of violence.

The U.S. embassy in Riyadh said on Monday that American citizens had been detained for filming recent events in Saudi Arabia, which has suffered a string of deadly attacks by Yemen's Houthis.

Iran rejects that route and demands that all vessels use a northern passage close to its own coastline, seeking permission from its military.
The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center, which monitors incidents in the region, had not reported any attacks on vessels Monday, but it noted at least two projectiles hitting vessels Sunday.
U.S., U.K., Australia, Canada and others condemn Iranian attacks, including "hybrid activities," after air base incident
The foreign ministers of the U.S., the U.K., Australia, Canada and 23 other countries, many in Europe, have released a joint statement condemning hostile activities by Iran on foreign soil.
The statement came on the heels of British Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying a recent security incident at England's RAF Fairford air base, which was until recently home to U.S. long-range bombers, was "almost certainly directed" by Iran's Revolutionary Guard.
The countries said Monday that they "condemn in the strongest terms Iran's use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners."
Linking the RAF Fairford incident to other recent attacks in Europe "targeting Jewish communities, Iranian journalists, and U.S. interests," the countries said: "Any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable."
"Anyone who conducts hostile activities on behalf of Iran, or any other state, should know that we will take action to identify, investigate, disrupt, and prosecute these acts."
U.K. prime minister says RAF Fairford air base plot "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran"
The security incident at a British base used by American bombers to strike Iran during the ongoing war was "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran" by the regime's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday.
British police have arrested and then released on bail seven men in connection with the alleged plot. The decision to free the men, whom British police say remain under investigation and monitoring, drew criticism from President Trump, who said in September the incident "might be" linked to Iran.

"We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," he added. "We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams."
Burnham said new sanctions against Iran would be announced.
Saudi Arabia vows response after deadly Houthi attacks on airports

Lethal airport strikes have rocked the world's top oil exporter since last week, which is pursuing an expensive economic reform drive aimed at attracting foreign investment.
Yemen's decade-old civil war, in which a Saudi-led military coalition supports the government against the Houthis, has reignited months into the U.S.-Iran conflict that has roiled energy markets and plunged the Middle East into crisis.
"Energy security can't be taken for granted," Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told an energy conference in Riyadh. "The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious."
Operations remained suspended at the sprawling King Khalid International Airport on Riyadh's outskirts Monday after the weekend's deadly Houthi strikes.
CCTV video of the deadliest strike, which killed 13 people on Saturday, released by Saudi authorities showed Muslim pilgrims in religious attire waiting in departure lounges before a sudden flash tore through the building and brought down flaming debris.
CBS/AFP

Turkish auto production shrinks 6 percent in January-September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:44:28 UTC
16:44:28 KST

Türkiye’s automotive production declined in the first nine months of 2026, while the domestic market also contracted, according to data released by the Automotive Manufacturers Association (OSD).
Total vehicle production fell 5.9 percent year-on-year in the January-September period to 971,159 units, while passenger car output dropped 17 percent to 528,366 units.
During the same period, the overall automotive market shrank 13 percent from a year earlier to 832,521 units. The passenger car market contracted 15.5 percent to 627,977 units.
Imported vehicles continued to dominate the passenger car market, accounting for 65 percent of sales in the first nine months of the year.
However, sales of imported passenger cars fell 23 percent year-on-year, while sales of domestically produced passenger cars increased 2 percent. Imported light commercial vehicle sales declined 9 percent, whereas domestic light commercial vehicle sales rose 11 percent, said OSD.
Despite weaker production and domestic sales, automotive exports increased in value terms. Total automotive exports rose 3 percent year-on-year to $30.5 billion in the January-September period.
Passenger car exports, however, declined 8 percent to $7.8 billion during the same period.
In September alone, total vehicle production increased 5.1 percent year-on-year to 129,571 units, while passenger car production decreased 3.8 percent to 70,197 units.

China Focus: Ancient southern China canal finds new life as living heritage
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:39:01 CST
16:39:01 KST

NANNING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- On free mornings, Ai Chenggang gets on his bicycle and rides along the Lingqu Canal, checking for rubbish tangled on the banks and watching out for children playing too close to the water.
Ai, in his 70s, has spent his life in Xing'an County in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, where the canal has flowed past homes and fields for more than two millennia.
"This canal is what home means to us," he said.
The waterway Ai tends, quiet and enduring, is drawing crowds of visitors from far and wide this week.
Canal experts and enthusiasts from around the world are gathering in the city of Guilin in Guangxi for the World Canals Conference, which opened on Monday. The Lingqu Canal, about 60 kilometers from downtown Guilin, is a centerpiece of the event.
The conference has brought together representatives from canal cities, research institutions and waterway organizations in more than 20 countries. It is the third time the event has been held in China and the first in Guangxi. Discussions focus on how to preserve historic waterways while maintaining their value for local communities along the banks.
AN ANCIENT LINK
Ai's work as a canal guardian follows a family tradition. He is a descendant of the doujun, canal keepers who once patrolled the banks, repaired embankments and operated water gates to keep boats moving safely.
This role faded when roads and railways replaced the canal as a transport route, and Ai now serves with a volunteer group protecting the waterway.
The 37-kilometer Lingqu Canal was built on the orders of Emperor Qinshihuang of the Qin Dynasty (221 B.C.-207 B.C.), connecting the Xiangjiang and Lijiang rivers and, through them, the Yangtze and Pearl river systems.
Originally built to transport supplies for Qin armies campaigning in Lingnan, it later became a vital trade route linking China's interior with the southern region.
Along with Dujiangyan and the Zhengguo Canal, Lingqu is regarded as one of ancient China's three major hydraulic projects.
No cargo ships travel its waters today, but the canal still irrigates farmland, aids flood control and feeds the Lijiang River flowing through Guilin's famous karst landscape. Locals walk and rest under old trees on its banks, while farmers continue to work nearby fields.
Chen Xinghua, a former deputy director of the Xing'an county museum, has studied Lingqu for decades.
Figurines depicting foreigners, dating to the Han Dynasty (202 B.C.-220 A.D.), have been unearthed near the canal, offering evidence of early cultural exchanges between China's interior and the outside world, he said.
"Lingqu was an important part of the ancient Maritime Silk Road," Chen noted. "Protecting it helps us better understand the past and draw lessons for the present."
In 2018, Lingqu was listed as a World Heritage Irrigation Structure, the first in Guangxi to receive this designation.
KEEPING IT ALIVE
Protecting a canal involves more than restoring old stonework.
Authorities have banned quarrying along the waterway, improved sewage treatment and cleared waste, while regional and local regulations provide legal protection for the site.
Further efforts will focus on preserving the canal's original structures, expanding archaeological research, and using digital technology to make its history more accessible to the public, according to Wu Xiaogang, spokesperson of the Guilin municipal government.
Tourism has grown alongside these efforts.
The 12,000-square-meter Lingqu Museum houses more than 10,000 cultural relics. An immersive theater, meanwhile, takes visitors on a simulated boat ride through different periods of the canal's history, with warships from the Qin Dynasty, passenger boats from the Tang Dynasty (618-907), and merchant vessels from the Ming and Qing dynasties (1368-1911) appearing on a 360-degree screen.
The Lingqu scenic area received more than 1 million tourist visits in 2025, including over 10,000 visits by participants in educational tours, boosting business for local restaurants, hotels and transport operators.
For local residents, protecting the Lingqu Canal and preserving its cultural heritage have become part of everyday life.
Zeng Jinglan, 69, grew up beside the canal. A finger painter whose works have been exhibited around the world, she returned to Xing'an three years ago and opened a studio nearby.
"I grew up drinking water from the canal," she said. "In summer, my friends and I ran along its banks, listened to stories about it and watched my father paint by the water."
Today, the canal's scenery, plants and wildlife inspire her paintings. She hopes her art will help keep its cultural heritage alive for future generations.
More than 2,000 years after Lingqu was built, another canal has opened in Guangxi. The 134.2-kilometer Pinglu Canal, which began operating in September this year, gives southwestern China a shorter waterway route to the sea.
Experts said the two canals underscore the enduring role of waterways in connecting regions, facilitating trade and driving China's development.
Ai still gets on his bicycle and follows the canal his ancestors once guarded. The cargo boats have disappeared. Generations of canal keepers have come and gone. But the water is still flowing.
"As long as the canal is here, our home has a root," Ai said. ■
