9th China Now Music Festival concludes in New York
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:38:56 CST
16:38:56 KST

Artists perform the symphonic oratorio Men of Iron and the Golden Spike during the ninth China Now Music Festival at Lincoln Center in New York, the United States, Oct. 11, 2026. The ninth China Now Music Festival concluded Sunday at Lincoln Center in New York City with a concert showcasing the resilience and aspirations that connect the American and Chinese peoples. (Photo by Zack Zhang/Xinhua)
NEW YORK, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The ninth China Now Music Festival concluded Sunday at Lincoln Center in New York City with a concert showcasing the resilience and aspirations that connect the American and Chinese peoples.
The symphonic oratorio Men of Iron and the Golden Spike returned to the New York stage after its premiere at the 2019 China Now Music Festival.
Featuring a large orchestra as well as 120 choristers and vocal soloists, the work honors thousands of Chinese laborers who helped build the United States' first transcontinental railroad in the 1860s.
"In this divisive moment in our country, I hope this piece reminds audiences that the United States has always been shaped by diverse ethnic communities, and that the stories of Chinese laborers deserve their rightful place in our shared history," said Zhou Long, Pulitzer-winning composer of the oratorio.
The closing concert also featured the premiere of symphonic suite Chasing the Sky, composed by Chinese composer Li Shaosheng.
The piece blends traditional Chinese instrument suona with a symphony orchestra, reflecting humanity's shared dream of reaching beyond the horizon.
"Symphony, rooted in the West, has continued to evolve, with styles constantly changing. Many outstanding works have emerged from Eastern countries," Li said. "I hope to see more and more Chinese symphonic works performed on stages in the United States."
The festival, which opened on Oct. 2, was co-hosted by the U.S.-China Music Institute of Bard College Conservatory of Music and the Central Conservatory of Music of China.
The annual event, created in 2018, is dedicated to promoting the understanding and appreciation of music from contemporary China through concerts and academic programs. ■

====================================================================================================

World Insights: Deadly Riyadh airport attack heightens security concerns, risks wider conflict
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:38:33 CST
16:38:33 KST

ADEN, Yemen, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- A deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh's main international airport has heightened the risk of regional escalation, putting pressure on Saudi Arabia to respond and raising the prospect of deeper involvement by outside powers.
Saturday's attack on a passenger terminal at King Khalid International Airport killed 12 people and injured 309 others, according to Saudi authorities. The Saudi-led coalition vowed a firm response, while U.S. President Donald Trump said Washington "may" join Saudi Arabia in striking the Houthis.
As the confrontation widens, analysts interviewed by Xinhua said the airport attacks are intended to shift the costs of war from Yemen's battlefields onto Saudi Arabia itself. Yet, they warned that a strategy designed to strengthen Houthi leverage could instead harden Riyadh's position, encourage deeper regional involvement and make the escalating conflict increasingly difficult to contain.
PRESSURE BEYOND BATTLEFIELD
"Targeting Riyadh's airport is about more than military damage. It's about undermining confidence, disrupting economic activity, and pressuring Riyadh to reconsider its involvement," Hisham Al-Omeisy, conflict analyst and senior Yemen advisor with the European Institute of Peace, told Xinhua.
He described the approach as "asymmetric warfare": unable to compete conventionally with Saudi Arabia, the Houthis can move pressure beyond Yemen's frontlines and threaten sensitive infrastructure deep inside the kingdom.
Jarrah Mutlaq Al-Qazaa, media adviser at the Kuwait Journalists Association, likewise viewed the airport attacks as part of a broader effort by the Houthis to shift the costs of the conflict onto Saudi Arabia, while emphasizing the wider implications of targeting such a prominent civilian facility.
"The objective goes beyond military retaliation," Al-Qazaa told Xinhua. "It is about raising the costs for Saudi Arabia in terms of national security, economic activity and international image."
He perceived an international airport as not merely a transport hub, but also a symbol of a country's connectivity, security and international standing. The repercussions of an attack, he said, could therefore extend beyond physical damage to flight disruptions, higher aviation insurance costs and broader perceptions of security in the kingdom.
Abdul-Ghani Al-Iryani, a senior researcher at the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies, told Xinhua that the pressure also serves a broader political objective. He said the Houthis are "seeking to pressure Saudi Arabia to return to a previously negotiated road map" that he described as favorable to the group at the expense of Yemen's internationally recognized government.
Yet, the analysts warned that the same strategy intended to build Houthi leverage could backfire after Saturday's civilian casualties. Al-Qazaa said that mounting civilian casualties could narrow rather than expand Riyadh's room for compromise.
"The higher the civilian toll, the more difficult it becomes for Saudi Arabia to make concessions amid domestic and international political pressure," he said.
Echoing those concerns, Yemeni political analyst Khalil Muthanna al-Omari told Xinhua that attacks on airports "raise the stakes considerably," potentially inviting stronger Saudi retaliation and broader international coordination against the group.
"With each escalation, the room for stepping back becomes narrower," al-Omari said.
DEFENSE CHALLENGE
The strikes have simultaneously exposed a second dimension of the confrontation: the difficulty of completely shielding Saudi Arabia's vast territory from increasingly diverse Houthi missile and drone threats, analysts said.
Ali Bin Hadi, an Aden-based military observer, told Xinhua that "repeated penetrations suggest potential gaps" in the defensive shield, arguing that "years of warfare have given the Houthis time to study Saudi defenses and adapt their methods."
Saudi Arabia's geography compounds the challenge, Bin Hadi said, with airports, cities and oil installations dispersed across a vast area while drones and low-flying cruise missiles can stretch expensive defensive systems.
The mounting pressure on Saudi defenses has also brought the potential roles of Pakistan and Türkiye, Saudi Arabia's security partners under the Mecca Agreement, into sharper focus, raising questions over how far they could become involved should the confrontation widen, according to analysts.
Al-Iryani said the precise scope of commitments under the Mecca Agreement remains unclear, and Bin Hadi cautioned that stronger defenses alone would not resolve the underlying conflict.
The same uncertainty surrounds Washington. Trump's suggestion that the United States could join Saudi strikes has raised the possibility of direct U.S. involvement, but the analysts differed over how readily Washington might cross that threshold.
Bin Hadi sees "little appetite in Washington for another confrontation with the Houthis" after previously seeking to disengage from that front. "Washington may help contain the fire, but it is unlikely to step into it," he said.
Al-Qazaa, however, said continued escalation could alter that calculation. He said the likelihood of direct U.S. military involvement would depend largely on whether Houthi attacks continue to cause heavy casualties, the extent to which Riyadh seeks U.S. participation, and whether Washington sees scope for limited strikes capable of restoring deterrence without drawing it into a prolonged war.
ROAD TO TALKS
Despite the intensifying confrontation, analysts broadly agreed that the path to diplomacy remains open, though they differed over what a viable political settlement would need to achieve.
Bin Hadi said Saudi Arabia "now faces a difficult choice" between a broader military confrontation with potentially heavy costs and renewed efforts at de-escalation, while years of aerial warfare have made the Houthis increasingly resilient to airstrikes.
"A prolonged state of neither full war nor genuine truce will continue to exhaust all sides," he said. "That equation is unlikely to remain sustainable."
Al-Omeisy went further, arguing that even a successful Saudi-Houthi accommodation would address only "one layer of the crisis." He said a viable settlement requires credible security guarantees, a more unified Yemeni government, and a political process that addresses the fundamental question of state authority.
"This is a Yemeni conflict, not simply a Saudi-Houthi dispute," Al-Omeisy said. "Ending Saudi-Houthi hostilities without addressing Yemen's underlying conflict would merely postpone the next war."
The Riyadh attack has therefore sharpened two intertwined questions: whether escalating pressure can produce deterrence without triggering a wider confrontation, and whether any eventual de-escalation can move beyond a Saudi-Houthi understanding toward resolving Yemen's underlying conflict.
As attacks increasingly cross national borders while fighting intensifies inside Yemen, the answers may determine not only the trajectory of the renewed war, but also how far its consequences spread across the Gulf and the wider region. ■

Nearly 1 bln people projected to have osteoarthritis by 2050: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:38:25 CST
16:38:25 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Nearly one billion people worldwide are projected to be living with osteoarthritis by 2050, up from about 600 million in 2023, according to a new roadmap released on Monday.
There remains no cure and no drug that can stop or slow the disease, prompting researchers to call for stronger health policies to address the growing global disability burden, according to a statement released Monday by Australia's Curtin University.
The global health policy roadmap published in The Lancet on World Arthritis Day by a Curtin University-led group of international researchers said osteoarthritis remained under-recognized in health policies globally and was often inadequately integrated into healthcare delivery for chronic diseases, and inconsistently and often inappropriately treated and prevented.
The roadmap calls on governments to recognize osteoarthritis as a major chronic disease, improve access to evidence-based care, invest in prevention by addressing excess body weight and joint injuries, and integrate osteoarthritis care with broader chronic disease and rehabilitation services.
"Osteoarthritis faces an image problem -- it's perceived and dismissed in communities as an unavoidable part of aging with limited management options," said the report's lead author Professor Andrew Briggs from Curtin University.
Professor Lyn March, a co-senior author from Australia's Kolling Institute, said the global disability burden attributed to osteoarthritis increased by 65 percent between 1990 and 2023.
Rising obesity rates, population aging and increasing joint injuries are expected to drive further growth in cases in coming decades, the researchers warned. ■

Brake-pedal failures in luxury EV put Chinese cars’ quality in regulatory spotlight

A safety failure spotted in tests of a Chinese electric vehicle (EV) made by a Huawei Technologies-backed luxury brand has raised doubts about the cars many consumers view as a source of national pride, and prompted regulators to step up policing of quality and reliability.

====================================================================================================

Houthis hit Riyadh airport again day after strike killing dozen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

Yemen's Houthi rebels on Sunday night carried out a fresh strike on a passenger terminal at Riyadh's international airport, the Saudi-led coalition said, one day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people.
Saudi authorities said one person, described as a Pakistani national, was killed, and 11 were injured in the latest attack on the domestic terminal complex at King Khalid International Airport.
The airport – struck four times in the past five days – has been closed since Saturday’s missile attack, which was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began. Over 300 other people were wounded, some critically.
The sharp escalation in the war's new front threatens to draw in greater U.S. military involvement. President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the Houthis. There was no White House comment Sunday.
India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died Sunday of injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, which would bring the toll to 13. Saudi authorities later said King Fahd International Airport in Dammam also was attacked, with few details. The city is on the Persian Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.
The latest strike in Riyadh came shortly after the Houthis said the airport in the rebel-held Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again, and blamed the Saudis.
On Sunday night the Houthi-run al-Masirah TV channel reported further strikes on Sanaa, blaming Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia has not commented on the strikes.
At stake, again, in this escalation are global supplies and prices of oil as well as commercial shipping through a crucial alternative waterway to the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz – along with civilians and aviation throughout the region.
There was no sign Sunday that Trump had followed up on plans to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who has been seeking assistance against the war-hardened rebel group that is currently Iran's most dynamic proxy.
A U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen, further restricting the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month.
The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces with Yemen's internationally recognized government, has been trying to seize them back.
The rebels' strikes against Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and military facilities highlight a problem. The kingdom is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the Iran war.
Some airlines have suspended flights serving Saudi airports and some embassies have cautioned citizens about the risks of using them, after multiple Houthi warnings about the rebels' use of Saudi airspace.
Sunday’s attack occurred as the Saudis hosted a major international energy conference in Riyadh, with other high-profile events including an investment gathering on the horizon.
Saudi Arabia under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has sought to open more to the world as a business and tourism destination, but the Houthi attacks threaten those efforts.
"There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix, we come out of the ashes all the time," the Saudi energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, told the conference.
He added that the kingdom is also working on pipelines in addition to the East-West one that was attacked and closed for days last month, with no details.
Earlier Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa.
The ministry also claimed 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks, 60% of them women and children.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims, as fighting in Yemen surges after a major military offensive was launched against the Houthis a week ago.
Inside Saudi Arabia, identities emerged for some of those killed in Saturday's attack in Riyadh, including an Egyptian flight attendant and a Syrian widow living in the kingdom.
The government has previously said the dead also include four Saudi citizens, as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, one Palestinian, one American, one Jordanian and one Sudanese national.
Early Monday, Saudi Arabia released videos of the moment of the strike captured by security cameras. They show people, many dressed in the white robes of Mecca-bound pilgrims, standing in line in a busy hall, while others scroll phones in a nearby seating area before a fireball erupts, following by people throwing themselves to the floor and running for safety.
The Houthis until recently had been largely on the Iran war’s sidelines. They have developed their military capabilities in recent years to become one of Tehran’s most powerful allies. Now they're pressuring its regional rival and a key U.S. ally.
Late Sunday, Saudi Arabia and Iran said their foreign ministers had spoken by phone. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he warned against insisting on a military approach and ignoring a political solution and said Tehran was ready to help start a dialogue between the Saudis and the Houthis.
The Saudis and Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen’s civil war on behalf of the government. Relative calm after a 2022 cease-fire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land.
The attack revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas. The rebels declared a blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Now the Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse Houthi territorial gains.
But the rebels' pressure tactics could backfire, said Ahmed Nagi, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Yemen: "Rather than pushing Riyadh to step back, attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure could make the Saudis more determined to continue the campaign."

Earlier Sunday, three Palestinians were killed and several others injured Sunday in an Israeli drone strike on a tent in southern Gaza.
A medical source at Nasser Hospital said the bodies of three Palestinians and several wounded people were brought to the facility after the strike near the hospital in the southern al-Buraq area of central Khan Younis.
Witnesses told Anadolu Agency (AA) that an Israeli drone fired at least one missile at the tent, which was being used as a mobile phone charging point.
Also Sunday, a medical source at al-Shifa Hospital said Jihad Iyad al-Ghandour, 6, died of serious wounds sustained Saturday when Israeli soldiers opened fire in the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza.
Separately, Israeli forces expanded the area under their control in eastern Gaza City early Sunday, injuring two Palestinians, including a pregnant woman and forcing dozens of families to flee their homes, according to local Palestinian sources.
The sources told AA that Israeli military vehicles advanced tens of meters beyond their existing positions in the Shujaiya neighborhood overnight from Saturday into Sunday, under cover of heavy gunfire and artillery shelling.
They said the troops were accompanied by armed Palestinian militias cooperating with and supported by the Israeli army, while quadcopter drones provided cover.
Israeli forces fired heavily toward the area stretching from the vegetable market in the east to the Shujaiya intersection on Salah al-Din Street in the west, the sources added.
For about a week, eastern areas of Gaza, particularly the eastern parts of the Tuffah and Shujaiya neighborhoods, have witnessed nighttime demolitions, gunfire, heavy artillery shelling and military vehicle movements near the "yellow line," according to the sources.
The line separates areas occupied by Israeli forces in the east from areas where Palestinians are permitted to remain in the west.
Israeli cease-fire violations have killed 1,488 Palestinians and injured 5,281 as of Sunday, according to the latest figures from Gaza's Health Ministry.
Since the war began in October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured, while around 90% of Gaza's infrastructure has been destroyed, according to the ministry.

The Cultural Life of Colors in Latin American Interiors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

A color has a biography. A color can have an origin, but it can also transform. It can move between materials and disciplines, from a local practice into architecture, from something ordinary into something symbolic. It can lose one association and acquire another, or persist without anyone consciously thinking of it as cultural. Its life unfolds through the conditions in which it is produced, used, repeated, and inhabited. As these conditions change, so do the meanings a color can carry.
The interior is a place where these histories converge. A color inside a room can carry traces of a territory, a material practice, a climate or a history of inhabitation. Its presence does not necessarily depend on an intention to represent any of these things.
Color can become part of a place through the continuity of materials and ways of living, acquiring significance beyond the surface on which it appears.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Two Coast Guard Administration (CGA) vessels reached the southernmost point ever visited by the agency during a two-day joint patrol of Palau’s exclusive economic zone.
The Chiayi and Penghu reached waters off Pulo Anna Island on Saturday afternoon. The island lies 217 nautical miles (402 kilometers) southwest of Koror State, according to a press release.
The mission follows last year’s first “Friendship Fleet,” when the CGA sent the Hualien and Taipei to Palau.
The vessels departed Malakal Port on Friday after a flag-raising ceremony marking Taiwan’s National Day was held aboard the Chiayi, Liberty Times reported.
Palauan maritime security official Lieutenant Jim Kloulechad thanked the CGA for patrolling Palau’s waters as the Penghu passed Pulo Anna.
He said only five people lived on the island and that it was good to check on their health and safety.
CGA Fleet Branch Director-General Huang Hsuan-kai (黃宣凱) said Taiwan and Palau have deepened maritime cooperation through joint patrols, maritime search-and-rescue exercises, and personnel exchanges since signing a bilateral agreement in 2019, per NOWnews.
He said the joint patrol not only helped safeguard Palau’s waters but also strengthened both sides’ maritime law enforcement and emergency-response capabilities.

Taiwan to boost vocational education
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:22:34 UTC
16:22:34 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) said Monday that the government will increase support for vocational education to help young people develop skills needed by industry.
Speaking at a meeting with Taiwan’s delegation to the 48th WorldSkills Competition, Lai said skilled workers are essential to economic growth. He pledged to strengthen cooperation among schools, training systems, and businesses to better prepare students for employment.
CNA reported that Taiwan sent 53 competitors to the WorldSkills Competition, which ended in Shanghai on Sept. 27. The team competed in 47 categories and won three gold, three silver, and seven bronze medals, along with 30 medallions for excellence, placing third among 68 teams.
Lai praised the competitors and thanked their coaches and support teams. He said skilled workers are just as important as technological advances in keeping domestic industries competitive.
With global supply chains changing and artificial intelligence reshaping industries, Lai said workers need practical skills, creativity, and knowledge across different fields. He stressed that vocational education must adapt to help students meet future job demands.
The government has allocated NT$16 billion (US$505 million) to the second phase of its youth employment program, which runs from 2023 through this year. Lai said the program had helped more than 800,000 young people find jobs as of August, with another phase being planned.
The government is also expanding overseas training opportunities for young people. The labor ministry plans to send young skilled workers to Japan this year, with similar exchanges planned for Germany and Australia.
Lai said these exchanges would allow participants to learn new skills and bring valuable experience back to Taiwan. He also encouraged the WorldSkills competitors to share their knowledge and help improve professional standards.
He said their achievements went beyond winning medals, as international competition had strengthened their confidence and problem-solving abilities. Lai urged them to continue developing their skills and contribute to the country’s industrial growth.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) said Monday that he hoped more F-16V Block 70 fighters would arrive in Taiwan before the end of October.
Koo said he expected more aircraft to pass acceptance inspections this month. The defense ministry will work with the US project office to expedite the delivery of aircraft that have completed flight testing, he said during a legislative hearing, per Liberty Times.
The minister said 63 aircraft were currently on the production line. Of the six aircraft furthest along in the delivery process, two have arrived in Taiwan, two are at a US base for training, and two remain under testing.

Koo added that Viper Shield must be integrated with the new fighters’ onboard systems and that integration testing must be completed within a specified period after delivery.
Under the Phoenix Rising program, US defense contractor Lockheed Martin and Taiwan’s Aerospace Industrial Development Corp. upgraded 140 F-16A/B fighters to the F-16V Block 20 configuration, Liberty Times said. The upgrades were completed in December 2023.
Under the separate Peace Phoenix Soaring program, the Air Force is spending NT$247.23 billion (US$7.75 billion) to procure 66 new F-16V Block 70 fighters.

Report: Saudi crown prince shuttles between bunker-equipped palaces as Houthi missiles hit Riyadh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:18:45 UTC
16:18:45 KST

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is moving between heavily guarded palaces equipped with bunkers, protected by a handpicked security team, as escalating Houthi missile attacks disrupt daily life in Riyadh and threaten the kingdom's economic stability, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing officials familiar with his movements.
The 41-year-old crown prince has sharply tightened his security as the Saudi capital increasingly comes under fire from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants. His last public appearance was Tuesday, when he donated blood as part of a national campaign, according to the report.
On Saturday, at least one Houthi missile struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, killing at least 12 people and injuring hundreds, many seriously. Two terminals sustained extensive damage, with sections of their roofs collapsing. Among the victims was a 28-year-old Egyptian flight attendant who bled to death after losing an arm, according to officials briefed on the attack.
Video verified by Storyful showed passengers evacuating the airport with their suitcases, passing a trail of blood on the floor. The attacks continued Sunday, when another projectile reportedly struck the closed airport, igniting a fire in Terminal 4 and causing further injuries.
The escalating strikes have transformed parts of Riyadh into a conflict zone. Residents have been forced to seek shelter as explosions echo across the capital. Workers in the city's financial district, students at several international schools and diplomats have been instructed to evacuate buildings or take cover.
On Thursday, debris from an intercepted ballistic missile struck a kindergarten and a medical clinic complex, highlighting the danger to civilian areas even when incoming missiles are successfully intercepted.
Saudi officials have warned that the kingdom is running low on missile interceptors, according to the Journal. With large areas to defend and attacks targeting multiple locations, Saudi Arabia has been moving air-defense batteries between strategic sites, including royal palaces and vital energy infrastructure.
The growing threat comes as Mohammed bin Salman faces mounting pressure over his ambitious economic transformation program. For years, the crown prince has sought to turn Saudi Arabia into a global destination for tourism, investment and technology, investing enormous sums in futuristic developments such as Neom and major new projects in Riyadh.
Those ambitions are now being threatened by the deteriorating security situation. Houthi attacks have targeted airports, refineries and the East-West oil pipeline, which allows Saudi Arabia to export oil through the Red Sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
The militants have also threatened Red Sea shipping, undermining another vital economic lifeline.
According to the Journal, a major international investment conference scheduled for late October is increasingly in doubt as the attacks threaten international travel and investor confidence.
The economic outlook was already deteriorating. Foreign investment declined during the first half of the year, several flagship megaprojects have stalled or come under review, and the Saudi Finance Ministry now expects the economy to contract by 3.6% in 2026.
Mohammed bin Salman is also facing difficult military decisions. Although Washington has provided military advisers, the United States has so far resisted Saudi requests for direct assistance in reversing Houthi territorial gains in Yemen, the Journal reported.
President Donald Trump said over the weekend that Washington was communicating with the Houthis but could join Saudi strikes against the group. "What they did was very bad," he said following the airport attack.
Saudi Arabia has also sought assistance from Pakistan and is searching internationally for additional air-defense systems, while exploring possible diplomatic solutions to contain the confrontation.
For the crown prince, the crisis now threatens both the security of his capital and the economic transformation on which he has staked much of his leadership. With missiles reaching Riyadh, civilian infrastructure under attack and his own movements taking place between fortified palaces, Saudi Arabia faces a growing challenge to its efforts to present itself as a safe destination for international business and investment.

florim channels venice’s textures and visual memory into tactile terrazzo surfaces

Unknown Publisher

16:00:40 KST

florim channels venice’s textures and visual memory into tactile terrazzo surfaces
florim introduces sensivenezia, a tactile porcelain stoneware collection that reinterprets classic venetian terrazzo for contemporary architecture.
FLORIM AND MATTEO THUN & PARTNERS EXPAND THE SENSI NARRATIVE
Florim captures the atmosphere of the Venetian lagoon in SensiVenezia, a tactile porcelain stoneware collection. Designed by Matteo Thun and Benedetto Fasciana, the series translates the city’s textures and visual memory into surfaces defined by material depth, channeling Carlo Scarpa’s compositional sensitivity references across twelve nuanced tones. Building on the sensory lineage of Sensi and SensiTerre, the collection reinterprets traditional Venetian terrazzo for modern spatial design, bringing historic craftsmanship into contemporary architecture through large-format slabs.
SENSIVENEZIA WEAVES MATERIAL culture AND SPATIAL PERCEPTION
Marking a new chapter in the ongoing partnership between the brand and architects Matteo Thun and Benedetto Fasciana, SensiVenezia explores the relationship between material, color, and space. Rooted in Italy’s landscapes and material culture, the collaboration pairs technical precision with regional heritage to translate Venetian craftsmanship into refined ceramic surfaces. Across the entire Sensi ecosystem, sensory experience serves as the foundational principle, blending memory, craft, and technology into a unified architectural language.
CHROMATIC PORTRAIT OF VENICE CRAFTED FOR CONTEMPORARY SPACES
The SensiVenezia collection features a palette of twelve distinct colors named after iconic Venetian sites, including Arsenale, Fenice, Rialto, and Giudecca. Drawing from the city’s architecture, canals, and surrounding lagoon, these earthy tones are offered in two distinct surface finishes: a uniform matte that creates visual continuity, and a soft finish that enhances tactile depth with subtle marble and glass highlights.
Designed for residential, hospitality, and commercial spaces, the porcelain stoneware collection comes in 9 mm and 20 mm thicknesses, with modular sizes and large-format slabs up to 120×120 cm. These large formats minimize joint lines to create continuous, enveloping surfaces that highlight the graphic rhythm of Venetian terrazzo. Completing the range is Scacchiera, a 30×30 cm mesh-mounted decorative element whose geometric layout forms a textile-like pattern. Underneath, a porphyry-effect body incorporates fine, medium, and large aggregates with subtle opalescent points that catch the light, adding material depth echoing time-worn stone.

name: SensiVenezia
company: Florim | florim_ceramiche
designers: Matteo Thun | @matteothun and Benedetto Fasciana | @benedettofasciana

Ministry of Defence scraps Type 31 support competition
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:00:27 BST
16:00:27 KST

The competition to provide through-life support for the Royal Navy’s Type 31 frigates has been discontinued after the department concluded that the assumptions behind it no longer held, according to answers given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what plans the Secretary of State had to replace the abandoned requirement, and separately in what way the assumptions underpinning it no longer held. Both questions referred to the corrigendum to tender 707770451, entitled Type 31 Through Life Support, published on 22 July.
Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said:
“The Type 31 Through Life Support procurement was discontinued following a review of the proposed approach. The Department concluded that the assumptions underpinning that procurement no longer reflected the most appropriate route for delivering support to the Type 31 class. Those assumptions included the delivery context for the programme and the way in which future support arrangements should be structured. The requirement to provide effective through-life support for the Type 31 fleet remains unchanged.
“The Department is now considering the most appropriate arrangements to meet that requirement. Any future procurement activity will be taken forward in accordance with Defence requirements, value for money considerations and established commercial procedures.”
A third question from Mr Obese-Jecty turned to the programme’s budget, asking when the minister planned to reset the Approved Budgetary Limit to mitigate the impact of inflation, with reference to the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority Major Projects Annual Report for 2025 to 2026.
Mr Pollard said: “The Ministry of Defence keeps the affordability of all major programmes under continual review. In common with other enterprises, the Type 31 programme is experiencing inflationary pressures, and the impact of possible costs is being assessed. Any changes to programme budgets and approvals will be considered through the Department’s established governance processes. It would therefore be inappropriate to speculate on the timing of any future decisions.”
The answers give no indication of what the revised support model might look like. Type 31 covers five Inspiration class frigates under construction by Babcock at Rosyth.

On the import side, the kingdom primarily brought in garment raw materials, construction supplies, vehicles, oil and gas, electronic goods, fertilizers, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, supplements, fruits, and food items.
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, said the double-digit growth reflected Cambodia's deepening regional economic integration and successful trade diversification.

Sri Lanka financial system remains stable despite global risks: central bank
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:43:45 CST
15:43:45 KST

COLOMBO, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka's financial system remains stable despite heightened global risks, while banking sector credit grew 23.6 percent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, up from 11.4 percent a year earlier amid strong private sector demand, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka said on Monday.
In its Financial Stability Review 2026, the central bank said the financial system remained stable during the first half of the year, supported by continued economic recovery, improved fiscal performance and adequate capital and liquidity buffers across banks and finance companies.
However, the bank warned that rapid credit growth, particularly household lending including vehicle financing and gold-backed lending, was creating potential systemic vulnerabilities. Rising household indebtedness, higher real estate prices and volatility in collateral values were also identified as emerging risks.
Household credit grew 25.4 percent year-on-year in the second quarter, compared with 14.8 percent a year earlier. Banks remained the main source of household financing, accounting for 62.5 percent of such credit.
Credit extended by finance companies expanded 45 percent year-on-year in the second quarter, driven largely by vehicle and gold-backed lending, compared with growth of 35.1 percent in the same period of 2025.
The central bank said geopolitical tensions, elevated energy and commodity prices, tighter global financial conditions and climate-related risks could spill over into the domestic economy through trade, tourism, remittances, capital flows and exchange rate movements.
The outlook for financial stability remains broadly positive, provided the economic recovery continues, fiscal consolidation progresses and prudent policies are maintained, the central bank said. ■

====================================================================================================

Letter from Mideast: Still waiting for peace near Gaza
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:43:44 CST
15:43:44 KST

This photo taken from an area near Israel's southern border on Oct. 6, 2026 shows Israeli military vehicles moving inside the Gaza Strip. (Photo by Gil Cohen Magen/Xinhua)
by Xinhua writer Wang Zhuolun
JERUSALEM, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- From a hill on the outskirts of Sderot, the Israeli city closest to the Gaza Strip, the devastation across the border is clearly visible. Shattered buildings form a jagged skyline just a few kilometers away, yet they seem worlds apart.
Three years ago, on Oct. 7, 2023, a Hamas-led attack on southern Israel triggered a new round of bloody conflict in Gaza. Militants entered Sderot and stormed the local police station, where fighting raged through the night. Israeli forces eventually demolished the building as they retook it.
I still remember crouching amid the ruins as I covered the war's early days: fighter jets roared overhead, fear emptied the streets, and acrid smoke hung in the air. Not far away, each Israeli strike on Gaza sent another plume into the sky.
Back then, no one knew how long the war would last, much less how its repercussions would spread across borders and engulf much of the Middle East.
Three years on, I returned. The ruins are gone. A memorial square now stands where the police station once stood, with newly planted greenery and paved walkways. Visitors stop to look around. Sderot is gradually reclaiming a sense of normalcy.
It took less than three years to turn ruins into a square. But how long will it take to turn war into peace?
In the West Bank city of Bethlehem, Ali Mansour told me he had been out of work since the war began. Before the conflict, he traveled daily to work in Israeli-controlled areas. Afterward, Israel sharply restricted work permits for Palestinian workers, leaving him without a job.
What he has been waiting for, Mansour said, is not just a job, but the chance to regain the dignity of an ordinary working life.
In Jerusalem's Old City, Palestinian souvenir seller Rami Hamdan has felt the war's toll in another way. In once-bustling shops, merchants now sit idle, waiting for customers who rarely come.
"I stopped watching the news long ago. I don't even want to know what's happening anymore," he said. "I just want to shut myself off from this world of endless war."
Perhaps this is war's most enduring consequence. An explosion has a time, a place, and a casualty count. It becomes a headline, then a photograph. But long after the smoke clears, war persists in less visible ways: in families mourning loved ones, workers waiting for jobs that never return, children growing up under air raid sirens, and ordinary people facing each day with uncertainty.
Over the past three years, the fighting has widened into a regional conflict.
It spread from Gaza to the Israel-Lebanon border and the Red Sea before escalating into large-scale direct military confrontations involving Israel, the United States, and Iran. Rockets, missiles, and drones repeatedly crossed Middle Eastern skies.
Over these three years, I have written "escalation" and "ceasefire takes effect" more times than I can remember. Again and again, just as a war seemed to be nearing its end, another round of fighting began.
The expanding battle fronts kept testing what I thought I understood about war. As a frontline correspondent, I have learned that the worst never stays the worst for long, and what looks like an ending can turn out to be the prelude to something worse.
Before leaving Sderot, I met Shalom Levi, a local resident. Now 60, he has lived his whole life near the Gaza border.
In Hebrew, "shalom" is both a greeting and the word for "peace." Levi told me his parents chose the name to express their hope for peace.
Behind him stood the memorial square built on the ruins of the police station. Beyond it lay Gaza, still scarred by war.
New monuments have risen from rubble. New grass has taken root in scorched earth.
But a man named "Peace" is still waiting for his name to become more than a promise. ■
A pedestrian walks past a memorial site for the latest round of Gaza conflict in Tel Aviv, Israel, Oct. 6, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Junqing)
Jewish people look toward the nearby Gaza Strip in Sderot, southern Israel, Oct. 6, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Zhuolun)

WASHINGTON, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- U.S. President Donald Trump announced an immediate "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday, drawing surprise from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said it was "news" to him.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, adding that "both parties have agreed."
The declaration came just two days after Trump unveiled a diesel supply deal with Russia.
However, Zelensky told U.S. news outlet Axios that Trump's announcement "was news for me."
"But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine will agree," Zelensky said.
On Saturday, Trump said Russia was willing to reach a deal to end the conflict in Ukraine, but accused Zelensky of resisting a negotiated settlement. He also called for Ukraine to hold an election and choose a new leader who could make a deal with Moscow.
Zelensky responded that he would call a vote if Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to a 60-day ceasefire, and that it was "up to Ukrainians" to choose their leader. Presidential elections, originally due in 2024, have been postponed under martial law.
"Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections," Zelensky told ABC News.
The Kremlin said Friday that Ukrainian drone attacks during Russia's parliamentary elections had effectively derailed prospects for an immediate resumption of peace talks.
The dispute over the ceasefire comes as rising energy prices have become a growing political concern for Trump ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
On Friday, Trump announced a deal with Putin under which Russia would supply diesel fuel to the United States and global markets. Trump described it as a necessary step to bring down soaring diesel prices, which he attributed largely to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
Zelensky rejected the suggestion that he was responsible for rising energy prices, saying that "everybody in the world" knew that the war in the Middle East was a bigger factor.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Sunday that the diesel deal "is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe."
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Sunday backed Trump's call "for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now," describing it as "the best route to get energy and fuel back into world markets."
French President Emmanuel Macron said Sunday that France supports a "real energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine.
"Currently, Russia continues to refuse that, by lately intensifying further its strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure," Macron said. "France will continue to stay by the side of Ukraine and President Zelensky."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen fully supported Zelensky's call for a ceasefire protecting global food supplies and energy infrastructure, according to her post on X on Sunday.

====================================================================================================

She vanished on a trip around the world. Did she end up a castaway in Australia's backyard?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:29:32 UTC
15:29:32 KST

in brief
- A new expedition is seeking to discover what happened to famous aviator Amelia Earhart.
- An object spotted on a Pacific island could be the remains of her plane.
A team of researchers is headed to a remote island they hope holds the secret to the disappearance of Amelia Earhart, an aviation pioneer whose feats made her one of the most famous figures in the early history of flight.
The researchers' primary target is the site of an unidentified object, first spotted in 2020 next to a lagoon off Kiribati's Nikumaroro island in the Pacific Ocean, located roughly halfway between Australia and Hawaii.
Nearly a century after Earhart's disappearance, a joint expedition between Purdue University, its research foundation, and the not-for-profit Archaeological Legacy Institute hopes to find out whether the object is the fuselage and tail of her plane.
After completing their final leg travelling by boat from Kiribati's capital to the atoll in the country's Phoenix Islands, the 17-person team will spend the following days searching the sandy landmass, stretching approximately 7.5km by 2.5km.
"There's something significant to flying over the Pacific Ocean," expedition member Sirisha Bandla said.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"As we finally arrived at our point of departure here in Tarawa, it struck home that we'd flown over a majority of the portion that Amelia Earhart and Fred Noonan were attempting to traverse when they were lost.
"Now we hope to have a chance to bring closure to their story."
The flight that ended in mystery
Born in 1897, Earhart was forever changed by a 10-minute plane trip she took at the age of 23.
"By the time I had got two or three hundred feet off the ground, I knew I had to fly," she later recalled.
She later became the first person to cross the Atlantic twice by air, having made the first crossing as a passenger in 1928 and the second alone in 1932 — the first woman to complete a solo flight across that ocean.
In the same year, she became the first woman to make a nonstop solo flight across the United States and in 1935 she became the first person to fly solo and nonstop from Hawaii to the US mainland.
She also broke multiple speed and altitude records in the decade preceding those journeys.
Despite having been awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross — a US decoration for heroism or extraordinary achievements in aerial flight — Earhart still had her sights on a new record: a flight around the world at the equator.
Between creating her own clothing line and helping to establish a support network for the advancement of female aviators, Earhart started working at Purdue University in 1935, where she eventually purchased a Lockheed Electra 10E.
The aircraft was nicknamed the "Flying Laboratory" for its developed technological communication and navigation systems.
However, in 1937, the plane would become the vessel of her final voyage.
Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan were last seen taking off from Lae, New Guinea, heading to Howland Island, an unincorporated territory of the US.
Radio operators on a US Coast Guard vessel received messages from the plane that it was running low on fuel and was struggling to locate the island.
After communication was lost and the pair failed to land, the US government began its largest-ever search for a missing aircraft. The 16-day mission, however, found no trace of the pair or the plane.
Several searches have been completed since.
The castaway theory
There are multiple conflicting theories about Earhart and Noonan's disappearance.
The US government's position is that, with limited radio communication and facing strong headwinds and cloud cover, Earhart and Noonan ran out of fuel before reaching their destination, crash-landing somewhere in the Pacific Ocean.
Another suggests the pair was running out of fuel but were able to land on Nikumaroro and lived out the rest of their lives as castaways on the remote coral island.
Human remains found on the atoll in 1940 have been the subject of ongoing academic debate.
While the original bones have been lost, measurements recorded by the doctor who examined them have been used by some to argue that they could be those of Earhart.
The clues left behind
The Taraia Object, a focus of investigations, has been visible on satellite imagery since 1938, the year after the pair went missing, according to Purdue University.
Remnants of a cosmetic jar of anti-freckle cream, as well as aeroplane-related materials and parts of a shoe, have also been found on Nikumaroro.
The researchers plan to heavily document the site, then complete a series of scans before any potential excavation work.
"We will start our remote sensing work using magnetometers and sonar to get a better idea of what is there before we actually uncover it. After that is all done, we will uncover it using a hydraulic dredge," expedition leader Rick Pettigrew said.
The team has visited a replica of the plane to study its parts and rivet patterns, to assist in identifying any potential wreckage.
They are scheduled to return to Kiribati's capital before the end of the month.
If the Taraia Object is the missing plane, the team hope for a full excavation next year, should they receive permission from the Kiribati government.
The mystery that refuses to die
Millions of dollars have been spent on several projects to search for the missing plane, despite none resulting in irrefutable evidence.
Competing Earhart explorer Ric Gillespie told news agency Reuters he believes the plane has been swept by tides into the sea, ultimately splitting apart and sinking.
Gillespie founded The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery. It's completed at least five expeditions to Nikumaroro over the last fifteen years.
He says the Taraia Object is more likely a fallen tree that has been swept into the lagoon.
"You can see the root ball. You can see the branches. It's a tree. People see what they want to see," he said.
The lack of definitive physical evidence has fostered a variety of speculations for what really happened to Earhart, ranging from being captured by the Japanese military to being returned to the US under an alias.

EU countries view the G7 agreement as the completion of March commitments rather than an additional release. The IEA said on Oct. 7 that about 100 million barrels pledged under the March agreement had yet to reach the market.

German labour minister quits Merz's fragile coalition
BERLIN, Oct 12 - Germany's labour minister and co-head of the centre-left SPD party resigned from both posts on Monday, citing the death of her stepdaughter and political attacks against her, adding to strain in Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition government.
"After my stepdaughter's death, I realised that I need time to come to terms with my grief," Baerbel Bas said in a statement, without giving further details.
Bas, whose ministry oversees large parts of Germany's welfare system, also said she had faced increasing "public attacks", including from members of the CDU/CSU conservative bloc, the SPD's coalition partners.
Bas had come under fire from lower ranks of the conservative party bloc over delays to a pension overhaul.
"The attacks against her during the past days of her mourning were inappropriate. That is unacceptable," said Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, the SPD's other co-leader, who cancelled a planned trip to India.
Merz's conservatives are seeking pro-business labour market deregulation to revive the economy amid a surge in energy prices and tough rivalry from China, while the SPD is pushing to preserve workers' rights and benefits.
STRUGGLING COALITION
Bas's exit adds pressure on the coalition, which trails the far-right AfD in opinion polls. It was shaken by major gains for both the far right and far left in regional elections last month.
Support for Merz will be further tested in five more regional elections next year that will impact his ability to get major legislation through the Bundesrat, a house of parliament filled by Germany's 16 states.
Nationwide elections are scheduled for 2029.
The SPD said that Alexander Schweitzer, the former state premier of Rhineland-Palatinate and one of the party's deputy leaders, would take over as labour minister.
Schweitzer lost his regional leadership role to a CDU rival after state elections in March. Under the coalition pact, the SPD does not need to consult with its CDU/CSU partners on who leads ministries that the party has been assigned.
The coalition partners have been working on changes to the nation's pay-as-you-go retirement system to address Germany's ageing society, a key element of a broader economic and social reform programme.
The labour market reform bill is under an initial review by the chancellor's staff.
Merz, whose party will wrap up a two-day strategy meeting in Berlin on Monday, struck a conciliatory tone on X, saying Bas's decision deserved respect and thanking her for her commitment.
It remained unclear who would succeed Bas as the SPD's co-leader or if Klingbeil would fill the role on his own. Bas said she would retain her seat in parliament. REUTERS

Scientists discover a hidden factor that can make or break chemical reactions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:24:46 UTC
15:24:46 KST

Scientists discover a hidden factor that can make or break chemical reactions
Scientists uncovered a hidden chemical variable and used it to boost reaction selectivity from 16% to 97%, potentially transforming how everyday materials are manufactured.
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- Seoul National University College of Engineering
- Summary:
- Researchers discovered a hidden factor that can determine whether chemical reactions succeed or fail, and then used it to boost the proportion of the desired product from 16% to 97%. By controlling acidity near electrodes, they developed a promising way to manufacture chemicals for plastics, medicines, and other products using oxygen and electricity instead of hazardous added oxidants.
- Share:
Scientists have identified a hidden factor that can determine whether a chemical reaction succeeds or fails. By controlling tiny changes in acidity near electrodes, researchers dramatically improved the production of valuable chemical ingredients, raising the proportion of the desired product from approximately 16% to 97%.
The breakthrough, led by Professor Jaeyune Ryu of the Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering at Seoul National University College of Engineering, could help make chemical manufacturing safer, cleaner, and more efficient. The researchers developed a method that uses oxygen and electricity to produce compounds used in plastics, medicines, adhesives, and other everyday materials without requiring the separate addition of peroxide oxidants.
Their discovery centers on a surprisingly overlooked factor called "local pH," which describes the acidity or alkalinity in the immediate surroundings of an electrode. By redesigning a chemical reactor to control the distance between electrodes and the movement of liquid through the system, the team found a way to manage these conditions and greatly improve the reaction's performance.
The work focused on two important families of chemicals: lactones and epoxides. Lactones are essential starting materials for biodegradable plastics and polyurethanes, while epoxides are used to manufacture adhesives, protective coatings, and epoxy resins found in electronic materials. Both also play important roles in producing pharmaceuticals and other specialized chemicals.
The findings were published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society (JACS), a leading chemistry journal published by the American Chemical Society (ACS).
The Hidden Chemistry That Can Make or Break a Reaction
The research builds on a technique known as organic electrosynthesis, which uses electrical energy to drive reactions that produce carbon-based chemical compounds.
This approach has attracted growing interest because it may reduce the need for some of the chemical oxidizing and reducing agents commonly used in traditional manufacturing. Such agents help reactions proceed by accepting or donating electrons, but some can be hazardous to handle and generate unwanted waste.
Until now, much of the effort to improve organic electrosynthesis has centered on familiar factors, including the electrical voltage, the materials used for electrodes, and the composition of the liquid in which reactions occur.
However, the researchers suspected that something important was being overlooked: the microscopic chemical environment directly next to each electrode.
This is where molecules exchange electrons and undergo chemical transformations. Although the surrounding solution may appear uniform, conditions within this tiny region can be dramatically different.
One particularly important factor is pH, a measure of how acidic or alkaline a substance is.
During an electrochemical reaction, hydrogen ions, also known as protons, can be produced or consumed at the electrodes. If these ions are generated or removed faster than they can move through the liquid, the pH near the electrode may become very different from the pH measured in the rest of the solution.
The researchers found that these local differences can influence several critical parts of a reaction. They can change how reactive oxygen species are produced, alter the behavior of the starting molecules, and even affect whether the finished products remain stable or begin to break down.
In other words, a reaction can fail even when the overall solution appears to have the right chemical conditions.
An Overlooked Problem May Affect Many Chemical Reactions
To determine whether this phenomenon might extend beyond their own experiments, the researchers examined more than 600 scientific papers on organic electrosynthesis published since 2010.
They found that approximately 89% of the studies involved reactions at one or more electrodes in which both electrons and protons were transferred.
This matters because the movement of protons can change local acidity. The finding suggests that overlooked pH differences near electrodes could influence a wide range of electrochemical reactions, rather than just a few specialized examples.
The team also measured how extreme these differences could become.
Even when the overall solution was essentially neutral, the researchers estimated that conditions near the cathode, the electrode where reduction occurs, could reach approximately pH 11, making the area strongly alkaline.
Meanwhile, the region around the anode, where oxidation takes place, could reach approximately pH 2.5, creating a strongly acidic environment.
These changes can have major consequences. Under such conditions, the reactive oxygen species needed to drive a reaction may become less available. Starting materials can change chemical form, and newly formed products may break down more rapidly.
Simply adjusting the acidity of the entire solution therefore may not solve the problem. What matters is the environment directly around the electrodes, where the chemistry actually happens.
Making Valuable Chemicals With Oxygen and Electricity
To demonstrate their discovery, the scientists investigated a well-established chemical process called Baeyer-Villiger oxidation.
This reaction adds an oxygen atom to a type of organic molecule known as a ketone, converting it into an ester or lactone. Lactones are ring-shaped compounds that serve as important building blocks for materials such as biodegradable plastics and polyurethanes.
Traditionally, Baeyer-Villiger oxidation often requires highly reactive oxidizing chemicals, including peroxyacids. Although effective, these substances can create difficulties involving safe handling, chemical waste, and the treatment of unwanted byproducts.
The Seoul National University team developed a different approach.
Instead of supplying these oxidants from outside the system, the researchers used electricity to activate oxygen gas at an electrode. This produced reactive oxygen species capable of transferring oxygen atoms into organic molecules.
To establish where the oxygen in the final products came from, the team conducted isotope-tracing experiments. These tests confirmed that the incorporated oxygen originated from oxygen gas rather than water.
The scientists also discovered that the two electrodes could work together in an important way.
At the cathode, oxygen reduction generates reactive oxygen species that initiate the oxygen-transfer reaction. Hydrogen peroxide formed during this process can then be converted back into reactive oxygen species at the anode.
This cooperation helps sustain the supply of reactive chemical species necessary for the reaction.
However, the entire process depends heavily on the acidity near the electrodes. If local pH becomes too extreme, the chemistry can become much less effective.
A Simple Reactor Redesign Boosts Selectivity From 16% to 97%
Once the researchers understood the importance of local pH, they investigated how to control it.
Using computer simulations and electrochemical measurements, they developed a reactor design that places the electrodes closer together while allowing the electrolyte, the electrically conductive liquid carrying the reaction ingredients, to flow between them.
The idea was to prevent extreme acidity differences from developing.
Because the area near the anode tends to become acidic while the area near the cathode becomes alkaline, bringing these regions closer together and circulating the liquid helps counterbalance their effects.
The results were striking.
Under conditions where local pH differences were not effectively controlled, approximately 16% of the relevant products formed were the desired target compound. With the improved reactor design, that selectivity rose to approximately 97%.
This increase in selectivity means the reaction became much better at producing the intended substance rather than unwanted products.
The researchers also discovered that changing the flow of the electrolyte had a powerful effect on production.
Across the flow rates they tested, the amount of product generated per unit time increased by approximately 14 times from the lowest to the highest flow rate.
Moving the electrodes closer together also made a difference. When the distance between them was reduced from 20 mm to 4 mm, the production rate increased by approximately 2.2 times.
Perhaps most revealing was what happened when the liquid was not allowed to flow.
Even though the applied voltage and the solution's composition remained unchanged, the researchers obtained almost none of the desired product.
This showed just how important the immediate chemical environment can be. The success of an electrochemical reaction depends on more than the ingredients, voltage, and electrode materials. The physical design of the reactor and the microscopic conditions it creates can be equally critical.
Applications for Biodegradable Plastics, Medicines, and Electronics
The researchers then explored whether their approach could be used to manufacture different kinds of useful chemicals.
Using their optimized conditions, they successfully synthesized lactones from 18 different ketone compounds.
One important example was ε-caprolactone, which they produced with an 82% yield.
This compound is a starting material for polycaprolactone, a biodegradable polymer used in medical applications such as surgical sutures and drug-delivery systems.
The researchers also applied their local pH control strategy to the production of epoxides, successfully obtaining products from six different alkene starting materials.
Epoxides are important ingredients in adhesives, surface coatings, and epoxy resins used in electronics. They are also valuable intermediates in the production of pharmaceuticals and fine chemicals.
Together, these experiments showed that controlling the microscopic environment around electrodes could have applications beyond a single reaction.
The findings suggest a potentially versatile way to improve the production of many commercially important chemical ingredients.
Toward Cleaner and More Sustainable Chemical Manufacturing
One of the most promising aspects of the technique is that it uses oxygen and electricity while reducing the need for externally added peroxide oxidants.
The reactions also take place at room temperature and normal atmospheric pressure, avoiding the need for separate equipment to heat or pressurize the system.
These characteristics could make certain chemical processes simpler and potentially safer.
Because electricity provides the energy needed to drive the reactions, the approach could eventually be combined with renewable energy sources to support more sustainable chemical manufacturing.
The researchers believe that pharmaceutical ingredients and other high-value specialty chemicals could be particularly promising applications.
These products often require careful control of reaction conditions and strict safety measures. Electrochemical methods may offer advantages by limiting the need to handle hazardous oxidizing agents and potentially allowing production in relatively compact equipment.
However, the technology is not yet ready for widespread industrial use. Further optimization and testing at larger production scales will be needed to determine whether the laboratory results can be reproduced economically and reliably in commercial manufacturing.
A New Way to Think About Chemical Reactions
Beyond its immediate applications, the discovery offers a different perspective on how electrochemical reactions should be designed.
Traditionally, researchers have concentrated on choosing the right starting materials, catalysts, electrode surfaces, voltages, and solution compositions.
The Seoul National University team's findings indicate that controlling the tiny environment where molecules actually react may be just as important.
This shifts attention toward "designing the environment in which molecules actually react."
Professor Jaeyune Ryu, who supervised the research, said, "This study transforms 'local pH' near the electrode from a hidden variable into a controllable design principle."
He added, "To improve the efficiency of organic electrosynthesis, we need to design not only the reaction substrates and catalysts, but also the environment in which the molecules actually react."
The researchers believe this principle could reveal opportunities to improve other electrochemical processes, particularly those involving the movement of both electrons and protons.
Rather than treating local acidity as an unavoidable side effect, future chemical reactors could be deliberately engineered to maintain conditions that favor the desired reactions.
The study's co-first authors were Seonghyeon Min and Junghoon Lee, both M.S. students in Seoul National University's Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering. Hanju Kim, an integrated M.S./Ph.D. student, participated as a co-author, with Professor Ryu overseeing the research.
Min and Lee plan to continue investigating how local reaction environments influence organic electrosynthesis, with the goal of extending the approach to a broader range of chemical reactions and manufacturing processes.
The research was supported by Seoul National University, the National Research Foundation of Korea, and the Institute for Basic Science (IBS).

Global poverty index rises for first time since its 2010 creation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:21:20 UTC
15:21:20 KST

More than half of those in acute poverty were children. (AFP Photo)
A U.N. global poverty index has risen for the first time since its creation in 2010, bringing the number of people affected to 1.2 billion, the United Nations Development Program reported on Oct. 12.
In the 2026 edition of their annual report, the UNDP and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative research center counted 51.5 million more people living in "acute" poverty compared to the previous year.
UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo said the increase in poverty should be a "wake-up call for the world."
"Behind these figures are 1.2 billion people facing hardships that reinforce one another: Hunger, missed schooling and a lack of clean water or electricity. This is unacceptable," he said in a press release.
However, UNDP said a major factor in the recorded increase was population growth, and new data was only available for 13 of the 108 developing countries covered by the report.
While the total number of people in poverty has increased, the report provides a mixed picture. Some 33 nations have halved the percentage of their people living in poverty as defined by the index in the past 15 years.
Those included six countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Among the countries that have made the most rapid progress were countries in Asia — China and Vietnam — UNDP said.
As in the previous year, the report found that the majority of the poorest people live in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, specifically the Indian subcontinent, the most densely populated region on Earth.
The poverty index used in the report includes indicators such as the lack of adequate housing, sanitation, electricity, cooking fuel, food and education.

designboom paris art week guide: what to see in and out of design miami and art basel 2026

designboom paris art week guide: what to see in and out of design miami and art basel 2026
designboom maps the art, design, and cultural encounters worth seeking out across paris this october.
What to see across Paris during Art Basel Paris 2026
Paris enters its busiest art and design week with a program that looks as much to what has already existed as to what comes next. Across museums, galleries, historic buildings, and temporary spaces, the 2026 season brings together fashion archives, modernist furniture, contemporary sculpture, photography, craft, and experimental forms of hospitality, with many projects reconsidering how objects and images acquire meaning over time.
At the center of the week, Art Basel Paris returns to the Grand Palais while Design Miami.Paris takes over the Hôtel de Maisons. Beyond the fairs, museums and cultural spaces across Paris present projects that span art, fashion, architecture, and design: Ibrahim Mahama brings a network of artists and Ghanaian cultural histories to Fondation Cartier; Prune Nourry revisits the overlooked legacy of women sculptors at the Petit Palais; Jenny Holzer activates the Musée d’Orsay with texts and images; and the Musée des Arts Décoratifs marks 40 years of its fashion collections through four decades of exhibitions and 40 significant silhouettes.
Galleries turn to material memory and transformation, from Jean Prouvé’s architecture and Japanese ceramics to Wendy Andreu’s reworked furniture and Ais’s layered paintings. Temporary projects also blur the boundaries between disciplines, including WE ARE ONA’s collaboration with Rirkrit Tiravanija and chef Dalad Kambhu, where a shared meal becomes part of the artwork itself. From major institutional exhibitions to intimate gallery presentations, collectible design, food, and temporary interventions, this is designboom’s guide to what to see across Paris during Art Basel Paris and Design Miami.Paris 2026.
design miami paris / art basel paris 2026
Art Basel Paris 2026
Art Basel Paris returns to the Grand Palais from October 23rd to 25th, 2026, with its fifth edition that brings together 211 galleries from 41 countries and regions, while expanding beyond the fair through an extensive public program across Paris. Under new director Karim Crippa, the edition foregrounds the galleries, museums, institutions, and public spaces of the city as part of the fair’s wider cultural context.
The fair is organized across three sectors: Galeries, with 183 exhibitors; Emergence, with 16 solo presentations; and Premise, with 12 historically focused projects. This year, Premise moves into the larger Salon Seine, while Conversations relocates to the Grand Palais Auditorium for the first time. A record 12 joint booths will also bring together 24 galleries.
Outside the Grand Palais, the Public Program spreads across nine Parisian venues, including the Petit Palais, Palais d’Iéna, Cité de l’architecture et du patrimoine, Beaux-Arts de Paris, and several public squares and gardens. Highlights include Alice Diop’s Geste de Consolation at Palais d’Iéna, Tracey Emin’s sculptures at the Parvis des Droits-de-l’Homme, Kutluğ Ataman’s Küba at Beaux-Arts de Paris, and Robert Indiana’s LOVE Wall at Place Clemenceau.
 what: Art Basel Paris 2026
when: October 23rd–25th, 2026
where: Grand Palais, 3 Avenue du Général Eisenhower, 75008 Paris
Alice Diop – Geste de Consolation presented by miu miu
For her first exhibition project, French filmmaker Alice Diop transforms the Palais d’Iéna into a multimedia journey for Miu Miu’s 2026 Art Basel Paris Public Program commission. Geste de Consolation brings together film, photography, sculpture, poetry, dance, music, and live performance, centering acts of consolation conceived by Black women artists.
The project takes over four interconnected spaces. It begins with work by South African artist Zanele Muholi and a two-screen video installation by Diop, bringing together archival images and film excerpts that have shaped her own way of looking. This leads into Chambre à soi, a living room and library featuring carpets with a motif by Mary Lee Bendolph and books drawn from Diop’s intellectual influences. The central library opens onto a performance space where texts by writers including Penda Diouf, Zora Neale Hurston, June Jordan, Audre Lorde, Marie Ndiaye, and Zadie Smith are performed live. Choreography by Nadia Beugré and music by Angel Bat Dawid and her ensemble further extend the project beyond the conventions of a static exhibition. Kutluğ Ataman brings Küba to the Chapelle des Petits-Augustins
Kutluğ Ataman’s Küba transforms the Chapelle des Petits-Augustins at the Beaux-Arts de Paris into a multi-screen portrait of a community shaped by migration, poverty, and survival. First created in 2004, the 40-screen video installation gives each television to a different resident of Küba, a former settlement on the outskirts of Istanbul founded in the late 1960s by people fleeing political persecution.
Set among mismatched armchairs and salvaged furniture, the screens show residents speaking directly to the camera about their memories, fears, beliefs, and dreams. Their stories overlap without one voice taking precedence, allowing visitors to gradually piece together a collective portrait while moving through the installation. Ataman uses individual testimony to consider how identity is formed through storytelling, giving the community’s own voices control over its representation.
 what: Küba, 2004
when: October 20th – 25th, 2026, 10am–7pm
where: Chapelle des Petits-Augustins, Beaux-Arts de Paris

Maison Parisienne
Pierre Renart and Maison Parisienne present a monumental wooden bench whose backrest unfolds into a curved ribbon, extending into a chaise longue. Made from a single flowing line of wood, the piece creates two facing seating areas designed for sitting and conversation.
Craftica Gallery
Craftica Gallery presents Korallion (2026), a birch plywood bench by Cyryl Zakrzewski that sits between sculpture and architecture. Designed for an outdoor setting, its fluid form responds to light, weather, and the passage of time while adding a sculptural element within the landscape.
Galerie Gastou
Galerie Gastou presents Irene Cattaneo’s Effi Briest, a group of monumental bronze swings inspired by the childhood swing in Theodor Fontane’s 1895 novel. Their weight and permanence contrast with the fleeting movement associated with swings, connecting the installation to the tension between childhood freedom and the social structures that shape adulthood.
Nilufar
Nilufar features a curated selection of vintage design alongside contemporary works, including Von Pelt Atelier’s Table Lamp Spring Fountain 2 (2025). Made in Spain, the lamp reinterprets the silver-plated decorative objects found in Spanish homes during the mid-to-late 20th century.
Galerie Patrick Seguin
 Galerie Patrick Seguin showcases furniture by Jean Prouvé, Charlotte Perriand, and Pierre Jeanneret alongside a 6×6 demountable house by Prouvé at Design Miami.Paris. The presentation brings together furniture and architecture to examine the shared ideas connecting the three designers’ practices.
The booth features Perriand’s Forme Libre low table from 1956, a Jeanneret sofa set from around 1955, and a Prouvé sideboard and Antony chair from around 1950. In the Hôtel de Maisons garden, Prouvé’s 1944 6×6 house is presented with a redesigned interior inspired by the chashitsu, the traditional Japanese tea pavilion.
Using natural materials including wood, the installation creates a dialogue between Prouvé’s architecture and Japanese approaches to living. It also draws on the designer’s connections with Japan, emphasizing affinities around simplicity, lightness, and material restraint.
