Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain – Ibrahim Mahama
Ghanaian artist Ibrahim Mahama transforms the Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain into a collective space for art, research, and exchange with The Harvest Season. For his first major exhibition in Paris, Mahama occupies the institution alongside nine artists and collectives connected through long-term collaborations, research, and exchanges, bringing together site-specific works and new versions of existing installations. The exhibition takes inspiration from the three art centers Mahama has established in Tamale, northern Ghana, since 2019. These spaces combine artistic production, education, and transmission, providing a model for thinking about how cultural institutions can emerge from local networks rather than operate separately from them. At the Fondation Cartier, this approach extends into a program of exhibitions, performances, music, talks, workshops, and masterclasses.
Among the central works is Parliament of Ghosts, a circular parliamentary chamber made from traditional Asante wooden stools. The installation refers to Ghana’s 1966 coup and the dissolution of its government, while also functioning as a stage for performances and discussions throughout the exhibition. Mahama also presents Things Fall Apart, a monumental reconstruction of a former Ghanaian glass bottle factory, using original materials to connect industrial heritage with questions of education, infrastructure, and possible futures. The exhibition expands through works by Dorothy Akpene Amenuke, Gideon Appah, James Barnor, CATPC, Courage Dzidula Kpodo, Zohra Opoku, Postbox Ghana, Tjaša Rener, and Feda Wardak. Their practices bring together textiles, photography, painting, architecture, archives, agricultural materials, and inherited infrastructure, extending Mahama’s interest in how histories and forms of knowledge can be carried forward and transformed.
 what: Ibrahim Mahama: The Harvest Season
when: October 22nd, 2026 – February 28th, 2027

The Musée de l’Orangerie marks the centenary of Claude Monet’s death with Monet: Painting Time, an exhibition examining how the artist’s work evolved from capturing fleeting impressions to exploring the experience of duration. Nearly 40 paintings trace this progression, from his Impressionist works of the 1870s through the Haystacks, Poplars, and Rouen Cathedral series to the Water Lilies that occupied him until his death in 1926.
The exhibition brings together works from the Musée d’Orsay and Musée Marmottan Monet, alongside loans from French and international collections. Its final section focuses on the Nymphéas, connecting the series to the Musée de l’Orangerie’s permanent panoramic installation, which Monet conceived as an immersive environment.

The Grand Palais presents Cezanne et nous, an exhibition tracing Paul Cézanne’s influence from the late 19th century to the present through nearly 180 works. Bringing together artists including Paul Gauguin, Henri Matisse, Pablo Picasso, Piet Mondrian, Joan Mitchell, Bridget Riley, and Peter Doig, the exhibition examines how successive generations have interpreted, appropriated, and challenged Cézanne’s approach to painting.
The exhibition follows Cézanne’s growing influence from the artists and collectors who discovered his work in Paris in the late 1880s through the avant-garde movements of the 20th century. At Musée du Luxembourg, Andy Warhol: La ligne et l’image places drawing at the center of Warhol’s artistic practice. Around 150 drawings, alongside paintings, screenprints, photographs, and archival documents, trace how drawing remained a site of experimentation throughout his career, from his early work as a commercial illustrator to his late drawings for The Last Supper.
The exhibition is organized around five themes: Warhol’s beginnings in advertising illustration, his use of handwritten text, his fascination with faces and masks, his exploration of gay imagery, and his recurring preoccupation with death. Drawings reveal the techniques behind his images, including stamps, transferred lines, stencils, and collage, highlighting the relationship between hand and mechanical reproduction that runs through his work.

La MEP – Maison Européenne de la Photographie – Irving Penn: PENN & FASHION
Maison Européenne de la Photographie (MEP) presents a major survey of Irving Penn’s fashion photography from 1947 to 2008. Drawn primarily from the MEP and the Nicola Erni Collection, with loans from The Irving Penn Foundation and the Miyake Issey Foundation, Penn & Fashion, traces the American photographer’s six-decade relationship with fashion and his long collaboration with Vogue. The exhibition moves from his photographs of Parisian haute couture in the 1950s, including Dior and Balenciaga, through the work of the 1970s and 1980s for designers such as Ungaro, Courrèges, Yves Saint Laurent, and Karl Lagerfeld. It also highlights Penn’s collaboration with Issey Miyake, whose sculptural garments became a particularly strong match for his controlled photographic compositions.
The presentation continues through Penn’s later fashion and beauty work, including photographs of creations by John Galliano, Christian Lacroix, and Chanel. Across the exhibition, his attention to silhouette, volume, texture, and composition demonstrates how his fashion commissions operated between photography, art, and commercial image-making.

Entre les lignes brings Milanese duo studioutte together with Italian artist Armando Marrocco at Galerie Chloé Perrin, translating the principle of Intreccio, or interweaving, that has shaped Marrocco’s practice since the 1960s into a spatial installation.
The gallery becomes a contemporary living interior where artworks, furniture, and architecture form a single landscape. Studioutte places its ERT chair, Osaka bench, Torch and Straal lights alongside The Ur, a new armchair created specifically for the exhibition, creating a dialogue between Marrocco’s work and the duo’s approach to objects and space.

Look! 40 ans de mode au musée
The Musée des Arts Décoratifs marks 40 years of its fashion museum with Look! 40 ans de mode au musée, bringing together 40 iconic silhouettes from four decades of exhibitions. The exhibition traces the processes that turn fashion into museum objects, from the first sketch and couture atelier to photography, conservation, restoration, and display.
The presentation follows the two lives of a garment: its creation before entering the collection and its transformation into cultural heritage once it reaches the museum. Drawings, embroidery samples, patterns, model deposits, and archival material reveal the work behind the clothes, while photographs and fashion shows demonstrate how garments have been presented as artistic performances. The 40 silhouettes span the museum’s exhibition history, from Moments de mode and Madeleine Vionnet to Christian Dior, couturier du rêve and Les Mondes surréalistes d’Elsa Schiaparelli.

For PASSAGES: Pas sages, the Quai d’Orsay opens the historic Hôtel du Ministre to a contemporary art exhibition during Art Basel Paris. Co-produced by artist-designers Thierry Lemaire and Harry Nuriev and curated by Krystyna Winckler, the exhibition brings contemporary art, design, craftsmanship, heritage objects, and diplomatic archives into dialogue across the ministry’s historic salons.
The exhibition focuses on the idea of passage as a form of transmission, connecting artists who have participated in France’s international residency network with works from the Manufactures Nationales, the Centre National des Arts Plastiques, and the diplomatic archives. Artists include Louise Bourgeois, Zao Wou-Ki, Betty Woodman, Raphaël Barontini, Jeanne Vicérial, Pol Taburet, Nour Awada, and Nelly Saunier, alongside historical furniture, ceramics, textiles, and Cypriot antiquities.
Lemaire and Nuriev develop the scenography as part of the exhibition itself, introducing contemporary interventions into rooms such as the King’s Bedroom and a cabinet of curiosities assembled from diplomatic documents and objects. The presentation also connects the exhibition to France’s network of more than 80 international artist residencies, positioning artistic exchange as part of cultural diplomacy.
 what: PASSAGES: Pas sages

where: Hôtel du Ministre, Quai d’Orsay, Paris

Five Easy Pieces presents five new editions of functional artworks that continue Owens and Lamy’s interest in architectural form and primal materials. Rusted steel and wood foreground processes of transformation, with the materials carrying associations with resistance, nature, and time. Running alongside it, Master Pieces brings together 16 works by 11 leading figures in 20th- and 21st-century Japanese ceramics. Spanning a century of practice, the selection highlights different approaches to historical techniques, form, surface, pattern, and material, with works that are seldom exhibited outside Japan.

UN global poverty index rises for first time, affecting 1.2 billion people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:15:10 UTC
15:15:10 KST

A UN global poverty index has risen for the first time since its creation in 2010, bringing the number of people affected to 1.2 billion, the United Nations Development Programme reported on Monday.
In the 2026 edition of their annual report, the UNDP and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative research center counted 51.5 million more people living in "acute" poverty compared to the previous year.
UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo said the increase in poverty should be a "wake-up call for the world."
"Behind these figures are 1.2 billion people facing hardships that reinforce one another: hunger, missed schooling and a lack of clean water or electricity. This is unacceptable," he said in a press release.
More than half of those in acute poverty were children.
However, UNDP said a major factor in the recorded increase was population growth, and new data was only available for 13 of the 108 developing countries covered by the report.
Multidimensional poverty rates
While the total number of people in poverty has increased, the report provides a mixed picture. Some 33 nations have halved the percentage of their people living in poverty as defined by the index in the past 15 years.
Those included six countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Among the countries that have made the most rapid progress were countries in Asia - China and Vietnam - UNDP said.
As in the previous year, the report found that the majority of the poorest people live in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, specifically the Indian subcontinent, the most densely populated region on Earth.
"In Egypt, Nepal, and Tajikistan, both the poverty rate and the number of people experiencing multidimensional poverty have decreased significantly," the press release said.
In Angola and Zambia, the poverty rate has also declined, but population growth has more than offset this decrease, resulting in an increase in the number of people living in poverty.
The poverty index used in the report includes indicators such as the lack of adequate housing, sanitation, electricity, cooking fuel, food and education.

Smotrich calls on Netanyahu, Katz to defy High Court over return of Palestinians to Jenin, Tulkarm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:15:00 UTC
15:15:00 KST

The High Court of Justice on Sunday ordered the state to provide a timetable for completing the measures it says are needed before Palestinians displaced from three refugee camps in the northern West Bank can return to their homes, and to say whether that work can be accelerated.
The justices also asked the state to address the petitioners’ claims about shortcomings in humanitarian aid to residents. The state must submit its response by November 23, 2026. The court did not order an immediate return or direct the IDF to withdraw from the camps.
The ruling came in a petition filed by six Palestinian residents and the Association for Civil Rights in Israel, which seeks to enable the residents’ return to their homes in the Jenin, Tulkarm, and Nur Shams refugee camps and to establish a mechanism for the return of other displaced residents. The petition also asks the state to provide for residents’ humanitarian needs until they can return.
The decision prompted Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich on Monday to call on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz to instruct the IDF not to cooperate with the court.
Supreme Court President Isaac Amit and Justices Alex Stein and Khaled Kabub noted that about one year and nine months had passed since the start of Operation Iron Wall, the IDF operation launched in the northern West Bank back in January 2025. According to the state, the security conditions needed for residents to return had still not been met.
Court seeks timeline to return West Bank residents to refugee camps
The case has been before the court since September 2025. In its preliminary response, filed on February 3, the state argued that continuing security needs prevented residents from returning. It said that the military had not ordered residents to leave and that most had left before the operation began. The response also acknowledged that residents could not return to the camps, except for limited purposes coordinated with the military. A Central Command officer filed an affidavit supporting the state’s account two days later.
At a hearing on March 30, the court heard from the parties and held a closed discussion with security officials. In a decision following the hearing, the justices noted that more than 400 buildings had been demolished in the camps on the military commander’s orders, in addition to buildings damaged or destroyed during fighting, and that some residents had yet to return. They asked the state to submit an update by July 1.
The state filed its update on August 24, after receiving extensions. It told the court that security conditions had not materially changed and that the military was continuing to find weapons and explosives in the camps. The state said the military needed to maintain operational control and that residents could not return under current conditions. It also said its review found that residents’ humanitarian needs were being adequately met.
In their September 17 response, the petitioners challenged both the state’s security justification and its assessment of humanitarian conditions. They argued that the state’s update described a continuing policy aimed at maintaining long-term security control and preventing future threats, rather than a need to keep residents away during active fighting. They also disputed the state’s account of the aid available to displaced families.
Smotrich called on Netanyahu and Katz to tell the IDF not to cooperate with the justices
After Sunday’s ruling, Smotrich accused the justices of endangering Israel’s security and warned that residents’ return would allow terrorist infrastructure to be rebuilt in the northern West Bank. He also compared the court’s involvement to its role in Gaza before the October 7 massacre and said the justices should themselves face investigation.
“I call on the prime minister and my colleague, the defense minister, to instruct the IDF not to cooperate with the court and not to allow the terrorist camps to be reestablished,” Smotrich said.
He argued that security decisions should rest solely with elected officials and reiterated his support for changes to Israel’s judicial system.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s former chief of staff, Tzachi Braverman, allegedly asked a Prime Minister’s Office stenographer to change the recorded time of a call between Netanyahu and his former military secretary, Avi Gil, on the morning of October 7, 2023, according to a transcript published by N12 on Sunday.
The transcript, which N12 dates to January 2024, reportedly shows Braverman speaking to a PMO stenographer and asking her to change the recorded time of Netanyahu’s secure-line call with Gil from 6:40 a.m. to 6:29 a.m.
“Wow, how beautiful. Look how sharp he is, Netanyahu. Look how sharp he is. It was at 6:29, not 6:40. Change the time,” Braverman said, according to the transcript.
The stenographer reportedly refused despite Braverman’s insistence, saying she was not permitted to change the computerized record.
However, despite her explicit objection and the fact that the record was an official, digitally signed document, Braverman did not back down, N12 reported. He allegedly took the printed transcript and changed the time in blue ink, writing it himself. The stenographer left the room and went to Gil to tell him what had happened.
Following the report, the information was passed on to the police investigation.
According to N12, Braverman wanted to change the time of the call between Gil and Netanyahu to suggest the prime minister received a detailed report immediately after the attack began.
Gil accuses Braverman of changing call log times
The account appears to align with what Gil said in an interview published by N12 and Israel Hayom on Thursday, in which he charged Braverman with making the changes.
"In January, one of the stenographers approached me and told me she had been instructed to retrieve the transcript of that 6:40 a.m. phone call and had been instructed [by Netanyahu's then chief of staff, Tzachi Braverman] to change the time of the call from 6:40 to 6:29," Gil said in the interview.
A statement shared with N12 on behalf of Braverman argued that the transcript is false.
"The stenographer was never told that Tzachi Braverman participated in the call. No such transcript of a conversation with her exists, and no such transcript was presented to him during his police questioning," the statement read.
"We regret that it was not reported that the military secretary failed to mention during his police questioning a conversation he had with Mr. Braverman at 6:33 a.m., during which he informed Braverman about the call at 6:29 a.m."
"We understand that after more than a year in which the case has been in the hands of the State Attorney's Office, and with indications that it is heading toward closure, it has been revived as part of a political campaign of which Mr. Braverman is a victim."
Braverman suspected of collecting classified protocols without authorization after Oct. 7
Separately, N12 reported on Sunday that Braverman has also been suspected of systematically collecting around 30 classified protocols without authorization in the month after the October 7 massacre.
The protocols reportedly included sensitive security discussions concerning the period leading up to the October 7 massacre, including those about Gaza and meetings with senior security officials concerning Hamas, according to N12.
According to N12, investigators suspected the documents had been collected to help shape the public narrative surrounding the events leading up to the massacre.
Braverman allegedly removed the documents without the required authorization, according to N12.
N12 noted that the case has been transferred to the Attorney General’s Office to decide whether to indict Braverman for violating procedures.

Startups are betting on AI to predict the future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:14:00 UTC
15:14:00 KST

Several startups are betting that they can leverage artificial intelligence (AI) to make better forecasts than even the most specialized experts when it comes to topics as varied as stock market movements, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, or how a Shakira song will perform on music charts.
By 2030, "we're going to feel that what we were doing for our decision-making was complete Stone Age thinking," Dan Schwarz, cofounder of the forecasting company FutureSearch, said.
AI forecasting models are already on par with the best "superforecasters" — gifted individuals whose estimates are markedly superior to those of ordinary people — thanks to troves of data acquired from both public and private sources.
In early September, two AI models made history when they took the top spots in the Metaculus Cup, a competition among prediction champions, both human and nonhuman.
FutureSearch's in-house human wizard, superforecaster Tom Liptay, is aware that "he's not secure in his job" in the medium term, Schwarz said. "He knows that these things are going to surpass him."
Theo Summer, who cofounded Preseen with Veniamin Veselovsky, used AI tools to turn $35 into $1.9 million in just seven months on the American prediction-making site Kalshi.
The idea is not to guarantee a result but to define a probability of occurrence, with the ability to cross-check assumptions related to several interconnected events — for example, changes in the price of oil and the war in the Middle East.
"Right now, the quickest buyers are normally the hedge funds, just because if they think they can make money off something, they can move pretty fast," Veselovsky said.
Algorithms have shaped Wall Street for more than a decade, but the rise of AI forecasting is likely to further increase the automation of financial markets.
"I think it's probably already having a small impact because we already have customers who use it when making trading decisions," said Toby Shevlane, the cofounder of another forecasting startup called Mantic.
Now-famous prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket, which are used by millions of Americans, are also becoming inundated by AI use.
It might soon be too late for retail investors, who don't have access to expensive AI tools, to profit on those types of consumer-oriented trading sites because "they will soon just be dominated by AI forecasting systems," Veselovsky said.
The most advanced models no longer just predict events, either.
They can also formulate their own questions about the future and then assign probabilities based on the different possible outcomes, Shevlane said.
Their sphere of influence is beginning to extend beyond finance, as well, with potential applications in government policy, corporate decision-making, scientific research, and insurance risk assessments.
Mantic provides a large American company with likely scenarios of regulatory developments in its sector and has also worked for the British government.
Companies "are interested in risks and how to monitor them," Shevlane said.
Meanwhile, other customers might be more interested in medical research, particularly to help make decisions around which types of treatments would be best to fund, Schwarz said.
Widespread access to these types of tools can come with costs, though.
"I think that good can be derived from this," Veselovsky said, but "I'm also a little bit scared because, you know, maybe Russia or China has better systems."

A new dawn for Didim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:01:55 UTC
15:01:55 KST

For centuries, the environs of Didim in Mid-Aegean Türkiye have carried the whisper of prophecy. It was here, at the monumental Temple of Apollo, that pilgrims once walked the Sacred Way from ancient Miletus to consult the oracle. Perched on a hill, overlooking the Maeander plain, Priene is one of the best-preserved sites of the Ionian league. Both Miletus and Priene still resonate with the impression of ancient times; one feels like walking through a time capsule. The mighty oracle of Apollon temple stands high and strong, as if whispering a secret, or maybe telling what will come next.
Only a few miles apart from each other, this magnificent trio of archaeological remains is not the only attraction of the Didim area; the natural park of Lake Bafa is another world to explore, from where the winding Meander River gently sweeps towards the Aegean through a verdant alluvial plain, and the picturesque villages like Doğanköy and Kayaköy are hidden gems to explore. Last, but not least, or maybe the foremost attraction is Altınkum beach, which literally translates as The Golden Sand. Strangely enough, despite having such a rich portfolio of history and natural beauty, Didim has never hit the stardom of other Aegean destinations. In modern times, as tourism swept across Türkiye’s western coast, the Mid-Aegean region (Orta Ege) found itself caught in a curious dichotomy. While Bodrum to the south became synonymous with flashy luxury and Alaçatı and Çeşme to the north with outgoing crowds, or in recent years, Urla as a gastronomy destination, Didim largely became associated with mass summer beach travel — its rich history and serene landscapes somewhat obscured by seasonal crowds.
New upcoming destination: Mid-Aegean
That narrative is now undergoing a profound transformation. The opening of Akra Didim — a visionary project by BHM Otelcilik, the group behind the 50-year legacy of Barut Hotels — signals a decisive turning point for the Mid-Aegean. It introduces an approach grounded not in ostentation, but in what they simply call “simplicity” referring to understated, subtle luxury rooted deeply in place, culture, and nature.
The property is gigantic, spreading to about 340,00 square-meter grounds, but the feel is not out of human scale. The architecture respects the coast rather than dominating it, with vast areas of open spaces, treating roofs as part of the landscape, creating a breathing environment which allows guests to slow down, enjoy the spatial atmosphere. The ‘Simplicity’ philosophy approaches comfort as the purest form of what is right, whilst creating a flow that allows guests to follow their own rhythm without having to organize anything. Based on six core principles – nature, harmony, balance, well-being, creation and production, and sharing – this approach ensures that diverse experiences come together as parts of a single whole at Akra Didim.
However, the term “simplicity” does not mean “simplistic” here. Everything is well-thought of, offering a diverse range of experiences for the guests. Coupled with world-class wellness facilities, extensive racket sports, including padel and pickleball, and a commitment to 12-month operation, the resort redefines Didim as a year-round haven for culture, sports, and well-being. Another emphasis is on intellectual and artistic enrichment. Through its Artist Residency Program and dedicated Art & Culture Village, the resort invites contemporary artists to reside, create, and display their work on site. Guests do not merely view art on hotel walls; they engage directly with creators in live ateliers.
Inspiration: The olive
Gastronomy is a strong tool that forms a vital part of the connection forged with the region’s natural environment and culinary culture. In Akra Didim, this is achieved by a special dining experience aptly named “Zeytin’lik,” which means “The Olive Grove” in Turkish, housed in a stone building nestled amongst olive trees. Here, the cooking is also in line with the philosophy of “simplicity,” featuring fire cooking only and reinterpreting the region’s culinary heritage through traditional methods such as open-fire grilling, stone ovens and pit fires. Zeytin’lik strongly emphasizes locality; it offers seasonal produce sourced from the region or grown in its own kitchen gardens and serves the day’s catch from the sea. Regional recipes collected from locals often feature in the menu, to be paired with wines made from indigenous grapes from the extensive wine cellar featuring only Turkish wines. Here, gastronomy transcends being merely a dining experience; it transforms into a journey experienced through the processes of production, cooking and sharing.
The Mid-Aegean possesses an extraordinary culinary heritage, anchored above all by the ancient olive tree. Didim sits in the heartland of the prized Memecik olive. Here, olive oil is not merely a cooking medium; it is the hero of the table. Zeytin-lik transforms regional gastronomy into an authentic story of place, where rustic Aegean heritage meets contemporary culinary finesse. If the oracle at Didyma were to speak today, it might well predict that the future of Aegean luxury lies not in extravagant grandeur, but in returning to the authentic, olive-scented soul of the region.

Houthi missile strike in Saudi Arabia exposes growing regional threat, Yemen expert warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
05:56:14 UTC
14:56:14 KST

The Houthis remain a significant threat to Saudi Arabia and other countries in the region despite recent territorial gains by forces backed by Riyadh, Yemen expert Inbal Nissim-Louvton told 103FM following a Houthi missile strike on a terminal in the Saudi capital.
Nissim-Louvton, a Yemen expert at Tel Aviv University's Moshe Dayan Center and the Open University, spoke with Ron Kofman and Aryeh Eldad on 103FM about the ongoing fighting between Saudi-backed forces and the Houthis, and the limitations facing countries seeking to weaken the terrorist organization.
Asked who was winning the confrontation between the Saudis and the Houthis, she replied: "It depends on whom you ask."
"I think we are still in the midst of it. Just a few weeks ago, the Houthis controlled the port of Mokha and Mayyun Island, overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. But now we can see that forces loyal to the internationally recognized government, which are backed by Saudi Arabia, have managed to regain control of those areas."
According to Nissim-Louvton, the fighting remains part of a broader conflict within Yemen.
Houthi control of Yemeni territory complicates Saudi military response
"There is still a certain dynamic to the fighting itself, which is part of the renewed civil war in Yemen and the collapse of the ceasefire between the Houthis and the Saudis, which had held up well until recently," she said.
"I think there is an asymmetry here that has worked in the Houthis' favor in the past and continues to play a role now," she added.
The expert emphasized that the Houthis' capabilities extend well beyond their missile arsenal, making them a persistent challenge for several countries in the region.
"The terrorist organization has more than just ballistic missiles. It is an organization that possesses the apparatus of a state, including the economic capabilities of a country, albeit a poor one like Yemen, but nevertheless," she said.
"They manage to control a considerable amount of territory in a country, with more than 50% of Yemen's population, and that makes them a major headache for the Saudis, the United Arab Emirates, and Israel."
Nissim-Louvton also explained that countries confronting the Houthis face significant limitations when attempting to strike infrastructure under the group's control, particularly ports essential to Yemen's civilian population.
"You can strike these ports only up to a certain point because they are the lifeline of most of Yemen's population. When you strike them beyond the limits that allow normal life to continue there, in the context of the civil war, you are effectively imposing a major humanitarian disaster on the population," she said.
Addressing the impact of the situation in Yemen and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Egypt, Nissim-Louvton noted that disruptions to maritime traffic have consequences beyond the countries directly involved in the fighting.
"Egypt was the main country harmed by the previous blockade or earlier rounds of fighting. This should be a headache for the international community because there is damage to and a violation of the security of freedom of movement along a maritime transport and trade route," she concluded.

World Insights: U.S. sanctions relief on Russian diesel unlikely to cool fuel prices
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:52:04 CST
14:52:04 KST

by Ben Xie
NEW YORK, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- The United States on Friday temporarily lifted sanctions on Russia's export of diesel in a bid to ease a global fuel shortage and curb soaring domestic prices, but analysts warn that limited supplies and damage to Russian refineries could possibly blunt the impact.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Friday that he had struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin during a phone call. On the same day, the U.S. Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control issued a temporary general license, authorizing Russian diesel transactions until April 7, 2027.
Under the phased schedule, Russia would deliver 2.25 million barrels in October, 3.75 million in November and 7.5 million "immediately thereafter," depending on the condition of Russian refineries. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed the volumes.
U.S. diesel averaged 6.28 dollars a gallon on Friday, according to the American Automobile Association, down from a record 6.53 dollars on Sept. 22, but still far above 3.68 dollars a year earlier, and up about 70 percent since the U.S.-Israel war with Iran began on Feb. 28.
A Pew Research Center survey released Oct. 8 found that 74 percent of Americans were "very concerned" about energy prices, and 84 percent of registered voters said the economy was "very important" to their vote in the Nov. 3 mid-term elections.
On Saturday, the Russian government partially lifted its diesel export ban with immediate effect, allowing 500,000 tons to reach the global market, with Novak saying domestic supplies would not be affected.
However, analysts said that the U.S. relief on sanctions on Russian diesel is unlikely to help tame domestic diesel prices, which hover at close to record-high levels and threaten Republican control of Congress in the upcoming elections.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) says the world is short about 1.6 million barrels of diesel daily. Even if all 36 million barrels Russia promised arrived at once, they would plug the gap for only about three weeks.
The October release alone is roughly 10 percent of what Russia exported in a typical month before Ukrainian drone strikes battered its refineries, according to analysts.
"It's kind of shuffling deck chairs on the Titanic," a report by The Seattle Times quoted Michael Lynch of the Energy Policy Research Foundation as saying. Russian diesel sent to the United States simply means that other buyers must look elsewhere. At best, he said, Americans might see "a tiny dip in prices locally in places like the New York-New Jersey area."
"It's clearly not a fix, but another stream to aid a very tight diesel market," Jim Mitchell, director of oil trading analytics at consultancy Wood Mackenzie, was quoted as saying by Reuters.
"The biggest concern is the refiners being able to do it," Ryan McKay, senior commodity strategist at TD Securities, a Canadian multinational investment bank and financial services provider, was quoted as saying by the Business Times.
The November shipment amounts to roughly one day of U.S. consumption, noted Chris Kennedy, lead for Economic Statecraft at Bloomberg Economics. He questioned whether Moscow can deliver given refinery damage, logistics and legal hurdles, with the largest later tranches explicitly conditioned on the state of Russia's refineries.
To make matters worse, Hurricane Isaias in the Gulf of Mexico has now shut down about 1.3 million barrels a day of U.S. oil production, which equals nearly 63 percent of total U.S. production in the gulf.
The Iran war also continues to disrupt flows through the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about 20 percent of global oil and fuel shipments before the war.
As part of an accelerated IEA emergency-stock release, Germany will release up to 15 million barrels of diesel, heating oil and crude, while France has committed 10 million barrels of diesel. Moreover, Italy says it has completed its 10 million-barrel commitment.
The Russian barrels address the shortage from the output side, while the stock releases address it from the inventory side. However, analysts say neither is large enough to repair the market on its own.
Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, predicted that the deal could result in a short-term reduction of 10 to 20 cents for a gallon of diesel. However, he said, it would be "difficult to achieve" Trump's import goals. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: Retracing the Long March: An Australian publisher's decades-long quest to understand China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:52:01 CST
14:52:01 KST

by Xinhua writer Xiong Wenyuan
MELBOURNE, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The Long March offers a key to understanding modern China, Australian publisher Harold Weldon has said, drawing on two journeys along the route and four decades of engagement with the country.
In a recent interview with Xinhua in Melbourne, Weldon compared the Long March, whose victory marks its 90th anniversary this year, to the spine of a body, saying it "goes right through the modern history of China."
Weldon, a writer and filmmaker who is also the founder and principal of Harold Weldon Advisory, first retraced the route in 1985, aged 19, and returned for the second journey in 2011.
A "WALKING UNIVERSITY"
His interest began at school. At 16, while studying Asian history, he read Edgar Snow's "Red Star Over China" and was drawn to its account of the Long March.
His father, also inspired by the book, later brought together international photographers to document China along the Long March route. Weldon had secured a university place, but his father encouraged him to join the family publishing company, describing the project as a "walking university."
Carrying Snow's book, Weldon joined a reconnaissance team that traveled by train and road and walked where vehicles could not go. On some stretches, donkeys carried their packs. He still keeps his diaries from the journey, with Polaroid photographs and pressed flowers.
At Jiaopingdu, a crossing on the Jinsha River, he met three surviving boatmen who had ferried the Red Army across. The elderly men came alive as they retold their stories.
On the climb back, Weldon ran out of water and became dizzy and exhausted. A girl of about 10 fetched her grandmother, who helped him rest in the shade of a mud-brick shelter and gave him spring water in a hollowed-out gourd.
The girl continued walking with him and, at one point, took his hand on the steep, narrow path.
"I've never forgotten her," he said. The demanding route he had walked just once was the children's daily journey to and from school.
ENDURANCE AND ADAPTABILITY
Weldon said his own hardships -- terrain, weather and fatigue -- had deepened his appreciation of what the Red Army endured while also facing pursuit and encirclement.
He believes the army's trials equipped it for later challenges. "Usually you say triumph over adversity, I say through adversity," he said.
Returning in 2011 also allowed him to revisit people and places from his first journey.
He recalled dozens of children crowding into the team's small room in Sichuan's grasslands in 1985 to sing simple songs. More than two decades later, Chinese colleagues tracked down one of those children, who was then working in the local tax bureau and helped locate the rest.
Weldon was reunited with eight of the former schoolchildren. He recalled crying when they met again.
He also recalled driving through unfinished tunnels in Sichuan in 2011, with only the headlights lighting the way. On a more recent visit, he saw elevated highways and tunnels threading through the gorges.
"Again, China just keeps going," he said.
For Weldon, adaptability connects the historical Long March with present-day development. The Red Army had to adjust to different environments and build relationships with local communities; the Communist Party of China must likewise respond to diverse regional conditions today.
Adaptability, he added, must go together with a clear purpose and a plan.
UNDERSTANDING CHINA THROUGH ITS PEOPLE
To introduce the Long March to overseas audiences, Weldon begins with human endurance, mutual support and perseverance. For Australian readers, he draws parallels with the spirit of the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, emphasizing endurance and comradeship.
He then connects those qualities with the places where the Long March unfolded, helping readers move from a story of human endurance to an understanding of the Chinese revolution.
"And then they learn it's not a myth -- it actually happened," he said.
He called for "bridge builders" who could tell Chinese stories in ways that Western audiences would be open to hearing, while remaining faithful to those stories. The same, he said, applied to presenting Australian stories to Chinese audiences.
His own connections reach back to that first journey. The interpreter who accompanied him in 1985 still works with him between Australia and China, he said.
Weldon encouraged Australians to visit Chinese villages and meet local people to better understand the country.
"You need to connect on a human level," he said, warning against preconceived ideas about a country one knows little about.
Reflecting on his continuing engagement with China, he said: "Every morning there is a horizon. You have to keep going."
Weldon hopes to retrace the full Long March route for the third time.
He still thinks about the girl who held his hand on the path above the Jinsha River. He holds onto a few photographs from the journey and looks forward to a possible reunion with her one day. ■

WELLINGTON, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's residential property values fell by an average of 1.5 percent in the three months to the end of September, according to property valuation company Quotable Value (QV).
The decline eased slightly from 1.9 percent in the previous monthly report, while the average home value stood at 892,580 NZ dollars (500,594.57 U.S. dollars), down 1.9 percent since the start of 2026 and 0.9 percent year on year, the latest QV House Price Index showed on Monday.
"There are some minor green shoots here and there, mostly in the South Island, but it's still overwhelmingly one-way traffic, with buyers firmly in the driver's seat," QV national spokesperson Simon Petersen said in a statement, adding the first month of spring had brought little evidence that a broad-based recovery was imminent.
Buyers remained in a strong negotiating position amid plentiful property listings, economic uncertainty and the approaching Nov. 7 general election, Petersen said.
Only three of the country's main urban areas recorded growth in the September quarter. Home values rose 3.1 percent in Queenstown and 0.5 percent in Invercargill on the South Island, while Tauranga on the North Island recorded a marginal 0.1 percent increase, QV showed.
By contrast, values fell 3.2 percent in Gisborne, 3 percent in the capital Wellington and Whangarei, and 2.5 percent across Auckland, New Zealand's largest city, it said.
"The economic recovery remains uneven and we're seeing that reflected in property values," Petersen was quoted as saying. ■

Redeveloped port opens for easier cross-border travel between China's Shenzhen, Hong Kong
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:51:19 CST
14:51:19 KST

HONG KONG/SHENZHEN, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The redeveloped Huanggang Port opened at 6:30 a.m. local time on Monday, streamlining cross-border passenger travel between China's Shenzhen and Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
The redeveloped port is positioned as the most important 24-hour passenger land boundary control point between Hong Kong and Shenzhen. It operates under a co-location arrangement with a new "collaborative inspection and joint clearance" mode, allowing travelers to complete both Hong Kong and Shenzhen immigration clearance in a single queue.
Under this new clearance mode, clearance time will be significantly reduced from around 30 minutes at the original Lok Ma Chau/Huanggang Port to approximately five minutes.
The design flow of the redeveloped port is 200,000 passenger trips per day, and could be further increased to about 300,000 upon the future commissioning of the Northern Link Spur Line of Hong Kong's MTR Corporation Limited.
The port has 134 "collaborative inspection" automated channels and 68 traditional manual counters set up side by side. In addition to the automated channels, travelers can also clear customs using the manual counters.
"It is very convenient and extremely fast," Ms. Wong, a traveler heading from Hong Kong to Shenzhen via Huanggang Port, said, adding that crossing the border previously required taking a shuttle bus, which was very time-consuming, but the new co-location arrangement has significantly improved efficiency.
"Officers from both sides work in the same area, allowing travelers to complete clearance procedures for both Hong Kong and Shenzhen in one go, which is highly efficient," Mr. Chen, a tourist visiting Hong Kong from Shenzhen, said.
The original Huanggang Port, which opened in 1989, was China's first large-scale land port with 24-hour clearance. It has served hundreds of millions of travelers, with daily passenger traffic peaking at over 60,000 and daily vehicle traffic reaching around 10,000.
Reconstruction on the original site began in 2019 to meet the surging demand for cross-border passage. ■

Malaysia suspends sale of Chery Omoda 5 after viral incident; Singapore cars not affected
Derryn Wong
- Malaysia’s JPJ has suspended new registrations of Chery’s Omoda 5 after a “serious incident” in Johor Bahru, and is now investigating the model, its production and suppliers.
- Chery Auto Malaysia recalled the Omoda 5 C and H variants on Oct 11, offering “comprehensive vehicle inspections” and possible parts replacement after a rear suspension failure with both wheels attached.
- This is the model’s second recall in two years, after a May 2024 case linked to incomplete welds; Singapore is not affected because the Omoda 5 is not sold there.
AI generated
SINGAPORE – Malaysia’s Road Transport Department, or Jabatan Pengangkutan Jalan (JPJ), has suspended new registrations of the Omoda 5 car from China carmaker Chery.
In a statement on Oct 11, JPJ said the vehicle’s type approval – the technical certification needed for a car to be registered for road use – has been temporarily rescinded, and it is conducting a technical investigation of the model, its production and suppliers.
The C and H variants of the Omoda 5 were recalled by Chery Auto Malaysia on Oct 11. It said that customers will receive “comprehensive vehicle inspections and any necessary follow-up action”, including component replacement.
The suspension follows a dramatic incident in Johor Bahru on Oct 6, where an Omoda 5 near Aeon Mall Tebrau City lost its entire rear suspension assembly with both wheels still attached.
Two recalls in two years
Hal Serudin of automotive consultancy Lampaki Consulting said: “This looks to be a serious incident, the second of its kind, where the manufacturer is now taken to task by JPJ.”
“The history and sequence of events suggests that the safety and communications processes need to be improved. In some markets, such as Australia, manufacturers know to initiate a voluntary recall when they discover a fault,” he added.
This is the second recall of the Omoda 5 in as many years.
In May 2024, Chery recalled some 600 units of the car due to the same issue – potential rear suspension and axle failure – again following an incident where an Omoda 5 lost its rear wheels while driving.
Some 60 units were affected and had their components replaced, and the recall was closed in June 2024.
The issue was traced to incomplete welds on the components arising from equipment miscalibration.
The model was updated in September 2025 with a new rear suspension assembly featuring a multi-link unit in place of the old torsion beam component.
It is not clear if the current recall is due to a new issue or older, pre-update cars that did not receive the update.
Singapore’s Omodas not affected
The Omoda 5 is a mid-sized sport utility vehicle with a 1.5-litre turbocharged engine. It is assembled in Malaysia by Inokom in Kedah.
Singapore is not affected by the recall as the Omoda 5 is not sold in the Republic.
A model from the same family, the E5, is available. However, it is the fully electric version and its multi-link suspension assembly is different from the Omoda 5’s.
According to Vertex Automobile, authorised distributor of Omoda and Jaecoo, all the Chery models sold in Singapore are manufactured in China. THE BUSINESS TIMES

FBI seizes Chinese hacker tools targeting Taiwanese infrastructure and universities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
05:37:08 UTC
14:37:08 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The FBI has seized scanning and phishing tools used by China-linked hackers to target Taiwanese universities and energy infrastructure, the US Department of Justice announced Thursday.
The operation has rendered the tools inoperable, according to the FBI, but experts warn that disrupting the campaign may not prevent the hackers from resuming their activities.
“Even if this company is sanctioned, it might set up another operation to start the same activities,” Wang Po-chi (王伯頎), an associate professor of criminal justice at Ming Chuan University, told PTS. “It may feel it has little to fear because the company might be based in one place, but the servers launching the attacks might be located elsewhere.”
The seized tools, known as Microscan and FishHub, were operated by hackers associated with Integrity Technology Group, a China-based cybersecurity company with government contracts, according to a press release by the US Justice Department.
Microscan, which scanned computer networks for vulnerabilities, targeted Taiwanese companies in the natural gas and power sectors, two Taiwanese universities, a US power company in South Carolina, airports in Japan and Poland, and an international non-governmental organization.
FishHub allowed hackers to gain remote access to targeted networks through spear-phishing and retrieve files to send to servers controlled by the Chinese company, the Justice Department said.
The FBI identified about 20 Taiwanese universities as confirmed victims of FishHub activity.
Chen Yun-nung (陳縕儂), a computer science professor at National Taiwan University, said malware can be difficult to detect when it operates through software already installed on a computer.
“The malicious program hides in existing management software and uses legitimate software for malicious acts,” Chen said. “For example, it can download and export your data, making it harder to detect because you will not see any additional programs running, just the original programs already there.”
The FBI said Integrity Technology Group, which was behind the major hacking campaign known as “Flax Typhoon,” is one of the companies helping the Chinese government “expand the reach and scale of its malicious cyber activity,” according to the press release.
The seizure is the latest US law enforcement action against the group, which the US Treasury Department sanctioned in January 2025 for its role in multiple cyber intrusions targeting US infrastructure.
In September 2024, the Justice Department announced an operation to disrupt a botnet of more than 200,000 internet-connected consumer devices infected by the company.

“Cities Are Mental Weapons”: Utopian Hours 2026 Returns to Turin with Sir Peter Cook and a Program on City-Making
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

The second part of the Utopian Hours 2026 international city-making festival will be held in Turin on October 16 and 17. After a first chapter in Rotterdam, the festival is marking its tenth anniversary edition by returning to its hometown in Italy. The event's lineup and cultural program are designed to explore how cities can respond creatively to the social, environmental, and political challenges of the 21st century. The Utopian Hours festival has been organized since 2017 by Stratosferica, a nonprofit cultural association dedicated to producing and sharing urban knowledge through content on the evolution of cities, urban communication strategies, events, community building and placemaking.
Archigram's Sir Peter Cook will travel to Turin to take part in the festival just one week before his 90th birthday. He will deliver a masterclass on the first day at La Centrale Lavazza about his experience imagining and studying cities, and the power of imagination. During the festival, Sir Peter Cook and Archigram will also be the subject of an exhibition with works never shown in Italy before. The program will also bring together Wim Walschap, CEO and senior partner at Herzog & de Meuron; Zahra Ebrahim, co-founder of Monumental, an organization building bridges between communities and institutions in Toronto; and Carolyn Steel, who explores the concept of Sitopia ("food-place").
Other international projects and practices in the program include Rotterdam Rooftop Days, which explores the potential of city roofs for climate adaptation and public space; Gleispool, a large public swimming pool proposed for a former railway yard in Basel; Helsinki's Crown Bridges project; Quatorze, the nonprofit practice advancing solidarity-based architecture; Nice Developers, whose work sets out to prove that developers do not need to be nasty; Madrid-based ENORME Studio, which explores the future of architecture through experimental, participatory and transformable design; and Powerhouse Company, the international practice working across housing, architecture and urban transformation.
The two-day program includes keynote lectures, masterclasses and the Urbanites Fair at La Centrale Lavazza, and participatory working sessions at Dorado Community Hub focused on generating responses to contemporary urban challenges. The exhibitions, which include Sir Peter Cook's The City Is a Garden and Urban Frames (presented in collaboration with CAMERA – Centro Italiano per la Fotografia), will also be held at Dorado. The festival is collaborating with the Architecture Film Festival Rotterdam (AFFR), bringing a selection of films dedicated to architecture and the city. The full schedule, with session times and venues, is available on the festival's online calendar; access to the roundtables at Dorado requires a Professional Pass.
 After witnessing in Rotterdam both the urgency of today's urban challenges and the extraordinary creativity with which cities are responding to them, we return to Torino with even greater ambition. For Part 2 of our Ten Years Edition, Utopian Hours will continue to push boundaries, bringing some of the world's most radical ideas about cities to our hometown. Because now more than ever, cities are mental weapons. – Luca Ballarini, co-founder of Stratosferica
Two projects for the city of Turin were announced this year. In April, UNS's design proposal for Turin's new Metro Line 2, developed in collaboration with Settanta7, Mijksenaar, Frigorosso, 3BA and WSP, was selected by an international jury of experts chaired by Dominique Perrault. Most recently, in July, MVRDV and Balance Architettura unveiled their proposal for the renovation of the Civic Gallery of Modern and Contemporary Art (GAM), following their selection through a public competition in December 2025. Also in Europe, Design Museum Gent recently opened a new wing by Carmody Groarke and ATAMA, and the Copenhagen Architecture Biennial announced the theme and dates for its second edition.

DAKAR – Senegal should halt its crackdown on same-sex relations, which calls into question the country’s compliance with the Olympic charter ahead of hosting the Youth Olympic Games, Human Rights Watch said on Oct 12.
In March, the west African nation adopted new legislation doubling the maximum penalty for same-sex relations to up to 10 years in prison.
The deeply religious, predominantly Muslim country has experienced a wave of homophobia in recent months.
Dozens of individuals have been arrested on suspicion of same-sex relations, including 71 men who in August were referred to trial for “acts against nature”, a term used to refer to same-sex relations.

Senegal’s law passed by an overwhelming majority in the National Assembly in March.
It also establishes criminal penalties for those found guilty of promoting or financing same-sex relationships.
LGBTQ rights advocacy is frequently denounced in Senegal as a tool used by Westerners to impose foreign values.

====================================================================================================

Will Indonesia’s New Foreign Minister Be Allowed to Do His Job?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
05:07:00 UTC
14:07:00 KST

On October 1, Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto finally replaced Sugiono, who had served as foreign minister for the past two years, with the veteran diplomat Arrmanatha Nasir. While one may welcome the appointment of a seasoned diplomat as foreign minister, it is unclear whether he will have enough power and presidential access to steer Indonesia’s foreign policy back to a steadier, more familiar course, as under previous administrations.
As the first foreign minister in decades without substantial foreign policy experience, Sugiono’s tenure was marked by consequential decisions that broke foreign policy precedent. During his time at the helm of the Foreign Ministry, Indonesia endorsed a joint statement with China that appeared to depart from its long-standing refusal to recognize its overlapping claim with China near the Natuna Islands, potentially lending credence to China’s illegal nine-dash line claim. Additionally, it joined both BRICS and U.S. President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, and signed the unequal Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with Washington, despite this having dubious benefits to Indonesia. Internally, Indonesian diplomats made anonymous complaints to Indonesian media regarding the chaotic Foreign Ministry workflow and being left in the dark about vital foreign policy decisions that were deliberated within Prabowo’s inner circle.
In this context, Nasir’s appointment comes as a breath of fresh air. In contrast to the inexperienced Sugiono, Nasir has 29 years of experience as a Foreign Ministry insider who has filled two ambassadorial-level postings and served a five-year stint as the Ministry’s spokesperson, among other roles. Therefore, the Foreign Ministry has returned to its decades-long tradition of having career diplomats at its helm. More importantly, during his tenure as Sugiono’s vice foreign minister, Nasir was responsible for the Ministry’s internal dynamics, suggesting he should have had direct knowledge of discontent among the Ministry’s diplomats and staff. Thus, under his tenure, diplomats’ involvement in technocratic deliberations on important foreign policy matters could be improved.
While there is no doubt about Nasir’s ability to steer Indonesia’s foreign policy in the coming years, it is less clear whether he will be given the necessary opportunities and access to do so. Reports in the Indonesian news magazine Tempo indicate that access to President Prabowo, even for ministers, is very limited and heavily curated by members of his inner circle at the presidential palace, thus handicapping close coordination between the president and his cabinet members across a wide range of governmental affairs.
Foreign policy is not immune to this, and at least three major foreign policy decisions under Sugiono’s tenure were made without properly following the Foreign Ministry’s recommendations. In the lead-up to the 2024 Sino-Indonesian joint statement, Indonesian diplomats were ordered to reject any stipulation regarding joint development in overlapping areas of the South China Sea, only for the president to sign it anyway. Some reports suggest that Prabowo followed the advice of his closest confidants, who view the dispute purely in economic terms.
Additionally, high-ranking Foreign Ministry officials expressed grave concern about the one-sidedness of the U.S.-Indonesia Agreement on Reciprocal Trade signed earlier this year, yet the president signed it regardless. Lastly, Indonesia joined the Board of Peace without proper deliberation with relevant Indonesian ambassadors in the Middle East, and several Indonesian diplomats anonymously complained that Indonesia’s decision to join the organization was problematic in terms of Jakarta’s policy of support for the Palestinian cause. Even Sugiono himself admitted publicly that the decision to join was made “quite fast.”
These phenomena suggest a gap in foreign policy formulation between career diplomats at the Foreign Ministry and politicians at the Presidential Palace. Ideally, the two should work in concert: Foreign Ministry staff should work out the technocratic and strategic foreign policy details, while the palace uses that advice to shape and consider broader implications beyond foreign policy, and vice versa. Additionally, bureaucrats typically spend years or decades in the Ministry, accumulating knowledge and experience that help ensure Indonesia’s foreign policy does not wildly deviate and remains consistent. If the Palace isolates itself, the views and analyses of seasoned, capable Foreign Ministry diplomats that help maintain policy stability and consistency may not be reflected in the final strategic decision, making it vulnerable to decisions of dubious benefit for Jakarta.
Nasir’s appointment, therefore, must be seen in that context. One may justifiably have little doubt about his ability to steer Indonesia’s foreign policy and muster the Ministry’s diplomats to that end. Yet, the President will have to allow the Minister quick and easy access to the Palace and ensure close coordination between it and the Ministry, such as inviting the Foreign Minister into policy deliberations with foreign policy implications and implementing his recommendations, as well as accepting the Minister’s request for an audience whenever necessary. Without proper access and consultation, no matter how brilliant or qualified the foreign minister may be, the Palace could make more major foreign policy decisions with dubious benefits and high risks.
While Prabowo wants to be more hands-on in foreign policymaking, if given access and proper consultation, an able foreign minister and diplomats can ensure that Prabowo leaves a better foreign policy legacy, since they will be able to make refined analyses and policies to achieve his goals more strategically. The question is, will the President finally muster his able foreign service to that end?
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own.

EU eyes COP31 climate deal to accelerate CO2 cuts, document shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
05:05:57 UTC
14:05:57 KST

EU eyes COP31 climate deal to accelerate CO2 cuts, document shows
BRUSSELS, Oct 12 - The European Union will use next month's COP31 climate summit to push for agreement on a "package" of efforts to reduce the greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet, an internal EU document seen by Reuters showed.
Even as the world suffers extreme weather due to climate change, governments at recent UN climate talks have failed to agree to tougher action - with large emerging economies and fossil fuel producers concerned about the impact of such measures on their growth and development.
At COP31 in Turkey in November, the EU will push for a "mitigation package" focussed on reducing emissions, by turning countries' existing climate pledges into real-world actions, a draft EU document showed.
A key EU demand will be to extend until 2040 the segment in UN climate negotiations where governments discuss how to reduce emissions, and identify areas where more can be done, the document said. This negotiation track - known as the "mitigation work programme" - is due to expire this year.
The EU will also push for countries to respond to the UN's confirmation last month that the world will miss the 2015 Paris agreement's target to limit global warming to 1.5C, the document said. It was drafted by Ireland, which holds the EU's rotating presidency.
"We will look to strengthen our partnerships to deliver practical progress on global climate action, specifically on the transition away from fossil fuels and on electrification,” Irish climate minister Darragh O'Brien said.
EU climate ministers will discuss their COP31 strategy at a meeting on Monday.
Countries' efforts to address climate change have come under geopolitical pressure after the U.S. pulled out of global climate negotiations.
After last year's COP30 summit in Brazil ended without stronger commitments to rein in greenhouse gas emissions, EU diplomats say the bloc is planning a different approach for COP31 - attempting to avoid public clashes over contentious issues and instead focus on working with countries to implement their climate commitments.
The internal document said there is "no scope" for new climate funding commitments at COP31 - a position likely to put European nations at odds with poorer countries seeking more support. REUTERS

Outdoor kitchens have evolved from exclusive luxury additions into natural extensions of the home. Beyond aesthetics, these new outdoor kitchens represent an evolution in how we experience open-air living. Durable materials and innovative technical solutions turn these designs into year-round settings, where cooking and sharing become parts of a single, unified experience.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The US International Trade Commission (USITC) on Friday launched a patent investigation involving Taiwan tech manufacturers Foxconn, Delta Electronics, and Quanta Computer.
The commission said it voted to investigate alleged patent infringement involving vertical power delivery systems, related components, and computing systems containing the technology. The case is being conducted under Section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which addresses unfair practices involving imported products.
The investigation stems from a Sept. 9 complaint by US power technology company Vicor Corp., which was supplemented the following day. Vicor alleges that the importation and sale of the products in the US infringe its patents and is seeking an order barring infringing products from entering the country, orders requiring the respondents to stop selling them, and a bond on affected imports during the 60-day presidential review period.
The respondents include Foxconn and its affiliates, Delta Electronics and its US subsidiaries, and Quanta Computer, Quanta Cloud Technology, and their US affiliates. Other respondents include Germany's Infineon Technologies, US-based Monolithic Power Systems, Flex, and Canada's Celestica, as well as Chinese subsidiaries of several companies.
The USITC's chief administrative law judge will assign the case to an administrative law judge, who will schedule an evidentiary hearing and issue an initial determination on whether Section 337 was violated. The commission may review that determination and set a target date to complete the investigation within 45 days of its launch.
The Ministry of Economic Affairs said Section 337 investigations typically take 12 to 16 months to complete, per Newtalk. If Vicor prevails, the commission could restrict affected products from entering the US market or order companies to stop selling them.
The ministry said the dispute concerns patent rights between private companies and remains under review. The government will monitor developments, maintain contact with the companies involved, and provide appropriate assistance if necessary.
Delta Electronics said it takes intellectual property rights and compliance with local laws seriously and would respond through the relevant legal procedures to protect its interests, Newtalk reported. The company said the investigation had not affected its products and declined to comment further while the proceedings were underway.

There are currently no plans to add funding, Huang said, adding that the administration would review the program's performance on a rolling basis.
Under the weekday accommodation scheme, eligible travelers staying at participating licensed hotels and guesthouses from Sunday through Thursday can receive discounts of up to NT$2,000 for two consecutive nights. The first night is eligible for a discount of up to NT$800, and the second up to NT$1,200. On offshore islands, the maximum combined discount is NT$2,500.
The program excludes national holidays and consecutive holiday periods. Travelers can stay at different participating properties for the two nights, provided the stays are consecutive and meet the program's requirements.
The administration also introduced a birthday accommodation voucher scheme. A total of 12,000 people were selected in September, with 1,000 winners for each birth month receiving NT$1,200 in accommodation subsidies. The birthday benefit can be combined with the weekday accommodation discount, subject to the program's rules, per CNA.
Other domestic tourism incentives include amusement park accommodation offers, corporate employee travel subsidies, and discounts on Taiwan PASS transportation packages.
The wider tourism promotion program also seeks to attract international visitors through incentives for repeat visits, travel associated with conventions and exhibitions, incentive group travel, and support for internationally recognized concerts.

Global poverty index rises for first time since its 2010 creation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
04:45:00 UTC
13:45:00 KST

Global poverty index rises for first time since its 2010 creation
- The UNDP said the global poverty index rose for the first time since 2010, with 1.2 billion people now in “acute” poverty and 51.5 million more than last year.
- UNDP chief Alexander De Croo called this a “wake-up call for the world” and said poor people face hunger, missed schooling, and no clean water or electricity.
- The report said population growth helped drive the rise, but 33 countries cut poverty rates. Most of the poorest people still live in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – A UN global poverty index has risen for the first time since its creation in 2010, bringing the number of people affected to 1.2 billion, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) reported on Oct 12.
In the 2026 edition of their annual report, the UNDP and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative research centre counted 51.5 million more people living in “acute” poverty compared to the previous year.
UNDP administrator Alexander De Croo said the increase in poverty should be a “wake-up call for the world”.
“Behind these figures are 1.2 billion people facing hardships that reinforce one another: Hunger, missed schooling and a lack of clean water or electricity. This is unacceptable,” he said in a press release.
More than half of those in acute poverty were children.
However, UNDP said a major factor in the recorded increase was population growth, and new data was only available for 13 of the 108 developing countries covered by the report.
While the total number of people in poverty has increased, the report provides a mixed picture. Some 33 nations have halved the percentage of their people living in poverty as defined by the index in the past 15 years.
Those included six countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Among the countries that have made the most rapid progress were countries in Asia – China and Vietnam – UNDP said.
As in the previous year, the report found that the majority of the poorest people live in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, specifically the Indian subcontinent, the most densely populated region on earth.
“In Egypt, Nepal, and Tajikistan, both the poverty rate and the number of people experiencing multidimensional poverty have decreased significantly,” the press release said.
In Angola and Zambia, the poverty rate has also declined, but population growth has more than offset this decrease, resulting in an increase in the number of people living in poverty.
The poverty index used in the report includes indicators such as the lack of adequate housing, sanitation, electricity, cooking fuel, food and education. AFP

Officers from Lahav 433, Israel's national major crimes investigation unit, raided approximately 30 locations, including municipal offices, as an undercover investigation lasting nearly a year and a half became public.

"The city was sold, nothing less than that," a source in the National Fraud Investigations Unit said, describing the suspected scale of the corruption.
Officials from the National Fraud Investigations Unit, part of Lahav 433, said the undercover investigation began in May 2025 after police received dozens of intelligence reports pointing to suspected widespread corruption at Kfar Saba City Hall, allegedly involving the mayor and his wife directly. According to investigators, although Saar's wife holds no official public position, she played a dominant and central role in the alleged scheme. "He is an elected official, she has no public standing, but she has a hand in everything," officials said.
During the covert investigation, detectives employed various investigative methods to substantiate their suspicions. According to information gathered, the couple allegedly worked to channel municipal tenders, properties and projects to associates, businesspeople and individuals with financial interests, some of whom are known to police as criminals. In return, investigators suspect Saar's wife received bundles of cash from those individuals, with whom she maintained direct contact.
The suspected method was straightforward: Businesspeople would approach the mayor's wife, establish a quid pro quo arrangement, and she would allegedly work to ensure they won municipal tenders and projects.
Police suspect that, to conceal preferential treatment of certain businesspeople and the alleged manipulation of tenders, projects were transferred from Kfar Saba City Hall to the municipal economic development company. Investigators believe the couple coordinated with the company's CEO, who allegedly knew in advance which bidder was supposed to win each tender brought before him.
Sources familiar with the investigation said detectives were surprised to discover that, in some cases, obstacles had allegedly been placed in the way of competing bidders until they were forced to withdraw. The projects were then allegedly awarded to businesspeople whose connections with the couple were suspected of benefiting them.
The allegations span nearly every area of municipal activity, including renovations of educational institutions, the placement of food trucks, the opening of businesses, the development of leisure and entertainment complexes, sports projects, transportation, traffic lights, street lighting and municipal cleaning services.
Another major element of the investigation concerns the couple's lifestyle and their allegedly extensive use of cash. According to National Fraud Investigations Unit officials, Saar and his wife maintained a lavish lifestyle, with numerous expenses paid in cash, including overseas travel, jewelry, clothing and handbags.
During police searches, investigators seized expensive jewelry and luxury watches, along with evidence of overseas flights and purchases. During the couple's most recent return from overseas, customs officials found 20,000 shekels in cash in Saar's wife's possession at Ben Gurion Airport, and she was questioned by customs authorities.
The couple also owned vehicles described by investigators as considerably more expensive than average. Saar drives a privately owned Tesla, while his wife recently purchased a new Audi.
"We are not investigating a technical violation involving the use of cash. If that were the issue, we would find a great many offenses of that kind," investigators explained, emphasizing that the cash transactions were being examined as part of the suspected bribery scheme.
During the police raids and searches, investigators discovered large quantities of cash, packaged and concealed in locations where detectives had anticipated finding it.
Investigators also revealed that Saar and his wife had grown increasingly concerned about the possibility that they were under surveillance. According to a source in the National Fraud Investigations Unit, rumors about the mayor's wife's influence over municipal affairs had circulated for some time, including reports in local newspapers suggesting that she effectively held the keys to running Kfar Saba.
The couple allegedly carried out technical checks to determine what surveillance methods might be used against them. Throughout the undercover investigation, they reportedly feared they were being monitored and investigated covertly.
"They had serious suspicions," the police source said. "There was a great deal of talk about the mayor's wife holding the key to running the city, and reports appeared in local newspapers. They conducted technical checks concerning measures that could be used against them. Throughout the investigation, they feared they were being monitored and investigated covertly. It sounded as though they believed they were the subject of a journalistic investigation, and they checked for devices that might have been installed but found nothing. Even so, their desire and sense of gratification blinded them."
Another line of investigation concerns suspected ties between Saar, his wife and criminal figures operating in the Sharon region. According to intelligence obtained by police, individuals known to the Israel Police's Central District for criminal activity allegedly helped Saar during the local election campaign.
Investigators suspect those individuals pressured political candidates running against Saar in an effort to influence the election. Police are examining the nature of the relationships between the criminal figures and the couple, as well as suspicions that those same individuals subsequently exerted pressure on the mayor and his wife.
The investigation centers on suspected bribery, fraud and breach of trust, with suspected money laundering and tax offenses also under examination. Among those arrested are businesspeople and individuals, some of whom are known to police for criminal activity. According to investigators, the common factor linking the suspects is their alleged involvement in quid pro quo arrangements in which financial interests were advanced in exchange for benefits.
Police said the investigation remains ongoing, with detectives examining the full scope of the suspected offenses and the alleged role of each individual involved. The case is being overseen by the Economic Department of the State Attorney's Office. Investigators are expected to seek extensions of detention for suspects where necessary at the Rishon LeZion Magistrate's Court.
