What is celebrated on October 13 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:48:12 EEST
10:48:12 KST

What is celebrated on October 13 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
Today, skeptics are honored, efforts are made to combat thrombosis and natural disasters, and No Bra Day and Costume Day are celebrated. Believers commemorate Venerable Veniamin.
Today, October 13, marks International Skeptics Day and No Bra Day, dedicated to raising awareness about breast health and cancer prevention, UNN reports.
International Skeptics Day
International Skeptics Day is dedicated to people who choose doubt over unconditional belief. This observance honors those who verify facts and carefully form their own convictions.
International Skeptics Day is an opportunity to reflect on how important critical thinking is in your life. After all, doubt is not the enemy of faith, but a tool for a deeper understanding of the world.
World Thrombosis Day
October 13 marks World Thrombosis Day, serving as a reminder of the “silent threat” that is often underestimated.
Thrombosis is the formation of a blood clot that partially or completely blocks a blood vessel. Normally, blood should clot to stop bleeding, but sometimes a clot forms unnecessarily or does not dissolve after healing—in which case it becomes dangerous.
A clot can stop blood flow, and if it breaks away, it can cause an embolism, leading to heart attacks, strokes, or pulmonary embolism.
Which foods thin the blood and what to eat for thrombosis prevention03.06.26, 19:50 • 116430 views
International Suit Day
October 13 marks International Suit Day around the world. On this day, men and women who uphold the tradition put on classic suits: pressed trousers, a white shirt, a tie, and a jacket. The main idea of the observance is to demonstrate style and confidence in any situation. A suit can be worn regardless of whether you work in an office, are at home, or even engage in sports.
No Bra Day
No Bra Day has been observed annually since 2011 and is dedicated to raising awareness about breast health and cancer prevention. On this day, women around the world forgo wearing bras, emphasizing the importance of regular screening and timely diagnosis.
The initiative quickly spread through social media under the hashtag #NoBraDay and now encompasses more than 30 countries. In addition, No Bra Day is often perceived as an act of protest or a political statement, as well as part of movements such as “Go Topless,” which advocate freedom of choice.
International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction
It is observed annually on October 13. The day was established by the UN General Assembly in 1989 as part of the International Decade for Natural Disaster Reduction, and the date was officially established in 2009. The purpose of the day is to raise awareness about preventing and mitigating the consequences of natural, environmental, and technological disasters, as well as to teach communities at risk to respond effectively to hazards.
According to statistics, about 184 people die from natural disasters every day, and risks are increasing with the growth of urbanization. The day serves as a reminder that many lives can be saved through preventive measures and greater preparedness.
Remembrance Day of Venerable Benjamin, the Recluse of the Caves
On this day, believers honor Venerable Benjamin, the Recluse of the Caves, one of the prominent ascetics of the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra. A former wealthy merchant, he gave his property to the poor, took monastic vows, and spent his final years in seclusion, devoting his life to prayer.
On this day, festive services are held; some believers observe a fast and also make pilgrimages to the Lavra to pray near his relics.

At least five people have died after Hurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel pummelled Mexico’s Pacific coast, causing flooding that downed trees and electricity poles, blocked roads and inundated homes.
Simon claimed the life of a 71-year-old man who died when a wall collapsed in Chilpancingo in the southern state of Guerrero, governor Evelyn Salgado said at a press conference.
The storm also damaged infrastructure and homes in the state’s coastal towns, including the major seaport of Acapulco, she said.
Tropical Storm Rachel is blamed for the deaths of four members of one family, including two children, whose bodies were found on the outskirts of the city of Ensenada in Baja California, the state’s prosecutor’s office reported.
Five more people remained missing, while security forces used helicopters to rescue 32 people, prosecutors said. Baja governor Marina del Pilar said officials were helping more than 50 people in temporary shelters.
Simon did not make landfall and, after weakening to category two on the five-point Saffir-Simpson scale, was moving away from the coast, authorities said. A rain alert remained in place.
The National Hurricane Center in Miami said heavy rainfall associated with Simon in west-central Mexico over the next few days might still produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides.
Officials warned waves of up to five metres high were still expected in some coastal areas. Flooding and landslides had already hit communities close to rivers and streams in the states of Michoacan and Colima.
The El Niño phenomenon, characterised by rising water temperatures in the Pacific, is fuelling a more intense hurricanes this season in the region.
Meteorologists say the 2026-27 El Niño, which causes global changes in winds and rainfall as well as erratic weather conditions, is certain to be the biggest ever recorded. Scientists now also think human-caused global heating is making El Niños more intense.

Bedbug infestation forces Qantas to ground plane in Rome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:21:25 UTC
13:21:25 KST

Qantas has been forced to ground a plane in Rome after bedbugs were discovered on the aircraft on its way from Perth.
The parasitic insects were found in the front of the economy section of the Boeing 787 Dreamliner as it made its way from Perth to Rome for the QF5 flight on 9 October, a source with knowledge of the incident confirmed on Tuesday.
Bedbugs are small insects that feed on the blood of some mammals, including humans, which can be hard to eradicate.
As first reported by the SMH, the aircraft had to be taken out of service for cleaning after its arrival in the Italian capital, resulting in the cancellation of the Qantas Rome to Perth service on 10 October.
A Qantas spokesperson said the flight was cancelled to allow its engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after “an issue identified on a small number of economy seats”.
They said the airline wanted to “sincerely apologise” to customers for the disruption.
Affected passengers were given accommodation and rebooked on alternative flights within 48 hours of their original departure, Qantas said.
The airline said its aircraft cabins were cleaned regularly and to an extremely high standard and treated with disinfectant every 50 days as a standard precautionary cleaning measure.
Prof Michelle Power, a parasitologist at Macquarie University, said the bedbugs had “more than likely” been brought on to the plane in someone’s luggage or on a passenger’s clothes and then escaped into the cabin.
“They’re associated with travel. People may go to a hotel that’s infested and because they like dark spaces and are attracted to the smell of human clothes, they make their way into someone’s luggage.”
“They’re a flightless insect, without planes,” she said.
Power said bedbugs were not dangerous, even though their bites could be itchy and irritating, but they were very difficult to get rid of and could hide in bedsheets and crevices for a long time without needing to feed.
She said there were “two sides to bedbugs”: on the one hand, wealthier people who travelled a lot got them and subsequently moved them around, whereas people already experiencing health inequities may not be able to afford pesticides or potentially heat water to the 55C required to kill them.

Whale meat curry for dinner? Study of bygone seafood recipes shows how UK tastes have narrowed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:05:13 UTC
13:05:13 KST

In days gone by, the UK’s domestic cooks were an adventurous lot when it came to seafood, prepared to dish up anything from an oyster cocktail to whale meat curry.
But an academic investigation of more than 1,000 fish and shellfish recipes published in a lifestyle magazine over the last century suggests tastes have become much narrower. Ruth Thurstan, from the University of Exeter, studied seafood recipes published in the British version of the magazine Good Housekeeping from 1923 to the present.
She found that 67 species had been included in recipes over the last 100 years but, since the 1970s, the “big five” – cod, haddock, tuna, salmon and prawns – have dominated, accounting for more than 60% of all mentions. The number of recipes featuring delicacies such as oysters, flatfish and herring have plunged.
Thurstan said: “For decades, British cooks have turned to published recipes for inspiration about what to put on the dinner table. I wondered whether these everyday sources could tell us how our relationship with fish has changed over time.”
She said there were three broad phases:
- Pre-1970s: A diverse mix of species in recipes. No single group ruled but flatfish, herring and oyster were prominent. Recipes emphasised domestic skills, economy and preparing whole fish.
- The 1970s shift: A decline in diversity of fish species in recipes, with increased focus on the “big five”.
- 1980s-present: “Big five” present in the majority of recipes, with a decline of other species – though not all have vanished entirely.
Recipes from the 1920s and 30s that Thurstan found included oyster cocktail, lobster canapes and halibut steaks in milk. The 1940s – when rationing was in force – featured recipes by the then Ministry of Food explicitly encouraging the consumption of fish and other protein sources – including a recipe for curried whale meat.
In the 1960s, recipes included plaice véronique and chilled prawn soup. Cooks of the 70s were asked to consider rustling up cod roe on toast and tuna soured cream quiche. There was also a sharp increase in recipes mentioning tinned fish.
Recipes in the 1990s featured the likes of herb-crusted salmon and prawn and peanut noodles while more “aspirational” dishes in the 2020s have included golden hasselback salmon, gochujang sticky cod and miso prawn skewers.
“The results reveal a striking story of change,” said Thurstan, whose research is conducted at the Centre for Ecology and Conservation within Exeter’s Penryn Campus in Cornwall.
“This wasn’t simply a case of fewer species being available – herring, oyster and lobster can all still be bought – but it reflects a genuine narrowing of what readers were being shown and encouraged to cook.”
According to the Marine Stewardship Council, the big five make up 80% of the fish and seafood consumed in the UK. Thurstan said this dominance carried environmental costs. She said cod, haddock and shrimp fishing, for example, could damage valuable habitats while salmon farming has come under intense scrutiny.
Thurstan said she had attempted a few of the recipes including “Fish baked in custard” from the 1920s. She said: “I tried it with pollack. While the recipe calls it a custard it isn’t sweet, so I think, perhaps with a name change, it has potential.”
She is also planning to try two 1930s recipes: oyster soup and kipper cream. The latter involves parboiling a kipper and then pounding it with melted butter, lemon juice or vinegar and cayenne until it is the consistency of a cream. “I think it would be similar to today’s mackerel paté, and just as delicious.”
The magazine Thurstan researched was originally published as British Good Housekeeping and is now Good Housekeeping UK. Once published, the paper – entitled “Declines in the diversity of fish represented in British domestic recipes over the past 100 years” – will be published in the journal People and Nature.
January 1923 – Fish baked in custard
“Purchase a slice of cod or halibut, or some filleted fish weighing about 1lb. Wipe it with a clean cloth and remove any black skin. Lay the fish in a greased and shallow baking-dish and sprinkle it with salt, a little white pepper, the grated rind of half a lemon, and a small onion finely chopped.
“Then break into a basin 1 or 2 eggs, add 2 tablespoonfuls of flour and a light seasoning of pepper and salt. Beat until smooth and add half pint fresh milk. Strain this custard over the fish, stand the dish in a tin containing some water and bake in a moderate oven until the custard is set and lightly browned (about 30 minutes). It is a good plan to baste the fish once or twice with the custard during the first part of the cooking. Potato chips or some mashed potatoes would be a good accompaniment to this dish.”
May 1934 – Potage aux huîtres
“One dozen oysters, 1 pint Court bouillon [a broth], 1 pint milk, 1 oz butter, 1 oz flour, 1 tablespoonful cream or unsweetened evaporated milk, seasoning. Oyster soup can be made with tinned oysters or fresh ones. There is no need, however, to buy the choicest variety, as the small ones answer quite well. In no circumstances should oysters be boiled, or they will become hard, leathery and indigestible.”

====================================================================================================
